Business Law & Practice.q: An individual (a sole trader) is unable to pay their debts as they fall due, and a creditor who is owed a sum exceeding the statutory minimum wishes to take formal insolvency proceedings against them. The debtor is an individual, not a company. A creditor seeks a court order dealing with the debtor's insolvency. The debtor runs a business as a sole trader, not through a company, and simply cannot meet the debts as they come due, so a creditor owed a sum above the statutory floor is looking to take formal insolvency proceedings that will put the debtor's assets into the hands of someone tasked with realising them for the creditors. Which of the following best describes the appropriate procedure and its effect?
o: A wrongful trading contribution order against the individual.
A members' voluntary liquidation of the individual's affairs.
A bankruptcy order, on which the debtor's estate vests in a trustee in bankruptcy to be realised for creditors.
A company voluntary arrangement binding the individual's creditors.
An administration order placing the individual under an administrator on these facts as a general rule.
Business Law & Practice.w: An individual who cannot pay their debts may be made bankrupt: a creditor owed at least the statutory minimum (or the debtor themselves) may seek a bankruptcy order. On bankruptcy, the debtor's estate vests in a trustee in bankruptcy, who realises the assets and distributes them to creditors in the statutory order; the bankrupt is usually discharged after one year.

n.0: Wrongful trading applies to directors of insolvent companies, not to an individual sole trader's bankruptcy.
n.1: Members' voluntary liquidation applies to solvent companies, not individuals.
n.3: A CVA is a company procedure; the individual equivalent is an IVA, not what a creditor imposes here.
n.4: Administration is a corporate insolvency procedure, not applicable to an individual.

Business Law & Practice.q: A general partnership has no written partnership agreement dealing with what happens on the death or bankruptcy of a partner. One of the partners then dies. The surviving partners assumed the firm would simply carry on unchanged, but a question arises as to the effect of the death on the partnership itself under the default statutory rules. The court considers the position under the Partnership Act 1890 in the absence of any contrary agreement. The supplier had dealt with the firm for years and simply carried on invoicing it just as before. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The death of a partner has no legal effect on the partnership in any circumstances.
The partnership is dissolved only if a majority of the surviving partners vote for it.
Subject to any agreement, the partnership is dissolved by the death of a partner.
The partnership is dissolved only where the deceased partner held a majority share.
The partnership always continues automatically, regardless of a partner's death.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.33 Partnership Act 1890, subject to any agreement between the partners, a partnership is dissolved by the death or bankruptcy of any partner. A well-drafted partnership agreement usually displaces this default by providing for continuation.

n.0: Death does have a legal effect under the default statutory rule.
n.1: No vote of the survivors is required under the default rule.
n.3: Dissolution is not confined to death of a majority-share partner.
n.4: The firm does not automatically continue in the absence of contrary agreement; death dissolves it.

Business Law & Practice.q: A growing business makes taxable supplies of goods and services, and its taxable turnover has now exceeded the statutory threshold over the relevant period. The owner wants to understand the business's obligations in relation to value added tax, including registration and how VAT is accounted for. The court considers the basic operation of VAT for a business making taxable supplies. The business had grown quickly and its sales had recently pushed past the registration threshold. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The business pays VAT only on its profits, in the same way as corporation tax.
The business must register for VAT once its taxable turnover exceeds the threshold, charging output VAT and reclaiming input VAT.
The business never needs to register for VAT, whatever its level of taxable turnover.
VAT is charged only on exports and never on domestic supplies of goods or services.
The business must register for VAT from the moment it is first incorporated, regardless of turnover on these facts as a general rule.
Business Law & Practice.w: A business making taxable supplies must register for VAT once its taxable turnover exceeds the registration threshold (and may register voluntarily below it). A registered business charges output VAT on its taxable supplies and can recover input VAT on its purchases, accounting to HMRC for the net amount.

n.0: VAT is charged on supplies, not on profits like corporation tax.
n.2: Registration becomes compulsory once the turnover threshold is exceeded.
n.3: VAT applies to domestic taxable supplies, not only exports.
n.4: Registration is triggered by turnover, not automatically on incorporation.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company proposes to make a loan of a significant amount to one of its directors to help the director with a personal purchase. The board wishes to know whether this can be done and what approval is required under the Companies Act 2006. The borrower is a director of the lending company and the loan is not within any exemption. The company wishes to act lawfully. A director has asked the company to lend them a sizeable sum to fund a personal purchase, the arrangement does not fall within any of the recognised exceptions, and the board wants to be sure it follows the correct procedure before advancing any money to one of its own number. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The loan requires the sanction of the court before it can be made.
The loan is absolutely prohibited and can never be made to a director.
The loan requires approval by special resolution of 75% of the members.
The loan generally requires approval by an ordinary resolution of the members.
The loan may be made by the board alone with no member approval at all.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.197 of the Companies Act 2006, a company generally may not make a loan to a director unless the transaction has been approved by a resolution of the members (an ordinary resolution), subject to certain exceptions (such as small loans and expenditure on company business). Approval by ordinary resolution is the general requirement.

n.0: Court sanction is not required.
n.1: Loans to directors are not absolutely prohibited; they may be made with member approval.
n.2: The requirement is an ordinary resolution, not a special resolution.
n.4: Board approval alone is generally insufficient for a loan to a director.

Business Law & Practice.q: Several professionals wish to carry on business together with limited liability but with the internal flexibility of a partnership. They form a limited liability partnership and register it. A creditor of the LLP, unpaid on a debt, seeks to make the individual members personally liable for the LLP's debts as if they were ordinary partners. The business is a duly registered LLP and the debt is that of the LLP itself. The professionals deliberately chose the LLP structure precisely to shield themselves from personal exposure while keeping a partnership-style internal arrangement, and the disappointed creditor is now testing whether it can look past that structure to the individuals behind it for payment of the debt. Which of the following best describes the members' liability?
o: The members are personally liable because an LLP has no separate legal personality.
The members are generally not personally liable for the LLP's debts, as the LLP is a separate legal person with limited liability.
The members are jointly liable without limit for the LLP's debts like ordinary partners on these facts as a general rule.
The members are liable in full unless the LLP has at least four designated members.
The members are liable only up to the amount of profits they have drawn.
Business Law & Practice.w: An LLP is a body corporate with separate legal personality, and its members generally have limited liability: the LLP itself is liable for its debts, not the members personally, save in exceptional cases (such as personal wrongdoing or clawback on insolvency). The creditor's claim lies against the LLP, not the members personally.

n.0: An LLP does have separate legal personality.
n.2: LLP members are not jointly liable without limit like ordinary partners.
n.3: Limited liability does not depend on having four designated members (an LLP needs at least two designated members, a different point).
n.4: Liability is not simply capped at profits drawn; the LLP itself bears the debt.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director learns, through their position, of a valuable business opportunity in which the company would be interested, and then takes that opportunity for themselves personally, without the company's informed consent, profiting from it. The company complains that the director has breached a general duty. The director argues that the company might not have pursued the opportunity anyway. The court considers the relevant directors' duty under the Companies Act 2006. The opportunity had come to the director's attention only because of their role within the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to declare an interest in an existing transaction with the company (s.182) on these facts.
The duty to avoid a situation in which the director's interests conflict with the company's (s.175).
The duty to exercise independent judgement in performing the role (s.173).
The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes (s.171).
The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the role (s.174).
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.175 Companies Act 2006, a director must avoid situations in which they have, or can have, a direct or indirect interest that conflicts, or may conflict, with the interests of the company — including the exploitation of property, information or opportunity — regardless of whether the company could have taken advantage of it.

n.0: Section 182 concerns declaring interests in existing transactions.
n.2: Section 173 concerns independent judgement.
n.3: Section 171 concerns constitutional limits.
n.4: Section 174 concerns care and skill, not conflicts.

Business Law & Practice.q: The partners in a firm have fallen out with one of their number and wish to expel that partner from the partnership against their will. The partnership agreement is silent on any power to expel a partner, and contains no express provision permitting expulsion. The majority argue that, because they are in the majority, they must be able to remove the difficult partner. The court considers whether a partner can be expelled under the Partnership Act 1890 in these circumstances. Relations had broken down completely, and the majority wanted the partner gone as soon as possible. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A partner may be expelled automatically once they have breached the agreement in any way.
A partner may always be expelled by a simple majority of the other partners.
A partner cannot be expelled by a majority unless the partnership agreement expressly confers that power.
A partner may be expelled by any two of the other partners acting together.
A partner may be expelled whenever the other partners consider it to be in the firm's interests.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.25 Partnership Act 1890, no majority of partners can expel a partner unless a power to do so has been conferred by express agreement between the partners. Without such an express power, the difficult partner cannot be expelled.

n.0: There is no automatic power of expulsion for a breach absent express agreement.
n.1: A majority cannot expel a partner without an express power to do so.
n.3: Two partners acting together cannot expel without an express power.
n.4: The other partners' view of the firm's interests does not create a power to expel.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director is personally interested in a transaction which the company is proposing to enter into — for example a contract with a business the director owns. Before the company commits to it, the director wishes to deal with the matter properly under the Companies Act 2006 so as not to be in breach. A question arises as to what the director must do about their interest in the proposed transaction. The court considers the relevant duty. The company was about to sign the contract at the next board meeting, unaware of the director's stake. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The director must simply resign from the board before the transaction is entered into on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The director must obtain the approval of the company's creditors for the transaction.
The director need do nothing, provided the transaction is at market value.
The director must declare the nature and extent of their interest to the other directors before the company enters into it (s.177).
The director must transfer their interest in the other business to the company.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.177 Companies Act 2006, a director who is in any way, directly or indirectly, interested in a proposed transaction or arrangement with the company must declare the nature and extent of that interest to the other directors before the company enters into it.

n.0: Resignation is not required; declaration of the interest is.
n.1: Creditor approval is not the requirement for declaring an interest.
n.2: Market value does not remove the duty to declare the interest.
n.4: The director need not transfer their outside interest to the company.

Business Law & Practice.q: A private company wishes to buy back some of its own shares from a shareholder who wants to exit. The directors are aware that a company purchasing its own shares engages the capital maintenance rules, and want to ensure the buyback is carried out lawfully. They ask about the sources from which a private company may fund a purchase of its own shares. The court considers the rules on a company buying back its own shares under the Companies Act 2006. The exiting shareholder wanted to be bought out, and the company had only modest distributable profits. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A company can never lawfully purchase any of its own shares in any circumstances.
Only a public company may ever purchase its own shares from a shareholder.
A company may fund a buyback only by borrowing the full amount from its bank.
A company may buy back its shares out of any funds at all, without restriction or procedure on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A company may buy back its own shares out of distributable profits or a fresh issue, and a private company may use capital subject to conditions.
Business Law & Practice.w: A company may purchase its own shares if permitted, generally funding the purchase out of distributable profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares. A private company may, in addition, purchase out of capital subject to the statutory conditions and procedure. The buyback must comply with the Companies Act 2006.

n.0: A company can lawfully buy back its shares if the procedure is followed.
n.1: Private companies may also purchase their own shares.
n.2: A buyback need not be funded by bank borrowing; permitted sources are specified.
n.3: A buyback must be funded from permitted sources, not any funds without restriction.

Business Law & Practice.q: A private company wishes to pass members' decisions without holding a physical meeting, using the written resolution procedure. The directors ask what majorities are needed to pass, by written resolution, a decision that would ordinarily require an ordinary resolution, and one that would ordinarily require a special resolution. The company is a private company using written resolutions. The decisions correspond to ordinary and special resolutions respectively. Rather than convening a meeting, the company intends to put decisions to the members in writing, and the directors want to be clear about the level of support required to carry, by that route, both a run-of-the-mill decision and one of the more important kind that would normally need a special resolution. Which of the following best describes the required majorities?
o: A written ordinary resolution needs a simple majority, and a written special resolution at least 75%, of eligible members votes.
Written resolutions require only a simple majority whatever the type of decision.
A written ordinary resolution needs 75% and a written special resolution needs 90% on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Written resolutions can only ever be passed unanimously by all eligible members.
Both written ordinary and special resolutions require unanimity of all members.
Business Law & Practice.w: For written resolutions of a private company, an ordinary resolution is passed by members representing a simple majority of the total voting rights of eligible members, and a special resolution by members representing not less than 75% of those voting rights. The thresholds mirror the votes needed at a meeting, but are measured against eligible members' total voting rights.

n.1: Special resolutions require 75%, so a simple majority is not enough for all decisions.
n.2: The thresholds are simple majority and 75%, not 75% and 90%.
n.3: Written resolutions need not be unanimous; the ordinary/special thresholds apply.
n.4: Written resolutions do not require unanimity of all members.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director allowed the company to keep trading and incurring credit at a time when they knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid going into insolvent liquidation, and did not take every step to minimise loss to creditors. On the company's insolvent liquidation, the liquidator seeks to make the director personally contribute to the company's assets. The court considers wrongful trading under the Insolvency Act 1986. The company had gone on ordering supplies long after rescue had become plainly hopeless. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The director can only be liable if the liquidator proves the director acted dishonestly on these facts as a general rule.
The director is liable only if they personally guaranteed the company's debts.
The director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading, without proof of dishonesty.
Wrongful trading applies only to the debts the director personally incurred.
A director can never be made personally liable for the debts of a limited company.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.214 Insolvency Act 1986, a director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets where, before the insolvent liquidation, they knew or ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation and did not take every step to minimise loss to creditors. Dishonesty need not be shown.

n.0: Wrongful trading does not require proof of dishonesty (unlike fraudulent trading).
n.1: Liability does not depend on a personal guarantee.
n.3: The contribution is not limited to debts the director personally incurred.
n.4: Directors can be made personally liable in insolvency, e.g. for wrongful trading.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company limited by shares proposes to return value to its shareholders in a way that would reduce the capital available to meet creditors' claims. A creditor is concerned, relying on the principle that a company's share capital is a fund that must in general be maintained for the protection of creditors. The court considers the doctrine of maintenance of share capital under company law. The proposal would hand cash back to the members while leaving creditors with a thinner buffer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Share capital may be distributed to shareholders whenever the directors think it appropriate on these facts as a general rule.
A company may return its share capital to shareholders freely at any time it chooses.
Capital maintenance applies only to public companies and never to private companies.
As a general rule a company must maintain its capital and may not return it to shareholders except by permitted procedures.
There is no principle of capital maintenance in modern company law at all.
Business Law & Practice.w: The capital maintenance doctrine provides that a company's share capital is, in general, to be maintained for the benefit of creditors, so it may not be returned to shareholders except through permitted procedures (such as a properly conducted reduction of capital, or a buyback complying with the Act).

n.0: Directors cannot simply distribute capital at will.
n.1: Capital cannot be returned freely; permitted procedures must be followed.
n.2: Capital maintenance applies to private companies too, albeit with some more flexible procedures.
n.4: Capital maintenance remains a principle of modern company law.

Business Law & Practice.q: A person is not formally appointed as a director of a company and is not recorded as such, but in reality either acts as a director (taking part in board decisions as though appointed) or is a person in accordance with whose directions the properly appointed directors are accustomed to act. The company's creditors argue that such a person should be subject to directors' duties and liabilities despite the absence of a formal appointment. The court considers the concepts of de facto and shadow directors. The person gave the orders and the board routinely did exactly as that person directed them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only a person formally appointed and registered as a director can ever owe directors' duties.
A shareholder automatically becomes a director simply by holding a majority of the shares.
A person may be treated as a de facto or shadow director and be subject to directors' duties despite no formal appointment.
A person who is not formally appointed can never incur any liability in relation to the company on these facts as a general rule.
Directors' duties apply only to executive directors who are also employees of the company.
Business Law & Practice.w: The law looks at substance: a de facto director (who acts as a director though not validly appointed) and a shadow director (a person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the directors are accustomed to act) can be subject to directors' duties and liabilities despite the absence of a formal appointment.

n.0: Duties are not confined to formally appointed, registered directors.
n.1: Holding a majority of shares does not automatically make someone a director.
n.3: An unappointed person can incur liability as a de facto or shadow director.
n.4: Directors' duties are not limited to executive director-employees.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director of a company simply does whatever a dominant shareholder tells them to do, mechanically following instructions and abdicating any personal assessment of what is best for the company, rather than forming and exercising their own view on the decisions before the board. A shareholder complains that the director has failed in a general duty owed to the company. The court considers which of the directors' general duties under the Companies Act 2006 is most directly engaged. The director never questioned the instructions and simply rubber-stamped whatever they were told. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to avoid conflicts of interest with the company (s.175).
The duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction with the company (s.177).
The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes (s.171).
The duty to exercise independent judgement in the performance of the role (s.173).
The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the role (s.174).
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.173 Companies Act 2006, a director must exercise independent judgement. Blindly following the instructions of another and abdicating their own judgement breaches this duty (subject to the ability to act under agreements duly entered into by the company or the constitution).

n.0: Section 175 concerns conflicts of interest.
n.1: Section 177 concerns declaring interests in transactions.
n.2: Section 171 concerns acting within powers.
n.4: Section 174 concerns competence and care, not independence of judgement.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director has breached their duties to the company, causing the company loss, but the wrongdoing directors control the board and will not cause the company to sue itself. A shareholder wishes to bring proceedings on the company's behalf to pursue the claim that belongs to the company. The cause of action is the company's, arising from a director's breach of duty. The shareholder seeks to enforce it despite board inaction. The wrong was done to the company itself and the loss is the company's, yet the very directors responsible control the board and will plainly never cause the company to sue them, so a shareholder is looking for a way to pursue the company's claim over the board's inaction. Which of the following best describes the mechanism available?
o: An unfair prejudice petition seeking a buy-out of the member's shares on these facts.
A petition to wind up the company on the just and equitable ground.
A personal claim by the member for damages payable to the member.
A direct claim by the member against the company's auditors.
A derivative claim brought by the member on the company's behalf, with the court's permission.
Business Law & Practice.w: A derivative claim under Part 11 of the Companies Act 2006 (ss.260-264) allows a member to bring an action on behalf of the company in respect of a cause of action vested in the company, arising from a director's negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust. The member must obtain the court's permission to continue the claim.

n.0: Unfair prejudice is a personal remedy for the member, not enforcement of the company's own cause of action.
n.1: Winding up on the just and equitable ground is a different remedy, not enforcement of the claim.
n.2: The loss is the company's; a personal claim for damages to the member is not the correct route.
n.3: The claim is against the director for breach of duty, not against the auditors.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director proposes to buy a valuable property from the company (or sell a valuable property to it) where the value of the asset exceeds the higher statutory threshold and is significant relative to the company's asset value. The board asks whether the transaction can simply be approved by the directors. The counterparty is a director and the asset is a substantial non-cash asset. The company wishes to comply with the Companies Act 2006. One of the directors wants to buy a substantial property from the company at a price well above the statutory threshold and significant in the context of the company's assets, and the board is trying to establish whether it can simply sign this off itself or must put it to the members. Which of the following best describes the approval required?
o: The transaction may be approved by the board of directors alone without member involvement.
The transaction is prohibited outright and can never be carried out.
The substantial property transaction must be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members.
The transaction requires approval by special resolution of 75% of members.
The transaction requires the approval of the company's creditors.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under ss.190-191 of the Companies Act 2006, an arrangement by which a director acquires from, or the company acquires from a director, a substantial non-cash asset (exceeding the statutory value thresholds) must be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members. Without approval the transaction is generally voidable and the director may have to account.

n.0: Board approval alone is insufficient for a substantial property transaction.
n.1: The transaction is not outright prohibited; it may proceed with member approval.
n.3: The requirement is an ordinary resolution, not a special resolution.
n.4: Creditor approval is not the applicable requirement.

Business Law & Practice.q: An individual carries on a business on their own account as a sole trader, without forming any company or partnership. The business runs into financial difficulty and cannot pay its trade creditors. The creditors wish to know whether they can look beyond the business assets to the individual's personal assets to satisfy the debts. The sole trader argues that only the business, and not they personally, is liable. The court considers the liability of a sole trader for business debts. The debts were considerable and the business had few assets of its own with which to meet them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The sole trader has no personal liability at all, as the business is a separate legal person.
The sole trader is liable only if they acted dishonestly in running the business.
The sole trader's liability is limited to the assets they invested in the business.
The sole trader is personally liable without limit for the debts of the business.
The sole trader is liable only up to the nominal value of any shares they hold.
Business Law & Practice.w: A sole trader and their business are not separate legal persons. The sole trader is personally liable, without limit, for all the debts and obligations of the business, so creditors may look to the trader's personal assets.

n.0: A sole trader business is not a separate legal person; there is no limited liability.
n.1: Liability arises from the debts, not only where the trader acted dishonestly.
n.2: A sole trader's liability is not limited to what they invested.
n.4: A sole trader has no shares; liability is personal and unlimited.

Business Law & Practice.q: An individual sells the whole of their trading business, which they have owned and run for many years, and makes a substantial chargeable gain on the disposal of the business assets. They ask their adviser whether any relief may reduce the rate of capital gains tax on the qualifying gain. The disposal is of a business the individual has owned and operated for the requisite period. The individual seeks to reduce the CGT payable on the qualifying gain. Having built up and run the business over many years, the individual is now selling it outright and stands to make a large gain on the business assets, and is asking whether any relief exists that could bring down the capital gains tax rate on the part of the gain that qualifies. Which of the following best describes a relief that may apply?
o: The gain is treated as trading income subject to income tax and national insurance on these facts as a general rule.
The gain is automatically exempt from capital gains tax with no conditions.
The gain is charged to corporation tax rather than capital gains tax.
Business Asset Disposal Relief may apply, reducing the rate of capital gains tax on qualifying gains up to a lifetime limit.
No relief of any kind is available on the disposal of a business.
Business Law & Practice.w: Business Asset Disposal Relief (formerly Entrepreneurs' Relief) may reduce the rate of capital gains tax on qualifying gains from the disposal of all or part of a trading business (or qualifying shares), subject to conditions including a minimum ownership period, up to a lifetime limit on qualifying gains. It reduces the CGT rate rather than exempting the gain entirely.

n.0: The gain is a capital gain, not trading income subject to income tax and NICs.
n.1: The gain is not automatically exempt; relief has conditions and a lifetime limit.
n.2: An individual's gain is charged to capital gains tax, not corporation tax.
n.4: Reliefs such as Business Asset Disposal Relief are available on qualifying business disposals.

Business Law & Practice.q: On a company's insolvent liquidation the liquidator discovers that, before the liquidation, the business had been carried on with the actual intention of defrauding creditors, and that a particular person was knowingly a party to carrying on the business in that way. The liquidator wishes to hold that person personally liable. The court considers fraudulent trading under the Insolvency Act 1986. Money and assets had been siphoned out of the company while its creditors went unpaid. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Only the company itself, and never any individual, can be liable for fraudulent trading.
Fraudulent trading liability arises only where the company was in fact solvent throughout on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Fraudulent trading is a purely civil matter and can never give rise to criminal liability.
Fraudulent trading requires no intention to defraud and is the same as wrongful trading.
A person knowingly party to carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors may be made personally liable for fraudulent trading.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.213 Insolvency Act 1986, if in the course of winding up it appears that the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the court may order those knowingly party to it to contribute to the assets. There is also a related criminal offence of fraudulent trading.

n.0: Individuals knowingly party to it can be personally liable.
n.1: It arises in the context of insolvency/winding up, not where the company was solvent throughout.
n.2: Fraudulent trading can also be a criminal offence, not purely civil.
n.3: Fraudulent trading requires intent to defraud, unlike wrongful trading.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director of a company has been involved in the management of several companies that have become insolvent, and their conduct as a director makes them unfit to be concerned in the management of a company. A regulator considers seeking an order to prevent the director from acting as a director in future. The court considers the disqualification of directors under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986. Several of the director's previous companies had collapsed leaving substantial unpaid debts. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Disqualification is automatic for any director whose company becomes insolvent.
A director can never be prevented from acting as a director of any company in the future on these facts.
A director may be disqualified only if they have been convicted of a criminal offence.
The court may disqualify a director from acting as a director for a period where their conduct makes them unfit.
Only the company's shareholders, and never the court, can disqualify a director.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986, the court may make a disqualification order (for a period up to 15 years) against a person whose conduct as a director makes them unfit to be concerned in the management of a company, among other grounds.

n.0: Disqualification is not automatic on insolvency; unfit conduct must be shown.
n.1: Directors can be disqualified in appropriate cases; it is not impossible.
n.2: Disqualification for unfitness does not require a criminal conviction.
n.4: Disqualification is ordered by the court, not by shareholders.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company goes into liquidation with limited assets and many claimants, including a bank with a fixed charge, a lender with a floating charge, employees owed wages, the liquidator's own fees, unsecured trade creditors, and the shareholders. The liquidator must distribute the available funds in the correct statutory order of priority. The court considers the order in which claims are paid in a corporate liquidation. The available funds fell far short of the total claims, so the order of payment would be decisive. Which of the following best describes the general order of priority?
o: Unsecured creditors are always paid in full before any secured creditor receives anything.
Shareholders are paid first, followed by unsecured creditors and only then secured creditors on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Fixed charge holders, then liquidation expenses, then preferential creditors, then floating charge holders, then unsecured creditors, then shareholders.
All creditors and shareholders are simply paid an equal share of whatever assets remain.
The order of payment is decided entirely at the liquidator's personal discretion.
Business Law & Practice.w: In a liquidation the general order is broadly: fixed charge creditors (from their charged asset), then the costs/expenses of the liquidation, then preferential creditors (e.g. some employee claims), then the prescribed part and floating charge creditors, then unsecured creditors, and finally any surplus to shareholders.

n.0: Secured creditors generally rank ahead of unsecured creditors, not behind.
n.1: Shareholders are paid last, not first.
n.3: Assets are not simply shared equally among all; priority applies.
n.4: The order is fixed by statute, not left to the liquidator's discretion.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company is in financial difficulty but is potentially viable, and its directors wish to reach a binding compromise with the company's creditors to pay its debts (in whole or in part) over time and avoid liquidation, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. The directors want a rescue procedure that binds unsecured creditors once approved. The company seeks a formal arrangement with creditors. The business is struggling but not beyond saving, and rather than let it collapse into liquidation the directors would prefer to strike a deal with the creditors to pay off the debts, wholly or in part, over a period, under the watch of an insolvency practitioner, in a way that ties in the unsecured creditors once enough of them agree. Which of the following best identifies the procedure?
o: A striking off of the company from the register by the Registrar.
A compulsory winding up by the court on a creditor's petition.
A members' voluntary liquidation, which is used only for solvent companies on these facts as a general rule.
A transaction at an undervalue set aside by a liquidator.
A company voluntary arrangement (CVA), binding on unsecured creditors if approved by the requisite majority.
Business Law & Practice.w: A company voluntary arrangement (CVA) under the Insolvency Act 1986 is a rescue procedure: the company (usually its directors) proposes to creditors an arrangement to pay its debts in whole or part over time, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. If approved by at least 75% in value of the unsecured creditors voting, it binds all unsecured creditors (secured and preferential creditors' positions are protected).

n.0: Striking off dissolves the company; it is not a creditor compromise.
n.1: Compulsory winding up ends the company, rather than rescuing it by agreement with creditors.
n.2: A members' voluntary liquidation is for solvent companies being wound up, not a rescue of a struggling one.
n.3: A transaction at an undervalue is a challengeable antecedent transaction, not a rescue procedure.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company grants a charge over its assets to secure a loan, but the charge is not delivered to Companies House for registration within the period allowed by the Companies Act 2006, and remains unregistered when the company later goes into liquidation. The lender assumed registration was a mere formality. The liquidator and other creditors challenge the security. The court considers the consequence of failing to register a registrable company charge in time. The lender had simply filed the paperwork away and never sent it to Companies House at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The charge is void against a liquidator, administrator and creditors, so the lender ranks as unsecured, though the debt remains payable.
Registration of charges is optional, so the failure has no legal consequence at all.
The charge is valid provided the lender registers it at any time before enforcement.
The failure to register makes the underlying loan itself void and unrecoverable.
The charge remains fully valid and enforceable despite the failure to register it in time on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Business Law & Practice.w: A registrable charge that is not delivered for registration at Companies House within the statutory period (21 days beginning with the day after creation) is void against a liquidator, administrator and any creditor of the company. The debt remains payable, but the lender loses the benefit of the security and ranks as an unsecured creditor.

n.1: Registration is not optional for registrable charges; failure has serious consequences.
n.2: Late registration generally requires a court order; it is not simply valid whenever registered before enforcement.
n.3: The underlying debt is not void; only the security is affected.
n.4: An unregistered registrable charge is not fully valid against a liquidator and creditors.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director, by reason of being a director of the company, is offered and accepts a valuable personal benefit from a third party who is seeking to influence how the director acts in relation to the company's affairs. The company did not authorise the director to accept the benefit. A shareholder complains that the director has breached a general duty under the Companies Act 2006. The court considers which duty is engaged. The benefit was a generous personal payment offered to sway how the director handled a contract. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty not to accept benefits from third parties conferred by reason of being a director (s.176).
The duty to exercise independent judgement in performing the role (s.173).
The duty to promote the success of the company for the members as a whole (s.172).
The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the role (s.174).
The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes (s.171) on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.176 Companies Act 2006, a director must not accept a benefit from a third party conferred by reason of their being a director, or their doing (or not doing) anything as a director, where acceptance could reasonably be regarded as likely to give rise to a conflict of interest.

n.1: Section 173 concerns independent judgement.
n.2: Section 172 concerns promoting the company's success.
n.3: Section 174 concerns care and skill.
n.4: Section 171 concerns constitutional limits and proper purposes.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company wishes to pay a dividend to its shareholders. The finance director is concerned about whether the company is legally permitted to make the distribution, given the company's accumulated financial position. A dividend can only lawfully be paid from a particular source. The court considers the rules on the payment of dividends and distributions under the Companies Act 2006. The company had built up losses in earlier years that exceeded its more recent trading profits. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A dividend may be paid out of any of the company's assets, whether or not it has any profits on these facts.
A dividend may always be paid out of the company's share capital to reward shareholders.
A dividend may only be paid out of profits available for distribution (accumulated realised profits less losses).
A dividend may be paid whenever the directors decide it would please the shareholders.
A dividend may be paid only if every creditor of the company first consents to it.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, a company may only make a distribution (such as a dividend) out of profits available for the purpose — broadly, its accumulated realised profits less its accumulated realised losses. Paying dividends otherwise contravenes the capital maintenance rules.

n.0: A dividend cannot be paid where there are no distributable profits.
n.1: Dividends cannot be paid out of share capital.
n.3: The directors' wish to please shareholders does not make a distribution lawful without profits.
n.4: Creditor consent is not the test; availability of distributable profits is.

Business Law & Practice.q: A newly incorporated private company limited by shares is formed without the members adopting any bespoke articles of association of their own, and nothing is registered to displace the default position. A dispute later arises about the internal rules governing how the company is to be run, such as directors' powers and the conduct of meetings. One member argues the company has no constitution at all. The court considers what governs the company's internal affairs in these circumstances. The company had been set up quickly online and the founders had never turned their minds to the articles. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company must adopt the articles of a public company until it drafts its own.
The company's internal affairs are governed solely by whatever the directors decide from time to time.
The company is automatically governed by the articles of the largest company in its sector.
The model articles apply as the company's default constitution where no bespoke articles are adopted.
The company has no constitution at all until the members draft and register their own articles.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, where a company is formed without registering bespoke articles, the relevant model articles (here for a private company limited by shares) apply by default as the company's constitution.

n.0: The private company model articles apply, not public company articles.
n.1: The internal affairs are governed by the articles, not simply the directors' say-so.
n.2: It is not governed by another company's articles.
n.4: The company is not left with no constitution; the model articles fill the gap.

Business Law & Practice.q: The shareholders of a company wish to remove a director from office before the end of their term, against the director's wishes, and the articles do not provide any special procedure. The shareholders want to know how, and by what majority, they can lawfully remove the director under the Companies Act 2006, and what procedural protections apply. The court considers the statutory power to remove a director. The director had a service contract, and the shareholders were determined to remove them regardless. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A director can be removed only by a special resolution passed by a 75% majority.
A director cannot be removed before the end of their term in any circumstances.
The members may remove a director by ordinary resolution, but special notice of the resolution is required (s.168).
A director may be removed by a simple decision of the other directors on the board.
A director can only ever be removed by a unanimous decision of all the shareholders on these facts as a general rule.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.168 Companies Act 2006, a company may by ordinary resolution (a simple majority) remove a director before the end of their term, notwithstanding anything in any agreement, but special notice of the resolution is required and the director has the right to make representations.

n.0: A special (75%) resolution is not required; an ordinary resolution suffices.
n.1: A director can be removed before the end of their term under s.168.
n.3: Removal under s.168 is by the members, not by the other directors alone.
n.4: Unanimity is not required; an ordinary resolution suffices (with special notice).

Business Law & Practice.q: A minority shareholder in a private company complains that the majority, who control the board, have excluded them from any involvement, stopped paying dividends, and are paying themselves excessive salaries, so that the company's affairs are being conducted in a way that harms the minority's interests as a member. The shareholder seeks a remedy, commonly an order that their shares be bought out at a fair value. The complaint is of conduct unfairly harmful to the member's interests. The minority shareholder put money into the company on the understanding of being involved, but the majority have frozen them out of decisions, turned off dividends and voted themselves generous pay, leaving the minority with an investment that yields nothing and no say in how it is run. Which of the following best identifies the statutory remedy?
o: A petition to wind the company up on the ground of insolvency.
A petition for relief from unfair prejudice under section 994 of the Companies Act 2006.
An application to strike the company off the register.
A claim for breach of the shareholder's employment contract.
A claim in the tort of conspiracy against the majority shareholders on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: A member may petition under s.994 of the Companies Act 2006 where the company's affairs are being or have been conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally or some part of them. The most common remedy is an order that the petitioner's shares be purchased at a fair value.

n.0: Winding up for insolvency is not the appropriate remedy for unfair prejudice to a member.
n.2: Striking off does not address unfair prejudice and would harm the petitioner.
n.3: The complaint concerns the member's interests as a member, not an employment contract.
n.4: The statutory unfair prejudice remedy, not a conspiracy claim, is the appropriate route.

Business Law & Practice.q: One partner in a trading firm enters into a contract with a third party which is of a kind usually made by businesses of that type, and which appears to be for carrying on the firm's business in the usual way. The third party does not know of any restriction on that partner's authority. The other partners say that they had privately agreed that no partner could make such a contract without the others' consent, and so the firm is not bound. The court considers a partner's authority to bind the firm under the Partnership Act 1890. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm is bound, because the partner had apparent authority to make a contract of that kind.
The firm is bound only if the contract turned out to be profitable for the firm.
The firm is not bound, because the partners had privately restricted that partner's authority.
The firm is bound only if the third party first checked the partnership agreement.
The firm is not bound unless all the partners signed the particular contract.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.5 Partnership Act 1890, the acts of a partner carrying on in the usual way business of the kind carried on by the firm bind the firm, unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that or did not believe them to be a partner. A private restriction unknown to the third party does not affect the firm's liability.

n.1: The firm is bound regardless of whether the contract proved profitable.
n.2: A private, undisclosed restriction does not protect the firm against a third party without notice.
n.3: A third party is not required to check the partnership agreement.
n.4: All partners need not sign; one partner's usual-business act binds the firm.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company wishes to change its articles of association to alter the way directors are appointed. The directors ask what type of members' decision is required to amend the articles under the Companies Act 2006. The proposal is to amend the company's existing articles. The company wishes to act validly. The company has decided to overhaul the way its directors are appointed and that means changing the wording of its existing articles, so the board needs to be clear about the level of member support the law requires before an amendment to the constitution can take effect. Which of the following best describes the resolution required to alter the articles?
o: A resolution of the board of directors alone.
The prior approval of the Registrar of Companies.
A special resolution of the members (at least 75%).
An ordinary resolution of the members (a simple majority).
A unanimous decision of all the members.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.21 of the Companies Act 2006, a company may amend its articles by special resolution, which requires a majority of at least 75%. A copy of the amended articles and the resolution must then be filed at Companies House. The board alone cannot alter the articles.

n.0: The board alone cannot amend the articles.
n.1: The Registrar's prior approval is not required; the resolution is filed after being passed.
n.3: An ordinary resolution is insufficient to alter the articles; a special resolution is required.
n.4: Unanimity is not required; a 75% special resolution suffices.

Business Law & Practice.q: A partner in a trading partnership, without the actual authority of the other partners, orders goods of a kind the firm usually buys from a supplier who deals with the firm and is unaware of any restriction on that partner's authority. The other partners refuse to pay, saying the partner had no authority. The transaction was in the ordinary course of the firm's business and the supplier did not know of any limit on authority. The partner placed a routine order of the sort the firm regularly makes, the supplier had dealt with the firm before and had no inkling of any private arrangement between the partners limiting who could order what, and only after delivery did the remaining partners try to disown the purchase. Which of the following best describes whether the firm is bound?
o: The firm is bound only if the supplier had made specific enquiries about authority.
The firm is bound because the partner had apparent authority to bind it in the firm's usual business.
The firm is bound only if the other partners later ratify the order in writing.
The firm is not bound because a partner never has authority without the others' express consent.
The firm is not bound because internal restrictions always defeat a third party's claim.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, the acts of a partner carrying on in the usual way the business of the kind carried on by the firm bind the firm and the other partners, unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew this or did not believe them to be a partner. Here the transaction was usual business and the supplier had no notice of any restriction, so the firm is bound.

n.0: A third party dealing in the usual course need not make specific enquiries about authority.
n.2: The firm is already bound by apparent authority; ratification is not required.
n.3: A partner has apparent authority in the firm's usual business without needing express consent each time.
n.4: Internal restrictions do not defeat a third party without notice of them.

Business Law & Practice.q: A partnership carries on a trade and makes profits, which are shared among the partners in the agreed proportions. The partners want to understand how those trading profits are taxed, and in particular whether the partnership itself is taxed as a separate entity or whether the partners are taxed individually on their shares. The court considers the taxation of the profits of a general partnership. The firm had several partners who each drew a share of the profits at the end of the year. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only the senior partner is taxed on the whole of the partnership's profits.
The partnership is taxed as a single entity, and the partners pay no tax at all.
The partnership is tax-transparent, so each partner is charged to income tax on their share of the profits.
The partnership's profits are entirely free of tax in the hands of the partners on these facts as a general rule.
The partnership pays corporation tax on its profits as if it were a company.
Business Law & Practice.w: A general partnership is tax-transparent: it is not itself a separate taxable entity for income tax. Instead, each partner is assessed to income tax (and pays national insurance) on their share of the partnership's trading profits.

n.0: All partners are taxed on their respective shares, not only the senior partner.
n.1: The partners are taxed on their shares; the profits are not tax-free at partnership level with no partner tax.
n.3: Partnership profits are taxable in the partners' hands, not tax-free.
n.4: A general partnership does not pay corporation tax; that applies to companies.

Business Law & Practice.q: A private company limited by shares proposes to give financial assistance (for example a loan or guarantee) to a person to help them acquire shares in that same company. The directors ask whether this is lawful, given that they have heard of a prohibition on financial assistance. The company is a private company, not a public company, and the assistance is for the acquisition of its own shares. The directors want to lend money, or give a guarantee, to help someone buy shares in their own company, but they have a vague memory of a statutory ban on that sort of thing and need to know whether it actually bites on a company of their kind or only on public companies. Which of the following best describes the position under the Companies Act 2006?
o: Financial assistance is lawful for any company provided the shares are fully paid.
Financial assistance is never lawful for any company in any circumstances.
A private company is absolutely prohibited from giving any financial assistance for the acquisition of its own shares on these facts.
Financial assistance is lawful only if approved by the SRA.
A private company may generally give financial assistance for the acquisition of its own shares, as the prohibition applies to public companies.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, the prohibition on a company giving financial assistance for the acquisition of its own shares applies to public companies (and their subsidiaries). The former prohibition on private companies was abolished, so a private company may generally give such assistance, subject to the general law (directors' duties, maintenance of capital and solvency considerations).

n.0: The rules turn on whether the company is public or private, not simply on whether shares are fully paid.
n.1: Financial assistance is not universally prohibited; the restriction targets public companies.
n.2: Private companies are not absolutely prohibited; the prohibition is on public companies.
n.3: SRA approval is irrelevant to company financial assistance.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company borrows money from a lender and grants security over its assets. The lender is considering whether to take a fixed charge over specific identified assets, or a floating charge over a class of assets that changes from time to time (such as stock in trade). The company wishes to understand the essential difference between the two, particularly the company's freedom to deal with the charged assets. The court considers the distinction between fixed and floating charges. The lender was weighing which form of security would best protect it if the company later failed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A fixed charge attaches to specific assets restricting dealings, while a floating charge hovers over a class of assets the company may deal with until crystallisation.
A floating charge attaches to specific assets and prevents any dealing with them at all.
A fixed charge allows the company to deal freely with the assets until the lender intervenes.
Only a floating charge can ever be taken over a company's property; fixed charges are not permitted on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There is no practical difference between a fixed charge and a floating charge.
Business Law & Practice.w: A fixed charge attaches to specific, identified assets and the company cannot dispose of them free of the charge without consent. A floating charge 'floats' over a fluctuating class of assets (such as stock), allowing the company to deal with them in the ordinary course of business until the charge crystallises and attaches to the assets then within the class.

n.1: The description is reversed; it is the fixed charge that attaches to specific assets restricting dealings.
n.2: A fixed charge restricts dealings; the freedom to deal is a feature of the floating charge before crystallisation.
n.3: Both fixed and floating charges may be taken over company property.
n.4: There are significant practical differences between the two.

Business Law & Practice.q: The partners in an existing firm wish to bring in a new person as a partner. There is no written partnership agreement making special provision about admitting new partners. One of the existing partners objects to the proposed new partner joining. The others argue that a simple majority should be enough to admit the newcomer. The court considers the default rule on the admission of a new partner under the Partnership Act 1890. The deceased had been an equal partner and no one had planned for what would happen on a death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No new partner may be introduced without the consent of all existing partners, absent contrary agreement.
A new partner may be admitted by a simple majority of the existing partners.
A new partner may be admitted only with the approval of the firm's principal creditors on these facts.
A new partner may be admitted by any single existing partner acting alone.
A new partner is admitted automatically once they contribute capital to the firm.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.24(7) Partnership Act 1890, no person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all existing partners, unless the partnership agreement provides otherwise. The objection of one partner therefore blocks the admission under the default rule.

n.1: A simple majority is not sufficient under the default rule.
n.2: Creditor approval is not the statutory requirement for admitting a partner.
n.3: A single partner cannot admit a new partner alone.
n.4: Contributing capital does not by itself make someone a partner.

Business Law & Practice.q: A shareholder in a private company wishes to transfer their shares to a buyer. The company's articles contain provisions restricting the transfer of shares, for example giving the directors a discretion to refuse to register a transfer, or conferring pre-emption rights on existing members. The selling shareholder argues that they can simply sell to whomever they like. The court considers the effect of transfer restrictions in a private company's articles. The company was a small family business whose articles were designed to keep ownership within the family. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer of shares may be restricted by the company's articles, which can bind the selling shareholder.
A shareholder may transfer shares only with the approval of the company's creditors.
Shares can never be transferred at all in a private limited company.
Transfer restrictions in the articles are automatically void and of no effect.
Shares in a private company are always freely transferable regardless of the articles on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: Unlike shares in a public/listed company, shares in a private company are commonly subject to transfer restrictions in the articles — such as directors' power to refuse registration or pre-emption provisions — which are valid and bind the members.

n.1: Creditor approval is not required to transfer shares.
n.2: Shares in a private company can be transferred, subject to the articles.
n.3: Transfer restrictions in the articles are valid, not automatically void.
n.4: Private company shares are not always freely transferable; the articles may restrict transfer.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director has breached one of their general duties to the company, causing the company loss and making a personal gain. The company (and its shareholders) consider what consequences follow from the breach, including whether the breach can be authorised or ratified. The director argues that a breach of a statutory duty has no real consequences. The court considers the remedies and consequences for breach of a director's general duties under the Companies Act 2006. The breach had enriched the director at the company's expense, and the members were weighing their options. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A breach of a statutory director's duty has no legal consequences whatsoever.
A breach of duty is always a criminal offence carrying a mandatory prison sentence.
Remedies mirror the equitable/common law consequences, and a breach may in some cases be ratified by ordinary resolution.
The only possible remedy is that the director must be disqualified from acting again on these facts as a general rule.
A breach of duty can never be ratified by the company in any circumstances at all.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.178 Companies Act 2006, the consequences of breach of the general duties are the same as would apply under the corresponding common law rule or equitable principle (for example, an account of profits, equitable compensation, or rescission). A breach may, in appropriate cases, be ratified by the members by ordinary resolution under s.239.

n.0: A breach of duty does carry legal consequences.
n.1: Breach of a general duty is not automatically a criminal offence.
n.3: Disqualification is not the only possible consequence; various remedies exist.
n.4: Breaches may be ratified by ordinary resolution in appropriate cases.

Business Law & Practice.q: A private company limited by shares wishes to reduce its share capital to return surplus capital to shareholders. The directors ask about a procedure available to a private company that does not require a court order. The company is a private company and its directors are willing to make a statement about its solvency. The company seeks the simplest lawful route. The company is sitting on surplus capital it would like to hand back to shareholders, it is a private company whose directors are willing to vouch formally for its solvency, and it is looking for the most straightforward lawful way to reduce its capital without going to court. Which of the following best describes the available procedure?
o: A special resolution confirmed by the court in every case.
The unanimous written consent of all the company's creditors.
A special resolution supported by a solvency statement from the directors.
An ordinary resolution alone, with no solvency statement required.
A board resolution alone, without any member involvement.
Business Law & Practice.w: A private company limited by shares may reduce its capital by special resolution supported by a solvency statement made by the directors (Companies Act 2006, ss.641-644), without needing court confirmation. The solvency statement must be made within a short period before the resolution and filed at Companies House. Public companies must use the court route.

n.0: Court confirmation is required for public companies, but the private-company route avoids it via the solvency statement.
n.1: Creditor consent is not the mechanism; a directors' solvency statement supports the resolution.
n.3: An ordinary resolution is insufficient; a special resolution plus solvency statement is needed.
n.4: A board resolution alone cannot reduce capital.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company makes taxable profits from its trading activities and from chargeable gains during its accounting period. A businessperson wants to understand which tax the company itself is liable to pay on those profits and gains, as distinct from taxes payable by its shareholders or employees. The court considers the tax to which a UK company is subject on its income and gains. The company had a profitable trading year and had also sold a property at a healthy gain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A company pays capital gains tax on its trading profits at the individual rate.
A company pays corporation tax on its taxable income profits and chargeable gains.
A company pays no tax at all on its profits; only its shareholders are taxed.
A company pays income tax on its profits in exactly the same way as an individual.
A company pays only VAT and is not subject to any tax on its profits.
Business Law & Practice.w: A UK company is chargeable to corporation tax on its taxable total profits, which comprise both its income profits (such as trading profits) and its chargeable gains, for each accounting period.

n.0: Companies pay corporation tax on gains, not capital gains tax at the individual rate.
n.2: A company is itself liable to tax on its profits.
n.3: Companies pay corporation tax, not income tax, on their profits.
n.4: A company is subject to corporation tax on profits, in addition to VAT on relevant supplies.

Business Law & Practice.q: An individual who runs a business through a company sells a business asset, or their shares, and makes a gain. Separately, a company disposes of a capital asset and makes a gain. The individual wants to understand the difference in how the gain is taxed depending on whether it is made by an individual or by a company. The court considers the taxation of capital gains for individuals and companies. The disposals produced substantial gains, and the taxpayers wanted to know their tax exposure. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Gains made by individuals are taxed as trading income under corporation tax rules.
Only companies, and never individuals, are ever charged to tax on capital gains.
Both individuals and companies pay capital gains tax on their gains in exactly the same way on these facts as a general rule.
Neither individuals nor companies pay any tax on gains from disposing of assets.
An individual's chargeable gains are subject to capital gains tax, while a company's gains are charged to corporation tax.
Business Law & Practice.w: An individual who makes a chargeable gain on the disposal of an asset is subject to capital gains tax (subject to reliefs and the annual exempt amount), whereas a company's chargeable gains are brought into its corporation tax computation and taxed as part of its total profits.

n.0: Individuals' gains are charged to CGT, not corporation tax.
n.1: Individuals are also chargeable on gains, via CGT.
n.2: Individuals pay CGT while companies pay corporation tax on gains; they are not identical.
n.3: Gains are taxable, not free of tax.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company was formed by two people on the basis of mutual trust to run a business together as quasi-partners, both participating in management. One has now been excluded from all management by the other, and although the company is solvent, the relationship of trust and confidence underlying it has irretrievably broken down. The excluded member wants the company brought to an end. The company is solvent but the basis on which it was formed has collapsed. The two set the company up as equals, each expecting to have a hand in running it, but one has now shut the other out of management entirely, and although the business is perfectly solvent the personal trust the venture depended on has completely collapsed. Which of the following best describes the remedy available?
o: A claim for wrongful trading against the controlling member.
A petition to wind up the company on the just and equitable ground under section 122(1)(g).
A derivative claim on behalf of the company against the excluded member.
An application to have the company administratively dissolved by the Registrar.
A petition to wind up the company on the ground that it is unable to pay its debts.
Business Law & Practice.w: Where a solvent company was formed as a quasi-partnership on a basis of mutual trust and participation, and that relationship has broken down (for example by exclusion from management), a member may petition to wind up the company on the just and equitable ground under s.122(1)(g) of the Insolvency Act 1986.

n.0: Wrongful trading concerns insolvent trading, not this quasi-partnership breakdown.
n.2: A derivative claim enforces the company's cause of action, not the exclusion complaint.
n.3: Administrative dissolution by the Registrar does not address the members' dispute.
n.4: Inability to pay debts is not the ground here; the company is solvent.

Business Law & Practice.q: A newly formed private company limited by shares is arranging its management. The founders ask how many directors the company must have and whether a particular proposed director, a 17-year-old individual, may be appointed. The company is a private company, not a public company. The proposed director is under 18 but over 16. The founders are keeping the management lean and would like to appoint just one director, and they are also keen to bring in a capable 17-year-old family member, so they need to know both the minimum number of directors and whether someone of that age can lawfully be appointed. Which of the following best describes the requirements as to directors?
o: A private company must have at least one director, and a director must be a natural person aged at least 16, so the 17-year-old may be appointed.
A private company need not have any directors at all.
A private company must have at least two directors, so one director is never sufficient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A director must be at least 18, so the 17-year-old cannot be appointed.
Only a public company may appoint a director under the age of 18.
Business Law & Practice.w: A private company must have at least one director (a public company at least two), and at least one director must be a natural person. A director must be at least 16 years old. As the proposed director is 17, and a private company needs only one director, the appointment is permissible.

n.1: A company must have at least one director; it cannot have none.
n.2: A private company needs a minimum of one, not two, directors.
n.3: The minimum age for a director is 16, not 18, so a 17-year-old qualifies.
n.4: The minimum age of 16 applies generally, not only to public companies.

Business Law & Practice.q: A general meeting of a private company with several members is convened. On the day, the directors are concerned that too few members are present for the meeting to transact business validly, and ask what the minimum number of members present is for a quorum, applying the default statutory position. The company has more than one member and the articles do not vary the default. The directors wish to know the quorum for the general meeting. On the morning of the meeting only a couple of members have turned up, the directors are worried that business transacted might later be challenged as invalid, and they want to confirm the smallest number of members whose presence will let the meeting proceed. Which of the following best describes the quorum requirement?
o: A quorum requires all the members to be present in person.
A quorum requires a majority of all the members of the company on these facts.
There is no quorum requirement for a general meeting.
A single member present is always sufficient to form a quorum.
Two qualifying persons (generally two members) present constitute a quorum.
Business Law & Practice.w: For a company with more than one member, the default quorum for a general meeting is two qualifying persons (broadly, two members present in person or by proxy, or corporate representatives). A single-member company has a quorum of one. The articles may vary the default, but two is the standard position here.

n.0: The quorum does not require all members to attend.
n.1: The quorum is a fixed number (two), not a majority of all members.
n.2: There is a quorum requirement for general meetings.
n.3: A single member is a quorum only for a single-member company, not one with several members.

Business Law & Practice.q: A person who is not a partner in a firm knowingly allows the firm to represent to a particular lender that they are a partner, and the lender, relying on that representation, advances credit to the firm. The firm later cannot pay, and the lender seeks to hold the non-partner liable. The individual knowingly permitted themselves to be held out as a partner and the lender gave credit in reliance. The individual let the firm describe them to the lender as one of the partners, said nothing to correct the impression, and the lender, reassured by the apparent involvement of someone it regarded as creditworthy, went ahead and extended the credit that the firm has now failed to repay. Which of the following best describes the individual's liability?
o: The individual has no liability because they were never actually a partner.
The individual is liable only if they received a share of the firm's profits on these facts as a general rule.
The individual is liable to all the firm's creditors regardless of reliance.
The individual is liable only if they signed the credit agreement personally.
The individual may be liable to the lender as a partner by holding out, having knowingly allowed the representation.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the doctrine of holding out (Partnership Act 1890, s.14), a person who by words or conduct represents themselves, or knowingly allows themselves to be represented, as a partner is liable as a partner to anyone who has, on the faith of that representation, given credit to the firm. The lender's reliance makes the individual liable here.

n.0: Not being an actual partner does not prevent liability by holding out.
n.1: Liability does not depend on receiving a share of profits.
n.2: Liability by holding out runs to those who relied on the representation, not automatically to all creditors.
n.3: Liability by holding out does not require signing the credit agreement.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director makes a decision on behalf of the company. In doing so, the director focuses only on short-term profit and ignores relevant matters such as the likely long-term consequences, the interests of employees, and the company's reputation, when they should have acted in the way they considered, in good faith, most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. A shareholder alleges a breach of duty. The court considers which duty is engaged under the Companies Act 2006. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes only (s.171) on these facts.
The duty not to accept benefits from third parties by reason of the office (s.176).
The duty to act in good faith to promote the success of the company for the members as a whole (s.172).
The duty to exercise independent judgement when acting for the company (s.173).
The duty to declare an interest in an existing transaction with the company (s.182).
