Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.172 Companies Act 2006, a director must act in the way they consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to factors including long-term consequences, employees, and the company's reputation.

n.0: Section 171 concerns constitutional limits and proper purposes.
n.1: Section 176 concerns benefits from third parties.
n.3: Section 173 concerns independent judgement, a distinct duty.
n.4: Section 182 concerns declaring interests in existing transactions.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company has more than one class of shares, and the rights attached to one class (for example preference shares) are to be altered in a way that affects that class specifically. The holders of the affected class are concerned that their special rights could be changed without their agreement. The court considers the protection given to a class of shareholders when their class rights are to be varied under the Companies Act 2006. The preference shareholders feared that their fixed dividend rights were about to be watered down. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Class rights may be varied by an ordinary resolution of the company as a whole.
Class rights may generally be varied only with the consent of the required proportion of that class of shareholders.
Class rights may be varied only with the unanimous consent of every shareholder in the company on these facts.
Class rights may be varied by the directors alone whenever they consider it appropriate.
Class rights can never be varied once they have been attached to a class of shares.
Business Law & Practice.w: The rights attached to a class of shares may be varied only in accordance with the variation of class rights procedure — generally requiring the consent in writing of holders of at least three-quarters in nominal value of the class, or a special resolution passed at a separate class meeting — protecting the affected class.

n.0: An ordinary resolution of the whole company is not sufficient to vary a class's rights.
n.2: Unanimity of every shareholder is not required; the class consent threshold governs.
n.3: Directors cannot vary class rights alone.
n.4: Class rights can be varied through the proper procedure; they are not immutable.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company is proposing two different decisions. One is a routine matter that requires only a simple majority of the members, and the other is a more fundamental matter, such as changing the company's articles of association, which the Companies Act 2006 requires to be approved by a higher threshold. The company secretary needs to know the majorities required. The court considers the difference between ordinary and special resolutions. One resolution was to approve the annual accounts and the other was to change the company's name. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An ordinary resolution needs a simple majority, while a special resolution needs at least 75%.
All company resolutions require the unanimous agreement of every member.
An ordinary resolution needs 75%, while a special resolution needs a simple majority.
Both ordinary and special resolutions require exactly the same simple majority.
A special resolution needs only a simple majority, provided 14 days' notice is given.
Business Law & Practice.w: An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority (more than 50%) of the votes, while a special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75%. Fundamental matters, such as altering the articles or changing the company name, require a special resolution.

n.1: Company resolutions do not generally require unanimity.
n.2: The thresholds are reversed in this option.
n.3: They do not require the same majority; special resolutions need 75%.
n.4: A special resolution requires 75%, not a simple majority.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company that is now in insolvent liquidation had, within the two years before the onset of insolvency, transferred a valuable asset to a connected person for far less than its true worth. The liquidator wishes to challenge the transaction and restore value to the estate. The transfer was at a significant undervalue and occurred within the relevant period before insolvency. The liquidator seeks to unwind it. Not long before the company slid into insolvent liquidation it handed a valuable asset to someone connected with it for a fraction of its real worth, leaving less for the creditors, and the liquidator now wants to unwind the deal and bring that value back into the estate. Which of the following best describes the basis of challenge?
o: The liquidator has no power to challenge past transactions of the company.
The liquidator may challenge it only with the unanimous consent of the creditors.
The liquidator may challenge it only if the company intended to defraud that particular creditor.
The liquidator may challenge it only if it occurred within six months before insolvency.
The liquidator may challenge it as a transaction at an undervalue and seek an order restoring the position.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.238 of the Insolvency Act 1986, a liquidator or administrator may challenge a transaction at an undervalue entered into within two years before the onset of insolvency, where the company was or became insolvent as a result. The court may make an order restoring the position to what it would have been had the transaction not occurred.

n.0: The liquidator does have power to challenge such transactions.
n.1: Creditor consent is not required for the liquidator to bring the challenge.
n.2: A transaction at an undervalue does not require proof of intent to defraud a particular creditor (that is a separate provision).
n.3: The relevant period for a transaction at an undervalue is two years, not six months.

Business Law & Practice.q: The members of a small private company want to pass a resolution without going to the trouble of holding a physical general meeting, because they are geographically dispersed. They wish to know whether their private company can take members' decisions in writing rather than at a meeting, and how such a written resolution is passed. The court considers the written resolution procedure available to private companies under the Companies Act 2006. The members were spread across the country and were rarely able to attend meetings in person. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A private company may generally pass members' resolutions as written resolutions, by the required majority, without a meeting.
A written resolution is valid only if signed by every member of the company in every case.
A private company must always hold a physical general meeting and can never use written resolutions on these facts.
Only a public company may use written resolutions to pass members' decisions.
Written resolutions may be used only for the removal of directors and auditors.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, a private company may pass most members' resolutions as written resolutions, requiring the same majority as at a meeting (a simple majority for an ordinary resolution, 75% for a special resolution), without the need to hold a general meeting. (Removal of a director or auditor cannot be done by written resolution.)

n.1: A written resolution needs the requisite majority, not the signature of every member.
n.2: Private companies are not required always to hold physical meetings.
n.3: It is private companies, not public companies, that may use written resolutions.
n.4: Written resolutions are available generally, not only for those specific matters (which are in fact excluded).

Business Law & Practice.q: A company grants a charge over its assets to a lender to secure a loan. The company secretary is aware that the charge must be registered but is unsure of the deadline, and of the consequence of missing it. The charge is one that is registrable at Companies House. The secretary wishes to preserve the lender's security. The loan has been drawn down against the security of the new charge, the secretary knows some registration step is required but is hazy on the timescale, and the lender is anxious that nothing be done, or left undone, that might jeopardise the security it has bargained for. Which of the following best describes the registration requirement and the effect of failure to register in time?
o: The charge must be registered with HM Land Registry within 21 days in every case.
The charge must be registered within 21 days, but failure only results in a fine with the charge remaining fully valid on these facts as a general rule.
The charge need not be registered at all, as registration is optional.
The charge must be registered at Companies House within 21 days of creation, failing which it is void against a liquidator, administrator and creditors.
The charge must be registered within 12 months, and late registration has no consequences.
Business Law & Practice.w: A registrable charge created by a company must be registered at Companies House within 21 days beginning with the day after its creation. If it is not, the charge is void against a liquidator, an administrator and any creditor of the company (though the debt itself remains payable and immediately becomes repayable).

n.0: Registration is at Companies House; Land Registry registration is a separate matter for land.
n.1: Failure does more than attract a fine; it renders the charge void against the specified persons.
n.2: Registration is not optional for registrable charges.
n.4: The period is 21 days, not 12 months, and failure has serious consequences.

Business Law & Practice.q: A private company needs to take a routine management decision about its day-to-day trading operations. A shareholder argues that all such decisions must be put to the shareholders in general meeting, while the directors say that ordinary management is a matter for the board. The company's articles follow the model articles. The court considers the general division of decision-making power between the board of directors and the shareholders in general meeting. The decision concerned a routine supply contract of the kind the company entered into every week. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All decisions of the company are for the directors alone, with no role for the shareholders on these facts as a general rule.
The directors are generally responsible for managing the company, while certain decisions are reserved to the shareholders.
Day-to-day decisions are taken by the company's creditors rather than its directors.
All decisions of the company must be taken by the shareholders in general meeting.
Every management decision must be approved by both the board and the shareholders together.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the model articles, the directors are responsible for the management of the company and may exercise all its powers, while certain important matters (such as altering the articles, or removing a director) are reserved to the shareholders by the Companies Act 2006 or the articles.

n.0: Some decisions are reserved to shareholders, so it is not all for the directors.
n.2: Creditors do not take the company's management decisions.
n.3: Not all decisions must go to the general meeting; day-to-day management is for the board.
n.4: Routine decisions do not require both board and shareholder approval.

Business Law & Practice.q: A businessperson is deciding whether to incorporate as a private limited company or a public limited company, and wants to understand a key legal difference between them. In particular, they have heard that only one of these types of company is permitted to offer its shares to the public at large. They also understand there are differences in minimum share capital requirements. The court considers a fundamental distinction between private and public companies under the Companies Act 2006. The businessperson planned eventually to raise capital from outside investors to grow the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A public company may offer its shares to the public and must meet a minimum share capital requirement, unlike a private company.
A private company may offer its shares to the public, but a public company may not on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Only a private company is a separate legal person; a public company is not.
There is no legal difference between private and public companies under the Act.
A public company cannot have limited liability, whereas a private company can.
Business Law & Practice.w: A key distinction is that a public limited company may offer its shares to the public and must have an allotted share capital of at least the statutory minimum (£50,000, a quarter paid up) and a trading certificate before trading, whereas a private company must not offer its shares to the public.

n.1: It is the public company, not the private company, that may offer shares to the public.
n.2: Both private and public companies are separate legal persons.
n.3: There are significant legal differences between the two types.
n.4: Both private and public companies can be limited by shares.

Business Law & Practice.q: Entrepreneurs wish to incorporate a private company limited by shares and ask what must be delivered to the Registrar of Companies to bring the company into existence. They intend to adopt the default constitution unless they provide their own. The company is to be a new private company limited by shares. The founders want to know what registration requires. The founders have settled on a private company limited by shares, are content to fall back on the default constitution unless they supply their own, and simply want to know what package of documents and information actually has to reach the Registrar before the company legally comes into being. Which of the following best describes what must be delivered to Companies House to form the company?
o: Nothing formal, as a company comes into existence simply by the founders trading together on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A court order approving the formation of the company.
Only a single signed partnership agreement between the founders.
Only the company's first set of annual accounts.
An application to register with the required documents, details and fee, following which a certificate of incorporation is issued.
Business Law & Practice.w: To form a company, an application for registration must be delivered to the Registrar with the required documents and information, including a memorandum of association, the proposed articles (or reliance on the model articles), a statement of capital, proposed officers and registered office, and the fee. The Registrar then issues a certificate of incorporation.

n.0: A company does not arise merely from trading together; registration is required.
n.1: No court order is needed to incorporate a company.
n.2: A partnership agreement does not form a company.
n.3: First accounts are not what brings a company into existence.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company is unable to pay its debts as they fall due, and a creditor who is owed a substantial undisputed sum wishes to take formal insolvency action to have the company wound up by the court and its assets realised and distributed. The creditor asks on what basis a company may be compulsorily wound up. The court considers compulsory winding up under the Insolvency Act 1986. The debt was long overdue and the company had ignored a formal statutory demand for payment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A company can never be wound up against the wishes of its shareholders.
A creditor may petition for the company to be compulsorily wound up on the ground that it is unable to pay its debts.
Only the company's own directors may ever apply to have the company wound up.
Compulsory winding up is available only where the company has acted fraudulently.
A creditor may wind up the company only if owed more than half of the company's total debts on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Insolvency Act 1986, a company may be wound up by the court on a petition (often by a creditor) on grounds including that the company is unable to pay its debts (inability being demonstrated, for example, by an unsatisfied statutory demand or unpaid judgment).

n.0: A company can be wound up against shareholders' wishes, e.g. on a creditor's petition.
n.2: Creditors, not only directors, may petition to wind up a company.
n.3: Inability to pay debts, not fraud, is the usual ground.
n.4: There is no rule that the creditor must be owed more than half the total debts.

Business Law & Practice.q: A general partnership has no written agreement dealing with how profits and losses are to be shared, or whether any partner is entitled to a salary. One partner contributed far more capital than the others and worked longer hours, and argues they should therefore receive a larger share of the profits and a salary for their extra work. The court considers how profits and losses are shared, and whether a partner is entitled to a salary, under the default rules of the Partnership Act 1890. The firm had traded successfully for several years without ever agreeing anything in writing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: In the absence of agreement, partners share profits and losses equally and are not entitled to a salary.
Profits are shared in proportion to the capital each partner contributed to the firm.
The partner who works the longest hours is automatically entitled to a salary.
Profits are shared equally, but losses fall only on the partner who caused them.
The partner with the largest capital contribution is entitled to the largest share of profits.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.24 Partnership Act 1890, in the absence of contrary agreement, partners share equally in the capital and profits of the business and must contribute equally to losses, and no partner is entitled to a salary for acting in the partnership business.

n.1: Profits are shared equally by default, not in proportion to capital.
n.2: There is no default entitlement to a salary for working longer hours.
n.3: Losses are shared equally, not borne only by the partner who caused them.
n.4: A larger capital contribution does not, by default, give a larger profit share.

Business Law & Practice.q: A promoter, acting to set up a company that has not yet been incorporated, enters into a contract 'on behalf of' the intended company with a supplier, before the company legally exists. After incorporation the company does not adopt or ratify the contract, and the supplier is not paid. The supplier seeks to recover from the promoter personally. The promoter argues that they contracted only as agent for the company. The court considers liability on a pre-incorporation contract under the Companies Act 2006. The promoter had signed the order in the company's name weeks before it was actually formed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The supplier's only remedy is against the company, which must ratify the contract.
The promoter is personally liable on the pre-incorporation contract, subject to any agreement to the contrary.
The promoter is liable only if they expressly guaranteed the contract in writing.
The company is automatically liable on the contract once it is later incorporated.
Neither the promoter nor the company is ever liable on a pre-incorporation contract on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.51 Companies Act 2006, a contract purporting to be made by or on behalf of a company before it is formed takes effect as one made with the person purporting to act for the company, who is personally liable on it, subject to any agreement to the contrary. The company cannot be bound by a contract made before it existed unless it makes a new contract after incorporation.

n.0: A company cannot ratify a contract made before it existed; a fresh contract is needed.
n.2: Personal liability under s.51 does not depend on an express written guarantee.
n.3: The company is not automatically bound; it did not exist when the contract was made.
n.4: The promoter is generally liable, so it is not the case that no one is.

Business Law & Practice.q: A sole trader carries on a business and makes trading profits during the tax year. The trader wants to understand how those business profits are taxed, and whether they are taxed in the same way as a company's profits or as the individual's own income. The court considers the taxation of a sole trader's business profits. The trader ran the business alone and had never incorporated it or taken on any partners. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The sole trader pays only VAT on the profits and no other tax at all.
The sole trader pays income tax (and national insurance) on the trading profits as part of their own income.
The sole trader pays corporation tax on the business profits as if the business were a company on these facts.
The sole trader pays no tax on the business profits, which are treated as tax-free.
The business itself is taxed as a separate legal entity distinct from the trader.
Business Law & Practice.w: A sole trader is not a separate legal or taxable entity. The trading profits form part of the individual's own income and are subject to income tax (and Class 2/Class 4 national insurance contributions) in the trader's hands.

n.0: The trader pays income tax on profits, not merely VAT.
n.2: A sole trader pays income tax, not corporation tax, on business profits.
n.3: The business profits are taxable, not tax-free.
n.4: The business is not a separate taxable entity from the sole trader.

Business Law & Practice.q: The directors of a private company with several directors wish to hold a board meeting to make a decision. They ask what is required for the board to act validly, in particular how many directors must be present and how a tie in voting is resolved, applying the model articles. The company has adopted the unamended model articles for private companies. The board wishes to take a decision at a meeting. The directors are gathering to take an important decision and want to be confident the meeting will be validly constituted, so they need to know how many of them must actually be present and what happens if the vote ends up evenly split between them. Which of the following best describes the position under the model articles?
o: The quorum is all the directors, who must decide unanimously.
The quorum is a majority of all the directors, with no casting vote available on these facts.
There is no quorum requirement for board meetings under the model articles.
The quorum for a board meeting is two directors, and the chair has a casting vote in the event of a tie.
A single director always forms a quorum and there is never a casting vote.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the model articles for private companies, the quorum for a directors' meeting is two (unless otherwise fixed, and subject to the special position of a sole-director company), and the chair of the meeting has a casting vote where votes are equal. This enables the board to act by a majority with a tie-breaker.

n.0: Board decisions are by majority, not unanimity, under the model articles.
n.1: The default quorum is a fixed number (two), not a majority of all directors.
n.2: The model articles do impose a quorum requirement.
n.4: The default quorum is two, and there is a casting vote, contrary to this option.

Business Law & Practice.q: An individual in financial difficulty wishes to avoid the consequences of bankruptcy by reaching a formal, binding arrangement with their creditors to pay part of what is owed over time, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. The debtor is an individual seeking an alternative to bankruptcy. The arrangement would bind creditors once approved. Anxious to keep clear of the stigma and consequences of being made bankrupt, the individual wants instead to put a formal proposal to their creditors to pay off part of what is owed over time under an insolvency practitioner's supervision, in a way that will bind the creditors once the necessary majority approves it. Which of the following best identifies the procedure?
o: A company voluntary arrangement, which is the correct procedure for an individual on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A creditors' voluntary liquidation of the individual.
An administration, placing the individual under an administrator.
An individual voluntary arrangement (IVA), supervised by an insolvency practitioner and binding creditors if approved by the requisite majority.
A bankruptcy order, which is the only option available to an insolvent individual.
Business Law & Practice.w: An individual voluntary arrangement (IVA) allows an insolvent individual to propose a binding arrangement to their creditors, typically to pay part of their debts over a period, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. If approved by at least 75% in value of creditors voting, it binds all unsecured creditors and enables the debtor to avoid bankruptcy.

n.0: A CVA is the company procedure; the individual equivalent is an IVA.
n.1: Creditors' voluntary liquidation applies to companies, not individuals.
n.2: Administration is a corporate procedure, not for individuals.
n.4: Bankruptcy is not the only option; an IVA is an alternative.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company wishes to raise capital by allotting new shares to an outside investor. The directors need to know whether they have authority to allot the shares and whether any shareholder approval is required, given the constitution and the Companies Act 2006. The company has more than one class of shares and the articles do not give the directors general authority to allot. The court considers the requirements for a valid allotment of shares. The company had ordinary and preference shares, and the board had no standing allotment authority. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only the shareholders, and never the directors, may ever allot new shares in the company.
The directors may always allot new shares freely, without any authority or shareholder involvement on these facts.
An allotment of shares requires the prior approval of the company's creditors.
An allotment is valid only if the new investor is an existing member of the company.
The directors need authority to allot, which may require shareholder approval where the articles do not confer it.
Business Law & Practice.w: Directors may only allot shares if authorised to do so — by the articles or by ordinary resolution of the members — except that directors of a private company with only one class of shares may generally allot without further authority unless the articles restrict it. Where such authority is absent, shareholder approval is required.

n.0: Directors can allot where duly authorised; it is not reserved solely to shareholders.
n.1: Directors cannot always allot freely; authority is required.
n.2: Creditor approval is not required for an allotment.
n.3: Shares can be allotted to new investors, not only existing members.

Business Law & Practice.q: A group of professionals wish to carry on business together in a way that gives them the flexibility of a partnership but also protects them from unlimited personal liability for the business's debts. They form a limited liability partnership (LLP) and register it appropriately. A question later arises about the legal status of the LLP and the members' exposure to its debts. The court considers the nature of a limited liability partnership. The members wanted the tax treatment of a partnership but the protection of a corporate body. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An LLP is identical to an ordinary partnership, with full personal liability for the members.
An LLP is a separate legal person, and the members generally have limited liability for its debts.
An LLP is not a separate legal person, and its members are personally liable without limit.
An LLP has limited liability only where every member has invested an equal amount of capital.
An LLP gives limited liability only to those members who take no part in management.
Business Law & Practice.w: A limited liability partnership, formed and registered under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000, is a body corporate with separate legal personality. Its members generally have limited liability for the LLP's debts, combining features of partnerships and companies.

n.0: An LLP is not identical to an ordinary partnership; it confers limited liability.
n.2: An LLP is a separate legal person; members are not generally personally liable without limit.
n.3: Limited liability does not depend on equal capital contributions.
n.4: Limited liability is not confined to non-managing members.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director causes the company to enter into a transaction which is outside the scope of the purposes and powers conferred on the directors by the company's constitution, using their position for a purpose that the constitution does not permit. A shareholder complains that the director has acted in breach of duty. The court considers the director's general duty relating to acting within the company's constitution under the Companies Act 2006. The transaction advanced the director's own agenda rather than any purpose the constitution allowed. Which of the following best describes the duty breached?
o: The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in managing the company (s.174) on these facts.
The duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction with the company (s.177).
The duty not to accept benefits from third parties in connection with the office (s.176).
The duty to avoid situations of conflict of interest with the company (s.175).
The duty to act within powers, that is in accordance with the constitution and for proper purposes (s.171).
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.171 Companies Act 2006, a director must act in accordance with the company's constitution and only exercise powers for the purposes for which they are conferred. Acting outside the constitution or for an improper purpose breaches this duty.

n.0: Section 174 concerns care and skill, not acting within the constitution.
n.1: Section 177 concerns declaring interests in transactions.
n.2: Section 176 concerns benefits from third parties.
n.3: Section 175 concerns conflicts of interest, not constitutional limits.

Business Law & Practice.q: The directors of a private company wish to call a general meeting of the members to consider a proposed ordinary resolution. They ask how much notice must be given to the members for the meeting, applying the default statutory position. The company is a private company and no shorter-notice consent has been obtained. The directors are calling a general meeting. The directors are fixing a date for a general meeting to put an ordinary resolution to the members, no one has agreed to accept the meeting on shorter notice, and they want to be sure they give the members the minimum period the default statutory rules require. Which of the following best describes the minimum notice required?
o: At least 28 clear days' notice for any general meeting.
At least 21 clear days' notice in every case without exception.
No notice is required provided a quorum happens to be present.
At least 14 clear days' notice, unless the members agree to short notice.
At least 7 clear days' notice for all private company meetings.
Business Law & Practice.w: A general meeting of a private company may generally be called on at least 14 clear days' notice. Shorter notice is possible if agreed by a majority in number of the members holding at least the requisite percentage of the shares (90% for a private company, or higher if the articles specify). Public company AGMs require 21 days.

n.0: 28 days is not the statutory minimum for a general meeting.
n.1: 21 days is the requirement for a public company AGM, not the general private-company default.
n.2: Proper notice is required; a chance quorum does not dispense with it.
n.4: 7 days is not the default minimum notice.

Business Law & Practice.q: Shortly before its insolvent liquidation, a company made a payment to one particular unsecured creditor which had the effect of putting that creditor in a better position, in the insolvency, than they would otherwise have been, and the company was influenced by a desire to produce that effect. The liquidator wishes to challenge the payment. The court considers the power to set aside a preference under the Insolvency Act 1986. The favoured creditor was a company connected to one of the directors of the failing business. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The liquidator may challenge the payment only if it was made after the winding up order.
A preference can be challenged only where it was made to a secured rather than unsecured creditor on these facts as a general rule.
Any payment to a creditor before liquidation is automatically valid and cannot be challenged.
The liquidator may challenge the payment as a preference where the company was influenced by a desire to prefer the creditor.
The liquidator may challenge the payment only if the creditor knew the company was insolvent.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.239 Insolvency Act 1986, a liquidator or administrator may apply to set aside a preference — where, within the relevant time before insolvency, the company did something that put a creditor in a better position on insolvency and was influenced by a desire to produce that effect (desire being presumed for connected persons).

n.0: The relevant conduct occurs before, not after, the winding up order.
n.1: Preferences can be challenged whether the creditor was secured or unsecured.
n.2: Pre-liquidation payments are not automatically immune from challenge.
n.4: The test focuses on the company's desire to prefer, not the creditor's knowledge.

Business Law & Practice.q: The members of a solvent company decide voluntarily to bring the company to an end and wind it up, and the directors are able to make a statutory declaration of solvency. In a different scenario, an insolvent company is wound up voluntarily with the creditors taking control of the process. A businessperson wants to understand the difference between the two kinds of voluntary liquidation. The court considers members' and creditors' voluntary liquidation under the Insolvency Act 1986. In one case the directors could confirm the company could pay its debts in full within twelve months. Which of the following best describes the distinction?
o: A members' voluntary liquidation is for a solvent company with a declaration of solvency; a creditors' voluntary liquidation is for an insolvent one.
There is no difference; both types are used only for insolvent companies.
A members' voluntary liquidation is used only for insolvent companies with no assets on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Both types can only ever be commenced by a petition presented by a creditor.
A creditors' voluntary liquidation requires an order of the court in every case.
Business Law & Practice.w: A members' voluntary liquidation is available where the company is solvent and the directors make a statutory declaration of solvency; a creditors' voluntary liquidation applies where the company is insolvent, so the creditors have the principal say in the conduct of the liquidation.

n.1: There is a clear difference based on solvency.
n.2: A members' voluntary liquidation is for solvent, not insolvent, companies.
n.3: Voluntary liquidations are commenced by resolution, not a creditor's petition.
n.4: A creditors' voluntary liquidation does not require a court order (unlike compulsory winding up).

Business Law & Practice.q: A partner retires from a general partnership which continues in business with the remaining partners. After the retirement, the firm incurs new debts to an existing supplier who had dealt with the firm before, and who was never told that the partner had left. The supplier seeks to hold the retired partner liable for the new debts. The retired partner argues they are no longer a partner and so cannot be liable. The court considers the position of a retired partner under the Partnership Act 1890. The contract was an everyday purchase of the sort the firm routinely made in its line of work. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The retired partner remains liable for all the firm's future debts forever, whatever notice is given on these facts.
The retired partner may remain liable to existing customers for new debts unless proper notice of retirement was given.
The retired partner is liable only for debts that existed at the exact date of retirement.
The retired partner is liable only if their name still appeared on the firm's bank account.
The retired partner is automatically free of all liability the moment they retire from the firm.
Business Law & Practice.w: A retiring partner remains liable to existing customers of the firm for debts incurred after retirement unless those customers are given actual notice of the retirement (and notice to the wider world requires publication, e.g. in the London Gazette) (s.36 Partnership Act 1890).

n.0: Proper notice can bring liability for future debts to an end, so it is not forever.
n.2: Liability can extend to post-retirement debts to existing customers absent notice, not only pre-existing debts.
n.3: Liability turns on notice to customers, not on the bank account details.
n.4: Retirement does not automatically end liability to those who dealt with the firm without notice.

Business Law & Practice.q: Creditors of an insolvent company seek to hold its individual shareholders personally liable for the company's debts by asking the court to disregard the company's separate legal personality — to 'pierce the corporate veil'. There is no suggestion of fraud or of the company being used as a mere facade to evade an existing legal obligation. The creditors simply argue it would be fair. The court considers when the corporate veil may be pierced. The company had been properly run and was simply the victim of a downturn in its market. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The corporate veil is pierced only rarely and in exceptional cases, not merely because it would be fair.
The corporate veil is pierced whenever a company is unable to pay its debts.
The corporate veil can never be pierced in any circumstances whatsoever.
The corporate veil is pierced whenever the court considers it would be fair to do so.
The corporate veil is pierced automatically where the company has only one shareholder on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: The separate personality established in Salomon is strongly protected. The courts will pierce the corporate veil only in very limited and exceptional circumstances (for example where the company is used as a mere facade to evade an existing obligation), and not simply because it would appear fair (Prest v Petrodel; VTB Capital).

n.1: Insolvency alone is not a ground for piercing the veil.
n.2: The veil can be pierced in rare cases, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: General fairness is not enough to pierce the veil.
n.4: A single shareholder does not lead to automatic piercing (Salomon itself involved concentrated ownership).

Business Law & Practice.q: A company proposes to enter into a service contract with one of its directors under which the director's employment is guaranteed for a fixed term of five years, during which the company cannot terminate it early for convenience. The board is unsure what internal approval, if any, is needed. The guaranteed term exceeds two years and the company is entering it with a director. The company seeks to comply with the Companies Act 2006. The company wants to reassure a key director by locking in employment for a fixed five-year term that it cannot cut short at will, and the board is now checking whether committing to a guaranteed period of that length is something it can agree on its own or whether the members must be involved. Which of the following best describes the approval required?
o: The service contract requires approval by special resolution of 75% of members.
The service contract is automatically void if it exceeds one year.
The service contract requires the prior consent of the Registrar of Companies.
The provision guaranteeing employment for more than two years must be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members.
No member approval is needed; the board alone may agree any length of service contract on these facts as a general rule.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.188 of the Companies Act 2006, a term of a director's service contract guaranteeing employment for a period longer than two years (a 'long-term service contract') must be approved by resolution of the members (an ordinary resolution). Without approval, the offending guaranteed-term provision is void and the contract is terminable on reasonable notice.

n.0: The required approval is an ordinary resolution, not a special resolution.
n.1: The contract is not automatically void for exceeding one year; the trigger is a guaranteed term over two years.
n.2: The Registrar's consent is not required.
n.4: Member approval is required; the board alone cannot bind the company to such a term.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director of a company, who is held out by the company as having authority to make contracts of a particular kind, enters into such a contract with a third party. In fact the board had not actually authorised this particular contract, but the third party did not know that and reasonably relied on the director's apparent authority. The company now denies it is bound. The court considers whether the company is bound by the acts of a person with ostensible (apparent) authority. The third party had dealt with the company through this director on several previous occasions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company is never bound by a director acting without actual authority in any circumstances.
The company is never bound unless the board expressly authorised the specific contract in advance on these facts.
The company is bound where it held the director out as having authority and the third party reasonably relied on it.
The company is bound only if the third party inspected the company's internal board minutes.
The company is bound only where the contract turned out to be beneficial to the company.
Business Law & Practice.w: A company may be bound by the acts of an agent with ostensible (apparent) authority: where the company, by its conduct, represents that the person has authority, and a third party reasonably relies on that representation, the company is bound even without actual authority (Freeman & Lockyer; and statutory protections also assist third parties).

n.0: A company can be bound by ostensible authority despite the absence of actual authority.
n.1: Express prior authorisation is not always required; ostensible authority can bind the company.
n.3: A third party is not required to inspect internal board minutes.
n.4: The company is bound regardless of whether the contract benefited it.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director takes decisions carelessly, without the degree of competence and diligence to be expected, causing loss to the company. The director has no particular expertise, but the question is what standard of skill and care the law requires of them. A shareholder alleges the director fell below the required standard. The court considers the standard of care applicable to a director under the Companies Act 2006. The director had relevant experience which made their careless handling of the matter harder to excuse. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The care and skill expected only of executive directors, and never of non-executive directors.
The care, skill and diligence of a reasonably diligent person, taking account of the director's actual knowledge and skill.
The care and skill of the most expert professional director available in the market.
The care and skill only of the particular director, judged purely by their own subjective abilities on these facts.
No standard of care at all, provided the director acted honestly and in good faith.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.174 Companies Act 2006, a director must exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence. The standard has an objective element (the reasonably diligent person carrying out the director's functions) and a subjective element (the general knowledge, skill and experience the particular director actually has), whichever is higher.

n.0: The duty applies to all directors, including non-executives.
n.2: It is not the standard of the most expert director available.
n.3: The standard is not purely subjective; there is an objective minimum.
n.4: Honesty and good faith do not remove the duty of care.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director continued to trade a company and incur further debts at a time when they knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid going into insolvent liquidation, and did not take every step to minimise loss to creditors. The company is now in insolvent liquidation with increased debts. The director carried on trading past the point of no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. The liquidator seeks a contribution. Well after it had become clear there was no realistic way of pulling the company back from insolvent liquidation, the director kept the business going and ran up yet more debts rather than stopping to protect creditors, and the liquidator, facing a bigger deficit, wants to make the director answer for it. Which of the following best describes the director's potential liability?
o: The director may be liable only if they personally guaranteed the company's debts.
The director may be liable only if the members pass a resolution to that effect.
The director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading.
The director is automatically criminally liable for fraud without further proof.
The director has no personal liability because the company is a separate legal person.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.214 of the Insolvency Act 1986, a director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading where, before insolvent liquidation, they knew or ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding it and failed to take every step to minimise loss to creditors. Liability is civil and does not require dishonesty.

n.0: Liability does not depend on a personal guarantee.
n.1: A members' resolution is not needed for the liquidator to pursue wrongful trading.
n.3: Wrongful trading is a civil liability; it does not require proof of fraud (that is fraudulent trading).
n.4: Separate legal personality does not shield a director from a wrongful trading contribution order.

Business Law & Practice.q: A trading company makes taxable profits in an accounting period. Its finance director is explaining to the board how the company itself is taxed on those profits, as distinct from how a partnership or sole trader would be taxed. The business operates through a company limited by shares. The board wishes to understand the company's own tax position. The board is comparing how their chosen structure is taxed against the alternatives, and the finance director is setting out how the company as a separate entity is charged on the profits it makes, as distinct from the way a partnership or a sole trader would be taxed on the same earnings. Which of the following best describes how the company's profits are taxed?
o: The company pays only value added tax on its profits.
The company's profits are taxed only in the hands of the shareholders as income tax.
The company pays income tax and national insurance like a sole trader.
The company is tax transparent, so each shareholder is taxed on a share of profits as they arise.
The company pays corporation tax on its taxable total profits, including income and chargeable gains.
Business Law & Practice.w: A company is a separate taxable person and pays corporation tax on its taxable total profits for the accounting period, which include its income profits and its chargeable gains. Shareholders are then separately taxed on distributions they receive. This differs from a partnership, which is tax transparent, and a sole trader, who pays income tax.

n.0: VAT is a tax on supplies, not a tax on the company's profits.
n.1: The company itself is taxed on its profits; they are not taxed only in shareholders' hands.
n.2: A company pays corporation tax, not income tax and NICs like a sole trader.
n.3: A company is not tax transparent; a partnership is.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company has been registered and the Registrar of Companies has issued a certificate of incorporation. Some months later, a person challenges the company's existence, alleging that a technical defect in the registration documents means the company was never properly formed. The certificate of incorporation has been duly issued by the Registrar. The challenge is to the validity of the company's formation. The company has been trading for some months on the strength of its certificate when a disgruntled counterparty, looking for a way out of a deal, claims that a paperwork slip at the registration stage means the company was never validly formed in the first place. Which of the following best describes the effect of the certificate of incorporation?
o: The certificate is only provisional and may be set aside for any documentary defect.
The certificate binds only the company, not third parties dealing with it.
The certificate proves the company exists only until its first annual return is filed.
The certificate has no legal effect and the company's existence must be separately proved on these facts as a general rule.
The certificate is conclusive evidence that the requirements of registration have been complied with and the company exists.
Business Law & Practice.w: The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the requirements of the Companies Act 2006 as to registration have been complied with and that the company is duly registered. Once issued, the company's existence cannot be attacked on the basis of alleged defects in the registration process.

n.0: The certificate is conclusive, not merely provisional or liable to be set aside for defects.
n.1: Its conclusive effect is not confined to the company; it establishes the company's existence generally.
n.2: Its conclusive effect is not limited to the period before the first annual return.
n.3: The certificate has decisive legal effect; separate proof of existence is not needed.

Business Law & Practice.q: Two people begin working together running a business, sharing the profits between them and making joint decisions, without ever signing any formal partnership agreement or forming any company. A dispute later arises about whether they are in partnership at all, which matters because it affects their legal relationship and liabilities. One of them denies that any partnership exists because nothing was written down. The court considers the definition of partnership under the Partnership Act 1890. The two had run the business together for over a year, splitting the profits as they went along. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A partnership exists where persons carry on a business in common with a view of profit, whether or not there is a written agreement.
A partnership exists only where the parties expressly called themselves partners.
No partnership can exist unless it has been formally registered with Companies House.
A partnership exists only where the business has made an actual profit in its first year on these facts as a general rule.
No partnership can exist unless the parties have signed a written partnership agreement.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.1 Partnership Act 1890, partnership is the relation which subsists between persons carrying on a business in common with a view of profit. It arises from the substance of the relationship and does not require any written agreement or registration.

n.1: The label the parties use is not decisive; the substance governs.
n.2: Ordinary partnerships are not registered at Companies House.
n.3: Only a view of profit is needed, not that a profit was actually made.
n.4: A written agreement is not required for a partnership to exist.

Business Law & Practice.q: The directors of a private company wish to call a general meeting of the shareholders to consider some ordinary business. They need to give the shareholders proper notice of the meeting, and want to know the minimum period of notice required by the Companies Act 2006 for a general meeting of a private company (in the absence of anything longer in the articles). The court considers the statutory minimum notice period for a general meeting. The articles said nothing about notice periods, so the statutory default had to be relied upon. Which of the following best describes it?
o: No notice at all is required, provided the meeting is held at the registered office on these facts.
A general meeting of a private company requires at least 28 clear days' notice.
A general meeting requires at least three months' notice to all the members.
A general meeting may be called on just 24 hours' notice in every case.
A general meeting of a private company must generally be called on at least 14 clear days' notice.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, the minimum notice for a general meeting of a private company is 14 clear days (subject to any longer period in the articles), though a meeting may be held on shorter notice if the requisite majority of members agree.

n.0: Notice is required; holding it at the registered office does not dispense with it.
n.1: 14 clear days, not 28, is the statutory minimum for a general meeting.
n.2: Three months is far longer than the statutory minimum.
n.3: 24 hours is not the statutory minimum for a general meeting.

Business Law & Practice.q: Shortly before going into insolvent liquidation, a company paid one particular unsecured creditor in full, putting that creditor in a better position than it would have been in the liquidation, and did so influenced by a desire to prefer that creditor. The creditor was a connected person. The payment was made within the relevant period and the company wished to improve that creditor's position. The liquidator seeks to challenge the payment. In the run-up to insolvency the company singled out one creditor, connected to it, and paid that creditor off in full while others went unpaid, apparently wanting to put that creditor ahead of the rest, and the liquidator is examining whether the payment can now be reversed. Which of the following best describes the basis of challenge?
o: The liquidator cannot challenge payments made to genuine creditors in any circumstances.
The liquidator may challenge it as a preference, the relevant period being two years for a connected person.
The liquidator may challenge it as a preference, but only if made within one month of insolvency.
The liquidator may challenge it only as a transaction at an undervalue.
The liquidator may challenge it only if the creditor knew the company was insolvent.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.239 of the Insolvency Act 1986, a preference arises where a company, influenced by a desire to prefer, puts a creditor in a better position on insolvency than they would otherwise have been. The relevant look-back period is six months, extended to two years where the creditor is a connected person, and a desire to prefer is presumed for connected persons.

n.0: Preferential payments can be challenged; genuine creditors are not immune where a preference is shown.
n.2: The connected-person period is two years, not one month.
n.3: This is a preference, distinct from a transaction at an undervalue.
n.4: The creditor's knowledge of insolvency is not the test; the company's desire to prefer is.

Business Law & Practice.q: A member of a company wishes to enforce a provision in the company's articles of association, arguing that the articles create binding legal obligations between the member and the company (and between members). Another member disputes that the articles have contractual effect at all. The provision in question concerns membership rights. The court considers the legal effect of a company's articles of association under the Companies Act 2006. The provision the member relied on concerned their rights as a shareholder in the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The articles bind the directors personally but never the members of the company.
The articles are enforceable only by the company, and never by an individual member.
The articles bind only those members who were shareholders when the company was first formed on these facts.
The articles are merely internal guidance with no binding legal effect on anyone.
The articles form a statutory contract between the company and its members, and between the members themselves.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.33 Companies Act 2006, the provisions of a company's constitution bind the company and its members to the same extent as if there were covenants on the part of the company and each member to observe them. The articles thus take effect as a statutory contract, enforceable in respect of membership rights.

n.0: The statutory contract binds the members, not only the directors.
n.1: Members can enforce membership rights under the articles, not only the company.
n.2: The contract binds current members, not only original ones.
n.3: The articles are not mere guidance; they have binding contractual effect.

Business Law & Practice.q: A person forms a private limited company to run their business, becoming its sole shareholder and director, and the company is duly incorporated. The business later fails owing money to creditors, who wish to pursue the shareholder personally for the company's debts, arguing that in reality the company and the individual are one and the same. The shareholder relies on the company's separate legal personality. The court considers the effect of incorporation on liability. The individual had run the same business as a sole trader before deciding to incorporate it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The shareholder is liable without limit because they are the only shareholder and director.
The company is a separate legal person, so the shareholder is generally not liable for its debts.
The company has no separate personality until it has traded for at least one full year.
The company's separate personality is ignored whenever the company cannot pay its debts.
The shareholder is always personally liable for the company's debts as its controller.
Business Law & Practice.w: On incorporation a company becomes a separate legal person distinct from its members (Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd). The shareholders' liability is generally limited to any amount unpaid on their shares, and they are not personally liable for the company's debts, even where one person owns and runs it.

n.0: Being sole shareholder/director does not create unlimited personal liability.
n.2: Separate personality arises on incorporation, not after a year's trading.
n.3: Separate personality is not disregarded simply because the company is insolvent.
n.4: A controlling shareholder is not, for that reason, personally liable for company debts.

Business Law & Practice.q: A general partnership incurs a substantial debt to a supplier in the ordinary course of its business. The partnership assets are insufficient to pay the debt in full, and the supplier wishes to recover the balance. The partners argue about the extent to which each of them is responsible for the firm's debts. The supplier seeks advice on the liability of the individual partners for the debts of the firm under the Partnership Act 1890. The debt had been run up buying stock for the firm in the ordinary course of its trading. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The partners have no personal liability, because the firm is a separate legal person.
The partners are liable only up to the amount of capital they each contributed to the firm.
Each partner is liable only for the share of the debt equal to their share of the profits.
Only the partner who incurred the particular debt is liable to the creditor for it.
The partners are jointly liable for the debts of the firm, and personally so without limit.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, partners are jointly liable for the debts and obligations of the firm incurred while they are partners, and that liability is personal and unlimited, so a creditor may pursue the partners' personal assets.

n.0: An ordinary partnership is not a separate legal person; partners are personally liable.
n.1: Liability is not capped at capital contributed.
n.2: Liability is not limited to each partner's profit share.
n.3: Liability is not confined to the partner who incurred the debt; partners are jointly liable.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company proposes to allot new ordinary shares for cash to a new outside investor. Existing shareholders complain that they were not first offered the chance to take up the new shares in proportion to their existing holdings, which would preserve their percentage stakes. The company had not passed any resolution to disapply the relevant rights. The court considers pre-emption rights on the allotment of shares under the Companies Act 2006. The new shares were being issued for cash, and the existing members held their shares in fixed proportions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Existing shareholders generally have statutory pre-emption rights and must be offered the new shares first, unless disapplied.
Pre-emption rights apply only to public companies and never to private companies.
Pre-emption rights apply only where the new shares are being issued for non-cash consideration.
Existing shareholders never have any right to be offered new shares before outsiders.
The directors may always ignore pre-emption rights whenever they consider it commercially sensible on these facts as a general rule.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.561 Companies Act 2006, where equity shares are allotted for cash, they must first be offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings (statutory pre-emption rights), unless those rights are excluded by the articles or disapplied by special resolution.

n.1: Pre-emption rights apply to private as well as public companies.
n.2: Statutory pre-emption applies to allotments for cash, not non-cash consideration.
n.3: Existing shareholders do generally have pre-emption rights.
n.4: Directors cannot simply ignore pre-emption rights; they must be disapplied or excluded.

Business Law & Practice.q: Two people run a business together and hold certain assets that are used in the business. A dispute arises as to whether particular assets are partnership property (belonging to the firm) or the personal property of one of the partners, which matters for how they are dealt with on dissolution. The assets were bought with the firm's money and used exclusively for the firm's business. The court considers what counts as partnership property under the Partnership Act 1890. The assets in question were vehicles bought entirely out of the firm's own bank account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All property used by the business automatically belongs personally to the senior partner on these facts.
Property bought with the firm's money belongs to whichever partner physically holds it.
There is no such thing as partnership property; all assets are always owned personally.
Property bought with the firm's money for the firm's purposes is presumed to be partnership property.
Property is partnership property only if the partnership agreement lists it by name.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, property bought with money belonging to the firm is presumed, unless a contrary intention appears, to have been bought on account of the firm and is partnership property. Such property must be held and applied by the partners exclusively for the purposes of the partnership.

n.0: Firm assets do not automatically belong to a senior partner personally.
n.1: Physical possession does not determine ownership of firm-bought assets.
n.2: Partnership property does exist as a distinct category.
n.4: Property need not be individually listed to be partnership property.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company has granted a floating charge over its assets to a lender. While the company continues to trade normally, it deals freely with the assets within the class covered by the charge. On the company's default and the occurrence of a specified event, the floating charge is said to 'crystallise'. The lender wishes to understand the effect of crystallisation on the charge. The court considers the crystallisation of a floating charge. The company had defaulted on the loan and had then ceased trading altogether soon afterwards. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Crystallisation releases the assets entirely, leaving the lender with no security over them.
Crystallisation converts the floating charge into an unsecured personal claim against the directors.
Crystallisation transfers ownership of the charged assets outright to the lender at once.
On crystallisation the floating charge attaches to the assets then within the class, becoming in effect a fixed charge over them.
Crystallisation has no effect, because a floating charge always operates as a fixed charge from the outset on these facts.
Business Law & Practice.w: A floating charge crystallises on the occurrence of certain events (such as the company's liquidation, appointment of a receiver, cessation of business, or a specified crystallising event). On crystallisation it ceases to float and attaches to the assets then within the charged class, taking effect much like a fixed charge over them.

n.0: Crystallisation fixes the charge on the assets; it does not release them.
n.1: Crystallisation strengthens the security over the assets; it is not a mere personal claim against directors.
n.2: Crystallisation does not transfer outright ownership to the lender.
n.4: A floating charge does not operate as a fixed charge from the outset; crystallisation changes its nature.

Business Law & Practice.q: A director has breached a duty to the company, but the breach is one the company is willing to overlook. The company proposes to ratify the director's conduct by resolution of the members, and a question arises about whose votes may count. The director in question is also a member and controls a substantial shareholding. The company proposes to ratify the breach. The board would rather draw a line under the director's breach than pursue it, and proposes to have the members approve what happened, but the director concerned also holds a large block of shares, which raises the question of whose votes may properly be counted in any such approval. Which of the following best describes the requirement for a valid ratification?
o: Ratification requires the unanimous consent of every member including the director on these facts as a general rule.
A breach of duty by a director can never be ratified by the members.
Ratification requires a special resolution with the director's votes fully counted.
Ratification is by ordinary resolution, but the votes of the director (and connected members) are disregarded.
Ratification may be effected by the board of directors alone.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.239 of the Companies Act 2006, a director's conduct amounting to a breach of duty may be ratified by ordinary resolution of the members, but the votes of the director (if a member) and any member connected with them are disregarded in determining whether the resolution is passed. This prevents the wrongdoer approving their own breach.

n.0: Ratification does not require unanimity; an ordinary resolution (excluding the wrongdoer's votes) suffices.
n.1: Many breaches of duty can be ratified by the members, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: An ordinary resolution suffices, and crucially the director's votes are not counted.
n.4: The board alone cannot ratify a breach of duty owed to the company.

Business Law & Practice.q: Shortly before going into insolvent liquidation, a company transferred a valuable asset to a connected person for far less than it was worth, depleting the assets available to creditors. The liquidator wishes to challenge the transaction and have the position restored for the benefit of the creditors. The court considers the power to set aside a transaction at an undervalue under the Insolvency Act 1986. The asset was transferred to the director's spouse for a fraction of its true market value. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The liquidator may apply to have a transaction at an undervalue set aside where it occurred within the relevant time before insolvency.
The transaction may be challenged only where the company received more than the asset was worth.
The liquidator may challenge the transaction only if it was made after the liquidation had already begun on these facts as a general rule.
Such transactions can never be challenged once they have been completed and the asset transferred.
Only the recipient of the asset may apply to have the transaction reviewed by the court.
Business Law & Practice.w: Under s.238 Insolvency Act 1986, where a company has entered a transaction at an undervalue within the relevant time before the onset of insolvency, the liquidator or administrator may apply to the court for an order restoring the position to what it would have been (subject to a defence of good faith and benefit to the company).

n.1: The provision targets undervalue transfers, where the company received less, not more.
n.2: The relevant transactions occur before the insolvency, not after liquidation begins.
n.3: Completed transactions at an undervalue can be challenged within the relevant time.
n.4: It is the liquidator/administrator, not the recipient, who applies.

Business Law & Practice.q: A company is in serious financial difficulty but has an underlying viable business, and its directors want to try to rescue it as a going concern, or at least achieve a better result for creditors than an immediate winding up, while obtaining protection from creditor action in the meantime. They are advised to consider a particular insolvency procedure. The court considers the procedure of administration under the Insolvency Act 1986. The business had valuable contracts and a viable core, but was crippled by short-term cash pressures. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Administration can only ever be used by companies that are completely solvent.
Administration hands control of the company back to its directors free of any oversight.
Administration aims to rescue the company or achieve a better result for creditors, with a moratorium protecting it from creditor action.
Administration is simply an immediate liquidation of the company with no attempt to rescue it on these facts as a general rule.
Administration is a procedure available only after the company has already been dissolved.
Business Law & Practice.w: Administration is a rescue and reorganisation procedure under the Insolvency Act 1986. An administrator is appointed to try to rescue the company as a going concern, or achieve a better result for creditors than winding up, or realise property for secured/preferential creditors, and a statutory moratorium protects the company from most creditor action during the process.

n.0: Administration is for companies in financial difficulty, not solvent ones.
n.1: An administrator, not the directors, takes control during administration.
n.3: Administration is not simply immediate liquidation; it aims at rescue.
n.4: Administration is not used after dissolution; the company still exists.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant makes a Part 36 offer to settle a money claim, which the claimant rejects. At trial the claimant succeeds but is awarded a sum that fails to beat the defendant's Part 36 offer. The offer had been made well before trial and remained open. The claimant did not obtain a judgment more advantageous than the defendant's Part 36 offer. The defendant had put a realistic settlement figure on the table months before trial, the claimant pressed on regardless, and although the claimant did win, the sum the judge awarded came out below what the defendant had already offered to pay to end the case. Which of the following best describes the usual costs consequence?
o: The claimant recovers all of its costs as the successful party, regardless of the offer on these facts.
The claimant is usually ordered to pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, with interest.
Each party simply bears its own costs because the claimant won at trial.
The defendant must pay the claimant's costs throughout, the offer being irrelevant.
The claim is dismissed because the claimant failed to beat the offer.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a claimant fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than a defendant's Part 36 offer, the usual order is that the claimant pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period (the date by which the offer could have been accepted), plus interest on those costs, even though the claimant technically won. This encourages reasonable settlement.

n.0: The claimant does not simply recover all its costs; the Part 36 offer shifts costs from the relevant period.
n.2: Costs do not simply lie where they fall; the Part 36 consequences apply.
n.3: The defendant does not pay the claimant's costs throughout where its offer was not beaten.
n.4: Failing to beat the offer affects costs, not the validity of the winning claim itself.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant is concerned that, if it successfully defends the claim, the claimant (which appears to have few assets and may be based outside the jurisdiction) will be unable to pay the defendant's costs. The defendant wishes to apply for an order requiring the claimant to provide security for the defendant's costs. The court considers the availability of security for costs under the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant appeared to have very little by way of assets within the jurisdiction to meet costs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Security for costs is ordered automatically against every claimant who brings a claim.
Security for costs may be ordered only where the claim is worth more than £1 million.
Security for costs may be ordered only against a defendant, never against a claimant.
Security for costs can never be ordered against a claimant in any circumstances at all on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may order the claimant to give security for costs where a statutory condition, such as being resident abroad, is satisfied and it is just.
Dispute Resolution.w: The court may order a claimant to provide security for the defendant's costs where one of the conditions in CPR 25.13 is met (for example the claimant is resident out of the jurisdiction in a non-enforcement country, or is a company that may be unable to pay costs) and it is just to make the order having regard to all the circumstances.

n.0: It is not ordered automatically against every claimant; conditions and justice apply.
n.1: There is no such value threshold for security for costs.
n.2: Security for costs is generally sought against the claimant, not the defendant.
n.3: Security for costs can be ordered where the conditions are met.

Dispute Resolution.q: Before issuing proceedings for a commercial debt, a prospective claimant ignores the relevant pre-action protocol and the general Practice Direction on pre-action conduct, issuing a claim without sending a proper letter of claim or attempting to narrow the issues. The claim later succeeds, but the defendant complains about the claimant's conduct before proceedings. The claimant failed to comply with pre-action requirements though ultimately winning. The prospective claimant was in a hurry and simply issued the claim, skipping the letter of claim and the exchange of information the protocol contemplates, and although the debt was clearly owed and the claim ultimately succeeded, the defendant is now drawing the court's attention to how the matter was handled before proceedings began. Which of the following best describes the likely consequence of the pre-action non-compliance?
o: The claim must be struck out automatically for failure to follow the protocol.
The court may impose costs or other sanctions to reflect the failure to comply with pre-action requirements.
There are no consequences, as pre-action conduct is entirely voluntary.
The defendant is barred from defending the claim because it did not object earlier on these facts.
The claimant automatically loses the right to recover any interest on the debt.
Dispute Resolution.w: Compliance with pre-action protocols and the Practice Direction on pre-action conduct is expected. Where a party fails to comply, the court may impose sanctions, particularly in costs (for example, depriving a successful party of some costs or interest, or ordering it to pay costs), even though the failure does not automatically defeat the claim.

n.0: Non-compliance does not automatically result in the claim being struck out.
n.2: Pre-action conduct is expected, not purely voluntary; non-compliance has consequences.
n.3: The defendant is not barred from defending for failing to object to the claimant's pre-action conduct.
n.4: Loss of interest is a possible sanction, not an automatic and inevitable one.

Dispute Resolution.q: A judgment creditor has a money judgment that remains unpaid. The creditor learns that the debtor holds a substantial credit balance in a bank account, that is, the bank owes money to the debtor. The creditor wishes to intercept that money to satisfy the judgment. A third party (the bank) owes money to the judgment debtor. The creditor wishes to have that money paid to it instead. The creditor has discovered that, while the debtor pleads poverty, the debtor is in fact holding a healthy credit balance at its bank, so that the bank effectively owes the debtor money, and the creditor wants that money diverted to itself before the debtor can move or spend it. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate enforcement method?
o: A third party debt order requiring the bank to pay the debt to the creditor.
An order for the debtor's committal to prison for non-payment on these facts.
A charging order over the debtor's land.
A writ of control against the debtor's goods.
An attachment of earnings order against the debtor's salary.
Dispute Resolution.w: A third party debt order (formerly garnishee order) requires a third party who owes money to the judgment debtor, such as the debtor's bank holding a credit balance, to pay that money directly to the judgment creditor to satisfy the judgment. An interim order is made first, followed by a final order after a hearing.
