n.1: Committal is not the route for enforcing an ordinary money judgment of this kind.
n.2: A charging order secures against land, not a bank debt.
n.3: A writ of control enforces against goods, not money held by a third party.
n.4: Attachment of earnings targets wages from an employer, not a bank balance.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party wishes to withhold from inspection documents such as communications with third parties and internal materials which were created when litigation was in reasonable contemplation and for the dominant purpose of that litigation — for example, an investigator's report obtained to defend an anticipated claim. The other party demands disclosure of them. The court considers litigation privilege in civil proceedings. The report had been commissioned specifically to help defend the claim that was plainly on its way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All documents connected with the dispute must always be disclosed to the other side.
Confidential documents created for the dominant purpose of litigation reasonably in contemplation are protected by litigation privilege.
Litigation privilege protects only communications directly between the lawyer and the client.
Documents created before proceedings are issued can never be privileged in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
Litigation privilege applies only to documents created after the trial has begun.
Dispute Resolution.w: Litigation privilege protects confidential communications between a party (or their lawyer) and third parties, and documents, created when litigation was in reasonable contemplation or on foot, for the dominant purpose of that litigation. Such documents may be withheld from inspection.

n.0: Not all documents connected with the dispute must be disclosed; privilege protects some.
n.2: Litigation privilege extends to third-party communications, not only lawyer-client ones.
n.3: Documents can be privileged before proceedings are issued if litigation was in reasonable contemplation.
n.4: Litigation privilege can attach to documents created before, not only after, trial begins.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party serves a document (not the claim form) on the other party by first-class post. A dispute arises about the date on which the document is treated as served, for the purpose of calculating subsequent time limits. The document was sent by first-class post to the correct address. The court applies the deemed service rules for documents other than the claim form. A time limit for the next step runs from service of the document, the parties disagree about when that clock started, and since the document was an ordinary one sent by first-class post rather than the claim form, the court must apply the deemed-service rules to fix the operative date. Which of the following best describes the deemed date of service?
o: Seven days after the document was posted in every case.
The day on which the document was actually posted.
The day the recipient actually reads the document, whenever that is.
The second business day after the document was posted.
The next calendar day after posting, including weekends.
Dispute Resolution.w: For documents other than the claim form served by first-class post (or another next-business-day service method), the deemed date of service is the second day after it was posted, provided that day is a business day, or if not, the next business day. This deemed date governs the calculation of subsequent procedural time limits.

n.0: The rule is the second business day, not a fixed seven days.
n.1: Service is not deemed on the day of posting for such documents.
n.2: Deemed service does not turn on when the recipient actually reads it.
n.4: The deemed date is the second business day, not simply the next calendar day.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant makes a Part 36 offer, and the claimant decides to accept it within the relevant period specified in the offer. The parties then dispute who bears the costs incurred up to the date of acceptance. The offer was accepted within the relevant period. The claimant accepted a defendant's Part 36 offer in time. Weighing up the risks of trial, the claimant decided to take the settlement the defendant had proposed, communicating acceptance while the offer was still within the period stated in it, and the parties are now sorting out who should bear the costs run up to that point. Which of the following best describes the usual costs position on acceptance within the relevant period?
o: The claimant must pay the defendant's costs as the price of accepting the offer on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant is usually liable to pay the claimant's costs up to the date on which the offer was accepted.
Costs are always reserved to be decided at a later trial.
No costs are payable at all where a Part 36 offer is accepted.
Each party bears its own costs on acceptance of a Part 36 offer.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a Part 36 offer is accepted within the relevant period, the claimant is generally entitled to its costs up to the date of acceptance (the defendant pays the claimant's costs to that point). Different consequences follow if a defendant's offer is accepted after the relevant period, when the claimant may have to pay the defendant's later costs.

n.0: The claimant does not pay the defendant's costs for accepting within the relevant period.
n.2: Costs are dealt with on acceptance under Part 36, not reserved to trial.
n.3: Costs are payable (by the defendant to the claimant) on such an acceptance.
n.4: Costs do not simply lie where they fall; the claimant is generally entitled to costs to acceptance.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant obtains a High Court money judgment for a substantial sum, which the defendant does not pay for a considerable period. The claimant wishes to recover interest for the period during which the judgment remained unpaid, in addition to the judgment sum itself. The judgment debt has remained outstanding since it was entered. The claimant seeks interest on the unpaid judgment debt. The defendant has left the substantial judgment sum unpaid for a long time, and the claimant, conscious that the money has been kept from it throughout that period, wants to recover interest for the delay in addition to the principal amount the court originally ordered. Which of the following best describes the position on interest on the judgment debt?
o: Interest accrues at whatever rate the claimant chooses to charge.
Interest accrues only from the date enforcement proceedings are commenced on these facts.
Interest accrues only if the original contract provided for it.
Interest generally runs on the outstanding judgment debt at the statutory rate until it is paid.
No interest can ever accrue on a judgment debt after judgment is entered.
Dispute Resolution.w: A money judgment debt generally carries interest at the statutory rate (currently 8% under the Judgments Act 1838 for High Court judgments, with similar provision for qualifying County Court judgments) from the date of judgment until payment. This is distinct from any interest awarded on the substantive claim up to judgment.

n.0: The rate is the statutory rate, not one the claimant chooses.
n.1: Interest runs from the date of judgment, not only from commencement of enforcement.
n.2: Statutory judgment interest does not depend on the original contract providing for interest.
n.4: Interest does continue to accrue on an unpaid judgment debt after judgment.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant has obtained a money judgment against a defendant who has not paid. The defendant owns valuable business equipment and stock at its premises. The claimant wishes to enforce by having an enforcement officer attend, take control of the defendant's goods, and sell them to satisfy the judgment. The judgment debtor has tangible goods of value at its premises. The claimant wishes to realise those goods to satisfy the debt. The judgment has gone unpaid for weeks, the debtor plainly has valuable equipment and stock sitting at its trading premises, and the creditor wants an enforcement officer physically to attend, take those goods into control and sell them so that the proceeds can be put towards the debt. Which of the following best identifies the enforcement method?
o: A writ or warrant of control, under which an enforcement officer takes control of and sells the debtor's goods.
A third party debt order directed at the debtor's bank.
A freezing injunction over the debtor's worldwide assets.
A charging order over the debtor's land.
An attachment of earnings order against the debtor's wages on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: Taking control of goods is effected by a writ of control (High Court) or warrant of control (County Court), under which an enforcement officer or bailiff may seize and sell the debtor's goods to satisfy the judgment. It is the appropriate method where the debtor has tangible goods of value that can be sold.

n.1: A third party debt order targets money owed to the debtor (e.g. by a bank), not tangible goods.
n.2: A freezing injunction preserves assets pending judgment; it is not a method of enforcing a judgment against goods.
n.3: A charging order secures the debt against land, not goods.
n.4: Attachment of earnings targets a debtor's wages, not goods.

Dispute Resolution.q: A default judgment has been entered against a defendant who failed to respond in time. The defendant applies to set the judgment aside, saying they have a defence with a real prospect of success, and explaining why they did not respond. There is no suggestion that the judgment was wrongly entered as a matter of procedure. The court considers the discretionary setting aside of a default judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant explained they had been abroad and had not seen the claim until judgment was entered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must always refuse to set aside a default judgment once it has been entered.
The court must set the judgment aside automatically whenever the defendant asks it to.
The court may set the judgment aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending or there is some other good reason.
The court may set the judgment aside only if the claimant consents to that being done.
The court can set aside a default judgment only where the amount claimed exceeded £100,000 on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a default judgment was regularly obtained, the court has a discretion to set it aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim, or if there is some other good reason to set it aside or allow the defendant to defend (also considering promptness of the application).

n.0: The court is not bound always to refuse; it has a discretion to set aside.
n.1: Setting aside is not automatic on request; the test must be met.
n.3: The claimant's consent is not required for the court to set the judgment aside.
n.4: There is no such value threshold governing setting aside.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party has repeatedly failed to comply with case management directions. The court makes an order requiring that party to take a specified step by a stated date, and providing that if it does not, its statement of case will be struck out without further order. The party then misses the deadline. The order was expressed to take effect automatically on default. The party failed to comply by the stated date. Exasperated by the party's repeated defaults, the court has spelt out one final requirement with a clear consequence attached, stating that if the step is not taken by the stated date the party's statement of case will fall away, and the deadline has now come and gone unmet. Which of the following best describes the effect of this type of order?
o: It is an 'unless order', and the specified sanction takes effect automatically on the party's default.
It merely warns the party, with no sanction following automatically on default.
It can never impose a sanction without a further hearing in every case.
It has no effect unless the innocent party issues a fresh application to enforce it on these facts.
It automatically ends the entire claim for all parties on any breach.
Dispute Resolution.w: An 'unless order' provides that, unless a party complies with a specified requirement by a stated time, a particular sanction (such as striking out its statement of case) will follow. On default, the sanction takes effect automatically, without the need for a further order, though the defaulting party may apply for relief from sanctions.

n.1: An unless order does more than warn; the sanction bites on default.
n.2: The sanction follows automatically; the defaulter must instead seek relief from sanctions.
n.3: The sanction operates automatically; a fresh enforcement application is not needed to trigger it.
n.4: It affects the defaulting party's position, not automatically ending the claim for everyone.

Dispute Resolution.q: At the end of a short interim hearing lasting less than a day, the court makes a costs order and must decide how the amount of costs is to be quantified. The receiving party has filed a statement of costs. One party argues the costs should be quantified there and then, while the other says a separate detailed process is required. The court considers summary and detailed assessment of costs under the Civil Procedure Rules. The hearing had taken only a couple of hours and the winning party had filed a schedule of its costs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Costs of a short interim hearing can only ever be assessed months later at a separate hearing on these facts as a general rule.
All costs must always be quantified by a later detailed assessment, never summarily.
The amount of costs is always fixed by a statutory scale regardless of the work done.
The court will generally assess the costs of a short hearing summarily there and then, rather than by a later detailed assessment.
The court has no power to quantify costs at the end of a hearing at all.
Dispute Resolution.w: The court will normally make a summary assessment of costs at the conclusion of a fast-track trial or of any other hearing lasting not more than a day, quantifying the costs immediately (often from the parties' statements of costs), rather than directing a later detailed assessment.

n.0: Summary assessment allows immediate quantification, not only a later separate hearing.
n.1: Short-hearing costs are usually assessed summarily, not always by detailed assessment.
n.2: Costs are assessed by reference to the work done, not a fixed scale in the ordinary case.
n.4: The court can and does quantify costs at the end of a hearing.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant is bringing a money claim for a debt and wishes to recover interest on the sum owed, in addition to the debt itself, up to the date of judgment. There is no contractual interest provision, and the claimant relies on a statutory power of the court to award interest. The court considers the recovery of interest on a debt or damages in civil proceedings. The debt had gone unpaid for a long time and the claimant wanted compensation for being kept out of the money. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Interest is recoverable only after the judgment has been paid in full by the defendant.
Interest is always awarded automatically at a fixed 20% rate without needing to be claimed on these facts.
The court has a discretion to award interest on debt or damages, and the claim for interest should be pleaded.
Interest can never be recovered on a debt or damages in civil proceedings.
Interest may be recovered only where the parties had a written contract providing for it.
Dispute Resolution.w: The court has a statutory discretion (for example under s.35A Senior Courts Act 1981 or s.69 County Courts Act 1984) to award simple interest on debt or damages for all or part of the period until judgment. A claim for interest should be included in the particulars of claim.

n.0: Pre-judgment interest is recoverable up to judgment, not only after payment.
n.1: Interest is not awarded automatically at a fixed 20% rate; it is discretionary.
n.3: Interest can be recovered, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Statutory interest does not depend on a contractual interest clause.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defended claim is for around £40,000 and is expected to be reasonably complex, with disclosure, witness evidence and possibly expert evidence, and a trial likely to last more than a day. The parties need to know the track to which such a claim is likely to be allocated. The court considers allocation between the fast track, intermediate track and multi-track under the Civil Procedure Rules. The case would need disclosure, witness statements and probably an expert on one issue. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A more complex claim of this value is likely to be allocated to the multi-track (or intermediate track).
The claim must be allocated to the small claims track because it is a money claim.
The claim will be allocated purely according to which party the court favours.
The claim will be allocated to the fast track in every case regardless of complexity or trial length.
The claim cannot be allocated to any track because its value exceeds £25,000.
Dispute Resolution.w: Higher-value or more complex claims are allocated to the multi-track (or, within a defined value band and complexity, the intermediate track). The fast track is generally for claims up to £25,000 capable of a one-day trial with limited expert evidence; a complex £40,000 claim is beyond that.

n.1: A £40,000 complex claim is not a small claims track matter.
n.2: Allocation is by reference to value and complexity, not favouritism.
n.3: The fast track is not used regardless of complexity; complex higher-value claims go to the multi-track.
n.4: Claims over £25,000 are allocated (to the multi-track), not left unallocated.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party is drafting a Part 36 offer and must specify the period within which, if the offer is accepted, the offeror will be liable to pay the offeree's costs. The party wants to ensure the offer carries the usual Part 36 costs consequences. The offer is made more than 21 days before the start of any trial. The party is fixing the 'relevant period' in the offer. The party wants the offer to carry the full protective costs consequences that Part 36 provides, is making it comfortably ahead of any trial date, and needs to be sure the acceptance window it writes into the offer is not so short that the offer falls outside the regime. Which of the following best describes the minimum relevant period that must be specified?
o: A period of not less than 21 days.
A period of not less than 14 days.
A period of not less than 28 days.
A period of not less than 7 days.
There is no minimum period; any period may be specified.
Dispute Resolution.w: For a Part 36 offer made more than 21 days before trial, the offer must specify a relevant period of not less than 21 days during which the offeror will be liable for the offeree's costs if the offer is accepted. This 21-day period is central to the timing of the Part 36 costs consequences.

n.1: Fourteen days is shorter than the 21-day minimum.
n.2: Twenty-eight days is longer than the required minimum, which is 21 days.
n.3: Seven days is shorter than the required minimum relevant period.
n.4: There is a minimum period of 21 days for offers made more than 21 days before trial.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party wishes to rely at trial on the evidence of a witness of fact as to what that witness saw and heard. The court has given directions for the exchange of witness statements. The party asks about the function of a witness statement and what happens if it is not served in time. The court considers witness statements under the Civil Procedure Rules. The witness had seen the key events and their account was central to the party's case at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A witness statement generally stands as the witness's evidence in chief, and a party who fails to serve one may need permission to call the witness.
Witness statements have no role, and all factual evidence must be given entirely orally without notice on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A witness statement is served only after the trial has concluded, as a record of the evidence.
A party may call any witness at trial without ever serving a witness statement in advance.
Witness statements are required only from the parties themselves, never from other witnesses.
Dispute Resolution.w: Parties must exchange witness statements of the factual witnesses they intend to call, in accordance with the court's directions. At trial the statement generally stands as the witness's evidence in chief. If a party fails to serve a statement, they may not call that witness without the court's permission.

n.1: Witness statements have a central role; evidence is not given wholly orally without notice.
n.2: Statements are exchanged before trial, not served afterwards.
n.3: Calling a witness without a served statement generally needs the court's permission.
n.4: Statements are required from the factual witnesses generally, not only the parties.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant suffers personal injuries in an accident caused by the defendant's negligence and wishes to bring a claim. A significant period has passed since the accident, and the claimant is unsure whether they are still in time. They need to know the limitation period that applies specifically to a personal injury claim and the date from which it runs. The court considers the limitation period for personal injury claims under the Limitation Act 1980. The claimant had spent a long time recovering from the injuries before turning to legal action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A personal injury claim must always be brought within one year of the accident occurring on these facts as a general rule.
A personal injury claim must generally be brought within three years of the injury or of the claimant's date of knowledge.
A personal injury claim must be brought within six years of the date of the accident.
A personal injury claim may be brought at any time, as there is no limitation period.
A personal injury claim must be brought within twelve years of the date of the accident.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the limitation period for a personal injury claim is three years, running from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the claimant's date of knowledge, subject to the court's discretion to disapply the period.

n.0: The period is three years, not one year.
n.2: Six years is the ordinary contract/tort period, not the personal injury period.
n.3: There is a limitation period for personal injury claims.
n.4: Twelve years does not apply to personal injury claims.

Dispute Resolution.q: During attempts to settle a dispute, the parties exchange correspondence marked 'without prejudice' in which they make concessions and settlement offers in a genuine attempt to resolve the claim. The dispute does not settle, and at trial one party wishes to put the other's without prejudice concessions before the court to show weakness in their case. The court considers the without prejudice rule. The letters had been written in a genuine effort to negotiate a settlement of the dispute. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The without prejudice label has no legal effect on the admissibility of communications.
Without prejudice communications may be relied on only by the claimant, never the defendant on these facts as a general rule.
The without prejudice rule applies only where both parties are represented by solicitors.
Without prejudice communications are always fully admissible in evidence at the trial.
Without prejudice communications in a genuine attempt to settle are generally not admissible to prove the parties' case.
Dispute Resolution.w: Communications made in a genuine attempt to settle a dispute (whether or not marked 'without prejudice') are generally protected by the without prejudice rule and cannot be put before the court as evidence of the parties' respective positions, encouraging free settlement negotiation (subject to recognised exceptions).

n.0: The rule (and the substance of genuine settlement communications) does have legal effect.
n.1: The protection applies for the benefit of both parties, not only the claimant.
n.2: The rule does not depend on both parties being represented.
n.3: Such communications are generally not admissible, contrary to this option.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant who has been sued wishes not only to defend the claim but also to bring their own claim against the claimant arising out of the same matter, and to bring a claim against a third party for a contribution towards any liability. The defendant asks how such additional claims are made within the existing proceedings. The court considers counterclaims and additional (Part 20) claims under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant said the claimant in fact owed them money arising out of the very same dealings. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defendant may bring a counterclaim only if it is for exactly the same amount as the claim.
A defendant can only ever defend the claim and may never bring any claim of their own.
A defendant must start entirely separate proceedings to make any claim against the claimant on these facts.
A defendant may never bring a third party into existing proceedings under any circumstances.
A defendant may bring a counterclaim against the claimant and, by an additional claim, bring in a third party.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under Part 20 CPR, a defendant may make a counterclaim against the claimant and may bring additional claims (for example for a contribution or indemnity, or a related claim) against a third party, so that connected disputes can be resolved in the same proceedings.

n.0: A counterclaim need not match the amount of the claim.
n.1: A defendant can bring claims of their own, not merely defend.
n.2: Separate proceedings are not required; a counterclaim can be made in the same action.
n.3: Third parties can be brought in by additional (Part 20) claims.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant seeks an interim injunction to restrain the defendant from doing something until trial, arguing that damages would not adequately compensate the harm. The court must decide whether to grant the interim injunction before the merits have been fully determined. The court considers the principles governing the grant of an interim (interlocutory) injunction. The claimant wanted to stop the defendant acting until the dispute could be tried in full. Which of the following best describes the approach?
o: The court can never grant any injunction before the trial of the action.
The court asks whether there is a serious issue to be tried, whether damages are an adequate remedy, and where the balance of convenience lies.
The court grants an interim injunction only where the claimant has already won at trial.
The court grants an interim injunction automatically whenever a claimant asks for one.
The court decides the full merits of the claim at the interim stage before granting relief on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the guidelines in American Cyanamid v Ethicon, in deciding whether to grant an interim injunction the court asks whether there is a serious question to be tried, whether damages would be an adequate remedy for either side, and where the balance of convenience lies, together with the usual cross-undertaking in damages.

n.0: Interim injunctions can be granted before trial; that is their purpose.
n.2: An interim injunction is by definition granted before, not after, trial.
n.3: Interim injunctions are not granted automatically on request.
n.4: The court does not decide the full merits at the interim stage.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant is drafting a defence in response to particulars of claim. The defence must respond to each of the claimant's allegations. The defendant fails to deal at all with one particular allegation of fact in the particulars of claim, neither admitting it, denying it, nor requiring it to be proved. The allegation was one the defence simply did not address. Working through the particulars of claim, the defence responded to most of the allegations but simply passed over one factual assertion altogether, neither accepting it, contesting it, nor putting the claimant to proof of it, and the claimant now relies on that silence. Which of the following best describes the effect of failing to deal with the allegation?
o: The court must strike out the entire defence for the omission.
The defendant is generally taken to admit the allegation not dealt with in the defence.
The allegation is automatically deemed denied because the defence was filed.
The failure has no effect provided the defence is verified by a statement of truth.
The allegation must always be proved by the claimant regardless of the defence.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, a defendant who fails to deal with an allegation in the defence is generally taken to admit it (subject to limited exceptions, such as where the defence sets out the nature of the case in relation to the issue). The defence should therefore state which allegations are admitted, denied, or not admitted (requiring proof).

n.0: The consequence is deemed admission of that allegation, not striking out the whole defence.
n.2: An unaddressed allegation is generally taken to be admitted, not deemed denied.
n.3: A statement of truth does not cure the failure to deal with the allegation.
n.4: Because it is taken as admitted, the claimant need not prove it.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant has been served with a claim form and particulars of claim and wishes to contest the claim, but needs more time to prepare a full defence than the initial period allows. They are considering filing an acknowledgment of service. The defendant wants to understand the time limits for responding to a claim and the effect of acknowledging service. The court considers the defendant's options for responding under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant genuinely wished to contest the claim but needed longer to prepare a full response. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant has no time limit at all and may file a defence whenever convenient.
The defendant may respond only by immediately paying the full amount claimed.
The defendant must file a full defence within 24 hours of being served with the claim on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Filing an acknowledgment of service admits the whole of the claimant's claim.
The defendant may file an acknowledgment of service within 14 days, extending the time to file a defence to 28 days from service of particulars.
Dispute Resolution.w: A defendant must generally respond within 14 days of service of the particulars of claim, by filing a defence or an acknowledgment of service. Filing an acknowledgment of service extends the time for filing the defence to 28 days after service of the particulars of claim.

n.0: There are strict time limits for responding to a claim.
n.1: Paying the claim is not the only permitted response; the defendant may defend.
n.2: A full defence is not required within 24 hours.
n.3: Acknowledging service does not admit the claim; it signals an intention to defend (or contest jurisdiction).

Dispute Resolution.q: A party needs a witness to attend trial to give evidence, but the witness is unwilling to attend voluntarily. The party wishes to compel the witness's attendance, and possibly the production of documents by that witness. The court considers the means of compelling a reluctant witness to attend and give evidence at trial. The witness had refused every request to attend court voluntarily to give their evidence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is no way to compel a reluctant witness; only willing witnesses can ever give evidence on these facts.
The party must simply ask the other side to persuade the witness to attend voluntarily.
The party may obtain a witness summons requiring the witness to attend court to give evidence or produce documents.
The party may compel attendance only by paying the witness a fee fixed by the other side.
A witness can be compelled to attend only in criminal, and never in civil, proceedings.
Dispute Resolution.w: A party may obtain a witness summons requiring a person to attend court to give evidence and/or to produce documents. Failure to comply with a validly served witness summons can amount to a contempt of court.

n.0: Reluctant witnesses can be compelled by a witness summons.
n.1: Persuasion by the other side is not the mechanism; a summons is.
n.3: Compulsion is by summons, not by a fee set by the opposing party.
n.4: Witness summonses are available in civil proceedings.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party failed to include an important document in its disclosure list and did not permit inspection of it, whether through oversight or otherwise. At trial that party now wishes to rely on the document to support its case. The other party objects that the document was never disclosed. The court considers the consequence of failing to disclose a document under the Civil Procedure Rules. The document had simply been overlooked when the party prepared and served its disclosure list. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A party may always rely on any document at trial, whether or not it was ever disclosed on these facts as a general rule.
The document is automatically admitted, and the other party must simply deal with it.
A party may not rely at trial on a document it failed to disclose or allow inspection of, without the court's permission.
The party may rely on the undisclosed document only if it helps the other side's case.
Failure to disclose a document has no consequence of any kind at trial.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, a party may not rely on any document which it failed to disclose or in respect of which it failed to permit inspection, unless the court gives permission. This encourages proper compliance with disclosure obligations.

n.0: Undisclosed documents cannot be relied on as of right; permission is needed.
n.1: An undisclosed document is not automatically admitted for the defaulting party.
n.3: The restriction is not limited by whether the document helps the other side.
n.4: Non-disclosure does have consequences for the ability to rely on the document.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party carrying out disclosure must look for the documents it is required to disclose. It has a very large number of documents, including archived and electronic material, and wonders how far it must go in searching for disclosable documents, and whether the duty ends once its list is served. The court considers the duty to search and the continuing nature of disclosure under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party held thousands of documents, many of them archived or held only in electronic form. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Once the list of documents is served, the duty of disclosure ends entirely.
A party must make a reasonable and proportionate search, and the duty of disclosure continues until proceedings end.
A party must search every document it holds regardless of cost or proportionality.
The duty to search applies only to paper documents and never to electronic material.
A party need not search at all and may simply disclose whatever comes easily to hand on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: A party must make a reasonable search for disclosable documents, the extent being judged by proportionality (number of documents, nature of the case, ease and cost of retrieval, significance). The duty of disclosure is continuing: documents that later come to light must be disclosed.

n.0: Disclosure is a continuing duty, not ended on service of the list.
n.2: The search must be reasonable and proportionate, not unlimited regardless of cost.
n.3: The duty extends to electronic as well as paper documents.
n.4: A party cannot simply disclose whatever is convenient; a reasonable search is required.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant applies to have the claimant's statement of case struck out, arguing that it discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing the claim, or is an abuse of the court's process. The claimant resists, saying the court has no power to end a claim without a trial. The court considers its power to strike out a statement of case under Part 3.4 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The particulars as drafted set out no facts capable of amounting to any recognised cause of action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must strike out any claim that a defendant asks it to strike out.
The court has no power to strike out a statement of case in any circumstances at all on these facts.
The court may strike out a statement of case that discloses no reasonable grounds or is an abuse of process.
The court may strike out a claim only where the claimant consents to the strike out.
The court may strike out a statement of case only after the trial has concluded.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under CPR 3.4, the court may strike out a statement of case (or part of it) if it discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing or defending the claim, is an abuse of the court's process, or if there has been a failure to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order.

n.0: Strike out is discretionary and requires the grounds to be met, not automatic on request.
n.1: The court does have a strike-out power.
n.3: Strike out does not require the claimant's consent.
n.4: Strike out is a pre-trial (or interim) remedy, not confined to after trial.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant has properly served a claim form and particulars of claim on a defendant in a money claim. The time for the defendant to respond has now passed, and the defendant has neither filed an acknowledgment of service nor filed any defence within the time allowed. The claimant wishes to obtain judgment without a trial. The court considers the claimant's ability to obtain default judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules. The deadline for the defendant to respond had come and gone with complete silence from them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant must always proceed to a full trial even where the defendant never responds.
The claim is automatically struck out where the defendant fails to file a defence.
The claimant may generally obtain default judgment where the defendant has failed to respond in time.
The claimant can never obtain judgment unless the defendant admits the claim in writing.
The claimant must wait a further twelve months before taking any step against the defendant.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a defendant has failed to file an acknowledgment of service or a defence within the relevant time in a claim for money or goods, the claimant may generally obtain judgment in default under Part 12 of the CPR, without the need for a trial.

n.0: A full trial is not required where the defendant has failed to respond; default judgment is available.
n.1: The defendant's failure to defend leads to default judgment for the claimant, not strike out of the claim.
n.3: A written admission is not required to obtain default judgment.
n.4: There is no twelve-month waiting period before seeking default judgment.

Dispute Resolution.q: At the end of a short interim application hearing lasting less than a day, the successful party asks the court to determine the amount of costs payable by the losing party there and then, rather than leaving the amount to be worked out in separate later proceedings. The hearing has lasted less than one day. The court is asked to fix the amount of costs immediately. The interim application took well under a day, the winning party has a schedule of its costs ready, and rather than putting everyone to the trouble and delay of a separate assessment process later, it asks the judge to fix the sum the loser must pay right there at the end of the hearing. Which of the following best describes the usual approach to assessing the costs of such a hearing?
o: The court cannot assess costs until the whole claim has concluded.
The court will refer the costs to be agreed by the parties without any assessment.
The court will order each party to bear its own costs of the hearing.
The court must always order a detailed assessment to be carried out later.
The court will usually assess the costs of the hearing summarily at the end of it.
Dispute Resolution.w: For a hearing lasting not more than one day, the court will generally undertake a summary assessment of costs at the conclusion of the hearing, fixing the amount payable immediately (aided by the parties' statements of costs). Detailed assessment, conducted later by a costs officer, is generally reserved for larger or more complex costs, such as those of a whole trial.

n.0: The court can and usually does assess the costs of the interim hearing immediately.
n.1: The court assesses rather than simply leaving costs to the parties to agree.
n.2: There is a successful party entitled to costs; the court does not simply order each side to bear its own.
n.3: Detailed assessment is not always required; short hearings are usually assessed summarily.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant needs to serve a claim form on a defendant company. The claimant is unsure of the correct place at which a company may validly be served with a claim form under the Civil Procedure Rules, and wants to ensure service is effective so as not to jeopardise the claim. The company has a registered office. The court considers valid methods of serving a claim form on a company. The claimant wanted to be sure the company could not later say it had never been served. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim form may be served on a company only at the home address of one of its shareholders.
A company cannot be served with a claim form at all and must instead be sued through its directors personally.
Service on a company is valid only if the claim form is served at the offices of its auditors.
A claim form may validly be served on a company by leaving it at, or posting it to, the company's registered office.
A company can only ever be served by handing the claim form personally to its managing director.
Dispute Resolution.w: A claim form may be served on a company by various permitted methods, including leaving it at or sending it by post to the company's registered office (and, under the Companies Act, service at the registered office is a recognised method), among other permitted places of business.

n.0: A shareholder's home address is not a valid place for serving the company.
n.1: A company can be served; it need not be sued only through its directors personally.
n.2: The auditors' office is not a valid place for service on the company.
n.4: Personal service on the managing director is not the only valid method.

Dispute Resolution.q: After statements of case have been served, a party realises that their pleaded case needs to be changed to correct an error and to add a new allegation. The other party does not consent to the change. The party wishes to know whether, and how, they can amend their statement of case at this stage. The court considers amendments to statements of case under the Civil Procedure Rules. A key date had been pleaded wrongly and a further allegation now needed to be added to the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A statement of case may be amended only during the trial itself and at no other time.
A statement of case can never be amended once it has been served on the other party.
A statement of case may be amended only if the amendment reduces the value of the claim.
After service, a statement of case may be amended only with the consent of all parties or the court's permission.
A party may amend its statement of case freely at any time without consent or permission on these facts.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, a party may amend a statement of case at any time before it has been served without permission. Once it has been served, it may be amended only with the written consent of all the other parties or with the permission of the court.

n.0: Amendment is not confined to the trial itself.
n.1: A served statement of case can be amended, with consent or the court's permission.
n.2: Amendment is not limited to those that reduce the value of the claim.
n.4: Amendment after service is not free; consent or permission is required.

Dispute Resolution.q: After standard disclosure has taken place, one party believes the other holds specific documents relevant to an issue that have not been disclosed, and which should have been. The party wishes the court to order the other side to carry out a further, targeted search and disclose those particular documents. Standard disclosure has already occurred but specific documents are said to be missing. The party seeks a targeted order. Standard disclosure has come and gone, but the party is convinced that particular documents bearing directly on a key issue exist and remain in the other side's hands undisclosed, and it wants the court to compel a further, focused search and production of exactly those documents. Which of the following best describes the appropriate application?
o: An application for specific disclosure, requiring a further search for and disclosure of identified documents or classes of document.
An application for a freezing injunction over the documents.
An application to strike out the other party's statement of case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An application for a wasted costs order against the other side.
An application for summary judgment on the whole claim.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a party considers that the other's disclosure is inadequate, it may apply for specific disclosure under the CPR, seeking an order that the other party carry out a further search and disclose specified documents or classes of document. The court will make such an order where it is necessary to deal with the case justly and proportionately.

n.1: A freezing injunction preserves assets, not the disclosure of documents.
n.2: Striking out is a disproportionate response to a disclosure shortfall; specific disclosure is the targeted remedy.
n.3: A wasted costs order concerns a representative's conduct, not inadequate disclosure.
n.4: Summary judgment disposes of a claim; it is not a disclosure remedy.

Dispute Resolution.q: The court is minded to grant a claimant an interim injunction before trial. The defendant is concerned that, if the injunction is granted but the claimant ultimately loses at trial, the defendant may suffer loss from having been wrongly restrained. The court considers what protection to require from the claimant as a condition of granting the injunction. The injunction would restrain the defendant pending a trial the claimant might lose. The defendant points out that being restrained now could cause it real loss if the claimant turns out at trial to have had no good claim, and the court, alive to that risk, considers what it should require of the claimant in return for granting relief before the rights and wrongs are decided. Which of the following best describes the protection the court will usually require?
o: A payment by the claimant of the defendant's costs of the whole action in advance.
A cross-undertaking in damages from the claimant to compensate the defendant if the injunction proves to have been wrongly granted.
A deposit paid into court equal to the full value of the claim.
Nothing, because a claimant granted an injunction owes no protection to the defendant on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A guarantee from the claimant's solicitors that the claimant will win at trial.
Dispute Resolution.w: As a condition of granting an interim injunction, the court will normally require the applicant to give a cross-undertaking in damages: an undertaking to compensate the respondent (and sometimes third parties) for any loss caused by the injunction if it later turns out the injunction should not have been granted. This protects the defendant against wrongful restraint.

n.0: The claimant is not required to pay the defendant's costs of the action in advance as the condition.
n.2: The usual protection is a cross-undertaking, not a deposit equal to the whole claim.
n.3: A claimant granted an injunction does owe protection, via the cross-undertaking.
n.4: Solicitors do not guarantee the outcome of the trial.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant makes a well-judged Part 36 offer to settle which the defendant rejects. At trial the claimant obtains a judgment that is at least as advantageous as the claimant's own offer — in other words, the claimant beats its own offer. The claimant seeks the enhanced consequences available in these circumstances. The court considers the costs and other consequences where a claimant matches or beats its own Part 36 offer. The claimant's offer had been a shrewd one that the defendant had been ill-advised to reject. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is automatically ordered to pay double the amount of the judgment.
The claimant is limited to its ordinary costs on the standard basis and nothing more.
The enhanced consequences apply only where the defendant is an individual, not a company on these facts.
The claimant may be awarded indemnity costs, enhanced interest and an additional amount, unless it is unjust.
The claimant gets no advantage at all from having beaten its own Part 36 offer.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a claimant obtains a judgment at least as advantageous as its own Part 36 offer, the court will usually order (unless unjust) enhanced consequences: interest on the sum awarded at an enhanced rate, costs on the indemnity basis with enhanced interest on costs, and an additional amount (a percentage uplift, subject to a cap).

n.0: The uplift is a capped additional amount, not automatically double the judgment.
n.1: The claimant is not limited to standard-basis costs where it beat its offer.
n.2: The enhanced consequences are not confined to cases where the defendant is an individual.
n.4: Beating one's own Part 36 offer does bring advantages for the claimant.

Dispute Resolution.q: During disclosure, a party wishes to withhold from inspection confidential written communications between the client and their solicitor which were created for the purpose of giving or obtaining legal advice, arguing that they are protected from disclosure to the other side. The other party demands to see them. The court considers legal advice privilege in civil proceedings. The letters recorded confidential advice the client had received from their own solicitor. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Confidential communications between lawyer and client for the purpose of legal advice are protected by legal advice privilege.
All documents in a party's possession must be produced to the other side, without exception.
Communications with a lawyer are protected only if the litigation has already commenced.
Legal advice privilege protects only documents created by the client, and never by the lawyer on these facts as a general rule.
Privilege is lost automatically as soon as a document is placed on the disclosure list.
Dispute Resolution.w: Legal advice privilege protects confidential communications between a lawyer and client made for the dominant purpose of giving or obtaining legal advice. Such documents may be disclosed (listed) but the party may withhold them from inspection.

n.1: Privileged documents may be withheld from inspection; not everything must be produced.
n.2: Legal advice privilege does not require litigation to have started.
n.3: It protects communications in both directions, not only from the client.
n.4: Listing a privileged document does not automatically waive privilege in it.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant considers that the defendant's defence is hopeless and has no real substance, and wishes to obtain judgment without the expense of a full trial, on the basis that the defence has no real prospect of success and there is no other reason for a trial. The claimant applies for judgment before trial. The court considers the test for summary judgment under Part 24 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The pleaded defence amounted to little more than a bare denial with nothing at all to support it. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Summary judgment is available only where the claim is worth less than £10,000.
Summary judgment may be given where a party has no real prospect of success and there is no other compelling reason for a trial.
Summary judgment must be granted whenever either party simply asks the court for it.
Summary judgment may be given only after all the witnesses have given oral evidence at trial on these facts as a general rule.
Summary judgment is available only to defendants and can never be sought by a claimant.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under Part 24 CPR, the court may give summary judgment against a claimant or defendant on the whole claim or an issue if that party has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue, and there is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at trial.

n.0: There is no such value limit on summary judgment.
n.2: It is not granted automatically on request; the test must be satisfied.
n.3: Summary judgment is decided before trial, not after oral evidence.
n.4: Summary judgment can be sought by claimant or defendant, not only defendants.

Dispute Resolution.q: The parties to litigation reach a settlement of their dispute and wish to record the agreed terms in a way that stays the proceedings but allows either party to return to court to enforce the settlement terms if the other defaults, without those terms all being set out in a public court order. The court considers the use of a Tomlin order to record a settlement. The parties had negotiated hard and wanted the agreed terms of their settlement to stay confidential. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A Tomlin order is available only in claims worth more than the multi-track threshold.
A Tomlin order stays the proceedings on agreed terms set out in a schedule, with liberty to apply to enforce them.
A Tomlin order requires all the confidential settlement terms to be read out in open court.
A Tomlin order can only be made after a full trial on the merits has taken place.
A Tomlin order brings the proceedings to a permanent end with no means of enforcing the settlement on these facts.
Dispute Resolution.w: A Tomlin order is a form of consent order that stays the proceedings on the terms set out in a schedule to the order (which can remain confidential), while giving the parties liberty to apply to the court to enforce those terms without needing to start fresh proceedings.

n.0: There is no such value threshold for a Tomlin order.
n.2: The confidential terms are in the schedule, not read out in open court.
n.3: A Tomlin order records a settlement; it does not require a prior trial.
n.4: It preserves a means of enforcement through the liberty to apply.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant fears that the defendant will destroy or conceal crucial documents or evidence before it can be obtained through the ordinary disclosure process, which would seriously damage the claimant's case. The claimant seeks an order permitting entry to the defendant's premises to search for and preserve that evidence. The court considers the availability of a search order. There was a real danger the crucial documents would vanish the moment the defendant was warned. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A search order may be granted in exceptional cases to preserve evidence at risk of destruction, subject to stringent safeguards.
A search order is granted routinely in every case as a standard step in litigation.
The court has no power to permit any search of a defendant's premises before trial.
A search order may be obtained by the claimant simply by writing to the defendant.
A search order allows the claimant to seize and keep the defendant's assets permanently on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: A search order (formerly an Anton Piller order) is an exceptional interim remedy permitting the applicant to enter the respondent's premises to search for, inspect and preserve evidence or documents that are at real risk of destruction or concealment. It is subject to stringent safeguards, including a supervising solicitor.

n.1: Search orders are exceptional, not a routine step in litigation.
n.2: The court does have power to grant a search order in a proper case.
n.3: A search order is granted by the court, not obtained by writing to the defendant.
n.4: A search order preserves evidence; it does not allow permanent seizure of assets.

Dispute Resolution.q: After lists of documents have been exchanged in the disclosure process, one party wishes to look at the actual documents disclosed by the other, and to take copies of them. The other party queries whether they are obliged to allow inspection of the documents on their list. The court considers the right to inspect disclosed documents under the Civil Procedure Rules. The other side had listed a number of documents that the party now wanted to examine closely. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A party generally has a right to inspect disclosed documents, except those no longer held, privileged or disproportionate to allow.
A party may inspect documents only after the trial has already concluded.
A party may inspect only documents that the disclosing party chooses to show them.
A party never has any right to inspect documents disclosed by the other side.
A party must pay a fixed statutory fee to the other side for each document inspected on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: A party to whom a document has been disclosed generally has a right to inspect it, except where the document is no longer in the disclosing party's control, the disclosing party has a right or duty to withhold inspection (for example privilege), or inspection would be disproportionate.

n.1: Inspection takes place during proceedings, not only after trial.
n.2: Inspection is not limited to what the disclosing party chooses to show.
n.3: There is a general right to inspect disclosed documents.
n.4: There is no such per-document statutory fee payable to the other side.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party realises they will not be able to meet a deadline set by the court and wishes to obtain more time. They are considering whether to seek the other side's agreement or to apply to the court, and are aware that some orders warn that failure to comply will result in an automatic consequence. The court considers extensions of time and 'unless' orders under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party could see it would not meet the looming deadline set out in the court's directions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Deadlines set by the court can never be extended in any circumstances whatsoever.
An 'unless' order has no effect and imposes no sanction for non-compliance.
A party may simply ignore any deadline without any consequence at all.
Only the court, and never the parties by agreement, can ever alter any time limit on these facts as a general rule.
Time may sometimes be extended by agreement, but an 'unless' order imposes an automatic sanction if its deadline is missed.
Dispute Resolution.w: Parties can sometimes agree short extensions of certain time limits (within limits set by the rules), or apply to the court. An 'unless' order specifies that, unless a step is taken by a stated time, an automatic sanction (such as strike out) will follow, so missing its deadline triggers the sanction without further order.

n.0: Court deadlines can be extended in appropriate circumstances.
n.1: An 'unless' order does impose a sanction on non-compliance.
n.2: Ignoring deadlines has consequences under the CPR.
n.3: Parties can agree some extensions; not every time limit requires a court order.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant is about to bring a civil claim and, before issuing proceedings, is expected to follow the steps set out in the relevant pre-action protocol or the Practice Direction on pre-action conduct, such as sending a detailed letter of claim and considering alternative dispute resolution. The claimant instead issues proceedings immediately without any pre-action steps at all. The defendant complains about the failure to comply. The court considers the consequences of failing to comply with pre-action conduct requirements. The defendant had been given no warning of the claim and no chance to resolve it before proceedings began. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant is barred from ever bringing the claim if they did not send a letter of claim first.
The court may impose costs or other sanctions for unreasonable failure to comply with pre-action conduct requirements.
Pre-action conduct is entirely optional and non-compliance can never have any consequence.
The claim is automatically struck out whenever the claimant fails to follow a pre-action protocol on these facts.
The defendant is automatically awarded judgment where the claimant ignored the protocol.
Dispute Resolution.w: Compliance with pre-action protocols and the Practice Direction on pre-action conduct is expected. Unreasonable non-compliance is not fatal to the claim, but the court may take it into account and impose sanctions, typically in costs (or by staying proceedings).

n.0: Failure to send a letter of claim does not permanently bar the claim.
n.2: Non-compliance can have consequences, so it is not without effect.
n.3: Non-compliance does not automatically strike out the claim.
n.4: The defendant is not automatically given judgment for the claimant's non-compliance.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant applies for an interim injunction to restrain the defendant pending trial. The court is satisfied there is a serious question to be tried. It must now decide whether to grant the injunction, considering whether damages would be an adequate remedy for either side and where the least risk of injustice lies. There is a serious issue to be tried and the court is applying the American Cyanamid guidelines. The court is prepared to accept that the claim is not fanciful and raises a genuine issue fit for trial, and now has to work through the remaining stages of the established interim-injunction guidelines before deciding whether restraining the defendant in the meantime is the right course. Which of the following best describes the next stage of the court's analysis?
o: Whether the claimant is more likely than not to win at the eventual trial on these facts as a general rule.
Whether the claim has been allocated to the multi-track.
Whether the defendant consents to the injunction being granted.
Whether damages would be an adequate remedy and, if not clearly so, where the balance of convenience lies.
Whether the claimant can prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the American Cyanamid guidelines, once a serious question to be tried is shown, the court asks whether damages would be an adequate remedy for the claimant (if so, an injunction is usually refused) and for the defendant if enjoined. If damages are not an adequate remedy for either or both, the court decides where the balance of convenience lies, often preserving the status quo.

n.0: The court does not, at the interim stage, decide who is likely to win at trial on the merits.
n.1: Track allocation is not part of the American Cyanamid test.
n.2: The defendant's consent is not the test; the court applies the guidelines.
n.4: The criminal standard of proof has no application to an interim injunction.

Dispute Resolution.q: A judgment creditor holds an unpaid money judgment against an individual debtor who is in regular employment earning a salary, but who has few other assets. The creditor wishes to have deductions made from the debtor's wages at source until the judgment is satisfied. The debtor is an employed individual with a regular wage. The creditor wishes to recover from the debtor's earnings over time. The debtor holds down a steady salaried job but owns almost nothing else worth pursuing, so rather than chasing assets that are not there, the creditor wants the debt recovered gradually by having deductions taken straight from the debtor's pay before it ever reaches the debtor's hands. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate enforcement method?
o: A third party debt order against the debtor's future wages on these facts as a general rule.
A freezing injunction over the debtor's salary.
An attachment of earnings order requiring the employer to deduct sums from the debtor's wages.
A charging order over the debtor's salary account.
A writ of control against the debtor's employer's goods.
Dispute Resolution.w: An attachment of earnings order directs the judgment debtor's employer to make deductions from the debtor's earnings and pay them to the creditor until the judgment is satisfied. It is available against an employed debtor with regular wages, and is well suited where the debtor lacks realisable assets but has an income.

n.0: A third party debt order attaches an existing debt, not a stream of future wages (which attachment of earnings addresses).
n.1: A freezing injunction preserves assets pending judgment; it does not enforce by deducting wages.
n.3: A charging order secures against land or investments, not a salary account in this way.
n.4: A writ of control targets the debtor's goods, not the employer's goods.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defended money claim proceeds and the court must allocate it to a case management track. The claim is for a sum of around £8,000, is factually straightforward, and does not involve any complex issues or a long trial. The parties want to know which track the claim is likely to be allocated to, and the general features of that track. The court considers allocation to the small claims track under the Civil Procedure Rules. The dispute was a simple unpaid consumer bill with no wider complications at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim will be allocated to the small claims track only if both parties are litigants in person on these facts.
The claim cannot be allocated to any track until the trial has already taken place.
The claim must be allocated to the multi-track, because all money claims go to the multi-track.
The claim is likely to be allocated to the small claims track, which has a limited costs regime and a simplified procedure.
The claim will be allocated to the fast track, because the small claims track no longer exists.
Dispute Resolution.w: The small claims track is the normal track for straightforward claims with a value of not more than £10,000 (with lower limits for some claim types). It uses a simplified procedure and a restricted costs regime under which recoverable costs are very limited.

n.0: Allocation to the small claims track does not depend on the parties being unrepresented.
n.1: Allocation happens before trial, as part of case management.
n.2: Low-value straightforward claims go to the small claims track, not automatically the multi-track.
n.4: The small claims track still exists; the fast track is for higher-value claims.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant has obtained a money judgment against a defendant who does not pay voluntarily. The claimant wishes to enforce the judgment against the defendant's assets or income. They ask what methods of enforcement are available to recover the judgment debt. The court considers the enforcement of a money judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules and related legislation. The defendant had the means to pay but was simply refusing to satisfy the judgment debt. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant must start a fresh claim from the beginning in order to recover the judgment debt.
The only way to enforce a money judgment is to have the defendant imprisoned for non-payment.
The claimant may choose from several methods, such as taking control of goods, a charging order, a third party debt order or attachment of earnings.
A judgment creditor has no means of enforcing a judgment if the defendant simply refuses to pay on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Enforcement is available only where the judgment debt exceeds £50,000.
Dispute Resolution.w: A judgment creditor has a range of enforcement methods, including a writ or warrant of control (taking control of goods), a charging order over the debtor's property, a third party debt order (against sums owed to the debtor, e.g. in a bank account), and attachment of earnings, choosing the method best suited to the debtor's circumstances.

n.0: A fresh claim is not required; enforcement proceeds on the existing judgment.
n.1: Imprisonment is not the ordinary method of enforcing a civil money judgment.
n.3: There are effective enforcement methods; the creditor is not without remedy.
n.4: Enforcement is not restricted to debts over £50,000.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party has obtained permission to appeal a first-instance decision and must identify the basis on which the appeal court may interfere. The appellant contends the judge below reached the wrong conclusion, or alternatively that the process was so flawed as to make the decision unjust. The appeal is against a decision of a lower court. The appellant must frame proper grounds. The would-be appellant needs to pin its complaint to a recognised basis for appellate intervention, arguing either that the judge below simply got the decision wrong or that the way the hearing was conducted was so seriously flawed that the resulting decision cannot stand as just. Which of the following best describes the grounds on which an appeal will be allowed?
o: Where new evidence is available, which is always admitted on appeal as of right.
Where the appeal court would prefer to substitute its own view on the facts in every case on these facts as a general rule.
Where the decision was wrong, or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity in the proceedings below.
Where any minor procedural error occurred, regardless of its effect on the outcome.
Where the appellant simply disagrees with the outcome and would have decided differently.
Dispute Resolution.w: An appeal will be allowed where the decision of the lower court was wrong (in law, fact or the exercise of discretion) or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity in the proceedings. Mere disagreement, or a trivial irregularity with no effect on the outcome, is insufficient, and appeals are generally reviews rather than rehearings.

n.0: New evidence is not admitted as of right on appeal; strict conditions apply.
n.1: An appeal is generally a review, not an occasion to re-decide the facts afresh at will.
n.3: The irregularity must be serious and render the decision unjust, not any minor error.
n.4: Mere disagreement with the outcome is not a ground of appeal.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party wishes to rely on expert evidence, for example a surveyor's or medical opinion, to support its case. It intends simply to instruct an expert and produce the report at trial. The other party objects that expert evidence cannot be used without the court's involvement. The court considers the control of expert evidence under the Civil Procedure Rules. The issue turned on technical matters on which only a qualified expert could properly assist. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Expert evidence may be relied on only with the court's permission, and the expert's overriding duty is to the court.
Expert evidence may be given only by an expert employed full-time by the court itself on these facts as a general rule.
An expert's duty is owed solely to the party who instructs and pays them.
Expert evidence is never admissible in civil proceedings under any circumstances.
A party may freely rely on any expert evidence it wishes without any court permission.
Dispute Resolution.w: Expert evidence is restricted to that which is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings, and no party may call an expert or put in an expert's report without the court's permission. The expert owes an overriding duty to help the court, which prevails over any duty to the instructing party.

n.1: Experts are instructed by the parties (or jointly), not employed by the court.
n.2: The expert's overriding duty is to the court, not solely to the instructing party.
n.3: Expert evidence is admissible with permission, not never.
n.4: Expert evidence requires the court's permission; it cannot be used freely.

Dispute Resolution.q: A civil claim is decided at trial, and one party is largely successful while the other loses. The successful party seeks an order that the losing party pay its costs. The losing party argues that each side should simply bear its own costs. The court considers the general rule on the incidence of costs following trial under the Civil Procedure Rules. The successful party had run the case efficiently and now wanted its legal costs paid by the loser. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The general rule is that the unsuccessful party pays the successful party's costs, though the court has a discretion.
The court has no power to make any order about costs after a trial.
Costs are always split equally between the parties regardless of who won.
Each party always bears its own costs, whatever the outcome of the trial.
The successful party always pays the unsuccessful party's costs as a matter of course on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: The general rule under CPR 44 is that the unsuccessful party will be ordered to pay the costs of the successful party ('costs follow the event'), although the court retains a broad discretion and may make a different order having regard to conduct, partial success and other factors.

n.1: The court does have power to make costs orders.
n.2: Costs are not automatically split equally.
n.3: Parties do not always bear their own costs; the loser usually pays.
n.4: It is the unsuccessful party who usually pays, not the successful one.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant brings a personal injury claim funded in the usual way, and is concerned that, if the claim fails, they will be ordered to pay the defendant's costs and be financially ruined. The claimant has heard that a special costs regime applies to personal injury claims which limits their exposure to the defendant's costs. The court considers qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS) in personal injury litigation. The claimant was of modest means and was anxious about the risk of a large adverse costs order. Which of the following best describes it?
o: QOCS means the defendant can never recover any costs from anyone in any circumstances.
Under QOCS, a losing personal injury claimant must always pay the defendant's costs in full.
Under QOCS, an unsuccessful personal injury claimant is generally protected from paying the defendant's costs, subject to exceptions.
QOCS applies to all civil claims of every kind, not only personal injury claims.
QOCS requires the claimant to pay the defendant's costs only if the claim was worth over £25,000 on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS) generally protects an unsuccessful claimant in a personal injury claim from having to pay the successful defendant's costs, subject to exceptions (such as fundamental dishonesty, claims struck out, or costs offset against damages/Part 36).

n.0: QOCS is qualified, with exceptions; it is not an absolute bar on any recovery.
n.1: QOCS protects the losing claimant; it does not require them to pay in full.
n.3: QOCS is specific to personal injury claims, not all civil claims.
n.4: QOCS protection does not turn on the claim exceeding £25,000.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party who has lost at first instance wishes to appeal. Before the appeal can proceed, the party must satisfy the court that the appeal should be allowed to go ahead. There is no automatic right to a full appeal hearing. The party is seeking to challenge the decision below. The party must first clear a threshold. Having lost below, the party is unhappy with the outcome and wants the matter looked at again by a higher court, but is aware that an appeal is not simply there for the asking and that some threshold must be crossed before the appeal will even be allowed to go ahead. Which of the following best describes the test for permission to appeal?
o: Permission is never required for an appeal to a higher court.
Permission is granted automatically to any party who files an appellant's notice.
Permission is granted only if both parties consent to the appeal.
Permission is granted only if the appeal has a real prospect of success or there is some other compelling reason for it to be heard.
Permission is granted only if the appellant proves the case beyond reasonable doubt on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: Permission to appeal is generally required and will be granted only where the court considers that the appeal would have a real prospect of success, or that there is some other compelling reason for the appeal to be heard. Permission may be sought from the lower court or the appeal court.

n.0: Permission is generally required, not dispensed with, for appeals.
n.1: Permission is not automatic on filing a notice.
n.2: The parties' consent does not determine whether permission is granted.
n.4: The criminal standard of proof has no role in the permission test.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party is dissatisfied with a first-instance decision and wishes to challenge it in a higher court. They believe they can appeal automatically as of right, simply because they disagree with the outcome. They ask about the requirements for bringing an appeal and the grounds on which an appeal may succeed. The court considers appeals in civil proceedings under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party felt the judge had misapplied the law and wanted the decision overturned on appeal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Permission to appeal is generally required, and an appeal succeeds only if the decision was wrong or unjust due to serious procedural irregularity.
An appeal will succeed whenever the appeal court would itself have reached a different view.
There is no right of appeal against any first-instance decision in civil proceedings.
A party may appeal automatically as of right simply because they disagree with the decision.
An appeal is a complete re-hearing at which fresh evidence is always heard as a matter of course on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: Permission to appeal is generally required (from the lower court or the appeal court), granted where there is a real prospect of success or some other compelling reason.
