An appeal is usually a review, not a re-hearing, and will be allowed only where the decision was wrong, or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity.

n.1: Mere disagreement or that the appeal court might differ is not the test; the decision must be wrong or unjust.
n.2: There is a route of appeal, subject to permission.
n.3: There is no automatic right of appeal merely on disagreement; permission is generally needed.
n.4: An appeal is usually a review, not a full re-hearing with fresh evidence as of right.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant accepts that part of the claimant's money claim is well founded, but disputes the rest. The defendant wishes to admit the part they accept so as to narrow the issues and limit their costs exposure, while continuing to defend the balance. The claimant asks what the effect of a partial admission is. The court considers admissions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant accepted part of the sum was plainly due but strongly disputed the rest of it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An admission by the defendant has no legal effect and can always be freely ignored.
A defendant who admits part of a claim is automatically taken to admit the whole of it on these facts.
A defendant can only ever admit the entire claim, and never just part of it.
An admission can only be made orally at the trial and never in writing beforehand.
A defendant may admit the whole or part of a claim, and the claimant may obtain judgment on the admitted part.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under Part 14 CPR, a party may admit the whole or part of another party's case, and admissions may be made in the statements of case or in writing. Where a defendant admits part of a money claim, the claimant may enter judgment on the admitted part and continue to litigate the disputed balance.

n.0: Admissions have legal effect and can found judgment.
n.1: Admitting part does not amount to admitting the whole.
n.2: Partial admissions are permitted, not only admission of the whole claim.
n.3: Admissions can be made in writing before trial, not only orally at trial.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party wishes to rely at trial on a statement made out of court by a person who will not be called as a witness, in order to prove the truth of what was stated — in other words, hearsay evidence. The other party argues that hearsay is simply inadmissible in civil proceedings. The court considers the admissibility of hearsay evidence in civil cases under the Civil Evidence Act 1995. The person who made the statement was abroad and could not be called to give evidence in person. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Hearsay evidence is admissible only where the maker of the statement has died.
Hearsay evidence is entirely inadmissible in civil proceedings in every case.
Hearsay evidence is admissible only in criminal, and never in civil, proceedings.
Hearsay evidence, if admitted, must always be treated as conclusive proof of the facts stated on these facts as a general rule.
Hearsay evidence is generally admissible in civil proceedings, subject to notice requirements and its weight being assessed.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the Civil Evidence Act 1995, evidence is not to be excluded in civil proceedings solely on the ground that it is hearsay. Such evidence is generally admissible, subject to notice requirements, with the court assessing the weight to be given to it.

n.0: Admissibility does not depend on the maker having died.
n.1: Hearsay is not inadmissible in civil proceedings.
n.2: Civil hearsay is admissible under the 1995 Act; the criminal rules differ.
n.3: Hearsay is not conclusive; its weight is assessed by the court.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party needs the court to make an order during the course of proceedings, before trial — for example an order about disclosure or an extension of time. They must make an interim application to the court. The party is unsure of the basic procedure for making such an application and what must accompany it. The court considers the procedure for interim applications under the Civil Procedure Rules. The order sought was needed well before trial to keep the case moving to the court's timetable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The party must file an application notice, usually supported by evidence, and serve it on the other party.
Interim orders can only ever be obtained at the final trial and never beforehand.
Interim applications require no notice to the other side in any circumstances at all.
Only the claimant, and never the defendant, may make an interim application to the court on these facts.
A party may obtain any interim order simply by telephoning the court informally.
Dispute Resolution.w: An interim application is generally made by filing an application notice (Form N244) setting out what order is sought and why, usually supported by evidence, and serving it on the respondent. Some applications may be made without notice where justified, but notice is the norm.

n.1: Interim orders are available before trial, not only at trial.
n.2: Notice to the other side is the norm, with without-notice applications being exceptional.
n.3: Either party may make an interim application, not only the claimant.
n.4: An informal phone call is not the proper procedure for an interim application.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant makes a Part 36 offer to settle, which the defendant rejects. At trial the claimant obtains a judgment that is at least as advantageous as its own Part 36 offer. The offer complied with the requirements of Part 36 and the relevant period had expired. The claimant equalled or bettered its own Part 36 offer at trial. The claimant had made a properly formulated offer to settle that the defendant turned down, the case went the distance, and at trial the claimant did at least as well as, if not better than, the figure it had proposed in that offer. Which of the following best describes the enhanced consequences that usually follow for the claimant?
o: The claimant recovers nothing extra because the defendant was entitled to reject the offer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The claimant must pay the defendant's costs for having gone to trial.
The claimant's enhanced entitlement depends on the defendant having made its own offer.
The claimant simply recovers its costs on the standard basis with no enhancement.
The claimant is usually entitled to indemnity costs and enhanced interest from the end of the relevant period, plus an additional amount.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a claimant obtains a judgment at least as advantageous as its own Part 36 offer, the court will usually order enhanced consequences: interest on the sum awarded at an enhanced rate, costs on the indemnity basis (with enhanced interest on costs), and an additional amount (a percentage uplift subject to a cap), unless it is unjust to do so.

n.0: Beating one's own Part 36 offer does bring extra entitlements, contrary to this option.
n.1: The claimant does not pay the defendant's costs where it beat its own offer.
n.2: The enhanced consequences do not depend on the defendant having made an offer.
n.3: The consequences are enhanced (indemnity costs and interest), not merely standard-basis costs.

Dispute Resolution.q: In a multi-track case, the parties are required to prepare and exchange documents setting out their estimated costs of each phase of the litigation, so that the court can make an order managing and controlling the parties' future costs. The case is proceeding on the multi-track and is subject to costs management. The parties must file documents estimating their costs by phase. The case is a substantial multi-track dispute in which the court intends to keep a grip on what each side can spend, and to that end the parties have been directed to put forward, phase by phase, their estimated costs so the court can decide how much of that future expenditure will be recoverable. Which of the following best describes what the parties must prepare?
o: A schedule of the value of the substantive claim rather than costs.
Costs budgets (in the prescribed form, Precedent H), which the court may then approve as a costs management order.
A Part 36 offer setting out each party's costs to date.
A single agreed bill of costs to be paid immediately by the losing party on these facts as a general rule.
A detailed assessment of costs to be conducted before the trial begins.
Dispute Resolution.w: In costs-managed cases (typically multi-track), the parties must file and exchange costs budgets in the prescribed form (Precedent H), setting out estimated costs by phase. The court may make a costs management order recording the extent to which budgets are agreed or approved, which then controls the recoverable costs of each phase.

n.0: Costs budgets concern costs, not the value of the substantive claim.
n.2: A Part 36 offer is a settlement offer, not a costs budget.
n.3: An immediate agreed bill payable by the loser is not what costs budgeting involves.
n.4: Detailed assessment happens after the case, not as the budgeting exercise before it.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant seeks an interim injunction that would require the defendant to take positive steps (a mandatory injunction), rather than merely to refrain from acting, before trial. The court recognises that ordering a party to do something at the interim stage is a more intrusive step than restraining action. The order sought would compel positive action pending trial. The court is deciding how cautiously to approach the application. What the claimant wants is not merely to stop the defendant doing something but to compel the defendant to take positive steps straight away, before the rights and wrongs have been tried, and the court is alert to the fact that ordering someone to act at this early stage is a weightier matter than restraining them. Which of the following best describes the court's approach to an interim mandatory injunction?
o: The court grants it automatically once a serious question to be tried is shown.
The court applies exactly the same low threshold as for any prohibitory injunction.
The court applies particular caution, generally needing a high degree of assurance that the claim would succeed at trial.
The court will never grant a mandatory injunction on an interim basis in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
The court treats a mandatory injunction as requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt.
Dispute Resolution.w: An interim mandatory injunction, requiring positive action before trial, is granted more cautiously than a prohibitory one. The court generally needs a high degree of assurance that, at trial, it will appear the injunction was rightly granted, because compelling action pending trial carries a greater risk of injustice if the claim ultimately fails.

n.0: They are not granted automatically on a serious question to be tried; more assurance is needed.
n.1: A higher threshold applies than for a prohibitory injunction, not the same low one.
n.3: Interim mandatory injunctions can be granted; they are not never available.
n.4: The criminal standard of proof does not apply to interim injunctions.

Dispute Resolution.q: During litigation, one party proposes mediation to try to settle the dispute, but the other party refuses to engage in any form of alternative dispute resolution at all, without any adequate justification for that refusal, and the matter proceeds to a trial that might have been avoided. At the end, the court considers costs. The court considers the costs consequences of an unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR. A short mediation could well have resolved the whole dispute long before it reached trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR may be penalised by the court in costs, even against an otherwise successful party.
A refusal to mediate is relevant only where the refusing party ultimately loses at trial on these facts as a general rule.
A refusal to engage in ADR can never have any effect on the court's decision about costs.
The court will always order the party who refused ADR to lose the case entirely.
Parties are compelled by law to settle every dispute through mediation before any trial.
Dispute Resolution.w: The court expects parties to consider ADR, and an unreasonable refusal to engage in it may be reflected in the costs order, potentially depriving even a successful party of some or all of its costs (Halsey v Milton Keynes; PGF II v OMFS).

n.1: An unreasonable refusal can be penalised even where the refusing party succeeds at trial.
n.2: An unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR can affect costs.
n.3: A refusal to mediate does not automatically cause the refusing party to lose the case.
n.4: There is no absolute legal compulsion to settle every dispute by mediation.

Dispute Resolution.q: A person has clearly been wronged (for example, their goods have been misappropriated online) but does not know the identity of the wrongdoer. A third party, who became innocently mixed up in the wrongdoing, holds information that would reveal the wrongdoer's identity. The applicant seeks an order compelling that third party to disclose the information so that proceedings can be brought. The third party is innocent but holds identifying information. The applicant needs that information to sue. The applicant has plainly been wronged but has no idea who is behind it, while a third party, itself blameless, became caught up in the events and holds the very information that would unmask the wrongdoer, and the applicant needs a way to prise that information loose so it can sue. Which of the following best identifies the order sought?
o: A charging order over the third party's property.
A third party debt order against the innocent party.
A freezing injunction against the innocent third party's assets on these facts as a general rule.
A wasted costs order against the third party.
A Norwich Pharmacal order requiring the third party to disclose information identifying the wrongdoer.
Dispute Resolution.w: A Norwich Pharmacal order may be granted against a third party who, though perhaps innocent, has become mixed up in another's wrongdoing and holds information (such as the identity of a wrongdoer) necessary to enable the applicant to bring a claim. It compels disclosure of that information, typically with the applicant paying the third party's reasonable costs.

n.0: A charging order is an enforcement method against property, not a disclosure order.
n.1: A third party debt order enforces a money judgment, not disclosure of a wrongdoer's identity.
n.2: A freezing injunction preserves assets; it does not compel identifying information.
n.3: A wasted costs order concerns a legal representative's conduct, not third-party disclosure.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party files a statement of case (such as particulars of claim or a defence) which sets out factual assertions on which they rely. The document must be verified in a particular way to confirm the party's belief in the truth of its contents, and there are consequences for verifying a false statement without an honest belief in its truth. The court considers the requirement for a statement of truth on statements of case under the Civil Procedure Rules. The document contained several detailed factual assertions central to the party's case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A statement of truth must be signed by the trial judge before the document can be used.
A statement of truth is required only on documents filed by litigants in person.
A statement of case needs no verification of any kind and may simply be filed as drafted on these facts as a general rule.
A false statement of truth has no consequences, provided the party later corrects it.
A statement of case must be verified by a statement of truth, and a false statement may lead to contempt proceedings.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, a statement of case must be verified by a statement of truth. A person who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth may be liable for contempt of court.

n.0: The statement of truth is given by the party (or representative), not the judge.
n.1: The requirement applies to represented parties as well as litigants in person.
n.2: Statements of case require verification by a statement of truth.
n.3: A false statement of truth can have serious consequences, including contempt.

Dispute Resolution.q: A judgment creditor is owed a substantial sum under an unpaid money judgment. The debtor owns a house with significant equity but has little available cash. The creditor wishes to secure the judgment debt against the property so that it will be paid out of the proceeds if the house is sold, and potentially to force a sale. The debtor's main asset is land with equity in it. The creditor wishes to secure the debt against that land. The debtor's wealth is locked up in a house carrying substantial equity while the debtor keeps little cash to hand, and the creditor wants to fasten the judgment debt onto that property so it will be paid out on any sale, and perhaps ultimately to press for the house to be sold. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate enforcement method?
o: A search order permitting entry to the debtor's home.
A charging order over the debtor's land, securing the judgment debt against the property.
A third party debt order against the equity in the property.
An attachment of earnings order against the debtor's rental income on these facts.
A writ of control over the fixtures in the house.
Dispute Resolution.w: A charging order imposes a charge over the judgment debtor's interest in land (or certain other assets) to secure the judgment debt, so that the creditor is paid out of the proceeds on any sale. The creditor may, in a further application, seek an order for sale to realise the charge. It is apt where the debtor's value is tied up in property.

n.0: A search order preserves evidence; it is not a method of enforcing a money judgment against land.
n.2: A third party debt order targets a debt owed to the debtor, not the debtor's own equity in land.
n.3: Attachment of earnings targets wages, not rental income enforcement against the property.
n.4: A writ of control enforces against goods, not the land itself.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant wishes to bring a claim for breach of contract, and separately is considering a claim in the tort of negligence (not involving personal injury). Time has been passing since the events in question, and the claimant is worried the claims may be too old to bring. They need to know the primary limitation period for these claims and from when it runs. The court considers the limitation periods under the Limitation Act 1980. The events giving rise to both potential claims had occurred a number of years ago now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The limitation period for both claims is twelve years from the date of the events complained of on these facts.
The limitation period for both claims is three years from the date the cause of action accrued.
The limitation period is one year for contract and six years for negligence claims.
The primary limitation period for both breach of contract and non-personal-injury negligence is six years from accrual.
There is no limitation period for contract or tort claims, which may be brought at any time.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the primary limitation period for a simple contract claim and for a tort claim (other than personal injury) is six years from the date the cause of action accrued (for contract, breach; for tort, when damage is suffered).

n.0: Twelve years applies to actions on a deed (specialty), not simple contract/ordinary tort.
n.1: Three years is the personal injury period, not the ordinary contract/tort period.
n.2: Both contract and this tort claim carry a six-year period, not one year for contract.
n.4: There is a limitation period; claims cannot be brought at any time.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant issues a claim form but does not serve it on the defendant straight away. The claimant is aware that a claim form has a limited period of validity for service, and wants to know how long they have to serve it and whether the period can be extended. The claim form is to be served within the jurisdiction. The court considers the time for serving a claim form under the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant had been trying to negotiate a settlement before committing to serving the claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim form remains valid for service indefinitely, with no time limit at all.
A claim form must generally be served within four months of issue, though the court may extend that period in limited circumstances.
A claim form must be served on the same day it is issued or it lapses immediately.
A claim form must be served within fourteen days of issue in every case.
A claim form may be served within ten years of issue without any need for an extension on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: A claim form for service within the jurisdiction must be served within four months of the date of issue. The court may, on application, extend the period for service, but only in limited circumstances, so claimants must act in good time.

n.0: A claim form's validity for service is time-limited, not indefinite.
n.2: A claim form need not be served the same day; there is a four-month window.
n.3: The period is four months, not fourteen days.
n.4: The validity period is four months, not ten years.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant fears that the defendant, against whom it has a strong claim, will dissipate or hide its assets before judgment so as to defeat any judgment the claimant may obtain. The claimant wishes to obtain an order freezing the defendant's assets pending the outcome of the litigation. The court considers the availability of a freezing injunction. There were signs the defendant was already moving money out of reach of any future judgment. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court can never restrain a defendant from dealing with its own assets before judgment.
A freezing injunction transfers ownership of the defendant's assets to the claimant at once on these facts as a general rule.
The court may grant a freezing injunction to restrain a party from dissipating assets where there is a real risk of dissipation.
A freezing injunction is granted automatically in every case where a money claim is brought.
A freezing injunction is available only after the claimant has already obtained judgment.
Dispute Resolution.w: A freezing injunction is an interim order restraining a party from disposing of or dealing with its assets (up to a specified value) where the applicant has a good arguable case and there is a real risk that a judgment would go unsatisfied because of dissipation of assets. It does not give the claimant any proprietary interest in the assets.

n.0: The court can restrain dissipation before judgment via a freezing injunction.
n.1: A freezing injunction does not transfer ownership of the assets to the claimant.
n.3: It is not granted automatically in every money claim; the conditions must be met.
n.4: A freezing injunction can be granted before judgment, indeed that is its purpose.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant wishes to bring a single set of proceedings against two defendants who are both said to be liable in respect of the same damage, and to include two related claims arising out of the same facts. The claimant wants to know whether multiple parties and claims can be dealt with together in one action. The court considers the joinder of parties and claims under the Civil Procedure Rules. Both potential defendants were said to have contributed to the same loss the claimant had suffered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Claims can only be joined if the defendants expressly consent to being sued together.
Each claim and each defendant must always be pursued in an entirely separate set of proceedings.
Multiple claims and parties may be joined in one set of proceedings where it is convenient to dispose of them together.
Multiple claims may be joined only where they exceed the multi-track value threshold.
A claimant may never sue more than one defendant in the same proceedings under any circumstances on these facts.
Dispute Resolution.w: The CPR permit a claimant to use a single claim form to start all claims which can be conveniently disposed of in the same proceedings, and multiple parties may be joined where there is a common question of law or fact or the claims arise out of the same transaction, so long as it is desirable to deal with them together.

n.0: Joinder does not require the defendants' consent.
n.1: Separate proceedings for every claim and defendant are not required.
n.3: Joinder is not gated behind the multi-track value threshold.
n.4: Multiple defendants can be sued together in appropriate cases.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defended claim has been allocated to a track, and the court must now give directions to manage the case through to trial, setting a timetable for steps such as disclosure, witness statements and expert evidence. The parties have completed and filed their directions questionnaires. A party asks about the court's role in actively managing the case. The court considers case management and the giving of directions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The parties had filed their directions questionnaires and the case now needed a timetable to trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Case management directions are given only in claims worth more than £1 million.
The court plays no active role and simply leaves the parties to run the case as they wish.
The court gives directions only if both parties jointly request a case management order.
The court fixes the trial date first and gives no other directions of any kind before trial on these facts as a general rule.
The court actively manages cases, giving directions and a timetable to bring the case to trial justly and at proportionate cost.
Dispute Resolution.w: Active case management is a central feature of the CPR. The court gives directions and sets a timetable (often standard directions for the fast track, or bespoke directions after a case/costs management conference on the multi-track) to further the overriding objective of dealing with cases justly and at proportionate cost.

n.0: Case management applies across the tracks, not only to very high-value claims.
n.1: The court does play an active management role; it does not leave everything to the parties.
n.2: Directions are given by the court as a matter of course, not only on joint request.
n.3: The court gives a range of directions, not merely a trial date.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant is preparing to issue a money claim and must decide in which court to start proceedings, choosing between the County Court and the High Court. The claim is a relatively modest money claim, well below the threshold at which High Court proceedings would be appropriate, and does not raise any special complexity or importance. The court considers the allocation of claims between the County Court and the High Court. The sum in dispute was a few thousand pounds owed under a single unpaid invoice. Which of the following best describes the position for a straightforward money claim of modest value?
o: A claimant may only ever start a money claim in the High Court, never the County Court.
The choice of court is irrelevant, because the two courts are identical in every respect on these facts.
A modest money claim must be started in the Supreme Court in the first instance.
All money claims, whatever their value, must be started in the High Court.
A straightforward money claim of relatively low value should generally be started in the County Court.
Dispute Resolution.w: Lower-value and straightforward money claims are generally started in the County Court. Only higher-value claims (broadly those exceeding the relevant threshold) or those of particular complexity, importance or specialist nature should be commenced in the High Court.

n.0: Money claims can be, and usually are, started in the County Court.
n.1: The two courts differ in the value and type of work they handle.
n.2: First-instance claims are not started in the Supreme Court.
n.3: Not all money claims must go to the High Court; modest ones go to the County Court.

Dispute Resolution.q: After a costs order is made, the amount of costs payable must be assessed, and the parties dispute the basis on which the assessment should be carried out. One party argues for an assessment that resolves doubt in favour of the paying party and requires proportionality, while the other seeks assessment on the more generous basis. The court considers the difference between the standard basis and the indemnity basis of assessing costs. A large bill of costs was in dispute and the basis of assessment would make a real difference to the sum. Which of the following best describes it?
o: On the indemnity basis the receiving party recovers nothing at all for its costs.
The basis of assessment is chosen by the paying party in every case.
On the standard basis all costs claimed are always allowed in full without question.
On the standard basis costs must be proportionate and doubt favours the paying party; the indemnity basis is more generous.
There is no difference between the standard basis and the indemnity basis of assessment on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Dispute Resolution.w: On the standard basis, the court allows costs that are proportionate to the matters in issue and reasonably incurred, resolving any doubt in favour of the paying party. On the indemnity basis, the requirement of proportionality does not apply and any doubt is resolved in favour of the receiving party, so it is generally more generous.

n.0: On the indemnity basis the receiving party recovers more, not nothing.
n.1: The basis is determined by the court, not chosen by the paying party.
n.2: Even on the standard basis, costs are scrutinised for proportionality and reasonableness.
n.4: There is a significant difference between the two bases.

Dispute Resolution.q: Two parties have a contract which contains a clause providing that any dispute between them is to be referred to arbitration rather than litigated in court. One party nonetheless issues court proceedings in respect of a dispute covered by the clause, and the other party wishes to hold them to the agreement to arbitrate. The court considers the effect of an arbitration agreement when one party sues in court, under the Arbitration Act 1996. The contract clearly required disputes of this kind to be resolved by arbitration, not by litigation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will ignore the arbitration agreement unless both parties now agree to arbitrate on these facts.
The court will strike out the claim entirely, leaving the claimant with no remedy at all.
The court will generally stay the court proceedings so the dispute can be referred to arbitration as agreed.
The arbitration clause has no effect and the court will simply hear the claim as normal.
Arbitration agreements are unlawful, so the court proceedings must always continue.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996, where a party brings court proceedings in respect of a matter that the parties agreed to refer to arbitration, the other party may apply for a stay, and the court will stay the proceedings (unless the arbitration agreement is null, void, inoperative or incapable of being performed), so the dispute goes to arbitration.

n.0: The court gives effect to the existing agreement; fresh agreement is not required.
n.1: The claim is stayed, not struck out, leaving arbitration as the forum.
n.3: The arbitration clause is given effect; the court does not simply hear the claim.
n.4: Arbitration agreements are lawful and enforceable, not unlawful.

Dispute Resolution.q: During litigation, one party's legal representative causes significant unnecessary costs to be incurred by the other side through an improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission in the conduct of the proceedings. The innocent party seeks an order that the costs so wasted be paid by the representative personally, rather than by the client. The wasted costs were caused by the representative's own conduct. The innocent party seeks a remedy against the representative directly. The wasted expense flowed not from anything the client did but from the representative's own improper and unreasonable handling of the case, and the party left out of pocket wants to recover those costs from the lawyer personally rather than pursuing a client who was not really at fault. Which of the following best identifies the order available?
o: A summary judgment against the legal representative.
An order for indemnity costs against the represented client on these facts.
A charging order over the representative's assets.
A third party debt order against the representative's firm.
A wasted costs order requiring the legal representative to meet the costs personally.
Dispute Resolution.w: A wasted costs order may be made against a legal representative personally where costs have been incurred as a result of any improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission by the representative (or which it is unreasonable to expect the client to pay). It is directed at the representative, not the client, and requires a causal link to the wasted costs.

n.0: Summary judgment disposes of a claim without trial; it is not the remedy for wasted costs.
n.1: An order against the client does not address the representative's own conduct.
n.2: A charging order is an enforcement method, not the remedy for a representative's misconduct.
n.3: A third party debt order enforces a money judgment against a debt owed to the debtor, not this situation.

Dispute Resolution.q: A civil dispute goes to trial, and the judge must decide the disputed factual issues and determine the outcome. A question arises about the standard to which the parties must prove the facts they assert in a civil (as opposed to criminal) case. The claimant asks what standard of proof the court applies to the facts in issue. The court considers the standard of proof in civil proceedings. The judge had to choose between two sharply conflicting accounts of what had happened. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Facts in a civil claim must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, as in a criminal trial.
The claimant must prove its case to a certainty before any facts can be found.
The standard of proof in a civil claim is decided differently by each individual judge on these facts.
Facts in a civil claim need not be proved at all; the judge decides on impression.
Facts in a civil claim must be proved on the balance of probabilities, that is more likely than not.
Dispute Resolution.w: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the balance of probabilities: a fact is proved if the court is satisfied that it is more likely than not to have occurred. This is a lower standard than the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

n.0: The criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt) does not apply in civil claims.
n.1: Proof to a certainty is not required; the balance of probabilities suffices.
n.2: The standard is a fixed legal standard, not chosen by each judge.
n.3: Facts must be proved to the civil standard, not decided on mere impression.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant applies for an urgent interim order without giving notice to the defendant, because giving notice might defeat the purpose of the order. The court is prepared to hear the application on a without-notice basis. The applicant is presenting the case with only its own side present. The application is made without notice to the respondent. Because tipping off the respondent might allow assets or evidence to disappear, the applicant has come to court with only its own side represented, and the judge is conscious that this one-sided procedure carries special obligations for the party seeking the order. Which of the following best describes a key duty the applicant owes on such an application?
o: No particular duty beyond that owed on an ordinary application on notice on these facts as a general rule.
A duty to notify the respondent immediately before the hearing begins.
A duty of full and frank disclosure, including disclosing matters that are adverse to the applicant's case.
A duty to prove the underlying claim to the criminal standard of proof.
A duty only to present the facts most favourable to the applicant's case.
Dispute Resolution.w: On a without-notice application, because the respondent is not present to put their side, the applicant owes a duty of full and frank disclosure: it must fairly present the application and disclose all material facts, including those adverse to its own case. Breach of this duty can lead to the order being set aside and costs sanctions.

n.0: A heightened duty of full and frank disclosure applies, beyond an ordinary on-notice application.
n.1: The point of a without-notice application is that the respondent is not notified in advance.
n.3: The criminal standard of proof does not apply to such applications.
n.4: The applicant must disclose adverse matters, not only favourable ones.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant, having started proceedings, decides that they no longer wish to pursue the claim and want to bring it to an end. They are aware that stopping a claim can have costs consequences. The claimant asks how a claim is brought to an end by the claimant's own choice, and what the usual costs consequence is. The court considers discontinuance of a claim under the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant had lost confidence in the claim and wanted to stop before incurring further costs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claimant who discontinues never has to pay any of the defendant's costs at all.
A claim can only be brought to an end by a full trial and judgment on the merits.
A claimant may discontinue only with the permission of the defendant in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A claimant may generally discontinue by filing and serving a notice, and will usually be liable for the defendant's costs to that date.
A claimant can never discontinue a claim once proceedings have been started.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under Part 38 CPR, a claimant may generally discontinue all or part of a claim at any time by filing and serving a notice of discontinuance (permission being needed only in certain cases). The usual costs consequence is that the discontinuing claimant is liable for the defendant's costs up to discontinuance.

n.0: Discontinuance usually carries liability for the defendant's costs.
n.1: A claim can be ended by discontinuance, not only by trial and judgment.
n.2: The defendant's permission is not generally required to discontinue.
n.4: A claimant can discontinue; it is not impossible once proceedings start.

Dispute Resolution.q: A party has failed to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order — for example missing a deadline — and as a result faces a sanction. The party applies for relief from the sanction so that they can continue with their case. The court must decide how to approach the application. The court considers the approach to relief from sanctions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party had missed an important deadline and now risked losing the right to rely on its evidence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must always grant relief from any sanction whenever a party asks for it.
The court decides the application purely at random with no structured approach.
The court must always refuse relief from sanctions in every case without exception.
The court applies the three-stage Denton approach: seriousness of the breach, the reason for it, and all the circumstances.
The court grants relief only where the party in default pays a fixed statutory penalty on these facts as a general rule.
Dispute Resolution.w: When considering relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9, the court applies the three-stage approach in Denton v TH White: assess the seriousness and significance of the breach; consider why the default occurred; and evaluate all the circumstances to deal with the application justly, including the need for compliance and efficient litigation.

n.0: Relief is not automatically granted on request.
n.1: The approach is structured (Denton), not random.
n.2: Relief is not automatically refused; it is assessed under Denton.
n.4: There is no fixed statutory penalty that secures relief.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant with a strong claim faces a long wait until trial and is suffering hardship because the money claimed is not yet available. The claimant applies for an order that the defendant make a payment on account of any damages or debt before the final judgment. The court considers the availability of an interim payment under the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant was in real financial difficulty while waiting many months for the trial to come on. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An interim payment is ordered automatically in every case as soon as a claim is issued on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may order an interim payment where, for example, liability is admitted or a substantial sum would be recovered.
An interim payment may be ordered only against a claimant, never against a defendant.
An interim payment may be ordered only where the claim is for less than £5,000.
An interim payment can never be ordered before the final trial has concluded.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, the court may order an interim payment on account of damages or a debt where certain conditions are met — for example the defendant has admitted liability, judgment has been obtained for damages to be assessed, or the court is satisfied the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial sum against that defendant.

n.0: They are not ordered automatically on issue of a claim.
n.2: An interim payment is ordered against a defendant, in the claimant's favour.
n.3: There is no such low value cap on interim payments.
n.4: Interim payments are available before final judgment.

Dispute Resolution.q: In a lower-value claim, the court is concerned about the cost and proportionality of each side instructing its own expert on a single, relatively narrow issue. The court is considering directing that the expert evidence on that issue be given by one expert instructed by both parties together. The court considers the use of a single joint expert under the Civil Procedure Rules. The issue was narrow and the cost of two separate experts would be out of proportion to it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court can never require the parties to share a single expert in any circumstances.
A single joint expert may be used only where both parties are litigants in person.
Each party is always entitled to instruct its own separate expert, whatever the court says on these facts.
The court may direct that evidence on an issue be given by a single joint expert instructed by both parties.
A single joint expert may be appointed only in claims worth more than £500,000.
Dispute Resolution.w: To control cost and further the overriding objective, the court may direct that expert evidence on a particular issue be given by a single joint expert instructed by both parties, particularly in lower-value or straightforward cases. This is common on the fast track.

n.0: The court can require a single joint expert; it is a recognised power.
n.1: The single joint expert mechanism is not confined to litigants in person.
n.2: Parties are not always entitled to their own separate expert; the court may order a single joint expert.
n.4: There is no such high-value threshold; single joint experts are typical in lower-value cases.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant issues a claim form but does not include the full particulars of claim within it, intending to serve them separately. The claimant wants to understand what the particulars of claim must contain and by when they must be served, so that the defendant knows the case they have to meet. The court considers the requirements for particulars of claim under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant needed to understand precisely what factual case they were being asked to meet. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The particulars of claim are optional and need never be served on the defendant at all.
The particulars of claim may be served at any time before the trial, however late.
The particulars of claim must set out all the evidence and legal argument the claimant will rely on at trial on these facts.
The particulars must set out a concise statement of the facts relied on and be served with or shortly after the claim form.
The particulars of claim need only state the amount of money the claimant wants to recover.
Dispute Resolution.w: The particulars of claim must contain a concise statement of the facts on which the claimant relies (and certain specific matters where relevant). They must be contained in or served with the claim form, or served within 14 days after service of the claim form (and within the claim form's validity period).

n.0: Particulars of claim are required, not optional.
n.1: They cannot be served at any time before trial; there are time limits.
n.2: They state the facts relied on, not all the evidence and legal argument.
n.4: The particulars must set out the material facts, not merely the sum claimed.

Dispute Resolution.q: A claimant has issued a claim form and must now serve it on the defendant to bring them into the proceedings. The claimant serves the claim form within the jurisdiction by first-class post. A question arises about the date on which the claim form is treated as having been served, which matters for calculating subsequent deadlines. The court considers the rules on deemed service of a claim form under the Civil Procedure Rules. The exact date of service mattered because the deadline for the defence turned upon it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim form served by first-class post is deemed served on the second business day after posting.
A claim form served by post is never validly served and must be handed over in person.
A claim form is deemed served only when the defendant actually reads and acknowledges it.
A claim form is deemed served twenty-eight days after it is posted to the defendant.
A claim form is deemed served the very moment it is placed in the post by the claimant.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under the CPR, a claim form served by first-class post (or another next-business-day method) within the jurisdiction is deemed served on the second business day after it was posted, regardless of when it actually arrives.

n.1: Postal service is a valid method of serving a claim form.
n.2: Deemed service does not depend on the defendant actually reading it.
n.3: The deemed service date is the second business day, not 28 days later.
n.4: Deemed service is not at the moment of posting; it is the second business day after.

Dispute Resolution.q: A court is exercising its powers and interpreting the Civil Procedure Rules in a case, and the parties disagree about how a particular procedural provision should be applied. One party urges the court to have regard to the fundamental purpose that underpins the entire body of rules. The court considers the overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules. The dispute over the rule would affect how much time and cost the whole case would consume. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The overriding objective is to make litigation as slow and thorough as possible.
The overriding objective is to maximise the costs recovered by the successful party on these facts.
The overriding objective is to ensure that the claimant always wins the case.
The overriding objective applies only to multi-track claims and no others.
The overriding objective is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
Dispute Resolution.w: The overriding objective in CPR 1.1 is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost, which includes ensuring the parties are on an equal footing, saving expense, dealing with cases proportionately, expeditiously and fairly, and allotting an appropriate share of the court's resources.

n.0: It seeks expeditious, proportionate handling, not slowness.
n.1: It aims at proportionate cost, not maximising costs recovery.
n.2: The objective is even-handed justice, not that the claimant always wins.
n.3: The overriding objective governs all cases, not only the multi-track.

Dispute Resolution.q: A multi-track claim reaches the disclosure stage, and the court makes an order for standard disclosure. A party is unsure which documents they are required to disclose, believing they need only produce the documents that support their own case. The other party says the obligation is wider than that. The court considers the scope of standard disclosure under the Civil Procedure Rules. There were documents that helped the other side which the party would have preferred not to reveal. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A party need only disclose the documents that support its own case, and no others.
A party must disclose every document it has ever created, whether or not relevant on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A party must disclose only the documents the other side specifically asks to see.
Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose documents relied on and those adversely affecting or supporting any party's case.
There is no obligation to disclose any documents to the other side before trial.
Dispute Resolution.w: Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose the documents on which it relies, and the documents which adversely affect its own case, adversely affect another party's case, or support another party's case (as well as documents required by a relevant practice direction), following a reasonable search.

n.0: Disclosure is not confined to documents that support one's own case.
n.1: It is limited to relevant documents within the standard disclosure categories, not everything ever created.
n.2: Standard disclosure is not confined to documents specifically requested.
n.4: There is an obligation to give disclosure where ordered.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant makes a formal offer to settle the claim, complying with the requirements of Part 36 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant does not accept it, proceeds to trial, and fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than the defendant's offer. The parties dispute the costs consequences. The defendant made the offer well before trial and it remained open. The court considers the costs consequences of a Part 36 offer that the claimant fails to beat. The defendant had put forward a realistic settlement figure that the claimant had gambled on beating at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant automatically loses the entire claim for having rejected the offer.
There are no costs consequences at all, because a Part 36 offer is only an informal negotiation on these facts.
The claimant will usually pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, plus interest, unless unjust.
The defendant must pay all of the claimant's costs, because the claimant still won some money.
The costs consequences apply only if the offer was made in the last week before trial.
Dispute Resolution.w: Where a claimant fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than a defendant's Part 36 offer, the usual costs consequence is that the claimant pays the defendant's costs from the expiry of the relevant period, together with interest on those costs, unless the court considers it unjust.

n.0: Failing to beat the offer affects costs, not the claimant's substantive success on the claim.
n.1: Part 36 has defined costs consequences; it is not merely informal negotiation.
n.3: The defendant does not pay all the claimant's costs where the offer was not beaten.
n.4: The consequences do not depend on the offer being made only in the final week.

Dispute Resolution.q: A defendant who is being sued alleges that, if the defendant is liable to the claimant, a third party (not currently a party) is liable to contribute to or indemnify the defendant in respect of that liability. The defendant wishes to bring that third party into the existing proceedings. The defendant seeks contribution or indemnity from someone not yet party to the claim. The defendant wants the third party's liability determined in the same action. The defendant accepts it might be found liable to the claimant but says that if so, a third party who is not yet involved in the action ought to bear all or part of that liability, and it wants that third party's responsibility sorted out within the same proceedings rather than in a fresh action. Which of the following best describes the appropriate step?
o: The defendant may make an additional claim (a Part 20 claim) against the third party for contribution or indemnity.
The defendant must apply to strike out the claimant's claim instead.
The defendant may counterclaim against the third party under Part 36.
The defendant may only bring entirely separate proceedings against the third party later on these facts.
The defendant may join the third party only with the claimant's consent.
Dispute Resolution.w: Under CPR Part 20, a defendant may bring an additional claim against a third party (a 'Part 20 claim'), for example for a contribution or indemnity in respect of the defendant's liability to the claimant. This allows the related liabilities to be determined in the same proceedings rather than in separate actions.

n.1: Striking out the claimant's claim is unrelated to obtaining contribution from a third party.
n.2: A counterclaim is against the claimant; Part 36 is about settlement offers, not additional claims.
n.3: The defendant need not bring wholly separate later proceedings; Part 20 allows it in the same action.
n.4: An additional claim against a third party does not require the claimant's consent (though court permission may be needed depending on timing).

Contract Law.q: A buyer pays a 10% deposit on exchanging contracts to buy property, the deposit being expressly stated to be paid as a deposit and earnest for performance. The buyer then wrongfully fails to complete, repudiating the contract, and the seller lawfully terminates. The buyer asks whether the deposit can be recovered, arguing it should be returned now the contract is at an end. The sum was a true deposit (a customary 10%), not merely an advance part-payment of the price. The sale had reached the point of exchange, the buyer handed over the customary sum expressly as a deposit and earnest for performance rather than as a mere instalment of the price, and then pulled out without any lawful excuse, leaving the seller to decide what could be kept. Which of the following best describes the buyer's ability to recover the deposit?
o: The deposit must be returned because all pre-payments are recoverable on termination.
The seller may generally forfeit and retain a true deposit where the buyer defaults.
The buyer may always recover a deposit in full once the contract is terminated.
The deposit must be shared equally between buyer and seller on default.
The deposit is recoverable because deposits are treated identically to penalties in every case.
Contract Law.w: A true deposit is an earnest for performance and may generally be forfeited and retained by the innocent seller if the buyer defaults, even if the seller's actual loss is less, provided the deposit is not so large as to be a disguised penalty. This differs from an advance part-payment, which may be recoverable subject to the seller's cross-claim for loss.

n.0: Not all pre-payments are recoverable; a true deposit is treated differently from a part-payment.
n.2: A defaulting buyer cannot always recover a true deposit; it may be forfeited.
n.3: The deposit is not split equally; the innocent seller may generally retain it.
n.4: A reasonable, customary deposit is not automatically treated as a penalty.

Contract Law.q: Two businesses sign a short document recording that they will work together on a project, and that they will 'negotiate in good faith and agree the price and detailed terms at a later date'. No price, quantity or key terms are in fact ever settled between them. When a dispute arises, one party tries to enforce the document as a binding contract, arguing that the parties clearly intended to be bound to work together. The other says that, because the essential terms were left to be agreed in the future, there is nothing the court can enforce. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a binding contract, and the court will simply fix a reasonable price and terms for the parties.
There is a binding contract, because the parties plainly intended to be legally bound to one another.
There is a binding contract, because putting the arrangement in a signed document makes it certain enough.
There is no binding contract, because an agreement to agree essential terms in the future is too uncertain to enforce.
There is a binding contract, because a duty to negotiate in good faith is fully enforceable in English law.
Contract Law.w: An agreement which leaves essential terms, such as price, to be agreed in the future is generally too uncertain to be an enforceable contract, and an agreement to negotiate in good faith is not enforceable in English law (Walford v Miles). There is therefore no binding contract.

n.0: The court will not write the contract for the parties by fixing terms they never agreed.
n.1: An intention to be bound cannot cure the fatal uncertainty of leaving essential terms unagreed.
n.2: Recording an incomplete agreement in signed form does not make its missing essential terms certain.
n.4: English law does not recognise an enforceable bare duty to negotiate in good faith.

Contract Law.q: A person books and pays for a package holiday which is described as offering particular facilities and enjoyment. The holiday turns out to be a great disappointment, falling far short of what was promised, and the traveller suffers distress and loss of enjoyment as a result, though little in the way of financial loss. The traveller claims damages for the disappointment and loss of enjoyment. The tour operator argues that damages for distress can never be awarded in contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages for distress are available in every contract wherever the claimant feels upset by a breach.
Damages for distress are available only if the traveller also suffered physical injury on the holiday.
Damages for distress and loss of enjoyment may be awarded, as an important object of this contract was enjoyment.
Damages are limited strictly to a refund of the price the traveller paid for the holiday.
Damages for distress and loss of enjoyment can never be awarded for any breach of contract.
Contract Law.w: Although damages for distress are generally not recoverable in contract, an exception applies where an important object of the contract was to provide pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind, such as a holiday. Damages for disappointment and loss of enjoyment may then be awarded (Jarvis v Swans Tours).

n.0: Distress damages are the exception, not available in every contract merely because a party is upset.
n.1: Physical injury is not a precondition to distress damages in an enjoyment contract.
n.3: The traveller is not confined to a refund; loss of enjoyment is compensable in such contracts.
n.4: Distress damages are not wholly barred in contract; the enjoyment exception applies here.

Contract Law.q: During negotiations, a seller makes a statement to the buyer that is literally true but tells only half the story, creating a misleading overall impression because the seller does not reveal an important qualifying fact. The buyer, relying on the misleading impression created, enters the contract and later suffers loss when the full picture emerges. The seller argues that, because everything actually said was true, there can be no misrepresentation. The buyer seeks advice on whether a misrepresentation claim can succeed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim can succeed only if the seller was under a fiduciary duty to the buyer.
There can be no misrepresentation, because everything the seller actually stated was literally true.
A claim can succeed only if the buyer specifically asked the seller about the qualifying fact.
A half-truth that creates a misleading overall impression can amount to an actionable misrepresentation.
There can be no misrepresentation, because a seller is never obliged to volunteer any information at all.
Contract Law.w: Although silence generally does not amount to misrepresentation, a statement which is literally true but misleading because it is only a half-truth can be an actionable misrepresentation, since the overall impression conveyed is false (Dimmock v Hallett; With v O'Flanagan principle).

n.0: No fiduciary duty is needed; the misleading statement itself founds the claim.
n.1: Literal truth of the words does not save a statement that is misleading as a half-truth.
n.2: A misleading half-truth is actionable whether or not the buyer asked about the missing fact.
n.4: The claim does not rest on a general duty to volunteer information, but on the misleading half-truth given.

Contract Law.q: A charterer hires a ship for two named voyages. The charterer's own conduct then makes it impossible to carry out those voyages as planned, and the charterer seeks to rely on that impossibility to say the contract has been frustrated and that it is therefore excused from liability. The shipowner argues that the charterer cannot rely on frustration where the frustrating event was brought about by the charterer's own choices and acts. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The charterer may rely on frustration, because frustration always applies wherever performance is impossible.
The charterer may rely on frustration, because the reason for the impossibility is legally irrelevant.
The charterer cannot rely on frustration, because the alleged frustrating event was self-induced.
The charterer may rely on frustration, provided it did not intend to bring the event about.
The charterer may rely on frustration, because the voyages did in fact become impossible to perform.
Contract Law.w: Frustration cannot be relied upon where the frustrating event was self-induced — that is, brought about by the choice or default of the party seeking to rely on it (Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers). The charterer's own conduct bars the plea of frustration.

n.0: Frustration does not apply to every impossibility; self-induced events are excluded.
n.1: The cause of the impossibility is very relevant; self-inducement defeats frustration.
n.3: Self-induced frustration is barred whether or not the party intended the specific outcome.
n.4: Impossibility caused by the party's own act does not count as frustration for that party.

Contract Law.q: A commercial contract for the supply of components contains a term requiring delivery to take place 'by 1 March', and the contract expressly states that time of delivery is of the essence. The supplier delivers on 5 March. The buyer, who has since found the delay has caused it real difficulty, wishes to terminate the whole contract and refuse the goods, as well as to claim damages. The supplier argues that a few days' delay should sound only in damages and does not entitle the buyer to walk away from the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer may claim damages only, because a short delay in delivery can never justify terminating a contract.
The buyer may neither terminate nor claim damages, because the goods were in fact delivered.
The buyer may terminate only if it can prove the delay caused it serious financial loss.
The buyer may terminate only if the supplier had previously delivered late on other occasions.
The buyer may terminate and claim damages, because breach of a condition entitles the innocent party to end the contract.
Contract Law.w: Where a term is a condition — as an express 'time of the essence' stipulation makes the delivery date — any breach, however slight, entitles the innocent party to terminate the contract and to claim damages, regardless of the seriousness of the consequences.

n.0: Because time was made of the essence, the term is a condition, so termination is available for any breach.
n.1: Late delivery is still a breach; delivery does not defeat the right to terminate a breached condition.
n.2: The right to terminate for breach of a condition does not depend on proving serious loss.
n.3: The right to terminate flows from the term being a condition, not from a history of late delivery.

Contract Law.q: A consumer engages a firm to service and repair the central heating in the consumer's home. The firm carries out the work carelessly, leaving a connection loose, so that the system leaks and has to be redone by another contractor. The consumer wants to know what standard the law required of the firm's work and what remedy may be available. The contract is a contract to supply a service to a consumer, governed by the Consumer Rights Act 2015. The complaint is about the quality of the workmanship rather than any goods supplied. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The consumer's only possible remedy is to reject the contract and recover nothing more.
The firm owed no particular standard because services carry no implied terms at all.
The service had to achieve a guaranteed result regardless of the care taken by the firm on these facts as a general rule.
The firm's obligations depend entirely on whatever the firm chose to promise orally.
The service had to be performed with reasonable care and skill, and the consumer may seek repeat performance or a price reduction.
Contract Law.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, a trader supplying a service to a consumer must perform it with reasonable care and skill. Where that term is breached, the consumer may be entitled to require repeat performance to put things right or, where that is not possible or not done in a reasonable time, to a price reduction, in addition to any damages.

n.0: The remedies include repeat performance and price reduction, not merely rejection with nothing more.
n.1: Consumer service contracts do carry statutory implied terms.
n.2: The statutory standard is reasonable care and skill, not a guaranteed result, unless a specific result was promised.
n.3: The statutory standard applies regardless of what the firm chose to say orally.

Contract Law.q: A rogue, pretending in writing to be a wealthy and creditworthy individual whose identity actually exists, induces a seller to contract at a distance and to part with goods on credit, the seller intending to deal only with that named, reputable person and not with the rogue. The rogue disappears and the goods end up with an innocent third party. Identity, not merely creditworthiness, was crucial to the seller, and the dealing was in writing rather than face to face. The seller intended to contract only with the specifically identified person. Which of the following best describes the effect on the contract with the rogue?
o: The contract is fully valid, because a mistake as to the other party's identity never matters.
The contract is voidable only, so a third party who buys in good faith always gets good title on these facts.
The contract may be void for unilateral mistake as to identity, so no title passes to the rogue or the third party.
The contract is valid because identity is only ever relevant in face-to-face dealings.
The contract is void for common mistake shared by both seller and rogue.
Contract Law.w: Where parties deal at a distance in writing and the seller intended to contract only with a specifically identified, existing third person (identity being material), a unilateral mistake as to identity can render the contract void, so no title passes to the rogue or on to a later buyer. This contrasts with face-to-face dealings, where the contract is usually only voidable.

n.0: A mistake as to identity can matter where identity is crucial and the dealing is at a distance.
n.1: If the contract is void (not merely voidable), even a good-faith third party gets no title.
n.3: Identity can be material in written dealings at a distance, not only face to face.
n.4: The mistake is unilateral (only the seller is mistaken), not a common mistake shared by both.

Contract Law.q: A commercial contract for the supply of services contains a clause purporting to exclude the supplier's liability for loss caused by its own negligence, other than death or personal injury (for example, damage to the customer's property). A dispute arises after the supplier's carelessness damages the customer's equipment, and the customer challenges the clause. The clause is contained in the supplier's written standard terms and is relied on to exclude liability for negligently caused property damage. The contract is a business-to-business contract subject to the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977. Which of the following best describes the clause's effectiveness?
o: The clause is automatically void because negligence liability can never be excluded on these facts as a general rule.
The clause is valid because reasonableness is irrelevant to property damage claims.
The clause is valid only if the customer separately insured against the loss.
The clause is automatically valid because the parties are both businesses.
The clause is effective to exclude liability for such negligence only so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness.
Contract Law.w: Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, a term excluding liability for negligence causing loss or damage other than death or personal injury is effective only in so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. Liability for negligently caused death or personal injury cannot be excluded at all, but property damage exclusions are tested for reasonableness.

n.0: Negligence liability for loss other than death/personal injury can be excluded if reasonable, so it is not always void.
n.1: Reasonableness is precisely the applicable test for excluding negligently caused property damage.
n.2: Validity turns on reasonableness under UCTA, not on whether the customer insured separately.
n.3: The clause is not automatically valid merely because both parties are businesses; reasonableness applies.

Contract Law.q: A buyer sends a seller a purchase order on the buyer's own standard terms. The seller replies with an acknowledgement that purports to accept the order but is expressed to be subject to the seller's own standard terms, which differ on a key point, and which include a tear-off slip for the buyer to sign and return. The buyer does not return the slip but says nothing further, and the seller then delivers the goods, which the buyer takes and uses. A dispute later arises as to whose standard terms govern the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is on the seller's terms: they fired the last shot, accepted by the buyer taking the goods.
The contract is on the buyer's terms, because the buyer's order was the first document sent in the exchange.
The contract is on the buyer's terms, because the buyer never signed and returned the seller's tear-off slip.
The contract is on a mixture of both sets of terms, with the court blending them into a single set.
There is no contract at all, because the two sets of standard terms never precisely matched one another.
Contract Law.w: In a 'battle of the forms', the traditional offer-and-acceptance analysis usually means the party who sends the last set of terms before performance, without objection, prevails (Butler Machine Tool v Ex-Cell-O). Here the seller's reply was a counter-offer on its terms, accepted by the buyer taking the goods.

n.1: Being first does not win the battle of the forms; the last shot before performance generally does.
n.2: Taking and using the goods amounted to acceptance of the seller's terms despite the unsigned slip.
n.3: The court does not usually blend the two sets of terms into a hybrid contract.
n.4: Performance by delivery and acceptance of the goods means a contract was formed despite the mismatch.

Contract Law.q: A debtor owes a creditor £10,000 which is due and undisputed. The creditor, wanting some payment rather than none, agrees to accept £6,000 in full and final settlement, and the debtor pays that sum. The creditor later sues for the remaining £4,000. There was no dispute about the sum owed and nothing new was given by the debtor beyond part of the existing debt. The debtor had pleaded cash-flow difficulty, the creditor reluctantly took what it could get to avoid the risk of recovering nothing at all, and the debtor gave nothing beyond a slice of the very sum already due before the creditor later changed its mind and pursued the shortfall. Which of the following best describes the creditor's ability to recover the balance?
o: The creditor cannot recover the balance, because accepting part payment always discharges the whole debt on these facts.
The creditor cannot recover the balance, because the debtor provided fresh consideration by paying early.
The creditor may recover only if the debtor acted dishonestly in negotiating the settlement.
The creditor may recover the balance only if the agreement was not put in writing.
The creditor may recover the balance, as part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the rest.
Contract Law.w: Under the rule in Pinnel's Case, affirmed in Foakes v Beer, payment of a smaller sum is not good consideration for a promise to release the balance of a larger debt. Absent fresh consideration (such as early payment, a different place, or a chattel) or an applicable estoppel, the creditor remains entitled to recover the outstanding £4,000.

n.0: Accepting part payment does not by itself discharge the whole debt.
n.1: On these facts the debtor gave nothing new; paying part of what was already due is not fresh consideration.
n.2: The rule does not turn on the debtor's honesty in negotiating.
n.3: Whether the agreement was in writing does not supply the missing consideration.

Contract Law.q: A guest checks in at the reception desk of a hotel and pays for a room, thereby concluding the contract there and then. Only after going up to the room does the guest see a notice on the back of the bedroom door which purports to exclude the hotel's liability for loss of or damage to guests' property. The guest's property is later stolen from the room, and the hotel relies on the notice to deny liability. The guest seeks advice on whether the exclusion applies to their contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The exclusion is incorporated, because the guest had the opportunity to read the notice before the theft.
The exclusion is incorporated, because a hotel is always entitled to limit liability for guests' property.
The exclusion is incorporated, because the notice was clearly displayed within the hotel room.
The exclusion is not incorporated, but only because it was printed on the back of the door.
The exclusion is not incorporated, because notice of it was given only after the contract had been concluded.
Contract Law.w: An exclusion clause is only incorporated if reasonable notice of it is given before or at the time the contract is made. Notice given after the contract was concluded at reception comes too late to be incorporated (Olley v Marlborough Court).

n.0: Being able to read it later does not matter; notice must be given by the time of contracting.
n.1: There is no rule that a hotel may always limit liability for guests' property.
n.2: Clear display does not help where the notice came after the contract was already made.
n.3: The problem is the timing of the notice, not the particular place it was displayed.

Contract Law.q: A commercial buyer tells a machinery seller, before contracting, that it needs a compressor capable of running continuously in a dusty foundry environment, and relies on the seller to select a suitable model. The seller, who deals in such equipment, supplies a compressor that is of good general quality but cannot cope with continuous dusty operation and fails within weeks. The buyer, a business, made its particular purpose known and relied on the seller's skill and judgement. The sale is a commercial sale of goods governed by the Sale of Goods Act 1979. Which of the following best describes the buyer's strongest implied-term claim?
o: Breach of the implied term that the goods be reasonably fit for the particular purpose made known.
No implied term applies, because the buyer inspected nothing before purchase.
Breach of the implied term that the goods correspond with their description only.
Breach of an implied term that the goods be of the very highest quality obtainable.
No implied term applies, because fitness for purpose is never implied in commercial sales.
Contract Law.w: Under s.14(3) of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, where the buyer expressly or impliedly makes known a particular purpose, and reasonably relies on the seller's skill and judgement, there is an implied term that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose. The compressor's inability to perform the disclosed continuous dusty operation breaches that term.

n.1: Fitness for a particular purpose does not depend on the buyer having inspected the goods.
n.2: Correspondence with description (s.13) is a different term; the issue here is fitness for the disclosed purpose.
n.3: The implied standard is reasonable fitness/satisfactory quality, not the very highest quality obtainable.
n.4: Fitness for purpose is implied in commercial sales where the s.14(3) conditions are met.

Contract Law.q: A company circulates to the public a notice promising a stated sum to anyone who uses its product as directed and still suffers a particular illness, stating that it has deposited money in a bank to show its sincerity. A member of the public buys and uses the product exactly as directed but still falls ill, and claims the sum. The company argues the notice was a mere advertising puff. The notice specified conduct that would earn the sum. The notice was widely circulated, framed in definite terms about exactly what a user had to do to qualify, and backed by the statement about money set aside to meet claims, and the claimant followed the directions to the letter and still contracted the illness the product was said to prevent. Which of the following best describes the notice's legal character?
o: It was a statement of opinion that could never give rise to contractual liability.
It was void for uncertainty because it was addressed to the public at large.
