It was a bilateral offer requiring the claimant to communicate acceptance in advance.
It was a unilateral offer that could be accepted by performing the specified conditions.
It was only an invitation to treat, incapable of forming a contract when acted upon.
Contract Law.w: An advertisement promising payment to anyone who performs specified conditions can be a unilateral offer, distinguishable from a mere invitation to treat, especially where (as here) the promisor shows an intention to be bound (the deposited money). It is accepted by performing the conditions, and prior communication of acceptance is not required.

n.0: The evidence of a deposited fund shows intention to be bound, so it is not a mere opinion or puff.
n.1: An offer to the world at large is not void for uncertainty; it can be accepted by anyone who performs.
n.2: A unilateral offer of this kind does not require acceptance to be communicated in advance of performance.
n.4: Unlike a shop display, this promise of payment on conditions is an offer, not a mere invitation to treat.

Contract Law.q: A small company is heavily dependent on a supplier and is contractually entitled to delivery of components at an agreed price. Knowing the company will be ruined if supply stops, the supplier refuses to deliver unless the company agrees on the spot to pay a much higher price, giving the company no realistic practical alternative but to agree in order to survive. The company agrees under protest and later refuses to pay the increase. The supplier sues for the higher price, and the company argues the variation is not binding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The variation is binding, because the company agreed to the new price rather than terminating.
The variation is binding, because the company continued to accept deliveries at the higher price.
The variation is void, because a price can never lawfully be changed once a contract is agreed.
The variation is binding, because economic pressure in commercial dealings is never unlawful.
The variation is voidable for economic duress, as illegitimate pressure left no real choice.
Contract Law.w: Economic duress makes a contract or variation voidable where illegitimate pressure (such as a threatened breach) is applied which leaves the victim no reasonable practical alternative but to agree (Atlas Express v Kafco; Pao On). Agreeing under protest to avoid ruin is a classic case.

n.0: Agreeing rather than terminating does not validate a variation extracted by duress.
n.1: Continued acceptance under the same coercion does not cure the duress or affirm the variation.
n.2: Prices can lawfully be varied by agreement; the vice here is the duress, not variation itself.
n.3: Illegitimate commercial pressure can amount to duress; it is not always lawful.

Contract Law.q: A consumer enters into a standard-form contract with a company for a service. Buried in the small print is a term, which was not individually negotiated, allowing the company to increase its charges by any amount it chooses at any time, without giving the consumer any right to cancel. The consumer challenges the term after a large and unexpected price rise. The company argues that the consumer signed up to the terms and is bound by all of them. The consumer seeks advice under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The term binds the consumer unless they can prove the company acted dishonestly in relying on it.
The term is automatically valid, provided it was written somewhere in the contract document.
The term binds the consumer, because price terms can never be assessed for fairness at all.
The term may not bind the consumer if it is unfair under the Consumer Rights Act 2015.
The term binds the consumer in full, because they agreed to the company's standard terms.
Contract Law.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, a term in a consumer contract that has not been individually negotiated is not binding on the consumer if it is unfair — that is, contrary to good faith it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights to the consumer's detriment. A one-sided price-variation term is a classic example.

n.0: Unfairness does not require proof of dishonesty; the imbalance-based test applies.
n.1: Mere inclusion in the document does not make a term automatically valid.
n.2: Only the core price itself, if transparent, is exempt from the fairness assessment; an open-ended variation term is not.
n.4: Agreement to standard terms does not prevent an unfair term being challenged under the Act.

Contract Law.q: A seller delivers goods to a buyer under a contract of sale, the property in the goods having passed to the buyer, and the buyer simply refuses to pay the agreed price of £12,000 although the goods conform to the contract in every respect. The seller does not want to claim damages for a lost bargain; it wants to recover the actual agreed price for goods the buyer now owns. The seller seeks advice on the appropriate claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The seller may only claim damages for its loss of profit, and never the agreed price itself.
The seller may bring an action for the price of the goods, as the property in them has passed to the buyer.
The seller may claim the price only if the contract expressly said the price was payable on delivery.
The seller must first resell the goods elsewhere before it can make any claim against the buyer.
The seller may recover nothing, because the buyer's refusal to pay is not a breach of contract.
Contract Law.w: Where goods have been sold and the property in them has passed to the buyer, and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay, the seller may maintain an action for the price under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (s.49), rather than being confined to a damages claim.

n.0: The seller is not limited to loss-of-profit damages; it may sue for the price where property has passed.
n.2: The action for the price arises where property has passed; it is not confined to an express payment-on-delivery term.
n.3: The seller need not resell first to claim the price where property has passed.
n.4: Refusing to pay for conforming goods is a breach on which the seller can sue.

Contract Law.q: A 17-year-old who has recently started an apprenticeship and lives independently buys a quantity of ordinary work clothing and basic tools from a supplier on credit, all of which are genuinely required for the apprenticeship and are suitable to the young person's actual needs and situation. The young person then refuses to pay for the goods, arguing that, because they are a minor, the contract cannot be enforced against them at all. The supplier seeks advice on whether it can recover payment for the clothing and tools. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is unenforceable, because contracts with minors are valid only if approved by a parent.
The contract is enforceable against the minor, because the goods were necessaries suitable to their condition and needs.
The contract is entirely unenforceable, because no contract with a minor can ever be enforced against them.
The contract is enforceable only for the tools, because clothing can never count as a necessary.
The contract is enforceable, because a minor who is working is treated in all respects as an adult.
Contract Law.w: Although contracts with minors are generally unenforceable against them, a minor is bound to pay a reasonable price for necessaries — goods suitable to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements — as well as for beneficial contracts of service such as apprenticeships. The goods here are necessaries.

n.0: Parental approval is not the test; the goods being necessaries is what makes the contract enforceable.
n.2: Contracts with minors are not all unenforceable; those for necessaries bind the minor.
n.3: Clothing suitable to the minor's needs can be a necessary; it is not excluded as a category.
n.4: A working minor is not treated as an adult across the board; the necessaries rule is the relevant exception.

Contract Law.q: A person hires a room overlooking a route, at a high price, for the specific purpose, known to both parties, of watching a royal procession that is due to pass by on a particular day. The procession is then cancelled because of the monarch's illness, although the room itself remains perfectly usable and the view unobstructed. The room owner sues for the agreed hire charge, and the hirer refuses to pay, arguing that the whole purpose of the contract has been destroyed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract stands, because frustration can never apply merely because an event is cancelled.
The contract is frustrated only if the room could not physically be entered on the day.
The contract stands and the hirer must pay, because the room remained available to be used.
The contract is likely frustrated: the cancelled procession destroyed its common foundation.
The hirer must pay, because watching the procession was only the hirer's private motive.
Contract Law.w: Where the occurrence of a particular event is the common foundation of the contract, known to both parties, its cancellation may frustrate the contract even though performance remains physically possible (Krell v Henry). The procession's cancellation destroyed the shared purpose of hiring the room.

n.0: Cancellation of the very event that is the contract's foundation can frustrate it.
n.1: Frustration here does not turn on physical inability to enter the room.
n.2: Continued availability of the room does not save the contract where its shared purpose has gone.
n.4: The purpose was not a mere private motive; it was the common basis of the contract known to both.

Contract Law.q: A company promises to pay a reward to anyone who completes a sponsored walk of a set route. A participant reads the offer, sets out, and has walked most of the route when the company purports to revoke the offer before the participant finishes. The participant completes the walk and claims the reward. The offer was of a unilateral kind, accepted by performing the act. The participant had trained for weeks, incurred expense and given up a day to take part, and was well over halfway round the set route relying on the promised reward when the company, worried about the cost, announced that the offer was withdrawn before anyone could finish. Which of the following best describes the effect of the attempted revocation?
o: The participant accepted the offer merely by reading it, so revocation was impossible from the outset on these facts.
The company may revoke provided it reimburses the participant's travel costs only.
No contract could arise because unilateral offers are never binding.
The offer was freely revocable at any time before the walk was actually completed.
The offer could not be revoked once the participant had begun performance, so the reward is payable on completion.
Contract Law.w: In a unilateral contract, acceptance occurs by full performance of the requested act, but the offeror cannot revoke once the offeree has embarked on performance. An implied obligation not to revoke arises once performance has begun, so the participant who completes the walk is entitled to the reward despite the purported revocation.

n.0: Merely reading the offer is not acceptance; performance is required.
n.1: The remedy is the promised reward on completion, not merely reimbursement of expenses.
n.2: Unilateral offers can be binding once accepted by performance.
n.3: The offer is not freely revocable once performance has started.

Contract Law.q: A consumer buys a new washing machine from a retailer. It proves faulty. The retailer is given one opportunity to repair it, but after the repair the same fault recurs within a short time, so the machine still does not conform to the contract. The consumer, having lost confidence, wants to return the machine and get money back rather than allow further attempts. The purchase is a consumer sale of goods governed by the Consumer Rights Act 2015, and a repair has already been attempted once without success. Which of the following best describes the consumer's remedy?
o: The consumer has a final right to reject and obtain a refund, which may be reduced for use in limited circumstances.
The consumer is entitled only to a further repair and never to a refund once repair has begun on these facts.
The consumer must allow the retailer unlimited further attempts to repair before any refund.
The consumer must accept a replacement and has no right to any refund at all.
The consumer may reject only within 30 days of purchase and has now lost all remedies.
Contract Law.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, after one repair or replacement has failed to bring the goods into conformity, the consumer has the final right to reject and obtain a refund. The refund may be reduced to reflect use in certain cases (and, outside the first six months, deductions are more readily made), but the consumer need not permit endless repair attempts.

n.1: A refund is available under the final right to reject, not only a further repair.
n.2: The consumer need not allow unlimited repair attempts; one failed attempt triggers the final right to reject.
n.3: The consumer is not obliged to accept a replacement instead of a refund at this stage.
n.4: The 30-day short-term right to reject is separate; the final right to reject arises after a failed repair.

Contract Law.q: A seller sends an offer to a buyer by email. The buyer sends an email accepting the offer, but owing to a problem on the buyer's own mail server the acceptance is not received by the seller until the following day, by which time the seller has sold the goods elsewhere. The buyer argues acceptance was complete when the email was sent. The communication was by an effectively instantaneous method. The buyer was keen to secure the goods and believed the deal was done the instant the reply was sent, the seller heard nothing that day and, treating the offer as still open, sold to another customer, and only afterwards did the delayed message finally surface on the seller's system. Which of the following best describes when the acceptance took effect?
o: When the buyer first decided to accept the offer, regardless of communication.
When the buyer clicked send, because acceptance is always effective on despatch on these facts as a general rule.
When the acceptance was actually received by the seller, as the postal rule does not apply to instantaneous communications.
When the seller chose to open and read the email, whenever that occurred.
Never, because acceptance by email is not recognised in contract law.
Contract Law.w: The postal rule (acceptance effective on posting) is an exception confined to non-instantaneous methods such as post. For instantaneous or effectively instantaneous communications such as email, the general rule applies: acceptance takes effect when and where it is received by the offeror. As it was received after the goods were sold, no contract was formed in time.

n.0: An uncommunicated intention to accept is not an effective acceptance.
n.1: The despatch rule is the postal-rule exception; it does not apply to instantaneous communications.
n.3: Receipt (arrival), not the moment the offeror chooses to read it, is generally the relevant point.
n.4: Acceptance by email is perfectly capable of forming a contract.

Contract Law.q: A landlord of a block of flats agrees, during a period of wartime difficulty, to accept half the normal ground rent from the tenant company, which relies on that promise and continues to occupy and manage the flats on that basis for several years. Once conditions return to normal and the flats are full again, the landlord seeks to recover the full rent for the future, and also to claim the arrears of the half-rent that was not paid during the difficult years. The tenant argues that the landlord is bound by the promise to accept half rent. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The landlord may use promissory estoppel as a cause of action to sue the tenant for the shortfall.
The landlord may recover nothing at all, because promissory estoppel extinguishes the debt entirely.
The landlord is permanently bound to accept half rent, because the tenant relied on the promise for years.
The landlord may be estopped from recovering the reduced rent for the past period, but may claim the full rent for the future.
The landlord may recover the full arrears for the whole period, because the promise to accept less lacked consideration.
Contract Law.w: On these facts (Central London Property Trust v High Trees House), promissory estoppel prevents the landlord going back on the promise to accept reduced rent for the period it was intended to cover and relied upon, but the strict right to full rent can be resumed for the future on reasonable notice.

n.0: Promissory estoppel is a shield, not a sword; it does not found a cause of action.
n.1: Promissory estoppel generally suspends rights; it does not wipe out the debt for all time.
n.2: Estoppel generally suspends rather than permanently extinguishes rights; full rent may resume for the future.
n.4: Estoppel prevents recovery of the shortfall for the period covered by the promise and relied upon.

Contract Law.q: A supplier is due to deliver a machine to a buyer on 1 June. On 1 May, well before the delivery date, the supplier writes to the buyer clearly stating that it will not be delivering the machine at all, as it has sold it elsewhere. The buyer does not want to wait until June and wishes to treat the contract as at an end straight away and to claim damages immediately, so that it can arrange a replacement without delay. The buyer seeks advice on whether it can act now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer cannot claim damages at all, because the delivery date has not yet arrived.
The buyer may accept the breach now, end the contract and sue immediately for damages.
The buyer must wait until the delivery date of 1 June before it can treat the contract as breached.
The buyer must first offer the supplier more time before it can treat the contract as at an end.
The buyer may sue immediately only if the supplier's refusal to deliver was made dishonestly.
Contract Law.w: An anticipatory breach — a clear refusal to perform before performance is due — entitles the innocent party to elect either to accept the breach, terminate immediately and sue for damages at once, or to affirm and await the date for performance (Hochster v De La Tour).

n.0: Damages can be claimed immediately on acceptance of the anticipatory breach.
n.2: The buyer need not wait until the performance date to act on a clear anticipatory breach.
n.3: There is no obligation to offer more time before accepting a clear repudiation.
n.4: The right to treat the contract as ended does not depend on the refusal being dishonest.

Contract Law.q: A buyer was induced to buy a business by a misrepresentation. However, after discovering the truth, the buyer continued for several months to run the business as its own, drew profits from it, and told the seller that it was happy to carry on with the purchase, before eventually changing its mind and seeking to rescind the contract and hand the business back. The seller argues that it is now too late for the buyer to rescind. The buyer seeks advice on whether the remedy of rescission remains available. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Rescission remains available, because rescission for misrepresentation can never be lost by the passage of time.
Rescission is likely to be barred, because the buyer affirmed the contract after learning of the misrepresentation.
Rescission is barred only if a court has already ordered the buyer to keep the business.
Rescission remains available, provided the buyer is willing to pay the seller a sum for its trouble.
Rescission remains available, because a buyer's conduct after the contract is legally irrelevant.
Contract Law.w: Rescission may be lost where the innocent party, with knowledge of the misrepresentation, affirms the contract (by words or conduct treating it as continuing). Running the business, taking profits and indicating satisfaction after discovering the truth amounts to affirmation, barring rescission.

n.0: Rescission can indeed be lost, including by affirmation and by lapse of time.
n.2: Affirmation bars rescission without any court order requiring the buyer to keep the business.
n.3: Offering a payment does not revive a right to rescind that has been lost by affirmation.
n.4: Post-contract conduct is highly relevant; affirmation is judged by it.

Contract Law.q: A customer pays a £3,000 advance to a supplier under a contract, and further sums are due to become payable later, in return for goods the supplier is to manufacture. Before any goods are delivered, and after the supplier has already incurred some expenses in starting the work, the contract is frustrated by a supervening event for which neither party is responsible. The customer wants its £3,000 back, and the supplier says it should be able to keep something for the expenses it incurred. The parties seek advice under the relevant statute. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The customer recovers the full £3,000 automatically, and the supplier can never retain any of it.
All sums paid before frustration are simply forfeited to the supplier, whatever expenses it incurred.
The contract continues despite frustration, so all the originally agreed sums remain payable.
The customer must additionally pay the sums that had not yet fallen due before frustration.
Sums paid before frustration are recoverable and sums then due cease, subject to an expenses allowance.
Contract Law.w: Under the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943, money paid before frustration is recoverable and money then payable ceases to be due, but the court may allow a party who incurred expenses in performance to retain or recover a just sum for those expenses out of sums paid or payable.

n.0: Recovery is not automatic and unqualified; the court may allow the supplier its expenses.
n.1: Pre-payment is not simply forfeited; it is recoverable subject to allowance for expenses.
n.2: Frustration discharges the contract; the originally agreed sums do not all remain payable.
n.3: Sums not yet due at frustration cease to be payable; the customer need not pay them.

Contract Law.q: A commercial supply contract contains a detailed force majeure clause which sets out what is to happen if performance is prevented or delayed by specified events beyond the parties' control, including extreme weather and government action. Performance is then prevented by exactly such an event which falls squarely within the clause. One party argues that the position should be governed by the general common-law doctrine of frustration instead of the clause. The other relies on the clause. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The doctrine of frustration always overrides any force majeure clause the parties have agreed.
The clause applies only if the event also amounts to frustration at common law.
The force majeure clause governs, as the parties have expressly allocated the risk of the specified events.
The clause is void, because it attempts to exclude the operation of the general law.
The clause is ineffective, because parties cannot agree in advance what happens on such events.
Contract Law.w: Where the parties have made express provision, through a force majeure clause, for the very event that has occurred, that clause governs the consequences and allocates the risk between them. The common-law doctrine of frustration is displaced to the extent the contract has dealt with the event.

n.0: Frustration does not override an applicable express allocation of risk agreed by the parties.
n.1: The clause operates on its own terms; it is not confined to events that also frustrate the contract.
n.3: A force majeure clause is a legitimate allocation of risk, not a void attempt to oust the law.
n.4: Parties can and do provide in advance for such events; the clause is not ineffective for that.

Contract Law.q: A decorator agrees to redecorate a house for a lump sum of £5,000. The decorator completes essentially all of the work to a proper standard, but leaves a few minor defects which would cost about £150 to put right. The client, seizing on the defects, refuses to pay anything at all, arguing that the decorator has not completely performed the contract. The decorator sues for the price. The client seeks advice on whether they can withhold the whole £5,000 for these minor outstanding defects. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client may withhold the whole price until the decorator returns and remedies every last defect.
The decorator may recover the full £5,000, and the client has no remedy for the minor defects.
The decorator may recover only if the client first agrees in writing to accept the work as done.
The decorator may recover the price less the cost of remedying the minor defects, having substantially performed.
The decorator may recover nothing at all, because the contract was not completely performed to the letter.
Contract Law.w: Where a party has substantially performed an entire obligation, subject only to minor defects, they may recover the contract price less the cost of remedying those defects (Hoenig v Isaacs). The client cannot refuse the whole price for trivial shortcomings.

n.0: The client may deduct the remedial cost but cannot withhold the entire price for minor defects.
n.1: The client is entitled to deduct the cost of the defects, so the full price is not payable.
n.2: No further written acceptance is needed once there has been substantial performance.
n.4: Substantial performance does entitle the party to payment, so recovering nothing is wrong.

Contract Law.q: An employee is wrongfully dismissed in breach of contract and is entitled to damages. Shortly afterwards, the employee is offered a broadly equivalent job with another employer at a similar salary, which they could reasonably take, but they unreasonably refuse it and remain out of work, letting their losses mount. They then claim damages from the original employer for the whole of their continuing lost earnings. The former employer argues that the employee should not be compensated for losses they could have avoided. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employee cannot recover losses that could reasonably have been avoided by taking the alternative job.
The employee's damages are unaffected, because there is no duty to reduce one's losses in contract.
The employee must accept the very first alternative offered, whatever its terms, or recover nothing at all.
The employee may recover in full, provided the alternative job was with a different employer.
The employee may recover all continuing losses in full, regardless of the alternative job offer.
Contract Law.w: An innocent party must take reasonable steps to mitigate its loss and cannot recover for losses which could reasonably have been avoided. By unreasonably refusing suitable alternative employment, the employee cannot claim the losses that this would have prevented.

n.1: There is a requirement to mitigate loss in contract; damages reflect it.
n.2: The duty is to act reasonably, not to accept the first offer whatever its terms.
n.3: That the job was with a different employer does not excuse the failure to mitigate.
n.4: The failure to mitigate reduces recovery; full continuing losses are not recoverable.

Contract Law.q: Two companies, A and B, make a contract under which A promises B that A will pay a sum of money to C, a third party who is not a party to the contract and who has given no consideration. The contract does not mention the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 or purport to give C any right to enforce it; it is simply an arrangement between A and B. A fails to pay C, and C wishes to sue A directly for the money. C seeks advice on whether it can enforce the promise. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: C can enforce the contract, because C is the person who was actually meant to receive the money.
C can enforce the contract, provided C later gives some consideration to A for the promise.
C can always enforce any contract that mentions C or is intended to benefit C in some way.
C can enforce the contract, because privity of contract has been entirely abolished in English law.
C generally cannot enforce the contract, because C is not a party to it and the doctrine of privity applies.
Contract Law.w: Under the doctrine of privity, only a party to a contract can generally enforce it. C is not a party and, absent an applicable exception (such as the contract satisfying the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, which is not engaged here), C cannot enforce A's promise.

n.0: Being the intended recipient of the money does not overcome privity by itself.
n.1: Later providing consideration does not make a non-party able to sue on the contract.
n.2: Merely mentioning or benefiting C does not, without more, give C an enforceable right.
n.3: Privity has not been abolished; it has been modified by statute in defined circumstances.

Contract Law.q: A buyer is induced to enter a contract by a statement of fact which was false but which the maker honestly and reasonably believed to be true when it was made — an innocent misrepresentation. The buyer, on discovering the truth, wishes to set the contract aside. The court, however, considers that rescission would be a disproportionate response given the minor nature of the matter, and that it would be more appropriate to keep the contract on foot and compensate the buyer instead. Which of the following best describes the court's power?
o: The court may award damages as of right, in addition to rescission, for an innocent misrepresentation.
The court has a discretion to award damages in lieu of rescission for an innocent misrepresentation.
The court can do nothing, because an innocent misrepresentation gives rise to no remedy at all.
The court may only refer the parties to renegotiate the contract between themselves.
The court must always grant rescission for an innocent misrepresentation if the buyer asks for it.
Contract Law.w: Under section 2(2) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967, where a person would be entitled to rescind for a non-fraudulent (including innocent) misrepresentation, the court has a discretion to declare the contract subsisting and award damages in lieu of rescission where it is equitable to do so.

n.0: Damages under s.2(2) are in lieu of rescission, not an additional as-of-right award.
n.2: An innocent misrepresentation is not remediless; rescission or damages in lieu may follow.
n.3: The court has its own statutory remedy; it is not confined to sending the parties back to negotiate.
n.4: Rescission for innocent misrepresentation is not an absolute right; s.2(2) allows damages in lieu.

Contract Law.q: A supplier breaches a contract with a buyer, but on the facts the breach has in fact caused the buyer no financial loss at all: the buyer was able to obtain identical goods elsewhere at the same price and suffered no additional expense or damage of any kind. The buyer nonetheless wishes to bring proceedings to establish that the supplier was in breach of the contract. The buyer seeks advice on what, if anything, a court would award in these circumstances. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will award the buyer the profit the supplier made from breaching the contract.
The court will dismiss the claim entirely, because a breach causing no loss cannot be sued upon.
The court will award damages equal to the full contract price as a matter of course.
The court may award nominal damages to recognise the breach, even though no real loss was suffered.
The court will award substantial damages, because any breach of contract must be compensated in full.
Contract Law.w: Breach of contract is actionable without proof of loss. Where the innocent party has suffered no actual loss, the court will award nominal damages — a small sum recognising that a legal right has been infringed — rather than substantial compensation.

n.0: Damages compensate the claimant's loss; they do not, as a rule, strip the defendant's profit.
n.1: A breach is actionable even without loss, so the claim is not dismissed outright.
n.2: There is no rule awarding the full contract price regardless of loss.
n.4: Substantial damages are not awarded where no loss has been suffered.

Contract Law.q: A 17-year-old, who is not yet an adult, orders a quantity of basic clothing suitable to their actual needs from a retailer, but then refuses to pay, arguing that as a minor they cannot be bound by the contract. The goods supplied were necessaries appropriate to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements. The minor has taken delivery of the clothing. The retailer supplied everyday items genuinely suited to the young person's needs and station in life rather than extravagant luxuries, the goods were delivered and used, and the young person is now attempting to avoid paying anything at all by relying simply on being under age. Which of the following best describes the minor's liability?
o: The minor is liable to pay the full contract price regardless of whether it was reasonable.
The minor is liable only if a parent or guardian countersigned the order.
The minor is liable to pay a reasonable price for necessaries actually sold and delivered.
The minor is liable only if the goods were luxuries rather than basic items.
The minor is not liable at all, because contracts with minors are always entirely void.
Contract Law.w: Contracts with minors for necessaries (goods suitable to the minor's condition in life and to their actual requirements at the time) are binding, but the minor is liable only to pay a reasonable price, not necessarily the agreed price. Basic clothing suitable to the minor's needs can be necessaries, so the minor must pay a reasonable price for what was delivered.

n.0: Liability for necessaries is to pay a reasonable price, which may differ from the contract price.
n.1: A parent's countersignature is not required to make a minor liable for necessaries.
n.3: Liability arises precisely because the items were necessaries, not luxuries.
n.4: Contracts with minors are not all void; those for necessaries bind the minor.

Contract Law.q: A local authority is already under a public duty to provide a certain level of policing at a venue. The venue owner promises to pay the authority a sum in return for the authority providing exactly that level of policing, and no more, that it is already obliged by law to provide. A dispute arises over whether the venue owner must pay. The authority did no more than its existing public duty required. The venue owner wanted a visible police presence for its own commercial reasons and offered to pay for it, but what it was promised in return was no more than the level of policing the force was already legally obliged to provide to the public in any event, with nothing extra laid on. Which of the following best describes the enforceability of the promise to pay?
o: The promise is unenforceable, as performing an existing public duty is not good consideration.
The promise is unenforceable, because public authorities can never enter into contracts.
The promise is enforceable, because the venue owner received a practical benefit in every case.
The promise is enforceable, because any performance by a public body is automatically good consideration.
The promise is unenforceable, because contracts with public bodies require statutory authority in writing.
Contract Law.w: Merely performing an existing public duty, without exceeding it, is not good consideration for a promise of payment. Had the authority provided policing over and above its existing duty, that extra provision would be good consideration; but doing only what the law already requires provides nothing new to support the promise.

n.1: Public authorities can and do enter into enforceable contracts.
n.2: There is no relevant 'practical benefit' where the body does only what it was already bound to do.
n.3: Performance by a public body is not automatically good consideration if it merely fulfils an existing duty.
n.4: The problem is the absence of consideration, not a formality about statutory authority in writing.

Contract Law.q: Two parties contract for the sale of a specific cargo of goods which, unknown to either of them, had already ceased to exist at the time the contract was made, having perished before the agreement. Neither party was at fault, and both genuinely believed the goods still existed and could be sold and bought. When the true position emerges, a dispute arises as to the status of the contract. The buyer seeks advice on the effect of the parties' shared mistaken belief about the existence of the goods. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is voidable at the seller's option, because only the seller bears the risk of the goods.
The contract is void for common mistake, because the subject matter did not exist when it was made.
The contract is valid and the buyer must pay, because both parties acted entirely in good faith.
The contract is valid, because a mistake shared by both parties can never affect a contract.
The contract is void only if the seller expressly promised that the goods still existed.
Contract Law.w: Where both parties enter a contract under a shared fundamental mistake as to the existence of the subject matter (res extincta) — the goods having already perished — the contract is void for common mistake (Couturier v Hastie; and see s.6 Sale of Goods Act 1979).

n.0: The contract is void, not merely voidable at one party's option.
n.2: Good faith does not save a contract for the sale of goods that no longer existed.
n.3: A sufficiently fundamental common mistake does affect the contract, rendering it void.
n.4: The contract is void for the mistake itself; it does not turn on an express promise of existence.

Contract Law.q: A contract contains an exclusion clause which is worded in a way that is genuinely ambiguous: on one reading it excludes liability for a particular kind of loss, and on another reading it does not. The party who drafted the clause, and who now seeks to rely on it to avoid liability, argues for the wider reading that would defeat the claim against it. The other party argues for the narrower reading. The court must decide how to resolve the ambiguity in the clause. Which of the following best describes the approach the court will take?
o: The court will simply strike the ambiguous clause out of the contract altogether.
The court will ask the drafting party what it intended the clause to mean and adopt that meaning.
Any ambiguity in the clause is construed in favour of the party seeking to rely on it.
The court will always adopt whichever reading gives the clause the widest possible effect.
Any ambiguity in the clause is construed against the party seeking to rely on it.
Contract Law.w: Under the contra proferentem principle, an ambiguous exclusion or limitation clause is construed against the party who put it forward and seeks to rely on it, so the narrower interpretation that preserves liability is generally preferred where the wording is genuinely unclear.

n.0: The court construes the clause; it does not simply delete it for ambiguity.
n.1: The drafting party's subjective account of intention does not govern the construction.
n.2: Ambiguity is resolved against, not in favour of, the party relying on the clause.
n.3: The court does not automatically give an ambiguous exclusion its widest effect.

Contract Law.q: A buyer is induced to enter a contract by the seller's misrepresentation. After discovering the truth, the buyer nevertheless proceeds to treat the contract as continuing, using the subject matter and making further payments for a considerable time without protest, before eventually seeking to unwind the contract. The buyer clearly elected to continue with the contract after learning the full facts. The buyer now seeks rescission of the contract. The buyer had every opportunity to complain once the truth came out but instead pressed on with the arrangement, drawing benefits from it and paying further instalments over many months, and only when the venture later disappointed did the buyer turn round and try to unwind the whole thing. Which of the following best explains why rescission is likely to be unavailable?
o: Rescission is unavailable because misrepresentation never gives a right to rescind.
Rescission is unavailable because only the party who made the statement may rescind.
Rescission is unavailable solely because some time has passed since the contract.
Rescission is unavailable because the buyer suffered no loss of any kind.
The right to rescind has been lost by affirmation of the contract after discovering the truth.
Contract Law.w: Rescission is an equitable remedy that may be barred, including by affirmation: where the misrepresentee, with knowledge of the truth and of the right to rescind, elects to continue with the contract, the right to rescind is lost. The buyer's continued use and payment after discovering the truth amount to affirmation, barring rescission.

n.0: Misrepresentation can give a right to rescind; the point is that the right has been lost here.
n.1: It is the misled party who may rescind; that is not the reason it is barred.
n.2: Mere lapse of time is a separate potential bar; here the clear bar is affirmation by conduct.
n.3: The bar to rescission is affirmation, not the absence of loss.

Contract Law.q: A seller of a remote farm, which has never been used for sheep farming, tells a prospective buyer during negotiations that in the seller's view the land 'would probably support about 2,000 sheep'. The seller has no special knowledge of the land's carrying capacity and honestly holds that view, and the buyer knows the land has not previously been used in that way. The land in fact supports far fewer sheep, and the buyer claims misrepresentation. The buyer seeks advice on whether the statement was actionable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The statement is actionable, because the buyer relied on it in deciding whether to buy the farm.
The statement is likely a non-actionable statement of opinion, not a statement of fact, on these facts.
The statement is actionable, because a seller is always taken to guarantee the accuracy of their views.
The statement is an actionable misrepresentation, because any statement inducing a contract is one of fact.
The statement is an actionable misrepresentation, because it turned out to be inaccurate.
Contract Law.w: A genuine statement of opinion, honestly held by someone with no special knowledge and where both parties are equally able to judge, is not a statement of fact and is not actionable as a misrepresentation (Bisset v Wilkinson). The carrying-capacity estimate here is such an opinion.

n.0: Reliance alone does not make an honest opinion actionable if it is not a statement of fact.
n.2: A seller does not guarantee honest opinions where they have no special knowledge.
n.3: Not every inducing statement is one of fact; opinions and mere puffs are excluded.
n.4: Mere inaccuracy of an honest opinion does not convert it into an actionable misstatement of fact.

Contract Law.q: A seller of a second-hand car tells the buyer that the car has never been involved in an accident. The seller in fact knows perfectly well that the car was seriously damaged in a collision and repaired, and makes the statement deliberately to secure the sale. The buyer relies on it and buys the car, later discovering the truth and suffering loss as a result. The buyer wishes to know not only about setting the contract aside but also about recovering damages for the loss caused. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer has no claim, because a buyer of a used car is expected to have it independently inspected.
The buyer may rescind and claim damages in the tort of deceit, as the misrepresentation was fraudulent.
The buyer may rescind, but damages are never available for any kind of misrepresentation.
The buyer may claim damages only if they can prove the seller was merely careless rather than dishonest.
The buyer may claim damages only for losses the seller could reasonably have foreseen at the time.
Contract Law.w: A fraudulent misrepresentation is a false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly (Derry v Peek). It entitles the innocent party to rescind and to claim damages in the tort of deceit, which cover all losses flowing directly from the misrepresentation.

n.0: An expectation to inspect does not defeat a claim founded on a deliberate lie relied upon.
n.2: Damages are available for misrepresentation; fraudulent misrepresentation clearly attracts them.
n.3: Fraud is established here; the buyer need not show mere carelessness to recover.
n.4: Deceit damages are not limited by reasonable foreseeability; all direct losses are recoverable.

Contract Law.q: Two parties have an existing contract and later wish to change one of its terms. One party agrees to accept a later delivery date, but receives nothing in return from the other party for agreeing to the change; the other party gives no additional consideration and undertakes no fresh obligation. A dispute later arises and the first party seeks to go back on the agreed variation, arguing that it was not binding. The parties seek advice on whether the variation was effective. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The variation is not binding, as a contract variation generally needs consideration.
The variation is binding, because both parties simply agreed to it between themselves.
The variation is not binding, because contracts can never be varied once they have been made.
The variation is binding, provided it was recorded in writing and signed by both parties.
The variation is binding, because a contract can always be varied by later agreement without more.
Contract Law.w: A variation of a contract is itself a contract and generally requires consideration to be binding. Where one party gives nothing in return for the other's agreement to vary, the variation is unsupported by consideration and is not binding (subject to any estoppel).

n.1: Mere agreement to vary is not enough; consideration (or estoppel) is generally required.
n.2: Contracts can be varied; the issue here is the absence of consideration, not an absolute bar.
n.3: Writing and signature do not supply the missing consideration for a simple contract variation.
n.4: A variation is not automatically binding just because it is a later agreement.

Contract Law.q: A music hall is hired out to a performer for a series of concerts on specified dates. A few days before the first concert, and without any fault on the part of either party, the music hall is entirely destroyed by an accidental fire, so that the concerts cannot possibly take place there. The performer, who has spent money advertising the concerts, sues the owner for breach of contract for failing to make the hall available. The owner argues that the contract came to an end automatically when the hall was destroyed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is frustrated, as destruction of the subject matter made performance impossible.
The contract is frustrated only if it contained an express clause dealing with fire.
The owner is liable for breach, because the owner was obliged to make the hall available whatever happened.
The performer must still pay the hire charge, because the destruction was nobody's fault.
The contract remains fully binding, because a contract can never be discharged by later events.
Contract Law.w: Where performance becomes impossible because the specific subject matter of the contract is destroyed, without the fault of either party, the contract is discharged by frustration (Taylor v Caldwell). Neither party is then liable for non-performance.

n.1: Frustration operates by law on impossibility; it does not require an express fire clause.
n.2: The owner is not liable for breach where destruction of the hall frustrated the contract.
n.3: Frustration discharges future obligations, so the performer is not bound to pay the hire.
n.4: Contracts can be discharged by frustrating events; they are not always binding regardless.

Contract Law.q: A company agrees to carry out work for a customer at an agreed price. After the contract is made, the company finds that, because of unexpected increases in the cost of materials and labour, performing the work will be far more expensive and much less profitable than it had anticipated, though the work remains entirely possible to carry out. The company argues that the contract has been frustrated by these changed economic circumstances and that it is released from its obligations. The customer disputes this. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is not frustrated; performance is merely more expensive, not radically different.
The contract is frustrated, provided the company can show the loss it will suffer is substantial.
The contract is frustrated, because performing it is now significantly less profitable than expected.
The contract is frustrated, because the company did not foresee the increase when it contracted.
The contract is frustrated, because any unexpected rise in costs discharges a contract.
Contract Law.w: Frustration requires performance to become impossible, illegal or radically different from what was undertaken. Mere increased cost, hardship or reduced profitability does not frustrate a contract (Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC), so the company remains bound.

n.1: The size of the loss does not turn mere expense into frustration.
n.2: Reduced profitability alone does not amount to frustration.
n.3: Failure to foresee a cost increase does not, by itself, frustrate the contract.
n.4: An unexpected rise in costs does not discharge a contract that remains possible to perform.

Contract Law.q: A textile manufacturer agrees to buy a large quantity of cloth from a wholesaler 'by sample', a small swatch having been shown and approved at the time of contracting. When the bulk is delivered, it matches the swatch in colour but, unlike the sample, contains a hidden weaving defect that a reasonable examination of the sample would not have revealed, making the bulk unusable. The contract was expressly a sale by sample under the Sale of Goods Act 1979. The bulk differs from the sample in a way not apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. Which of the following best describes the buyer's position?
o: The buyer may claim for breach of the implied term that the bulk correspond with the sample in quality.
The buyer has no claim, because a sale by sample implies no terms about the bulk.
The buyer has no claim, because inspection of a sample always waives all later complaints on these facts.
The buyer may claim only if the bulk also failed to match the sample in colour.
The buyer may claim only if the wholesaler expressly guaranteed the bulk in writing.
Contract Law.w: On a sale by sample under s.15 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, there are implied terms that the bulk will correspond with the sample in quality and that the goods will be free from any defect making quality unsatisfactory that would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. The hidden weaving defect breaches those implied terms.

n.1: A sale by sample does imply terms linking the bulk to the sample.
n.2: Examining a sample does not waive complaints about defects not reasonably apparent from the sample.
n.3: The correspondence term covers quality, not only colour, so a quality defect suffices.
n.4: The implied terms arise by statute and do not depend on an express written guarantee.

Contract Law.q: A buyer contracts to buy goods from a seller for £10,000, intending to resell them. The seller fails to deliver, and by the time of the breach the market price of equivalent goods has risen so that the buyer has to pay £13,000 to buy replacements elsewhere. The buyer claims damages from the seller for the breach of contract. The seller argues that it should only have to refund any deposit, and should not have to compensate the buyer for the higher price paid to a substitute supplier. Which of the following best describes the measure of damages?
o: Damages should put the buyer in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed.
Damages are limited to refunding any deposit the buyer had actually paid to the seller.
Damages should put the buyer in the position it was in before the contract was ever made.
Damages are limited to the seller's own lost profit on the transaction that was not performed.
Damages are not available at all, because the buyer was able to obtain substitute goods elsewhere.
Contract Law.w: The normal measure of contractual damages is the expectation measure: to put the innocent party, so far as money can, in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed. Here that is broadly the extra £3,000 the buyer had to pay for replacement goods.

n.1: Damages are not limited to a refund of the deposit; they protect the buyer's expectation.
n.2: The pre-contract position is the reliance measure, not the normal expectation measure.
n.3: Damages compensate the buyer's loss, not the seller's lost profit.
n.4: Obtaining substitutes does not remove the claim; the extra cost of doing so is the loss.

Contract Law.q: Two businesses contract on one party's written standard terms of business. Those terms include a clause excluding all liability for defective goods, including liability for the goods being of unsatisfactory quality. When the goods prove defective and the buyer complains, the seller relies on the clause. The buyer accepts that the clause was properly incorporated into the contract, but argues that it should not be allowed to operate to defeat the claim entirely. The court must decide whether the clause is effective. Which of the following best describes the test the court applies?
o: The clause is effective only if the buyer expressly agreed to it in a separate signed document.
The clause is effective only so far as it satisfies the UCTA 1977 reasonableness requirement.
The clause is automatically void, because a business can never exclude liability for defective goods.
The clause is effective only if the seller can show the buyer suffered no real loss.
The clause is automatically effective, because it was validly incorporated into the contract.
Contract Law.w: Where one business deals on the other's written standard terms, a clause excluding liability for breach (including the statutory implied terms as to quality in a business sale) is subject to the requirement of reasonableness under UCTA 1977, and is effective only so far as it is reasonable.

n.0: A separate signed document is not the statutory test; reasonableness is.
n.2: Businesses can exclude some liability for defective goods if the clause is reasonable, so it is not automatically void.
n.3: The test is the reasonableness of the clause, not whether the buyer suffered loss.
n.4: Valid incorporation is not enough; such a clause must also satisfy the reasonableness test.

Contract Law.q: A buyer agrees to buy a cargo of cotton from a seller 'to arrive on the ship Peerless from Bombay'. Unknown to either party, there are in fact two ships called Peerless sailing from Bombay, one in October and one in December. The buyer means the October ship and the seller means the December ship, and there is nothing to show which was objectively intended. When the goods arrive on the later ship, the buyer refuses to take them, and a dispute arises as to whether any contract was ever formed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a binding contract, and the court will simply choose whichever ship is more convenient.
There is a binding contract on the seller's understanding, because the seller shipped the goods.
There is a binding contract on the buyer's understanding, because the buyer spoke first in negotiations.
There is no contract, because the parties were at cross purposes on a fundamental matter with no agreed meaning.
There is a binding contract, because the written term named a ship called Peerless in any event.
Contract Law.w: Where the parties are genuinely at cross purposes over a fundamental term and there is no objective basis to prefer one meaning, there is no consensus and hence no contract (Raffles v Wichelhaus). The ambiguity as to which Peerless was meant prevents agreement.

n.0: The court will not pick a meaning for the parties where the term is truly ambiguous.
n.1: Shipping the goods does not impose the seller's meaning where there was never consensus.
n.2: Who spoke first does not resolve a mutual mistake; there is simply no agreement.
n.4: Naming 'Peerless' does not create agreement when the name identified two different ships.

Contract Law.q: A commercial contract for the operation of a business is silent on a particular point, and a dispute arises about an obligation that the contract does not expressly address. One party argues that a term should be implied into the contract to give it business efficacy, because without it the contract would not work as the parties must obviously have intended. The other party resists implying any term that the parties did not expressly write down. The court considers whether to imply the term in fact. Which of the following best describes the test the court applies?
o: A term may be implied whenever it would be fair and reasonable to include it in the contract.
A term may never be implied into a contract that the parties have reduced to writing.
A term is implied in fact only if necessary for business efficacy or obvious (officious bystander).
A term may be implied only where one party can show the other acted in bad faith.
A term may be implied whenever it would make the contract more commercially advantageous to one party.
Contract Law.w: A term is implied in fact only where it is necessary to give the contract business efficacy, or is so obvious that it goes without saying (the officious bystander test). It is not enough that the term would merely be fair, reasonable or commercially desirable.

n.0: Mere fairness or reasonableness is not the test for implying a term in fact; necessity or obviousness is.
n.1: Terms can be implied into written contracts where the strict test is met.
n.3: Bad faith by one party is not the basis for implying a term in fact.
n.4: Commercial advantage to one party is not a ground for implication; necessity is.

Contract Law.q: A seller posts a written offer to a buyer to sell goods, and the parties have throughout conducted their dealings by ordinary post. On receiving the offer the buyer immediately posts a letter of acceptance, properly addressed and stamped. Unknown to the buyer, that letter is delayed and then lost in the post, and it never reaches the seller at all. Before anything further happens, the seller, having heard nothing, sells the goods to someone else, and the buyer claims there was already a binding contract between them. The buyer seeks advice on whether a contract was formed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No contract was formed, because a lost letter of acceptance can never take effect in law.
Acceptance took effect when the letter was posted, so a binding contract was formed at that moment.
A contract was formed only if the buyer can prove the seller in fact received the letter of acceptance.
No contract was formed, because acceptance is only ever effective when it actually reaches the offeror.
A contract was formed only when the seller ought reasonably to have expected the letter to arrive.
Contract Law.w: Under the postal rule, where post is a reasonable means of acceptance, acceptance takes effect when the letter is posted, not when it is received, even if it is delayed or lost (Adams v Lindsell; Household Fire Insurance v Grant). A contract was therefore formed when the buyer posted the acceptance.

n.0: A properly posted acceptance is effective even though the letter is lost.
n.2: Actual receipt need not be proved where the postal rule applies.
n.3: For postal acceptance the general receipt rule is displaced by the postal rule.
n.4: The rule fixes the time of acceptance at posting, not at the seller's expected delivery date.

Contract Law.q: A company markets a health product with a widely published advertisement promising to pay £100 to any purchaser who uses the product correctly and still catches influenza, and stating that it has deposited a sum with its bank to show its sincerity. A customer buys the product, uses it exactly as directed, and nevertheless catches influenza. When the customer claims the £100, the company argues that the advertisement was mere sales talk, that the customer never communicated any acceptance to the company, and that there was therefore no binding contract. The customer seeks advice on whether they are entitled to the £100. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A contract formed when the customer performed the act; acceptance need not be separately communicated.
There is no contract, because the deposit with the bank was not a genuine offer to the public.
There is no contract, because an advertisement of this kind can never amount to a binding offer.
There is no contract, because the customer never notified the company that they accepted the offer.
There is a contract, but only if the customer had told the company in advance that they would use the product.
Contract Law.w: A unilateral offer, made to the world and intended to be acted upon, is accepted by performing the required act, and full performance dispenses with the need to communicate acceptance in advance (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co). Using the product as directed formed a binding contract.

n.1: The deposit reinforced, rather than negated, the intention to be bound by the promise.
n.2: An advertisement can amount to a binding unilateral offer where it shows an intention to be bound.
n.3: For a unilateral offer, performance is acceptance; separate communication is not required.
n.4: Advance notification of intention to perform is not required for acceptance of a unilateral offer.

Contract Law.q: A retailer displays a television in its shop window with a price label attached reading '£299'. A customer sees the label, goes into the shop, and tells a member of staff that they wish to buy the television at that price. The staff member, having just realised that the label was wrong and that the television should have been priced at £499, refuses to sell it at £299. The customer insists that, by displaying the price, the shop made an offer which the customer has now accepted, so that there is a binding contract at £299. The customer seeks advice on whether that is correct. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The display is a firm offer, so the customer's acceptance created a binding contract at the labelled price of £299.
The display is an offer, and the shop is bound to sell at £299 unless the mistake was caused by the customer.
The display is a firm offer, but the shop may withdraw it at any time even after the customer has accepted it.
The display is an offer to the world, which anyone who tenders the labelled price is automatically entitled to accept.
The display is an invitation to treat, so it is the customer who makes the offer, which the shop may accept or reject.
Contract Law.w: Goods displayed in a shop window or on the shelves, with a price, are an invitation to treat, not an offer (Fisher v Bell; Pharmaceutical Society v Boots). The customer makes the offer to buy, which the shop is free to accept or reject, so there is no contract at £299.

n.0: A priced display is an invitation to treat, not an offer capable of acceptance.
n.1: There is no offer by the shop, so the cause of the mistake is irrelevant to formation.
n.2: As the display is not an offer, no contract arose that could be withdrawn.
n.3: A shop display is not an offer to the world; that analysis applies to certain unilateral offers, not priced displays.

Contract Law.q: A business buys a quantity of steel from another business for use in manufacturing. The steel supplied turns out to be of a lower grade than steel of that description should be, and is not of the quality that a reasonable person would regard as satisfactory given the price and description. The buyer, which is not a consumer, wishes to know the legal basis on which it can complain about the quality of the goods it received under this commercial sale. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The Sale of Goods Act 1979 implies terms of satisfactory quality and correspondence with description.
The buyer has no remedy, because quality obligations apply only where the buyer is a consumer.
The buyer has no remedy unless the contract expressly promised a particular quality of steel.
The buyer's only remedy is in the tort of negligence against the manufacturer of the steel.
The buyer may rely only on the Consumer Rights Act 2015, which governs all sales of goods.
Contract Law.w: In a business-to-business sale, the Sale of Goods Act 1979 implies terms that the goods will be of satisfactory quality (s.14), fit for purpose where relevant, and correspond with their description (s.13). The buyer can rely on those implied terms even without an express quality clause.

n.1: Quality obligations are not limited to consumers; the SGA 1979 implies them into business sales.
n.2: The implied terms apply automatically; an express quality promise is not required.
n.3: The buyer has contractual remedies against the seller under the implied terms, not only a tort claim.
n.4: The Consumer Rights Act governs consumer contracts; business sales are governed by the SGA 1979.

Contract Law.q: A charterer hires a ship under a contract containing a term that the vessel is to be 'in every way fitted for ordinary cargo service'. On delivery the vessel has some engine problems and an inefficient crew, which cause delays while repairs are carried out, but the vessel remains available for a substantial part of the charter period and can still perform the essential purpose of the contract. The charterer purports to terminate the whole charter for breach of that term. The shipowner disputes the right to terminate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The charterer may terminate only if the shipowner acted deliberately or dishonestly.
The charterer may terminate only if the contract expressly labelled the term a condition.
The charterer may never terminate, because a seaworthiness term is only ever a warranty.
Whether the charterer may terminate depends on how serious the breach and its consequences actually are.
The charterer may terminate automatically, because any breach of a seaworthiness term ends the contract.
Contract Law.w: A term of this kind is an innominate (intermediate) term. The remedy depends on the seriousness of the breach and its consequences: only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract may they terminate (Hong Kong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki).

n.0: The right to terminate turns on the seriousness of the breach, not the shipowner's state of mind.
n.1: The consequences-based approach applies even without an express 'condition' label.
n.2: Such a term is not automatically a mere warranty either; it depends on the breach.
n.4: An innominate term is not treated as a condition breached by any deviation.

Contract Law.q: An elderly parent, who relies heavily on their adult child for advice and management of their financial affairs and reposes complete trust in them, transfers a valuable property to that child at a substantial undervalue, in a transaction that is not readily explicable by the ordinary relationship between them. The parent received no independent advice. The parent later wishes to set the transfer aside, arguing that it resulted from the influence the child had over them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transaction stands, because undue influence applies only between spouses, not parent and child.
The transaction may be set aside, as undue influence is presumed from the relationship and suspicious transaction.
The transaction stands, because a parent is always free to give property to their own child.
The transaction can be set aside only if the child obtained the property by a written misrepresentation.
The transaction can be set aside only if the parent proves the child made explicit threats.
Contract Law.w: Where there is a relationship of trust and confidence and a transaction that calls for explanation, undue influence is presumed and the burden shifts to the party benefiting to rebut it (e.g. by showing independent advice). Absent such rebuttal, the transaction may be set aside (Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge).

n.0: Undue influence is not confined to spouses; parent–child is a recognised relationship of influence.
n.2: Freedom to make gifts does not prevent a transaction being set aside for undue influence.
n.3: Undue influence does not depend on a written misrepresentation.
n.4: Presumed undue influence does not require proof of explicit threats.

Contract Law.q: A buyer contracts to purchase goods 'described as new' from a seller. The written contract describes the goods by that description, and the buyer relies on the description in agreeing to buy. When the goods arrive they are in fact second-hand and reconditioned, and so do not correspond with the description under which they were sold. The buyer wishes to know the basis on which it can complain, and in particular whether the description formed part of the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The description is a term of the contract, and goods sold by description must correspond with that description.
The description binds the buyer, not the seller, so the buyer must accept the goods as delivered.
The description is a mere representation, so the buyer's only possible claim is for misrepresentation.
The description has no legal effect, because descriptions of goods are always mere sales talk.
The description is a term only if the buyer inspected the goods before agreeing to buy them.
Contract Law.w: Where goods are sold by description and the buyer relies on that description, there is an implied condition that the goods will correspond with the description (s.13 Sale of Goods Act 1979). The description is a contractual term, and delivering non-conforming goods breaches it.

n.1: The description binds the seller to supply conforming goods, not the buyer to accept whatever arrives.
n.2: A description relied upon in a sale by description is a term, not merely a representation.
n.3: Contractual descriptions of goods are not merely sales talk; they have legal effect.
n.4: Correspondence with description does not depend on the buyer having inspected the goods.

Contract Law.q: A seller offers in writing to sell a car to a buyer, stating that the offer will remain open for a week. Two days later, and before the buyer has said anything in response, the seller telephones the buyer and clearly tells them that the offer is withdrawn because the seller has decided to keep the car. The buyer, who had not yet paid anything or given anything in return for the promise to keep the offer open, nonetheless purports the next day to accept the original offer, insisting that it had to stay open for the full week. The buyer seeks advice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The revocation was ineffective, because the seller had promised to keep the offer open for a week.
The revocation was ineffective, because it was made by telephone rather than in writing.
The revocation was effective, because it was communicated to the buyer before the offer was accepted.
The revocation was effective only if the seller returned any deposit the buyer had paid.
The revocation was ineffective, because an offer can never be withdrawn once it has been made.
Contract Law.w: An offer may be revoked at any time before acceptance, provided the revocation is communicated to the offeree. A promise to keep an offer open is not binding without consideration, so the seller was free to revoke, and did so effectively before the buyer accepted.

n.0: The promise to keep the offer open was not supported by consideration, so it did not bind the seller.
n.1: Revocation may be communicated in any way that reaches the offeree, including by telephone.
n.3: No deposit had been paid, and its return is not a condition of effective revocation here.
n.4: Offers can generally be revoked before acceptance; they are not irrevocable.

Contract Law.q: An elderly parent transfers a valuable property to an adult child for little or no payment. The parent had come to rely heavily on the child in all financial matters and reposed complete trust and confidence in the child, and the transaction is one that calls for explanation as it is not readily explicable by the ordinary motives of people in such a relationship. No independent advice was taken. The relationship was one of trust and confidence and the transaction is not readily explicable by ordinary motives. Which of the following best describes the parent's strongest ground to set the transfer aside?
o: Economic duress, arising from an illegitimate threat by the child.
Presumed undue influence, arising from the relationship of trust and a transaction calling for explanation.
Common mistake, because both parties misunderstood the transaction on these facts as a general rule.
Frustration, because circumstances changed after the transfer.
Breach of an implied term that gifts be fair in amount.
Contract Law.w: Presumed undue influence can arise where there is a relationship in which one party reposes trust and confidence in the other and the transaction calls for explanation (is not readily explicable by ordinary motives). Those elements raise a presumption of undue influence, which the other party may rebut, typically by showing the transferor had independent advice.

n.0: Duress requires illegitimate pressure/threats, which is not what is described.
n.2: There is no shared mistake about the transaction; the concern is influence over the parent.
n.3: Frustration concerns supervening events defeating performance, not the fairness of a gift.
n.4: There is no implied term requiring gifts to be fair; the doctrine in point is undue influence.

Contract Law.q: During pre-contract discussions to sell a car, the seller tells the buyer that the car has 'done only 20,000 miles', which the seller genuinely believes. The parties later sign a detailed written contract for the sale which contains a clause stating that it constitutes the entire agreement between them and that no statement made during negotiations forms part of the contract. The mileage statement turns out to be wrong. The buyer wishes to sue for breach of contract, treating the mileage statement as a contractual term. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The mileage statement is a term, because the entire agreement clause is automatically void.
The mileage statement is unlikely to be a term, given the entire agreement clause.
The mileage statement is automatically a term, because it was important to the buyer's decision.
The mileage statement is a term, because any statement made before a contract becomes part of it.
The mileage statement is a term, because the seller genuinely believed that it was true.
Contract Law.w: An 'entire agreement' clause is designed to confine the contract to its written terms and to exclude prior statements from forming part of the contract. Its presence makes it unlikely that the pre-contract mileage statement is a contractual term, though it may still found a misrepresentation claim.

n.0: Entire agreement clauses are generally effective and are not automatically void.
n.2: Importance to the buyer does not make a statement a term where an entire agreement clause excludes prior statements.
n.3: Not every pre-contract statement becomes a term; many are representations only.
n.4: The seller's honest belief goes to whether any misrepresentation was innocent, not to whether the statement is a term.

Contract Law.q: An individual is injured when a machine, hired to them under a written business contract, malfunctions because of the supplier's negligence. The hire contract contains a clause stating that the supplier accepts no liability whatsoever for death or personal injury, however caused, including by its own negligence. The supplier relies on that clause to defeat the injured person's claim for their physical injuries. The injured person seeks advice on whether the clause can lawfully exclude liability for the personal injury. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The clause is ineffective only if the supplier acted deliberately rather than merely negligently.
The clause is ineffective to exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.
The clause is effective, provided it passes the general test of reasonableness.
The clause is effective, because the parties freely agreed to it in a written contract.
The clause is effective, because the injured person is treated as a business rather than a consumer.
Contract Law.w: Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence cannot be excluded or restricted by a contract term at all. Such a clause is automatically ineffective and does not even reach the reasonableness test.

n.0: The clause fails because it excludes negligence liability for injury, not because of any lack of intent.
n.2: This category is a blanket prohibition, not subject to the reasonableness test.
n.3: Free agreement does not save a clause excluding liability for negligent personal injury.
n.4: The prohibition applies regardless of whether the injured party is a business or consumer.

Contract Law.q: An elderly person with poor eyesight is asked to sign a document by someone they trust. They are told it is a minor form of one kind, when in fact it is a deed of a fundamentally different character that disposes of a valuable asset. Without reading it (being unable to do so) and relying on the misdescription, they sign. They later discover the true nature of what they signed and seek to escape it entirely. The signer was fundamentally mistaken about the very nature of the document, not merely its terms, and was not careless in the circumstances. Which of the following best describes the plea available to the signer?
o: The signer may rescind only, so a good-faith third party would still take free.
The signer has no remedy because non est factum has been abolished.
The signer may plead non est factum, so that the signature is not binding.
The signer is bound absolutely, because a signature always binds regardless of the circumstances.
The signer may rely on common mistake shared with the other party.
