Contract Law.w: The plea of non est factum ('it is not my deed') may be available, exceptionally, where a signer is fundamentally mistaken as to the very nature (not merely the contents) of the document, and was not careless. If made out, the document is void, not merely voidable, so the signer is not bound. The plea is narrow and rarely succeeds.

n.0: A successful non est factum renders the document void, going further than mere rescission.
n.1: Non est factum has not been abolished; it survives as a narrow doctrine.
n.3: A signature does not always bind where non est factum is genuinely made out.
n.4: The signer's mistake is unilateral and fundamental, not a common mistake shared by both parties.

Contract Law.q: A buyer contracts to purchase a particular house, a unique property, and the seller then refuses to complete the sale in breach of contract, having received a higher offer from someone else. The buyer does not want damages; it wants the house itself, which is exactly what it bargained for and which cannot readily be replaced by buying an equivalent elsewhere. The buyer seeks advice on whether the court can compel the seller to go through with the sale. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will order specific performance automatically for any breach of any contract.
The court will refuse specific performance, because it never compels the sale of property.
The court may order specific performance, as damages are inadequate where the subject matter is unique land.
The court can never order specific performance, and the buyer's only remedy is damages.
The court will order specific performance only if the seller acted dishonestly in refusing to complete.
Contract Law.w: Specific performance is a discretionary equitable remedy granted where damages are an inadequate remedy. Contracts for the sale of land are the classic case, because each piece of land is regarded as unique, so the court may order the seller to complete the sale.

n.0: Specific performance is discretionary and not granted automatically for every contract.
n.1: The court does order the sale of land by specific performance; that is the classic example.
n.3: Specific performance is available for land; the buyer is not confined to damages.
n.4: The remedy does not depend on proving dishonesty by the seller.

Contract Law.q: A consumer buys a new washing machine from a retailer. Ten days after delivery, the machine develops a serious fault which means it does not work properly and is not of satisfactory quality. The consumer returns to the retailer and says that they no longer want the machine and want their money back straight away, rather than a repair or replacement. The retailer says the consumer is only entitled to a repair. The consumer seeks advice on their rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The consumer may reject the goods only if the retailer is first given a chance to repair them.
The consumer may reject the goods only within 14 days of delivery, and that period has now expired.
The consumer's only entitlement is to a repair or replacement, and never to a refund of the price.
The consumer has no rights at all, because the machine worked when it was first delivered.
The consumer has the short-term right to reject and get a refund, the fault appearing within 30 days.
Contract Law.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, goods must be of satisfactory quality, and the consumer has a short-term right to reject faulty goods and obtain a refund if they do so within 30 days of ownership passing. The consumer here is within that period.

n.0: The short-term right to reject does not require giving the retailer a chance to repair first.
n.1: The short-term right to reject lasts 30 days, not 14, so it has not expired.
n.2: The consumer is not confined to repair or replacement; the short-term right to reject gives a refund.
n.3: Later failure to meet satisfactory quality still gives rights, even if the machine initially worked.

Contract Law.q: A person, at another's request, carries out substantial services for that other in circumstances where both understood the services were to be paid for, but no price was ever fixed or agreed between them. When the work is complete, the parties fall out over payment, and it emerges that there was never a concluded agreement as to the amount to be paid. The person who did the work wishes to be paid a fair sum for the work actually done and requested. Which of the following best describes the basis of the claim?
o: The person may claim nothing, because no price for the services was ever agreed between the parties.
The person may claim only if the services were provided under a fully concluded written contract.
The person may claim only the amount they personally hoped to be paid for the work.
The person may claim a quantum meruit — a reasonable sum for the value of the services requested and provided.
The person may claim the highest price that any provider could conceivably have charged.
Contract Law.w: Where services are requested and provided on the understanding that they will be paid for, but no price is agreed, the provider may recover a quantum meruit — a reasonable sum for the value of the work done — under the law of restitution or an implied term as to reasonable remuneration.

n.0: The absence of an agreed price does not defeat the claim; a reasonable sum is recoverable.
n.1: A quantum meruit can arise without a concluded written contract fixing the price.
n.2: The measure is an objectively reasonable sum, not the claimant's private hopes.
n.4: The claim is for a reasonable sum, not the highest conceivable charge.

Contract Law.q: A seller during negotiations makes an accurate statement of fact to the buyer, but before the contract is signed the position changes so that the statement, though true when made, has become false by the time of contracting. The seller becomes aware of the change but says nothing to the buyer, who enters the contract still relying on the original statement. When the buyer discovers the true position, they claim misrepresentation. The seller argues that the statement was true when it was originally made. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There may be an actionable misrepresentation, as a statement that becomes false before contracting must be corrected.
There is a misrepresentation only if the change of circumstances was caused by the seller's own act.
There is a misrepresentation only if the buyer expressly asked the seller to confirm the statement again.
There is no misrepresentation, because a seller is never under any duty to update earlier statements.
There is no misrepresentation, because the statement was entirely true at the time it was first made.
Contract Law.w: A representation is treated as continuing until the contract is made. If a statement, true when made, becomes false before contracting and the representor knows this, they must correct it; failing to do so can be an actionable misrepresentation (With v O'Flanagan).

n.1: The duty to correct does not depend on the seller having caused the change of circumstances.
n.2: The duty to correct arises whether or not the buyer asks for reconfirmation.
n.3: There is a duty to correct a continuing representation that has become false before contracting.
n.4: Truth at the time of making does not excuse failing to correct a statement that later becomes false.

Contract Law.q: During negotiations to buy a horse from his nephew, a man writes to the nephew saying that, if he hears nothing more, he will consider the horse to be his at a stated price. The nephew does not reply to that letter, but privately tells an auctioneer to keep the horse out of a forthcoming sale because he intends to sell it to his uncle. The auctioneer mistakenly sells the horse anyway, and the uncle claims that a binding contract to buy the horse had already been formed with his nephew by the time of the sale. The uncle seeks advice on whether that is correct. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a contract, because the uncle validly stipulated that silence would count as acceptance.
There is a contract, because the nephew's silence amounted to acceptance of the uncle's offer.
There is a contract, because the nephew's instruction to the auctioneer was itself the acceptance.
There is no contract, because an offer to buy a horse must always be made in writing signed by both.
There is no contract, because silence cannot be imposed on the nephew as a mode of acceptance.
Contract Law.w: An offeror cannot stipulate that the offeree's silence will constitute acceptance; acceptance must generally be communicated (Felthouse v Bindley). The nephew's uncommunicated intention did not create a contract, so no binding agreement had been formed when the horse was sold.

n.0: An offeror cannot validly impose silence as a mode of acceptance on the offeree.
n.1: Silence does not amount to acceptance, even where the offeror purports to treat it as such.
n.2: The nephew's private instruction to the auctioneer was not communicated to the uncle as an acceptance.
n.3: There is no rule requiring a contract for the sale of a horse to be in signed writing.

Contract Law.q: A building contractor engages a carpenter to complete joinery work on a development for a fixed price. Part-way through, the carpenter runs into financial difficulty and warns that he may not finish on time, which would expose the contractor to heavy penalties under the main building contract. To keep the work on track, the contractor promises the carpenter an extra payment for each flat completed on time. The carpenter completes the remaining flats on time in reliance on that promise, but the contractor then refuses to pay the extra sums, saying the carpenter was only doing what he was already contractually bound to do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The extra payment is unenforceable, because the carpenter merely performed an existing contractual duty.
The extra payment is unenforceable, because a promise to pay more for the same work is always void.
The extra payment is enforceable, but only if the carpenter first threatened to stop work altogether.
The extra payment is enforceable: completing on time gave a practical benefit and there was no duress.
The extra payment is unenforceable, because the original fixed price can never afterwards be varied.
Contract Law.w: Where a party promises extra payment to secure performance of an existing contractual duty and thereby obtains a practical benefit (such as avoiding a penalty and the trouble of finding another contractor), that can be good consideration, provided the promise was not obtained by economic duress (Williams v Roffey Bros).

n.0: Performing an existing duty can be consideration where it confers a practical benefit, as here.
n.1: A promise to pay more for existing work is not automatically void.
n.2: A threat to stop work is not required; indeed such duress would defeat the claim.
n.4: A fixed price can be varied where the variation is supported by consideration such as a practical benefit.

Contract Law.q: A party to a contract wishes to transfer to a third party not only the benefit of the contract (the right to receive performance) but also the burden (its own obligations to perform), so as to be released from those obligations. The other contracting party has not agreed to release the transferor. The transferor seeks to shed its own contractual obligations. The contracting party wants to offload not just the right to receive performance but its own side of the bargain, its obligations, onto a third party and walk away free of them, but the other party to the contract has never agreed to let the transferor off the hook. Which of the following best describes the position on assigning the burden of a contract?
o: Neither the benefit nor the burden of a contract can ever be transferred.
The burden of a contract can be freely assigned in the same way as the benefit on these facts as a general rule.
The burden passes automatically to anyone who receives the benefit.
The burden can be assigned provided notice is given to the other party.
The burden of a contract cannot generally be assigned without the other party's consent; only the benefit is assignable.
Contract Law.w: While the benefit of a contract can generally be assigned, the burden (a party's obligations) cannot be transferred to a third party without the other party's consent. To transfer obligations and be released, the parties must novate the contract (a tripartite agreement replacing the old contract with a new one), rather than simply assigning.

n.0: The benefit can be assigned, so it is not the case that nothing can be transferred.
n.1: The burden is not freely assignable like the benefit.
n.2: Receiving the benefit does not automatically impose the burden.
n.3: Mere notice does not transfer the burden; the other party's agreement (novation) is needed.

Contract Law.q: A wholesaler tells a retailer that it will not enforce the full contract price for a delivery, and the retailer, relying on that assurance, forgoes arranging alternative finance. No fresh consideration is given by the retailer for the wholesaler's assurance. Later the wholesaler seeks to recover the full price, and the retailer argues the assurance is binding. The retailer relied on the assurance but gave nothing in return. The retailer took the wholesaler at its word, decided against lining up alternative finance it could otherwise have arranged, and ordered its affairs accordingly, only for the wholesaler to change its position and demand the whole contract price after all, leaving the retailer to argue the earlier assurance still binds. Which of the following best describes the likely effect of promissory estoppel here?
o: Estoppel permanently extinguishes the wholesaler's right to the balance in all cases on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Estoppel has no possible application because the retailer gave no consideration.
Estoppel gives the retailer a free-standing right to sue the wholesaler for damages.
Estoppel applies only where the parties intended to create a deed.
Estoppel may prevent the wholesaler going back on the assurance for now, but it is a shield and generally suspensory, not a cause of action.
Contract Law.w: Promissory estoppel can prevent a promisor going back on a clear promise, intended to be relied on and in fact relied on, where it would be inequitable to resile. But it operates as a defence ('a shield not a sword'), does not require consideration, and is generally suspensory: it may postpone rather than permanently extinguish the right, which can sometimes be reasserted on reasonable notice.

n.0: Its effect is generally suspensory, not automatically permanent extinction in all cases.
n.1: Estoppel can apply precisely where there is no consideration; that is its purpose here.
n.2: Estoppel does not create a free-standing cause of action for damages.
n.3: Estoppel does not depend on the parties intending to create a deed.

Contract Law.q: A joiner agrees to build and fit a complete bespoke staircase for a fixed lump sum of £8,000, payable on completion of the whole job. After doing a substantial part of the work, the joiner abandons the project entirely and never returns, leaving the staircase unusable and unfinished. The client has to engage another joiner to finish it. The original joiner now claims to be paid a proportion of the £8,000 for the work he did carry out. The client refuses to pay him anything. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The joiner cannot recover any of the price, as it was payable only on complete performance.
The joiner may recover the price, because the client will benefit from the finished staircase.
The joiner may recover the full £8,000, because he did the greater part of the work involved.
The joiner may recover the price in full, subject only to a small deduction for the unfinished part.
The joiner may recover a fair proportion of the price for the work he actually did before abandoning it.
Contract Law.w: Where payment is due only on completion of an entire obligation, a party who fails to complete cannot recover the price, or any part of it, for incomplete performance (Cutter v Powell; Sumpter v Hedges). The joiner, having abandoned the job, cannot claim the lump sum or a proportion of it.

n.1: The client's eventual benefit from another joiner's work does not entitle the defaulting joiner to payment.
n.2: Doing the greater part does not entitle him to the full price where the obligation is entire and unfinished.
n.3: He is not entitled to the price less a deduction, because he did not substantially perform.
n.4: An entire obligation must be completed before the price is earned; part performance earns nothing.

Contract Law.q: A contractor is engaged to perform services over a period. Part-way through, the client indicates in advance that it will not perform its side of the bargain, an anticipatory breach which the contractor could accept and terminate. The contractor, however, decides not to accept the repudiation, and instead insists on continuing to perform the whole contract itself and then claims the full contract price, even though the client made clear it did not want the services to continue. The client argues the contractor should simply have stopped and claimed damages. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The innocent party must always accept an anticipatory breach and can never elect to continue performing.
The innocent party loses all remedies entirely if it does not accept the repudiation immediately.
The innocent party may always complete performance and claim the full price, whatever the circumstances.
The innocent party may sometimes affirm and perform, but only with a legitimate interest in doing so.
The innocent party may continue performing only if the contract expressly permits it to do so.
Contract Law.w: Faced with anticipatory breach, the innocent party may affirm and perform, keeping the contract alive (White & Carter v McGregor). But the right to do so is limited: it may not be exercised where the party has no legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages, or where performance requires the other's cooperation.

n.0: The innocent party is not obliged always to accept the breach; affirmation is an option.
n.1: Failing to accept immediately does not strip the innocent party of remedies; it may affirm.
n.2: The right to complete and claim the price is not unlimited; a legitimate interest is required.
n.4: Affirmation does not depend on an express contractual permission to continue.

Contract Law.q: Before entering a contract to buy a business, the buyer asks the seller whether there are any undisclosed disputes with major customers. The seller, knowing of a serious ongoing dispute, replies that relations with customers are 'excellent', which is literally true of most customers but conceals the one major dispute, creating a misleading overall impression. The buyer relies on the answer and later suffers loss when the dispute surfaces. The seller made a statement that was technically true in part but misleading as a whole, and did so knowing the true position. Which of the following best describes the nature of any misrepresentation and the measure of damages?
o: Fraudulent misrepresentation, for which the buyer may recover all losses flowing directly from entering the contract.
A mere statement of opinion, which cannot found any misrepresentation claim.
No misrepresentation at all, because the statement was literally true of most customers.
Negligent misstatement only, limited to losses that were reasonably foreseeable.
Innocent misrepresentation only, for which damages are never available in any circumstances on these facts.
Contract Law.w: A half-truth that creates a misleading overall impression can be a misrepresentation, and a statement made knowingly or without belief in its truth is fraudulent. In the tort of deceit the claimant may recover all losses flowing directly from entering the contract, whether or not foreseeable, which is a wider measure than for negligence.

n.1: This is a statement of fact creating a false impression, not a mere opinion.
n.2: A misleading half-truth can amount to a misrepresentation despite being partly true.
n.3: The maker's knowledge makes it fraudulent, attracting the wider deceit measure, not merely the negligence measure.
n.4: Innocent misrepresentation is not the correct classification where the maker knew the truth.

Contract Law.q: A supplier and a manufacturer enter a contract under which the manufacturer is to deliver goods and be paid in monthly instalments as each batch is delivered and accepted, each delivery being separately priced. After several batches have been delivered, paid for and accepted without complaint, a dispute arises over one later batch. The manufacturer argues that, because the contract is a single overall agreement, any problem with one batch entitles it to be paid for none of them. The supplier disputes this analysis of the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The obligations are likely divisible, so payment is earned batch by batch as each delivery is completed.
The contract is entire, so the manufacturer must repay everything already received for earlier batches.
The contract is divisible only if it expressly uses the word 'severable' in its wording.
The obligations are entire, because any contract for a series of deliveries is treated as a single whole.
The contract is entire, so no payment at all is earned unless every batch is delivered without any issue.
Contract Law.w: Where a contract provides for separate deliveries to be separately priced and paid for as they are made, the obligations are divisible (severable). Payment is earned for each completed and accepted delivery, and a problem with one instalment does not defeat payment for the others.

n.1: Divisible obligations already earned do not have to be repaid because of a later dispute.
n.2: Divisibility depends on the structure of the obligations, not on using the word 'severable'.
n.3: A series of separately priced deliveries is not automatically treated as a single entire obligation.
n.4: The contract is not entire; separately priced deliveries make the obligations divisible.

Contract Law.q: A UK company contracts to supply and export goods to a buyer in another country. After the contract is made, but before delivery, the UK government lawfully imposes a trade embargo which makes it a criminal offence to export goods of that kind to that country. Performance of the contract as agreed would now be unlawful. The buyer nevertheless demands delivery and threatens to sue for breach if the goods are not shipped. The seller seeks advice on the effect of the embargo on the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is frustrated only if the seller can show the embargo was aimed specifically at it.
The seller is liable for breach, because a party must always perform whatever the law later provides.
The contract is merely suspended until the embargo is lifted, however long that takes.
The contract is frustrated by supervening illegality, as performance has become unlawful after it was made.
The contract remains binding, and the seller must ship the goods despite the embargo.
Contract Law.w: Where a change in the law after the contract renders performance illegal, the contract is discharged by frustration through supervening illegality. The parties are excused, and the seller is not liable for refusing to do something that has become unlawful.

n.0: Frustration by illegality does not require the embargo to target the particular seller.
n.1: A party is not required to perform an act that the law has since made illegal.
n.2: Supervening illegality frustrates the contract; it is not merely suspended indefinitely.
n.4: The contract does not remain binding so as to require unlawful shipment.

Contract Law.q: Two commercial parties enter into a detailed written agreement, but include a clause stating that the arrangement is 'binding in honour only' and is not intended to give rise to legal relations or be enforceable in any court. A dispute later arises and one party seeks to sue on the agreement. The agreement is between businesses dealing at arm's length. The parties are experienced businesses who negotiated the deal at arm's length and deliberately inserted the clause to keep the arrangement out of the courts, and now that the deal has gone wrong one of them regrets that wording and wants to sue on the agreement despite it. Which of the following best describes the effect of the honour clause on intention to create legal relations?
o: The clause converts the agreement into a unilateral contract instead of a bilateral one.
The clause is ignored, because commercial agreements are always legally binding.
The clause rebuts the usual presumption of intention, so the agreement is not legally enforceable.
The clause is void as an unlawful attempt to oust the jurisdiction of the court.
The clause is effective only if both parties are companies rather than individuals.
Contract Law.w: In commercial dealings there is a strong presumption of an intention to create legal relations, but it can be rebutted by clear words. An express 'binding in honour only' clause shows the parties did not intend legal enforceability, so the presumption is displaced and the agreement is not a legally binding contract.

n.0: An honour clause negatives intention; it does not turn the agreement into a unilateral contract.
n.1: The commercial presumption is strong but rebuttable by clear contrary words.
n.3: Such a clause is not treated as an unlawful ouster; it defines the parties' own intentions.
n.4: The clause's effect does not depend on whether the parties are companies or individuals.

Contract Law.q: In negotiations for a business contract, one party makes a statement of fact to the other which turns out to be false, and which induced the contract. The statement was not made dishonestly, but the maker had no reasonable grounds for believing it was true. The innocent party has suffered loss and wishes to claim damages. The party who made the statement argues that, since they were not fraudulent, no damages can be claimed against them. The innocent party seeks advice under the Misrepresentation Act 1967. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages are available under s.2(1) unless the maker proves a reasonable belief in the statement's truth.
No damages are available at all, because the maker of the statement was not fraudulent.
Damages are available only if the innocent party has already rescinded the whole contract.
Damages are available only where the statement later became an express term of the contract.
Damages are available only if the innocent party first proves the maker was negligent.
Contract Law.w: Under section 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967, once a misrepresentation inducing the contract is shown, the representor is liable in damages unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the statement was true. The burden of disproving negligence lies on the representor.

n.1: Damages are available under s.2(1) even without fraud.
n.2: Damages under s.2(1) do not depend on the contract first having been rescinded.
n.3: A s.2(1) claim does not require the statement to have become a contractual term.
n.4: The claimant need not prove negligence; the representor must disprove it.

Contract Law.q: A commercial contract between two businesses of equal bargaining power contains a clause requiring the party in breach to pay a fixed sum on a particular breach. The sum was a genuine attempt to protect the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance and is not extravagant or out of all proportion to that interest. When the clause is triggered, the paying party argues that it is an unenforceable penalty and that only the actual loss should be payable. The other party relies on the clause as agreed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The clause is enforceable only if the fixed sum exactly matches the actual loss suffered.
The clause is enforceable if it protects a legitimate interest and is not out of all proportion.
The clause is automatically unenforceable, because any fixed pre-agreed sum is a penalty.
The clause is unenforceable, because businesses can never agree damages in advance.
The clause is enforceable only where the innocent party can prove it suffered no loss at all.
Contract Law.w: A pre-agreed damages clause is enforceable as liquidated damages, not a penalty, provided it does not impose a detriment out of all proportion to a legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance (Cavendish Square v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis). A genuine, proportionate clause is binding.

n.0: The sum need not match the actual loss exactly; that is not the modern test.
n.2: Not every fixed pre-agreed sum is a penalty; proportionate clauses are enforceable.
n.3: Businesses can agree damages in advance through liquidated damages clauses.
n.4: Enforceability does not depend on the innocent party proving it suffered no loss.

Contract Law.q: During negotiations for the sale of a specialist business, the seller makes a statement to the buyer about the level of the business's past turnover. The statement is one of past fact, is made shortly before the contract is signed, and the seller has particular expertise and access to the figures which the buyer does not. The buyer relies on the statement in deciding to buy, and it later proves inaccurate. The buyer wishes to argue that the statement was a term of the contract rather than a mere representation. Which of the following factors most supports treating the statement as a term?
o: The statement was made a considerable time before the contract was finally signed.
The seller invited the buyer to check the accuracy of the figures independently.
The buyer did not actually rely on the statement in deciding whether to buy.
The seller had special knowledge or expertise about the matter compared with the buyer.
The parties later signed a contract containing an entire agreement clause.
Contract Law.w: In distinguishing a term from a representation, the courts look at factors such as the relative expertise of the parties. Where the maker of the statement has special knowledge or skill relative to the other party, this points towards the statement being a contractual term (Oscar Chess; Dick Bentley).

n.0: A statement made long before signing points away from it being a term, not towards it.
n.1: Inviting the other party to verify the statement points away from treating it as a term.
n.2: Absence of reliance points against the statement being a term (or a misrepresentation).
n.4: An entire agreement clause points against the statement forming part of the contract.

Contract Law.q: A buyer and seller agree that, in place of the seller's original obligation to deliver goods (which the seller can no longer conveniently perform), the seller will instead pay the buyer a sum of money, and the buyer accepts this new arrangement in full satisfaction of the original obligation. The buyer provides its agreement to give up the original right in return for the new promise. The seller pays the sum. The buyer later tries to sue on the original obligation as well. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer may sue on the original obligation, because it has already received the substitute payment.
The original obligation is discharged only if the substitution was ordered by a court.
The original obligation survives, because replacing delivery with money is not permitted in law.
The original obligation is discharged by accord and satisfaction, so the buyer cannot sue on it.
The original obligation survives, because an obligation once created can never be discharged by agreement.
Contract Law.w: A contractual obligation can be discharged by agreement where there is accord (agreement to release) and satisfaction (fresh consideration for the release). Here the buyer agreed to accept a money payment in place of delivery, and that new arrangement discharges the original obligation.

n.0: Having accepted the substitute in satisfaction, the buyer cannot also enforce the original obligation.
n.1: Accord and satisfaction operates by agreement of the parties, without any court order.
n.2: Substituting a money payment for delivery, by agreement, is perfectly permissible.
n.4: Obligations can be discharged by agreement supported by consideration; they are not indelible.

Contract Law.q: Two parties reach an agreement for the sale of a business, but a term fixing the price is expressed only as a figure 'to be agreed between the parties in due course', with no formula or machinery for resolving the matter if they fail to agree. They never reach agreement on the price and one party seeks to enforce the sale. There is no external standard or mechanism provided for setting the price. The parties shook hands on the broad shape of the deal but left the crucial matter of price hanging, recording only that it would be settled between them later, and they provided no formula, valuer or other mechanism to fix it if, as happened, they could never actually agree a figure. Which of the following best describes the enforceability of the agreement?
o: The contract is binding, and the court will simply fix whatever price it considers fair.
The contract is binding, because price is never regarded as an essential term.
There is likely no binding contract, as an agreement to agree an essential term is too uncertain to enforce.
The contract is void for mistake because the parties misunderstood the price.
The contract is binding, and the price defaults automatically to the market value in every case on these facts.
Contract Law.w: An agreement that leaves an essential term, such as price, simply 'to be agreed' later, with no machinery or objective standard for resolving it, is generally too uncertain to be an enforceable contract: the courts will not make the parties' bargain for them. The position differs where the contract provides a formula or mechanism, or a statutory implied term applies.

n.0: The court will not simply impose whatever price it thinks fair where the parties left it to be agreed.
n.1: Price is generally an essential term for a sale of a business.
n.3: The problem is uncertainty/incompleteness, not a shared mistake about the price.
n.4: There is no automatic default to market value where the parties agreed to agree with no mechanism.

Contract Law.q: A seller offers to sell a piece of machinery to a buyer for £20,000. The buyer writes back saying that they will pay £18,000 for it. The seller replies that they are not prepared to reduce the price and hears nothing further for a few days. The buyer then writes again, saying that on reflection they accept the original price of £20,000 after all, and asserts that there is now a binding contract at that figure. The seller, who has in the meantime found another purchaser, denies that any contract exists. The buyer seeks advice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's counter-offer merely paused the original offer, which revived once the seller rejected it.
A binding contract arose at £18,000, because the seller failed to reject that figure quickly enough.
The counter-offer of £18,000 destroyed the original offer, which the buyer could no longer accept.
The original offer of £20,000 remained open, so the buyer's later acceptance created a binding contract.
A binding contract arose at £20,000, because the buyer eventually agreed to the seller's original price.
Contract Law.w: A counter-offer rejects and destroys the original offer, which cannot then be accepted later (Hyde v Wrench). By offering £18,000 the buyer rejected the £20,000 offer, so their subsequent purported acceptance of £20,000 was itself only a new offer, which the seller was free to decline.

n.0: A counter-offer destroys the original offer; it does not merely suspend it.
n.1: The seller's silence did not create a contract at the counter-offer figure.
n.3: The original offer did not remain open once it had been met by a counter-offer.
n.4: By the time the buyer agreed to £20,000, that offer had already been destroyed by the counter-offer.

Contract Law.q: A rogue, pretending in a face-to-face meeting to be a wealthy and creditworthy individual, persuades a private seller to sell them goods and to accept a cheque in payment. The seller deals with the rogue in person and, although mistaken about the rogue's creditworthiness and honesty, intends to sell to the individual physically present. The cheque bounces, and the rogue sells the goods on to an innocent third party. The seller argues there was never any contract with the rogue because of the mistake as to identity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is void, because identity is always a fundamental matter in any face-to-face sale.
The contract is fully valid and unaffected, because the seller received a cheque in payment.
There is a presumption the seller intended to deal with the person present, so the contract is voidable, not void.
The contract is void, because a seller is always mistaken when dealing with a dishonest rogue.
The contract is automatically void for mistake as to identity, so no title could pass to the third party.
Contract Law.w: In a face-to-face dealing there is a strong presumption that a party intends to contract with the person physically present, whatever their assumed identity. The contract is therefore voidable for fraudulent misrepresentation, not void for mistake, so an innocent third party who buys before rescission can acquire good title (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay).

n.0: Identity is not automatically fundamental in a face-to-face sale; the presumption is the opposite.
n.1: Payment by cheque does not render the contract unaffected; the fraud makes it voidable.
n.3: The mere fact the rogue was dishonest does not make the contract void for mistake.
n.4: Face-to-face identity mistakes generally render the contract voidable, not automatically void.

Contract Law.q: A husband and wife have separated. As part of arrangements on separation, the husband promises in writing to transfer the house to the wife once she has paid off the outstanding mortgage instalments, which she then does. The husband refuses to transfer the house, arguing that agreements between spouses are not intended to be legally binding. The promise was made after the couple had separated and involved defined obligations. The couple were no longer living together and were sorting out their finances on the breakdown of the marriage, the promise was recorded in writing with a clear condition attached, and the wife duly did what was asked before the husband tried to disown the arrangement as a mere family understanding. Which of the following best describes the position on intention to create legal relations?
o: The agreement is unenforceable, because arrangements between spouses can never be binding.
The agreement is enforceable only if the wife provided no consideration at all.
The agreement is unenforceable, because domestic arrangements are always presumed non-binding without exception.
The agreement is enforceable only if it was made before the couple separated.
The presumption against intention in domestic arrangements is rebutted, so the agreement is enforceable.
Contract Law.w: Domestic and social arrangements are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations, but the presumption is rebuttable. Where spouses are separating and enter a definite agreement, often in writing and with each side undertaking obligations, the presumption is rebutted and the agreement is legally enforceable.

n.0: Agreements between spouses can be binding where intention is shown.
n.1: The wife did provide consideration by paying the instalments; enforceability does not require the absence of consideration.
n.2: The domestic presumption is rebuttable, not absolute.
n.3: An agreement on separation, made after separating, is a classic situation where the presumption is rebutted.

Contract Law.q: A well-known performer agrees in a contract that, for a period, they will sing exclusively for one venue and will not perform for any competitor. The performer then proposes to breach that negative undertaking by performing for a rival venue. The original venue does not seek to force the performer to sing for it, but does want to stop the performer singing for the competitor in breach of the exclusivity promise. The venue seeks advice on the remedy available. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will order the performer to sing for the original venue by way of specific performance.
The court can grant no remedy at all, because promises about personal services are unenforceable.
The court may grant a prohibitory injunction to restrain the performer from breaching the negative undertaking.
The court will refuse any injunction, because that would indirectly compel personal service.
The court will grant an injunction only if the performer has already begun performing for the rival.
Contract Law.w: A court will not order specific performance of a contract for personal services, but it may grant a prohibitory injunction to enforce a negative undertaking (such as a promise not to perform for competitors), provided this does not in substance compel the personal service (Lumley v Wagner; Warner Bros v Nelson).

n.0: The court will not order the performer to sing for the venue; that is specific performance of personal service.
n.1: Negative undertakings in personal-service contracts can be enforced by injunction, so a remedy exists.
n.3: An injunction restraining the negative promise is permissible where it does not compel the service itself.
n.4: An injunction may be granted to prevent a threatened breach, not only after it starts.

Contract Law.q: A carrier contracts to transport a mill owner's broken crankshaft to be copied, but is not told that the mill is standing idle and will remain so until the new shaft arrives. The carrier delays delivery, and the mill owner claims the profits lost during the extended stoppage, which were far greater than the carrier could have anticipated from the limited information given. The carrier was not made aware of the special circumstances (the idle mill) that caused the unusually large loss of profit. Which of the following best describes whether the lost profits are recoverable?
o: The lost profits are recoverable because remoteness is irrelevant in contract.
All the lost profits are recoverable, because any loss factually caused by breach is recoverable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The lost profits are recoverable only if the carrier acted deliberately.
The unusual lost profits are irrecoverable, being neither ordinary losses nor within the carrier's contemplation from known special circumstances.
No damages of any kind are recoverable, because the loss was consequential.
Contract Law.w: Under the rule in Hadley v Baxendale, recoverable losses are those arising naturally in the ordinary course (first limb) or within the parties' reasonable contemplation from special circumstances actually communicated (second limb). As the special circumstances (the idle mill) were not made known, the unusually large lost profits were too remote to be recovered.

n.0: Remoteness is a central limit on damages in contract, not irrelevant.
n.1: Not every factually caused loss is recoverable; remoteness limits recovery.
n.2: Recoverability turns on remoteness, not on whether the breach was deliberate.
n.4: Some damages (ordinary losses) may still be recoverable; the point is the special lost profits are too remote.

Contract Law.q: A creditor is owed money under a contract (a chose in action) and wishes to transfer the benefit of that debt to a third party, so that the third party can enforce it and sue for it in their own name. The creditor wants to make a legal (statutory) assignment of the debt. The right assigned is a purely contractual benefit. The creditor is owed a debt under a contract and wants to hand the benefit of that debt over to a third party outright, so that the third party can chase and sue for it in its own name, and is trying to make the transfer as a full legal assignment rather than merely an equitable one. Which of the following best describes the requirements for a valid legal assignment under section 136 of the Law of Property Act 1925?
o: No formality is required; a legal assignment can be inferred from conduct on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The assignment must be absolute, in writing signed by the assignor, and express written notice must be given to the debtor.
The assignment may be made orally provided the debtor is aware of it.
The assignment requires the debtor's consent before it can take effect.
The assignment must be made by deed and registered at Companies House.
Contract Law.w: For a legal (statutory) assignment of a chose in action under s.136 of the Law of Property Act 1925, the assignment must be absolute (not by way of charge only), in writing signed by the assignor, and express notice in writing must be given to the debtor. The assignee can then sue in their own name. An assignment not meeting these requirements may still take effect in equity.

n.0: A legal assignment requires the statutory formalities; it is not inferred from conduct.
n.2: An oral assignment does not satisfy s.136; writing and written notice are required.
n.3: The debtor's consent is not required to assign the benefit (the burden is different).
n.4: A deed and Companies House registration are not the s.136 requirements.

Contract Law.q: Two parties make a contract which contains an express term stating that a named third party is entitled to enforce a particular benefit conferred on them by the contract, and the third party is expressly identified by name. The promisor then fails to confer that benefit, and the named third party wishes to enforce the term directly against the promisor. The promisor argues that, as the third party is not a party to the contract, they cannot sue on it. The third party seeks advice under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The third party may enforce the term only after first joining the original promisee to the claim.
The third party can never enforce the term, because only the original contracting parties can sue.
The third party may enforce the term only if the promisor agrees to let them do so.
The third party may enforce the term only if they provided consideration for the promise.
The third party may enforce the term, as the contract expressly provides that they may do so.
Contract Law.w: Under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, a third party may enforce a term of a contract if the contract expressly provides that they may, or if the term purports to confer a benefit on them (and it is not shown the parties did not intend it to be enforceable). Here the contract expressly so provides.

n.0: The third party need not join the promisee to enforce a right conferred under the Act.
n.1: The 1999 Act allows a qualifying third party to enforce; enforcement is not limited to the original parties.
n.2: Enforcement does not require the promisor's separate agreement once the Act is satisfied.
n.3: A third party enforcing under the Act need not have provided consideration.

Contract Law.q: A carrier is engaged to deliver a broken mill shaft to be used as a pattern for a replacement, and delays delivery. Unknown to the carrier, the mill is entirely stopped for want of the shaft, and the delay causes the mill owner substantial loss of profits during the extra downtime. The mill owner claims those lost profits from the carrier. The carrier did not know, and was not told, that the mill would be wholly idle until the shaft was returned. The mill owner seeks advice on whether the lost profits are recoverable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The lost profits are never recoverable, because loss of profit can never be claimed for late delivery.
The lost profits are always recoverable in full, however unusual or unforeseeable the loss.
The lost profits are recoverable simply because they were in fact caused by the carrier's delay.
The lost profits are recoverable only if within the parties' reasonable contemplation when contracting.
The lost profits are recoverable only if the carrier acted deliberately rather than carelessly.
Contract Law.w: Under the remoteness rule in Hadley v Baxendale, losses are recoverable only if they arise naturally from the breach, or were within the reasonable contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting. Unusual losses (here, total stoppage) are recoverable only if the special circumstances were communicated.

n.0: Loss of profit can be recoverable if within reasonable contemplation, so 'never' is wrong.
n.1: Damages are limited by remoteness; not all losses, however unforeseeable, are recoverable.
n.2: Mere factual causation is not enough; the loss must also not be too remote.
n.4: Remoteness, not the defendant's state of mind, governs recoverability here.

Contract Law.q: During negotiations for the sale of a restaurant, the seller tells the buyer that the premises are let to a tenant who is 'a most desirable tenant', when in fact the seller knows the tenant is heavily in arrears with the rent and unreliable. The buyer, relying on that statement, agrees to buy the restaurant. Shortly after completion the true position about the tenant emerges, and the buyer wishes to unwind the transaction. The buyer seeks advice on the primary remedy available for the seller's false pre-contract statement. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's only possible remedy is to claim damages, and rescission is never available for misrepresentation.
The buyer may rescind the contract, because the seller made an actionable misrepresentation that induced it.
The buyer may rescind only if the statement was also written into the contract as an express term.
The buyer has no remedy, because the statement was made before the contract and so has no effect.
The buyer has no remedy, because a statement about a tenant is only ever a matter of opinion.
Contract Law.w: An actionable misrepresentation is an unambiguous false statement of fact made by one party which induces the other to enter the contract. Its primary remedy is rescission, setting the contract aside, and damages may also be available depending on the type of misrepresentation.

n.0: Rescission is the primary remedy for misrepresentation; damages are additional, not the only option.
n.2: Misrepresentation does not require the statement to have become an express contractual term.
n.3: A pre-contract inducing statement is precisely what founds a misrepresentation claim.
n.4: The statement was one of fact that the seller knew to be untrue, not mere opinion.

Contract Law.q: A landowner grants a company the right to use a strip of land in return for the company paying 'one peppercorn' per year if demanded. The arrangement is otherwise intended to be a binding contract. A dispute arises and one party argues the arrangement is unenforceable because a single peppercorn is of negligible value compared with the right granted. The parties genuinely agreed the peppercorn as the price. The right granted was commercially valuable and the parties deliberately chose a token annual payment as the price rather than a market rent, and now, the relationship having soured, one side is trying to escape the bargain by pointing to the glaring mismatch between the peppercorn and the value of the right. Which of the following best describes the position on consideration?
o: The consideration is sufficient even though it is not adequate, so the arrangement is enforceable.
The consideration fails because it must be adequate, that is, roughly equal in value to the right granted.
The consideration fails because a peppercorn cannot in law be consideration at all.
The arrangement is unenforceable because only money can constitute valid consideration.
The arrangement is enforceable only if the peppercorn is actually demanded and paid each year.
Contract Law.w: Consideration must be sufficient (of some recognised value in the eyes of the law) but need not be adequate (equal in value to what is promised in return). A nominal consideration such as a peppercorn is legally sufficient, so the parties' bargain is enforceable regardless of the disparity in value.

n.1: The law does not require consideration to be adequate; sufficiency is enough.
n.2: A peppercorn is a classic example of sufficient (if nominal) consideration.
n.3: Consideration need not be money; goods or other things of value will do.
n.4: Enforceability does not depend on the peppercorn actually being demanded.

Contract Law.q: A husband, about to go to work abroad for an extended period, promises his wife that he will pay her a monthly allowance of £200 while he is away. The couple are on good terms at the time and nothing is written down or formalised. Some months later the marriage breaks down, the husband stops the payments, and the wife sues him to enforce the promise of the monthly allowance, arguing that it was a clear agreement supported by their relationship. The husband denies that the arrangement was ever legally binding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a binding contract, because the wife plainly relied on the promise of the allowance.
There is a binding contract, because any clear promise of money between spouses is legally enforceable.
There is no binding contract: domestic arrangements are presumed to lack intention to create legal relations.
There is no binding contract, because a promise between spouses can never be legally enforceable.
There is a binding contract, because the promise concerned a specific sum payable each month.
Contract Law.w: Agreements made between spouses in a domestic or social context are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour). On these facts that presumption is not rebutted, so the promise of the allowance is not an enforceable contract.

n.0: Reliance alone does not rebut the presumption against intention in a domestic arrangement.
n.1: Not every promise of money between spouses is enforceable; the domestic presumption applies.
n.3: Spousal promises can be enforceable where intention is shown, so 'never' is too absolute.
n.4: Specifying a monthly sum does not, by itself, rebut the presumption against legal intention.

Contract Law.q: A supplier is owed £10,000 by a customer under a contract. The customer, who could in fact afford to pay in full, tells the supplier that they are short of money and offers to pay £6,000 'in full and final settlement' of the whole debt. The supplier, wanting at least something quickly, agrees in a telephone call to accept the £6,000 and to write off the rest. The customer pays the £6,000. Some weeks later the supplier changes their mind and sues the customer for the remaining £4,000. The customer argues that the debt was settled. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because accepting part payment always discharges the whole debt.
The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because the customer honestly said they were short of money.
The supplier may recover the £4,000 only if the original contract was made in writing.
The supplier may still recover the £4,000, as part payment is not consideration for giving up the balance.
The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because the agreement to accept £6,000 was a binding variation.
Contract Law.w: Under the rule in Pinnel's Case, affirmed in Foakes v Beer, payment of a smaller sum is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the balance of a debt. Absent fresh consideration or an applicable estoppel, the creditor may still sue for the unpaid £4,000.

n.0: Part payment does not, by itself, discharge the whole debt.
n.1: The debtor's honest statement of shortage does not supply the missing consideration.
n.2: Whether the original contract was in writing is irrelevant to this rule.
n.4: The promise to accept less lacked consideration, so it was not a binding variation.

Contract Law.q: A company spends a large sum preparing for a venture in reliance on a contract, incurring expenditure that is wasted when the other party breaches the contract. Because the venture was new and untested, the company cannot reliably prove what profit it would have made, so it cannot readily establish its expectation loss. It wishes instead to recover the money it actually spent in reliance on the contract being performed. The other party argues the company can only ever claim lost profits. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company may claim only nominal damages, because its expectation loss is unproven.
The company may instead claim its wasted expenditure incurred in reliance on the contract.
The company may claim its expenditure only if the other party acted in bad faith.
The company may recover nothing, because it cannot prove the profit it would have made.
The company may claim wasted expenditure only if the contract expressly allowed for it.
Contract Law.w: Where expectation loss (lost profit) is too speculative to prove, the innocent party may instead elect to claim the reliance measure — the expenditure wasted in reliance on the contract — provided the expenditure was not going to be lost anyway (Anglia Television v Reed).

n.0: The company is not confined to nominal damages; wasted expenditure is recoverable.
n.2: Reliance damages do not depend on the other party having acted in bad faith.
n.3: Inability to prove profit does not leave the company remediless; it may claim reliance loss.
n.4: Recovery of reliance loss does not require an express contractual provision.

Contract Law.q: A business owner signs a written contract to buy an automatic vending machine, without reading it. The document she signs contains, in ordinary print, a clause excluding the seller's liability for the machine's failure to perform. The machine proves seriously defective, and when the buyer complains the seller relies on the exclusion clause. The buyer argues that she should not be bound by the clause because she never actually read it before signing. She seeks advice on whether the clause was incorporated into the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The clause is incorporated only if the seller expressly drew the buyer's attention to it before signing.
The clause is not incorporated, because the buyer did not in fact read it before signing the document.
The clause is incorporated, because a party who signs a contractual document is generally bound by its terms.
The clause is not incorporated, because an exclusion clause can never be included in a signed contract.
The clause is not incorporated, because the buyer was a business rather than a consumer.
Contract Law.w: A person who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms whether or not they have read them, in the absence of misrepresentation (L'Estrange v Graucob). The signed exclusion clause is therefore incorporated, subject to any statutory controls on its effectiveness.

n.0: With a signed document, special notice of the clause is not required for incorporation.
n.1: Failing to read a signed document does not prevent its terms binding the signatory.
n.3: Exclusion clauses can be, and often are, included in signed contracts.
n.4: The signature rule applies to businesses as well; the buyer's status does not defeat incorporation.

Contract Law.q: A homeowner contracts for a swimming pool to be built to a specified depth. The pool is built slightly shallower than specified, but it is still perfectly safe to use and dive into, and the shortfall makes no difference to the pool's value. Rebuilding the pool to the exact depth would cost a very large sum, out of all proportion to any real loss suffered. The homeowner nonetheless claims the full cost of rebuilding. The builder argues that such an award would be wholly unreasonable. Which of the following best describes the likely measure of damages?
o: The court is likely to award a modest sum for loss of amenity, rather than the disproportionate cost of rebuilding.
The court will award the difference in the market value of the pool, which here is substantial.
The court must award the full cost of rebuilding the pool to the specified depth.
The court will award nothing at all, because the pool is safe and usable as built.
The court will award the full rebuilding cost, provided the homeowner promises to carry out the work.
Contract Law.w: Where the cost of cure is wholly disproportionate to the benefit to be obtained and the diminution in value is nil, the court may instead award a modest sum for loss of amenity — reflecting the consumer surplus lost — rather than the unreasonable cost of reinstatement (Ruxley Electronics v Forsyth).

n.1: The diminution in value here is nil, so that measure would give nothing meaningful.
n.2: The full rebuilding cost is not awarded where it is out of all proportion to the loss.
n.3: The homeowner is not left with nothing; loss of amenity is recognised.
n.4: A promise to do the work does not justify a disproportionate cost-of-cure award on these facts.

Contract Law.q: Two businesses have dealt with each other regularly over several years, and on every previous occasion the seller's delivery notes have incorporated the seller's standard terms, including a limitation clause, of which the buyer has always been aware. On the latest order the goods are delivered first and the delivery note handed over only afterwards, but the course of dealing has been consistent and well known to the buyer. The parties are experienced commercial contractors with a long, consistent history of dealing on these terms. Which of the following best describes whether the limitation clause is incorporated?
o: The clause is automatically incorporated into every contract between any businesses.
The clause cannot be incorporated because it was handed over after delivery on this occasion.
The clause may be incorporated by the parties' consistent prior course of dealing.
The clause can never be incorporated unless separately signed on each occasion.
The clause is incorporated only if the buyer expressly re-agreed to it for this order.
Contract Law.w: Terms can be incorporated by a consistent and well-known course of dealing between the parties. Where experienced commercial parties have regularly contracted on the same standard terms, those terms may be incorporated into a further transaction even if, on the particular occasion, the document containing them was provided after the moment of contracting.

n.0: Terms are not automatically incorporated into every contract between businesses; a basis such as course of dealing is needed.
n.1: Late delivery of the note on one occasion does not defeat incorporation built on a consistent prior course of dealing.
n.3: A fresh signature on each occasion is not required where a course of dealing exists.
n.4: Express re-agreement for the specific order is not necessary given the established course of dealing.

Contract Law.q: A man carries out extensive repairs and improvements to his friend's house, entirely of his own accord and without any prior request or promise of payment. After all the work has been completed and the man has gone home, the grateful friend says to him, 'In return for everything you have done to the house, I promise to pay you £2,000.' The friend later refuses to pay anything, and the man seeks to enforce the promise of £2,000, pointing to all the work he did on the house. The man seeks advice on whether the promise is enforceable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The promise is unenforceable, because a promise to pay for building work must always be made in writing.
The promise is enforceable, because the work done to the house was plainly good consideration for it.
The promise is enforceable, because the friend clearly intended to be legally bound by their promise.
The promise is enforceable, because the value of the work far exceeded the £2,000 that was promised.
The promise is unenforceable, because the work was past consideration, having been done before the promise was made.
Contract Law.w: Consideration must not be past: an act already completed before a promise is given cannot generally be consideration for that promise (Re McArdle). As the work was done before the friend promised to pay, the promise is unsupported by consideration and is unenforceable.

n.0: There is no general requirement that a promise to pay for building work be in writing.
n.1: Although work was done, it was completed before the promise and so is past consideration.
n.2: An intention to be bound cannot supply the consideration that the promise lacks.
n.3: The adequacy or value of the work is irrelevant; the problem is that the consideration is past.

Contract Law.q: A supplier and a buyer negotiate the sale of industrial equipment by an exchange of documents. The buyer sends a purchase order on the buyer's standard terms. The supplier replies with an acknowledgement on the supplier's own standard terms, which differ on liability. The buyer takes delivery of the equipment without further comment. A dispute later arises about which set of terms governs the contract. Applying the ordinary 'battle of the forms' analysis, Neither party read the other's small print with care, each simply assumed its own conditions applied, and the equipment has since developed a fault that engages the very liability terms on which the two documents differ, so everything now turns on which set of standard terms became part of the deal. which of the following best describes whose terms are likely to govern?
o: Neither party's terms, so no contract can ever be formed on these facts.
The supplier's terms, as the last set sent before performance which the buyer accepted by taking delivery.
A neutral set of terms imposed by the court to balance the parties.
Whichever terms are more favourable to the party later found to be in breach on these facts as a general rule.
The buyer's terms, because the buyer sent the first document in the exchange.
Contract Law.w: On the traditional analysis, each set of standard terms sent in response to the other operates as a counter-offer that rejects the previous terms. The last counter-offer before performance (here the supplier's acknowledgement) is accepted by the other party's conduct in taking delivery, so the contract is generally on the terms of the last document fired in the exchange.

n.0: Conduct in performing usually shows a contract was formed, so 'no contract at all' is wrong here.
n.2: The court applies offer-and-acceptance analysis rather than imposing its own neutral terms.
n.3: Which terms govern turns on the sequence of offer and acceptance, not on who is in breach.
n.4: The first document is treated as an offer superseded by later counter-offers, not as the governing terms.

Contract Law.q: Goods are put up for sale at an auction advertised as being 'without reserve'. The auctioneer invites bids, and the highest bid is made by a particular bidder. The auctioneer, dissatisfied with the level of the bidding, refuses to knock the item down to the highest bidder and withdraws it from sale. The bidder complains. The auction was expressly without reserve. The item had attracted keen interest precisely because the sale had been billed as one where the goods would go to the top bidder whatever the level, and the highest bidder had come specifically on that basis before the auctioneer changed course and pulled the lot. Which of the following best describes the bidder's position?
o: The auctioneer may withdraw the item at will, as bids create no obligations of any kind.
The bidder can compel the auctioneer to transfer the goods by specific performance.
The auctioneer may be liable for breach of a collateral undertaking to sell to the highest bidder.
The advertisement of the auction was itself a binding offer to sell to any bidder.
A binding contract of sale was completed the moment the highest bid was called out.
Contract Law.w: At an auction, each bid is an offer accepted by the fall of the hammer, so no sale contract is completed merely by making the highest bid. However, in an auction without reserve there is a separate collateral contract that the auctioneer will sell to the highest bidder; refusing to do so breaches that collateral undertaking, entitling the bidder to damages.

n.0: Bids do create a collateral obligation in a no-reserve auction, so it is not true that they create none.
n.1: The remedy for breach of the collateral contract is damages, not specific performance of a sale.
n.3: The advertisement of the auction is generally not itself a binding offer to sell.
n.4: The main sale contract is completed on the fall of the hammer, not when the highest bid is called.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently causes a claimant a leg injury which leaves the claimant with a slightly weakened leg. Some time later, the claimant, well aware of the weakness, chooses to descend a steep staircase that has no handrail, in an unreasonable way and without any need to do so, and falls, suffering a much more serious injury. The original defendant accepts responsibility for the first injury but denies responsibility for the second. The claimant argues the whole chain of loss flows from the original negligence. The defendant says the claimant's own conduct broke the chain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The original defendant is liable for all later injuries, whatever the claimant subsequently chooses to do.
The chain of causation can only ever be broken by the act of a third party, and never by the claimant.
The claimant's own unreasonable conduct may break the chain of causation for the later, more serious injury.
The claimant's conduct is irrelevant, because the defendant's original negligence started the sequence of events.
The defendant is liable for the second injury only if it was more serious than the first injury.
Tort.w: The chain of causation may be broken by the claimant's own conduct where that conduct is so unreasonable as to be regarded as a new intervening cause (McKew v Holland). The claimant's unreasonable act in descending the staircase may relieve the defendant of liability for the later injury.

n.0: The defendant is not automatically liable for all subsequent injuries.
n.1: The claimant's own act can break the chain, not only a third party's act.
n.3: The claimant's own unreasonable conduct is very relevant to legal causation.
n.4: The break in causation does not turn on which injury was more serious.

Tort.q: A worker develops a lung condition caused by inhaling dust at work. Some of the dust exposure was due to the employer's negligence (the 'guilty' dust) and some was innocent exposure that could not have been avoided. Medical evidence shows the disease was caused by the cumulative effect of all the dust, and that the guilty dust made a material contribution to the total. The condition is a 'divisible' one, worsened cumulatively by the total dust inhaled. Over the years the worker breathed in dust from the factory air, some of it the product of the employer's failure to provide proper extraction and some of it exposure that no reasonable precaution could have prevented, and the medical evidence links the disease to the combined burden of all the dust inhaled. Which of the following best describes the basis on which the employer may be liable?
o: The employer's liability depends solely on the 'but for' test being satisfied on the balance of probabilities.
The employer escapes liability because the innocent dust also contributed to the harm.
The employer is liable because the guilty dust made a material contribution to the cumulative harm.
The employer is liable in full only if the guilty dust alone would have caused the disease.
The employer is liable only if it can be shown which single particle of dust caused the disease.
Tort.w: Where a condition results from the cumulative effect of tortious and non-tortious exposure and the tortious exposure made a material (more than negligible) contribution to the harm, the defendant is liable (Bonnington Castings). The claimant need not prove that the guilty exposure alone would have caused the disease, nor satisfy a strict 'but for' test in these cumulative-cause cases.

n.0: In cumulative-cause cases material contribution, not strict 'but for', is the applicable test.
n.1: The presence of innocent exposure does not defeat liability where guilty exposure materially contributed.
n.3: It is enough that the guilty dust materially contributed; it need not alone have caused the disease.
n.4: The claimant need not identify the precise particle responsible.

Tort.q: A customer lawfully visits a shop and is injured when they slip on a spillage that the shop had negligently failed to clean up or warn about. The customer sues the shop as occupier of the premises. The shop accepts the customer was a lawful visitor but disputes the standard of care it owed. The customer seeks advice on the duty owed by an occupier to a lawful visitor under the relevant legislation. The spillage had been on the floor for some time and staff had repeatedly walked past it without dealing with it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier's duty depends solely on whether the visitor paid an entry fee to come in.
The occupier owes a common duty to take reasonable care to keep visitors reasonably safe for the purposes of their visit.
The occupier owes only the lesser duty that is owed to trespassers who are not permitted to be there on these facts.
The occupier owes lawful visitors no duty of care at all in respect of the state of the premises.
The occupier owes visitors an absolute duty to ensure that they come to no harm whatsoever.
Tort.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, an occupier owes lawful visitors the 'common duty of care' — a duty to take such care as is reasonable in all the circumstances to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which they are permitted to be there.

n.0: The duty does not turn simply on whether an entry fee was paid.
n.2: Lawful visitors are owed the 1957 Act duty, higher than that owed to trespassers.
n.3: An occupier does owe a duty to lawful visitors regarding the state of the premises.
n.4: The duty is one of reasonable care, not an absolute guarantee of safety.

Tort.q: A solicitor is instructed by an elderly client to prepare a will leaving a substantial legacy to a named intended beneficiary. The solicitor negligently delays and fails to prepare the will before the client dies, with the result that the intended beneficiary receives nothing they would otherwise have inherited. The disappointed beneficiary, who was never the solicitor's client and had no contract with the solicitor, wishes to claim their lost inheritance from the solicitor in the tort of negligence. The intended legacy was substantial, and the beneficiary had been clearly identified in the client's instructions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiary can never recover, because they had no contract with the solicitor.
The beneficiary can recover only if they can show the solicitor acted dishonestly rather than carelessly on these facts.
The beneficiary can never recover, because a solicitor owes duties only to the living client.
The disappointed beneficiary may recover, as the solicitor is treated as owing them a duty despite the lack of contract.
The beneficiary can recover only their own out-of-pocket expenses, and not the lost legacy.
Tort.w: In this special situation, a solicitor who negligently fails to carry out a testator's instructions may be liable to a disappointed intended beneficiary who loses their legacy, even though the beneficiary was not the client and there was no contract, because the assumption of responsibility extends to them (White v Jones).

n.0: The absence of a contract does not defeat the claim in this recognised category.
n.1: The liability is for negligence; dishonesty is not required.
n.2: The duty here extends beyond the living client to the intended beneficiary.
n.4: The recoverable loss is the lost legacy, not merely out-of-pocket expenses.

Tort.q: A person is injured in an accident caused by another's negligence and wishes to bring a personal injury claim, but a considerable amount of time has now passed since the accident occurred. The potential defendant argues that the claim is now too old to be pursued and is barred by the passage of time. The injured person seeks advice on the time limit that applies to a personal injury claim in negligence and from when it runs. The claimant has only recently taken legal advice and is anxious about whether it is now too late to sue at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A personal injury claim can never be brought more than one year after the accident occurred.
A personal injury claim must always be brought within six years of the accident, without exception.
A personal injury claim may be brought at any time, because there is no time limit for such claims on these facts.
A personal injury claim must generally be brought within three years of the injury or of the claimant's knowledge of it.
A personal injury claim must be brought within twelve years, as for actions concerning deeds.
Tort.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the primary limitation period for a personal injury claim is three years, running from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the claimant's date of knowledge, subject to the court's discretion to extend the period.

n.0: The period is three years, not one year.
n.1: The personal injury period is three years, not the six-year period for ordinary contract/tort claims.
n.2: There is a time limit for personal injury claims; they cannot be brought at any time.
n.4: Twelve years applies to certain actions on deeds, not to personal injury claims.

Tort.q: A long-established factory begins to emit noise and smells that interfere with the comfort of neighbouring residents in what has always been a quiet residential area. The residents sue in private nuisance in respect of the loss of amenity, and the factory argues the interference is not unreasonable. The complaint concerns interference with comfort and enjoyment, not physical damage to the land. The character of the locality is residential. The area had always been peaceful and residential, the factory's noise and odours now intrude on the residents' day-to-day comfort at home, and the argument centres on whether an interference of that character, in a neighbourhood of this kind, crosses the line into an unreasonable one. Which of the following best describes the relevance of the locality to the claim?
o: The character of the locality is relevant only to claims for physical damage to land.
