The character of the locality means an industrial user can never be liable in a residential area.
The character of the locality determines liability solely according to who was there first.
The character of the locality is relevant to whether an amenity interference is unreasonable.
The character of the locality is irrelevant to every private nuisance claim.
Tort.w: In private nuisance the character of the locality is relevant to whether an interference with comfort or amenity is unreasonable: what counts as a nuisance in a quiet residential area may not in an industrial one. Locality is not, however, relevant where the nuisance causes physical damage to property, which is actionable regardless of the neighbourhood.

n.0: Locality is relevant to amenity claims, not (as stated) only to physical damage claims.
n.1: An industrial user can still be liable in a residential area; locality is one factor, not a shield.
n.2: Priority in time ('coming to the nuisance') does not by itself determine liability.
n.4: Locality is relevant to amenity nuisance, so it is not irrelevant.

Tort.q: A woman is not present at a disaster but later learns that her adult child was caught up in it. She attends the hospital some hours afterwards, sees her injured child, and subsequently develops a recognised psychiatric illness. She was never herself in any physical danger. She claims damages for her psychiatric injury as a secondary victim. The defendant argues that she cannot satisfy the requirements the law imposes on such claims. By the time she reached the hospital the immediate rescue was long over and her child had already been treated. Which of the following best describes the requirements she must meet?
o: She may recover provided she learned of the event from a reliable third party or the media.
She must show a close tie of love and affection, closeness in time and space to the event or its aftermath, and perception by her own senses.
She may recover on the same basis as if she had been in physical danger herself.
She need only show that her psychiatric illness was in fact caused by the defendant's negligence on these facts as a general rule.
She may recover simply because she is a parent of the person who was injured in the disaster.
Tort.w: A secondary victim must satisfy the control mechanisms in Alcock: a close tie of love and affection with the immediate victim, proximity in time and space to the incident or its immediate aftermath, and perception of the event through their own unaided senses. Mere causation is not enough.

n.0: Being told by a third party or via the media does not satisfy the perception requirement.
n.2: A secondary victim is not treated the same as a primary victim in physical danger.
n.3: Causation alone is insufficient for a secondary victim; the control mechanisms must be met.
n.4: Being a parent creates the tie, but the other Alcock requirements must also be satisfied.

Tort.q: An employee, in the course of doing their job for their employer, negligently injures a member of the public. The injured claimant wishes to sue the employer rather than the employee, because the employer is better able to meet a claim. The employer argues that it should not be responsible for the wrongdoing of another person and that only the employee who actually caused the injury should be liable. The claimant seeks advice on the basis on which the employer may be held responsible. The employee was carrying out an ordinary task assigned to them when the injury to the claimant occurred. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer is liable only if the employee cannot afford to pay the claim themselves.
The employer is liable only where it personally instructed the employee to commit the tort.
The employer is liable only where the employee is an independent contractor rather than a true employee.
The employer may be vicariously liable for a tort committed by an employee acting in the course of employment.
The employer can never be liable for a tort committed by its employee against a third party.
Tort.w: An employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee acting in the course of their employment. This is a form of strict, secondary liability that does not require the employer itself to have been at fault.

n.0: Vicarious liability does not depend on the employee's inability to pay.
n.1: The employer need not have instructed the tort; course of employment suffices.
n.2: Vicarious liability arises for employees; it does not generally apply to independent contractors.
n.4: Employers are routinely liable for employees' torts through vicarious liability.

Tort.q: A claimant, fully aware of an obvious and serious risk, freely and voluntarily chooses to take part in an activity in which that very risk then materialises and injures them. There was no pressure on the claimant to take part, they understood the nature and extent of the risk, and they willingly accepted it. The defendant argues that, in these particular circumstances, the claimant's voluntary acceptance of the risk provides a complete answer to the claim in negligence. No one had encouraged the claimant to take part, and they had joined in entirely of their own free choice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defence applies automatically whenever the claimant knew that some risk existed.
The claimant's knowledge of the risk is legally irrelevant to any claim in negligence.
The defence of consent (volenti) may provide a complete defence where the claimant freely accepted a fully understood risk.
The claimant's voluntary acceptance of the risk can only ever reduce, and never defeat, the claim on these facts.
The defence applies only where the claimant was paid to accept the risk in question.
Tort.w: Volenti non fit injuria is a complete defence where the claimant, with full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk, freely and voluntarily agreed to accept it. It requires genuine, informed and voluntary consent, and, if made out, defeats the claim entirely.

n.0: Mere knowledge that some risk exists is not enough; free and full acceptance is required.
n.1: The claimant's knowledge and acceptance of risk are central to the defence, not irrelevant.
n.3: Volenti, unlike contributory negligence, is a complete defence, not merely a reduction.
n.4: Payment is not a requirement of the defence.

Tort.q: A claimant establishes that the defendant is committing a continuing private nuisance which substantially interferes with the enjoyment of the claimant's land, and which is likely to continue into the future unless something is done. The claimant primarily wants the nuisance stopped, not merely to be paid for past interference. The court considers what remedy to grant, weighing the claimant's prima facie entitlement against the possibility of awarding money instead. The interference recurred almost daily and showed every sign of continuing indefinitely into the future. Which of the following best describes the position on remedies?
o: The court may grant an injunction to restrain the nuisance, and has a discretion to award damages in lieu.
The court must always grant an injunction, and can never award damages instead of one.
The court may act only after the local authority has first taken enforcement action.
The court may only ever award damages, and can never grant an injunction to stop a nuisance.
The court can grant no remedy at all unless the nuisance has caused physical damage to property.
Tort.w: The primary remedy for a continuing nuisance is an injunction to restrain it, an equitable and discretionary remedy. The court also has a discretion to award damages in lieu of an injunction in appropriate cases (Shelfer; Coventry v Lawrence). Self-help by abatement may also be available.

n.1: An injunction is discretionary, and damages in lieu may be awarded instead.
n.2: A civil nuisance claim does not depend on prior local-authority enforcement.
n.3: The court is not confined to damages; an injunction is the primary remedy for nuisance.
n.4: Interference with enjoyment is actionable in nuisance without physical property damage.

Tort.q: An employee is given a job that involves interacting with members of the public on the employer's behalf. In the course of carrying out that role, the employee commits a serious wrongful act against a customer which is closely connected with the duties the employee was employed to perform, even though the act was itself a gross abuse of the employee's position. The victim sues the employer. The employer argues that a deliberate wrongful act by the employee cannot possibly be within the course of employment. The employee had been placed in a position of trust and authority over the very customer who was harmed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer may still be vicariously liable if the wrongful act was closely connected with the employee's duties.
The employer is liable only for careless acts by employees, and never for intentional ones on these facts.
The employer is never liable for a deliberate or criminal wrongful act by an employee.
The employer is liable for any act at all committed by an employee at any time or place.
The employer is liable only where it expressly authorised the wrongful act in question.
Tort.w: An employer may be vicariously liable even for an employee's intentional or criminal wrongdoing where there is a sufficiently close connection between the wrongful act and the acts the employee was authorised to do, such that it is fair to impose liability (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud).

n.1: Vicarious liability is not limited to careless acts.
n.2: Deliberate or criminal acts can fall within vicarious liability under the close-connection test.
n.3: Not every act by an employee attracts liability; a close connection with the employment is needed.
n.4: Express authorisation of the wrong is not required.

Tort.q: A consumer is injured by a defective product and also suffers damage to a private item of property worth several hundred pounds, as well as damage to the defective product itself. The consumer claims under the Consumer Protection Act 1987. The private property damaged was for the consumer's own private use and its value exceeds the statutory threshold. The consumer wants to know what losses are recoverable under the Act. The fire not only injured the consumer but also ruined a valuable personal possession kept nearby and destroyed the appliance itself, and the consumer is trying to work out which of these various heads of loss the statutory product-liability regime will actually allow to be recovered. Which of the following best describes the damage recoverable under the Consumer Protection Act 1987?
o: Damage to any property, including business property and the defective product itself.
Only the cost of replacing the defective product, and nothing else.
Death or personal injury, and damage to private property above the statutory threshold, but not the defective product itself.
Only death or personal injury, with no recovery for any property damage at all.
Any and all financial losses flowing from the defect, including the cost of the product itself on these facts as a general rule.
Tort.w: The Consumer Protection Act 1987 allows recovery for death or personal injury, and for damage to private (non-business) property exceeding the statutory threshold (£275). It does not allow recovery for damage to the defective product itself, nor for pure economic loss; those must be pursued, if at all, in contract or ordinary negligence.

n.0: Business property and the product itself are excluded, so 'any property' is wrong.
n.1: Recovery is not limited to replacing the product; personal injury and qualifying property damage are covered.
n.3: Property damage (to qualifying private property) is recoverable, not only personal injury.
n.4: The cost of the defective product itself is not recoverable under the Act.

Tort.q: A business carries on an unusually delicate manufacturing process on its premises which is exceptionally sensitive to small changes in temperature or vibration. A neighbouring occupier carries on an ordinary and reasonable activity next door which would not trouble a normal user of land at all, but which interferes with the claimant's abnormally sensitive process. The claimant sues in private nuisance for the disruption to its delicate operation. The defendant argues that its activity is entirely ordinary and only affects the claimant because of the claimant's exceptional sensitivity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claimant generally cannot recover in nuisance for interference arising only from an abnormally sensitive use of land.
The claimant recovers, because the defendant's activity in fact interfered with the claimant's use of its land.
The claimant recovers in full, because any interference with its business is an actionable nuisance.
The claimant recovers, provided its sensitive process is a lawful and legitimate business activity.
The claimant recovers, because a defendant is always liable for any consequences of its own activities.
Tort.w: Historically a claimant could not complain of interference that affected only an abnormally sensitive use of land where an ordinary use would not have been troubled. The touchstone is whether the interference was an unreasonable one judged by ordinary use; special sensitivity does not, by itself, make an otherwise reasonable activity a nuisance.

n.1: Mere factual interference is not enough where it stems from the claimant's exceptional sensitivity.
n.2: Not every interference with a business is actionable; abnormal sensitivity is the problem here.
n.3: The lawfulness of the claimant's process does not make the neighbour's ordinary activity a nuisance.
n.4: A defendant is not liable for all consequences; the interference must be unreasonable.

Tort.q: A doctor adopts a particular method of treatment that is supported by a responsible body of medical opinion. The claimant argues the doctor was negligent, and calls expert evidence that the practice, although followed by some practitioners, is not capable of withstanding logical analysis and exposes patients to a risk that has no proper justification. The court must decide how to treat the fact that some professionals support the practice where its logic is challenged. The practice is followed by some but is said to be indefensible on logical analysis. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?
o: A doctor is judged by the standard of the most skilled specialist in the field in every case.
A practice supported by a body of opinion still must withstand logical analysis to avoid a finding of breach.
The court substitutes its own preferred treatment for the doctor's whenever experts disagree.
A practice supported by any body of medical opinion is always conclusive against a finding of breach.
A doctor cannot be negligent so long as a single other doctor would have done the same.
Tort.w: Under Bolam a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a responsible body of medical opinion, but Bolitho qualifies this: the court must be satisfied that the body of opinion has a logical basis and withstands analysis. A practice that cannot be logically defended will not shield the doctor from a finding of breach.

n.0: The doctor is judged by the standard of the ordinary competent practitioner in the field, not the most skilled specialist.
n.2: The court does not simply prefer its own treatment whenever experts differ.
n.3: Support by a body of opinion is not conclusive if the opinion is not logically defensible.
n.4: One supportive doctor is not enough; the opinion must be responsible and logically sound.

Tort.q: An employee is injured at work because the equipment provided was inadequate, the system of work was unsafe, and fellow workers were not competent. The employer argues it delegated safety to a manager and so should not be personally liable. The claim is framed as a breach of the employer's own duty to its employee, not merely vicarious liability. The failures relate to staff, equipment, system of work and the workplace. The injured worker points to a combination of failings, unsafe machinery, a badly designed system of work and inadequately trained colleagues, and the employer's answer is simply that it had handed the whole question of safety to a manager, which it says should be enough to shift responsibility away from itself. Which of the following best describes the nature of the employer's duty here?
o: The employer owes a duty only in respect of equipment, not the system of work or staff.
The employer's duty is strict, making it liable for any injury however it was caused.
The employer owes a personal, non-delegable duty to take reasonable care for the employee: competent staff, adequate equipment, a safe system and a safe workplace.
The employer's only possible liability is vicarious liability for the acts of the manager.
The employer owes no personal duty because responsibility for safety can be fully delegated to a manager on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Tort.w: An employer owes each employee a personal, non-delegable duty to take reasonable care for their safety. This is traditionally analysed as duties to provide competent fellow workers, adequate plant and equipment, a safe system of work, and a safe place of work. Because the duty is non-delegable, delegating its performance does not discharge the employer's responsibility.

n.0: The duty covers staff, equipment, system of work and workplace, not equipment alone.
n.1: The duty is to take reasonable care, not a strict liability for any injury.
n.3: The employer can be personally liable for breach of its own duty, not only vicariously.
n.4: The duty is non-delegable; delegating to a manager does not remove the employer's responsibility.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently leaves a dangerous obstacle, and a boy is injured when, in an unforeseeable way, an unexpected explosion occurs, causing burns. Burns from contact with the danger were a foreseeable type of harm, but the precise sequence of events producing them was not foreseeable. The defendant argues the harm is too remote because the exact manner in which it happened could not have been predicted. The type of harm (burns) was foreseeable although the manner in which it came about was not. Children were known to play in the area, the boy was drawn to the hazard the defendant had carelessly left unguarded, and although burns from the danger were an obvious risk, the particular chain of events that produced them unfolded in a freakish and unexpected way that nobody could have predicted in detail. Which of the following best describes the position on remoteness?
o: The damage is too remote because the exact sequence of events must be foreseeable.
The damage is recoverable only if every step in the chain of events was individually foreseeable on these facts.
The damage is recoverable regardless of whether any type of harm was foreseeable at all.
The damage is not too remote, as harm of a foreseeable type occurred even if the precise manner was unforeseeable.
The damage is too remote because the defendant must foresee the precise extent of the injury.
Tort.w: Damage is not too remote if it is of a kind or type that was reasonably foreseeable; the precise manner in which it comes about, and its exact extent, need not be foreseeable (Hughes v Lord Advocate). As burns were a foreseeable type of harm, the injury is recoverable despite the unforeseeable sequence of events.

n.0: The exact sequence of events need not be foreseeable.
n.1: Each individual step need not be foreseeable; foreseeability of the type of harm suffices.
n.2: Foreseeability of the type of harm is required; it is not irrelevant.
n.4: The precise extent of the injury need not be foreseeable, only the type.

Tort.q: A visitor to a building is injured by faulty construction work carried out on the premises by a specialist independent contractor whom the occupier had engaged. The occupier took reasonable care to select a competent and reputable contractor for the job, and the work was of a kind that required specialist skill which the occupier did not have. The injured visitor sues the occupier under the occupiers' liability legislation. The occupier relies on the fact that the work was done by an independent contractor. The occupier had checked the contractor's references and qualifications carefully before engaging it for the specialist work. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier is never liable for anything done by an independent contractor in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
The occupier is liable unless the visitor knew that an independent contractor had done the work.
The occupier is always liable for any injury caused by work done on its premises, whoever did it.
The occupier may avoid liability if it acted reasonably in entrusting the work to a competent contractor and checking it where reasonable.
The occupier is liable only if it failed to insure against injuries on the premises.
Tort.w: Under s.2(4)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, an occupier is not liable for a visitor's injury caused by the faulty work of an independent contractor if the occupier acted reasonably in entrusting the work to the contractor and took reasonable steps to check competence and, where appropriate, that the work was properly done.

n.0: The occupier can be liable for a contractor's work if it did not act reasonably; 'never' is wrong.
n.1: The visitor's knowledge of who did the work is not the test.
n.2: The occupier is not automatically liable for all work done on the premises.
n.4: Liability does not turn on whether the occupier had insurance.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured in a road accident caused by the defendant's negligent driving. However, the claimant was not wearing a seatbelt at the time, and the medical evidence shows that their injuries were significantly more serious than they would have been had they been belted in. The defendant accepts liability for the accident but argues that the claimant's own carelessness for their safety should reduce the compensation payable. The seatbelt was fitted and working, and there was no good reason for the claimant not to have worn it. Which of the following best describes the effect of the claimant's failure to wear a seatbelt?
o: The claimant's damages are automatically halved whenever a seatbelt was not worn.
The claimant's damages are reduced only if the failure to belt up actually caused the accident itself.
The claimant recovers in full, because the defendant caused the accident in the first place.
The claimant's damages may be reduced for contributory negligence to reflect their share of responsibility.
The claimant recovers nothing at all, because failing to wear a seatbelt is a complete defence.
Tort.w: Under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945, where a claimant's own want of care for their safety contributes to the damage they suffer, their damages are reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable. Failing to wear a seatbelt is a classic example of contributory negligence.

n.0: There is no fixed automatic reduction; the court assesses a just and equitable figure.
n.1: Contributory negligence applies to carelessness contributing to the damage, not only to the accident.
n.2: The claimant does not recover in full where their own carelessness increased the injuries.
n.4: Contributory negligence reduces damages; it is not a complete defence.

Tort.q: A person is injured by a defective product and wishes to bring a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, but is unsure who can be held liable. The product was manufactured abroad, imported into the United Kingdom by an importer, and sold under a supermarket's own brand name, and the ultimate producer cannot easily be identified by the consumer. The injured person seeks advice on who may be liable for a defective product under the Act. The consumer wrote to the supermarket asking who had produced the item but received no useful reply at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Liability may fall on the producer, an own-brander who holds themselves out as producer, or the importer into the UK.
No one can be liable unless the consumer can identify the exact original producer abroad on these facts as a general rule.
Only the shop that physically sold the product to the consumer can ever be liable.
Only the individual factory worker who actually made the product can be held liable.
Liability falls only on whoever the consumer chooses to sue, regardless of their role.
Tort.w: Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, those who may be liable include the producer (manufacturer), a person who holds themselves out as the producer by putting their own brand on the product ('own-brander'), and the person who imported the product into the UK. A mere supplier may be liable only if it fails to identify the producer on request.

n.1: Own-branders and importers can be liable even where the original overseas producer is not identified.
n.2: A mere retailer is generally liable only where it cannot identify the producer on request.
n.3: Liability is not limited to the individual worker who made the item.
n.4: Liability attaches to defined categories of person, not simply whoever is chosen as defendant.

Tort.q: A person trespasses onto industrial land by climbing over a fence, and is injured by a dangerous piece of machinery there. The occupier knew the machinery was dangerous, knew that people sometimes climbed in at that spot, and could reasonably have offered some protection against the danger, but did nothing. The trespasser sues the occupier. The occupier argues that it owes no duty at all to someone who was not permitted to be on the land. Warning signs had been torn down some time earlier, and the gap in the perimeter fencing had never been repaired. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier may owe a duty to the trespasser under the 1984 Act where the statutory conditions are met.
The occupier owes a trespasser exactly the same common duty of care as it owes to lawful visitors.
The occupier owes no duty of any kind to a trespasser in any circumstances whatsoever.
The occupier owes a duty to a trespasser only if the trespasser was a child rather than an adult.
The occupier owes a duty to a trespasser only once the trespasser has actually been injured.
Tort.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, an occupier may owe a duty to a non-visitor (trespasser) where it is aware of the danger, knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser may come into its vicinity, and the risk is one against which it may reasonably be expected to offer some protection.

n.1: The 1984 Act duty is narrower than the common duty of care owed to lawful visitors.
n.2: A trespasser may be owed a duty under the 1984 Act, so 'no duty ever' is wrong.
n.3: The 1984 Act duty is not confined to child trespassers.
n.4: The duty exists on the conditions being met; it does not arise only after injury occurs.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently causes a fire. Owing to a wholly unforeseeable and unusual chain of events, the fire leads to a highly unexpected type of damage to the claimant's property, of a kind that no reasonable person could have anticipated from the defendant's carelessness. Ordinary fire damage would have been foreseeable, but the particular type of harm that occurred was not. The claimant claims for the unforeseeable type of damage. The court must apply the rules on remoteness of damage. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is liable for all damage that in fact flows directly from the breach, foreseeable or not.
The defendant is liable only if the exact extent of the damage was precisely foreseeable.
The defendant is liable for no damage at all, because the events were unusual and unexpected.
The defendant is liable only for damage of a type that was reasonably foreseeable here.
The defendant is liable for the unforeseeable damage, provided some damage of any kind was foreseeable.
Tort.w: Under the remoteness rule in The Wagon Mound (No 1), a defendant is liable only for damage of a kind or type that was reasonably foreseeable as a result of the breach. Damage of an unforeseeable type is too remote and not recoverable, even if some damage was foreseeable.

n.0: Liability is limited by foreseeability of the type of harm, not all directly-flowing damage.
n.1: The precise extent need not be foreseeable, but the type of damage must be.
n.2: Some liability may still arise for foreseeable types; it is the unforeseeable type that is too remote.
n.4: It is the type of harm that must be foreseeable, not its precise extent.

Tort.q: A claimant argues that the defendant should be liable in negligence for failing to act — for a pure omission — where the defendant simply stood by and did nothing while the claimant came to harm, even though the defendant could easily have intervened to help. There was no special relationship between them, the defendant did not create the danger, and the defendant had assumed no responsibility for the claimant. The claimant says the defendant should have acted as any decent person would. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is liability because a bystander always owes a legal duty to rescue those in peril.
There is generally no liability in negligence for a pure omission to act, absent a recognised exception.
There is liability whenever the defendant could easily have prevented the harm but chose not to.
There is always liability for failing to help another person who is in danger.
There is liability because failing to act is treated in law exactly like a positive act of harm.
Tort.w: The common law generally imposes no liability in negligence for a pure omission — a mere failure to confer a benefit or to rescue — absent a recognised basis for a duty, such as a special relationship, assumption of responsibility, control, or the defendant having created the danger.

n.0: A bystander does not generally owe a legal duty to rescue.
n.2: Ease of prevention alone does not create a duty to act.
n.3: There is no general duty to help; liability for omissions is exceptional.
n.4: The law distinguishes omissions from positive acts; they are not treated identically.

Tort.q: A bank, at the request of a customer's supplier, gives the supplier a reference about the customer's creditworthiness. The bank does so carelessly and the reference is inaccurate. The supplier, reasonably relying on the reference, extends credit to the customer and loses a large sum when the customer cannot pay. The supplier sues the bank in negligence for the purely financial loss. The bank argues that it owed the supplier no duty of care for a careless statement causing only financial loss. The supplier had no other means of assessing the customer's finances and took the reference at face value. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A duty arises automatically whenever one party gives another any information at all.
A duty arises only where the maker of the statement acted dishonestly rather than merely carelessly.
A duty may arise for a negligent statement where the maker assumes responsibility and the claimant reasonably relies on it.
No duty can ever arise for a careless statement that causes only financial rather than physical loss on these facts.
A duty arises only where there was a contract between the maker of the statement and the claimant.
Tort.w: A duty of care can arise for negligent misstatement causing pure economic loss where there is a special relationship: the maker of the statement, having relevant skill, assumes responsibility for it and the claimant reasonably relies on it to their detriment (Hedley Byrne v Heller).

n.0: A duty does not arise for every statement; a special relationship is required.
n.1: Liability can arise for careless statements, not only dishonest ones.
n.3: Pure economic loss from a negligent statement can be recoverable via the Hedley Byrne principle.
n.4: A contract is not required; the assumption of responsibility can arise without one.

Tort.q: A person buys a house next to an existing workshop and then sues the workshop owner in private nuisance for noise that the workshop has been generating in the same way for many years, from before the claimant arrived. The workshop owner argues that the claimant 'came to the nuisance' and so cannot complain. The activity pre-dated the claimant's arrival but the claimant's use of the land is otherwise ordinary. The workshop had been operating in exactly the same way for many years before the claimant ever moved in next door, and the owner's central point is that the claimant knowingly bought a house beside a working workshop and cannot now be heard to complain about the very activity that was always there. Which of the following best describes the effect of the claimant having come to the nuisance?
o: It is a complete defence that the claimant came to the nuisance.
It is generally no defence that the claimant came to the nuisance.
It prevents any remedy but allows the claimant to recover nominal damages only.
It is a defence because an established activity acquires immunity from any later neighbour.
It is a defence only if the activity had continued for more than five years.
Tort.w: It is generally no defence to a claim in private nuisance that the claimant came to the nuisance, that is, acquired or began using their land after the defendant's activity had begun. The defendant cannot rely on the prior existence of the activity to defeat the claim, though the claimant's use of land and locality remain relevant to reasonableness.

n.0: Coming to the nuisance is not a complete defence.
n.2: The claimant is not limited to nominal damages merely for having come to the nuisance.
n.3: An established activity does not acquire general immunity against later neighbours by mere continuation.
n.4: There is no rule making it a defence after a fixed period such as five years (contrast prescription's twenty years).

Tort.q: A family lives together in a rented house which is affected by a persistent nuisance emanating from a neighbouring property. Several members of the household are troubled by it, but only one of them, the tenant, has any legal interest in the land; the others are family members and licensees living there with no proprietary interest of their own. They all wish to sue the neighbour in private nuisance. The neighbour argues that most of the household have no standing to bring such a claim. The nuisance had continued for many months and troubled the whole household throughout that period. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No one may sue in private nuisance unless they also own the neighbouring land causing it.
Any person who is in fact troubled by the interference has standing to sue in nuisance.
Only the owner of the freehold, and never a mere tenant, may sue in private nuisance.
Only a person with a proprietary interest in the affected land can generally sue in private nuisance.
Anyone who lives in the affected property may sue in private nuisance, whatever their interest.
Tort.w: Private nuisance protects rights in land, so generally only a person with a proprietary interest in the affected land (such as a freeholder or tenant in possession) has standing to sue. Mere occupiers without such an interest cannot bring the claim (Hunter v Canary Wharf).

n.0: The claimant need not own the offending land; they must have an interest in the affected land.
n.1: Being troubled by the interference is not enough without a proprietary interest.
n.2: A tenant in possession does have a sufficient interest to sue; it is not confined to freeholders.
n.4: Mere residence without a proprietary interest does not give standing in private nuisance.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured and sues the defendant in negligence. It is accepted that the defendant was careless, but there is a dispute about whether that carelessness actually caused the claimant's injury. The evidence shows that, even if the defendant had taken all proper care, the very same injury would still have occurred in exactly the same way. The claimant argues that the defendant's breach is enough on its own to establish liability. The court must apply the test for factual causation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails on causation, because the injury would have occurred even without the defendant's breach.
The claim fails only if the claimant was also partly at fault for the injury.
The claim succeeds, because the defendant admitted that they had been careless.
The claim succeeds, because a proven breach of duty automatically establishes causation of the injury.
The claim succeeds, provided the injury was of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable.
Tort.w: Factual causation is generally decided by the 'but for' test: the claimant must show that, but for the defendant's breach, the harm would not have occurred. Where the injury would have happened anyway, causation is not established and the claim fails (Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital).

n.1: The claim fails on causation regardless of any fault of the claimant.
n.2: An admission of carelessness does not prove that the carelessness caused the harm.
n.3: Breach alone does not establish causation; the 'but for' test must be satisfied.
n.4: Foreseeability goes to duty and remoteness, not to factual causation.

Tort.q: A company carries out an activity that affects a large section of the local community: it causes obstruction and noxious fumes affecting a whole neighbourhood of residents and road users, rather than just one landowner. One resident suffers particular, additional damage over and above the general inconvenience shared by everyone else in the area. That resident wishes to bring a civil claim arising out of the situation. The resident seeks advice on the basis of a claim in public nuisance. The obstruction lasted for weeks and affected residents, shopkeepers and road users right across the area. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Public nuisance is purely a criminal matter, and no individual can ever bring a civil claim for it on these facts as a general rule.
An individual may sue in public nuisance only if they have suffered special damage beyond that suffered by the public generally.
The resident may sue only if they also have a proprietary interest in affected land.
The resident may sue only if the company intended to harm the local community.
Any member of the affected public may bring a civil claim in public nuisance without more.
Tort.w: Public nuisance is an act affecting a class of the public. An individual can bring a civil claim in public nuisance only where they have suffered special (particular) damage over and above that suffered by the public at large.

n.0: Public nuisance, though a crime, can also found a civil claim where there is special damage.
n.2: A proprietary interest in land is required for private nuisance, not for a public nuisance special-damage claim.
n.3: Intention to harm is not required for public nuisance.
n.4: An ordinary member of the affected public cannot sue without showing special damage.

Tort.q: A motorist drives carelessly through a junction and collides with a pedestrian who is lawfully crossing the road, causing the pedestrian serious physical injuries and financial loss. The pedestrian wishes to bring a claim in the tort of negligence against the motorist. The motorist accepts that they were driving without proper care, but questions whether they owed the pedestrian any relevant legal duty at all in these circumstances. The pedestrian seeks advice on whether a duty of care existed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No duty of care is owed to pedestrians, because a duty in negligence is owed only to other drivers.
No duty of care arises, because the motorist did not intend to cause the pedestrian any harm.
A duty of care exists only if the court applies the full three-stage Caparo test to these facts.
A road user owes a well-established duty of care to other road users, including pedestrians.
No duty of care arises unless the pedestrian and motorist had some prior relationship with one another.
Tort.w: Duties of care are established in recognised categories, and it is long settled that road users owe a duty of care to other road users, including pedestrians. Where the relationship falls within an established category, there is no need to apply the incremental Caparo analysis afresh.

n.0: The duty extends to pedestrians and other road users, not only to other drivers.
n.1: Negligence does not require an intention to cause harm; carelessness suffices.
n.2: The full Caparo test is for novel situations; this is an established duty.
n.4: No prior relationship is needed; the road-user duty is an established category.

Tort.q: A young child lawfully visits a park run by a local authority and is injured by an attractive but dangerous feature which drew the child in but which an adult would have recognised and avoided. The authority argues it took the care that would keep an ordinary adult visitor safe, and that this should be enough. The child's parents sue under the occupiers' liability legislation, arguing a higher standard applied because the visitor was a child. The feature was brightly coloured and obviously tempting to a young child exploring the park with little supervision. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An occupier owes children exactly the same standard as adults, with no allowance for their age.
An occupier discharges its duty to children simply by displaying a warning notice that adults could read on these facts.
An occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults, so a greater standard of care may be required.
An occupier owes no duty at all to child visitors, who are the responsibility of their parents alone.
An occupier's duty to children arises only where the child paid to enter the premises.
Tort.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults. A danger that is not a trap to an adult may be an allurement to a child, so a higher standard of care may be needed to keep child visitors reasonably safe.

n.0: The Act expressly requires allowance for children being less careful than adults.
n.1: A notice an adult could read may not discharge the duty owed to a young child.
n.3: An occupier does owe duties to child visitors under the 1957 Act.
n.4: The duty to child visitors does not depend on payment of an entry fee.

Tort.q: A claimant suffers a leg injury caused by the defendant's negligence, leaving the claimant with a permanent limp and reduced earning capacity. Before trial, the same leg is seriously injured again in an entirely separate incident, which would in any event have caused the same disability. The defendant argues that the second injury reduces the damages payable for the first. The first tortfeasor's negligence caused an injury whose effects were later overtaken by a separate tortious injury. The first accident left the claimant with a permanent limp and a settled reduction in earning capacity, and then, entirely by chance and through a wholly unconnected wrongdoer, the very same leg was badly hurt again before the case came to trial, prompting the first defendant to argue its own responsibility had shrunk. Which of the following best describes the effect on the first defendant's liability?
o: The first defendant's liability ends completely at the moment the second injury occurs.
The first defendant is liable only for losses arising after the second injury, not before.
The first defendant remains liable for the continuing effects of the original injury despite the later separate injury.
The first defendant becomes jointly liable with the person who caused the second injury for everything on these facts.
The second injury automatically extinguishes all damages for the first injury from the outset.
Tort.w: Where a claimant's tortious injury is later overtaken by a second, separate tortious injury producing the same disability, the first tortfeasor remains liable for the continuing loss caused by the original injury (Baker v Willoughby). The later tort does not wipe out the first defendant's responsibility for the damage it caused.

n.0: The first defendant's liability does not cease when the second injury occurs.
n.1: The first defendant remains liable for the ongoing effects, including after the second injury.
n.3: The first defendant is not made jointly liable for the separate second tort.
n.4: The second injury does not extinguish damages for the first from the outset.

Tort.q: A trespasser climbs over a fence onto industrial premises at night and is injured by a dangerous piece of machinery. The occupier knew the machinery was dangerous, knew that people sometimes climbed in at that point, and could readily have offered some protection against the risk. The injured person was not a lawful visitor. The occupier was aware of the danger and of the likelihood of trespassers coming into its vicinity. There had been previous incidents of people getting into the yard at that spot, the machine was left accessible and unguarded, and the occupier was well aware both of how dangerous it was and that intruders were apt to come near it, yet took no steps to fence it off or warn. Which of the following best describes when the occupier owes a duty to the trespasser under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984?
o: A duty arises where the occupier is aware of the danger, knows a trespasser may come, and it is reasonable to offer protection.
The occupier owes a trespasser exactly the same common duty of care as a lawful visitor on these facts as a general rule.
A duty arises automatically whenever any trespasser is injured on the premises.
A duty arises only if the occupier deliberately intended to injure the trespasser.
No duty is ever owed to a trespasser, whatever the occupier knew or could have done.
Tort.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, an occupier owes a duty to a non-visitor if it is aware of the danger (or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists), knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser may come into its vicinity, and the risk is one against which, in all the circumstances, it may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. Those conditions are satisfied here.

n.1: The duty owed to trespassers is narrower than the common duty owed to lawful visitors.
n.2: The duty does not arise automatically on any injury; the statutory conditions must be met.
n.3: The duty does not require an intention to injure; it turns on knowledge and reasonableness.
n.4: A duty can be owed to trespassers under the 1984 Act, so 'never' is wrong.

Tort.q: A claimant succeeds in a personal injury claim in negligence, having suffered a serious physical injury, considerable pain, a long period off work with lost earnings, and various out-of-pocket expenses for treatment and care. The claimant wishes to understand what the damages award is intended to include. The defendant accepts liability but disputes some heads of loss. The claimant seeks advice on the general nature of the damages recoverable for a personal injury of this kind. The claimant was off work for many months and incurred significant costs for treatment and rehabilitation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages cover only pain and suffering, and never any award for lost earnings or expenses.
Damages are limited to a fixed statutory sum that is the same for every personal injury claim on these facts as a general rule.
Damages are payable only where the injury has left the claimant permanently disabled.
Damages cover only the claimant's actual financial losses, and nothing for pain or suffering.
Damages cover both general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and special damages for quantifiable financial losses.
Tort.w: Damages for personal injury comprise general damages (non-pecuniary loss such as pain, suffering and loss of amenity, and future losses that cannot be precisely calculated) and special damages (pecuniary losses accrued to trial, such as lost earnings and expenses that can be quantified).

n.0: Damages include lost earnings and expenses as well as pain and suffering.
n.1: There is no single fixed statutory sum; damages are assessed on the facts.
n.2: Damages are not confined to cases of permanent disability.
n.3: Damages include non-pecuniary loss such as pain and suffering, not only financial loss.

Tort.q: Two teenagers of the same age are playing together with plastic rulers when one ruler snaps and a fragment injures the other's eye. The injured teenager sues the other in negligence. The defendant is a child, and the question arises as to the standard of care by which a child defendant's conduct is to be judged when deciding whether they were negligent. The claimant argues the defendant should be judged like an adult. Both children were of exactly the same age and were playing together in the ordinary way that children of that age do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A child is judged by exactly the same standard of care as a reasonable adult would meet.
A child is judged by the standard of a reasonable child of the same age, not by the adult standard.
A child is judged purely by their own individual level of maturity and understanding.
A child is judged by the standard of the most careful child that could be imagined.
A child can never be liable in negligence, whatever the child's age or conduct.
Tort.w: Where the defendant is a child, the standard of care is that of a reasonable and careful child of the defendant's age, not the adult standard (Mullin v Richards). The test remains objective, but calibrated to the defendant's age.

n.0: A child is not held to the full adult standard of care.
n.2: The standard is objective for a child of that age, not the child's own subjective maturity.
n.3: The standard is the reasonable child of that age, not the most careful child imaginable.
n.4: Children can be liable in negligence if they fall below the standard of a reasonable child of their age.

Tort.q: An organisation engages an individual whose relationship with it, although not a formal contract of employment, is akin to employment: the individual is integrated into the organisation's activities and works on its behalf rather than running an independent business of their own. The individual commits a tort connected with that work, and the claimant seeks to hold the organisation vicariously liable. The relationship is closely analogous to employment rather than that of an independent contractor. The individual wore the organisation's uniform, was told what to do and how to do it, and was in practice absorbed into the organisation's operation rather than trading independently on their own account, so the question is whether that relationship is close enough to employment to carry vicarious liability. Which of the following best describes when vicarious liability may arise from such a relationship?
o: Vicarious liability arises only where there is a formal written contract of employment.
Vicarious liability may arise where the relationship is akin to employment, even without a formal contract of employment.
Vicarious liability arises automatically for anyone doing any work for the organisation.
Vicarious liability arises for the acts of any independent contractor engaged by the organisation on these facts.
Vicarious liability can never arise unless the wrongdoer is a direct employee.
Tort.w: Vicarious liability requires a relationship of employment or one 'akin to employment'. Where a person is integrated into the defendant's organisation and works on its behalf rather than running their own independent business, the relationship may be sufficiently analogous to employment to found vicarious liability, even without a formal employment contract. True independent contractors generally fall outside it.

n.0: A formal written contract of employment is not essential; an akin-to-employment relationship suffices.
n.2: It does not arise automatically for anyone doing any work; the relationship must be employment or akin to it.
n.3: Vicarious liability does not generally arise for the acts of a genuine independent contractor.
n.4: It can arise for relationships akin to employment, not only for direct employees.

Tort.q: A claimant suffers a novel type of loss in circumstances that do not fall within any previously recognised category in which a duty of care has been held to exist. The claimant argues that the defendant should nonetheless owe them a duty of care in the tort of negligence. The court must decide whether to recognise a duty of care in this new situation, and considers the established approach to determining whether a duty arises in a case of this kind. Which of the following best describes the test the court applies?
o: The court imposes a duty of care in every case in which the claimant has in fact suffered a loss.
The court asks whether harm was foreseeable, proximity exists, and a duty is fair, just and reasonable.
The court refuses a duty of care in any situation that is not already an established category.
The court imposes a duty of care only where the defendant and claimant had a contract between them.
The court imposes a duty of care whenever the defendant could afford to pay compensation.
Tort.w: In a novel situation, the court decides whether to recognise a duty of care using the threefold approach derived from Caparo v Dickman: reasonable foreseeability of harm, a relationship of proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, developed incrementally by analogy with established cases.

n.0: A duty does not arise merely because loss was suffered; the threefold test must be satisfied.
n.2: Novel duties can be recognised incrementally; the law is not frozen to existing categories.
n.3: A contract is not required for a duty of care in negligence.
n.4: The defendant's ability to pay is irrelevant to whether a duty of care exists.

Tort.q: A business occupier of premises to which paying visitors come displays a prominent notice at the entrance which purports to exclude all of its liability for personal injury caused by the negligence of the occupier or its staff. A visitor is injured through the occupier's negligence and, when they claim, the occupier relies on the exclusion notice to defeat the claim for the physical injury. The visitor seeks advice on whether the occupier can exclude liability for their personal injury in this way. The visitor had paid an entrance fee and had no realistic opportunity to negotiate the terms of entry. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury provided the notice is large and clearly displayed.
The occupier cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, as statute prohibits it.
The occupier can exclude all liability by a clear notice, because visitors are taken to accept its terms.
The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury provided the visitor had paid to enter the premises.
The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury unless the visitor is a consumer rather than a business.
Tort.w: An occupier's ability to exclude the common duty of care is constrained by statute. Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (business liability) and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (for consumers), liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded or restricted at all.

n.0: Size and prominence of the notice do not overcome the statutory prohibition.
n.2: A clear notice cannot exclude liability for negligently caused personal injury.
n.3: Payment to enter does not permit excluding liability for personal injury.
n.4: The bar on excluding personal-injury liability protects consumers and applies to business visitors under UCTA too.

Tort.q: A householder in a quiet residential street is disturbed by a neighbour who has started running a noisy business from home, generating loud noise and vibration late into the evening on most days of the week. The noise substantially interferes with the householder's ordinary use and enjoyment of their home over a sustained period. The householder wishes to bring a claim in private nuisance. The neighbour argues that they are entitled to use their own property as they wish. The householder seeks advice on how the court assesses whether there is an actionable nuisance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim succeeds only if the noise has caused physical damage to the householder's property.
Any interference with a neighbour's enjoyment of their land is automatically an actionable nuisance.
The claim succeeds only if the householder can prove the neighbour intended to cause the disturbance on these facts.
There can be no nuisance, because a person may always use their own property however they wish.
The court asks whether the interference is unreasonable, considering factors such as locality, duration and intensity.
Tort.w: Private nuisance is an unlawful, unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of their land. Whether the interference is unreasonable is judged by factors including the nature of the locality, the duration and frequency, the intensity of the interference, and any malice.

n.0: Nuisance covers interference with enjoyment, not only physical property damage.
n.1: Not every interference is a nuisance; it must be unreasonable.
n.2: Intention is not required, though malice may be relevant to reasonableness.
n.3: The right to use one's land is limited by the obligation not to cause an unreasonable nuisance.

Tort.q: An employee, during the working day, abandons their assigned duties entirely and goes off on a substantial personal errand of their own, wholly unconnected with their job and for their own purposes. While engaged in that purely personal venture, and far removed from anything they were employed to do, the employee negligently injures a third party. The injured party sues the employer, seeking to rely on vicarious liability. The employer argues that the employee was on a frolic of their own at the time. The personal errand had taken the employee several miles away from their assigned place of work that day. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer is liable, because the injury happened during the employee's normal working hours.
The employer is liable, because the employee was still technically employed at the time of the injury.
The employer is liable, because an employer is responsible for everything an employee does all day.
The employer is liable, provided the employee was using the employer's vehicle when the injury occurred on these facts.
The employer is unlikely to be liable, because the employee was on a frolic of their own outside the course of employment.
Tort.w: Vicarious liability arises only where the employee is acting in the course of employment. Where the employee has abandoned their duties on a purely personal venture — a 'frolic of their own' — unconnected with the job, the act falls outside the course of employment and the employer is not vicariously liable.

n.0: Merely occurring in working hours does not bring a personal frolic within the course of employment.
n.1: Still being employed does not make a personal frolic part of the course of employment.
n.2: An employer is not responsible for everything an employee does regardless of connection to the job.
n.3: Using the employer's vehicle does not, by itself, bring a personal frolic within employment.

Tort.q: An employee is injured at work because of unsafe working arrangements. The problems included incompetent fellow workers who had not been properly vetted, defective equipment, an unsafe workplace, and no safe system of work in place. The employer argues that it delegated health and safety to a manager and so should not itself be liable. The injured employee seeks advice on the nature of the duty the employer owed. The employer had a large workforce but had never carried out any proper risk assessment of the tasks involved. Which of the following best describes the employer's primary liability?
o: An employer owes no personal duty to employees and is liable only vicariously for others' acts.
An employer owes a personal, non-delegable duty to provide competent staff, safe equipment, a safe workplace and a safe system of work.
An employer discharges its duty completely by delegating health and safety to a competent manager.
An employer's duty is limited to providing safe equipment, and does not extend to the system of work on these facts as a general rule.
An employer owes a duty only to employees who have worked for it for a minimum qualifying period.
Tort.w: An employer owes each employee a personal, non-delegable duty of care to take reasonable steps to provide competent fellow employees, adequate equipment, a safe place of work and a safe system of work. Delegating the task to another does not discharge the employer's own duty.

n.0: The employer owes a personal primary duty, not merely vicarious liability.
n.2: Because the duty is non-delegable, delegation to a manager does not discharge it.
n.3: The duty covers the system of work, not just equipment.
n.4: The duty is owed to employees generally, not only after a qualifying period.

Tort.q: A defendant carried out an activity that created only a very small risk of harm, where the cost and difficulty of eliminating that small risk entirely would have been very high, and where the activity itself had significant social utility. An accident nonetheless occurred and the claimant was injured. The claimant argues the defendant should have taken every possible precaution regardless of cost. The court must weigh the relevant factors in deciding whether the defendant breached the standard of care. Which of the following best describes how breach is assessed?
o: Breach weighs the likelihood and seriousness of harm against the cost of precautions and utility.
The defendant is in breach unless they eliminated every conceivable risk, whatever the cost.
Breach depends only on whether harm was in fact caused to the claimant.
Breach is assessed purely by asking whether the defendant could have afforded better precautions.
The defendant is never in breach so long as the activity had some social utility of any kind.
Tort.w: Whether the standard of care has been breached involves balancing the magnitude of the risk (likelihood and seriousness of harm) against the cost and practicability of precautions and the social utility of the defendant's activity (Bolton v Stone; Watt v Hertfordshire).

n.1: A defendant need not eliminate every conceivable risk regardless of cost; the test is a balance.
n.2: The occurrence of harm does not by itself establish breach.
n.3: Affordability alone is not the test; the full balancing of factors applies.
n.4: Social utility is one factor in the balance, not a complete answer to any risk.

Tort.q: Professional rescuers (emergency service employees) attend the scene of a disaster caused by an employer's negligence and later develop recognised psychiatric illnesses from what they experienced, though they were not themselves in physical danger. They argue they should be treated as primary victims simply because they acted as rescuers. They were not exposed to danger to their own physical safety. They were deployed to a catastrophe brought about by their employer's failings, spent hours amid harrowing scenes doing their professional duty, and later developed diagnosed psychiatric conditions, and they now argue that their status as rescuers should by itself place them in the more favourable category of claimant. Which of the following best describes their position in claiming for psychiatric injury?
o: Rescuers can never recover for psychiatric injury in any circumstances.
Rescuers recover only if they are related to those they attempted to rescue.
Rescuers are always primary victims entitled to recover for psychiatric injury without more on these facts.
Rescuers recover automatically provided their distress was foreseeable to the defendant.
Rescuers are not a special category and must satisfy the ordinary primary or secondary victim requirements.
Tort.w: Rescuers are not given any special status for psychiatric injury claims (White v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire). To recover, a rescuer must qualify as a primary victim (for example, by being exposed to danger or reasonably believing themselves to be) or satisfy the secondary victim control mechanisms; simply acting as a rescuer is not enough.

n.0: Rescuers can recover if they meet the ordinary requirements, so 'never' is wrong.
n.1: There is no requirement that a rescuer be related to those rescued.
n.2: Rescuers are not automatically primary victims entitled to recover without more.
n.3: Foreseeability of distress alone does not guarantee recovery.

Tort.q: A learner driver, on one of their first lessons, drives carelessly and injures a passenger. When sued in negligence, the learner argues that, because they are inexperienced and still learning, they should be judged more leniently and held only to the standard that could fairly be expected of a beginner rather than of a competent driver. The injured passenger disputes this. The court must decide the standard of care to which the learner driver is held. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The learner is held only to the standard reasonably expected of an inexperienced beginner.
The learner is judged purely by their own honest efforts to drive as well as they could.
The learner owes no duty of care at all until they have passed their driving test.
The learner is held to the very high standard of a professional driving instructor.
The learner is held to the standard of the reasonably competent driver.
Tort.w: The standard of care is objective and does not make allowance for the defendant's inexperience. A learner driver is held to the same standard as a reasonably competent, qualified driver (Nettleship v Weston).

n.0: No lower standard is applied to beginners; the objective standard governs.
n.1: Honest effort does not set the standard; it is objective.
n.2: A learner driver does owe a duty of care to passengers and other road users.
n.3: The learner is held to the competent driver's standard, not that of a professional instructor.

Tort.q: A cricket club has played on its ground for decades. On a rare occasion a ball is hit out of the ground, over a high fence, and injures a passer-by, something that has happened only a handful of times in many years. The passer-by sues the club in negligence. The likelihood of a ball escaping and causing injury was very small, and the club had taken sensible precautions such as a high boundary fence. The risk that materialised was small and infrequent. Which of the following best describes whether the club is likely to be in breach?
o: The club is unlikely to be in breach, as the low probability of harm meant reasonable care did not require more.
The club is in breach because any foreseeable risk, however small, must always be eliminated on these facts.
The club is in breach because sporting clubs are strictly liable for injuries to passers-by.
The club is automatically in breach because injury in fact occurred to the passer-by.
The club is in breach because it should have ceased playing cricket altogether.
Tort.w: Whether there is a breach depends on what the reasonable person would do in response to the risk. Where the likelihood of harm is very small and reasonable precautions have been taken, the reasonable person may not be required to do more, and there is no breach, even though harm has in fact occurred on a rare occasion.

n.1: Not every foreseeable risk must be eliminated; the probability and cost of precautions are weighed.
n.2: There is no strict liability here; the question is whether reasonable care was taken.
n.3: The occurrence of harm does not automatically establish breach.
n.4: Reasonable care did not require abandoning the activity altogether given the small risk.

Tort.q: A person is injured when attacked by a third party in the street, and argues that the police were negligent in failing to protect them from the attacker, of whom the police had some general awareness. The police did not create the danger, did not assume responsibility towards this individual, and were not in control of the attacker at the time. The claimant seeks to hold the police liable in negligence for failing to prevent harm caused by a third party. The attacker was someone the police had encountered before and had some general information about, but no promise of protection had been made to this particular victim and the police had taken no step that placed the victim in a worse position than if they had done nothing at all. Which of the following best describes the likely position on duty of care?
o: The police owe a duty because public bodies are subject to a stricter test than private defendants on these facts.
The police are wholly immune from negligence claims in the exercise of any function.
The police always owe a duty to protect any member of the public from any criminal.
The police owe a duty identical to that owed by a private bodyguard hired to protect the claimant.
The police generally owe no duty to protect an individual from harm caused by a third party absent special circumstances.
Tort.w: Applying ordinary negligence principles, the police (like others) are generally under no duty to protect a person from harm inflicted by a third party, absent special circumstances such as an assumption of responsibility or control over the wrongdoer. There is no blanket immunity, but nor is there a general duty to prevent third-party harm.

n.0: Public bodies are judged by ordinary principles, not a stricter test that creates liability here.
n.1: The police are not wholly immune; ordinary principles apply, but usually yield no duty here.
n.2: There is no general duty to protect everyone from every criminal.
n.3: They do not owe the duty of a specifically retained private bodyguard.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently causes a road accident. As a foreseeable result the claimant is taken to hospital, where entirely ordinary and competent medical treatment is given, but the claimant nonetheless suffers a complication that is a recognised risk of such treatment. The defendant argues that the medical treatment broke the chain of causation. The medical treatment given was ordinary and competent, not grossly negligent. After the collision the claimant was taken to hospital in the ordinary way, the doctors treated the injuries competently and without any fault, yet the claimant still suffered a complication that is simply a known and accepted risk of that treatment, which the defendant seizes on as an intervening event. Which of the following best describes the effect of the medical treatment on the defendant's liability?
o: The defendant's liability ends as soon as the claimant is admitted to hospital.
The chain of causation is always broken whenever medical treatment intervenes.
The defendant is liable only if the doctors were also negligent in their treatment.
The chain of causation is broken because any hospital treatment is a new intervening act.
The chain of causation is not broken, so the defendant remains liable for the complication.
Tort.w: Only grossly negligent or wholly unreasonable medical treatment will break the chain of causation. Ordinary, competent treatment, and complications that are recognised risks of it, are treated as within the risk created by the defendant's original negligence, so the defendant remains liable for the consequences.

n.0: Admission to hospital does not end the defendant's liability.
n.1: Intervening medical treatment does not always break the chain.
n.2: The defendant remains liable even though the doctors were not negligent.
n.3: Competent hospital treatment is not a novus actus; only gross negligence would be.

Tort.q: During an emergency, fire officers rushing to save a life carry heavy lifting equipment on an ordinary vehicle not designed for it, because no suitable vehicle is available in time. A rescuer is injured when the equipment shifts. The claimant argues the service was negligent to transport the equipment that way. In assessing breach, the court weighs the risk against the importance of the objective being pursued. The activity was undertaken to save a human life in an emergency. Which of the following best describes how the social utility of the activity affects the breach analysis?
o: The social utility of an activity is irrelevant to whether the defendant fell below the standard of care on these facts.
Any risk taken in an emergency automatically amounts to a breach of duty.
The social utility of saving life is weighed in the balance and may justify taking a risk that would otherwise be a breach.
The defendant is judged by a lower standard than ordinary care simply because it is a public service.
The only relevant factor is the seriousness of the harm, never the purpose of the activity.
Tort.w: Breach is assessed by weighing the magnitude of the risk (likelihood and seriousness of harm) against factors including the cost of precautions and the social utility of the defendant's conduct. Where the activity serves a valuable purpose, such as saving life in an emergency, that utility may justify running a risk that would otherwise constitute a breach.

n.0: Social utility is a recognised and relevant factor in the breach balance.
n.1: Taking a risk in an emergency is not automatically a breach; utility is weighed.
n.3: The standard remains reasonable care; the utility is weighed within it, not a lower standard.
n.4: The purpose and utility of the activity are relevant, not only the seriousness of harm.

Tort.q: An occupier of industrial premises knows that adults sometimes trespass across a corner of the site where there is a deep, dangerous excavation. To address the risk, the occupier puts up prominent and clearly worded warning signs at the point where trespassers enter, warning of the excavation and telling people to keep out. An adult trespasser ignores the clear signs, goes to the excavation anyway, and is injured. The trespasser sues under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, and the occupier relies on the warning it gave. The excavation was several metres deep and lay only a short distance beyond the point where trespassers got in. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A clear warning may discharge the occupier's duty to an adult trespasser under the 1984 Act.
The occupier is liable because it knew people trespassed there, whatever warning it gave.
The occupier owes no duty at all, so the adequacy of the warning is entirely irrelevant.
A warning can never discharge an occupier's duty to a trespasser in any circumstances.
The occupier remains fully liable, because a trespasser is always owed the common duty of care.
Tort.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, the duty to a trespasser may be discharged by taking such steps as are reasonable to give warning of the danger or to discourage people from taking the risk. A clear warning to an adult trespasser may therefore be enough to discharge the duty.

n.1: Knowledge that people trespass does not make the occupier liable regardless of an adequate warning.
n.2: A duty may be owed to trespassers under the 1984 Act, so the warning is relevant.
n.3: A warning can discharge the 1984 Act duty; it is a recognised way of doing so.
n.4: Trespassers are not owed the common duty of care owed to lawful visitors.

Tort.q: A company stores a large quantity of a hazardous liquid in tanks on its industrial site as part of a non-ordinary use of the land. Through no negligence on its part, the liquid escapes and floods neighbouring land, causing damage of a kind that was a foreseeable consequence of such an escape. The neighbour sues under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. The company brought and accumulated the substance for its own purposes in a non-natural use of the land, and it escaped. Which of the following best sets out what the claimant must establish under that rule?
o: That the defendant was negligent in allowing the dangerous thing to escape.
That the dangerous thing was naturally present on the land before it escaped.
That the defendant intended the dangerous thing to escape onto the neighbour's land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
That the defendant brought and accumulated a dangerous thing in a non-natural use of land, which escaped and caused foreseeable damage.
That the escape caused only pure economic loss to the neighbour.
Tort.w: Under Rylands v Fletcher (a form of strict liability), the claimant must show the defendant brought onto and accumulated on its land a thing likely to do mischief if it escaped, in a non-natural (extraordinary) use of the land, that the thing escaped, and that damage of a foreseeable type resulted. Negligence and intention need not be proved.

n.0: Negligence need not be proved; liability under the rule is strict.
n.1: The thing must be brought onto the land, not naturally present; natural accumulations are excluded.
n.2: Intention to cause the escape is not required.
n.4: The rule addresses property/physical damage from escape, not pure economic loss.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured partly through the defendant's negligence and partly through the claimant's own failure to take reasonable care for their own safety, such as not wearing an available seatbelt, which made the injuries worse. The defendant admits primary liability but argues the damages should be reduced. The claimant's own carelessness contributed to the extent of the harm suffered. The defendant's careless driving caused the collision that put the claimant in hospital, but the claimant had also neglected an obvious precaution for their own safety that made the resulting injuries considerably worse than they would otherwise have been, and the defendant now seeks a corresponding reduction in what must be paid. Which of the following best describes the effect of the claimant's conduct on the award?
o: Damages must always be reduced by exactly 50% where the claimant is partly at fault.
Damages may be reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable to reflect the claimant's share of responsibility.
The claim fails entirely because any fault by the claimant is a complete defence.
The claimant's conduct reduces damages only if it was the sole cause of the injuries.
The claimant's conduct is irrelevant once the defendant's primary liability is established on these facts as a general rule.
Tort.w: Contributory negligence is a partial defence under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945. Where the claimant's own want of care contributes to their injury, damages are reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility. It reduces, rather than defeats, the claim.

n.0: There is no fixed 50% reduction; the reduction reflects the claimant's share of responsibility.
