n.2: Contributory negligence is a partial, not a complete, defence.
n.3: Contributory negligence applies to a contributory cause; it need not be the sole cause (which would defeat causation entirely).
n.4: The claimant's contributory fault is relevant and reduces the award.

Tort.q: A defendant's factory lawfully carries on an activity expressly authorised by statute, and does so without negligence and strictly within the terms of that statutory authority. An inevitable consequence of carrying on the authorised activity in the manner permitted is some escape or interference affecting neighbouring land, which would otherwise be actionable. A neighbour sues in nuisance and under Rylands v Fletcher. The defendant relies on the fact that the activity was authorised by, and conducted in accordance with, statute. The statute set out in detail how the activity was to be carried on, and the factory had followed it exactly. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is liable because statutory authority protects only public bodies, never private businesses.
The defendant remains fully liable, because carrying on any activity that harms a neighbour is always actionable on these facts.
The defendant is liable unless the neighbour consented in writing to the activity beforehand.
Statutory authority is never a defence to a claim in nuisance or under Rylands v Fletcher.
Statutory authority may provide a defence where the harm is an inevitable consequence of the authorised activity done without negligence.
Tort.w: Where a defendant acts under statutory authority and the interference or escape is an inevitable consequence of doing the authorised thing in the authorised manner, without negligence, statutory authority can provide a defence to nuisance and to a claim under Rylands v Fletcher.

n.0: The defence is not confined to public bodies; it turns on acting under statutory authority.
n.1: Not all harm to a neighbour is actionable; a valid statutory-authority defence may apply.
n.2: The defence does not depend on the neighbour's prior written consent.
n.3: Statutory authority can be a defence to these claims in appropriate circumstances.

Tort.q: A worker is directly involved in a serious accident at work caused by the employer's negligence. The worker is physically in the zone of danger and reasonably fears for their own safety, and although they escape physical injury they suffer a recognised psychiatric illness as a result of the terrifying event. The worker claims damages for the psychiatric injury. The employer argues that damages for psychiatric harm are subject to the strict control mechanisms that apply to bystanders. The worker had to be helped from the scene and has been unable to return to work since the incident. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: As a primary victim in the zone of physical danger, the worker can recover if some personal injury was foreseeable.
The worker must satisfy the strict secondary-victim control mechanisms before recovering anything.
The worker can recover only if the psychiatric illness was foreseeable in a person of ordinary fortitude, judged separately from physical risk.
The worker can recover only if a close relative was also injured in the same accident.
The worker cannot recover, because damages for psychiatric injury are never available without physical injury.
Tort.w: A primary victim — someone within the range of foreseeable physical injury — can recover for consequent psychiatric illness provided physical injury of some kind was foreseeable; it is not necessary that the psychiatric harm itself was foreseeable (Page v Smith). The strict secondary-victim controls do not apply.

n.1: The secondary-victim control mechanisms do not apply to a primary victim.
n.2: For a primary victim, foreseeability of physical injury suffices; separate foreseeability of psychiatric harm is not required.
n.3: A primary victim need not show a close relative was injured.
n.4: Psychiatric injury can be recovered even without physical injury, especially by a primary victim.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured when a barrel falls from an upper window of the defendant's warehouse onto the street below as they pass. The claimant cannot point to any specific act of carelessness, and does not know exactly how or why the barrel came to fall, because that information is entirely within the defendant's knowledge. However, barrels do not normally fall from warehouse windows if those in control of them take proper care. The claimant seeks to rely on the circumstances of the accident itself. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim must fail, because the claimant cannot identify the precise negligent act that caused the accident.
The burden is on the claimant throughout to disprove every innocent explanation for the accident.
The claimant can succeed only if there was an eyewitness to the defendant's carelessness.
The claimant must prove exactly how the barrel fell before the court can find any negligence.
The claimant may rely on res ipsa loquitur, so the burden shifts to the defendant to rebut negligence.
Tort.w: Where the thing causing harm was under the defendant's control, the accident is one that does not ordinarily happen without negligence, and the cause is unknown to the claimant, res ipsa loquitur applies: the circumstances themselves raise an inference of negligence which the defendant must rebut (Scott v London & St Katherine Docks).

n.0: The claimant need not identify the precise negligent act where res ipsa loquitur applies.
n.1: Res ipsa loquitur casts an evidential burden on the defendant to explain the accident.
n.2: An eyewitness is not required; the circumstances themselves can raise the inference.
n.3: Proof of the exact mechanism is not required in such circumstances.

Tort.q: A patient is treated by a doctor and later alleges that the treatment was negligent. The doctor followed a particular course of treatment which is supported by a responsible body of medical opinion within the profession, even though another respectable body of doctors would have taken a different approach. The patient argues that, because some doctors would have acted differently, the doctor must have been negligent. The court must decide the standard by which the doctor's professional conduct is judged. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The doctor is negligent unless every doctor in the profession would have acted in the same way.
The doctor is judged solely by whether the treatment happened to produce a good outcome.
The doctor is not negligent if they followed a responsible and logical body of professional opinion.
The doctor is negligent whenever any other doctor would have chosen a different course of treatment.
The doctor is judged by the standard of an ordinary reasonable person with no medical training.
Tort.w: A professional is judged by the standard of the ordinary skilled member of that profession. A doctor is not negligent if they acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion, provided that body's view withstands logical analysis (Bolam, as qualified by Bolitho).

n.0: Unanimity is not required; a responsible body of opinion suffices.
n.1: Negligence is judged by the standard of conduct, not simply by the outcome.
n.3: The existence of a different school of thought does not make the doctor negligent.
n.4: Professionals are judged by the standard of their profession, not the ordinary person.

Tort.q: A neighbour, purely out of spite following a disagreement, deliberately sets out to disturb the claimant by banging on the party wall and making loud noises whenever the claimant is trying to give music lessons, doing so with the specific intention of ruining the claimant's peaceful enjoyment of their home. The activity would perhaps be tolerable if done innocently, but it is done maliciously to annoy. The claimant sues in private nuisance and the defendant argues that noise-making on one's own property can never be a nuisance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails, because music lessons are themselves a sensitive and non-ordinary use of land.
Malice is entirely irrelevant in nuisance, so the defendant's motive makes no difference at all on these facts.
The defendant's malice is relevant and may make an otherwise borderline interference an actionable nuisance.
There can be no nuisance, because making noise on one's own property is always lawful.
The claim succeeds only if the noise caused physical damage to the claimant's property.
Tort.w: Malice is a relevant factor in assessing the reasonableness of an interference in private nuisance. Conduct done deliberately to annoy a neighbour may be an actionable nuisance even where the same activity, done innocently, might not be (Christie v Davey).

n.0: Giving music lessons at home is an ordinary use; the vice is the malicious interference.
n.1: Malice is relevant to reasonableness in nuisance, not irrelevant.
n.3: Making noise on one's own land can be a nuisance, especially where done maliciously.
n.4: Nuisance covers interference with enjoyment; physical damage is not required.

Tort.q: A defendant admits owing the claimant a duty of care, but disputes that they fell below the required standard. The defendant is an ordinary person carrying out an everyday activity, and did what they genuinely thought was sensible at the time. The claimant argues that the defendant's honest belief that they were being careful is beside the point, and that the defendant must be judged against an objective yardstick. The court must decide the standard against which the defendant's conduct is measured. Which of the following best describes the standard of care?
o: The defendant is judged only by their own honest belief that they were acting carefully at the time.
The defendant is judged by whatever standard the defendant personally considers appropriate.
The defendant is judged against the standard of a reasonable person doing that activity, objectively assessed.
The defendant is judged against a purely subjective standard tailored to their own abilities.
The defendant is judged against the standard of the most careful and skilful person imaginable.
Tort.w: The standard of care in negligence is objective: the defendant is measured against the standard of the reasonable person carrying out the activity in question, not against their own honest belief or subjective view of what was careful (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks).

n.0: The defendant's honest belief does not set the standard; it is objective.
n.1: The defendant cannot set their own standard of care.
n.3: The standard is objective, not tailored subjectively to the individual defendant's abilities.
n.4: The standard is that of the reasonable person, not perfection or the most skilful person.

Tort.q: A consumer is injured when a new domestic appliance overheats and catches fire because of a manufacturing flaw. The consumer brings a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 against the producer, who argues that the product was not 'defective'. The appliance was less safe than persons generally are entitled to expect, taking into account how it was marketed and any instructions and warnings given. The claim is brought under the strict liability regime for defective products. The appliance had been bought new and used entirely as intended, it bore no unusual warnings that might have alerted the user to the risk, and it failed in a way that made it plainly less safe than an ordinary purchaser would be entitled to assume of such a product. Which of the following best describes the meaning of 'defect' under that Act?
o: A product is defective if it is merely of poor quality or fails to work well.
A product is defective only where the consumer proves exactly how the flaw arose.
A product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect.
A product is defective only if the producer was negligent in making it.
A product is defective only if it is more dangerous than every rival product on the market.
Tort.w: Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, a product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect, taking account of all the circumstances including its marketing, instructions and warnings, and what might reasonably be expected to be done with it. Liability is strict, so the claimant need not prove negligence.

n.0: The test is about safety, not mere poor quality or performance.
n.1: The claimant need not prove the precise mechanism of the flaw, only that the product was unsafe as defined.
n.3: Liability is strict; the claimant need not prove the producer was negligent.
n.4: The product need not be more dangerous than every rival; the test is public safety expectation.

Tort.q: A defendant accumulates a hazardous substance on its land in a non-natural use. The substance escapes and damages a neighbour's property, but the escape was caused entirely by the deliberate, unforeseeable act of a trespassing stranger over whom the defendant had no control and whose conduct it could not have anticipated. The neighbour sues under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. The escape resulted solely from the unforeseeable act of a third-party stranger. The defendant had contained the substance carefully, but an intruder with no connection to the defendant deliberately interfered with the tanks in a way the defendant could not have foreseen or guarded against, and it was that stranger's act alone that brought about the escape onto neighbouring land. Which of the following best describes the defendant's position?
o: The defendant is liable because only an act of God can ever provide a defence.
The defendant is liable unless it can prove the stranger was insolvent.
The defendant is strictly liable regardless of who caused the escape.
The defendant may rely on the defence of act of a stranger to escape liability.
The defendant is liable because the act of a stranger is never a defence under the rule.
Tort.w: Liability under Rylands v Fletcher is strict but not absolute. Recognised defences include the act of an unforeseeable stranger: where the escape is caused by the deliberate and unforeseeable act of a third party over whom the defendant has no control, the defendant is not liable. Other defences include act of God, the claimant's own default, consent and statutory authority.

n.0: Act of God is not the only defence; act of a stranger is also recognised.
n.1: The defence does not depend on the stranger's solvency.
n.2: Liability is strict but subject to defences, so it is not regardless of who caused the escape.
n.4: The act of a stranger is a recognised defence, contrary to this option.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured as a result of the combined negligence of two different defendants, each of whom contributed to causing the same damage. The claimant sues and recovers the whole of their damages from the first defendant, who was the easier to pursue. The first defendant, having paid the full amount, considers that the second defendant should bear a fair share of the liability, since both were responsible for the harm. The first defendant seeks advice on recovering a contribution from the second defendant. Both defendants had been careless in different ways, and together they brought about the single injury. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The first defendant must recover exactly half from the second defendant in every case.
The first defendant may recover a contribution only if the two defendants had a contract between them on these facts.
The first defendant has no remedy, because a defendant who pays a claim cannot pursue anyone else.
The first defendant can recover nothing, because it has already paid the claimant in full.
The first defendant may recover a contribution from the second, assessed as just and equitable to their responsibility.
Tort.w: Under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978, a person liable for damage may recover a contribution from any other person also liable for the same damage. The amount is such as the court finds just and equitable having regard to each party's responsibility.

n.0: Contribution is apportioned according to responsibility, not fixed at half.
n.1: A contribution claim under the Act does not require a contract between the defendants.
n.2: A defendant who has paid may pursue others liable for the same damage for a contribution.
n.3: Paying the claimant in full does not prevent a contribution claim against another tortfeasor.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured by the conduct of a worker and wishes to hold the worker's employer vicariously liable. However, on examination it turns out that the worker's conduct, although careless-looking, did not actually satisfy the elements of any recognised tort at all: no duty was breached and no actionable wrong was committed by the worker. The claimant nonetheless argues that the employer should pay because it is a business and the worker was at work. The employer disputes that vicarious liability can arise. On analysis the worker had neither owed nor breached any duty of care to the claimant at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There can be no vicarious liability unless the employee has actually committed a tort.
The employer is liable because the worker was on duty when the incident happened.
The employer is liable because it is better able than the worker to meet the claim.
The employer is liable in any event, because vicarious liability does not require an underlying tort.
The employer is liable provided the worker was acting within the course of employment.
Tort.w: Vicarious liability is secondary liability for another's tort. It requires that the employee (or person in an analogous relationship) has actually committed a tort. If no tort was committed by the worker, there is nothing for which the employer can be held vicariously liable.

n.1: Being on duty does not create liability where no tort was committed.
n.2: The employer's greater means do not create liability absent a tort by the employee.
n.3: Vicarious liability is parasitic on an underlying tort; it does not arise without one.
n.4: Course of employment matters only once a tort by the employee is established.

Tort.q: A strong swimmer is walking past a lake when they see a stranger, with whom they have no relationship and for whom they have no responsibility, struggling in the water. The swimmer could easily have effected a rescue at no risk but chooses to walk on, and the stranger drowns. The stranger's family wish to sue the swimmer in negligence for failing to act. The swimmer did nothing to create the danger and had assumed no responsibility for the stranger's safety. Which of the following best describes the swimmer's liability in negligence for the pure omission to act?
o: There is liability because everyone owes a general legal duty to rescue strangers in peril.
There is generally no liability for a pure failure to act absent a recognised duty to act.
There is liability because failing to rescue is always treated the same as causing the harm.
There is liability because the swimmer's skill created a special duty to all swimmers in difficulty.
There is automatic liability whenever a person could easily have prevented harm to another.
Tort.w: The common law generally imposes no liability for pure omissions: a person is not ordinarily liable for merely failing to confer a benefit or prevent harm to another. A duty to act arises only in recognised situations, such as where the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control over the claimant or a third party. None applies here.

n.0: English law imposes no general duty to rescue a stranger in peril.
n.2: A pure omission is not equated with positively causing the harm absent a duty to act.
n.3: Merely being a capable swimmer does not create a special duty to those in difficulty.
n.4: Ease of prevention does not by itself create a duty to act.

Tort.q: A contractor negligently cuts through a power cable in the road, cutting off electricity to a nearby factory. As a result the factory suffers three kinds of loss: physical damage to metal that solidified in its furnaces during the power cut, the loss of profit on that damaged metal, and additional loss of profit on other batches it simply could not process while the power was off. The factory claims all three losses from the contractor in negligence. The factory had no back-up generator, and the power was off for several hours before it was restored. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All three heads of loss are fully recoverable, because they were all caused by the contractor's negligence on these facts.
Only the loss of profit is recoverable, and the physical damage to the metal is treated as too remote.
None of the losses is recoverable, because economic loss can never be claimed in the tort of negligence.
All the losses are recoverable, provided the factory had no insurance covering the power cut.
The pure economic loss unconnected to physical damage is not recoverable, though the physical damage and its related loss are.
Tort.w: In negligence, pure economic loss (financial loss not consequent on damage to the claimant's own property) is generally irrecoverable. The factory can recover the physical damage to the metal and the profit on that metal, but not the profit lost on batches it simply could not process (Spartan Steel v Martin).

n.0: Pure economic loss standing alone is not recoverable, so not all three heads succeed.
n.1: The physical damage is recoverable and is not too remote; it is the pure economic loss that fails.
n.2: Economic loss consequent on physical damage to one's own property is recoverable, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Recoverability does not depend on whether the claimant was insured.

Tort.q: An employee, in the course of carrying out the job they are employed to do, commits a wrongful act that injures a customer. The wrongful act is closely connected with the duties the employee was engaged to perform, being a misguided execution of those very duties rather than an independent personal venture. The claimant seeks to hold the employer vicariously liable. There is an employment relationship and the act is closely connected to the employee's authorised duties. Which of the following best describes the test for whether the act was in the course of employment?
o: Whether the wrongful act occurred strictly within the employee's contracted working hours only on these facts as a general rule.
Whether the employer expressly authorised the precise wrongful act committed.
Whether the wrongful act was so closely connected with the employee's authorised duties that it is fair to impose liability.
Whether the employee was acting solely for the employer's benefit at the time.
Whether the employee had been specifically warned not to commit that kind of act.
Tort.w: Vicarious liability for an employee's tort turns on the 'close connection' test: the employer is liable where the wrongful act is so closely connected with the acts the employee was authorised to do that it may fairly and properly be regarded as done in the course of employment. Express authorisation of the wrong, or acting for the employer's benefit, is not required.

n.0: The act need not fall strictly within contracted hours; close connection is the test.
n.1: Express authorisation of the precise wrongful act is not required.
n.3: Acting solely for the employer's benefit is not the test; a wrong can be closely connected even if not beneficial.
n.4: A prior warning against the act does not determine whether it was in the course of employment.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently injures the claimant, causing a modest wound. The claimant is then taken to hospital, where a doctor administers grossly negligent treatment that is completely outside the range of any competent care, and it is this second, egregious act which causes the claimant's much more serious final condition. The original defendant argues that the doctor's grossly negligent treatment broke the chain of causation, so that the original defendant is not responsible for the more serious harm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The original defendant is always liable for all consequences, because nothing can break the chain of causation.
A grossly negligent intervening medical act may break the chain of causation, relieving the original defendant of liability for the later harm.
The original defendant remains liable for everything, because the claimant would not have been in hospital but for the original wound.
The chain is broken only where the claimant deliberately injured themselves after the accident.
The chain of causation is broken by any medical treatment at all, however careful, that the claimant receives.
Tort.w: An intervening act (novus actus interveniens) may break the chain of causation where it is sufficiently independent and unreasonable. Medical treatment usually does not break the chain, but grossly negligent treatment, so far outside competent care, can do so, relieving the original defendant of liability for the additional harm.

n.0: An intervening act can break the chain; the original defendant is not liable come what may.
n.2: 'But for' the wound is not enough; a sufficiently unreasonable intervening act can still break legal causation.
n.3: A grossly negligent third-party act, not only self-harm, can break the chain.
n.4: Ordinary or merely careless medical treatment does not break the chain; only grossly negligent treatment may.

Tort.q: An occupier of commercial premises engages an apparently reputable and suitably qualified specialist contractor to carry out electrical work. The occupier checks the contractor's competence and, so far as it reasonably can, that the work has been done properly. A visitor is later injured because of a latent defect in the contractor's work that the occupier could not reasonably have detected. The visitor sues the occupier under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957. The occupier acted reasonably in selecting the contractor and in checking the work. Which of the following best describes the occupier's likely liability?
o: The occupier is strictly liable for any injury caused by a contractor's work on the premises.
The occupier is liable unless the visitor was expressly warned about the electrical work.
The occupier is liable because a contractor's negligence is always attributed to the occupier.
The occupier is likely not liable, having acted reasonably in entrusting the work to a competent contractor and checking it.
The occupier is liable because the common duty of care can never be discharged through a contractor on these facts.
Tort.w: Under s.2(4)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, where damage is caused by the faulty work of an independent contractor, the occupier is not liable if it acted reasonably in entrusting the work to a contractor and took reasonable steps to satisfy itself that the contractor was competent and (where appropriate) that the work had been properly done. Those conditions are met here.

n.0: The occupier is not strictly liable for a contractor's faulty work.
n.1: Discharge turns on the reasonableness of entrusting and checking the work, not on warning the visitor.
n.2: A competent independent contractor's negligence is not automatically attributed to the occupier.
n.4: The common duty of care can be discharged by reasonably entrusting specialist work to a contractor.

Tort.q: A buyer purchases a building that later proves to have been negligently constructed with defective foundations. No person is injured and no other property is damaged; the only loss is the cost of repairing the defective building itself and the reduction in its value. The buyer sues the negligent builder in the tort of negligence for that cost. The loss claimed is the cost of making good the defect in the thing itself, with no personal injury or damage to other property. Which of the following best describes the recoverability of this loss in negligence?
o: It is recoverable because economic loss is freely recoverable in the tort of negligence.
It is recoverable because defective buildings are treated as physical damage to other property.
It is always recoverable in negligence as ordinary consequential loss.
It is recoverable provided the defect was merely difficult, rather than impossible, to discover on these facts.
It is generally irrecoverable in negligence, being pure economic loss in respect of a defective product or building.
Tort.w: The cost of repairing a defect in the product or building itself, and its diminution in value, is pure economic loss, which is generally not recoverable in the tort of negligence (Murphy v Brentwood). Such loss is usually recoverable, if at all, only in contract or under a specific assumption of responsibility, not in ordinary negligence.

n.0: Pure economic loss is generally not freely recoverable in negligence.
n.1: A defect in the thing itself is not damage to 'other property'.
n.2: This kind of loss is not treated as ordinary recoverable consequential loss in negligence.
n.3: Recoverability does not turn on how difficult the defect was to discover.

Tort.q: A claimant develops an industrial disease after being exposed to a harmful substance by several different employers over the years, each of whom was in breach of duty. Because of the nature of the disease, it is scientifically impossible to say which particular exposure actually triggered it, so the claimant cannot satisfy the ordinary 'but for' test against any single defendant. The claimant argues they should not be left without a remedy simply because of this scientific uncertainty. The court considers how to approach causation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails entirely, because the claimant cannot prove which exposure caused the disease.
Only the last employer to expose the claimant can be held liable for the disease.
Only the first employer to expose the claimant can ever be held liable for the disease.
The claim succeeds only if the claimant can identify the exact exposure that caused the disease.
Each employer that materially increased the risk of the disease may be held liable.
Tort.w: Where scientific uncertainty makes the 'but for' test impossible to satisfy in certain cases (such as mesothelioma from asbestos), a defendant who materially increased the risk of the claimant's harm may be held liable (McGhee; Fairchild). The claimant is not left remediless because of the impossibility of pinpointing the exposure.

n.0: The claim does not automatically fail; the material-increase-in-risk approach may apply.
n.1: Liability is not confined to the last exposing employer.
n.2: Liability is not confined to the first exposing employer.
n.3: The claimant need not identify the exact causative exposure in these special cases.

Tort.q: A consumer buys a household appliance which, because of a manufacturing defect present when it left the factory, catches fire and injures the consumer and damages their other property. The consumer wishes to claim compensation for the personal injury and property damage caused by the defective product, but is worried about having to prove exactly how the manufacturer was careless. The consumer seeks advice on a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987. The appliance was only a few months old and had been used entirely in the ordinary domestic way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The producer is liable only where the defect caused financial loss rather than physical harm.
The producer may be strictly liable for damage caused by a defective product, without proof of negligence.
The consumer must prove the manufacturer was negligent before any claim can succeed at all.
The consumer has no claim, because liability for products arises only in contract with the seller.
The producer is liable only if the consumer bought the product directly from the producer.
Tort.w: Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, a producer is strictly liable for damage caused by a defect in their product, so the injured person need not prove negligence. A product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect.

n.0: The Act covers death, personal injury and certain property damage, not just financial loss.
n.2: The Act imposes strict liability, so negligence need not be proved.
n.3: The claim under the Act is not confined to those in a contract with the seller.
n.4: Liability does not require the claimant to have bought the product from the producer.

Tort.q: A claimant succeeds in establishing a continuing private nuisance from a neighbour's activity and asks the court what remedy it will grant. The interference is ongoing and substantial, but the defendant argues that the court should not shut down its activity and should instead order it to pay a sum of money. The claimant primarily seeks to stop the continuing interference. The interference is continuing and shows no sign of stopping, the claimant wants it brought to an end rather than simply to be paid off year after year, while the defendant, whose activity has some wider value, urges the court to let it carry on in exchange for money. Which of the following best describes the court's approach to remedies in private nuisance?
o: An injunction is the prima facie remedy, but the court has a discretion to award damages in lieu.
Damages are the only remedy ever available in private nuisance.
An injunction must always be granted whenever a nuisance is established.
The court may only order the defendant to abate the nuisance itself, with no other remedy.
The claimant must choose between an injunction and damages before the hearing begins.
Tort.w: For a continuing nuisance the prima facie remedy is an injunction to restrain the interference, together with damages for past loss. However, the court retains a discretion to award damages in lieu of an injunction in appropriate cases, weighing factors such as the public interest and the effect on the parties. It is not obliged to grant an injunction in every case.

n.1: Damages are not the only remedy; an injunction is the primary remedy.
n.2: An injunction is not automatic; the court may award damages in lieu.
n.3: Court-ordered self-help abatement is not the only remedy available.
n.4: The claimant need not irrevocably elect before the hearing; the court exercises its discretion.

Tort.q: A woman is not present when her close family member is involved in an accident caused by the defendant's negligence, but she comes upon the immediate aftermath very shortly afterwards and, through her own unaided senses, witnesses the horrifying scene, suffering a recognised psychiatric illness as a result. She was not physically endangered herself. She was not a participant but perceived the immediate aftermath with her own senses and has a close tie to the victim. She rushed to the scene as soon as she heard, arriving within minutes to find her relative gravely injured and the aftermath still raw and untouched, and what she saw with her own eyes brought on a diagnosed psychiatric condition even though she herself was never in any physical danger. Which of the following best describes what she must establish as a secondary victim?
o: A close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath, and perception through her own senses.
Only that the psychiatric harm to her was reasonably foreseeable, with no further requirements on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
That the defendant intended to cause her psychiatric harm.
That she was within the zone of physical danger at the time of the accident.
Only that she suffered some distress or grief as a result of the accident.
Tort.w: A secondary victim must satisfy the control mechanisms in Alcock: a close tie of love and affection with the primary victim, proximity in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath, perception of the event (or aftermath) through their own unaided senses, and a recognised psychiatric illness caused by a sudden shock. Mere grief or foreseeability alone is insufficient.

n.1: Foreseeability alone does not suffice for secondary victims; the control mechanisms must be met.
n.2: There is no requirement to prove the defendant intended psychiatric harm.
n.3: Being within the zone of danger would make her a primary victim, which she is not.
n.4: Ordinary distress or grief, short of a recognised psychiatric illness, is not enough.

Tort.q: A defendant negligently causes a minor injury to the claimant. Because the claimant happens to have an unusually thin skull, a rare medical susceptibility unknown to anyone, that minor injury triggers far more serious consequences than the same blow would have caused to an ordinary person. The defendant argues that they should only be liable for the modest harm that a normal person would have suffered, not for the exceptional harm caused by the claimant's hidden vulnerability. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant must take the claimant as they find them and is liable for the full extent of the harm.
The defendant's liability is reduced in proportion to the claimant's pre-existing vulnerability.
The defendant is liable for the full harm only if they knew about the claimant's condition beforehand.
The defendant is liable only for the harm an ordinary person without the vulnerability would have suffered.
The defendant is not liable at all, because the serious harm was caused by the claimant's own condition.
Tort.w: Under the 'eggshell skull' rule, a defendant must take the claimant as they find them. Provided some injury of the relevant type was foreseeable, the defendant is liable for the full extent of the harm, even though its severity was increased by the claimant's unforeseeable pre-existing susceptibility (Smith v Leech Brain).

n.1: Damages are not reduced for a pre-existing vulnerability under this rule.
n.2: Knowledge of the condition is not required for the eggshell skull rule to apply.
n.3: Liability is not limited to the harm an ordinary person would have suffered.
n.4: The claimant's own susceptibility does not relieve the defendant where some injury was foreseeable.

Tort.q: A solicitor negligently fails to issue a client's personal injury claim before the limitation period expires, with the result that the client's otherwise strong claim becomes statute-barred and worthless. The client sues the solicitor. The solicitor accepts the mistake but argues that, because the client never actually obtained any judgment in the original claim, the client cannot show they have suffered any recoverable loss. The client seeks advice on the basis of a claim against the solicitor. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor is liable only in contract, and the client can recover nothing in the tort of negligence.
The solicitor is liable only if the client can now still bring the original claim despite the limitation bar.
The solicitor has no liability, because the client never obtained a judgment in the original claim.
The solicitor is liable in professional negligence for the value of the lost, time-barred claim.
The solicitor has no liability, because missing a limitation date is never regarded as negligent.
Tort.w: A solicitor owes their client a duty to exercise reasonable care and skill. Allowing a good claim to become statute-barred is a breach, and the client's recoverable loss is assessed by reference to the value of the claim that has been lost (its prospects and likely value).

n.0: The client may sue in tort as well as contract for the solicitor's negligence.
n.1: The loss arises precisely because the original claim is now barred; that is the damage.
n.2: The lost claim is the recoverable loss; a prior judgment is not required.
n.4: Missing a limitation date through carelessness is a classic example of negligence.

Tort.q: A claimant is injured while they and the defendant are jointly engaged in committing a serious criminal offence together, the injury arising directly out of that joint criminal enterprise. The claimant then sues the defendant in negligence for the injuries suffered during the crime. The defendant argues that the court should not allow the claimant to found a claim on their own serious criminal wrongdoing. The two had planned the offence together in advance and were in the act of carrying it out when the injury occurred. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim is merely reduced for contributory negligence, but is never barred by illegality.
The claim is barred only if the claimant was convicted of the offence before suing.
The claim succeeds in full, because illegality is never a defence to a claim in negligence.
The claim succeeds, because the defendant was also involved in the same criminal enterprise on these facts.
The claim may be barred by the illegality defence, as it arises directly from the claimant's own serious criminal act.
Tort.w: The defence of illegality (ex turpi causa non oritur actio) may bar a claim which is founded on, or arises directly out of, the claimant's own serious criminal conduct, where allowing recovery would be contrary to public policy and the integrity of the legal system.

n.0: Illegality can bar the claim entirely, not merely reduce it.
n.1: A prior conviction is not a precondition to the illegality defence.
n.2: Illegality can be a defence in negligence; it is not always excluded.
n.3: The defendant's own involvement in the crime does not automatically defeat the illegality defence.

Tort.q: A defendant keeps a large volume of water on its land in a reservoir, a non-natural use, which then escapes and floods a neighbour's property. The escape, however, was caused entirely by the deliberate and unforeseeable act of a malicious stranger who broke in and opened the sluices, and over whom the defendant had no control at all. The neighbour sues under Rylands v Fletcher. The defendant argues that, because the escape was caused by a stranger's act, it should not be strictly liable. The stranger had climbed over a secure boundary fence at night specifically in order to cause the flooding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is liable unless it can prove the stranger was acting on the defendant's behalf.
The defendant is liable, because it chose to keep the water on its land in the first place.
The defendant is strictly liable regardless, because liability under Rylands v Fletcher has no defences.
The defendant may escape liability under the defence that the escape was caused by the act of a stranger.
The defendant is liable because a malicious act by a stranger is always foreseeable in law.
Tort.w: Liability under Rylands v Fletcher is subject to recognised defences, including the act of a stranger (an unforeseeable act of a third party over whom the defendant had no control), act of God, the claimant's own default, consent, and statutory authority. The stranger's act here may provide a defence.

n.0: The defence applies precisely because the stranger was not acting for the defendant.
n.1: Merely keeping the water does not defeat the act-of-a-stranger defence.
n.2: Rylands v Fletcher liability does have defences; it is not without exception.
n.4: An unforeseeable malicious act by a stranger is not treated as always foreseeable.

Tort.q: A patient attends a doctor with symptoms, and the doctor negligently fails to diagnose a serious illness. By the time the illness is correctly diagnosed, the patient's chance of a successful recovery has fallen, but even with prompt correct diagnosis the patient would, on the balance of probabilities, more likely than not have suffered the same poor outcome anyway. The patient claims damages for the reduced chance of recovery caused by the delay. The doctor argues that causation is not made out on the ordinary balance of probabilities. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim succeeds, because the doctor's negligence undoubtedly worsened the patient's position.
The claim fails only if the patient made a full recovery despite the delay in diagnosis.
The claim is likely to fail, because loss of a less-than-even chance of recovery is generally not recoverable.
The claim succeeds automatically, because the doctor admitted failing to diagnose the illness.
The claim succeeds, because any reduction in the chance of recovery is always compensable in full on these facts.
Tort.w: In clinical negligence, the claimant must generally prove on the balance of probabilities that the negligence caused the adverse outcome. Where the lost chance of recovery was less than even, the courts have generally refused to allow recovery for the reduced chance itself (Gregg v Scott).

n.0: Worsening the position is not enough without proving causation on the balance of probabilities.
n.1: The difficulty is the standard of proof of causation, not whether the patient recovered.
n.3: An admission of failure to diagnose does not establish causation of the outcome.
n.4: A reduction in a less-than-even chance is not generally compensable, so recovery is not automatic.

Tort.q: A company stores a large quantity of a hazardous chemical in tanks on its industrial site as part of an unusual and high-risk operation, an activity not regarded as an ordinary use of land in the area. The chemical unexpectedly escapes from the site and causes damage to neighbouring land of a kind that was a foreseeable consequence of such an escape. The neighbour sues, seeking to rely on strict liability rather than having to prove negligence. The company argues that it took all reasonable care and so should not be liable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company is not liable, because strict liability has no place in the modern law of tort.
The company is liable for the escape only if the damage caused was entirely unforeseeable.
The company is liable only if it intended the chemical to escape from its site.
The company is liable only if the neighbour can prove that the company was actually negligent on these facts.
The company may be strictly liable under Rylands v Fletcher for the escape from its non-natural use of land.
Tort.w: Under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher, a person who, for their own purposes, brings and keeps on their land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, in a non-natural use of the land, is strictly liable for foreseeable damage caused by its escape, without the need to prove negligence (Cambridge Water requires foreseeability of the type of damage).

n.0: Rylands v Fletcher strict liability remains part of English law.
n.1: Liability requires that the type of damage was foreseeable, not that it was unforeseeable.
n.2: Intention to cause the escape is not required for liability.
n.3: The rule imposes strict liability, so proof of negligence is not required.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A local authority, which is a public body exercising statutory functions, makes a decision affecting an individual in a way that interferes with that individual's Convention rights. The authority is not required by any incompatible primary legislation to act as it did. The individual considers challenging the authority's conduct. The authority exercised a statutory function in the way it chose, not because any Act compelled that particular course, and the individual affected wants to know whether the way the authority acted can be said to be unlawful given the body's public character and its obligations under the Act. Which of the following best describes the position under section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998?
o: Only central government, not local authorities, is bound by Convention rights.
It is unlawful for the public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right.
A public authority may act incompatibly provided it later apologises.
A public authority is free to act incompatibly with Convention rights if it chooses.
Convention rights bind private individuals in the same way as public authorities.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with a Convention right, unless primary legislation requires it to act that way. A local authority exercising statutory functions is a public authority for this purpose.

n.0: Local authorities, not just central government, are public authorities bound by section 6.
n.2: A later apology does not make the incompatible act lawful.
n.3: A public authority is not free to breach Convention rights at will.
n.4: The Act principally binds public authorities, not private individuals directly.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A decision-maker reaches a decision that adversely affects an individual without giving that individual any opportunity to make representations, and where one of the decision-makers had a personal interest in the outcome. The individual seeks judicial review, complaining about the way the decision was reached rather than its substance. The complaint concerns the fairness of the process. The individual was given no chance to put their side before the decision was taken, and it later emerged that one of those deciding stood to gain personally from the result, so the challenge is directed not at the wisdom of the outcome but at the manner in which the decision was arrived at. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review relied on?
o: Error of fact going to jurisdiction.
Proportionality of the resulting interference.
Irrationality in the outcome of the decision.
Illegality through misdirection as to the law.
Procedural impropriety.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Procedural impropriety covers failure to observe procedural rules and breaches of the rules of natural justice, including the right to a fair hearing (the opportunity to make representations) and the rule against bias (no personal interest in the outcome). The complaint here is squarely about the fairness of the process.

n.0: Error of fact going to jurisdiction is a distinct, narrower ground.
n.1: Proportionality assesses whether an interference is excessive, not procedural fairness.
n.2: Irrationality attacks the substance of a decision, not the fairness of the procedure.
n.3: Illegality concerns legal error or exceeding powers, not a want of fair process.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A district judge is case managing a civil claim and must apply the guiding principle that underpins the Civil Procedure Rules when giving directions and making case management decisions. Counsel refers the judge to the fundamental principle stated at the very start of the rules. The judge is exercising case management powers. The parties are pressing competing applications and each accuses the other of running up disproportionate costs, and the judge, before ruling, wants to anchor the decision in the guiding principle the rule-makers placed at the very front of the Civil Procedure Rules to govern how the court manages litigation. Which of the following best describes the overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules?
o: To ensure the claimant always succeeds if a claim is issued on these facts.
To decide cases as slowly as necessary to avoid any error.
To resolve every case by a full trial regardless of cost.
To enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
To give priority to the wealthier party's convenience.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost. This includes ensuring the parties are on an equal footing, saving expense, dealing with cases proportionately, expeditiously and fairly, and allotting an appropriate share of the court's resources.

n.0: The objective is to deal with cases justly, not to guarantee the claimant's success.
n.1: Cases are to be dealt with expeditiously, not as slowly as possible.
n.2: Proportionality is central; not every case requires a full trial regardless of cost.
n.4: The objective promotes equal footing, not the wealthier party's convenience.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A litigant is told that the High Court is organised into separate divisions, each dealing broadly with particular types of work, such as general civil and commercial claims, trusts and property and business disputes, and family matters. The litigant wants to understand this structure. The High Court is divided into divisions by subject matter. The litigant seeks the correct description. Told that the High Court is not a single undifferentiated body but is split into parts each handling broadly different work, from general civil and commercial claims to trusts, land and business disputes and to family matters, the litigant wants the correct names of those three divisions. Which of the following best describes the three divisions of the High Court?
o: The Criminal Division, the Civil Division, and the Appeals Division.
The Commons Division, the Lords Division, and the Monarch's Division.
The King's Bench Division, the Chancery Division, and the Family Division.
The Magistrates' Division, the Crown Division, and the Youth Division.
The Small Claims Division, the Fast Track Division, and the Multi-Track Division.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The High Court is organised into three divisions: the King's Bench Division (general civil and commercial claims, and some specialist courts), the Chancery Division (trusts, probate, land, company and insolvency, and business disputes), and the Family Division (family and matrimonial matters). Cases are allocated to the appropriate division by subject matter.

n.0: 'Criminal/Civil/Appeals' describes divisions of the Court of Appeal, not the High Court.
n.1: There are no 'Commons', 'Lords' or 'Monarch's' divisions of the High Court.
n.3: Magistrates', Crown and youth are other courts, not divisions of the High Court.
n.4: Small claims, fast and multi are case management tracks, not High Court divisions.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is charged with theft, an offence which the law treats as capable of being tried either in the magistrates' court or in the Crown Court, depending on its seriousness and the choices made at the allocation stage. The defendant's solicitor explains the flexible position for this category of offence. The offence falls in the middle classification. The allegation is one that, depending on the amount involved and the circumstances, might be dealt with as a relatively minor matter or as something much more serious, and the solicitor is explaining to the client that this middle category of offence can end up in one of two different courts. Which of the following best describes where an either-way offence may be tried?
o: In whichever court the prosecution alone selects, without any allocation procedure.
In either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, depending on allocation and any election.
In the High Court, which decides all either-way offences.
In the magistrates' court only, with no possibility of the Crown Court.
In the Crown Court only, with no possibility of summary trial.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Either-way offences (such as theft) may be tried either summarily in the magistrates' court or on indictment in the Crown Court. Following the plea before venue and allocation procedure, the magistrates decide whether the case is suitable for summary trial, and if it is, the defendant may still elect trial in the Crown Court.

n.0: There is an allocation procedure; the prosecution does not simply choose the court alone.
n.2: The High Court does not decide either-way offences.
n.3: Either-way offences can go to the Crown Court, so 'magistrates only' is wrong.
n.4: They can also be tried summarily, so 'Crown Court only' is wrong.

England & Wales Legal System.q: The Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) is considering whether it is bound by one of its own previous decisions in a case where following it might result in an individual being wrongly imprisoned. Counsel argues the criminal division has a degree of flexibility not available in civil appeals. The case concerns the liberty of the subject. The court weighs following its own precedent. The earlier decision is directly in point and, if followed, would leave the appellant convicted and imprisoned on a basis the court now doubts, and counsel presses that the division dealing with criminal appeals is not shackled to its own precedent quite as tightly as the civil side, precisely because a person's liberty is at stake. Which of the following best describes the position of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)?
o: It may depart from its own decisions only with the consent of the parties.
It is never bound by any of its own previous decisions in any circumstances.
It is bound only by decisions of the Court of Appeal (Civil Division).
It may depart from its own previous decision with rather more flexibility where following it would cause injustice to the subject.
It is absolutely bound by its own previous decisions with no exceptions whatsoever on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The Court of Appeal is generally bound by its own previous decisions (subject to the Young v Bristol Aeroplane exceptions), but the Criminal Division has somewhat greater flexibility to depart from its own precedent where following it would cause injustice, because the liberty of the subject is at stake.

n.0: Departure does not depend on the parties' consent.
n.1: It is generally bound by its own decisions subject to exceptions, so 'never bound' is wrong.
n.2: It is not bound by the Civil Division; each division generally follows its own decisions.
n.4: It is not absolutely bound with no exceptions; it has some added flexibility in criminal cases.

England & Wales Legal System.q: In a criminal trial, the defendant wishes to raise a particular defence. The judge must decide who bears the burden of putting enough evidence of the defence before the court to make it a live issue, as opposed to the ultimate burden of disproving it. A distinction is drawn between raising an issue and proving it. The defence must first be sufficiently raised. The defendant wants to run a particular defence, and the judge has to separate two different questions, first whether enough evidence has been put forward to make that defence a live issue at all, and second who must ultimately prove or disprove it once it is in play. Which of the following best describes the evidential burden as distinct from the legal burden?
o: The evidential burden is the burden of adducing enough evidence to raise an issue, while the legal burden is the burden of proving it.
The evidential and legal burdens are the same thing under a different name.
The evidential burden is irrelevant once a plea of not guilty is entered.
The evidential burden always rests on the defendant for every element of the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The evidential burden requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the whole case.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The evidential burden is the burden of adducing sufficient evidence to raise an issue for the tribunal to consider (for example, enough evidence of self-defence to make it live). The legal (persuasive) burden is the burden of actually proving the issue to the required standard. For many defences the defendant bears the evidential burden, but the prosecution then bears the legal burden of disproving the defence.

n.1: The two burdens are distinct: raising an issue versus proving it.
n.2: The evidential burden remains relevant to which issues are live at trial.
n.3: The evidential burden does not rest on the defendant for every element; the prosecution proves the offence.
n.4: The evidential burden is about raising an issue, not proving the whole case to the criminal standard.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is convicted after a summary trial in the magistrates' court and wishes to challenge both the finding of guilt and the sentence, arguing that on the evidence the court should not have convicted. The defendant wants the matter looked at afresh rather than confined to a point of law. The defendant pleaded not guilty at trial. The defendant maintains that the prosecution witnesses were not credible and that the bench reached the wrong conclusion on the evidence, and wants a fresh tribunal to hear the witnesses again and decide guilt afresh rather than simply reviewing a question of law. Which of the following best describes the appropriate appeal route?
o: Appeal to the Crown Court, which conducts a rehearing.
Judicial review of the conviction in the County Court.
Appeal directly to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
Appeal to a differently constituted bench of the same magistrates' court.
Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court on the facts.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A defendant convicted in the magistrates' court after pleading not guilty may appeal to the Crown Court against conviction and/or sentence. The Crown Court conducts a full rehearing of the case. Appeal by way of case stated, by contrast, lies to the High Court and is confined to points of law or jurisdiction.

n.1: The County Court is a civil court and does not judicially review criminal convictions.
n.2: There is no direct appeal from the magistrates' court to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
n.3: The appeal is to the Crown Court, not to another bench of magistrates.
n.4: Case stated goes to the High Court and is for points of law, not a factual rehearing.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A judge is sentencing an offender for an offence for which the Sentencing Council has issued a definitive guideline setting out the approach and sentencing ranges. The judge is considering how much weight must be given to the guideline. There is nothing exceptional making the guideline inappropriate on these facts. The offence is a common one for which the Sentencing Council has published a detailed step-by-step guideline with categories and ranges, the facts fall squarely within the ordinary run of such cases, and the judge is conscious of the need to explain how far the guideline dictates the outcome. Which of the following best describes the judge's obligation in relation to the sentencing guideline?
o: The judge must follow the guideline unless satisfied it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.
The judge must apply the guideline only if the prosecution asks for it.
The judge is absolutely bound by the guideline in every case without exception on these facts as a general rule.
The judge must refer the guideline to the Court of Appeal before sentencing.
The judge may disregard the guideline entirely at personal discretion.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A court must follow any relevant sentencing guideline unless it is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. This gives the guidelines strong effect while leaving the court a limited power to depart where the interests of justice require it.

n.1: The duty to follow the guideline does not depend on a prosecution request.
n.2: The obligation is strong but not absolute; departure is possible in the interests of justice.
n.3: There is no requirement to refer the guideline to the Court of Appeal before sentencing.
n.4: The judge cannot simply disregard a relevant guideline at will.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court is applying a provision of an Act of Parliament that, read in its natural sense, would operate in a way that interferes with a person's rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. Counsel argues the provision can reasonably be read in a different, Convention-compatible way. The court is considering its duty under the Human Rights Act 1998. The provision was drafted before the point now in issue arose, its ordinary meaning would cut across a right the claimant enjoys under the Convention, and counsel maintains that a perfectly natural alternative reading exists that would respect that right, so the court must be clear about how far its interpretive duty stretches. Which of the following best describes the court's obligation under section 3 of the Act?
o: It must refer the legislation to the European Court of Human Rights for a ruling.
It must suspend the legislation until Parliament amends it.
It must strike down the legislation as invalid because it interferes with Convention rights on these facts.
It must apply the natural meaning and disregard the Convention entirely.
It must read and give effect to the legislation compatibly with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998 requires courts, so far as it is possible to do so, to read and give effect to primary and subordinate legislation in a way that is compatible with Convention rights. This is a strong interpretive obligation, but it does not permit the court to strike down primary legislation.

n.0: Domestic courts do not refer legislation to the European Court of Human Rights for rulings.
n.1: The court has no power to suspend an Act of Parliament pending amendment.
n.2: Courts cannot strike down primary legislation for incompatibility; section 3 is interpretive.
n.3: The court cannot simply disregard the Convention; section 3 imposes a positive duty.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Parliament delegates law-making power to various bodies, and the resulting law takes different forms depending on who makes it and how. Examples include rules made by ministers, rules made by local authorities, and legislation made in the exercise of the royal prerogative. The question concerns the forms of delegated legislation. Various bodies exercise delegated powers. Parliament routinely hands out law-making power to others, and the resulting rules come in more than one shape depending on who exercises the power and how, from ministerial rules to local rules to instruments made in the name of the Crown, and the student is trying to name the principal forms this secondary legislation takes. Which of the following best describes the main forms of delegated legislation?
o: Only Acts of Parliament, which are the sole form of legislation.
Only European Union regulations, which remain the main source of delegated law.
Statutory instruments (made by ministers), byelaws (made by local authorities and certain bodies), and Orders in Council.
Only decisions of the courts, which make all delegated legislation.
Only royal proclamations, which are the exclusive form of delegated legislation on these facts as a general rule.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Delegated (secondary) legislation takes several forms: statutory instruments, the most common, made by ministers under powers in a parent Act; byelaws, made by local authorities and some other bodies for their areas or functions; and Orders in Council, often used in the exercise of the royal prerogative or in emergencies. All derive their authority from enabling powers.

n.0: Acts of Parliament are primary, not delegated, legislation; they are not the only form of law.
n.1: EU regulations are not the main source of domestic delegated legislation, particularly post-Brexit.
n.3: Courts develop the common law but do not make delegated legislation.
n.4: Royal proclamations are not the exclusive form of delegated legislation.

England & Wales Legal System.q: An Act of Parliament has received Royal Assent, but a person wishes to know when its provisions actually take legal effect, as the Act itself contains a section dealing with when it is to come into force. The Act has been passed but its operative date is in question. The Act contains provision about commencement. The Act has cleared all its stages and received Royal Assent, but a party needs to know from what moment its provisions actually bite, and, noticing that the Act itself contains a section dealing with commencement, wants to understand the default position and how it can be varied. Which of the following best describes when an Act's provisions come into force?
o: Only after a further vote of both Houses of Parliament following Royal Assent on these facts.
On Royal Assent, unless the Act provides for a different commencement date or for commencement by order.
Only when a court first applies the Act in a decided case.
Always immediately on Royal Assent, regardless of any provision in the Act.
Only once the Act has been in existence for at least one year.
England & Wales Legal System.w: An Act comes into force on the date of Royal Assent unless the Act itself provides otherwise. Many Acts specify a later commencement date, or provide that some or all provisions come into force on a day appointed by a minister through a commencement order (a statutory instrument), so different parts may come into force at different times.

n.0: No further parliamentary vote is needed after Royal Assent for the Act to commence.
n.2: An Act's force does not depend on a court first applying it.
n.3: Commencement can be deferred by the Act; it is not always immediate on Royal Assent.
n.4: There is no rule requiring a year to pass before an Act can take effect.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A judge in the County Court is considering an earlier judgment of a higher court. Part of that judgment sets out the legal principle essential to the earlier decision on its facts, and another part consists of the judge's general observations on a hypothetical situation that did not arise. The County Court judge must decide which part binds the court. The earlier judgment ran to many pages, weaving together the reasoning that decided the actual dispute with wider commentary on situations that were not before the court, and the County Court judge must separate the part that governs the present case from the part that does not. Which of the following best describes what is binding under the doctrine of precedent?
o: Neither the ratio nor obiter is binding on a lower court in any circumstances.
The ratio decidendi of the earlier decision is binding, while obiter remarks are only persuasive.
Both the ratio decidendi and the obiter remarks are equally binding.
Only the final order of the earlier court is binding, not any reasoning.
The obiter remarks are binding, while the ratio decidendi is merely persuasive on these facts.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The binding element of a precedent is the ratio decidendi: the legal reasoning necessary to the decision on its material facts. Obiter dicta, such as observations on hypothetical situations not essential to the decision, are persuasive only and do not bind a later court.

n.0: The ratio of a higher court's decision does bind a lower court.
n.2: Obiter remarks are not binding; only the ratio binds.
n.3: It is the ratio (the reasoning), not merely the order, that binds.
n.4: This reverses the position; obiter is persuasive, not binding.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A jury in the Crown Court has been deliberating for a considerable time and has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. The judge is considering whether a verdict on which the jury is not unanimous can be accepted. The jury cannot agree unanimously after sufficient time. The judge considers the rules on verdicts. After many hours locked in disagreement the jury still cannot all agree, and the judge, conscious that the law does not always insist on unanimity, must decide whether and on what basis a verdict that not every juror supports can properly be received. Which of the following best describes when a majority verdict may be accepted?
o: A majority verdict (such as 10-2) may be accepted after the jury has deliberated for a minimum period and cannot reach unanimity.
Only a unanimous verdict of all twelve jurors can ever be accepted.
The judge may enter a verdict without any agreement of the jury.
A simple majority of seven to five is always sufficient from the outset.
A majority verdict may be accepted immediately, without any minimum deliberation time on these facts as a general rule.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A jury is first asked to reach a unanimous verdict. If it cannot do so after a minimum period of deliberation (at least two hours, in practice longer), the judge may accept a majority verdict, such as 10-2 or 11-1 (or 10-1/9-1 where the jury has fewer than twelve members). A verdict of 9-3 or narrower is not acceptable.

n.1: A verdict need not always be unanimous; a qualifying majority may be accepted.
n.2: The judge cannot enter a verdict without the jury's agreement.
n.3: A 7-5 split is not a sufficient majority; the permitted majorities are narrower (e.g. 10-2).
n.4: A minimum deliberation period must pass before a majority verdict may be taken.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A person receives a jury summons and asks whether they are eligible to serve, having heard that eligibility depends on age, registration to vote and residence, subject to certain disqualifications and the right to seek excusal. The person has been summoned for jury service. They query their eligibility. Having received a summons to attend for jury service, the recipient is unsure whether they actually qualify, having gathered that it turns on matters such as age, being on the electoral register and residence, with certain people disqualified and others able to seek to be excused. Which of the following best describes eligibility for jury service?
o: Anyone of any age may be compelled to serve with no exceptions.
Only qualified lawyers are eligible to serve as jurors.
Jurors are appointed for life once they have served on one jury on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A person is generally eligible if aged 18 to 75, on the electoral register and resident as required, unless disqualified or excused.
Only property owners are eligible to serve on a jury.
England & Wales Legal System.w: To be qualified for jury service a person must generally be aged 18 to 75, be registered as a parliamentary or local government elector, and have been ordinarily resident in the UK for the required period. Certain people are disqualified (for example, due to certain criminal convictions or mental health grounds), and some may be excused or have service deferred.

n.0: There are age limits and exceptions; not everyone of any age must serve.
n.1: Jury service is not confined to qualified lawyers; ordinary citizens serve.
n.2: Jurors are not appointed for life; they serve when summoned.
n.4: Eligibility is not based on property ownership.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A litigant has already appealed once, from a first-instance decision to an appeal court, and now wishes to bring a further, second appeal to an even higher court. They are told that a stricter test applies to obtaining permission for a second appeal. This would be a second appeal, not a first appeal. The litigant seeks permission. The litigant has already taken the case up once, from the original decision to an appeal court, and, still dissatisfied, now wants to climb another rung to a higher court again, only to be warned that getting permission for a further appeal of this kind is harder than it was the first time. Which of the following best describes the test for permission for a second appeal?
o: Permission for a second appeal is granted on exactly the same basis as a first appeal on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Permission for a second appeal is granted automatically to any dissatisfied party.
Permission is granted only where the appeal raises an important point of principle or practice, or there is some other compelling reason.
Permission for a second appeal is never available in any circumstances.
Permission for a second appeal depends solely on the value of the claim.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A stricter test applies to second appeals: permission will be granted only where the appeal would raise an important point of principle or practice, or there is some other compelling reason for the appeal court to hear it. This is a higher threshold than for a first appeal (a real prospect of success or other compelling reason).

n.0: The second-appeal test is stricter than the first-appeal test, not the same.
n.1: Permission is not automatic; a demanding test applies.
n.3: Second appeals are possible where the higher threshold is met, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: The test turns on importance of principle/practice or a compelling reason, not solely on claim value.

England & Wales Legal System.q: An enabling Act provides that regulations made under it will not come into force unless and until they have been approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament. The minister prepares regulations and must secure a positive vote before they can take effect. Parliament's active approval is required. The Act makes clear that the minister cannot simply lay the instrument and let it take effect; instead nothing happens until each House has actively voted its approval, reflecting a deliberate choice by Parliament to keep a tighter grip on this particular power. Which of the following best describes the parliamentary control procedure applicable to these regulations?
o: The negative resolution procedure.
A procedure requiring no parliamentary involvement at all.
The procedure for granting Royal Assent to Bills.
The procedure for issuing a declaration of incompatibility.
The affirmative resolution procedure.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the affirmative resolution procedure, a statutory instrument requires the positive approval of Parliament, by a resolution of each House (or, for some financial matters, the Commons), before it can come into force or continue in force. It involves a higher level of scrutiny than the negative procedure.

n.0: The negative procedure requires no positive vote; the instrument stands unless annulled.
n.1: This procedure does involve Parliament; approval is expressly required.
n.2: Royal Assent concerns primary legislation, not delegated legislation.
n.3: A declaration of incompatibility is a court remedy under the HRA, not a legislative procedure.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Two parties in dispute wish to try to resolve it out of court. They are considering a process in which an independent third party gives a non-binding evaluation of the likely outcome of the dispute, to help them assess their positions and negotiate a settlement. The neutral gives an opinion, not a binding decision. The process is a form of alternative dispute resolution. Anxious to avoid the cost and risk of a trial, the two sides are attracted to a process in which a respected neutral looks at the dispute and tells them frankly, without binding anyone, how it is likely to come out, so that each can take a more realistic view in negotiations. Which of the following best identifies this process?
o: Arbitration, in which the neutral imposes a binding award on the parties on these facts.
Litigation, in which a judge determines the dispute at trial.
A Part 36 offer made by one party to the other.
Early neutral evaluation, in which a neutral gives a non-binding assessment of the merits.
A freezing injunction preventing the parties from dealing with assets.
