England & Wales Legal System.w: Early neutral evaluation is a form of alternative dispute resolution in which an independent, neutral evaluator (sometimes a judge) gives the parties a non-binding assessment of the likely outcome or of particular issues, to inform their negotiations and encourage settlement. It does not impose a binding decision, unlike arbitration.

n.0: Arbitration produces a binding award; early neutral evaluation is non-binding.
n.1: Litigation is a court determination, not this out-of-court evaluative process.
n.2: A Part 36 offer is a formal settlement offer, not a neutral evaluation of the merits.
n.4: A freezing injunction preserves assets; it is not a dispute-resolution evaluation.

England & Wales Legal System.q: An individual is dissatisfied with a decision made by a government department about a statutory entitlement, such as a welfare benefit or tax matter, and wishes to challenge it before a specialist body rather than the ordinary courts. A colleague mentions the tribunals system. The challenge concerns a specialist administrative decision. The decision concerns a statutory entitlement of exactly the sort Parliament has assigned to specialist adjudication rather than the ordinary courts, and the individual, wanting both an initial hearing before people expert in the field and a route to challenge an adverse result, asks how the tiered system fits together. Which of the following best describes the structure of the tribunals system?
o: All such disputes are decided at first instance in the Crown Court.
The First-tier Tribunal decides such cases, with onward appeal (usually on a point of law) to the Upper Tribunal.
Tribunals have no appeal structure; their decisions are always final.
Tribunal decisions can only ever be challenged by judicial review, never by appeal on these facts as a general rule.
Such disputes must be brought in the County Court like ordinary civil claims.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the unified tribunals structure, specialist disputes (such as tax, social security and immigration matters) are decided at first instance in the First-tier Tribunal, with an onward right of appeal, usually on a point of law, to the Upper Tribunal, which is a superior court of record. This provides a specialist, tiered system distinct from the ordinary courts.

n.0: Such administrative disputes are not decided at first instance in the Crown Court.
n.2: There is an appeal structure; tribunal decisions are not always final.
n.3: There is a statutory right of appeal to the Upper Tribunal, not only judicial review.
n.4: These disputes go to the tribunal, not the County Court as ordinary civil claims.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant brings a High Court claim worth several million pounds that raises numerous complex issues of fact and law, will require extensive expert evidence, and is expected to occupy a lengthy trial. The court must allocate the claim to the appropriate case management track. The claim is high in value and highly complex. The dispute concerns an alleged breach of a major commercial agreement, the pleadings raise numerous distinct issues, several experts in different disciplines will be needed, and the trial is expected to run for weeks, so the court is looking for the track designed to manage substantial and complicated litigation. Which of the following best identifies the track to which the claim would ordinarily be allocated?
o: The intermediate track.
The fast track.
The multi-track.
The summary track.
The small claims track.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The multi-track is the normal track for claims that are of the highest value or that involve complexity beyond the scope of the small claims, fast and intermediate tracks. A multi-million pound, factually and legally complex claim requiring extensive expert evidence and a long trial is a paradigm multi-track case.

n.0: The intermediate track is for less complex claims up to £100,000.
n.1: The fast track is for claims up to £25,000 with a one-day trial.
n.3: There is no case management track called the 'summary track'.
n.4: The small claims track is for straightforward claims of £10,000 or less.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A judge in the High Court is referred to a recent decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on the very point in issue. Counsel accepts the decision is not from a court in the ordinary domestic hierarchy but urges the judge to attach considerable weight to it. There is no directly binding domestic authority on the point. The overseas appeal happens to have been decided by many of the same senior judges who sit in the domestic final court, the reasoning is directly on the disputed point, and counsel is candid that it comes from outside the ordinary ladder of English courts while urging that it should still carry real weight. Which of the following best describes the status of a Privy Council decision in the courts of England and Wales?
o: It automatically overrules any conflicting House of Lords decision.
It is binding on all courts below the Supreme Court without exception.
It has no relevance whatsoever and must be ignored.
It is persuasive but not strictly binding on the domestic courts.
It binds the High Court but not the Court of Appeal.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are not part of the ordinary domestic court hierarchy and are therefore persuasive rather than strictly binding on the courts of England and Wales. Given the seniority of its members, however, such decisions are usually treated as highly persuasive.

n.0: They do not automatically overrule House of Lords or Supreme Court authority.
n.1: Privy Council decisions are not strictly binding on the domestic courts.
n.2: They are relevant and often highly persuasive, so they cannot be ignored.
n.4: They are persuasive at every level, not binding on the High Court alone.

England & Wales Legal System.q: In the same Crown Court trial, the client asks what the judge, as opposed to the jury, is responsible for during and after the trial. Counsel explains the distinct functions of the trial judge. The proceedings are a jury trial on indictment. With the legal argument and the factual conflict both live in the case, the client, having heard how the jury's responsibilities are defined, now wants the mirror-image explanation of what falls to the judge before, during and after the jury delivers its verdict. Which of the following best describes the role of the judge?
o: The judge has no role once the jury has been sworn in.
The judge decides the facts and returns the verdict on guilt.
The judge decides questions of law, directs the jury on the law, and passes sentence.
The judge decides the credibility of the witnesses instead of the jury.
The judge simply records whatever verdict the jury reaches and does nothing further.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The trial judge decides all questions of law, makes rulings on the admissibility of evidence, directs the jury on the relevant law and how to approach their task, and, following a conviction, determines and passes the sentence. The jury remains responsible for the factual questions and the verdict.

n.0: The judge has a central role throughout the trial, not none after swearing the jury.
n.1: Deciding the facts and returning the verdict is the jury's role, not the judge's.
n.3: Assessing witness credibility is a matter of fact for the jury.
n.4: The judge does more than record the verdict; the judge sentences and rules on law.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Two parties to a commercial contract have agreed that any dispute will be referred to a private tribunal whose decision they will accept as final. A dispute arises, it is referred, and the tribunal issues its decision. One party now wonders whether the decision can simply be ignored. The parties agreed to this process in their contract. Their contract contained a clause committing any dispute to a private determination whose outcome they promised to treat as final, the process has now run its course and produced a result, and the party who came off worse is testing whether that result carries any real legal force. Which of the following best describes the effect of an arbitration award?
o: The award is merely advisory and neither party is obliged to comply.
The award takes effect only if later approved by a judge at trial.
The award can be freely disregarded because arbitration is informal.
The award binds only the party that referred the dispute.
The award is binding on the parties and can be enforced through the courts.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Arbitration produces a binding award. Where parties agree to arbitrate, the arbitrator's award is final and binding on them and can be enforced through the courts, with only limited grounds for challenge. This distinguishes arbitration from facilitative processes such as mediation, which do not impose a binding outcome.

n.0: An arbitration award is binding, not merely advisory.
n.1: The award is binding without needing subsequent approval by a judge at trial.
n.2: An award cannot be freely disregarded; it is enforceable despite arbitration's flexibility.
n.3: The award binds both parties, not only the party that referred the dispute.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A student is asked to identify the principal sources of law in England and Wales and how they rank where they conflict. The sources include Acts of Parliament, case law developed by the courts, and delegated legislation. A conflict between a statute and a common law rule is given as an example. The student must explain the hierarchy of sources. Asked to set out where the law of England and Wales actually comes from, the student lists Acts of Parliament, the case law built up by the judges, and delegated legislation, and is then pressed to explain what happens, and which source wins, when a statute and a rule of the common law point in opposite directions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Delegated legislation always prevails over Acts of Parliament.
Case law always prevails over Acts of Parliament where they conflict on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
All sources of law rank equally and conflicts cannot be resolved.
Custom is the highest source of law and overrides statute.
Legislation (primary and valid delegated legislation) prevails over inconsistent case law, reflecting parliamentary sovereignty.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The principal sources of law include legislation (Acts of Parliament and delegated legislation) and case law (common law and equity). Reflecting parliamentary sovereignty, a valid Act of Parliament prevails over inconsistent case law, and case law can be overridden by statute. Delegated legislation must be within the powers of its parent Act, and custom is a very limited source.

n.0: Delegated legislation is subordinate to Acts of Parliament, not superior.
n.1: Case law does not prevail over statute; statute can override the common law.
n.2: The sources are ranked; conflicts are resolved by that hierarchy.
n.3: Custom is a minor source and does not override statute.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court must interpret a statutory provision whose words, given their ordinary grammatical meaning, produce a clear result. One party argues the court should simply apply the words as written, even though the outcome is not the one that party would prefer. The words are not ambiguous and the result is not absurd. The dispute turns entirely on a single subsection whose wording, read naturally, admits of only one meaning, and the party disadvantaged by that meaning is pressing the court to look behind the words, while the opponent insists the court should simply take the provision as it stands. Which of the following best describes the approach the court is being invited to take?
o: The mischief rule, focusing on the gap the statute aimed to remedy.
The golden rule, modifying the words to avoid an absurd result.
The ejusdem generis rule, limiting general words by a preceding list.
The literal rule, giving the words their ordinary and natural meaning.
The purposive approach, giving effect to the statute's broader aims.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The literal rule requires the court to give the words of a statute their ordinary, plain and natural meaning, applying them even if the result seems harsh, provided the words are clear and unambiguous. The other approaches only come into play where the literal meaning is ambiguous or produces absurdity.

n.0: The mischief rule looks beyond the words to the defect being remedied, not the plain meaning.
n.1: The golden rule departs from the literal meaning to avoid absurdity, which is not the case here.
n.2: Ejusdem generis is a specific aid for general words following a list, not the approach described.
n.4: The purposive approach looks to the statute's aims rather than simply applying clear words.

England & Wales Legal System.q: The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is hearing an appeal and is referred to one of its own previous decisions directly on the point in issue. Counsel argues that the earlier decision was wrongly decided and asks the court not to follow it. There is no relevant Supreme Court authority overruling the earlier decision. The earlier authority is squarely on the point and was decided only a few years ago by a differently constituted division of the same court, and counsel accepts it is directly in point but urges that the court is not rigidly tied to it in the way it might at first appear. Which of the following best describes when the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) may decline to follow its own previous decision?
o: Only in limited exceptional situations, such as where the earlier decision was per incuriam or conflicts with a higher court.
Only where the earlier decision is more than ten years old.
Never, because the Court of Appeal is always bound by its own decisions without exception on these facts as a general rule.
In any case where the current court simply considers the earlier decision wrong.
Only where all the parties to the later appeal agree that it should not be followed.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is generally bound by its own previous decisions, subject to the limited exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane: where there are two conflicting Court of Appeal decisions, where its decision conflicts with a later Supreme Court/House of Lords decision, or where the earlier decision was made per incuriam.

n.1: The age of the decision is not one of the recognised exceptions.
n.2: It is not the case that there are no exceptions at all.
n.3: Merely thinking the decision wrong is not enough; the exceptions are limited.
n.4: The parties' agreement does not release the court from precedent.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant and their solicitor agree that, instead of charging on the usual basis, the solicitor's fee will be a percentage of the damages actually recovered if the claim succeeds, and nothing by way of that fee if it does not. The fee is a share of the sums recovered. The arrangement is a form of contingency funding. Rather than bill in the ordinary way, the solicitor offers to take, as the fee, an agreed slice of whatever damages the client actually recovers, so that the firm shares in the winnings if the claim succeeds and takes nothing by way of that fee if it does not. Which of the following best identifies this arrangement?
o: An after-the-event insurance policy covering the opponent's costs.
A fixed fee payable in advance whatever the outcome.
A conditional fee agreement charging the normal fees plus a capped success fee on these facts.
A damages-based agreement, under which the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the damages recovered.
A legal aid arrangement funded from central government.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A damages-based agreement (DBA) is a form of contingency fee arrangement under which the lawyer's fee is calculated as an agreed percentage of the financial benefit (damages) recovered by the client, subject to statutory caps, and is payable only on success. It differs from a conditional fee agreement, where the fee is the normal fee plus a success fee.

n.0: After-the-event insurance covers costs risk; it is not the fee arrangement described.
n.1: A DBA is contingent on success and linked to damages, not a fixed advance fee.
n.2: A conditional fee agreement charges normal fees plus a success fee, not a percentage of damages.
n.4: A DBA is private funding, not legal aid.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is charged with a very serious offence, such as murder, which by law must be tried in the higher criminal court before a judge and jury. Although the first hearing takes place in the magistrates' court, the case cannot remain there for trial. The offence is of the most serious classification. The client faces an allegation at the very top of the scale of seriousness, the first hearing has been listed before the magistrates as a matter of routine, and the solicitor is explaining that despite that starting point the trial itself can only take place in one particular court before a jury. Which of the following best describes where an indictable-only offence is tried?
o: In the Crown Court, before a judge and jury.
In the High Court, before a single judge.
In the County Court, before a district judge.
In the magistrates' court only.
In the magistrates' court, unless the defendant elects otherwise.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Indictable-only offences, the most serious category (such as murder and robbery), can only be tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury. The first appearance is in the magistrates' court, but the case is then sent to the Crown Court for trial; it cannot be tried summarily.

n.1: The High Court does not conduct criminal trials of such offences at first instance.
n.2: The County Court has no criminal trial jurisdiction.
n.3: Indictable-only offences are not tried in the magistrates' court.
n.4: There is no summary trial option, with or without the defendant's election.

England & Wales Legal System.q: During a Crown Court trial, disputes arise both about what the law requires and about which witnesses are telling the truth. Counsel is explaining to the client how responsibility for these different questions is divided between the judge and the jury. The trial is on indictment before judge and jury. The case has thrown up genuine legal argument about what the prosecution must establish, alongside a sharp factual conflict between witnesses whose honesty is in question, and the client is anxious to understand which of these matters will be decided by the twelve members of the jury. Which of the following best describes the jury's role?
o: The jury decides questions of law and directs the judge accordingly.
The jury decides questions of fact and returns the verdict on guilt.
The jury advises the judge, who alone decides guilt.
The jury decides both the law and the sentence to be imposed.
The jury determines only the sentence once the judge convicts.
England & Wales Legal System.w: In a Crown Court trial the jury is the tribunal of fact: it decides the disputed factual questions, including the credibility of witnesses, and returns the verdict of guilty or not guilty. The judge decides questions of law, directs the jury on the law, and passes sentence following conviction.

n.0: Questions of law are for the judge, not the jury.
n.2: The jury decides guilt by its verdict; it does not merely advise.
n.3: The jury does not decide the law or the sentence.
n.4: The jury decides guilt, not sentence; sentencing is for the judge.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A statute was passed to remedy a specific defect in the previous law. The precise words of the provision do not squarely cover the situation before the court, but the situation is plainly within the kind of problem the statute was designed to address. The court wishes to interpret the provision so as to suppress that problem. The court focuses on the defect in the old law. The provision was enacted in response to a well-documented problem in the earlier law, the facts before the court fall within the spirit of that problem even if not neatly within the words, and the court is minded to construe the section so as to address the very defect that prompted it. Which of the following best describes the interpretive approach being applied?
o: The mischief rule, interpreting the statute to suppress the mischief it was intended to remedy.
The presumption that statutes do not bind the Crown.
The literal rule, confining interpretation to the ordinary meaning of the words.
The noscitur a sociis principle, reading words in the context of surrounding words on these facts.
The golden rule, altering the words only to avoid an absurd outcome.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The mischief rule (from Heydon's Case) directs the court to consider the defect or 'mischief' in the law that the statute was passed to remedy, and to interpret the provision so as to suppress that mischief and advance the remedy. It looks beyond the literal words to the statute's remedial purpose.

n.1: The Crown-binding presumption is a separate matter unrelated to this interpretation.
n.2: The literal rule would confine the court to the ordinary meaning of the words.
n.3: Noscitur a sociis is about reading words in the light of their neighbours, not the mischief.
n.4: The golden rule is concerned with avoiding absurdity, not the pre-existing defect in the law.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A statute lists specific items followed by general words, for example 'cats, dogs and other animals'. A court must decide whether the general words ('other animals') are limited by the class of the specific items that precede them. The general words follow a list of specific items of the same kind. The court applies a rule of language. The section sets out a run of specific examples and then tacks on a sweeping general phrase, and the argument is about whether that catch-all phrase should be read at large or cut down to cover only more things of the same character as the specific items that came before it. Which of the following best identifies the rule the court is applying?
o: The ejusdem generis rule, by which general words following a list are limited to the same class as the specific items.
The literal rule, giving the general words their widest possible meaning.
The expressio unius principle, meaning the express mention of one excludes others on these facts as a general rule.
The golden rule, modifying the words to avoid absurdity.
The mischief rule, focusing on the defect in the earlier law.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The ejusdem generis ('of the same kind') rule is a rule of language: where general words follow a list of specific words forming a class, the general words are read as limited to things of the same class. So 'other animals' following 'cats, dogs' might be read as limited to domestic animals of that kind.

n.1: The literal rule concerns ordinary meaning generally, not this list-and-general-words situation.
n.2: Expressio unius is a different maxim (express mention of one excludes others), not the class-limiting rule here.
n.3: The golden rule addresses absurdity, not the limiting of general words by a preceding class.
n.4: The mischief rule looks at the defect in the old law, not rules of language.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A business pursues a defended County Court debt claim valued at £70,000. The claim is not especially complex, is likely to need a trial of no more than three days, and requires only limited expert evidence from no more than two fields. The court is deciding on the appropriate track. The value is above £25,000 but below £100,000. The dispute is a business debt claim that turns on a relatively confined set of issues, the parties anticipate a trial of two to three days with limited expert input, and the value sits comfortably in the band that a newer track was specifically introduced to handle proportionately. Which of the following best identifies the track most likely to apply?
o: The tribunal track.
The fast track.
The multi-track, regardless of complexity.
The intermediate track.
The small claims track.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The intermediate track is the normal track for less complex claims with a value above £25,000 but not more than £100,000, where the trial is not expected to exceed three days and expert evidence is limited. A £70,000 claim of modest complexity is well suited to the intermediate track.

n.0: There is no case management 'tribunal track' for such a County Court claim.
n.1: The fast track is generally for claims up to £25,000.
n.2: The multi-track is not the automatic destination for such a claim where the intermediate track fits its value and complexity.
n.4: The small claims track is for straightforward claims of £10,000 or less.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court interpreting a statute wishes to use aids to construction. Some aids are found within the statute itself (such as its long title, headings and interpretation sections), while others are external to it (such as dictionaries and, in limited circumstances, Hansard). The court is distinguishing between the two categories of aid. The court considers internal and external aids to interpretation. Wrestling with an ambiguous provision, the judge wants to draw on every legitimate aid to work out its meaning, some sitting inside the four corners of the Act itself and others lying outside it, and counsel invites the court to be clear about which category each proposed aid falls into. Which of the following best describes the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic aids?
o: Only extrinsic aids may ever be used to interpret a statute.
Intrinsic aids are external sources, and extrinsic aids are parts of the Act.
Intrinsic aids are found within the Act itself, while extrinsic aids are sources outside the Act.
Intrinsic aids are always binding, whereas extrinsic aids are always prohibited on these facts.
Intrinsic and extrinsic aids are identical and interchangeable terms.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Intrinsic (internal) aids to interpretation are found within the statute itself, such as the long and short titles, preamble, headings, marginal notes and interpretation sections. Extrinsic (external) aids lie outside the Act, such as dictionaries, earlier statutes, reports of law reform bodies and, within the limits of Pepper v Hart, Hansard.

n.0: Both intrinsic and extrinsic aids may be used, not only extrinsic ones.
n.1: This reverses the definitions: intrinsic aids are within the Act, extrinsic outside it.
n.3: Intrinsic aids are not automatically binding, and extrinsic aids are not always prohibited; both may assist.
n.4: The two are distinct categories, not interchangeable.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A client needs an advocate to conduct a trial in the Crown Court. The client is aware that both solicitors and barristers exist but is unclear about who may appear as an advocate in the higher courts. The client asks about rights of audience. The matter will be heard in the Crown Court. The client has been told that lawyers in England and Wales come in more than one kind and is unsure whether the person who advises on a case is necessarily the same person who can stand up and argue it in the higher courts, so wants the position on who may act as an advocate spelt out. Which of the following best describes the position on rights of audience in the higher courts?
o: Only solicitors may appear as advocates in the higher courts.
Only barristers may ever appear as advocates in any court in England and Wales.
Barristers have rights of audience in the higher courts, and solicitors may obtain higher rights as solicitor advocates.
Neither solicitors nor barristers may appear; only the client may address the court on these facts as a general rule.
Rights of audience in the higher courts are granted only by the Supreme Court.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Barristers traditionally have full rights of audience in all courts, including the higher courts. Solicitors have rights of audience in the lower courts and may obtain higher rights of audience, qualifying as solicitor advocates able to appear in the higher courts. Rights of audience are regulated by the approved regulators.

n.0: Rights of audience in the higher courts are not confined to solicitors.
n.1: Solicitors can obtain higher rights of audience, so advocacy is not confined to barristers.
n.3: Qualified advocates, not only the client, may address the court.
n.4: Rights of audience are granted through the regulatory framework, not by the Supreme Court.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A student confuses the European Convention on Human Rights with European Union law, assuming both come from the same institutions. In fact the Convention is a product of a different international organisation and is enforced by a different court from the EU institutions. The Convention and EU law have distinct origins. The student seeks clarification. The student has muddled the Convention on Human Rights with the law of the European Union, assuming both flow from the same Brussels institutions, when in truth the Convention springs from a quite separate international body and is policed by a different court altogether, a confusion the tutor wants to correct. Which of the following best describes the position of the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: It is enforced by the UK Supreme Court sitting as an EU court.
It is a treaty of the Council of Europe, enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, separate from the EU.
It is a piece of European Union legislation enforced by the Court of Justice of the EU on these facts as a general rule.
It is a domestic UK statute with no international dimension.
It ceased to have any effect in the UK when the UK left the European Union.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The European Convention on Human Rights is a treaty of the Council of Europe (a separate international organisation from the European Union), and alleged breaches can ultimately be taken to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. It is given effect domestically by the Human Rights Act 1998 and is entirely distinct from EU law; UK membership of the Convention was unaffected by leaving the EU.

n.0: It is enforced ultimately by the Strasbourg court, not by the UK Supreme Court acting as an EU court.
n.2: The Convention is not EU legislation and is not enforced by the Court of Justice of the EU.
n.3: It is an international treaty, not merely a domestic statute (though the HRA gives it domestic effect).
n.4: Leaving the EU did not end the UK's participation in the Convention.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant wishes to bring a modest civil money claim and a more substantial civil claim, and asks in which court civil claims are generally commenced and tried at first instance, as distinct from the criminal courts. The claims are civil, not criminal. The claimant is considering the appropriate civil court. The client has one small money claim and one larger, more involved dispute, both purely civil rather than criminal, and wants to know in which court civil proceedings of this kind are normally started and tried at first instance, as opposed to the courts that deal with crime. Which of the following best describes the civil trial courts of first instance?
o: The County Court handles most civil claims, with the High Court dealing with higher-value or more complex claims.
The Supreme Court hears all civil claims at first instance.
The Crown Court is the main court for civil claims at first instance.
Civil claims can only ever be commenced in a tribunal, never a court on these facts as a general rule.
The magistrates' court tries all civil claims of any value.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Civil claims at first instance are generally brought in the County Court, which handles the bulk of civil litigation, while the High Court deals with higher-value, more complex or specialist claims (through its King's Bench, Chancery and Family Divisions). The Crown Court and magistrates' court are principally criminal courts.

n.1: The Supreme Court is the final appeal court, not a first-instance civil court.
n.2: The Crown Court is principally a criminal court, not the main civil first-instance court.
n.3: Many civil claims are brought in the ordinary courts, not only in tribunals.
n.4: The magistrates' court has very limited civil functions, not all civil claims.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Parliament has conferred power on a minister to make regulations by statutory instrument. The relevant Act provides that such regulations are to be laid before Parliament and will become law unless either House passes a resolution to annul them within the prescribed period. No positive vote of approval is required. The minister makes regulations accordingly. The Act allows the minister to legislate by statutory instrument and sets the terms on which Parliament will scrutinise the result, providing that the instrument stands as law once laid unless one of the Houses moves within the prescribed period to strike it down, without any need for a positive vote. Which of the following best describes the parliamentary control procedure being used?
o: The super-affirmative resolution procedure.
A hybrid instrument procedure.
The affirmative resolution procedure.
The negative resolution procedure.
The Royal Assent procedure for primary legislation.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the negative resolution procedure, a statutory instrument is laid before Parliament and becomes (or remains) law unless it is annulled by a resolution of either House within the prescribed period (commonly 40 sitting days). No affirmative vote of approval is needed; the instrument takes effect unless objected to.

n.0: The super-affirmative procedure involves enhanced scrutiny beyond a simple approval vote.
n.1: A hybrid instrument procedure applies to instruments affecting particular private interests differently.
n.2: The affirmative procedure requires a positive vote of approval, which is not the case here.
n.4: Royal Assent is part of the process for primary legislation, not delegated legislation.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A party dissatisfied with a decision of the First-tier Tribunal on a specialist matter wishes to challenge it. They are told there is a specialist appellate tribunal that hears such appeals, generally on a point of law, and which is itself a superior court of record. The challenge is from the First-tier Tribunal. An onward appeal route exists. Unhappy with how the First-tier Tribunal decided their specialist matter, the party wants to take the point higher, and is told that a dedicated appellate tribunal, itself a superior court of record, exists to hear such appeals, generally confined to questions of law. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The First-tier Tribunal's decisions can only ever be challenged by judicial review on these facts as a general rule.
Appeals from the First-tier Tribunal lie directly to the Supreme Court.
Appeals from the First-tier Tribunal lie to the Crown Court.
There is no route of appeal from the First-tier Tribunal at all.
An appeal generally lies, usually on a point of law, to the Upper Tribunal, with a further onward route in appropriate cases.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Within the unified tribunals structure, an appeal from the First-tier Tribunal generally lies, usually on a point of law and often with permission, to the Upper Tribunal, which is a superior court of record. From the Upper Tribunal a further appeal may lie to the Court of Appeal in appropriate cases.

n.0: There is a statutory appeal route to the Upper Tribunal, not only judicial review.
n.1: Appeals go to the Upper Tribunal, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.2: Appeals do not lie to the Crown Court, which is a criminal court.
n.3: There is a route of appeal from the First-tier Tribunal, so 'no route' is wrong.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A dispute arises about the relationship between an Act of Parliament and a rule of the common law developed by the courts. The Act, validly passed, contains a clear provision that is inconsistent with the pre-existing common law rule. A party argues the court should prefer the common law. The Act is clear and unambiguous. The judge-made rule had governed this area for many years until Parliament legislated, and the statute now says something plainly at odds with it, leaving the court to decide which source of law must give way where a clear statute and an established common law rule cannot both stand. Which of the following best describes the position under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty?
o: The common law rule prevails because it is older and judge-made.
The Act of Parliament prevails over the inconsistent common law rule.
The Act is invalid because it conflicts with the common law.
The two rules apply equally and the party may select either.
The court may choose whichever rule it considers fairer.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament is the supreme law-making body. A clear and valid Act of Parliament prevails over any inconsistent rule of the common law; the courts give effect to the statute. The common law can be overridden or altered by statute.

n.0: The common law does not prevail over a clear inconsistent statute merely because it is older.
n.2: An Act is not invalid for conflicting with the common law; statute overrides common law.
n.3: The rules do not apply equally; the statute takes precedence.
n.4: The court must give effect to the statute, not simply choose the rule it prefers.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court is faced with a statutory provision that is genuinely ambiguous. Counsel wishes to refer the court to a clear statement made by the responsible minister during the Parliamentary debates on the Bill, as recorded in Hansard, to help resolve the ambiguity. The statement is clear and was made by the promoter of the Bill. The provision is capable of bearing two quite different meanings, neither obviously right, and counsel has located a passage in the official record of the Parliamentary debates in which the responsible minister explained precisely what the clause was meant to do, and wishes to rely on it. Which of the following best describes when the court may have regard to such Parliamentary material?
o: Only where both Houses of Parliament formally consent to its use.
Never, because reference to Parliamentary debates is always prohibited on these facts as a general rule.
In every case, as a routine first step in interpreting any statute.
Where the legislation is ambiguous or obscure, and the statement relied on is a clear ministerial statement.
Only in criminal cases and never in civil proceedings.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under Pepper v Hart, a court may refer to Hansard as an aid to interpretation where the legislation is ambiguous, obscure or leads to absurdity, where the material relied on consists of a clear statement by the minister or promoter of the Bill, and where that statement is itself clear. It is not a routine or unrestricted practice.

n.0: Formal consent of both Houses is not required.
n.1: It is not always prohibited; Pepper v Hart created a limited exception.
n.2: Reference to Hansard is not a routine first step; the conditions must be met.
n.4: The principle is not confined to criminal cases.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A prospective claimant cannot afford to pay legal fees as the case proceeds, and their solicitor offers an arrangement whereby the solicitor will be paid only if the claim succeeds, taking a success fee in that event, and nothing (for their fees) if it fails. The funding is contingent on success. No public funding is involved. The prospective claimant simply cannot fund the case as it goes along, so the solicitor proposes to act on the footing that the firm will be paid for its work, with an agreed uplift, only if the claim comes off, and will not charge its fees at all if the claim fails. Which of the following best describes this funding arrangement?
o: A legal aid certificate funding the case from public funds throughout.
An arrangement under which the lawyer must personally pay the client's opponent's costs on these facts as a general rule.
A retainer under which the client pays all fees in advance regardless of outcome.
A damages-based agreement in which the lawyer is paid a fixed hourly rate win or lose.
A conditional fee agreement, under which the lawyer's fees (and any success fee) are payable only if the case is won.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A conditional fee agreement ('no win, no fee') provides that the lawyer's fees are payable only if the case is successful, usually with a success fee (an uplift on the normal fees, capped) payable on success. It is a form of private funding, distinct from legal aid and from a damages-based agreement (where the fee is a percentage of the damages recovered).

n.0: Legal aid is public funding; a CFA is a private no-win-no-fee arrangement.
n.1: A CFA does not make the lawyer personally liable for the opponent's costs.
n.2: A CFA is not payment of all fees in advance regardless of outcome.
n.3: A damages-based agreement links the fee to a percentage of damages, not a fixed rate win or lose.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is tried on indictment in the Crown Court before a judge and jury and is convicted. The defendant believes there were serious errors in the judge's directions to the jury and wishes to challenge the conviction. The trial took place in the Crown Court. The defendant was tried before a judge and jury on a serious charge, was convicted, and complains that the summing-up misdirected the jury on the law, and is now taking advice on the court to which such a challenge to a conviction returned by a jury must be directed. Which of the following best identifies the court to which an appeal against conviction on indictment ordinarily lies?
o: The High Court, by way of case stated.
The magistrates' court, exercising a supervisory role.
The Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
The Crown Court, before a different judge.
The Supreme Court, as the first appeal court.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A defendant convicted on indictment in the Crown Court appeals against conviction (and/or sentence) to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave. Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court is available from the magistrates' court and from the Crown Court in its appellate capacity, not from trial on indictment.

n.0: Case stated to the High Court is not the route for a conviction on indictment.
n.1: The magistrates' court has no supervisory role over Crown Court convictions.
n.3: The appeal does not go to another Crown Court judge.
n.4: The Supreme Court is not the first appeal court from the Crown Court.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant of limited means is charged with a criminal offence and wishes to know whether they can obtain publicly funded legal representation. Their solicitor explains that eligibility depends on more than just the defendant's financial position. The defendant faces criminal proceedings. The defendant has very little income but the solicitor is careful to explain that a grant of public funding does not turn on finances alone, since the seriousness of the charge, the risk to the defendant's liberty and the complexity of the case all feed into a separate assessment that must also be satisfied. Which of the following best describes the basis on which criminal legal aid is granted?
o: It is granted automatically to every defendant regardless of circumstances.
It is available only after the defendant has been convicted.
It depends on both a means test and an interests of justice test.
It depends only on whether the offence is triable in the Crown Court.
It depends solely on the defendant's income, with no other requirement.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Criminal legal aid for representation is generally subject to two requirements: a means test (assessing the defendant's financial resources) and an interests of justice test (considering, for example, whether the defendant risks loss of liberty, the complexity of the case, and the ability to understand proceedings). Both must be satisfied.

n.0: Legal aid is not granted automatically to every defendant.
n.1: Legal aid is to fund representation during proceedings, not only after conviction.
n.3: Eligibility is not determined only by whether the offence is Crown Court triable.
n.4: Income alone is not the sole criterion; the interests of justice test also applies.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A member of the public wishes to complain about the conduct of a solicitor and separately about the conduct of a barrister, and asks which bodies are responsible for regulating each branch of the profession. The two branches of the profession have different frontline regulators. The person wants to direct each complaint correctly. The complainant has grievances about two lawyers, one a solicitor and the other a barrister, and, understanding that the two branches of the profession answer to different frontline regulators, wants to be sure each complaint is directed to the body that actually oversees that kind of lawyer. Which of the following best describes the regulation of solicitors and barristers?
o: Solicitors are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority and barristers by the Bar Standards Board.
Neither solicitors nor barristers are subject to any professional regulation on these facts as a general rule.
Both solicitors and barristers are regulated directly by the government.
Solicitors and barristers are both regulated by the Bar Council alone.
Both solicitors and barristers are regulated solely by the Law Society.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The legal profession has separate frontline regulators: solicitors are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (the regulatory arm of the Law Society), and barristers by the Bar Standards Board (the regulatory arm of the Bar Council). Both operate under the oversight of the Legal Services Board created by the Legal Services Act 2007.

n.1: Both branches are subject to professional regulation.
n.2: The professions are regulated by independent regulators, not directly by the government.
n.3: The Bar Council (through the BSB) regulates barristers, not solicitors as well.
n.4: The Law Society's regulatory functions are exercised by the SRA, and barristers are regulated by the BSB, not the Law Society.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is to be tried summarily in the magistrates' court and asks who will decide the case, having heard that magistrates' courts are made up of different kinds of judicial officer. The trial is a summary trial in the magistrates' court. The defendant asks about the tribunal's composition. About to be tried summarily, the defendant has heard that the magistrates' court can be made up in more than one way and wants to know who will actually decide the case, whether a group of lay justices helped by a legal adviser or a single professional judge sitting alone. Which of the following best describes who sits in the magistrates' court?
o: Always a judge and a jury of twelve members.
Either a bench of (usually three) lay magistrates advised by a legal adviser, or a single legally qualified district judge.
Always a panel of qualified barristers acting as judges.
Always the same twelve lay magistrates for every case in the area on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Always a single High Court judge sitting alone.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Cases in the magistrates' court are heard either by a bench of lay magistrates (justices of the peace), usually three, who are not legally qualified and are advised on the law by a legal adviser (justices' clerk), or by a single district judge (magistrates' courts), who is legally qualified and sits alone.

n.0: There is no jury in the magistrates' court.
n.2: The court is composed of lay magistrates or a district judge, not a panel of barristers.
n.3: Benches are drawn from a pool; it is not the same twelve magistrates for every case, nor twelve in number.
n.4: A High Court judge does not sit in the magistrates' court.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A consumer brings a straightforward County Court claim against a trader for £6,000 in respect of faulty goods. The claim raises no complex issues of law or fact and is defended. When directions are given the court must allocate the claim to a case management track. The claim is a modest, uncomplicated money claim. The goods were a household appliance that failed shortly after purchase, the consumer wants a refund plus a modest sum for consequential expense, the trader disputes liability, and the sums and issues involved are exactly the kind the civil rules channel into a streamlined, low-cost procedure with limited costs recovery. Which of the following best identifies the track to which the claim would ordinarily be allocated?
o: The multi-track.
The fast track.
The Crown Court list.
The intermediate track.
The small claims track.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The small claims track is the normal track for straightforward claims with a value not exceeding £10,000. A defended, uncomplicated claim for £6,000 falls within it, providing a streamlined and low-cost procedure with limited recovery of costs.

n.0: The multi-track is for the highest value or most complex claims.
n.1: The fast track is generally for claims above £10,000 up to £25,000.
n.2: The Crown Court is a criminal court and has no role in allocating a civil money claim.
n.3: The intermediate track is for certain claims above £25,000 up to £100,000.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A government minister makes a decision that goes beyond the powers actually conferred on the minister by the enabling Act of Parliament, purporting to do something the statute does not authorise. A person affected seeks to challenge the decision in judicial review proceedings. The decision exceeds the statutory power. The enabling Act set out in some detail what the minister could and could not do, the step actually taken falls outside that grant of power, and the person affected is framing the challenge around the fact that the minister simply had no authority to do what was done. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review being relied on?
o: Procedural impropriety.
Proportionality of the interference.
Illegality.
Irrationality.
Legitimate expectation arising from a promise.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Illegality as a ground of judicial review arises where a decision-maker acts outside the powers conferred on it, misdirects itself in law, or fails to give effect to the law. Acting beyond the powers conferred by the enabling Act (ultra vires) is a classic instance of illegality.

n.0: Procedural impropriety concerns unfair procedure or breach of natural justice, not acting ultra vires.
n.1: Proportionality assesses whether an interference is excessive, not whether the power existed.
n.3: Irrationality concerns a decision so unreasonable no reasonable authority could reach it, not exceeding powers.
n.4: Legitimate expectation involves reliance on a promise or practice, which is not what is described.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A public body reaches a decision that, although within its legal powers and taken by a fair procedure, is so extreme that no reasonable authority properly directing itself could ever have arrived at it. A claimant seeks judicial review, focusing on the quality of the decision itself rather than the procedure. The decision defies logic and accepted standards. There is no complaint that the body lacked the power or that the procedure was unfair; the objection is to the decision itself, which the claimant says is so far removed from anything a sensible authority could have decided that it cannot be allowed to stand on review. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review relied on?
o: Procedural impropriety through a breach of natural justice.
Breach of a substantive legitimate expectation.
Failure to give reasons for the decision.
Irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness).
Illegality through acting outside statutory powers.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Irrationality, or Wednesbury unreasonableness, is a ground of judicial review that applies where a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority, properly directing itself, could have made it. It targets the substance or quality of the decision rather than the legality of the power or the fairness of the procedure.

n.0: Procedural impropriety concerns unfair procedure, which is not the focus here.
n.1: Legitimate expectation involves reliance on a promise or practice, not extreme unreasonableness.
n.2: Failure to give reasons is a distinct procedural complaint, not irrationality.
n.4: Illegality concerns exceeding or misusing legal powers, not the extreme quality of a lawful-powered decision.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Following the United Kingdom's departure from the European Union, a question arises about the status of certain EU-derived law that was preserved in domestic law at the end of the implementation period. A party wishes to know what body of law now governs the point, given that the UK is no longer an EU member. The point turns on preserved EU-derived rules. The rule in question originated in EU law and was carried over into domestic law at the end of the implementation period, and with the UK now outside the EU the party wants to understand on what footing, if any, that preserved body of law continues to operate in the courts of England and Wales. Which of the following best describes the status of that preserved law within the domestic legal system?
o: It ceased to have any effect in domestic law immediately on the UK leaving the EU on these facts as a general rule.
It can only be applied by the Court of Justice of the European Union.
It automatically overrides any later Act of Parliament.
It continues to have effect domestically as assimilated (formerly retained) EU law, as modified by Parliament.
It continues to bind the UK courts exactly as EU law did before, without change.
England & Wales Legal System.w: On leaving the EU, a large body of EU-derived law was preserved in domestic law (originally 'retained EU law', now 'assimilated law'). It continues to have effect as part of domestic law, but is subject to amendment and repeal by Parliament and to changes in its status and interpretation made by domestic legislation.

n.0: EU-derived law was preserved domestically rather than ceasing to have effect immediately.
n.1: It is applied by domestic courts, not exclusively by the Court of Justice of the EU.
n.2: It does not automatically override later Acts of Parliament; Parliament remains sovereign.
n.4: It does not continue to bind exactly as before; its status and supremacy have been changed by domestic law.

England & Wales Legal System.q: In a criminal trial in the Crown Court, the judge must direct the jury on the standard of proof they must apply before they can convict the defendant of the offence charged. Defence counsel emphasises the importance of the direction being correctly given. The proceedings are criminal. The case against the accused rests largely on circumstantial evidence, defence counsel is concerned that the jury might convict on suspicion rather than proof, and the correct formulation of how sure the jury must be before they may return a guilty verdict has become the focus of the summing-up. Which of the following best describes the standard of proof the prosecution must meet?
o: The jury need only find guilt more likely than not.
The jury must find the defendant probably guilty on balance.
The jury must be sure of guilt (beyond reasonable doubt).
The jury must be satisfied on clear and convincing evidence.
The jury must find a prima facie case established.
England & Wales Legal System.w: In criminal proceedings the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, that is, so that the jury (or magistrates) are sure of guilt. This is a higher standard than the civil balance of probabilities, reflecting the seriousness of a criminal conviction.

n.0: 'More likely than not' is the civil balance of probabilities, not the criminal standard.
n.1: 'Probably guilty on balance' is the civil standard, insufficient for conviction.
n.3: The criminal standard is being sure/beyond reasonable doubt, not a 'clear and convincing' test.
n.4: A prima facie case is not the standard required to convict.

England & Wales Legal System.q: The Supreme Court is asked to decide a case in which one of its own earlier decisions (from when the court's predecessor was the House of Lords) is said to be wrong and to be producing injustice. Counsel invites the court to depart from that earlier decision. The court is the final appellate court for the jurisdiction. The point has significant commercial consequences, the earlier authority has been criticised by academics and judges over the years, and counsel submits that the time has come for the final court to reconsider it, so the court must first be clear about the extent of its own freedom to do so. Which of the following best describes the Supreme Court's position in relation to its own previous decisions?
o: It may only depart from a previous decision with the consent of Parliament.
It is absolutely bound by its own previous decisions in every case.
It is bound by decisions of the Court of Appeal on the same point.
It may never overrule a decision made when it sat as the House of Lords.
It may depart from its own previous decisions when it appears right to do so.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the 1966 Practice Statement (which the Supreme Court continues to apply), the final appellate court, while treating its former decisions as normally binding, may depart from a previous decision when it appears right to do so. Its decisions bind all lower courts.

n.0: Parliament's consent is not required for the court to depart from its own precedent.
n.1: It is not absolutely bound by its own decisions; the Practice Statement allows departure.
n.2: The Supreme Court is not bound by the Court of Appeal, which is a lower court.
n.3: It can depart from House of Lords decisions as well as its own.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A potential claimant wishes to sue for breach of a simple contract that occurred some years ago. Before advising on the merits, the solicitor must consider whether the claim can still be brought in time, given the statutory limitation rules. The claim is founded on a simple contract. The alleged breach happened several years ago, the prospective claimant has only recently decided to pursue it, and before spending time on the merits the solicitor must work out whether the passage of time has already barred the claim under the statutory limitation regime for this kind of action. Which of the following best describes the ordinary limitation period for a claim in simple contract?
o: Twelve years from the date the contract was signed.
There is no limitation period for contract claims.
One year from the date the claimant discovered the breach.
Three years from the date of the breach in every case.
Six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the ordinary limitation period for an action founded on a simple contract is six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued (generally the date of breach). Different periods apply to certain claims, such as personal injury (three years) and specialties/deeds (twelve years).

n.0: Twelve years applies to specialties (contracts by deed), not simple contracts, and runs from accrual not signing.
n.1: There is a limitation period for contract claims.
n.2: One year is not the general contractual limitation period.
n.3: Three years is the usual period for personal injury claims, not simple contract.

England & Wales Legal System.q: Two commercial parties in dispute wish to resolve matters without a trial. They agree to appoint a neutral third party to help them communicate and negotiate towards their own settlement, but who will not impose any decision on them. The client asks how this form of dispute resolution works. The neutral will not decide the dispute. Both businesses want to preserve their commercial relationship and avoid the cost and publicity of a trial, they have identified an independent person acceptable to both to help them talk the matter through, and it is understood from the outset that this person will not hand down any decision. Which of the following best describes this form of alternative dispute resolution?
o: Adjudication, in which a court officer issues a final judgment.
Litigation, in which a judge determines the dispute at trial.
A reference to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
Mediation, in which a neutral facilitator helps the parties reach their own settlement.
Arbitration, in which the neutral imposes a binding decision on the parties.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Mediation is a form of alternative dispute resolution in which an independent, neutral mediator facilitates negotiation between the parties to help them reach their own voluntary settlement. The mediator does not decide the dispute or impose any outcome; any settlement is agreed by the parties themselves.

n.0: Adjudication (in this sense) involves an imposed decision, unlike facilitative mediation.
n.1: Litigation involves a judge determining the dispute, not a facilitator.
n.2: A reference to the Court of Justice concerns EU law questions, not this settlement process.
n.4: Arbitration involves the neutral imposing a binding decision, which is expressly not the case here.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A judge sitting alone in the High Court is referred to a previous decision of another High Court judge on the same point of law. The judge must decide whether that earlier decision is binding or merely persuasive. Both decisions are at first instance in the High Court. The earlier decision is of a fellow High Court judge. Sitting alone at first instance, the judge is shown a ruling by a fellow High Court judge on the identical point and has to decide whether that earlier decision ties their hands or merely carries weight that they would ordinarily respect but could, if persuaded it was wrong, decline to follow. Which of the following best describes the status of the earlier decision?
o: It binds all courts in the country including the Supreme Court.
It has no relevance whatsoever and must be ignored.
It binds the judge only if it was decided more recently than any other case on these facts as a general rule.
It is of persuasive authority only; a High Court judge is not strictly bound by another High Court judge's decision.
It is strictly binding; High Court judges always bind one another.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A decision of a High Court judge at first instance is not strictly binding on another High Court judge, though it is of strong persuasive authority and will usually be followed for consistency unless considered wrong. (A Divisional Court decision, by contrast, generally binds a single High Court judge.)

n.0: A first-instance High Court decision does not bind higher courts such as the Supreme Court.
n.1: The earlier decision is persuasive and usually followed, not irrelevant.
n.2: Its status does not turn simply on which case is more recent.
n.4: High Court judges do not strictly bind one another at first instance.

England & Wales Legal System.q: The Supreme Court, hearing a case, considers a legal principle established in an entirely separate earlier case decided by the Court of Appeal some years before. The Supreme Court concludes that the principle in that earlier, unrelated case was wrong and declares that it should no longer be followed. The two cases are different cases with different parties. The earlier authority arose from a completely separate dispute between different litigants years ago, the principle it laid down has troubled the courts since, and the final court has now concluded, in the course of deciding the present unrelated case, that the old principle should no longer stand. Which of the following best describes what the Supreme Court is doing to the earlier decision?
o: Affirming the earlier decision.
Overruling the earlier decision.
Quashing the earlier decision under judicial review.
Reversing the earlier decision.
Distinguishing the earlier decision.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Overruling occurs where a higher court, in a later and separate case, decides that the legal principle laid down in an earlier case was wrong and should no longer be followed. It is distinct from reversing, which is the appellate court changing the outcome of the very same case on appeal.

n.0: Affirming would uphold, not reject, the earlier decision.
n.2: Judicial review quashes administrative decisions, not the legal principle of an earlier judgment.
n.3: Reversing changes the result of the same case on appeal, not a different earlier case.
n.4: Distinguishing avoids a precedent on the facts without saying it was wrong.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant brings a defended County Court claim for £18,000 arising from a contractual dispute. The issues are not especially complex, the trial is expected to last no more than one day, and limited expert evidence may be required. The court is allocating the claim to a track. The value falls between £10,000 and £25,000. The parties disagree about whether goods supplied met the contract specification, the evidence is contained mainly in documents and correspondence with perhaps one expert report, and the case can realistically be disposed of within a single day of trial, all of which bears on where it belongs. Which of the following best identifies the track to which the claim would ordinarily be allocated?
o: The fast track.
The commercial arbitration track.
The multi-track.
The intermediate track.
The small claims track.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The fast track is the normal track for claims with a value above £10,000 but not more than £25,000, where the trial is likely to last no longer than one day and expert evidence is limited. An £18,000 claim of modest complexity fits within it.

n.1: There is no 'commercial arbitration track' in the case management tracks; arbitration is a separate process.
n.2: The multi-track is reserved for higher value or more complex claims.
n.3: The intermediate track is for certain claims above £25,000 up to £100,000.
n.4: The small claims track is generally for claims of £10,000 or less.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant wishes to challenge a public authority's decision by judicial review. Some months have passed since the decision was made, and the defendant argues the claim is too late. The claimant asks about the time within which a judicial review claim must be brought. The grounds arose when the decision was made. The decision under attack was taken and communicated to the claimant some months ago, the claimant took time to gather evidence and seek advice before acting, and the defendant now says that even if there is a good point on the merits the challenge has simply been left too late to proceed. Which of the following best describes the time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review?
o: The claim must be brought within twelve months of the grounds arising.
The claim must be filed promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising.
The claim must be brought within twenty-one days of the decision without exception.
There is no time limit for bringing judicial review proceedings.
The claim may be brought at any time within six years of the decision.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A claim for judicial review must be filed promptly, and in any event not later than three months after the grounds to make the claim first arose. The requirement of promptness means a claim may be too late even within the three months, though the court has a limited discretion to extend time.

n.0: Twelve months is longer than the three-month limit.
n.2: The general time limit is three months (with a promptness requirement), not a fixed 21 days.
n.3: There is a time limit; judicial review cannot be brought at any time.
n.4: The six-year limitation period applies to certain contract and tort claims, not judicial review.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is convicted in the magistrates' court. The defendant does not dispute the facts found but contends that the magistrates misapplied the law in reaching their decision, and wishes to challenge the conviction specifically on that point of law. The challenge is on a point of law only. The defendant accepts the facts as the magistrates found them and does not want the evidence heard again, but maintains that on those very facts the law did not permit a conviction, so the challenge is confined to the legal analysis the bench applied. Which of the following best describes the appropriate route of appeal from the magistrates' court?
o: Appeal directly to the Supreme Court on the point of law.
Appeal to the Crown Court for a full rehearing of the evidence.
Application to the same magistrates to reconsider their decision.
Appeal directly to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Where the challenge to a magistrates' court decision is on a point of law (or that they acted in excess of jurisdiction), the appropriate route is an appeal by way of case stated to the High Court (a Divisional Court of the King's Bench Division). Appeal to the Crown Court is for a rehearing, generally on fact and/or sentence.

n.0: There is no direct appeal from the magistrates' court to the Supreme Court.
n.1: An appeal to the Crown Court is a rehearing of the evidence, not the route for a pure point of law.
n.2: Asking the same magistrates to reconsider is not an appeal route on a point of law.
n.3: Appeals do not go directly from the magistrates' court to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant brings a substantial contract claim in the High Court. After trial, judgment is given against the claimant, who believes the judge made an error of law and wishes to challenge the decision. The claim was heard at first instance in the High Court. The claimant's solicitor considers to which court a first appeal against the High Court's decision would ordinarily lie. The claim was worth several hundred thousand pounds and was tried by a High Court judge in the King's Bench Division, and the claimant, having lost, is now taking advice on where and how a challenge to the judgment on a point of law would have to be brought and whether permission would be needed. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate appeal court?
o: The County Court, as the court with general civil jurisdiction.
The Crown Court, exercising its civil appellate jurisdiction.
The Court of Appeal (Civil Division).
A different judge of the High Court sitting alone.
The Supreme Court, as the next court above the High Court.
England & Wales Legal System.w: An appeal from a decision of the High Court at first instance ordinarily lies to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division), usually with permission. The Supreme Court hears appeals from the Court of Appeal (and occasionally by the leapfrog procedure), not routine first appeals from the High Court.

n.0: The County Court is a lower civil court and does not hear appeals from the High Court.
n.1: The Crown Court has no civil appellate jurisdiction over the High Court.
n.3: An appeal is not reheard by another High Court judge at the same level.
n.4: The Supreme Court is not the ordinary first appeal court from the High Court.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A vacancy arises for a judicial appointment, and a candidate asks how judges are selected, having heard that appointments are made on merit through an independent process rather than by political patronage. The appointment is to a judicial office. The candidate asks about the selection process. A vacancy has arisen on the bench and a would-be applicant, keen to dispel the notion that judgeships are handed out as political favours, wants to understand the modern route by which candidates are chosen on merit through an independent, open competition rather than by patronage. Which of the following best describes how judicial appointments are generally made?
o: Judges are elected by public vote at general elections.
Candidates are selected on merit through the independent Judicial Appointments Commission process.
Judges are appointed by the monarch acting entirely on personal choice.
Judges are appointed directly by the Prime Minister on political grounds on these facts.
Judges are chosen by existing judges from among their own families.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Judicial appointments are made on merit through a process run by the independent Judicial Appointments Commission (established by the Constitutional Reform Act 2005), which selects candidates through fair and open competition. This independence from political patronage supports judicial independence and public confidence in the judiciary.

n.0: Judges are not elected by public vote.
n.2: The monarch formally appoints, but on the basis of the independent selection process, not personal choice.
n.3: Judges are not appointed by the Prime Minister on political grounds.
n.4: Judicial office is obtained on merit through open competition, not by family connection.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is charged with a minor road traffic offence which, by statute, can only be dealt with in one particular court. The defendant's solicitor explains that this type of offence is not one that can ever be sent to the Crown Court for trial by jury. The offence is of the least serious classification. The charge is a low-level motoring matter that carries only limited penalties, the client is anxious about the prospect of a jury trial, and the solicitor is explaining that for an offence of this least-serious category there is in fact only one venue in which the matter can be heard. Which of the following best describes where a summary offence is tried?
o: In the County Court sitting in its criminal jurisdiction.
In the High Court at first instance.
In the Crown Court only.
In either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court at the defendant's election.
In the magistrates' court only.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Summary offences, the least serious category of criminal offence, are tried only in the magistrates' court. There is no right to trial by jury for a summary offence, and it cannot be sent to the Crown Court for trial (though sentence may occasionally be committed there in limited circumstances).

n.0: The County Court is a civil court with no criminal trial jurisdiction.
n.1: The High Court does not try criminal offences at first instance.
n.2: Summary offences are not tried in the Crown Court.
n.3: A defendant cannot elect Crown Court trial for a summary offence.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A public authority interferes with an individual's right to respect for private and family life, a Convention right of a kind that is not absolute but may be limited in defined circumstances. The authority argues the interference is justified. The individual challenges it under the Human Rights Act. The right in question is a qualified right. The interference affects the individual's private life rather than any right the Convention treats as incapable of limitation, the authority insists it acted for good reason and within the law, and the court must apply the recognised conditions that alone can justify limiting a right of this qualified kind. Which of the following best describes when interference with such a qualified right may be justified?
o: Where it is in accordance with the law, pursues a legitimate aim, and is necessary and proportionate.
Only where the individual has consented in writing to the interference.
Where the public authority simply considers the interference desirable on these facts as a general rule.
Whenever primary legislation is silent on the point.
In no circumstances, because all Convention rights are absolute.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Qualified Convention rights, such as the right to respect for private and family life, may be interfered with only where the interference is in accordance with (or prescribed by) law, pursues a legitimate aim recognised by the Convention, and is necessary in a democratic society, meaning it is proportionate to that aim. Absolute rights, by contrast, cannot be interfered with.

n.1: The individual's written consent is not the test for justifying interference.
n.2: Mere desirability in the authority's view does not justify interference; the test is stricter.
n.3: Silence in primary legislation does not itself justify interference with a qualified right.
n.4: Not all Convention rights are absolute; qualified rights can be limited on defined conditions.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A claimant succeeds in judicial review proceedings, persuading the court that a public authority's decision was unlawful. The claimant wants the unlawful decision to be deprived of legal effect so that the matter can be reconsidered lawfully. The court is considering the appropriate remedy. The court has accepted that the authority acted unlawfully, the claimant does not want damages but wants the tainted decision stripped of legal effect so the authority can look at the matter again and decide it properly, and the court turns to which remedy achieves that. Which of the following best describes the principal remedy that sets aside an unlawful decision in judicial review?
o: A declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act.
An order for specific performance of the decision.
A quashing order, which the court grants at its discretion.
An award of exemplary damages as of right.
A binding direction that the authority reach a particular outcome.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A quashing order sets aside an unlawful decision, so that it has no legal effect and the matter can, if appropriate, be reconsidered lawfully. Judicial review remedies (quashing, prohibiting and mandatory orders, declarations, injunctions) are discretionary; the court is not bound to grant a remedy even where a ground is established.

n.0: A declaration of incompatibility relates to primary legislation under the HRA, not quashing an administrative decision.
n.1: Specific performance is a private-law contractual remedy, not a judicial review remedy.
n.3: Damages are not available as of right in judicial review and require a recognised private-law cause of action.
n.4: The court generally requires reconsideration lawfully rather than dictating the substantive outcome.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A minister makes a statutory instrument that purports to do something falling outside the scope of the powers granted by the parent Act of Parliament.
