A person adversely affected wishes to challenge the instrument in the courts, arguing it should have no legal effect. The instrument exceeds the enabling power. The parent Act granted the minister a defined power, the instrument reaches beyond what that power permits, and a person disadvantaged by it wants to know whether a court, faced with subordinate legislation that strays outside its statutory foundation, can do anything about its validity. Which of the following best describes the courts' power in relation to such delegated legislation?
o: The courts may hold the delegated legislation ultra vires and of no effect.
The courts may quash the parent Act of Parliament as well.
The courts must refer the instrument back to Parliament for a vote.
The courts have no power to review delegated legislation once it is made.
The courts may only comment on the instrument but not affect its validity.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Unlike an Act of Parliament, delegated legislation can be challenged in the courts. Where a statutory instrument goes beyond the powers conferred by the enabling Act, the courts may declare it ultra vires and therefore invalid and of no legal effect. This is an important control on the exercise of delegated law-making power.

n.1: The courts cannot strike down the parent Act of Parliament itself.
n.2: The court determines validity; it does not simply refer the instrument back for a vote.
n.3: The courts do have power to review delegated legislation for vires.
n.4: The court can affect validity by holding the instrument ultra vires, not merely comment.

England & Wales Legal System.q: The High Court concludes that a provision in an Act of Parliament simply cannot be read compatibly with a Convention right, even applying the strong interpretive obligation available to it. The claimant asks the court to grant a formal remedy recognising the incompatibility. The court is satisfied the provision is incompatible. The court has already tried and failed to find any Convention-compatible reading of the words, however generously it approaches the task, and the claimant now presses for the formal step that acknowledges the clash between the statute and the Convention while leaving it to Parliament to respond. Which of the following best describes the remedy the High Court may grant, and its effect?
o: A declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the provision.
An injunction preventing any public authority from ever applying the Act.
An order quashing the offending Act of Parliament with immediate effect.
A declaration of incompatibility, which automatically strikes down the provision on these facts as a general rule.
An order suspending the Act until Parliament repeals it.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Under section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a court (the High Court and above) is satisfied that a provision of primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right and cannot be read compatibly, it may make a declaration of incompatibility. This does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the provision; it is for Parliament to decide whether to change the law.

n.1: The court does not injunct all public authorities from applying primary legislation.
n.2: Courts cannot quash an Act of Parliament for incompatibility.
n.3: A declaration of incompatibility does not strike the provision down; it leaves it operative.
n.4: A declaration does not suspend the Act; the provision remains in force.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court is interpreting domestic legislation and adopts an approach that seeks to give effect to the underlying purpose and objectives of the legislation as a whole, rather than being confined strictly to the ordinary meaning of individual words. This broad, purpose-driven method is increasingly favoured in modern statutory interpretation. The court looks to the aim behind the legislation. Rather than dwelling on the precise meaning of isolated words, the court stands back and asks what the legislation as a whole was trying to achieve, treating that overall objective as the key to resolving the interpretive question before it. Which of the following best describes this approach?
o: The literal rule applied strictly to individual words.
The purposive approach to statutory interpretation.
The rule against double jeopardy in criminal proceedings.
The rule that penal statutes are construed narrowly.
The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The purposive approach interprets legislation so as to give effect to the purpose or object underlying it, looking at the statute as a whole and its aims rather than being restricted to the literal meaning of isolated words. It is the approach most commonly associated with modern interpretation.

n.0: The literal rule is the opposite: it confines the court to the ordinary meaning of the words.
n.2: Double jeopardy is a criminal-law principle, not a method of statutory interpretation.
n.3: Narrow construction of penal statutes is a specific presumption, not this general purposive method.
n.4: Parliamentary sovereignty concerns Parliament's law-making supremacy, not an interpretive approach.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court is interpreting a statute that could, on one reading, operate to impose criminal liability without any fault, or to apply to events before it came into force. The court applies established presumptions of statutory interpretation unless the statute clearly displaces them. The statute is silent or ambiguous on these points. The court applies interpretive presumptions. The wording could be read either to punish a person who had no idea they were doing anything wrong, or to reach back and catch things done before the Act existed, and the court, finding the statute unclear on both points, turns to the settled presumptions that fill such gaps unless Parliament has plainly displaced them. Which of the following best describes how such presumptions operate?
o: The court ignores all presumptions and applies only the literal words.
The court presumes that statutes always bind the Crown automatically.
The court presumes that all statutes operate retrospectively unless stated otherwise on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court presumes that criminal offences never require any mental element.
The court presumes, unless clear words show otherwise, against retrospective effect and in favour of requiring mens rea for criminal offences.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Courts apply certain presumptions when construing statutes, rebuttable by clear words: for example, a presumption against retrospective operation, a presumption that mens rea is required for criminal offences, a presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts, and a presumption that statute does not bind the Crown. These guide interpretation where the statute is unclear.

n.0: The court does apply presumptions; it does not ignore them entirely.
n.1: The presumption is that statute does not bind the Crown, not that it always does.
n.2: The presumption is against, not in favour of, retrospective operation.
n.3: The presumption is that criminal offences do require mens rea, not that they never do.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A campaigning individual with no direct personal stake in a decision wishes to bring judicial review proceedings against a public authority. Before the claim can proceed, the court must be satisfied that the claimant is a proper person to bring it. The court considers the requirement of standing. The claimant has campaigned on the issue for years and feels strongly about it but has no personal financial or proprietary stake in the particular decision, so the court must decide, as a threshold matter, whether this is a person the law regards as entitled to bring the challenge at all. Which of the following best describes the test for standing in judicial review?
o: The claimant must have a sufficient interest in the matter to which the claim relates.
The claimant must have suffered direct personal financial loss from the decision.
The claimant must obtain the prior consent of the defendant authority.
Any member of the public may bring a claim without any interest requirement.
Only the Attorney General may bring judicial review proceedings.
England & Wales Legal System.w: To bring a claim for judicial review the claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' in the matter to which the claim relates (Senior Courts Act 1981, s.31(3)). This is applied flexibly, and can extend to campaigning bodies or individuals acting in the public interest, but a mere busybody with no real interest would not qualify.

n.1: Direct personal financial loss is not required; a sufficient interest is broader.
n.2: The defendant authority's consent is not needed to bring the claim.
n.3: There is an interest requirement; not literally anyone may claim regardless of interest.
n.4: Judicial review is not confined to the Attorney General.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is charged with an either-way offence. At the allocation hearing the magistrates decide that the case is suitable for summary trial and are willing to keep it. The defendant, however, would prefer to be tried by a jury. The magistrates have accepted jurisdiction. The magistrates have indicated they are prepared to keep the case and deal with it themselves, but the client, distrustful of summary justice for the allegation faced, would rather put the matter before a jury of ordinary citizens, and wants to know whether that choice remains available. Which of the following best describes the defendant's position on the venue for trial?
o: The defendant may choose the High Court instead of either court.
The defendant may only be tried in the Crown Court if the prosecution agrees.
The defendant may elect to be tried in the Crown Court by a jury.
The defendant must be tried in the magistrates' court once they accept jurisdiction.
The defendant has no say; the magistrates' decision on venue is final.
England & Wales Legal System.w: For an either-way offence, even where the magistrates accept jurisdiction and are content to try the case summarily, the defendant retains the right to elect trial on indictment in the Crown Court before a jury. The defendant's election overrides the magistrates' willingness to keep the case.

n.0: The High Court is not an option for trial of the offence.
n.1: The defendant's right to elect Crown Court trial does not depend on the prosecution's agreement.
n.3: The defendant is not compelled to accept summary trial once magistrates accept jurisdiction.
n.4: The defendant does have a say; the election is the defendant's, not the magistrates'.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A person of limited means wishes to obtain public funding for a civil claim. Their adviser explains that civil legal aid is available only for certain types of case and is subject to tests of the applicant's finances and the merits of the case. The claim is a civil matter and the applicant has low income. Public funding is being considered. The prospective claimant has very little money and hopes the state will fund the civil claim, but the adviser cautions that public funding of this kind is now confined to particular categories of case and is hedged about with tests looking at both the applicant's finances and the strength of the claim. Which of the following best describes the availability of civil legal aid?
o: Civil legal aid has been entirely abolished for all civil matters.
Civil legal aid depends solely on the applicant's means, with no merits test.
Civil legal aid is available only for categories of case within scope and subject to means and merits tests.
Civil legal aid is available only to companies, not to individuals.
Civil legal aid is available for every civil claim regardless of means or merits on these facts as a general rule.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Civil legal aid is limited: since LASPO 2012, only certain categories of civil case remain within scope, and funding is subject to a means test (assessing the applicant's income and capital) and a merits test (assessing, for example, the prospects of success and proportionality). Many civil matters are now out of scope.

n.0: Civil legal aid has been reduced in scope, not entirely abolished.
n.1: Both a means test and a merits test apply, not means alone.
n.3: Legal aid is available to eligible individuals, not only companies.
n.4: Civil legal aid is not available for every civil claim; scope, means and merits all limit it.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A government Bill is progressing through Parliament. Having been formally introduced, it has been debated on its general principles, examined in detail line by line, reconsidered, and passed by the House in which it started, and it now moves to the other House to undergo a similar process. A trainee asks what remains before the Bill can become law. All parliamentary stages in both Houses are being completed. The Bill has already been read a first time as a formality, debated on its principles, scrutinised clause by clause in committee, reconsidered at report stage and passed at third reading in its originating House, and it is now repeating that journey in the second House, so the trainee is trying to picture what still stands between it and the statute book. Which of the following best describes the final step required for the Bill to become an Act of Parliament?
o: It must be ratified by a national referendum.
It must be registered with the European Court of Human Rights.
It must be approved by the Supreme Court.
It must be countersigned by the Lord Chancellor.
It must receive Royal Assent.
England & Wales Legal System.w: After a Bill has passed through all its stages in both Houses (first reading, second reading, committee, report and third reading in each), it must receive Royal Assent from the monarch before it becomes an Act of Parliament and part of the law. Royal Assent is the final formal step.

n.0: A referendum is not a general legal requirement for a Bill to become an Act.
n.1: Registration with the European Court of Human Rights plays no part in enacting UK legislation.
n.2: The Supreme Court does not approve legislation; it adjudicates disputes.
n.3: The Lord Chancellor's countersignature is not the step that makes a Bill law.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant is charged with an offence for which a statute expressly places a specific legal burden on the defendant to establish a particular defence. The defendant accepts that this reverse burden applies but disputes the standard to which the defence must be proved. A legal burden, not merely an evidential one, rests on the defendant. The statute creating the offence expressly requires the defendant, rather than the prosecution, to establish the particular matter relied on by way of defence, and while the defendant accepts that this unusual reverse burden bites, the argument now is about how convincingly the defence must be made out. Which of the following best describes the standard the defendant must meet to discharge such a burden?
o: Absolute certainty as to the defence.
The balance of probabilities.
A prima facie evidential threshold only.
So that the tribunal is sure of the defence.
Beyond reasonable doubt, as for the prosecution.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Where a statute places a legal (persuasive) burden on the defendant to prove a defence, the defendant must discharge it only on the balance of probabilities, the civil standard. The defendant is not required to prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt; that higher standard applies to the prosecution's proof of guilt.

n.0: Absolute certainty is not required.
n.2: A legal burden requires proof on the balance of probabilities, not merely raising a prima facie evidential issue.
n.3: Being 'sure' equates to the criminal standard, which the defendant need not meet.
n.4: The defendant need not prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A High Court case turns on a point of law of general public importance that is bound, whatever the Court of Appeal decides, to end up before the Supreme Court. To save time and cost, the parties wish to bypass the Court of Appeal and appeal directly from the High Court to the Supreme Court. The trial judge grants a certificate. Both sides accept that the issue is of general public importance and that a further appeal to the highest court is inevitable whatever the intermediate court might decide, so they are keen to find a way of shortening the litigation and reaching a final ruling sooner. Which of the following best describes the procedure that allows this?
o: The reference procedure, requiring the case to be sent to the Court of Justice.
The leapfrog procedure, allowing a direct appeal to the Supreme Court with permission.
An interlocutory appeal, which must always go to the Court of Appeal first.
The Attorney General's reference on a point of law.
The case stated procedure from the High Court to the Court of Appeal.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The leapfrog procedure permits an appeal to be made directly from the High Court to the Supreme Court, bypassing the Court of Appeal, where the trial judge grants a certificate (typically involving a point of law of general public importance) and the Supreme Court gives permission to appeal.

n.0: A reference to the Court of Justice concerns EU law questions, not a domestic leapfrog appeal.
n.2: The point of the leapfrog is that it does not go to the Court of Appeal first.
n.3: An Attorney General's reference is a distinct criminal procedure, not this appeal route.
n.4: Case stated is a different procedure and does not describe a leapfrog to the Supreme Court.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A journalist wishes to attend and report on court proceedings. A party argues the case should be heard entirely in private and never reported. The court considers the general principle that justice should be administered openly, subject to limited exceptions. The starting point is that hearings are public. The court weighs open justice against any need for privacy. A journalist wants to sit in and report on the hearing, but one of the parties is pressing for the whole case to be conducted behind closed doors and kept out of the press entirely, forcing the court to weigh the long-standing expectation that justice is done in public against any genuine need for privacy. Which of the following best describes the principle of open justice?
o: Open justice means the public may attend but reporting is always prohibited.
Only the parties, and never the public or press, may ever attend any hearing.
All court proceedings must always be held in private with no reporting permitted on these facts as a general rule.
Justice should generally be administered in public and be capable of being reported, subject to limited exceptions.
The principle of open justice has no application to civil proceedings.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Open justice is a fundamental principle: justice should generally be administered in public, hearings should usually be open to the public and press, and proceedings should be capable of being reported. There are limited exceptions (for example, to protect children, national security or genuinely confidential matters), where hearings may be in private or reporting restricted.

n.0: Open justice generally permits reporting, not a blanket prohibition on it.
n.1: The public and press may generally attend, not only the parties.
n.2: Proceedings are not always held in private; the norm is public hearings.
n.4: Open justice applies to civil as well as criminal proceedings.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A party argues that a previous decision of a higher court should not be treated as binding because, in reaching it, the court overlooked a relevant statutory provision that, had it been considered, would have led to a different result. The provision was in force at the time but was not cited to the court. The later court must decide how to treat that earlier decision. The overlooked provision was directly relevant and, on any view, would have pointed the earlier court towards the opposite conclusion, and the party now before the later court argues that this omission is exactly the kind of flaw that frees a court from an otherwise binding authority. Which of the following best describes the relevant exception to precedent?
o: The earlier decision is automatically overruled by the later court's disapproval.
The earlier decision becomes binding only on courts of equal standing.
The earlier decision may be treated as per incuriam and not binding.
The earlier decision is persuasive in criminal but not civil cases.
The earlier decision remains fully binding despite the oversight.
England & Wales Legal System.w: A decision reached per incuriam, that is, in ignorance or forgetfulness of a relevant statutory provision or binding authority which would have affected the result, need not be followed. It is one of the recognised exceptions allowing a court not to be bound by what would otherwise be precedent.

n.0: Disapproval alone does not automatically overrule; per incuriam is the applicable doctrine.
n.1: Per incuriam status is not limited to courts of equal standing.
n.3: The per incuriam exception is not confined to criminal cases.
n.4: An oversight of a relevant provision can render a decision per incuriam, so it is not fully binding.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A judge is faced with an earlier decision of a higher court that a party says is binding. The judge concludes that the material facts of the present case are genuinely and significantly different from those in the earlier case, so that the earlier legal principle does not apply. The judge does not say the earlier case was wrongly decided. On close analysis the earlier case involved a materially different factual setting, such that the reasoning that decided it simply does not reach the situation now before the court, and the judge is careful to make clear that nothing turns on any suggestion that the earlier court got it wrong. Which of the following best describes what the judge is doing when declining to apply the earlier decision on this basis?
o: Distinguishing the earlier decision on its facts.
Reversing the earlier decision on appeal.
Departing under the 1966 Practice Statement.
Making a per incuriam finding about the earlier decision.
Overruling the earlier decision as wrongly decided.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Distinguishing is the process by which a court avoids being bound by an otherwise applicable precedent by identifying material differences in the facts, so that the ratio of the earlier case does not apply to the case before it. The earlier decision is not criticised as wrong; it is simply held not to govern the present facts.

n.1: Reversing changes the outcome of the same case on appeal, not a different case.
n.2: The Practice Statement concerns the Supreme Court departing from its own decisions, not distinguishing on facts.
n.3: A per incuriam finding is about an earlier decision made in ignorance of relevant law.
n.4: Overruling declares the earlier decision wrong, which is not what is happening here.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A court is interpreting a statute where applying the words in their ordinary literal sense would produce a manifestly absurd result that Parliament plainly cannot have intended. The court wishes to adopt an interpretation that avoids the absurdity while remaining faithful to the statutory language so far as possible. The literal meaning is clear but the outcome would be absurd. Read in their ordinary sense the words would require an outcome so strange that Parliament can hardly have intended it, and the court is anxious to reach a sensible result without straying any further from the statutory language than the absurdity makes necessary. Which of the following best describes the interpretive approach the court is applying?
o: The literal rule, applying the ordinary meaning regardless of absurdity.
The presumption against retrospective effect of legislation.
The expressio unius principle, excluding what is not expressly mentioned.
The mischief rule, examining the common law before the statute was passed.
The golden rule, modifying the literal meaning to avoid an absurd result.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The golden rule allows the court to depart from the ordinary literal meaning of statutory words to the extent necessary to avoid a result that is absurd or repugnant, while otherwise adhering to the language. It is applied where the literal rule would produce such an absurdity.

n.0: The literal rule would apply the ordinary meaning despite the absurdity, which is what the court is avoiding.
n.1: The presumption against retrospectivity is a separate interpretive presumption.
n.2: Expressio unius is a distinct maxim about implied exclusion, not about absurd results.
n.3: The mischief rule focuses on the defect the statute addresses, not on avoiding absurdity in clear words.

England & Wales Legal System.q: A defendant in a criminal trial declines to give evidence and argues that it is not for the defendant to prove innocence. The court must direct itself on who bears the burden of proving the elements of the offence. No statutory reverse burden applies to the offence charged. The defendant has chosen to say nothing in evidence and rests on the contention that the case against them has not been made out, so the court must be clear about which side carries the obligation to prove the elements of the offence and how the presumption of innocence operates here. Which of the following best describes where the legal burden of proof generally lies in a criminal trial?
o: The court itself bears the burden of establishing the facts.
The defendant bears the burden of proving innocence.
The burden lies on whichever party called the first witness.
The prosecution bears the burden of proving the defendant's guilt.
The burden is shared equally between prosecution and defence.
England & Wales Legal System.w: Reflecting the presumption of innocence, the legal burden of proving the elements of a criminal offence generally rests on the prosecution, which must make the tribunal sure of guilt. The defendant is not required to prove innocence, save where a statute expressly places a specific burden on the defence.

n.0: The court does not bear a burden of proof; it adjudicates.
n.1: The defendant does not generally have to prove innocence.
n.2: The burden does not depend on who called the first witness.
n.4: The burden is not shared equally; it rests on the prosecution.

England & Wales Legal System.q: In a civil claim for breach of contract, the judge must decide whether the claimant has proved the disputed facts on which the claim depends. Counsel asks the judge to direct themselves as to the standard the claimant must meet before the facts can be found in the claimant's favour. This is a civil, not a criminal, matter. The parties give directly conflicting accounts of what was agreed and whether the goods conformed, there is no independent documentary tie-breaker, and the judge must be clear about how convinced the court needs to be before treating the claimant's version of the disputed facts as established. Which of the following best describes the standard of proof the claimant must satisfy?
o: Absolute certainty on the evidence.
The balance of probabilities.
Clear and convincing evidence to a near certainty.
Beyond reasonable doubt.
A prima facie case only.
England & Wales Legal System.w: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the balance of probabilities: the party bearing the burden must show that the fact in issue is more likely than not to be true. This is a lower standard than the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

n.0: Absolute certainty is not required in civil (or indeed criminal) proceedings.
n.2: English civil law does not use a distinct 'clear and convincing' near-certainty standard.
n.3: Beyond reasonable doubt is the criminal standard, not the civil standard.
n.4: Establishing a prima facie case is not the ultimate standard for proving the claim.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A student is surprised to learn that the United Kingdom does not have a single document setting out its constitution, and asks a solicitor to explain where the rules of the UK constitution are actually found. The rules come from a variety of sources rather than one codified text. The solicitor considers the sources and nature of the UK constitution. The student had expected a single document like the constitutions of many other countries. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The UK has no constitution of any kind, written or unwritten.
The UK constitution consists solely of Acts of the European Union.
The UK constitution is contained entirely in a single codified written document on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The UK constitution is made up only of decisions of the monarch.
The UK has an uncodified constitution drawn from statutes, case law, conventions and other sources, rather than a single written document.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The UK constitution is uncodified: rather than a single written document, it is found in a range of sources including Acts of Parliament, case law (common law), constitutional conventions, the royal prerogative, and works of authority. It is often described as 'unwritten' in the sense of not being codified.

n.0: The UK does have a constitution, albeit uncodified.
n.1: The constitution is not made up solely of EU law.
n.2: The UK constitution is not contained in a single codified document.
n.3: The constitution is not simply the monarch's decisions.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A concern is raised that the executive might pressure judges by threatening their removal or pay if they decide cases against the government. A commentator points to constitutional protections designed to keep the judiciary independent of the other branches. The issue is the constitutional protection of judicial independence. The separation of powers is engaged. Concern is voiced that a government displeased with judgments going against it might try to lean on judges by threatening their positions or their pay, and a commentator points to the constitutional arrangements specifically designed to insulate the judiciary from that kind of executive pressure. Which of the following best describes a key protection of judicial independence?
o: Judges serve entirely at the pleasure of the government of the day.
The executive may reduce judges' salaries whenever it disapproves of their decisions on these facts as a general rule.
Senior judges have security of tenure and protected salaries, and can be removed only through strict constitutional processes.
Judicial independence has no legal or constitutional protection in the UK.
Ministers may dismiss any judge who rules against the government.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Judicial independence is protected constitutionally: senior judges hold office during good behaviour with security of tenure (removable only on an address by both Houses of Parliament), their salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund and protected from executive reduction, and the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 places a duty on ministers to uphold judicial independence.

n.0: Judges do not serve at the government's pleasure; they have security of tenure.
n.1: The executive cannot reduce judges' salaries in response to their decisions.
n.3: Judicial independence is protected by law and convention, not unprotected.
n.4: Ministers cannot dismiss judges for ruling against the government.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The UK Parliament proposes to legislate on a matter that is within the devolved competence of a devolved legislature, such as the Scottish Parliament. A question arises about the constitutional expectation that applies where Westminster legislates on devolved matters. A solicitor is asked about the convention governing this situation. The solicitor considers the Sewel convention. The proposed law would operate in an area normally handled by the devolved legislature. Which of the following best describes it?
o: By the Sewel convention Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent, but legally retains the power.
The devolved legislature can veto any UK legislation on any subject whatsoever.
The UK Parliament requires the monarch's personal consent before legislating on devolved matters.
The UK Parliament is legally prohibited from ever legislating on any devolved matter.
The Sewel convention is a legally enforceable rule that the courts will uphold with an injunction on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: By the Sewel convention, the UK Parliament will not normally legislate with regard to devolved matters without the consent of the relevant devolved legislature. However, this is a constitutional convention: the UK Parliament retains legal sovereignty to legislate, and the convention is not enforceable by the courts.

n.1: The devolved legislature cannot legally veto UK legislation.
n.2: The monarch's personal consent is not the requirement.
n.3: The UK Parliament is not legally prohibited from legislating on devolved matters.
n.4: The Sewel convention is not legally enforceable by the courts.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A decision affecting an individual is taken by a decision-maker who had a personal connection to the outcome such that a fair-minded and informed observer might conclude there was a real possibility of bias, even though there is no proof of actual bias. The individual challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked about the test for disqualifying bias in public decision-making. The solicitor considers the rule against bias. The decision-maker had a personal stake in the outcome that troubled the losing party. Which of the following best describes the test?
o: The rule against bias applies only to judges and never to administrative decision-makers.
A decision can be challenged for bias only where actual bias is positively proved.
Any connection at all between the decision-maker and the parties automatically invalidates the decision on these facts as a general rule.
Bias is legally irrelevant to the validity of a public body's decision.
A decision may be quashed for apparent bias where a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The rule against bias includes apparent bias: a decision may be set aside where a fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the decision-maker was biased (Porter v Magill). Actual bias need not be proved, and there is automatic disqualification for a direct interest in the outcome.

n.0: The rule against bias applies to administrative decision-makers too.
n.1: Actual bias need not be proved; apparent bias suffices.
n.2: Not every connection disqualifies; the fair-minded observer test applies.
n.3: Bias is highly relevant to the validity of a decision.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A member of the public asks a solicitor about the composition of the UK Parliament and how the members of the principal, elected chamber come to hold their seats. They understand that this chamber is central to the democratic legitimacy of law-making. The solicitor considers the composition of the House of Commons and general elections. They were curious about how the people in the main chamber actually came to sit there. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The House of Commons is composed of judges chosen by the government.
The House of Commons is composed of Members of Parliament elected from constituencies at general elections.
The House of Commons is composed entirely of hereditary peers.
The House of Commons is composed of members appointed for life by the monarch.
The House of Commons is composed of members selected at random from the electorate on these facts.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The House of Commons is the elected chamber of Parliament, made up of Members of Parliament each returned for a constituency at a general election under the first-past-the-post system. Its elected character underpins the democratic legitimacy of the legislature.

n.0: The Commons is not composed of government-chosen judges.
n.2: Hereditary peers sit (in limited numbers) in the Lords, not the Commons.
n.3: MPs are elected, not appointed for life by the monarch.
n.4: MPs are elected, not selected at random.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant wishes to bring judicial review proceedings against a body, but a question arises about whether that body's decision is capable of being judicially reviewed at all, given the nature of the body and the function it was performing. The body performs a public function under statutory powers. A solicitor is asked when a body's decision is amenable to judicial review. The solicitor considers amenability to judicial review. The body was not a government department but was carrying out functions of a plainly public character. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A decision is amenable to judicial review where the body is exercising a public function, whether or not it is a governmental body.
Only decisions of central government departments can ever be judicially reviewed.
Any decision by any person or body at all can be judicially reviewed, including purely private ones on these facts as a general rule.
Amenability depends solely on whether the body describes itself as a public authority.
A decision can be judicially reviewed only where the claimant has a contract with the body.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Judicial review is available in respect of the exercise of public functions. What matters is the nature of the function rather than merely the identity of the body, so even a non-governmental body may be amenable to judicial review when exercising a public function; purely private or contractual functions are generally not.

n.1: Amenability is not confined to central government departments.
n.2: Purely private functions are generally not amenable to judicial review.
n.3: It is the nature of the function, not the body's self-description, that governs.
n.4: A contract with the body is not the test; the public nature of the function is.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A body that is not a core organ of government, but which exercises certain functions of a public nature (alongside private activities), acts in a way said to be incompatible with a Convention right when performing one of those public functions. A claimant wishes to rely on the Human Rights Act 1998. The body is a hybrid body performing some public functions. The act complained of relates to a public function. The body sits somewhere between the public and private spheres, running some genuinely public functions alongside its ordinary commercial activities, and the act complained of arose in the course of one of those public functions, so the claimant must show the body counts as a public authority for that purpose. Which of the following best describes when such a body is bound by the Human Rights Act?
o: It is bound by the Act in respect of all its activities, public and private alike.
It can never be bound by the Human Rights Act because it is not a core public authority on these facts as a general rule.
It is a public authority in respect of its functions of a public nature, and is bound when performing those functions.
It is bound only where it consents to be treated as a public authority.
It is bound only if it is wholly owned by central government.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998, 'public authority' includes any person certain of whose functions are functions of a public nature (a 'hybrid' or functional public authority). Such a body is bound by the Act when exercising its public functions, but not in relation to acts of a private nature.

n.0: It is bound only for its public functions, not its private acts.
n.1: A hybrid body can be bound in respect of its public functions, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Its status does not depend on its consent; it turns on the nature of its functions.
n.4: Being bound does not depend on being wholly owned by central government.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A statute is drafted in general words which, read literally, could be taken to authorise an interference with a fundamental common-law right, such as access to the courts, without expressly saying so. A court is asked to interpret the statute. A solicitor is asked about the interpretive presumption the courts apply where fundamental rights are at stake. The solicitor considers the principle of legality in statutory interpretation. The words were wide enough, on their face, to strip the person of access to the courts. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Under the principle of legality, fundamental rights are presumed not to be overridden by general words; clear express language is required.
The principle of legality means the courts must ignore fundamental rights when reading statutes on these facts as a general rule.
The courts will interpret any ambiguous statute so as to remove as many rights as possible.
General words in a statute are always read as overriding any fundamental right.
Fundamental rights can be overridden only by a decision of a government minister.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under the principle of legality, the courts presume that Parliament does not intend to interfere with fundamental common-law rights (such as access to justice) by general or ambiguous words. Such rights can be overridden only by clear and express statutory language, so the courts read general words restrictively to protect those rights (R v Home Secretary, ex p Simms).

n.1: The principle of legality protects, rather than ignores, fundamental rights.
n.2: The courts protect rights on interpretation; they do not maximise their removal.
n.3: General words are not read as overriding fundamental rights; express words are needed.
n.4: Fundamental rights are overridden by clear statute, not a minister's decision.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body with a discretionary power adopts a rigid policy under which it will always decide cases in a particular way, and refuses even to consider whether an individual case might justify a different outcome, effectively shutting its mind to the exercise of discretion. A claimant challenges this. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged. The solicitor considers the fettering of discretion as a ground of review. The body announced it would refuse every application of this kind without exception. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A body may fetter its discretion provided it acts in good faith throughout.
A body unlawfully fetters its discretion if it applies a rigid policy without being willing to consider exceptions.
A body is never permitted to have any policy at all when exercising a discretion.
A body may always apply a fixed policy and refuse to consider any individual circumstances on these facts.
The way a body exercises a discretion can never be judicially reviewed.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A body with a discretion may adopt a policy to guide the exercise of that discretion, but it must not fetter its discretion by applying the policy so rigidly that it refuses to consider whether an individual case justifies departing from it. Doing so is a form of illegality.

n.0: Acting in good faith does not cure an unlawful fetter on discretion.
n.2: A body may have a policy, so long as it does not apply it rigidly; the issue is fettering.
n.3: A body cannot apply a fixed policy while refusing to consider individual circumstances.
n.4: The exercise of discretion is reviewable.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A court finds that a provision in an Act of Parliament is incompatible with a Convention right, and it is not possible to read the provision compatibly under the interpretive obligation. The court cannot invalidate the Act. A solicitor is asked what the higher courts can do where primary legislation is found incompatible with a Convention right. The solicitor considers section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998. No compatible reading of the statute was possible, however hard the court tried. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must simply ignore the Act and decide the case as if it did not exist.
A higher court may make a declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the validity of the Act but signals the incompatibility to Parliament.
The court may strike down and invalidate the incompatible Act of Parliament.
The court may amend the Act itself to remove the incompatibility.
The court can do nothing at all where primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a higher court is satisfied that a provision of primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right and cannot be read compatibly, it may make a declaration of incompatibility. This does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the Act, but signals to Parliament that it may wish to amend the law.

n.0: The court does not ignore the Act; it applies it but may declare incompatibility.
n.2: The court cannot strike down or invalidate the Act.
n.3: The court does not itself amend the Act; that is for Parliament.
n.4: The court can make a declaration of incompatibility, so it is not powerless.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant wishes to challenge a public law decision affecting their public law rights. Rather than using the judicial review procedure with its safeguards (such as the permission stage and time limits), the claimant tries to raise the public law issue by ordinary civil claim to avoid those safeguards. The claim is essentially a public law challenge to a public body's decision. The claimant seeks to avoid the judicial review procedure. Rather than face the permission stage and the tight time limit that judicial review carries, the claimant has dressed up what is really a public law attack on a public body's decision as an ordinary civil claim, and the defendant objects that this is an attempt to sidestep the safeguards of the proper procedure. Which of the following best describes the principle of procedural exclusivity?
o: Judicial review safeguards apply only where the claimant chooses to use them.
Ordinary civil procedure is the required route for all challenges to public bodies on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Public law challenges can never be raised except by petitioning Parliament.
Public law challenges should generally be brought by judicial review, and evading its safeguards by ordinary procedure may be an abuse.
Public law issues may always be raised freely in any form of ordinary civil claim.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under the principle of procedural exclusivity (O'Reilly v Mackman), a claimant seeking to vindicate public law rights should generally proceed by judicial review, and it may be an abuse of process to use ordinary civil procedure to evade the protections of judicial review (such as the permission requirement and short time limit), though the rule is applied flexibly, especially where public law arises collaterally.

n.0: The safeguards are not optional at the claimant's choice; the proper route is judicial review.
n.1: Judicial review, not ordinary civil procedure, is the general route for public law challenges.
n.2: Public law challenges are brought by judicial review, not by petitioning Parliament.
n.4: Public law issues cannot always be raised freely in ordinary claims; procedural exclusivity constrains this.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A general election is held to elect members to the House of Commons. The country is divided into constituencies, and in each the candidate with the most votes is elected, whether or not they have an overall majority of votes cast. The system elects one member per constituency on a plurality basis. The question concerns the voting system for the Commons. Polling day has arrived for a Commons election, the country is carved into individual constituencies each returning a single member, and in each seat whoever polls the most votes wins it, regardless of whether that tally amounts to more than half of all the votes cast there. Which of the following best describes the electoral system used?
o: A system in which members are chosen by lot from the electorate.
The first-past-the-post system, under which the candidate with the most votes in each constituency is elected.
A system in which the monarch appoints all members of the House of Commons.
A single national ballot electing all members from one countrywide list.
A system of proportional representation allocating seats in proportion to national vote share on these facts.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Members of the House of Commons are elected using the first-past-the-post (simple plurality) system: the UK is divided into constituencies, each returning one member, and the candidate who receives the most votes in a constituency is elected, even without an overall majority of the votes cast.

n.0: Members are elected by voters, not chosen by lot.
n.2: The monarch does not appoint members of the elected House of Commons.
n.3: There is no single countrywide list; members are elected constituency by constituency.
n.4: The Commons is not elected by national proportional representation.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body has a statutory power granted for one particular purpose, but exercises the power in order to achieve a different objective that Parliament did not intend the power to be used for. A claimant challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked which aspect of illegality is engaged where a power is used for an unauthorised purpose. The solicitor considers the improper purpose ground of judicial review. The power had been granted for one aim but was used to pursue a quite different objective. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The purpose for which a statutory power is used is legally irrelevant.
The decision may be unlawful because the power was used for an improper purpose, not the purpose for which it was conferred.
The decision is lawful because a public body may use its powers for any purpose it chooses on these facts as a general rule.
Using a power for a different purpose is permissible provided the outcome is beneficial.
The decision can be challenged only if the body acted in bad faith or dishonestly.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A statutory power must be exercised only for the purpose for which it was conferred. Using a power for an ulterior or improper purpose (even without dishonesty) is a form of illegality that may render the decision unlawful and liable to be quashed.

n.0: The purpose of the power is highly relevant.
n.2: A power may not be used for any purpose; it must serve its statutory purpose.
n.3: A beneficial outcome does not legitimise use for an improper purpose.
n.4: Improper purpose does not require bad faith or dishonesty.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A person facing a decision by a public tribunal that could deprive them of an important interest complains that they were given no proper opportunity to present their case and that the tribunal was not impartial. They wish to rely on a Convention right guaranteeing a fair hearing. The complaint concerns the fairness and impartiality of the determination of the person's civil rights. A Convention right is engaged. The individual stands to lose something important through a tribunal's determination of their civil rights, yet complains they were shut out of properly putting their case and that those deciding were not impartial, which brings into play the Convention guarantee concerned with the fairness of such hearings. Which of the following best identifies the relevant Convention right?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial (a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal).
Article 10, the right to freedom of expression.
Article 1 of the First Protocol, the protection of property.
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life.
Article 3, the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment on these facts as a general rule.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees the right to a fair trial: in the determination of civil rights and obligations or a criminal charge, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The complaint about a fair hearing and impartiality engages Article 6.

n.1: Article 10 concerns freedom of expression.
n.2: Article 1 of the First Protocol concerns peaceful enjoyment of possessions.
n.3: Article 8 concerns private and family life, not the fairness of a hearing.
n.4: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not fair hearings.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: An Act of Parliament contains a provision empowering a minister, by secondary legislation, to amend or repeal provisions of primary legislation, including the Act itself. A commentator is concerned about the breadth of such a power. A solicitor is asked to explain what such a provision is and its constitutional significance. The solicitor considers so-called Henry VIII powers. The provision let a minister rewrite primary legislation by order, which troubled the commentator. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A Henry VIII power is a provision that abolishes the monarchy.
A Henry VIII power allows the courts to strike down Acts of Parliament.
A Henry VIII power lets secondary legislation amend or repeal primary legislation, and is construed strictly.
A Henry VIII power is a type of prerogative power exercised personally by the monarch on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A Henry VIII power is a rule that prevents any amendment of legislation whatsoever.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A 'Henry VIII power' is a provision in an Act that authorises the amendment or repeal of primary legislation by means of secondary (delegated) legislation. Such powers are constitutionally significant because they allow the executive to change primary law, and the courts construe them strictly.

n.0: A Henry VIII power does not abolish the monarchy.
n.1: It does not give the courts power to strike down Acts.
n.3: It is a statutory delegated power, not a personal prerogative of the monarch.
n.4: It permits, rather than prevents, amendment of legislation.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant, unhappy with an Act of Parliament, brings a claim asking the court to declare the Act invalid because, they argue, Parliament followed a flawed process and the statute is unjust. The government argues the court cannot entertain such a challenge to primary legislation. A solicitor is asked whether the courts can question the validity of an Act of Parliament. The solicitor considers the courts' role in relation to primary legislation. The claimant was determined to have the offending statute declared void by the court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The courts cannot question the validity of an Act of Parliament, though they interpret it and may declare it incompatible with Convention rights.
The courts may rewrite an Act of Parliament to achieve a fairer result.
The courts may refuse to apply an Act of Parliament that a majority of judges dislike on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The courts may strike down an Act of Parliament for procedural defects in its passage.
The courts may declare an Act of Parliament void whenever they consider it unjust.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: As a consequence of parliamentary sovereignty and the 'enrolled bill' rule, the courts cannot question the validity of a duly enacted Act of Parliament or inquire into the process of its enactment. They interpret and apply it, and under the Human Rights Act 1998 may make a declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the Act's validity.

n.1: The courts interpret, but do not rewrite, statutes.
n.2: Judicial dislike is not a basis for refusing to apply an Act.
n.3: The courts do not examine the internal process of enactment (the enrolled bill rule).
n.4: The courts cannot void an Act for being unjust.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A court is interpreting a statutory provision that, on its ordinary meaning, would appear to conflict with a Convention right. The court is considering whether it can read the provision in a way that is compatible with the Convention right. A solicitor is asked about the interpretive obligation on the courts under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The ordinary reading of the provision would have produced a clear breach of a Convention right. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Section 3 applies only to secondary legislation and never to Acts of Parliament.
So far as it is possible to do so, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights.
The court must strike down any statute that is incompatible with a Convention right.
The court must always apply the literal meaning of a statute even if it breaches Convention rights on these facts.
The court may rewrite any statute freely to achieve any result it considers desirable.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.3 of the Human Rights Act 1998, so far as it is possible to do so, primary and subordinate legislation must be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Convention rights. This is a strong interpretive obligation, though it cannot be used to go against a fundamental feature of the legislation.

n.0: Section 3 applies to both primary and subordinate legislation.
n.2: The courts cannot strike down primary legislation; s.3 (and s.4) reflect this.
n.3: Section 3 requires a compatible reading where possible, not always the literal meaning.
n.4: Section 3 permits a strained reading where possible, but not unlimited rewriting.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body is under a clear public law duty to make a decision on an application, but has simply refused or failed to make any decision at all, leaving the applicant in limbo. The applicant seeks a remedy in judicial review that would compel the body to perform its duty. The body has unlawfully failed to perform a public law duty. The applicant wants it compelled to act. The public body was plainly obliged to determine the application but has simply sat on its hands, making no decision at all and leaving the applicant stranded, and the applicant now wants an order from the court that will actually force the body to get on and perform its duty. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate remedy?
o: An award of damages as the primary remedy for the failure to decide.
A declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act.
A quashing order setting aside the decision that has not been made.
A mandatory order requiring the public body to perform its public law duty.
A prohibiting order preventing the body from acting.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A mandatory order (formerly mandamus) compels a public body to perform a public law duty it has unlawfully failed to perform, such as making a decision it is obliged to make. A quashing order sets aside an unlawful decision, and a prohibiting order restrains unlawful action, so neither fits a failure to act; a mandatory order does.

n.0: Damages are not generally available in judicial review merely for a failure to decide, and are not the primary remedy.
n.1: A declaration of incompatibility concerns primary legislation under the HRA, not compelling a decision.
n.2: A quashing order sets aside a decision made; here no decision has been made to quash.
n.4: A prohibiting order restrains action; the problem here is inaction.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The government advises the monarch to prorogue Parliament for an unusually long period at a critical time, with the effect of preventing Parliament from carrying out its constitutional functions of legislating and holding the government to account. The exercise of the prerogative power has a serious frustrating effect on Parliament. A claimant challenges the prorogation. Ministers advised a lengthy suspension of Parliament at a moment of acute national importance, with the practical effect of shutting Parliament out of legislating and scrutinising the executive for weeks, and a claimant now argues the courts can and should examine whether that use of the prerogative was lawful. Which of the following best describes the courts' approach following recent authority?
o: The prerogative to prorogue is entirely beyond the reach of the courts in all circumstances on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Prorogation is always lawful provided the monarch formally approves it.
The courts may review prorogation only if Parliament first passes a resolution.
Prorogation can be challenged only in the European Court of Human Rights.
The exercise of the prerogative to prorogue is justiciable and may be unlawful if it frustrates Parliament without reasonable justification.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Following R (Miller) v The Prime Minister, the exercise of the prerogative power to prorogue Parliament is justiciable: a prorogation will be unlawful if it has the effect of frustrating or preventing, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions. The court may declare an unlawful prorogation to be of no effect.

n.0: The prerogative to prorogue is not wholly beyond the courts; its effects can be reviewed.
n.1: Formal approval does not make a prorogation with an unlawful frustrating effect lawful.
n.2: The courts' jurisdiction does not depend on Parliament first passing a resolution.
n.3: The challenge is a domestic public law matter, not confined to the European Court of Human Rights.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A person is detained by the state, and challenges the detention as arbitrary and without lawful basis or proper procedure. They wish to rely on the Convention right concerned with freedom from unlawful detention. The complaint is about deprivation of physical liberty by the state. A specific Convention right is engaged. The individual has been taken into custody by the state and says the deprivation of their liberty was arbitrary, lacking any lawful basis or proper procedure, and they want to invoke the particular Convention guarantee that protects a person against being unlawfully detained. Which of the following best identifies the relevant Convention right?
o: Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life.
Article 1 of the First Protocol, protection of property.
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of the person.
Article 6, the right to a fair trial.
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Article 5 of the Convention protects the right to liberty and security of the person: no one is to be deprived of their liberty except in defined cases and in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. A challenge to arbitrary or unlawful detention engages Article 5, which also provides related rights such as prompt information and access to a court to test the lawfulness of detention.

n.0: Article 8 concerns private and family life.
n.1: Article 1 of the First Protocol concerns property, not liberty.
n.3: Article 6 concerns fair trial, not deprivation of liberty as such.
n.4: Article 9 concerns freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant succeeds in a judicial review claim, having shown that a public body's decision was unlawful, and wishes to know what the court can actually order as a result — for example to undo the unlawful decision or to compel the body to act. A solicitor is asked about the remedies available in judicial review. The solicitor considers the remedies in a judicial review claim. The claimant wanted the unlawful decision undone and the body compelled to think again. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The court may grant remedies such as a quashing order, a prohibiting order, a mandatory order, a declaration or an injunction, at its discretion.
The only remedy available in judicial review is an award of damages to the claimant.
The court has no power to grant any remedy in judicial review proceedings.
The court must always quash the decision automatically once any unlawfulness is shown on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may only advise the public body and can make no binding order at all.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The remedies available in judicial review include a quashing order (to set aside the decision), a prohibiting order, a mandatory order (to compel action), a declaration, and an injunction. These remedies are discretionary, so the court may decline relief (for example for delay or where it would make no difference).

n.1: Damages are not the primary remedy in judicial review and are limited.
n.2: The court does have remedial powers in judicial review.
n.3: Remedies are discretionary; quashing is not automatic.
n.4: The court can make binding orders, not merely advise.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant wishes to challenge a public body's decision by judicial review, but some time has already passed since the decision was made, and the claimant is unsure whether they are still in time to bring the claim. A solicitor advises that judicial review has strict time requirements. The solicitor considers the time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review. The decision had been made a couple of months earlier and the claimant had been slow to act. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A claim may be brought within twelve years, as for actions concerning land.
A claim must be brought promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising, subject to any shorter or extended period.
A claim for judicial review may be brought at any time within six years of the decision on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A claim must be brought within 24 hours of the decision being made.
There is no time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A claim for judicial review must be made promptly and in any event within three months of the date on which the grounds to make the claim first arose (with shorter periods in some contexts, such as planning). The court may extend time in limited circumstances, but delay can be fatal.

n.0: Twelve years does not apply to judicial review.
n.2: The judicial review period is three months, not six years.
n.3: The limit is three months (and promptly), not 24 hours.
n.4: There is a strict time limit for judicial review.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public authority interferes with a right such as the right to respect for private and family life, which is a qualified Convention right that may be interfered with only where the interference is justified. The claimant argues the interference was not justified. A solicitor is asked about how interference with a qualified Convention right is assessed. The solicitor considers the structure of qualified Convention rights (such as Articles 8 to 11). The authority had interfered with the person's private life and had to justify doing so. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Interference with a qualified right is permitted only if it is in accordance with the law, pursues a legitimate aim, and is necessary and proportionate.
Qualified rights may be interfered with only where the individual consents in writing.
Interference with a qualified right requires no justification of any kind.
A public authority may interfere with a qualified right for any reason it considers convenient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Qualified Convention rights are absolute and can never be interfered with in any circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Qualified Convention rights (such as Articles 8 to 11) may be interfered with, but only where the interference is in accordance with the law, pursues one of the legitimate aims specified in the article, and is necessary in a democratic society — that is, a proportionate response to a pressing social need.

n.1: Justification is by the legal/legitimate-aim/proportionality test, not the individual's written consent.
n.2: Interference with a qualified right does require justification.
n.3: Interference cannot be for any convenient reason; it must be justified.
n.4: Qualified rights are not absolute; that describes rights like Article 3.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A Bill has completed all its stages in both Houses of Parliament and is presented to the monarch for Royal Assent. A commentator suggests the monarch might refuse assent because the monarch personally disapproves of the Bill. The Bill has passed both Houses and awaits Royal Assent. The question is whether assent may be withheld. Everything has been done bar the final step, the Bill having cleared both Houses, and a commentator idly wonders aloud whether the monarch, said to dislike the measure, might simply decline to sign it off, which raises the settled constitutional understanding about the granting of assent. Which of the following best describes the constitutional position on Royal Assent?
o: Royal Assent may be refused whenever the government of the day requests it.
Royal Assent is a mere formality that Parliament may dispense with entirely.
The monarch routinely exercises a personal choice whether to assent to Bills on these facts.
By convention the monarch does not refuse Royal Assent to a Bill duly passed by Parliament.
The monarch must obtain the Prime Minister's permission to grant assent.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Although Royal Assent is legally required for a Bill to become an Act, by firmly established convention the monarch does not refuse assent to a Bill that has been duly passed by both Houses (or under the Parliament Acts). The monarch acts on advice and as a constitutional monarch, so assent is granted as a matter of course.

n.0: Assent is not refused on the government's request; the convention is that it is granted.
n.1: Royal Assent is legally necessary; it cannot simply be dispensed with.
n.2: The monarch does not exercise a personal choice to withhold assent by convention.
n.4: The monarch does not need the Prime Minister's permission to grant assent.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body made a clear and unambiguous promise to an individual that they would receive a particular substantive benefit, and the individual relied on that promise, but the body now seeks to go back on it. The individual argues they are entitled to the benefit itself, not merely to a fair procedure. A solicitor is asked whether a public body can be held to a substantive promise. The solicitor considers substantive legitimate expectation. The individual had reorganised their affairs in reliance on the promised benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A public body is always bound to honour every promise it ever makes, without exception.
A public body may resile from any promise simply because circumstances have changed at all.
Substantive legitimate expectation applies only to promises made in writing under seal.
In limited circumstances a clear promise may give rise to a substantive legitimate expectation, and resiling from it may be an abuse of power.
A substantive legitimate expectation can never be enforced against a public body in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: In limited circumstances the courts recognise a substantive legitimate expectation: where a public body has made a clear, unambiguous promise of a substantive benefit on which a person has relied, resiling from it may be so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power, and the court may hold the body to the promise unless there is a sufficient overriding public interest (R v North and East Devon HA, ex p Coughlan).

n.0: A public body is not bound to honour every promise regardless of the public interest.
n.1: A body may resile only where justified by an overriding public interest, not for any change at all.
n.2: There is no requirement that the promise be under seal.
n.4: Substantive legitimate expectation can be enforced in limited circumstances.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body, in reaching a decision, takes into account a matter that it should legally have ignored, or fails to take into account a matter that it was legally required to consider. A claimant challenges the decision by judicial review. A solicitor is asked which aspect of illegality is engaged where a decision-maker considers the wrong matters. The solicitor considers relevant and irrelevant considerations as a ground of review. The decision-maker had focused on a matter that had nothing to do with the statutory scheme. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The considerations a body takes into account are never a basis for judicial review.
A decision can be challenged only if the decision-maker considered no matters at all.
A decision-maker may take account of whatever considerations it wishes, relevant or not on these facts as a general rule.
A decision may be unlawful if the body took account of irrelevant considerations or failed to consider relevant ones.
A decision is lawful provided the body considered at least one relevant matter.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: As part of illegality, a decision-maker must have regard to considerations that are legally relevant and must not have regard to legally irrelevant ones. Taking into account an irrelevant consideration, or failing to take into account a relevant one, can render the decision unlawful.

n.0: The considerations taken into account are a recognised ground of review.
n.1: The challenge is not confined to cases where nothing was considered.
n.2: A body may not consider whatever it wishes; relevance is controlled by law.
n.4: Considering one relevant matter does not save a decision that ignored other required ones or took account of irrelevant ones.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: In a genuine national emergency threatening the life of the nation, a state wishes to take measures that would otherwise breach certain Convention rights, and considers whether it may formally suspend some of its obligations. The measures respond to a public emergency threatening the life of the nation. Only certain rights are involved. Facing a grave crisis said to threaten the life of the nation, the state wants to take emergency measures that would otherwise cut across some Convention guarantees, and it is considering whether it can formally suspend a measure of its obligations to do so, and within what limits. Which of the following best describes the position on derogation under the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: Derogation is permitted only with the consent of every other Convention state.
Derogation automatically repeals the Human Rights Act 1998 during the emergency.
A state may derogate from all Convention rights without limit during any emergency on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A state may never derogate from any Convention right in any circumstances.
A state may derogate from certain Convention rights in a public emergency, to the extent strictly required, but not from non-derogable rights.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Article 15 of the Convention permits a state, in time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation, to derogate from certain Convention obligations to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation. However, some rights are non-derogable (for example, the prohibition of torture), and derogations are subject to conditions and scrutiny.

n.0: Derogation does not require the consent of every other state.
n.1: Derogation does not repeal the Human Rights Act; it concerns specific obligations.
n.2: Derogation is limited to what is strictly required and excludes non-derogable rights, not unlimited.
n.3: Derogation is possible in a qualifying emergency, so 'never' is wrong.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body's decision interferes with an individual's rights, and the challenge is brought in a context (such as a human rights or, historically, an EU law matter) where the court examines whether the interference was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, rather than merely whether it was rational. A solicitor is asked about the intensity of review in such contexts. The solicitor considers the principle of proportionality. The measure struck at a protected right and the court had to weigh it against the aim pursued. Which of the following best describes it?
o: In human rights (and certain other) contexts the court applies proportionality, asking whether the measure is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
Proportionality applies to every judicial review claim in exactly the same way as irrationality on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Proportionality allows the court to quash any decision the claimant considers unfair.
Proportionality has no place in UK public law in any circumstances.
Proportionality means the court simply defers entirely to the decision-maker in every case.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: In cases engaging Convention rights under the Human Rights Act (and formerly in EU law contexts), the court applies a proportionality analysis: whether the objective is sufficiently important, whether the measure is rationally connected to it, whether a less intrusive measure could have been used, and whether a fair balance has been struck. This is a more intensive review than Wednesbury irrationality.

n.1: Proportionality is not the general standard for all judicial review; it applies in particular contexts.
n.2: Proportionality is not simply a test of the claimant's sense of unfairness.
n.3: Proportionality does have a role in UK public law, notably under the HRA.
n.4: Proportionality is a structured, intensive review, not complete deference.
