Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A solicitor is advising on a Convention right that is not absolute but is 'limited' — capable of interference only in the specific circumstances set out in the article itself, rather than being subject to a general proportionality justification like the qualified rights. A client asks how such limited rights differ from qualified and absolute rights. The solicitor considers the categories of Convention rights. The client was trying to work out how this right differed from the absolute and qualified ones. Which of the following best describes a limited right?
o: A limited right may be interfered with only in the specific, defined circumstances permitted by the article itself.
A limited right may be interfered with for any reason the public authority considers appropriate.
A limited right may be balanced away under a general proportionality test like a qualified right.
A limited right is identical in every respect to an absolute right and can never be interfered with on these facts.
A limited right applies only to companies and never to individuals.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Convention rights fall into categories: absolute rights (which cannot be interfered with at all), limited rights (which may be interfered with only in the specific, defined circumstances set out within the article itself, such as the exceptions to the right to liberty in Article 5), and qualified rights (which may be interfered with where justified under a general legitimate-aim and proportionality test).

n.1: A limited right cannot be interfered with for any reason; only in the defined circumstances.
n.2: A limited right is interfered with within its own defined exceptions, not by a general proportionality balance like qualified rights.
n.3: A limited right is not identical to an absolute right; it can be limited in defined ways.
n.4: Convention rights are not confined to companies.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A devolved legislature passes an Act dealing with a matter, and a question arises whether the Act is within the legislature's legislative competence, given that certain matters are reserved to the Westminster Parliament. The Act may stray into a reserved matter outside the devolved legislature's competence. Its validity is challenged. The devolved legislature has passed an Act that arguably strays into territory reserved to Westminster and so beyond its own powers, and a party affected by it is asking the courts to rule on whether the measure is within competence or must be struck down. Which of the following best describes how such a challenge is determined?
o: Devolved legislation always overrides Acts of the Westminster Parliament.
A devolved Act is valid provided the devolved legislature intended it to be.
Only the Westminster Parliament, not the courts, may rule on devolved competence on these facts as a general rule.
Devolved legislation is immune from challenge in the courts in all circumstances.
The courts may determine whether the devolved Act is within legislative competence and, if it is outside it, hold it invalid.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Devolved legislatures have limited legislative competence: they cannot legislate on reserved matters or outside their defined powers. Unlike Acts of the sovereign Westminster Parliament, a devolved Act can be challenged in the courts, which may determine whether it is within competence and, if not, hold the provision to be not law (invalid).

n.0: Devolved legislation does not override Westminster Acts; Westminster remains sovereign.
n.1: The legislature's intention does not cure an Act that is outside its competence.
n.2: The courts, not only Parliament, rule on devolved competence.
n.3: Devolved legislation is not immune from challenge; competence can be tested in the courts.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A statute confers a decision-making power on a named minister or body, but the power is in fact exercised by a different person or body to whom it has been handed over, without any lawful authority to delegate it. A claimant challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged where a power is exercised by the wrong person. The solicitor considers unlawful delegation of power. The statute named a particular officer, but someone else had actually taken the decision. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Delegation of a statutory power is never capable of being unlawful.
A statutory power may always be delegated to anyone the decision-maker chooses on these facts as a general rule.
The identity of the person exercising a statutory power is legally irrelevant.
A decision can be challenged only where the delegate acted dishonestly.
The decision may be unlawful because the power was unlawfully delegated to a person not authorised to exercise it.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a statute confers a power on a particular person or body, it must generally be exercised by that person or body. Exercising it through an unauthorised delegate (unlawful sub-delegation) is a form of illegality, subject to limited exceptions such as the Carltona principle for ministers and their departments.

n.0: Unlawful delegation is a recognised ground of illegality.
n.1: A statutory power cannot always be freely delegated.
n.2: The identity of the decision-maker matters where the statute confers the power on a specific person.
n.3: Unlawful delegation does not require dishonesty by the delegate.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A person in Scotland asks about the powers of the Scottish Parliament and the relationship between devolved government and the UK Parliament at Westminster, given that some matters are decided in Edinburgh and others remain reserved to Westminster. A solicitor is asked to explain the basic constitutional position of devolution. The solicitor considers devolution in the UK. Some laws affecting the person were made in Edinburgh and others still at Westminster. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Devolution transfers all powers to the devolved legislatures, leaving Westminster with none on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Devolution has no effect on law-making, which remains entirely with Westminster alone.
Devolution confers law-making powers on the devolved legislatures over devolved matters, while certain matters remain reserved to Westminster.
Devolution means the devolved nations are fully independent states outside the UK.
Devolution means the UK Parliament has been abolished and replaced by regional assemblies.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Devolution has conferred law-making and executive powers on the devolved institutions (for example the Scottish Parliament and Senedd Cymru) over devolved matters, while certain matters (reserved matters) remain within the competence of the UK Parliament, which in law retains sovereignty over the whole UK.

n.0: Not all powers are transferred; reserved matters remain with Westminster.
n.1: Devolution does change law-making by conferring powers on devolved bodies.
n.3: The devolved nations remain part of the UK, not fully independent states.
n.4: The UK Parliament has not been abolished.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A dispute arises about a well-established practice by which those in government behave in a particular way — for example that the monarch acts on ministerial advice — even though no statute or case requires it, and a party argues this practice is legally enforceable in the courts. A solicitor is asked about the status of such non-legal but binding constitutional practices. The solicitor considers constitutional conventions. The practice had been observed for generations, yet was written down in no statute at all. Which of the following best describes them?
o: Constitutional conventions have no significance and are freely ignored without any consequence on these facts.
Constitutional conventions can be enforced by the courts through an award of damages.
Constitutional conventions are rules of EU law binding on the UK institutions.
Constitutional conventions are binding practices of the constitution but are not legally enforceable in the courts.
Constitutional conventions are statutes that can be directly enforced by the courts.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Constitutional conventions are non-legal rules of constitutional behaviour that are regarded as binding in practice by those who operate the constitution (for example, that the monarch assents to bills passed by Parliament), but they are not laws and are not directly enforceable by the courts.

n.0: Conventions are significant and generally observed, not freely ignored.
n.1: Breach of a convention does not sound in damages in the courts.
n.2: Conventions are domestic constitutional practices, not rules of EU law.
n.4: Conventions are not statutes and are not directly enforceable in the courts.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A member of a decision-making body has a direct personal financial interest in the outcome of the very matter the body is deciding, and participates in the decision. A party challenges the decision on the ground of bias. The decision-maker had a direct pecuniary interest in the outcome. The challenge is on the ground of bias. It has emerged that one of those who sat in judgment on the matter stood to gain financially from the very outcome they helped to decide and yet took part anyway, and the losing party now attacks the decision on the ground that the tribunal was tainted by that interest. Which of the following best describes the effect of such a direct interest?
o: A decision-maker with a direct personal (for example pecuniary) interest is automatically disqualified, and the decision may be set aside.
A direct financial interest is irrelevant provided the decision-maker felt able to be fair on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Bias must always be proved as actual bias in the decision-maker's mind.
A direct interest disqualifies the decision-maker only in criminal proceedings.
A decision-maker's interest matters only if the affected party consents to it.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A decision-maker with a direct personal interest in the outcome, such as a pecuniary interest (or a relevant non-financial interest, as in Pinochet), is automatically disqualified from acting, without any need to prove actual bias, and a decision so tainted may be quashed. Beyond automatic disqualification, the test is whether a fair-minded observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias.

n.1: A direct interest is not cured by the decision-maker's own confidence in their fairness.
n.2: Actual bias need not be proved where there is automatic disqualification or apparent bias.
n.3: Automatic disqualification is not confined to criminal proceedings.
n.4: The interest is not rendered acceptable merely by the party's consent in this context.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: After the end of the implementation period, a court is dealing with a body of EU-derived law that was preserved in domestic law, and must decide how to treat pre-exit case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union when interpreting it. The rules concern assimilated (formerly retained) EU law. The court is considering the status of retained EU case law. The dispute turns on a slice of EU-derived law carried over into domestic law after the implementation period ended, and the judge has to work out how much weight to give to rulings the Court of Justice handed down before exit when construing that preserved body of law today. Which of the following best describes the position of the higher courts?
o: Retained EU case law has been entirely abolished and may never be referred to.
All UK courts remain absolutely bound by CJEU case law exactly as before Brexit.
Only the Court of Justice of the European Union may interpret retained EU law.
UK courts must refer all questions of retained EU law to the CJEU for a ruling.
Certain higher courts may depart from retained EU case law where it appears right to do so.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Following the UK's departure from the EU, retained (now assimilated) EU case law continues to be relevant to interpreting retained EU law, but certain higher courts (such as the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal) are empowered to depart from it, applying a test similar to that for departing from their own precedent, rather than being bound by it as before.

n.0: Retained EU case law is not abolished; it remains relevant to interpretation.
n.1: UK courts are not absolutely bound by CJEU case law as before; higher courts may depart.
n.2: UK courts, not only the CJEU, interpret retained/assimilated EU law after Brexit.
n.3: UK courts no longer make references to the CJEU for such rulings.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: Following the UK's departure from the European Union, a solicitor is advising on the status of EU-derived law that was preserved in the domestic legal system at the end of the implementation period. A client asks whether EU-derived rules simply ceased to have any effect in the UK, or whether they were carried over into domestic law. The solicitor considers retained (now assimilated) EU law under the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018. The client wanted to know what had happened to the EU rules their business had relied on for years. Which of the following best describes it?
o: EU-derived law was largely converted into domestic 'retained' (now assimilated) EU law, subject to amendment and repeal by the UK.
EU-derived law can never be amended or repealed by the UK Parliament.
The UK is still bound to follow all new EU legislation as a member state.
EU law continues to apply in the UK exactly as before, with full supremacy over domestic law on these facts as a general rule.
All EU law ceased to have any effect in the UK the moment the UK left the European Union.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, a large body of EU-derived law was converted into domestic law as 'retained EU law' (now 'assimilated law') to provide continuity at the end of the implementation period. It forms part of UK law but can be amended or repealed domestically, and its special status has been progressively reduced.

n.1: Retained/assimilated EU law can be amended or repealed by the UK.
n.2: The UK is no longer bound as a member state to follow new EU legislation.
n.3: EU law no longer applies with full supremacy; that ended on withdrawal.
n.4: EU-derived law did not all simply cease; much was retained in domestic law.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant lodges a claim for judicial review. Before the substantive hearing, the court must decide whether to allow the claim to proceed to a full hearing at all, applying a threshold test at an initial stage. The claim is at the initial stage of judicial review proceedings. The court must decide whether it can go forward. The claim for judicial review has only just been lodged, and before anyone reaches the merits the court must apply the initial filter that decides whether a claim of this kind is even allowed to go forward to a full hearing at all. Which of the following best describes the permission stage in judicial review?
o: The court decides the substance of the claim finally at this initial stage.
Permission is granted only where the claimant proves the case beyond reasonable doubt.
The claimant must obtain permission, granted where there is an arguable case with a realistic prospect of success.
Every judicial review claim proceeds automatically to a full hearing without any filter on these facts.
Permission depends solely on whether the defendant public body consents.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Judicial review has a permission (leave) stage acting as a filter: the claimant must obtain the court's permission to proceed, which is generally granted where the claim is arguable and has a realistic prospect of success (and the claimant has standing and is in time). Unmeritorious claims can be stopped at this stage before a full hearing.

n.0: The permission stage is a filter, not a final determination of the substance.
n.1: The threshold is arguability/realistic prospect, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.
n.3: Claims do not proceed automatically; permission is required.
n.4: Permission does not depend on the defendant's consent.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A decision affecting a party is taken by an adjudicator who has a direct personal financial interest in the outcome of the very matter being decided. The party challenges the decision on the ground of bias, without needing to show a real possibility of bias. A solicitor is asked about the position where the decision-maker has a direct interest in the outcome. The solicitor considers automatic disqualification for bias. The adjudicator stood to gain financially from the very decision they were being asked to make. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Automatic disqualification applies only to full-time salaried judges.
A direct financial interest in the outcome is irrelevant unless actual bias is proved.
A decision-maker may always decide a case in which they have a financial interest.
A decision-maker with a direct personal interest in the outcome is automatically disqualified, without proof of bias.
A direct interest disqualifies the decision-maker only if the losing party objects in advance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a decision-maker has a direct personal interest in the outcome — classically a direct pecuniary interest — they are automatically disqualified from acting, and the decision is liable to be set aside without any need to investigate whether there was a real possibility of bias (Dimes v Grand Junction Canal).

n.0: Automatic disqualification is not confined to salaried judges.
n.1: A direct interest disqualifies automatically; proof of actual bias is not needed.
n.2: A decision-maker may not decide a case in which they have such an interest.
n.4: Automatic disqualification does not depend on an advance objection.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: Parliament has passed a statute that comprehensively regulates a particular area which was previously governed by the royal prerogative. The government seeks to rely on the prerogative to act in a way inconsistent with the statutory scheme. The statute now covers the same ground as the former prerogative. The government prefers to use the prerogative. Parliament has since enacted a detailed statutory scheme covering exactly the territory the prerogative once occupied, but the government, finding the statute inconvenient, wants to fall back on the old prerogative power to act in a way the statute would not permit, forcing the question of which source of power now governs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The statute is invalid because it interferes with the royal prerogative.
The prerogative always prevails over any inconsistent Act of Parliament.
The government may freely choose between the statute and the prerogative on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Where statute covers the same ground, the government must act under the statute, and the prerogative is displaced to that extent.
The prerogative can be used to suspend the operation of the statute.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a statute regulates an area formerly governed by the prerogative, the executive must act under the statute; the prerogative is displaced or goes into abeyance to the extent of the statutory scheme (Attorney General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel; Fire Brigades Union). The prerogative cannot be used to circumvent or frustrate the will of Parliament expressed in the statute.

n.0: The statute is valid; Parliament may legislate over prerogative areas.
n.1: The prerogative does not prevail over statute; statute displaces the prerogative.
n.2: The government cannot freely choose the prerogative where statute covers the ground.
n.4: The prerogative cannot be used to suspend a statute's operation.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body proposes to make a decision that will adversely affect an individual's interests, but does so without telling the individual what is being considered or giving them any chance to respond before the decision is taken. The individual challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked about the individual's entitlement to be heard before an adverse decision is made. The solicitor considers the right to a fair hearing in procedural fairness. The person only learned of the decision after it had already been taken against them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A person is entitled to a full court trial before any administrative decision is made.
A person may be heard only after the decision has already been made against them.
The right to be heard applies only in criminal proceedings, never in administrative decisions on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A person has no right to be heard before a public body makes a decision affecting them.
Fairness generally requires that a person affected be given notice and a fair opportunity to make representations before an adverse decision.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The common-law rules of natural justice require procedural fairness, including that a person whose interests are adversely affected should generally be given notice of what is proposed and a fair opportunity to make representations before the decision is made. What fairness requires varies with the context.

n.0: Fairness requires a fair opportunity to be heard, not necessarily a full court trial.
n.1: The opportunity to be heard should come before, not only after, the decision.
n.2: Fairness applies to administrative decisions, not only criminal proceedings.
n.3: There is generally a right to be heard before an adverse decision.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A bill has been passed by the House of Commons but the House of Lords is refusing to agree to it, and the Government wishes to know whether the bill can nonetheless become law without the Lords' consent. A solicitor is asked about the respective roles of the two Houses and the mechanism that can allow the Commons to prevail. The solicitor considers the role of the House of Lords and the Parliament Acts. The Lords kept sending the bill back and the Government was anxious to get it onto the statute book. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The Lords is mainly a revising chamber; under the Parliament Acts the Commons can sometimes legislate without its consent.
The House of Commons can never pass any legislation without the agreement of the Lords.
The House of Lords is the elected chamber and the Commons is the appointed one.
The House of Lords has an absolute veto over all legislation, which can never be overridden on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The House of Lords alone can make law without any involvement of the House of Commons.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The House of Lords is principally a revising chamber that scrutinises and can delay legislation. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, in defined circumstances a bill may be presented for royal assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords, so the elected Commons can ultimately prevail.

n.1: The Commons can, via the Parliament Acts, legislate without the Lords in defined cases.
n.2: The Commons is the elected chamber; the Lords is largely appointed.
n.3: The Lords does not have an absolute, unoverridable veto.
n.4: The Lords cannot make law alone without the Commons.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: In judicial review proceedings, the public body defendant holds documents and information relevant to the lawfulness of its decision, including material that is unhelpful to its own case. A question arises about the body's obligations of disclosure and openness to the court. A solicitor is asked about the special duty owed by a public body in judicial review. The solicitor considers the duty of candour. The body held internal documents that shed real light on how the decision had been made. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A public body owes no duty of disclosure of any kind in judicial review proceedings.
A public body owes a duty of candour to assist the court with full and fair disclosure of relevant material, including material unhelpful to its case.
A public body need only disclose the material that supports its own defence.
A public body may conceal relevant material from the court if it considers it embarrassing on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The duty of candour applies only to the claimant and never to the public body.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: In judicial review, public authorities owe a duty of candour and cooperation: they must assist the court with full and accurate explanations of the decision under challenge and disclose relevant material, including documents that undermine their own case, so that the court can perform its supervisory role fairly.

n.0: There is a duty of candour/disclosure in judicial review.
n.2: The duty is not limited to helpful material; it includes unhelpful material.
n.3: A body may not conceal relevant material because it is embarrassing.
n.4: The duty of candour applies to the public body (and to claimants too).

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body reaches a decision that a claimant argues is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority, properly directing itself, could ever have arrived at it. The claimant does not allege illegality or unfairness, but attacks the decision itself as irrational. A solicitor is asked about the standard the court applies to such a challenge. The solicitor considers the ground of irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness). The claimant accepted the body had power to decide, but attacked the decision as absurd. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A decision may be quashed as irrational whenever the claimant strongly disagrees with it.
A decision may be quashed simply because the court would itself have reached a different decision on these facts.
A decision is irrational whenever it produces an outcome that is unpopular with the public.
A decision may be quashed as irrational only if it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it.
Irrationality is not a recognised ground of judicial review in English law.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under the ground of irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness), the court will only quash a decision on this basis if it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority, properly directing itself, could have made it. This is a high threshold that respects the decision-maker's role and does not allow the court to substitute its own view.

n.0: The claimant's strong disagreement does not make a decision irrational.
n.1: Mere disagreement by the court is not enough; the threshold is high.
n.2: Unpopularity does not equate to irrationality.
n.4: Irrationality is a recognised ground of judicial review.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public authority makes a decision that interferes with an individual's rights protected by the European Convention on Human Rights, and the individual argues that the authority acted unlawfully by breaching those rights. A solicitor is asked about the obligation of a public authority in relation to Convention rights under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The authority's decision plainly cut across a right protected under the Convention. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Convention rights are relevant only in the European Court of Human Rights and never in UK courts on these facts.
It is unlawful under s.6 HRA 1998 for a public authority to act in a way incompatible with a Convention right.
The Human Rights Act binds only private individuals and not public authorities.
Public authorities are entirely free to disregard Convention rights when making decisions.
A public authority may breach Convention rights provided it acts in good faith.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998, it is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way which is incompatible with a Convention right, unless primary legislation requires it to do so. This allows Convention rights to be enforced against public authorities in the UK courts.

n.0: Convention rights are enforceable in the UK courts under the HRA, not only in Strasbourg.
n.2: The HRA binds public authorities, not (directly) private individuals.
n.3: Public authorities are not free to disregard Convention rights; s.6 binds them.
n.4: Good faith does not excuse acting incompatibly with a Convention right.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A commentator observes that, in the UK constitution, law-making, the administration of government, and the resolution of legal disputes are carried out by broadly distinct institutions — Parliament, the executive, and the judiciary — with various checks between them, although the separation is not complete. A solicitor is asked to explain the constitutional principle this describes. The solicitor considers the separation of powers. The commentator was trying to make sense of how power is shared between the branches of the state. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The separation of powers means Parliament decides the outcome of individual court cases.
The separation of powers is a rule that the monarch personally exercises all three functions.
The separation of powers requires the judiciary to be controlled directly by the government of the day.
The separation of powers means that a single institution exercises all governmental functions together on these facts as a general rule.
The separation of powers distributes functions between the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, with checks and balances between them.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The separation of powers refers to the distribution of governmental functions between the legislature (which makes law), the executive (which implements it), and the judiciary (which resolves disputes and interprets the law), with checks and balances between them, although in the UK the separation is partial rather than absolute.

n.0: Parliament does not decide individual court cases; that is for the judiciary.
n.1: The monarch does not personally exercise all three functions.
n.2: Judicial independence from government is a key aspect, not government control of the judiciary.
n.3: Separation of powers means functions are distributed, not concentrated in one body.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The government wishes to take a particular executive action relying on historic powers of the Crown that do not derive from any statute, such as certain powers relating to foreign affairs. A claimant argues that these powers are unlimited and beyond the scrutiny of the courts. A solicitor is asked about the nature of these non-statutory executive powers and their reviewability. The solicitor considers the royal prerogative. The government relied on ancient Crown powers rather than on any Act of Parliament at all. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The prerogative is a modern statutory power created by a recent Act of Parliament.
The prerogative gives the government unlimited powers that the courts can never review at all on these facts as a general rule.
The prerogative may be used to override or suspend Acts of Parliament at will.
The prerogative comprises residual non-statutory powers of the Crown, whose exercise is in principle reviewable by the courts.
The prerogative belongs to Parliament rather than to the Crown and the executive.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The royal prerogative comprises the residual common-law powers of the Crown, exercised in practice by ministers, which do not derive from statute. Its existence and extent, and increasingly its exercise, are reviewable by the courts, and prerogative power cannot be used to override statute.

n.0: The prerogative is a common-law source, not a recent statutory creation.
n.1: Prerogative power is not unlimited and is subject to judicial review.
n.2: The prerogative cannot override or suspend Acts of Parliament.
n.4: The prerogative belongs to the Crown/executive, not Parliament.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A campaigning organisation, which is not itself directly affected by a public body's decision but has a genuine concern about the issue, wishes to bring judicial review proceedings challenging that decision. The public body argues the organisation has no right to bring the claim. A solicitor is asked whether the claimant is entitled to bring judicial review. The solicitor considers the requirement of standing in judicial review. The organisation had genuine expertise and a real concern about the lawfulness of the decision. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The claimant must have a sufficient interest in the matter, which can include a suitably concerned campaign group in appropriate cases.
Standing in judicial review depends solely on whether the claimant can afford the court fees.
A campaign group can never have standing to bring judicial review under any circumstances.
Only a person directly and personally affected in their private rights can ever bring judicial review on these facts as a general rule.
Anyone at all may bring judicial review, with no requirement of any interest in the matter.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: To bring judicial review a claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' in the matter to which the claim relates. This is applied flexibly and, depending on the context, a public-interest group or campaigning body with genuine expertise and concern may be found to have sufficient interest to bring a claim.

n.1: Standing depends on sufficient interest, not the ability to pay fees.
n.2: Campaign groups can, in appropriate cases, have standing.
n.3: Standing is not confined to those personally affected in their private rights.
n.4: There is a requirement of sufficient interest; not anyone may bring a claim.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public authority makes a decision that adversely affects an individual, who believes the decision was made unlawfully and wishes to challenge it in the courts. The individual is not seeking to appeal the merits but to challenge the legality of the decision-making. A solicitor is asked about the mechanism for challenging the lawfulness of a public body's decision. The solicitor considers the nature and scope of judicial review. The individual wanted the decision reviewed for legality, not a fresh decision on the merits of their case. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Judicial review allows the court to substitute its own decision on the merits for that of the public body.
Judicial review is an appeal on the facts against any decision the claimant dislikes.
Judicial review is available to challenge the decisions of private individuals in private disputes.
Judicial review is the court's supervisory jurisdiction to review the lawfulness of decisions of public bodies.
Judicial review allows the court to award damages as of right for any unlawful decision.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Judicial review is the process by which the courts exercise a supervisory jurisdiction over the exercise of public functions, reviewing the lawfulness (not generally the merits) of decisions, actions and omissions of public bodies against grounds such as illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.

n.0: The court reviews legality, not the merits; it does not substitute its own decision.
n.1: It is not an appeal on the facts.
n.2: Judicial review concerns public functions, not purely private disputes.
n.4: Damages are not available as of right in judicial review.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A UK court is determining a claim involving Convention rights and is considering how much weight to give to decisions of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. A solicitor is asked about the extent to which UK courts are bound by, or must have regard to, Strasbourg case law under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers section 2 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The parties disagreed about how far the UK court had to follow the Strasbourg case law. Which of the following best describes it?
o: UK courts are strictly bound to follow every decision of the European Court of Human Rights on these facts.
UK courts may consider Strasbourg case law only with the consent of the Government.
UK courts must take into account relevant Strasbourg jurisprudence, but are not strictly bound to follow it.
UK courts must ignore Strasbourg case law entirely when deciding human rights claims.
Strasbourg case law overrides Acts of Parliament in the UK courts.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.2 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a court determining a question in connection with a Convention right must take into account relevant judgments and decisions of the European Court of Human Rights, but it is not strictly bound to follow them; it gives them appropriate weight.

n.0: UK courts are not strictly bound to follow Strasbourg decisions.
n.1: Considering Strasbourg case law does not require Government consent.
n.3: UK courts must take Strasbourg case law into account, not ignore it.
n.4: Strasbourg case law does not override Acts of Parliament.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public authority's conduct is alleged to amount to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, engaging a Convention right that is framed in absolute terms. The authority argues it should be able to justify its conduct by reference to a pressing public interest. A solicitor is asked whether such a right can be interfered with or balanced against other interests. The solicitor considers absolute Convention rights, such as the prohibition of torture. The authority insisted a pressing public need justified how it had treated the individual. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An absolute right, such as the prohibition of torture, cannot be interfered with, balanced away or derogated from, whatever the circumstances.
All Convention rights, including the prohibition of torture, may be interfered with if justified in the public interest on these facts.
Absolute rights may be balanced against competing interests in exactly the same way as qualified rights.
Absolute rights may be breached provided the public authority acted in good faith.
Absolute rights apply only in times of peace and may be suspended in any emergency at will.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Some Convention rights are absolute — most notably Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). Absolute rights cannot be interfered with, balanced against other interests, or derogated from, even in a public emergency, however compelling the asserted justification.

n.1: Not all rights can be interfered with; absolute rights cannot.
n.2: Absolute rights are not balanced like qualified rights.
n.3: Good faith does not permit breach of an absolute right.
n.4: Absolute rights like Article 3 are non-derogable, even in emergencies.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant wishes to sue in relation to statements made by a Member of Parliament during a debate in Parliament, and to have the court examine and rule on what was said in parliamentary proceedings. A solicitor is asked whether the courts can inquire into things said and done in Parliament. The issue concerns the protection given to parliamentary proceedings. The solicitor considers parliamentary privilege. The words complained of had been spoken by the member during a heated parliamentary debate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The courts may freely examine and rule on anything said during proceedings in Parliament.
Parliamentary privilege means the courts must decide all disputes about parliamentary procedure on these facts as a general rule.
Members of Parliament have no protection at all for what they say in debates.
Parliamentary proceedings are protected by parliamentary privilege and generally cannot be questioned or impeached in the courts.
Parliamentary privilege prevents Parliament itself from discussing any legal matter.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under parliamentary privilege (reflected in Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689), the freedom of speech and proceedings in Parliament may not be impeached or questioned in any court. The courts will not generally inquire into or adjudicate on what is said or done in the course of parliamentary proceedings.

n.0: The courts cannot freely examine parliamentary proceedings; privilege protects them.
n.1: Privilege keeps such matters out of the courts, rather than requiring the courts to police procedure.
n.2: MPs have significant protection (privilege) for what they say in debate.
n.4: Privilege protects Parliament's proceedings; it does not stop Parliament debating matters.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body makes an important decision affecting an individual's liberty or livelihood but gives no reasons at all for its decision, leaving the individual unable to understand why the decision went against them or whether it might be challengeable. The individual argues they were entitled to reasons. A solicitor is asked whether a public body must give reasons for its decisions. The solicitor considers the duty to give reasons in public law. The individual was left completely in the dark about why the decision had gone against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A public body is never required to give reasons for any decision it makes.
A public body must always give full written reasons for every decision, however trivial on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There is no universal duty to give reasons, but fairness increasingly requires reasons, especially where important interests are affected.
A public body must give reasons only to those who can afford to pay for them.
Reasons are required only where the statute expressly says so and in no other case.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: There is no general common-law duty to give reasons for every decision, but fairness will often require reasons, particularly where important interests (such as liberty or livelihood) are at stake or where a decision appears aberrant. Statute may also impose a duty to give reasons (R v Home Secretary, ex p Doody).

n.0: There is no blanket rule that reasons are never required.
n.1: There is no universal duty to give reasons for every trivial decision.
n.3: The duty to give reasons does not depend on payment.
n.4: Fairness can require reasons even without an express statutory duty.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A person aggrieved by a public body's decision wishes to bring judicial review immediately, but there is a statutory appeal or internal complaints procedure available that has not yet been used, which could resolve the complaint. A suitable alternative remedy exists and has not been pursued. The claimant wishes to proceed straight to judicial review. The claimant is impatient to get straight to court by way of judicial review, but there is an untried statutory appeal or internal grievance route sitting available that could well resolve the very complaint, and the court must consider how that unused alternative bears on whether judicial review should proceed. Which of the following best describes the court's likely approach?
o: The claimant has an unqualified right to judicial review regardless of alternative remedies on these facts.
Alternative remedies are irrelevant to whether judicial review may be pursued.
The court may refuse permission for judicial review where a suitable alternative remedy has not been exhausted.
The court must always require the claimant to use judicial review rather than any appeal.
Judicial review is available only after every possible civil claim has been tried.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Judicial review is a remedy of last resort. Where there is a suitable alternative remedy (such as a statutory right of appeal or an effective internal procedure), the court will normally expect it to be used first and may refuse permission for judicial review if it has not been exhausted, save in exceptional circumstances.

n.0: There is no unqualified right to judicial review; alternative remedies matter.
n.1: Alternative remedies are highly relevant to whether judicial review will be entertained.
n.3: The court often expects an available appeal to be used rather than judicial review.
n.4: Judicial review does not require every possible civil claim to be tried first; it concerns suitable alternative remedies.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body has, by a clear promise or an established practice, led an individual to expect that a particular procedure (such as consultation) will be followed before a decision is made, but the body then departs from that procedure without good reason. The individual challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked about the individual's ability to hold the body to the expected procedure. The solicitor considers procedural legitimate expectation. The body had always consulted before such decisions, and people had come to rely on that. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A public body may always depart from any promise or practice it has established, without any consequence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A clear promise or established practice may give rise to a legitimate expectation that a procedure will be followed, which the body cannot depart from unfairly.
Legitimate expectation requires the individual to have paid the public body for the expectation.
A public body's past promises are never relevant to the lawfulness of its decisions.
Legitimate expectation applies only where the individual has a contract with the public body.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a public body, by a clear and unambiguous representation or an established practice, creates a legitimate expectation that a particular procedure (such as consultation) will be followed, it may be procedurally unfair to depart from that expectation without good reason, giving rise to a ground of review.

n.0: A body cannot always resile from a promise or practice without consequence.
n.2: It does not depend on payment.
n.3: A body's representations and practices can be relevant to the lawfulness of its decisions.
n.4: Legitimate expectation does not require a contract.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A later general statute contains general words that, read literally, might be taken to repeal or override an earlier statute of major constitutional importance, but the later Act does not expressly address that earlier statute. A party argues the earlier constitutional statute has been impliedly repealed. The earlier statute is a 'constitutional' statute. The later Act uses only general words. A later Act framed in broad general terms could, if read at face value, be said to sweep away part of an earlier statute of real constitutional weight, even though the later Act never mentions it, and a party is arguing that the earlier measure has simply been repealed by implication. Which of the following best describes the position under the doctrine concerning constitutional statutes?
o: Constitutional statutes override all later Acts regardless of Parliament's intention.
Constitutional statutes are not subject to implied repeal and can be repealed only by clear express words or unavoidable implication.
Constitutional statutes can never be repealed or amended by Parliament at all.
Constitutional statutes lose all effect as soon as any later statute is passed.
Constitutional statutes are repealed by any later inconsistent statute in the ordinary way on these facts as a general rule.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Following Thoburn v Sunderland City Council, certain 'constitutional' statutes are not subject to the doctrine of implied repeal: they can be repealed or amended only by express words in a later statute, or by words so specific that the inference of an intention to repeal is irresistible. General words in a later Act will not impliedly repeal them.

n.0: Constitutional statutes do not override later Acts regardless of intention; express repeal is possible.
n.2: Parliament can repeal constitutional statutes by clear express words, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: They do not lose effect automatically on any later statute; express repeal is required.
n.4: Constitutional statutes are protected from implied repeal, unlike ordinary statutes.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant establishes that a public authority acted unlawfully by breaching their Convention rights, and wishes to know what remedy the court may grant, including whether financial compensation is available. A solicitor is asked about the remedies a court may give for a breach of Convention rights. The solicitor considers section 8 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The claimant had suffered real harm and wanted to know what the court could actually do for them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Damages for a breach of Convention rights are available as of right in every case.
The court may only make a declaration and can never grant any other form of relief.
The court may grant such relief as it considers just and appropriate, and may award damages where necessary to afford just satisfaction.
The court must always award substantial damages for any breach of a Convention right on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court has no power to grant any remedy for a breach of Convention rights.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.8 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a court finds that a public authority has acted unlawfully under s.6, it may grant such relief or remedy within its powers as it considers just and appropriate, and may award damages, but only where necessary to afford 'just satisfaction' — so damages are not automatic.

n.0: HRA damages are not available as of right in every case.
n.1: The court may grant a range of remedies, not only a declaration.
n.3: Damages are not always awarded; they are discretionary and subject to the just satisfaction test.
n.4: The court does have remedial powers under s.8.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A court reviewing a public authority's decision that interferes with a Convention right must decide how intensively to scrutinise it. Counsel argues that mere Wednesbury unreasonableness is not the right test where a Convention right is engaged, and that a more structured and intensive assessment applies. A Convention right is engaged by the interference. The intensity of review is in issue. The decision under challenge bites directly on a Convention right, and the claimant argues that the old, deferential unreasonableness standard is simply not searching enough in such a case, pressing the court to subject the interference to a more structured and demanding form of scrutiny. Which of the following best describes the applicable standard?
o: No review at all, because interference with rights is a matter for the executive on these facts.
A review confined to whether the decision-maker acted in good faith.
Only traditional Wednesbury unreasonableness, with no more intensive scrutiny.
Proportionality, a more intensive and structured review than traditional Wednesbury unreasonableness.
A pure merits review in which the court substitutes its own decision as of right.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a Convention right is engaged, the court applies a proportionality assessment, which is more intensive and structured than traditional Wednesbury review. It considers whether the objective is sufficiently important, whether the measure is rationally connected to it, whether a less intrusive measure could have been used, and whether a fair balance has been struck.

n.0: There is review; interference with rights is not immune from scrutiny.
n.1: Review is not confined to good faith; proportionality is a structured, substantive test.
n.2: Traditional Wednesbury is not the applicable standard where a Convention right is engaged.
n.4: Proportionality is not a pure merits review; the court does not simply substitute its own view as of right.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body reaches a decision seriously affecting an individual without following a fair procedure — for example without giving the person any opportunity to put their case. The individual challenges the decision by judicial review, not on its merits but on the way it was reached. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged where the decision-making procedure was unfair. The solicitor considers the ground of procedural impropriety. The individual complained not about the outcome but about how unfairly the decision had been reached. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Procedural fairness applies only where the statute expressly requires a fair procedure.
The way a decision is reached is legally irrelevant, provided the outcome is reasonable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Procedural impropriety is not a recognised ground of judicial review.
A decision can be challenged only on its substance and never on the procedure followed.
The decision may be quashed for procedural impropriety, which includes a breach of the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Procedural impropriety is a recognised ground of judicial review. It includes a failure to observe the rules of natural justice and common-law procedural fairness (such as the right to a fair hearing and the rule against bias), as well as a failure to follow statutory procedural requirements.

n.0: Procedural fairness can be implied at common law, not only where the statute requires it.
n.1: The procedure followed is very relevant, not merely the outcome.
n.2: Procedural impropriety is one of the classic grounds of review.
n.3: Decisions can be challenged on procedure as well as substance.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A government department makes a serious policy failure, and there is public debate about who should answer to Parliament for the conduct of the department and its ministers. A solicitor is asked to explain the constitutional convention that governs ministers' accountability to Parliament for their departments and their own conduct. The solicitor considers ministerial responsibility. The failure had caused a public outcry and questions about who should answer for it. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Ministers are accountable only to the civil servants who work in their departments.
Ministerial responsibility is a statutory rule enforceable in the courts by damages on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Ministers are accountable only to the monarch and never to Parliament.
Ministers have no responsibility to anyone for the conduct of their departments.
By convention, ministers are individually and collectively responsible and accountable to Parliament for their conduct and their departments.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: By constitutional convention, ministers are accountable to Parliament: individual ministerial responsibility makes a minister answerable for their own conduct and the running of their department, and collective ministerial responsibility binds the government to support agreed policy publicly. These are conventions, not legally enforceable rules.

n.0: Ministers answer to Parliament, not merely to their civil servants.
n.1: Ministerial responsibility is a convention, not a statutory rule enforced by damages.
n.2: Ministers are accountable to Parliament, not only to the monarch.
n.3: Ministers do bear responsibility for their departments by convention.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A person wishes to bring a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998 alleging that a public authority has acted incompatibly with their Convention rights, but a question arises about whether this particular claimant is entitled to bring such a claim. The claimant must show they are affected in the right way. A solicitor is asked who may bring a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers the victim requirement under section 7 of the Act. The claimant had to show they were personally affected by the authority's conduct. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Anyone at all may bring a Human Rights Act claim, whether or not they are affected on these facts.
Only a person who is (or would be) a victim of the unlawful act may bring a claim under the Human Rights Act.
Only the Government may bring proceedings under the Human Rights Act.
A claim may be brought only by a person who has suffered financial loss.
Human Rights Act claims may be brought only by companies and not by individuals.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.7 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a person may bring proceedings against a public authority for acting incompatibly with a Convention right only if they are (or would be) a victim of the unlawful act — broadly, a person directly affected by it. This is narrower than the 'sufficient interest' test in ordinary judicial review.

n.0: The claimant must be a victim; not anyone may claim.
n.2: HRA claims are brought by victims, not the Government.
n.3: Financial loss is not the test; being a victim is.
n.4: Individuals (and in some cases organisations that are victims) may bring HRA claims.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A statute contains a clause purporting to prevent any court from questioning or reviewing decisions of a particular tribunal, appearing to exclude judicial review entirely. A claimant nonetheless seeks to challenge a decision of that tribunal that was made without jurisdiction. A solicitor is asked about the effect of such an ouster clause. The solicitor considers the approach of the courts to ouster clauses. The tribunal had made a fundamental error, yet the statute seemed to shut out any challenge. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The courts will always give an ouster clause its widest possible meaning.
Ouster clauses are automatically void and have no effect whatsoever on the courts.
The courts construe ouster clauses very narrowly and a decision made outside jurisdiction may still be reviewable.
An ouster clause completely and effectively excludes judicial review in all circumstances on these facts.
Ouster clauses can be relied on only by private bodies, never by public ones.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The courts construe ouster clauses very restrictively, in accordance with the principle that access to judicial review will not be excluded except by the clearest words. In Anisminic, a clause purporting to oust review did not protect a decision that was a nullity for error of law/excess of jurisdiction.

n.0: The courts construe such clauses narrowly, not widely.
n.1: Ouster clauses are not automatically void, but are narrowly construed.
n.3: Ouster clauses are not treated as wholly effective to exclude review.
n.4: Ouster clauses concern public law decisions, not a private/public distinction of this kind.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: During the UK's membership of the EU, a directive that had not been properly implemented into domestic law by the deadline conferred a clear, precise and unconditional right. An individual sought to rely on the directive against a state body, and separately another individual sought to rely on it against a private employer. The directive was unimplemented but sufficiently clear and unconditional. Reliance was sought against both a state body and a private party. The deadline for turning the directive into national law had passed with nothing done, yet its terms were clear and unconditional enough to be relied on, and two claimants tested it in different directions, one against an arm of the state and the other against an ordinary private employer. Which of the following best describes the direct effect of directives as it then operated?
o: A directive had direct effect only against private parties, never the state.
A directive had direct effect only once formally implemented into domestic law.
A directive could have vertical direct effect against the state, but not horizontal direct effect against a private party.
A directive always had full horizontal and vertical direct effect against anyone on these facts as a general rule.
A directive could never have any direct effect in any circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: An unimplemented directive that was sufficiently clear, precise and unconditional could be relied upon by an individual against the state or an emanation of the state (vertical direct effect), but not against another private party (no horizontal direct effect). This reflected the position developed in EU law during membership.

n.0: This reverses the position: direct effect ran against the state, not private parties.
n.1: The whole point of vertical direct effect was reliance on an unimplemented directive against the state.
n.3: Directives did not have horizontal direct effect against private parties.
n.4: Sufficiently clear, unconditional directives could have vertical direct effect, so 'never' is wrong.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The government proposes to use prerogative powers in a way that would frustrate, or render ineffective, the purpose of an existing Act of Parliament, effectively bypassing the statute. A claimant challenges this use of prerogative power. A solicitor is asked about the relationship between the royal prerogative and statute where the two come into conflict. The solicitor considers the limits of the prerogative in the face of legislation. The proposed use of the power would have gutted the very statute Parliament had recently passed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The prerogative is entirely unaffected by any statute Parliament may pass.
The prerogative and statute have equal status, and the government may choose which to apply on these facts.
The prerogative cannot be used to frustrate or override an Act of Parliament; statute prevails over the prerogative.
The prerogative always overrides any Act of Parliament that conflicts with it.
The prerogative may be used to repeal an Act of Parliament without a further Act.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Statute prevails over the prerogative: where an Act of Parliament covers the ground, the prerogative is displaced or curtailed, and the executive cannot use prerogative power to frustrate the purpose of, or act inconsistently with, legislation (Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel; R v Home Secretary, ex p Fire Brigades Union).

n.0: Statute can and does curtail the prerogative.
n.1: Statute and prerogative are not of equal status; statute prevails.
n.3: The prerogative does not override an Act of Parliament.
n.4: The prerogative cannot repeal an Act; only Parliament can.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The government seeks to introduce fees that would in practice prevent many people from bringing claims to enforce their legal rights before a tribunal, effectively denying them access to justice. A claimant challenges this by reference to a fundamental constitutional principle. A solicitor is asked which principle is engaged where access to the courts is impeded. The solicitor considers the rule of law and the right of access to justice. The proposed fees were set so high that ordinary people could not realistically bring claims. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Access to the courts is a fundamental aspect of the rule of law, and measures that unjustifiably impede it may be unlawful.
Access to the courts is a mere privilege that the government may remove at will for any reason on these facts as a general rule.
Access to justice is guaranteed only to those who can afford to pay for it in full.
The courts cannot consider any challenge to fees set by the government.
The rule of law has nothing to do with whether people can bring claims to court.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Access to the courts is a constitutional right and a fundamental element of the rule of law. Measures (such as prohibitive fees) that effectively prevent people from vindicating their legal rights may be held unlawful as an unjustified interference with that right (R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor).

n.1: Access to justice is a constitutional right, not a privilege removable at will.
n.2: Access to justice is not confined to those who can pay any fee set.
n.3: The courts can and do review measures impeding access to justice.
n.4: The rule of law is closely concerned with access to the courts.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A government Bill has been passed by the House of Commons but the House of Lords repeatedly refuses to agree to it, seeking to block it. The government wishes the Bill to become law despite the Lords' opposition, relying on a statutory mechanism. The Bill has Commons support but is being blocked by the Lords. The government invokes the relevant statutory procedure. The elected government has the numbers in the Commons but the Lords keeps sending the Bill back, determined to stop it, and ministers, unwilling to let an unelected chamber thwart their programme, are looking to the statutory route that lets the Commons have its way despite the Lords. Which of the following best describes the effect of the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949?
o: The House of Lords has an absolute veto over all legislation the Commons proposes on these facts as a general rule.
The Commons can never pass legislation without the agreement of the Lords.
The Bill must be abandoned entirely if the Lords refuse to agree to it.
In defined circumstances a Bill may be presented for Royal Assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords.
The monarch may personally override the Lords and enact the Bill by decree.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 allow certain public Bills passed by the Commons to be presented for Royal Assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords, subject to conditions and delay (and immediately for money bills). They reflect the primacy of the elected Commons over the unelected Lords.

n.0: The Lords has no absolute veto; the Parliament Acts limit its power to a delay.
n.1: The Commons can, in defined circumstances, legislate without the Lords' agreement.
n.2: The Bill need not be abandoned; the Parliament Acts provide a route around the Lords.
n.4: Legislation is enacted by Parliament with Royal Assent, not by monarchical decree.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public authority has acted unlawfully in breach of a claimant's Convention rights, and the claimant has suffered as a result. The claimant seeks financial compensation under the Human Rights Act 1998. A breach of a Convention right by a public authority is established. The claimant seeks damages. The public authority has been found to have acted unlawfully in breach of the claimant's Convention rights and the claimant has suffered as a result, so the claimant now presses for financial compensation and needs to know on what basis, if any, money can be awarded under the Act. Which of the following best describes the availability of damages under the Act?
o: Damages are payable as of right and in full for every breach of a Convention right.
Damages must always match the maximum awarded by the European Court of Human Rights on these facts as a general rule.
Damages are never available for a breach of a Convention right.
Damages are available only if the claimant also proves a breach of contract.
A court may award damages where necessary to afford just satisfaction, but they are discretionary and not automatic.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under s.8 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a court that finds an act of a public authority unlawful may grant such relief as it considers just and appropriate, including damages, but only where necessary to afford 'just satisfaction'. Damages are discretionary, not available as of right, and the court takes account of the principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights.

n.0: Damages under the HRA are discretionary, not payable as of right for every breach.
n.1: Awards need not match a maximum; the court assesses just satisfaction.
n.2: Damages can be available for a breach, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: HRA damages do not require proof of a separate breach of contract.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body takes a decision that goes beyond the powers conferred on it by the statute under which it was acting — it simply had no legal power to do what it did. A claimant challenges the decision by judicial review. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged where a body acts outside its legal powers. The solicitor considers the ground of illegality (acting ultra vires). The statute simply gave the body no power to make the decision it had purported to make. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The decision can be challenged only if it was also irrational, and illegality is not a ground by itself.
The decision is lawful provided the body acted honestly, whatever its statutory powers.
The decision is valid because a public body may do anything it considers to be in the public interest.
Acting beyond statutory powers is never a ground for judicial review.
The decision may be quashed for illegality, because the body acted beyond the powers conferred on it (ultra vires).
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Illegality is a core ground of judicial review: a public body must act within the powers conferred on it by law. Where it acts beyond those powers (ultra vires), or misdirects itself in law, the decision is unlawful and may be quashed.

n.0: Illegality is a freestanding ground; it need not be coupled with irrationality.
n.1: Acting honestly does not cure acting outside statutory powers.
n.2: A public body cannot do anything it likes; it must act within its powers.
n.3: Acting ultra vires is precisely a ground for judicial review.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A public body decides to carry out a consultation before making a policy decision, and an affected group argues that the consultation was so inadequate — for example giving no real information and no genuine opportunity to respond — that it was unlawful. A solicitor is asked about the standard a lawful consultation must meet. The solicitor considers the requirements of a fair consultation. The consultation had been rushed, with little information given and no real time to respond. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A consultation may be conducted in any way the body pleases, however inadequate.
A consultation is required to reach the outcome that the majority of consultees prefer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A lawful consultation must be at a formative stage, give sufficient information and time, and the responses must be conscientiously taken into account.
There is no requirement to consider the responses received to a consultation.
A consultation is lawful provided at least one person is asked for their view.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Where a public body consults (whether by choice or by legal duty), the consultation must be fair: undertaken when proposals are still at a formative stage, giving sufficient reasons and information to permit intelligent consideration and response, allowing adequate time, and the product of the consultation must be conscientiously taken into account (the Gunning/Sedley criteria).

n.0: A consultation cannot be conducted in any inadequate way; it must be fair.
n.1: The body need not simply adopt the majority view, but must genuinely consider responses.
n.3: Responses must be conscientiously considered.
n.4: Asking one person is not a fair consultation.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: In litigation against the government, a party seeks disclosure of documents, but the government resists on the ground that disclosing them would cause real harm to an important public interest, such as national security. A solicitor is asked about the basis on which the government may seek to withhold relevant documents from disclosure in the public interest. The solicitor considers public interest immunity. The documents were plainly relevant, but the government said releasing them would harm the public interest. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Public interest immunity is decided solely by the government minister with no role for the court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Public interest immunity may allow documents to be withheld where the public interest in non-disclosure outweighs disclosure.
Relevant documents can never be withheld from disclosure on any public interest ground.
Public interest immunity applies only to documents held by private companies.
The government may withhold any document it wishes simply by asserting it is confidential.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Public interest immunity may justify withholding otherwise disclosable documents where the public interest in withholding them (for example national security or the proper functioning of the public service) outweighs the public interest in disclosure. The court, not the government alone, weighs the competing interests and decides.

n.0: The court, not solely the minister, decides PII.
n.2: Documents can be withheld on PII grounds where justified.
n.3: PII concerns public interest documents, typically held by public bodies, not only private companies.
n.4: A mere assertion of confidentiality is not enough; the court balances the interests.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A newly enacted Act of Parliament changes the law in a way that some consider undesirable, and a campaigner argues that a court should strike the Act down as invalid because it conflicts with earlier legislation and with what they say the constitution requires. A solicitor is asked about the fundamental principle governing the status of an Act of Parliament in the UK constitution. The solicitor considers the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty. The campaigner insisted the courts had power to overturn any statute they thought went too far. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An Act of Parliament is valid only if it is approved by the general public in a referendum.
An Act of Parliament can be overridden by an earlier statute that conflicts with it.
The courts may strike down any Act of Parliament they consider to be unwise or unconstitutional on these facts.
Parliament cannot change the law without the consent of the courts and the monarch personally.
Parliament may make or unmake any law, and the courts cannot strike down a validly enacted Act of Parliament.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can make or unmake any law, no Parliament can bind its successors, and the courts cannot strike down or refuse to apply a validly enacted Act of Parliament (they interpret and apply it).

n.0: A referendum is not a condition of the validity of an Act.
n.1: A later Act prevails over an earlier conflicting one (implied repeal), not the reverse.
n.2: The courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament for being unwise or unconstitutional.
n.3: Parliament does not need the courts' consent to legislate.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A government minister makes a piece of delegated (secondary) legislation, such as a statutory instrument, under powers conferred by a parent Act of Parliament. A claimant argues that the statutory instrument goes beyond what the parent Act authorises. A solicitor is asked whether, and how, secondary legislation can be challenged in the courts, in contrast to primary legislation. The solicitor considers the status and review of secondary legislation. The instrument appeared to go well beyond anything the parent Act had actually authorised. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Secondary legislation can never be challenged in the courts under any circumstances.
Secondary legislation is valid only if approved by the public in a referendum.
Secondary legislation has exactly the same immunity from challenge as an Act of Parliament on these facts as a general rule.
Secondary legislation may be challenged only by another government minister.
Secondary legislation may be challenged and quashed by the courts if it is ultra vires the parent Act, unlike primary legislation.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Unlike an Act of Parliament, secondary (delegated) legislation is not protected by parliamentary sovereignty. It may be challenged by judicial review and quashed if it is ultra vires — outside the powers conferred by the parent Act — or made for an improper purpose or in breach of other public law principles.

n.0: Secondary legislation can be challenged in the courts.
n.1: Secondary legislation does not require a referendum to be valid.
n.2: Secondary legislation does not share the immunity of primary legislation.
n.3: Challenge is not confined to government ministers.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A member of the public is confused about the role of the monarch in modern government, having read that the monarch formally opens Parliament, gives royal assent to legislation, and appoints the Prime Minister. A solicitor is asked to explain the constitutional position of the monarch in the UK today. The solicitor considers the role of the Crown as a constitutional monarch. The member of the public assumed the monarch still ran the country on a day-to-day basis. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The monarch may veto legislation and dismiss governments at personal discretion whenever they wish on these facts.
The monarch has no role of any kind in the modern constitution.
The monarch personally decides the outcome of legal disputes in the courts.
The monarch is a constitutional monarch who acts on ministerial advice, exercising largely formal and ceremonial functions.
The monarch personally governs the country and makes all the key political decisions.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The UK is a constitutional monarchy: the monarch is head of state but by convention acts on the advice of ministers. The monarch's functions (such as giving royal assent, opening Parliament and formally appointing the Prime Minister) are largely formal and ceremonial, with real political power exercised by the elected government.
