n.0: By convention the monarch does not veto legislation or dismiss governments at personal whim.
n.1: The monarch has an established, if largely formal, constitutional role.
n.2: The monarch does not decide court cases.
n.4: The monarch does not personally govern or make key political decisions.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A solicitor is explaining the historical relationship between EU law and domestic law during the period of the UK's membership of the European Union, and how conflicts between the two were resolved at that time. A student asks how the courts dealt with a UK statute that conflicted with directly effective EU law while the UK was a member. The solicitor considers the supremacy of EU law as it operated during membership. The student was trying to grasp how conflicts were handled back when the UK was still a member. Which of the following best describes it?
o: During membership, directly effective EU law took precedence over conflicting domestic law, which the courts would disapply.
During membership, the monarch personally decided whether EU or domestic law applied on these facts as a general rule.
During membership, domestic statutes always prevailed over any conflicting EU law.
EU law never had any effect in the UK even during the period of membership.
During membership, conflicts were resolved by a public vote in each case.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: During the UK's membership of the EU, by virtue of the European Communities Act 1972 and cases such as Factortame, directly effective EU law took precedence over conflicting domestic legislation, and the courts would disapply the conflicting domestic provision. This relationship ended on the UK's withdrawal.

n.1: The monarch did not personally resolve such conflicts.
n.2: Domestic statutes did not always prevail over EU law during membership.
n.3: EU law did have effect in the UK during membership.
n.4: Conflicts were resolved by the supremacy principle, not a public vote.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A tribunal or public body makes a decision based on a misunderstanding or misapplication of the law — an error of law — which affects the outcome. A claimant challenges the decision by judicial review. A solicitor is asked whether such an error is a basis for the courts to intervene, and how it relates to jurisdiction. The solicitor considers error of law as a ground of judicial review. The tribunal had plainly misunderstood the legal test it was required to apply to the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An error of law by a public body can never be corrected by the courts.
An error of law is generally reviewable; since Anisminic most such errors are treated as going to jurisdiction.
The courts may correct only errors of fact and never errors of law.
An error of law is reviewable only where the body admits that it made a mistake.
Errors of law are relevant only in appeals and can never be raised in judicial review on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: An error of law is a form of illegality and is generally reviewable. Following Anisminic and later authority, most errors of law made by a public body or tribunal are treated as taking it outside its jurisdiction, rendering the decision a nullity, so the courts can quash the decision.

n.0: Errors of law can be corrected by the courts.
n.2: The courts review errors of law (more readily than errors of fact).
n.3: Review does not depend on the body admitting its mistake.
n.4: Errors of law can be raised in judicial review, not only on appeal.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A newly elected government seeks to pass legislation implementing a specific promise contained in the manifesto on which it won the general election. The House of Lords is considering how to treat the Bill at second reading. The Bill gives effect to a government manifesto commitment. The Lords is deciding whether to block it. The government won the election on a platform that expressly promised this very measure, the Bill simply enacts that pledge, and the Lords, weighing whether to vote it down at second reading, must reckon with a long-standing understanding about how the unelected chamber treats manifesto commitments. Which of the following best describes the relevant constitutional convention?
o: By convention manifesto Bills bypass both Houses entirely.
By convention the monarch decides whether manifesto Bills proceed.
By convention the Commons must obtain the Lords' consent to any manifesto Bill on these facts as a general rule.
By the Salisbury convention, the Lords will not normally block a Bill implementing a government manifesto commitment.
By convention the Lords must block any Bill it disagrees with on principle.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: By the Salisbury convention, the House of Lords does not normally vote against, or wreck, a Bill at second reading that seeks to implement a commitment in the governing party's election manifesto. It reflects respect for the electoral mandate of the elected government and the primacy of the Commons.

n.0: Manifesto Bills still pass through the parliamentary process; they do not bypass both Houses.
n.1: The monarch does not decide whether manifesto Bills proceed.
n.2: The convention supports manifesto Bills proceeding, not requiring Lords' consent to them.
n.4: The convention restrains, rather than requires, the Lords blocking such Bills.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: The government proposes to take a significant action, such as entering into a treaty with another state or deploying the armed forces, relying on powers that do not derive from any statute. A commentator asks what the legal source of such powers is. The powers are non-statutory executive powers exercised in the name of the Crown. The government relies on them for foreign affairs and defence. The government is proposing to do something significant on the international and defence stage, entering a treaty or committing the armed forces, and points out that it relies for this not on any Act of Parliament but on longstanding powers exercised in the name of the Crown, prompting the question of their legal source. Which of the following best describes the source of these powers?
o: The direct authority of the electorate expressed at a general election.
The inherent legislative power of the courts to authorise executive action.
The royal prerogative, comprising residual non-statutory powers of the Crown exercised by ministers.
A general statutory power conferred on ministers by a single Act of Parliament on these facts.
The powers of the devolved legislatures acting collectively.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Actions such as making treaties, conducting foreign affairs, deploying the armed forces, and granting mercy derive from the royal prerogative: the residue of non-statutory powers historically vested in the Crown, now exercised in practice by ministers. The prerogative is subject to the courts' supervision and can be displaced by statute.

n.0: The powers derive from the Crown's prerogative, not directly from the electorate.
n.1: The courts do not confer such executive powers; they supervise their exercise.
n.3: These powers are prerogative powers, not a single general statutory power.
n.4: They are central executive prerogative powers, not powers of the devolved legislatures.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A government bill has passed through the House of Commons and the House of Lords and is in its final stages before becoming law. A member of the public asks a solicitor how a bill becomes an Act of Parliament, and what the final step is that turns it into law. The solicitor considers the legislative process for primary legislation. The bill had cleared both Houses and everyone was waiting for the final step to make it law. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A bill becomes law as soon as it is introduced into the House of Commons.
A bill becomes an Act once it has passed both Houses (or the Commons under the Parliament Acts) and received royal assent.
A bill becomes an Act only if it is approved by the public in a referendum.
A bill becomes law once a government minister signs it, without any parliamentary stages on these facts as a general rule.
A bill becomes an Act only if the courts confirm that it is constitutional.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: A public bill generally passes through readings and committee and report stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords (with the Parliament Acts allowing the Commons to proceed in limited circumstances without the Lords' consent), and becomes an Act of Parliament (law) once it receives royal assent.

n.0: A bill is not law merely on introduction; it must complete its stages and receive royal assent.
n.2: A referendum is not a general requirement for a bill to become an Act.
n.3: A minister's signature does not turn a bill into law; parliamentary stages and royal assent are required.
n.4: The courts do not confirm the constitutionality of Acts as a condition of validity.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A government minister proposes to detain individuals without any legal authority and to deny them access to the courts to challenge their treatment, arguing that the executive should be free to act as it sees fit. A solicitor is asked which fundamental constitutional principle this proposal offends, given that it involves acting without legal authority and removing access to justice. The solicitor considers the rule of law. The minister claimed the executive should be free to act without any check from the courts. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The rule of law requires that all laws be approved by the courts before they take effect.
The rule of law applies only to private individuals and never to the government or its ministers.
The rule of law requires that power be exercised according to law, that no one is above the law, and that people have access to the courts.
The rule of law means that the government may do whatever it considers to be in the public interest on these facts as a general rule.
The rule of law means that the executive is entirely above and immune from the ordinary law.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: The rule of law requires, among other things, that governmental power be exercised in accordance with the law, that everyone (including the government) is subject to and equal before the law, that the law is applied by independent courts, and that individuals have access to justice to challenge unlawful action.

n.0: The rule of law does not require the courts to pre-approve all legislation.
n.1: The rule of law applies to the government as well as to individuals.
n.3: The rule of law constrains the government to act within the law, not simply as it thinks best.
n.4: The executive is subject to the law, not above it.

Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.q: A claimant succeeds in judicial review and, in addition to having the unlawful decision quashed, wishes to recover financial compensation for losses caused by the public body's unlawful decision. A solicitor is asked whether damages can be awarded simply because a decision was unlawful in public law. The solicitor considers the availability of damages in judicial review. The claimant had lost money as a result of the decision and hoped to recover it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages can never be recovered in connection with any public law decision.
Damages are not available in judicial review merely for unlawfulness; a recognised private law cause of action (or HRA claim) is required.
Damages are automatically awarded to a successful claimant in every judicial review claim.
Damages are the standard remedy in judicial review and require no separate cause of action on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Damages are awarded in judicial review purely at the claimant's request.
Constitutional, Administrative & EU Law.w: Damages are not available in judicial review simply because a public body has acted unlawfully. A claimant can recover damages only if they can establish a recognised private law cause of action (such as a tort) or a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998, in addition to the public law unlawfulness.

n.0: Damages can be recovered where a private law or HRA claim is made out.
n.2: Damages are not automatic on success in judicial review.
n.3: A separate cause of action (or HRA claim) is required for damages.
n.4: Damages are not awarded merely on request; a legal basis is required.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is asked to give a professional undertaking to a third party as part of a fast-moving transaction. The particular wording proposed by the other side is loose and open to more than one interpretation, and part of what it appears to promise in fact depends upon the actions of other people over whom the solicitor has no control at all. Keen to keep the deal moving and not to be seen as obstructive, the solicitor is tempted simply to sign the undertaking as drafted and to worry about its precise meaning and effect later on. A more experienced colleague advises caution. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Undertakings must be clear and unambiguous, and any ambiguity will be interpreted against the solicitor who gave it.
The solicitor may sign a loosely worded undertaking, provided they privately intend to perform only part of it.
An undertaking may safely promise the acts of third parties, since the solicitor is not answerable for those.
The precise wording of an undertaking does not matter, because undertakings are not strictly enforced anyway.
Any ambiguity in an undertaking will always be interpreted in favour of the solicitor who gave it.
Legal Services.w: Because undertakings are binding and enforceable, they should be drafted clearly and precisely. Any ambiguity is generally construed against the giver, and a solicitor should not undertake to procure the acts of people beyond their control, so loose wording should be resisted.

n.1: A private intention to perform only part of a signed undertaking does not limit its binding effect.
n.2: A solicitor should not give an undertaking dependent on the acts of third parties they cannot control.
n.3: The wording matters greatly; undertakings are strictly enforced.
n.4: Ambiguity is construed against the giver, not in their favour.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is conducting a piece of civil litigation for a client and expects to appear as the advocate at the forthcoming trial in order to keep the client's costs down. As the case develops, however, it becomes clear that the solicitor personally witnessed a key event that is now in dispute between the parties, and is therefore very likely to be called to give evidence about it as a material witness at that same trial. The solicitor would still prefer to carry on as the advocate as well, to save the client the expense of instructing counsel. The solicitor considers whether this is proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may act as advocate and witness, provided doing so saves the client the cost of counsel.
The solicitor may always act as both advocate and witness, because the two roles never come into any conflict.
The solicitor should not act as advocate at the trial if they are likely to be a material witness in the same case.
The solicitor may act as advocate and witness, provided the evidence they give is entirely truthful.
The solicitor may act as advocate and witness, provided the client gives written consent to the arrangement.
Legal Services.w: Acting as advocate while also being a material witness undermines the independence of the advocate and risks damaging the administration of justice, because the advocate's own credibility is in issue. The solicitor should not take on both roles in the same case.

n.0: Saving costs does not justify combining the roles of advocate and material witness.
n.1: The roles do conflict where the advocate's own evidence and credibility are in issue.
n.3: The truthfulness of the evidence does not remove the difficulty of combining the two roles.
n.4: Client consent does not cure the risk to the administration of justice.

Legal Services.q: The SRA opens an investigation into a firm's handling of client money and writes to a solicitor at the firm, formally requiring the solicitor to provide certain documents and to explain in writing what actually happened. The solicitor is worried about what the documents may reveal about their own conduct, and is tempted either simply to ignore the request altogether, or else to give the SRA an account that quietly plays down the problems and leaves out the most damaging facts. The solicitor considers what the conduct rules require of them in dealing with their own regulator. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may ignore the SRA's request, because a solicitor is under no duty to assist an investigation into themselves.
The solicitor must cooperate with the SRA, provide the information it properly requires, and must not mislead it.
The solicitor may give a partial account, provided nothing they positively state is actually untrue.
The solicitor must respond only after first obtaining the consent of the firm's other partners.
The solicitor need respond only if the SRA first obtains a court order compelling them to do so.
Legal Services.w: Solicitors must be open and cooperative with their regulator. They must provide information the SRA reasonably requires, respond to its enquiries, and must not mislead or attempt to mislead the SRA, whether by positive misstatement or by omission of material facts.

n.0: There is a positive duty to cooperate with the regulator, even in an investigation into oneself.
n.2: Playing down the problems by omission still amounts to misleading the SRA.
n.3: The duty to respond does not depend on the other partners' consent.
n.4: A court order is not a precondition to the duty to provide information the SRA properly requires.

Legal Services.q: A person who has never qualified as a solicitor, and who is not on the roll of solicitors or the holder of any practising certificate, sets up in business advising members of the public on their legal problems for a fee. In marketing that business, the person repeatedly describes themselves to clients and prominently on their website as a 'solicitor', genuinely believing that, because they give legal advice for a living, they are entitled to use the title. A qualified solicitor is asked whether an unqualified person may lawfully describe themselves as a solicitor in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided they make clear that they are not regulated by the SRA.
The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided their clients do not object to their doing so.
Only a person on the roll with a current practising certificate may practise as, or hold themselves out as, a solicitor.
Anyone who gives legal advice to the public may lawfully describe themselves as a solicitor to their clients.
The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided they do not carry out any court work for their clients.
Legal Services.w: The title 'solicitor' is protected. It is an offence for an unqualified person wilfully to pretend to be, or to take or use any name or title implying that they are, a solicitor. Only those on the roll with a practising certificate may practise as, or hold out as, solicitors.

n.0: A disclaimer about SRA regulation does not permit an unqualified person to use the title.
n.1: The clients' lack of objection does not legitimise holding out as a solicitor.
n.3: Giving legal advice does not entitle a person to the protected title of solicitor.
n.4: Avoiding court work does not make the misuse of the title lawful.

Legal Services.q: A firm conducting personal injury work is offered payments by a claims management company in return for the referral of personal injury clients to the firm, and considers whether it may pay or receive such referral fees. The work is a personal injury claim. Referral fees are proposed in connection with it. A claims management company offers the firm payments in exchange for steering personal injury clients its way, and the firm, doing this kind of work, must decide whether paying or pocketing such referral fees is something it is allowed to do in the personal injury context. Which of the following best describes the position on referral fees in this context?
o: Referral fees in relation to personal injury claims are prohibited, so the firm must not pay or receive them.
Referral fees are permitted in personal injury cases without any restriction.
Referral fees are always permitted provided they are disclosed to the client on these facts as a general rule.
Referral fees are permitted provided they are paid to the SRA.
Referral fees are prohibited only where the client objects to them.
Legal Services.w: Under section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, referral fees in relation to personal injury claims are prohibited: regulated persons must not pay or be paid a referral fee in connection with such claims. In other areas referral arrangements may be permitted subject to conduct requirements such as disclosure and independence.

n.1: Referral fees in personal injury claims are restricted (prohibited), not unrestricted.
n.2: Disclosure does not make referral fees lawful in personal injury claims; they are prohibited.
n.3: Referral fees are not made lawful by paying them to the SRA.
n.4: The prohibition applies regardless of whether the client objects.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor learns, in confidence from a client, information suggesting that a third party is at risk of serious physical harm. The solicitor is bound by the duty of confidentiality but is considering whether disclosure may exceptionally be justified to prevent that harm. The information was received in confidence. There is a risk of serious harm to another. In confidence, the client has let slip information suggesting that someone else faces a real risk of serious physical harm, and the solicitor, bound as a rule to keep the client's confidences, is wrestling with whether this is one of the rare situations in which disclosure can be justified. Which of the following best describes when confidentiality may be overridden here?
o: Confidentiality may be overridden whenever the solicitor personally thinks it would be convenient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Confidentiality may be overridden where disclosure is justified to prevent serious physical or mental harm, or is otherwise permitted or required by law.
Confidentiality can never be overridden in any circumstances whatsoever.
Confidentiality may be overridden only with the client's express consent in every case.
Confidentiality automatically ends as soon as any third party is mentioned.
Legal Services.w: The duty of confidentiality is fundamental but not absolute. It may be overridden in limited circumstances, including where disclosure is required or permitted by law, or where the solicitor reasonably believes disclosure is necessary to prevent the client or a third party committing a serious criminal offence or causing serious physical or mental harm. Disclosure should be limited to what is necessary.

n.0: Mere convenience does not justify breaching confidentiality.
n.2: Confidentiality can be overridden in limited circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: The harm and legal exceptions do not depend on the client's consent.
n.4: Confidentiality is not lost merely because a third party is mentioned.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor faces a situation where acting in the client's immediate best interests would require conduct that undermines the proper administration of justice. The solicitor must decide which of the SRA Principles takes precedence, as two Principles appear to pull in different directions. The client's interests and the public interest in the administration of justice conflict. The solicitor must resolve the clash of Principles. The solicitor is caught between what the client wants and the wider demands of the justice system, with two of the SRA Principles apparently pointing in opposite directions, and needs to know which of them must give way when they cannot both be honoured at once. Which of the following best describes how the SRA Principles are prioritised?
o: Where two or more Principles conflict, the one that best serves the wider public interest (especially the rule of law and administration of justice) takes precedence.
All the Principles rank equally and a conflict between them cannot be resolved.
The solicitor may choose whichever Principle produces the best outcome for the client.
The Principle requiring the solicitor to act in the client's best interests always takes precedence over all others on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The most recently published Principle automatically overrides the earlier ones.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Principles must be complied with, but where two or more come into conflict, the Principle which takes precedence is the one that best serves the wider public interest, in particular the public interest in the proper administration of justice and upholding the rule of law. The duty to the client does not override these wider public interest duties.

n.1: The Principles are not all equal in a conflict; there is an order of priority.
n.2: The solicitor cannot simply pick the Principle best for the client.
n.3: The client's best interests do not always take precedence; wider public interest Principles prevail.
n.4: Priority does not depend on which Principle was most recently published.

Legal Services.q: Having formed a genuine suspicion of money laundering in relation to a client's property transaction, a solicitor duly makes a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency and awaits the appropriate consent before proceeding any further. Shortly afterwards the client telephones the solicitor to chase progress and to ask why completion is being delayed. Wanting to give a helpful explanation, the solicitor is tempted to tell the client that a report has been made and that the matter is on hold while consent is awaited. The solicitor pauses to consider whether saying this to the client would itself be a criminal offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must tell the client about the report, so that the client can explain the source of funds.
The solicitor may freely tell the client about the report, because the client is entitled to know of it.
The solicitor may tell the client, provided the solicitor does not mention the National Crime Agency by name.
The solicitor may tell the client, because tipping off only applies to disclosures made to third parties.
The solicitor risks committing the offence of tipping off by telling the client that a report has been made.
Legal Services.w: Under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, it is the offence of 'tipping off' to disclose that a suspicious activity report has been made where that disclosure is likely to prejudice any resulting investigation. The solicitor must therefore not alert the client to the report.

n.0: There is no duty to tell the client of the report; doing so is prohibited.
n.1: The client is not entitled to be told of the report; disclosing it risks the tipping-off offence.
n.2: Omitting the agency's name does not save a disclosure that reveals a report has been made.
n.3: Tipping off includes alerting the very person whose transaction was reported.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is instructed to recover a substantial unpaid commercial debt for a client. In order to increase the pressure on the debtor to pay up quickly, the solicitor proposes writing to the debtor to say that, unless the outstanding sum is paid in full within seven days, the client will report the debtor to the police for fraud. The alleged fraud is wholly unconnected with the recovery of the debt and would be raised only as a lever to force a settlement of the civil dispute. The solicitor asks a colleague whether this course of action is proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must not do this, as it is improper to threaten criminal proceedings merely to gain an advantage in a civil matter.
The solicitor may do this, because any lawful pressure that helps to recover the client's money is entirely permitted.
The solicitor may do this, because reporting a suspected crime to the police is always in the wider public interest.
The solicitor may do this, provided the alleged fraud is something that the client genuinely and reasonably suspects.
The solicitor may do this only if counsel first advises that making the threat is reasonable in the circumstances.
Legal Services.w: It is a breach of professional conduct to use, or threaten to use, criminal or regulatory proceedings solely to obtain an advantage in a civil dispute. This amounts to taking unfair advantage and does not serve the proper administration of justice.

n.1: Not all pressure is legitimate; threatening criminal action as leverage in a civil matter is improper.
n.2: The threat here is made to gain civil advantage, not out of a genuine public-interest report.
n.3: A genuine suspicion does not make it proper to deploy the threat as leverage in the civil dispute.
n.4: Counsel's approval cannot make an improper threat proper.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor whose practice consists entirely of residential conveyancing is asked by a regular and valued client to take on a complex and highly specialised immigration appeal, an area of law in which the solicitor has had no training, supervision or experience whatsoever. Anxious not to lose the client's goodwill or to send the work elsewhere, the solicitor accepts the instruction and attempts to handle the appeal personally, without obtaining any assistance, training or supervision, and makes a series of serious errors as a result. The client complains about the poor standard of the service they received. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor breached only the duty of confidentiality by handling the client's sensitive immigration information.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, because errors of judgement can never amount to a regulatory breach.
The solicitor acted properly, provided the client was told the solicitor usually does only conveyancing work.
The solicitor breached the duty to provide a competent service, as they must only act on matters within their competence.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor is qualified to take on any type of legal work for a client.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires a solicitor to provide a competent service and to maintain their competence, which includes only carrying out work they are competent to do, or obtaining appropriate supervision or expertise. Taking on unfamiliar, specialised work unaided breaches that duty.

n.0: The failing here is competence and standard of service, not confidentiality.
n.1: A serious failure to provide a competent service can indeed be a regulatory breach.
n.2: A general warning about the firm's usual work does not cure the lack of competence to do this matter.
n.4: Being a qualified solicitor does not mean being competent in every field of law.

Legal Services.q: Part-way through a straightforward matter, a solicitor becomes frustrated with a client who is slow to respond to requests for information, and decides that they would simply rather not continue acting for that client. There is no conflict of interest, the client is fully up to date with the firm's bills, and there is nothing at all improper about the instructions the client has given; the solicitor has just lost enthusiasm for the work. The solicitor proposes to stop acting straight away, without any notice, leaving the client to find another firm. The solicitor asks whether they may terminate the retainer in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may only cease acting where there is good reason to do so and on giving the client reasonable notice.
The solicitor may never cease acting once instructed, and must see every matter through to its conclusion.
The solicitor may cease acting at any time and for any reason, as a retainer is terminable instantly at will.
The solicitor may cease acting immediately, provided the client is sent a final bill for the work done so far.
The solicitor may cease acting without notice, provided another firm has already agreed to take the matter on.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor may only stop acting for a client where there is good reason to do so and on reasonable notice, so as not to leave the client's interests unprotected. Mere reluctance to continue, without good reason or notice, does not justify terminating the retainer.

n.1: A solicitor is not bound to continue in every case; they may cease acting for good reason on notice.
n.2: A retainer is not terminable instantly at will for any reason; good reason and reasonable notice are required.
n.3: Sending a final bill does not, by itself, satisfy the requirements of good reason and reasonable notice.
n.4: Another firm's willingness to take over does not dispense with the need for good reason and proper notice.

Legal Services.q: A firm takes on a new corporate client, a private limited company, on a substantial commercial property purchase, and must complete customer due diligence before it starts work. The fee-earner obtains and verifies the identity of the single director who is giving the firm its instructions, and treats that as sufficient to satisfy the firm's obligations. In fact the company is owned and ultimately controlled, behind the scenes, by several other individuals whose identities the fee-earner has not checked or even asked about. The firm's money laundering reporting officer reviews the file. Which of the following best describes what due diligence requires here?
o: Beneficial owners need only be identified if the company is based in another country entirely.
Due diligence on a company client requires identifying and verifying its beneficial owners.
No due diligence is needed on a company at all, because only individual clients present a money laundering risk.
Verifying the director who gives instructions is always enough, because a company acts only through its directors.
It is enough to note the company's registered number, without identifying any of the individuals behind it.
Legal Services.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require, for a corporate client, that the firm identifies and takes reasonable measures to verify the company's beneficial owners — broadly, individuals who ultimately own or control it — as well as the person giving instructions.

n.0: The duty to identify beneficial owners is not confined to overseas companies.
n.2: Companies are within the money laundering regime; corporate clients are not exempt.
n.3: Verifying the instructing director does not satisfy the requirement to identify the beneficial owners.
n.4: Noting the registered number does not identify the individuals who own or control the company.

Legal Services.q: A fee-earner receives, through the post, a cheque representing completion monies which are client money held on behalf of a client. Instead of banking the cheque, the fee-earner simply leaves it sitting in the matter file for around two weeks before it is finally paid into the client account, purely because the file is busy and other work keeps taking priority over it. The money is not spent, misdirected or used by the firm at any point during that period. The firm's compliance officer later reviews the file and raises the delay. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Client money need only ever be banked once the matter to which it relates has been fully completed and billed.
Client money may be held outside a client account indefinitely, provided that it is eventually banked at some point.
The delay is acceptable in these circumstances, because the money was not spent or misapplied during the period.
A cheque is not client money until it has actually cleared, so no accounts rule was engaged by the delay here.
Client money must be paid promptly into a client account, so leaving the cheque unbanked for around two weeks was a breach.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be paid promptly into a client account. A cheque representing client money must be banked without delay; holding it for around two weeks is a breach even though the money was not misapplied.

n.0: The obligation to bank promptly does not wait until the matter completes.
n.1: Client money cannot be held outside a client account indefinitely; it must be banked promptly.
n.2: The absence of misapplication does not excuse the failure to bank the money promptly.
n.3: Money received as client money is client money on receipt; the promptness obligation is not deferred until clearance.

Legal Services.q: A firm is instructed by two clients jointly on a single matter, both of them having exactly the same interest in it at the outset of the retainer. Part-way through the work, however, the two clients fall out badly and begin to take directly opposing positions, so that advancing the interests of one of them would now clearly damage the interests of the other. The fee-earner would much prefer to carry on acting for both, since the firm has already done a great deal of work on the matter, and asks whether the firm may properly continue. Which of the following best describes the firm's position under the conflict of interest rules?
o: The firm may continue to act for both, provided that neither client objects to the arrangement in writing.
The firm may continue to act for both, as a conflict between existing clients can always be managed by a barrier.
A conflict has now arisen, so the firm must stop acting for at least one, and usually both, of the clients.
The firm may continue to act for both of the clients, because it was originally retained by them together jointly.
The firm may simply continue acting for whichever of the two clients is prepared to pay it the higher fee.
Legal Services.w: Where a conflict of interest arises between two clients and no exception applies, the solicitor must cease acting for one or both. An information barrier does not cure a conflict between clients' own competing interests in the same matter.

n.0: Absence of a written objection does not remove the conflict.
n.1: An information barrier does not cure a conflict of interest between two clients in the same matter.
n.3: An original joint retainer does not entitle the firm to continue once the clients' interests conflict.
n.4: The firm cannot resolve a conflict by preferring the higher-paying client.

Legal Services.q: A firm holds confidential information from a former client that is material to a new client's matter, and there is a risk to that confidential information if it acts for the new client. The firm wishes to act for the new client and considers putting arrangements in place to protect the former client's confidential information. The firm owes a continuing duty of confidentiality to the former client. The firm wishes to act for the new client. The firm still holds confidential information from a former client that bears directly on a new client's matter, and, wanting to take on the new client without betraying the old one, it is weighing whether erecting internal safeguards would be enough to let it act consistently with its continuing duty of confidentiality. Which of the following best describes when the firm may act using an information barrier?
o: The firm may act provided it charges the new client a higher fee.
The firm may act only if effective safeguards (an information barrier) protect the confidential information and, generally, the affected clients give informed consent.
The firm may act only if the former client's matter has fully concluded, with no further safeguards needed on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm may act freely because the duty of confidentiality ends when the retainer ends.
The firm may never act for a new client whose matter relates to a former client.
Legal Services.w: The duty of confidentiality continues after the retainer ends. A firm must not act for a new client against a former client where it holds confidential information material to the new matter, unless effective safeguards (such as an information barrier separating those with the information) protect the confidentiality and, generally, informed consent is obtained. The former client's confidentiality outweighs the new client's interest in disclosure.

n.0: Charging a higher fee does not address the confidentiality risk.
n.2: Mere conclusion of the former matter, without safeguards, does not make it safe to act.
n.3: The duty of confidentiality does not end with the retainer; it continues.
n.4: The firm may act in some cases with proper safeguards, so 'never' is too absolute.

Legal Services.q: A firm in the regulated sector takes on a new client who holds a prominent public position (or is a close associate of such a person), which the firm's risk assessment identifies as carrying a higher money laundering risk. The client is a politically exposed person for anti-money-laundering purposes. The firm must apply the appropriate level of due diligence. The new client holds a prominent public office, or is closely connected to someone who does, and the firm's risk assessment flags the relationship as carrying a heightened money laundering risk, prompting the firm to consider what level of due diligence and monitoring it must apply. Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation?
o: The firm must apply enhanced due diligence and ongoing monitoring, given the higher risk posed by a politically exposed person.
The firm need carry out no due diligence at all on a public figure.
The firm may apply simplified due diligence because such clients are inherently low risk on these facts as a general rule.
The firm must report the client to the NCA merely for being a public figure.
The firm must refuse to act for any politically exposed person in every case.
Legal Services.w: Under the money laundering regulations, a politically exposed person (PEP), or a family member or close associate of one, presents a higher risk, so the firm must apply enhanced due diligence measures, including senior approval to act, establishing the source of wealth and funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring. Acting is not prohibited, but heightened scrutiny is required.

n.1: Due diligence is required, not dispensed with, for a PEP.
n.2: Simplified due diligence is inappropriate; PEPs are higher, not lower, risk.
n.3: Being a PEP does not, by itself, warrant a suspicious activity report to the NCA.
n.4: Acting for a PEP is not prohibited; enhanced due diligence is required.

Legal Services.q: A firm has carried out full customer due diligence on a client at the very start of a transaction that falls within the money laundering regime, obtaining and carefully recording evidence of the client's identity and of the source of the funds being used. The transaction then completes without incident and the file is closed. A fee-earner, tidying up the office and short of storage space, proposes to destroy all of the due diligence records straight away, on the basis that the matter is now completely finished. The firm's money laundering reporting officer intervenes. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm need not keep any due diligence records at all once identity has originally been verified.
The firm must keep the due diligence records for about five years after the relationship ends.
The firm need keep the records only until the client's next matter, whenever that happens to be.
The firm may destroy the due diligence records immediately, because the transaction has now completed.
The firm must keep the records permanently and may never destroy them under any circumstances.
Legal Services.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require firms to keep records of the customer due diligence carried out, and of the transaction, for a prescribed period (broadly five years) after the business relationship ends or the transaction is completed, so records must not be destroyed immediately.

n.0: Records of the due diligence must be kept, not merely the fact that identity was once checked.
n.2: Retention is measured by the prescribed period, not by whenever the client next instructs the firm.
n.3: Completion of the transaction does not permit immediate destruction of the records.
n.4: Permanent retention is not required; the obligation is to keep them for the prescribed period.

Legal Services.q: During a case management hearing, a solicitor makes a statement of fact to the court, on the client's instructions, which the solicitor genuinely and reasonably believes to be true at the time it is made. Later that same day, on reviewing newly received documents, the solicitor discovers that the statement was in fact false, so that the court has been misled on a point that is material to the issues it must decide. When the solicitor explains this to the client, the client refuses to allow the position to be corrected, insisting that the court be left with the false impression. The solicitor considers what they must now do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may leave the false impression uncorrected, provided the solicitor personally says nothing further about it.
The solicitor may correct the statement only if the opposing party first notices the error and raises it.
The solicitor need do nothing, because the statement was made in good faith and was believed true at the time.
The solicitor must at once disclose the client's confidential explanation to the court to put the record straight.
The solicitor must not allow the court to remain misled and, if the client will not consent to correction, must cease to act.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor who realises the court has been misled, even innocently, must not allow that state of affairs to continue. They should seek the client's consent to correct it; if the client refuses, the solicitor must cease to act, but must not disclose privileged information to the court.

n.0: Staying silent while the court remains misled is itself a breach of the duty to the court.
n.1: The duty to act does not wait until the other side happens to spot the error.
n.2: Good faith at the time does not excuse leaving the court misled once the truth is known.
n.3: The solicitor cannot disclose the client's privileged explanation to the court.

Legal Services.q: A firm holds a sum of money in the client account on behalf of a client, out of which the firm intends to take payment of its own professional fees for the work it has carried out on the matter to date. A fee-earner, keen to get the firm paid without delay, proposes simply transferring the amount of the firm's costs straight out of the client account and into the firm's own office account, without first sending the client any bill or other written notification of the costs being charged. The firm's compliance officer questions whether this may be done. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money may be moved from the client account to the office account for costs only after a bill has been delivered to the client.
The firm may take its costs from the client account first and deliver a bill to the client at some later date.
The firm may never take its own costs from money held in the client account in any circumstances at all.
The firm may take its costs from the client account without a bill, provided the amount taken is reasonable.
The firm may transfer its costs from the client account at any time, since the money is held for that client anyway.
Legal Services.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, money held for a client may be transferred to the office account in respect of the firm's costs only once a bill of costs or other written notification of the costs incurred has been given to the client.

n.1: The bill must precede the transfer, not follow it.
n.2: The firm may properly take costs from client money, but only after delivering a bill.
n.3: Reasonableness of the amount does not dispense with the requirement for a bill first.
n.4: Holding the money for the client does not permit taking costs before a bill is delivered.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is instructed to act for both the borrower and the lender on the grant of a mortgage over a residential property, on the footing that their interests are aligned and only the lender's standard terms are involved. During the transaction the lender gives the solicitor certain confidential instructions which, if they were disclosed to the borrower, would seriously prejudice the borrower's position, and it becomes clear that the interests of borrower and lender have begun to diverge. The solicitor realises they can no longer act fairly for both at the same time. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?
o: The solicitor may continue acting for both, because acting for borrower and lender together is always permitted.
The solicitor may continue for both, provided the solicitor privately decides which client's interests to prefer.
The solicitor may pass the lender's confidential instructions to the borrower to keep both clients fully informed.
The solicitor may continue for both, because a mortgage transaction cannot as a matter of law give rise to a conflict.
A conflict has arisen, with confidentiality and disclosure duties clashing, so the solicitor must stop acting for at least one.
Legal Services.w: Acting for borrower and lender is permissible only while their interests are aligned. Once a conflict arises and the duty of confidentiality to one client cannot be reconciled with the duty of disclosure to the other, the solicitor must cease acting for at least one of them.

n.0: Acting for borrower and lender is not always permitted; it depends on their interests remaining aligned.
n.1: The solicitor cannot secretly prefer one client while purporting to act for both.
n.2: The solicitor cannot disclose one client's confidential instructions to the other.
n.3: A mortgage transaction can give rise to a conflict once interests diverge.

Legal Services.q: A client instructs a solicitor to transfer the client's only substantial asset, a valuable property, into the sole name of a relative for no payment at all, and tells the solicitor quite frankly that the entire purpose of doing so is to put the property beyond the reach of the client's creditors, who are about to enforce a large judgment against the client. The client insists that the solicitor carry out the transfer straight away and without asking any questions. The solicitor recognises that giving effect to the instruction would involve them in unlawful conduct. Which of the following best describes how the solicitor must respond?
o: The solicitor may carry out the transfer, provided the relative is unaware of the client's true purpose.
The solicitor must refuse to act on the instruction and, if the client insists, must cease to act altogether.
The solicitor must carry out the transfer, because a solicitor is bound to follow the client's lawful instructions.
The solicitor may carry out the transfer, provided the client signs a written statement accepting all responsibility.
The solicitor may carry out the transfer, provided the creditors have not yet actually obtained their judgment.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must not act where doing so would involve them in a breach of the law or a failure to uphold the rule of law. A transfer designed to defraud creditors is improper, so the solicitor must refuse to give effect to it and must cease acting if the client insists.

n.0: The relative's ignorance of the purpose does not cure the impropriety of the transaction.
n.2: The duty to follow instructions is confined to lawful instructions; this instruction is not lawful.
n.3: A client-signed acceptance of responsibility does not make it proper for the solicitor to assist an unlawful purpose.
n.4: The transaction is objectionable regardless of the precise stage the creditors' claim has reached.

Legal Services.q: A member of the public attends a solicitor for an initial, exploratory meeting to discuss whether or not to instruct the firm on a sensitive and difficult dispute. During that meeting they disclose a good deal of confidential information about their situation and their opponent. In the end, however, they decide not to instruct the firm at all, and no retainer is ever entered into. Some time later, the firm is approached by the opposing side in that very same dispute and asked to act for them. The firm considers what duties, if any, it owes in respect of the information the prospective client disclosed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The duty lapses automatically as soon as the person decides not to instruct the firm.
The information may be freely used, provided the firm does not charge the prospective client for the meeting.
No duty of confidentiality arises at all, because the person never actually became a client of the firm.
The duty of confidentiality applies to a prospective client's information, even if they never instruct the firm.
A duty arises only if the firm expressly promised, at the meeting, to keep the information confidential.
Legal Services.w: The duty of confidentiality attaches to information imparted in confidence, including by a prospective client at an initial meeting, whether or not a retainer is ultimately entered into. The firm must protect that information and be alert to any resulting conflict.

n.0: Deciding not to instruct the firm does not release the information from confidentiality.
n.1: Whether or not a fee was charged is irrelevant to the duty of confidentiality.
n.2: Confidentiality does not depend on the person actually becoming a client.
n.4: The duty arises from the confidential nature of the information, not from an express promise.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is acting for a client in negotiating the settlement of a contractual dispute with an opponent who is not represented by any lawyer and who is plainly unfamiliar with the relevant legal position. In the course of the negotiations the solicitor realises that the opponent has seriously misunderstood their own rights, in a way that happens to be very favourable to the solicitor's client, and the solicitor is tempted to exploit that misunderstanding in order to extract particularly harsh settlement terms. The solicitor asks how they may properly deal with the unrepresented opponent. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may exploit the opponent's misunderstanding fully, because the solicitor's only duty is to their own client.
The solicitor must not take unfair advantage of the opponent, but may still act in the client's interests without advising the opponent.
The solicitor may take advantage of the opponent, provided nothing said to the opponent is actually untrue.
The solicitor must refuse to deal with the opponent at all until the opponent instructs their own solicitor.
The solicitor must give the unrepresented opponent full legal advice so that both sides are on an equal footing.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code prohibits a solicitor from taking unfair advantage of any person, including an unrepresented opponent. The solicitor may still pursue the client's legitimate interests, but must not exploit the opponent's lack of understanding, while also not acting as the opponent's adviser.

n.0: A duty to the client does not permit taking unfair advantage of the opponent.
n.2: Taking unfair advantage can occur even where nothing untrue is said.
n.3: There is no duty to refuse to deal with an unrepresented opponent altogether.
n.4: The solicitor should not advise the opposing party; they are not the solicitor's client.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is taking instructions from an elderly client whose ability to understand and make decisions about the matter appears to be in doubt. The solicitor must ensure they act only on the proper instructions of a client able to give them. There are indications the client may lack capacity for this decision. The solicitor is considering how to proceed. The elderly client's grasp of the matter and ability to weigh the decision seem shaky, and the solicitor, who may only act on a client's proper instructions, has to decide how to satisfy themselves that the client can actually give the instructions being sought before acting on them. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's obligation?
o: The solicitor may take instructions from a relative instead without further inquiry on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor must satisfy themselves that the client has the mental capacity to give the instructions before acting on them.
The solicitor must refuse to act for any elderly client as a matter of course.
The solicitor must obtain a court order before acting for any client.
The solicitor may always act on whatever the client says, regardless of capacity.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must act in the client's best interests and on the client's proper instructions, which requires the client to have the mental capacity to give those instructions for the particular decision. Where capacity is in doubt, the solicitor must satisfy themselves that the client has capacity (obtaining a medical or other assessment if needed) before acting, applying the Mental Capacity Act principles.

n.0: A relative cannot simply substitute their instructions without proper authority.
n.2: Age alone is not a reason to refuse to act; capacity must be assessed.
n.3: A court order is not routinely required to act for a client.
n.4: The solicitor cannot act on instructions the client lacks capacity to give.

Legal Services.q: A successful non-lawyer entrepreneur wishes to invest in, and to take a substantial ownership stake in, a new business that will provide legal services directly to the public, and also to sit on its management board, working alongside the qualified solicitors who will actually carry out the legal work. The entrepreneur has been told by an acquaintance that non-lawyers are completely barred from owning any part of a legal practice in England and Wales. A solicitor is asked whether there is in fact any lawful structure through which a non-lawyer may own and help to manage a provider of legal services. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This is permitted only if the non-lawyer first qualifies as a solicitor before taking any ownership stake.
This is permitted only where the non-lawyer holds a minority stake of no more than a fixed small percentage.
This is permitted through a licensed alternative business structure (ABS), which allows non-lawyers to own and manage it.
This is not permitted in any circumstances, because only qualified lawyers may ever own a legal services provider.
This is permitted without any regulation, because ownership of legal businesses is entirely unrestricted.
Legal Services.w: The Legal Services Act 2007 introduced alternative business structures (ABSs), which may be licensed to allow non-lawyers to own and manage bodies providing legal services, subject to approval and regulation. Non-lawyer ownership is therefore possible, but only through a licensed and regulated ABS.

n.0: The non-lawyer need not qualify as a solicitor; the ABS regime permits their involvement.
n.1: There is no fixed small percentage cap; a licensed ABS can permit substantial non-lawyer ownership.
n.3: Non-lawyer ownership is possible through a licensed ABS, so it is not barred outright.
n.4: Ownership of legal businesses is regulated, not unrestricted; a licence is required.

Legal Services.q: A partner at a mid-sized firm is concerned about a claim that has just been intimated by a former client of the firm. An employed solicitor at the firm made a serious drafting error in a commercial agreement some months ago, and as a direct result the client has suffered a substantial financial loss and now threatens to sue the firm for professional negligence. The partner wants to know whether the firm's compulsory professional indemnity insurance must respond to a claim of this kind, given that the mistake was made by an employee rather than by one of the partners personally. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The insurance responds only where the loss suffered by the client exceeds a fixed statutory minimum figure.
The insurance need not respond, because a firm's policy only ever covers negligence committed personally by the partners.
The firm's professional indemnity insurance must respond, as compulsory cover extends to civil liability for employees' negligence.
The insurance responds only if the client can first prove that the employee acted dishonestly rather than carelessly.
The insurance need not respond, because professional indemnity cover is entirely optional for solicitors' firms.
Legal Services.w: The SRA's rules require firms to hold professional indemnity insurance meeting minimum terms and conditions, covering civil liability arising from the practice, including liability for the negligent acts of the firm's employees. Such a claim therefore falls within the compulsory cover.

n.0: There is no loss threshold that the client must exceed before the cover responds.
n.1: Cover is not limited to the partners' own acts; it extends to liability for employees' negligence.
n.3: The cover responds to negligence; it does not depend on proving dishonesty.
n.4: Professional indemnity insurance meeting the minimum terms is compulsory, not optional.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is making an urgent application to the court, without notice to the other side, for a freezing injunction over a defendant's assets before those assets can be dissipated. Because the defendant will have no opportunity to be heard before the order is made, the solicitor is aware that a special obligation attaches to the way in which the application must be presented to the judge. There are certain facts, known to the solicitor, which are distinctly unhelpful to the applicant's case, and the solicitor is tempted simply to leave those facts out of the material put before the court. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's duty?
o: The solicitor need present only the facts that support the applicant's case, as in any ordinary contested hearing.
The solicitor may omit the adverse facts, provided they would in any event have come out at a later hearing.
The solicitor must give full and frank disclosure of all material facts, including any adverse to the applicant.
The solicitor may omit the adverse facts, provided the applicant genuinely believes the injunction is justified.
The solicitor may present a one-sided case, because the defendant can always apply later to set the order aside.
Legal Services.w: On a without-notice application, the applicant's advisers owe a duty of full and frank disclosure to the court, which requires them to draw the court's attention to all material facts, including those adverse to the applicant, since the other side is not present to do so.

n.0: A without-notice application is not an ordinary contested hearing; adverse facts must be disclosed.
n.1: The duty is not excused because the facts might emerge later.
n.3: The applicant's belief in the merits does not permit withholding material adverse facts.
n.4: The availability of a later set-aside application does not justify a one-sided presentation.

Legal Services.q: In the course of administering a deceased's estate, a solicitor is asked by the executors to advise on and arrange the sale of a portfolio of shares held by the estate and to reinvest the proceeds in specific named financial products chosen by the beneficiaries. This work would involve carrying on activities that are regulated under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, and the firm itself is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. The solicitor wants to know on what basis, if any, the firm may lawfully carry out this investment work for the estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may carry out the work simply because it is being done in the course of administering an estate.
The firm may do such work only if authorised, or the activity is exempt as incidental to its legal services.
The firm may never carry out any activity that is regulated under the Act in any circumstances whatsoever.
The firm may carry out any financial services work it wishes, because solicitors are wholly outside the scope of the Act.
The firm may carry out the work, provided the client signs a written waiver of the statutory protections involved.
Legal Services.w: Carrying on a regulated activity under FSMA 2000 requires FCA authorisation, unless it is an exempt regulated activity carried on incidentally to the provision of legal services and supervised by the SRA under Part XX. Estate administration does not automatically bring the work outside the regime.

n.0: Doing the work within an estate does not, by itself, make it exempt from the regime.
n.2: Firms can carry on some regulated activities through the exempt regime, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Solicitors are not outside FSMA; they must be authorised or fall within the exempt regime.
n.4: A client waiver cannot displace the statutory authorisation requirements.

Legal Services.q: In the course of acting, a firm receives a commission from a third party (for example, from a financial provider) in connection with the client's matter. The firm wishes to keep the commission. The commission arises out of work done for the client. The firm considers its obligations regarding the commission. In the course of the retainer the firm has picked up a commission from a third party connected with the client's matter, and, tempted to keep it, must first work out what its duty to the client requires it to do about a payment that has arisen out of the work it is doing for that client. Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation?
o: The firm must refuse all commissions in every circumstance.
The firm must always pay any commission to the SRA.
The firm may keep the commission provided it is less than the firm's fees on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm must account to the client for the commission unless the client has given informed consent to the firm keeping it.
The firm may keep any commission received without telling the client.
Legal Services.w: A firm must properly account to the client for any commission received in the course of acting for the client, arising out of that work. It may only retain the commission if the client has given informed consent to it doing so. Silently keeping a commission would breach the duties to act in the client's best interests and with integrity.

n.0: The firm need not refuse all commissions; it may retain them with informed consent.
n.1: Commission is accounted for to the client, not paid to the SRA.
n.2: Retention is not permitted merely because the commission is smaller than the fees; informed consent is required.
n.4: The firm cannot silently keep a commission without informing the client.

Legal Services.q: An authorised firm is required to designate individuals with specific responsibility for compliance. One is responsible for the firm's compliance with its regulatory obligations generally, and another for compliance with the accounts rules. The firm is an authorised body and must appoint compliance officers. The roles cover general regulatory compliance and accounts compliance respectively. As an authorised body the firm has to allocate formal responsibility for compliance, one person overseeing its regulatory obligations at large and another its handling of client money, and the firm wants to identify the two designated roles the rules require it to fill. Which of the following best describes these roles?
o: The SRA appoints the firm's compliance officers on its behalf.
The firm must have a Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP) and a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA).
Compliance officers are required only for firms that are alternative business structures.
A single partner automatically holds all compliance responsibilities without formal designation on these facts as a general rule.
The firm need not appoint any compliance officers at all.
Legal Services.w: An authorised firm must have a Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP), responsible for compliance with the firm's authorisation and regulatory obligations and for recording and reporting breaches, and a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA), responsible for compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules. Both must be approved by the SRA.

n.0: The firm nominates its compliance officers (subject to SRA approval); the SRA does not appoint them.
n.2: COLP and COFA are required for authorised firms generally, not only ABSs.
n.3: The roles must be formally designated and SRA-approved, not automatically assumed.
n.4: Compliance officers are required; the firm cannot simply have none.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor acting on a transaction has formed a genuine suspicion of money laundering and, through the firm's nominated officer, a suspicious activity report seeking a defence (consent) has duly been submitted to the National Crime Agency. The relevant statutory period for a response has not yet expired, and no consent has so far been given or refused. The client, who knows nothing of the report, is meanwhile pressing very hard for the transaction to complete without any further delay at all. The solicitor considers whether they may go ahead and complete the transaction in the meantime. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may proceed immediately, because submitting the report is by itself enough to allow completion.
The solicitor may proceed, provided the client signs a declaration accepting responsibility for the funds.
The solicitor may proceed, provided the transaction is completed within the firm rather than through a bank.
The solicitor may proceed, because a client is always entitled to have their transaction completed on time.
The solicitor must not proceed with the transaction until the appropriate consent is given or the statutory period expires.
Legal Services.w: Where a defence (consent) has been sought under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, the person must not carry out the prohibited act until consent is granted or the statutory notice/moratorium period has expired. Proceeding beforehand risks committing a money laundering offence.

n.0: Merely submitting the report does not permit completion; consent or expiry of the period is required.
n.1: A client declaration does not remove the statutory prohibition on proceeding.
n.2: Where the transaction completes is irrelevant to the prohibition on proceeding.
n.3: The client's wish for timely completion does not override the statutory prohibition.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor becomes aware of facts which indicate a serious breach of the SRA's regulatory arrangements, whether by the solicitor's own firm or by another person. The solicitor is considering their reporting obligations to the regulator. The facts are capable of amounting to a serious breach. The solicitor must consider their duty to report. The solicitor has come across facts that look capable of amounting to a serious breach of the regulatory arrangements, whether by their own firm or by someone else in the profession, and is considering exactly what their duty to the regulator requires them to do about it. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's obligation?
o: The solicitor need only report serious breaches once a year in a routine return.
The solicitor must never report another person to the SRA, only their own conduct on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The solicitor may report only breaches that have caused actual financial loss.
The solicitor has no duty to report any breach unless the SRA asks first.
The solicitor must report promptly to the SRA facts they reasonably believe capable of amounting to a serious breach of the regulatory arrangements.
Legal Services.w: Solicitors and firms are under a duty to report promptly to the SRA (or otherwise ensure it is informed of) any facts or matters that they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the SRA's regulatory arrangements, whether committed by themselves or others. There is also a duty to cooperate with, and not mislead, the SRA.

n.0: Serious breaches must be reported promptly, not merely in an annual return.
n.1: The duty extends to serious breaches by others, not only one's own conduct.
n.2: Reporting is not limited to breaches causing actual financial loss.
n.3: The duty to report does not depend on the SRA asking first.

Legal Services.q: A commercial client asks a solicitor to draw up a written contract and to date it as though it had been signed some weeks earlier than it is in fact going to be signed, so that the client can then tell a third party that the agreement was already in place at that earlier date. The effect of backdating the document in this way would be to give the third party a false impression about when the contract truly came into existence. The client presents the request as no more than a harmless administrative convenience. The solicitor considers whether they may properly do as the client asks. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Backdating the document to give a false impression would breach the duty to act with integrity and must not be done.
The solicitor may backdate the document, provided no third party is likely ever to discover the true date.
The solicitor may backdate the document, because the date on a contract is a mere formality of no real effect.
The solicitor may backdate the document, because a solicitor must carry out the client's lawful instructions.
The solicitor may backdate the document, provided the client accepts responsibility for any consequences.
Legal Services.w: Backdating a document so as to give a false impression to a third party offends the SRA Principles requiring solicitors to act with integrity and honesty, and to uphold public trust. The solicitor must not do it, whatever the client's instructions.

n.1: The likelihood of discovery is irrelevant; the conduct lacks integrity regardless.
n.2: The date is not a mere formality where it is used to create a false impression.
n.3: The duty to act on instructions does not extend to producing a misleading, backdated document.
n.4: The client accepting responsibility does not make it proper for the solicitor to act without integrity.

Legal Services.q: A firm is instructed by a new client who holds a prominent public office in an overseas government, and who is therefore a politically exposed person, and whose funds for the matter are being routed to the firm through a jurisdiction that is well known to present a high risk of money laundering. The fee-earner proposes simply to carry out the firm's standard identity checks, on the basis that exactly the same procedure is applied to every single client the firm takes on. The firm's money laundering reporting officer questions whether standard checks are really sufficient in a case like this. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm need carry out no due diligence at all, because a person holding public office is inherently trustworthy.
The firm need only carry out its standard due diligence, because the same checks apply to every client alike.
The firm must carry out enhanced due diligence, because this situation presents a higher risk of money laundering.
The firm may carry out reduced due diligence, because a public official's identity is a matter of public record.
The firm may proceed without further checks, provided the client signs a declaration about the source of the funds.
Legal Services.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require enhanced due diligence in higher-risk situations, including where the client is a politically exposed person or funds involve a high-risk jurisdiction. Standard checks are not sufficient in such cases.

n.0: Holding public office is a risk factor for enhanced checks, not a reason to omit them.
n.1: Higher-risk situations require more than the standard level of due diligence.
n.3: Being a public figure does not justify reduced due diligence; the opposite applies.
n.4: A client declaration does not replace the required enhanced due diligence.

Legal Services.q: An elderly client instructs a solicitor to prepare a new will and explains that they wish to leave a very substantial legacy to the solicitor personally, as a mark of gratitude for many years of good service. The proposed gift is significant, both in absolute terms and in the context of the size of the client's estate. The solicitor is perfectly willing to prepare the will and is confident that the client is acting entirely of their own free will, but is unsure how to proceed with the gift in a way that is professionally proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must refuse the instruction outright and may never prepare a will that benefits the solicitor in any way.
The solicitor may prepare the will including the gift, provided a colleague in the same firm witnesses the client sign it.
The solicitor must advise the client to take independent legal advice, and decline to act if they do not.
The solicitor may prepare the will including the gift, provided the solicitor is satisfied that the client is acting freely.
The solicitor may accept the gift without any special step, because a client is always free to benefit their own solicitor.
Legal Services.w: Where a client proposes to make a significant gift (including by will) to the solicitor or someone connected to the solicitor, the Code requires the solicitor to advise the client to take independent legal advice, and to decline to act on that gift if the client does not do so.

n.0: The rule requires independent advice, not an absolute refusal in every case.
n.1: A colleague witnessing the signing does not satisfy the requirement for independent legal advice.
n.3: The solicitor's own satisfaction that the client acts freely does not replace the need for independent advice.
n.4: A significant gift to the solicitor is not something to accept without the safeguard of independent advice.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is running a matter for a client on an hourly-rate basis, and the fees are steadily mounting month by month. The solicitor privately forms the clear and settled view that the client's claim now has very poor prospects of success and is really no longer worth continuing, but deliberately says nothing to the client about any of this. Instead the solicitor continues to encourage the client to press on, and keeps on billing, precisely because the ongoing work is profitable for the firm.
