The client later discovers just how weak the claim always was. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor breached only the rules on client money by continuing to render bills for the work.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor is entitled to keep earning fees for as long as a client will pay them.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, provided the work that was actually billed was genuinely carried out.
The solicitor breached the duties of honesty and best interests by concealing the poor prospects while continuing to bill.
The solicitor acted properly, because it is always for the client alone to decide whether to continue a claim.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must act with honesty and integrity and in the client's best interests. Deliberately withholding advice about the poor prospects of the claim, so as to keep generating fees, breaches those duties, whatever the client would ultimately have decided.

n.0: The core failing is the dishonest withholding of advice, not merely a client-money matter.
n.1: The entitlement to charge does not permit keeping the client in the dark to generate fees.
n.2: That the billed work was done does not excuse concealing the claim's true prospects.
n.4: Although the decision is the client's, it must be an informed one; the solicitor must give the advice.

Legal Services.q: In the course of acting on a residential property purchase, a solicitor becomes genuinely suspicious that the money the client is using to fund the transaction represents the proceeds of crime. The client is pressing hard for the purchase to complete as quickly as possible and is impatient at any suggestion of delay. The solicitor is conscious of the various obligations imposed on them by the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and wants to be clear about how they must act before taking any further step in the matter. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor must do?
o: Take no action at all unless and until the sum involved exceeds a fixed statutory reporting threshold amount.
Make a suspicious activity report to the NCA, do not proceed without consent, and avoid tipping off the client.
Proceed with the purchase as normal, because legal professional privilege prevents any disclosure to the authorities.
Immediately tell the client of the suspicion, so that the client has a chance to explain the source of the funds.
Simply return the funds to the client and close the file, without taking any other step in relation to the matter.
Legal Services.w: Under POCA 2002, a person who suspects money laundering must make a suspicious activity report to the NCA, obtain appropriate consent before proceeding, and must avoid tipping off. Privilege does not protect communications made to further a criminal purpose.

n.0: There is no minimum threshold that removes the reporting obligation once suspicion is formed.
n.2: Privilege does not extend to the iniquity here and does not permit the solicitor to proceed regardless.
n.3: Telling the client of the suspicion risks the criminal offence of tipping off.
n.4: Simply returning the funds and closing the file does not discharge the reporting duty and may itself tip off the client.

Legal Services.q: A firm is keen to attract new clients and prepares an advertising campaign to run across its website and its social media channels. The draft marketing material prominently claims that the firm has 'the highest success rate of any firm in the country' and offers every client a 'guaranteed win or your money back'. In truth the firm cannot substantiate either statement, and both of them are inaccurate and likely to mislead members of the public who read them. A partner reviewing the campaign before it goes live is concerned about whether the firm may lawfully publish these claims. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm's publicity must not be false or misleading, so the unsubstantiated claims breach the rules and must not be published.
The firm may publish the claims, provided the firm genuinely hopes that they will turn out to be true.
The firm may publish the claims, provided a disclaimer in small print appears somewhere on the website.
The firm may publish the claims, because advertising by law firms is not subject to any professional restrictions.
The firm may publish the claims, because clients are expected to treat all advertising with healthy scepticism.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires that a firm's publicity is not false or misleading. Unsubstantiated or inaccurate claims of this kind are misleading and breach the rules, regardless of any disclaimer or the firm's hopes.

n.1: A hope that claims may prove true does not make publishing inaccurate claims proper.
n.2: A small-print disclaimer does not cure headline claims that are false or misleading.
n.3: Law firm advertising is subject to professional rules and must not mislead.
n.4: The rule against misleading publicity does not depend on how sceptical clients are.

Legal Services.q: A client instructs a firm on a contested commercial matter that is likely to be both lengthy and expensive to run to trial. At no point does the fee-earner give the client any estimate of the likely overall cost, any explanation of how the firm's fees will be calculated, or any update as the costs steadily mount over the following months. When the matter concludes the client receives a very large final bill and is genuinely shocked, having had no idea that the work would cost anything approaching that amount. The client complains about the complete lack of any costs information. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor acted properly, provided the fees charged were reasonable for the work actually carried out.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor is never required to estimate costs before the work is finished.
The solicitor breached only the rules on client money by delivering a single bill at the very end.
The solicitor breached the duty to give the client the best possible information about the likely overall cost of the matter.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, because the client could have asked about the costs at any time.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires a solicitor to give clients the best possible information about the likely overall cost of a matter, both at the outset and as it progresses, so the client can make informed decisions. Providing no costs information at all breaches that duty.

n.0: Charging a reasonable fee does not cure the failure to give proper costs information.
n.1: A solicitor is required to give costs information at the outset and updates, not only at the end.
n.2: The breach concerns costs information and client care, not the client money rules.
n.4: The duty to inform rests on the solicitor; it is not answered by saying the client could have asked.

Legal Services.q: A firm of solicitors that is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority wishes to give its clients a certain amount of advice on investments as part of the wider legal services it provides, for example when winding up deceased persons' estates or advising on the division of assets in matrimonial settlements. A partner simply assumes that, because the firm is a firm of solicitors, it must be free to carry on any investment work it likes as an ordinary part of its practice. The firm seeks advice on the basis, if any, on which such activities may lawfully be carried on. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may carry on any investment activities it wishes, simply because it is a firm of solicitors.
The firm is completely barred from any investment activity unless it becomes authorised by the FCA.
The firm may carry on investment activities freely, provided it does not charge a separate fee for them.
The firm may do such work only if it is incidental to its legal services and SRA-compliant.
The firm may carry on investment activities, provided each client signs a waiver of FCA protection.
Legal Services.w: A firm without FCA authorisation may only carry on 'exempt regulated activities' under Part 20 FSMA where they arise out of, or are complementary to, the provision of legal services, and it complies with the SRA's financial services rules as a profession supervised by a designated professional body.

n.0: Being a firm of solicitors does not permit unrestricted investment work.
n.1: The firm is not wholly barred; the exempt regime allows incidental activities.
n.2: Not charging separately does not remove the need to fall within the exempt regime.
n.4: A client waiver cannot substitute for the statutory and regulatory basis required.

Legal Services.q: In the course of ongoing litigation, the opposing party's solicitors write to demand disclosure of the written legal advice which a solicitor had earlier given to their own client about the merits and weaknesses of the client's case. That advice was given confidentially, in writing, for the sole purpose of advising the client on the very dispute now before the court. The client is anxious that the advice should not be handed over to the other side, and the solicitor must explain the legal basis on which it can properly be withheld. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The advice must be disclosed, because there is no protection for communications passing between a solicitor and a client.
The advice must be disclosed, because the professional duty of confidentiality never applies once litigation has begun.
The advice may be withheld only if the solicitor personally objects to disclosing their own work to opponents.
The advice is protected by legal professional privilege, which belongs to the client.
The advice may be withheld only until the opposing party offers to keep it confidential in return.
Legal Services.w: Confidential communications between a solicitor and client made for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice attract legal professional privilege. The privilege belongs to the client and cannot be overridden by an opponent without the client's waiver.

n.0: Solicitor–client advice communications are protected, so they are not disclosable as of course.
n.1: Privilege is not lost simply because litigation has commenced.
n.2: The protection is the client's privilege, not a matter of the solicitor's personal objection.
n.4: Withholding does not depend on the opponent agreeing to keep the advice confidential.

Legal Services.q: A new client instructs a firm on the purchase of a residential property and, on the very first attendance, offers to pay £5,000 towards the firm's fees in cash. The fee-earner, keen to get the matter moving, accepts the cash without carrying out any check on the client's identity and without making any enquiry at all into the source of the funds, and the transaction then proceeds towards exchange. Some weeks later the firm's money laundering reporting officer reviews the file and questions the way in which the retainer was set up. Which of the following best explains the breach under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017?
o: Customer due diligence under the Regulations is only required where the client is a company rather than an individual person.
Due diligence checks are optional in any case where the firm expects a long-standing relationship with the client.
A solicitor is entitled to assume that a new client is honest and so need not carry out any identity checks on them.
Customer due diligence, including identity checks, is mandatory here for conveyancing, so accepting the funds without them was a breach.
Cash payments below £10,000 are exempt, so no customer due diligence was required before accepting the money on these facts.
Legal Services.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require customer due diligence, including identity verification, when a business relationship is established in a relevant activity such as conveyancing. There is no blanket cash threshold that removes the obligation on these facts.

n.0: Customer due diligence applies to individual clients as well as to companies.
n.1: An expected long relationship does not dispense with due diligence at the outset.
n.2: A solicitor may not simply assume honesty; the Regulations require positive verification.
n.4: There is no general exemption for cash under £10,000 that removes the CDD obligation here.

Legal Services.q: An elderly client attends a solicitor's office to give instructions for a substantial lifetime gift of money to a recent acquaintance. During the meeting the client appears increasingly confused, cannot consistently recall who the acquaintance actually is, and gives shifting and contradictory reasons for wishing to make the gift, leaving the solicitor with real and growing doubts about whether the client genuinely understands what they are proposing to do. The solicitor considers how they ought to proceed in the face of these doubts about the client's mental capacity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may proceed on the acquaintance's assurance that the client knows exactly what they are doing.
The solicitor must satisfy themselves that the client has capacity and take appropriate steps to protect a client who may lack it.
The solicitor must simply carry out the instructions, because every adult client is presumed to have capacity absolutely.
The solicitor may proceed, provided a member of the client's family is willing to approve the gift instead.
The solicitor must refuse to have any further dealings at all with a client who shows any sign of confusion.
Legal Services.w: While capacity is presumed, a solicitor who has real doubts must not simply act on the instructions. They must take appropriate steps to assess the client's capacity to make the particular decision (for example obtaining a medical opinion) and act so as to protect a client who may lack capacity.

n.0: The acquaintance who benefits is not a reliable source of assurance about the client's capacity.
n.2: The presumption of capacity is rebuttable and does not require the solicitor to ignore clear warning signs.
n.3: A family member cannot supply the client's own capacity to make the decision.
n.4: Signs of confusion call for appropriate steps, not an outright refusal to deal with the client.

Legal Services.q: In the course of a hard-fought piece of civil litigation, a solicitor repeatedly misses court-imposed deadlines and turns up to hearings without having prepared properly, causing several hearings to be adjourned and putting the opposing party to significant additional and entirely unnecessary legal costs. The opposing party is understandably aggrieved by all this and applies to the court for an order that the solicitor personally, rather than the solicitor's own client, should bear the extra costs that the solicitor's conduct has caused. The court considers the application. Which of the following best describes the court's power?
o: The court has no power to order a solicitor personally to pay costs, which can only ever fall on the litigant client.
The court may order the solicitor to pay costs only where the solicitor is shown to have acted dishonestly.
The court may order the solicitor to pay costs only if the client first formally complains about the solicitor's conduct.
The court may make a wasted costs order against the solicitor personally for their improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct.
The court may penalise the solicitor only by reporting the matter to the SRA, and not by any order for costs.
Legal Services.w: Under the court's wasted costs jurisdiction, a legal representative may be ordered to pay costs personally where those costs have been caused by the representative's improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission. Dishonesty is not required.

n.0: The court can order a legal representative personally to pay wasted costs; the liability is not confined to the client.
n.1: Improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct suffices; dishonesty need not be shown.
n.2: A wasted costs order does not depend on a prior complaint by the client.
n.4: A wasted costs order is itself a costs sanction, separate from any regulatory referral.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is faced with a difficult situation in which two of the SRA Principles pull in opposite directions. Acting in the way the client is pressing for would serve the solicitor's duty to act in the client's best interests; but doing so would at the same time undermine the solicitor's duty to uphold the rule of law and the proper administration of justice. The solicitor cannot possibly satisfy both duties at once, and must decide which of the two competing Principles should take precedence in resolving the dilemma. Which of the following best describes how a conflict between the Principles is to be resolved?
o: The Principle that best serves the public interest, especially the public interest in the proper administration of justice, takes precedence.
The most recently introduced of the conflicting Principles automatically takes precedence over the older one.
The Principle requiring the solicitor to act in the client's best interests always takes precedence over every other Principle.
Neither Principle applies once they conflict, so the solicitor is free to act however they think best.
The solicitor may simply choose whichever of the two conflicting Principles they personally consider the more important.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Principles provide that, where two or more Principles come into conflict, the one which takes precedence is the one that best serves the wider public interest, and in particular the public interest in the proper administration of justice.

n.1: Precedence does not turn on which Principle is newer.
n.2: The duty to the client does not automatically override the wider public interest Principles.
n.3: A conflict does not disapply the Principles; one of them must be given precedence on the public-interest test.
n.4: Resolution is not a matter of personal preference; the public-interest test governs.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor who is advising a client on a property purchase recommends that the client use a particular surveying company to carry out the survey of the property. What the solicitor does not tell the client is that the solicitor personally owns a substantial shareholding in that very surveying company, and so stands to benefit financially if the client goes on to instruct it. The recommendation is presented to the client as entirely impartial professional advice about the best firm to use for the job. The solicitor considers whether this is a proper way to proceed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may keep the interest private, because a solicitor is free to recommend any business they choose.
The solicitor may keep the interest private, provided the surveying company does competent work for the client.
The solicitor must disclose the financial interest and must not act where that interest conflicts with the client's own interests.
The solicitor has no obligation at all, because recommending other businesses falls outside professional regulation.
The solicitor may keep the interest private, provided the client is not actually charged any more as a result.
Legal Services.w: An undisclosed financial interest in a business the solicitor recommends creates an own-interest conflict and undermines the independence of the advice. The solicitor must disclose the interest and must not act where that interest conflicts, or risks conflicting, with the client's interests.

n.0: The freedom to recommend does not extend to concealing a personal financial interest.
n.1: Competent work by the recommended firm does not cure the undisclosed conflict of interest.
n.3: Recommending businesses in which the solicitor has an interest is subject to the conduct rules.
n.4: The absence of extra charge does not remove the conflict or the duty to disclose.

Legal Services.q: Two clients wish to instruct the same firm in relation to the same asset or objective which they are both trying to acquire, so that they are effectively competing with each other. There is a conflict of interest between them, but the clients ask whether the firm may nonetheless act for both. The clients are competing for the same objective. The firm is considering the conflict of interest rules. Two would-be clients each want the firm to help them secure the very same asset, so that in substance they are bidding against one another, and although that plainly sets up a conflict between them, they are asking whether the firm can nonetheless act for both under one of the recognised exceptions. Which of the following best describes when the firm may act for both despite the conflict?
o: The firm may act for both only with the permission of the SRA in each case.
The firm may act for both only if it charges each of them the same fee.
The firm may never act for two clients who have any conflict of interest in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm may always act for both clients regardless of any conflict.
The firm may act for both under the competing-for-the-same-objective exception, if the safeguards including informed consent and confidentiality are met.
Legal Services.w: Generally a firm must not act where there is a conflict of interest, but there are two exceptions. One applies where the clients are competing for the same objective (such as bidding for the same asset). The firm may then act for both if the conditions are met, including that the clients have given informed written consent, effective safeguards protect confidential information, and it is reasonable to act.

n.0: The exception does not require case-by-case SRA permission.
n.1: Acting for both does not turn on charging identical fees.
n.2: There are exceptions; it is not the case that a firm can never act where there is a conflict.
n.3: A firm cannot always act despite a conflict; the exception's conditions must be satisfied.

Legal Services.q: A fee-earner working on a transaction at a firm forms a genuine suspicion that a client may be engaged in money laundering. The fee-earner is unsure of the correct first step to take, and wonders whether they should personally telephone the National Crime Agency straight away, or perhaps put the concern directly to the client, or simply do nothing at all for the time being. The firm, like most firms of its size, has appointed a nominated officer to handle exactly these matters internally. The fee-earner considers what they are actually required to do first. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The fee-earner must make an internal report to the firm's nominated officer, who then decides whether to report to the NCA.
The fee-earner should first put the concern to the client, to give them a chance to explain matters.
The fee-earner should simply record the suspicion on the file and take no further action of any kind.
The fee-earner must personally report the suspicion directly to the National Crime Agency without telling anyone at the firm.
The fee-earner need do nothing at all unless and until the nominated officer specifically asks them about it.
Legal Services.w: Within a firm that has a nominated officer (MLRO), an individual who suspects money laundering discharges their obligation by making an internal report to that nominated officer, who then considers whether an external suspicious activity report to the NCA is required. The fee-earner must not tip off the client.

n.1: Putting the concern to the client risks the offence of tipping off.
n.2: Merely noting the suspicion on the file, without an internal report, does not discharge the duty.
n.3: In a firm with a nominated officer, the internal report goes to that officer, not directly and secretly to the NCA.
n.4: The fee-earner has a positive duty to report the suspicion internally, not to wait to be asked.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is employed in the legal department of a large commercial company as an in-house solicitor, and holds a current practising certificate. A dispute arises between the company and one of its major suppliers which is likely to end up in contested court proceedings. The company wishes its own in-house solicitor to conduct that litigation on the company's behalf, so as to save the cost of instructing an external firm to do the work. The solicitor is unsure whether, as an employed solicitor rather than one in private practice, they are actually permitted to conduct litigation for their employer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An employed solicitor may act for their employer only in non-contentious matters, and never in any litigation.
An employed solicitor may conduct the litigation only if the company also instructs an external firm alongside them.
An employed solicitor may act for their employer, including conducting litigation on the employer's behalf.
An employed solicitor may conduct the litigation only after obtaining the SRA's specific prior permission to do so.
An employed solicitor may never conduct litigation, because that is reserved to solicitors in private practice.
Legal Services.w: An employed (in-house) solicitor who holds a practising certificate may provide legal services to, and act for, their employer, including exercising rights of audience and conducting litigation on the employer's behalf. Restrictions mainly concern acting for third parties, not for the employer itself.

n.0: The in-house solicitor's ability to act for the employer is not limited to non-contentious work.
n.1: There is no requirement to instruct an external firm alongside the in-house solicitor.
n.3: No specific prior SRA permission is required to act for the employer in this way.
n.4: Conducting litigation is not reserved to those in private practice; in-house solicitors may do it for their employer.

Legal Services.q: A client instructs a firm on the all-cash purchase of an expensive property and, when asked to do so, is able to prove their identity without any difficulty at all. However, the very large sum of money being used to fund the purchase appears wholly out of keeping with what little the firm knows of the client's apparently modest means, and the client becomes noticeably evasive whenever the subject of where the money has actually come from is gently raised. The fee-earner is satisfied as to identity and is minded to proceed on that basis alone. Which of the following best describes what the firm must do?
o: The firm may proceed, provided the purchase price is paid to the firm by way of a bank transfer.
The firm may proceed, because the source of a client's funds is never any concern of the solicitor.
The firm may proceed, because a client who can prove their identity is presumed to be acting honestly.
The firm need do nothing further, because verifying the client's identity is all that the Regulations ever require.
The firm must obtain evidence of the source of the funds, and not simply rely on having verified the client's identity.
Legal Services.w: Customer due diligence is risk-sensitive and, where the circumstances suggest a higher risk, extends beyond identity to scrutinising and obtaining evidence of the source of the client's funds. Unexplained wealth inconsistent with the client's profile is a classic warning sign requiring further enquiry.

n.0: Payment by bank transfer does not answer the concern about where the money originated.
n.1: The source of funds is very much the solicitor's concern under the money laundering regime.
n.2: Proving identity does not displace the need to scrutinise suspicious funding.
n.3: Verifying identity is not the whole of due diligence; source of funds must be addressed where risk arises.

Legal Services.q: A client is dissatisfied with the service provided by a firm and has exhausted the firm's own complaints procedure without resolution. The client wishes to take the complaint further to an independent body that can investigate and, if appropriate, order redress. The complaint concerns poor service rather than misconduct alone. The firm's internal complaints process is exhausted. The client is unhappy not with any dishonesty but with the poor standard of service received, has been right through the firm's own complaints process without getting anywhere, and now wants to take the matter to an independent body able to investigate and, if warranted, order the firm to put things right. Which of the following best describes the appropriate avenue?
o: The client may complain only to the SRA, which resolves all service complaints on these facts as a general rule.
The client may complain to the Legal Ombudsman, which can investigate service complaints and order redress.
The client has no further avenue once the firm's own procedure is exhausted.
The client may complain only to the police about the firm's service.
The client must bring a negligence claim in the High Court as the only option.
Legal Services.w: Where a client is dissatisfied with a firm's service and the firm's own complaints procedure has not resolved matters, the client may refer the complaint to the Legal Ombudsman, which handles service complaints and can direct remedies such as an apology, correction of work, or payment of compensation up to its limit. The SRA, by contrast, deals with breaches of professional conduct.

n.0: The SRA deals with conduct breaches; the Legal Ombudsman handles service complaints.
n.2: There is a further avenue (the Legal Ombudsman) after the firm's procedure.
n.3: Service complaints go to the Legal Ombudsman, not the police.
n.4: A negligence claim is not the only option; the Legal Ombudsman handles service complaints.

Legal Services.q: A firm is instructed by a new client on a transaction that clearly falls within the scope of the money laundering regime. Keen to make quick progress, and anxious not to lose the client to a competitor firm down the road, the fee-earner begins substantive work on the transaction immediately, intending to get round to carrying out the client identity and due diligence checks at some later and more convenient point once the matter is properly under way. The firm's money laundering reporting officer questions the timing of those checks. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Due diligence may be postponed indefinitely where the fee-earner judges the client to be trustworthy.
Due diligence is only required once the firm has actually received any money from the client.
Customer due diligence must be completed before the firm establishes the business relationship and starts acting on the matter.
Due diligence need only be done at the very end of the matter, as part of closing the file.
Due diligence may be carried out at any convenient time, provided it is finished before the matter finally completes.
Legal Services.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require customer due diligence to be carried out before a business relationship is established or an occasional transaction is carried out (subject to narrow exceptions), so the firm should not begin acting before the checks are completed.

n.0: A subjective view that the client is trustworthy does not justify postponing the checks.
n.1: The obligation is not triggered by, or deferred to, the receipt of money.
n.3: Due diligence belongs at the outset, not at file-closing.
n.4: Due diligence must precede acting, not merely be finished before completion.

Legal Services.q: A firm specialising in personal injury work is approached by a claims management company which offers to pass it a steady stream of road traffic accident clients. In return for each personal injury client it refers, the company asks the firm to pay it a fixed fee. The firm is keen to grow its caseload quickly and sees the arrangement as a convenient source of new work. Before agreeing to anything, the firm's managing partner asks whether the firm may lawfully agree to pay the company a fee for each such personal injury client that is referred to it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may pay the referral fee, provided the claims management company is itself a regulated business.
The firm may pay the referral fee, provided the arrangement is kept confidential from the referred clients.
The firm may pay the referral fee, provided it does not increase the amount the client is ultimately charged.
The firm must not pay the referral fee, because paying for the referral of personal injury clients is prohibited by statute.
The firm may pay the referral fee in any event, because referral fees are entirely unregulated in England and Wales.
Legal Services.w: Referral fees in personal injury cases are prohibited by section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012. More generally, any permitted referral arrangements must be disclosed to the client and must not compromise the solicitor's independence or the client's interests.

n.0: The referrer being regulated does not lift the statutory ban on PI referral fees.
n.1: Concealing the arrangement makes it worse, not permissible; the prohibition still applies.
n.2: The statutory prohibition applies regardless of whether the client is charged more.
n.4: Referral fees are regulated, and are banned outright for personal injury work.

Legal Services.q: A client with quite limited funds asks a solicitor to help with just one discrete part of a dispute — reviewing and advising on a single settlement offer that has been made — rather than taking on the conduct of the whole matter, which the client intends otherwise to handle themselves. The solicitor is perfectly willing to provide this limited, 'unbundled' service, but is unsure how to do so properly, and in particular what duties they will still owe to the client when acting only on part of the matter. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A limited-scope retainer is permitted, but only if the client agrees never to complain about the service.
A limited-scope retainer relieves the solicitor of any professional duties at all in relation to the work done.
A limited-scope retainer is permitted, provided its limits are made clear and the agreed work is done competently.
A limited-scope retainer is permitted only where the client has been refused help by every other firm first.
A solicitor may never act on only part of a matter, and must always take on the client's whole dispute.
Legal Services.w: Acting on a limited or 'unbundled' basis is permissible. The solicitor must make the scope and limits of the retainer clear to the client, and must still act competently and in the client's best interests in carrying out the agreed, limited work.

n.0: The client cannot be required to give up the right to complain as a condition of a limited retainer.
n.1: A limited retainer narrows the scope of the work, but does not remove professional duties within that scope.
n.3: There is no requirement that the client be turned away elsewhere before a limited retainer can be offered.
n.4: A solicitor may act on part of a matter; there is no rule requiring conduct of the whole dispute.

Legal Services.q: A person who is a client of the firm, but who is not currently engaged on any active legal matter, asks a solicitor whether the firm will receive a large sum of money into its client account on their behalf, hold it for a while, and then pay it out later in instalments to various people the client will nominate from time to time, purely as a convenient way of moving the money around. No legal service, transaction or matter being handled by the firm is connected in any way with these payments. The solicitor considers whether the firm may operate its client account in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm must not provide banking facilities through its client account for payments unconnected to any legal service.
The firm may pass the money through its client account, because a client account may be used however the client wishes.
The firm may do this, provided the firm charges the client a fee for handling the movement of the money.
The firm may do this, provided each individual payment out is below a fixed statutory reporting threshold.
The firm may do this, provided the source of the money is documented in the file for the record.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Accounts Rules prohibit using a client account to provide banking facilities: money moving through the client account must relate to an underlying legal service or transaction the firm is delivering. Passing unconnected funds through the account breaches that rule and carries money laundering risk.

n.1: A client account cannot be used as the client pleases; movements must relate to legal services.
n.2: Charging a fee does not turn a prohibited banking facility into a permitted use.
n.3: There is no payment threshold that permits the client account to be used as a banking facility.
n.4: Documenting the source does not make it proper to provide a banking facility.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is asked to act for two separate companies, each of which is bidding against the other for the same government contract, in relation to the preparation and submission of their competing bids. Both companies know that the solicitor's firm is also acting for the other, and neither has objected, but neither has given any written consent to the arrangement, and neither has been told about the safeguards, such as separate teams, that the firm would put in place. A dispute later arises about whether the firm was entitled to act for both of them at all. Which of the following best explains the solicitor's regulatory position under the conflict of interest rules?
o: The firm may act for both clients provided the SRA grants its prior approval for the joint retainer between them.
The conflict is automatically avoided because both clients know the firm acts for the other, whether or not they have consented.
There is no conflict provided that neither client actually suffers any financial loss as a result of the arrangement.
There is a conflict, so the firm may act only under the 'competing for the same objective' exception, with consent and safeguards.
There is no conflict of interest, because a conflict can only arise where two clients are already in litigation against one another.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must not act where there is a conflict, or a significant risk of conflict, between two clients unless an exception applies. Competing for the same objective is such an exception, but only with each client's informed consent and appropriate safeguards; bare awareness is not informed consent.

n.0: There is no requirement, or mechanism, for prior SRA approval of such a retainer; the safeguard is informed consent plus protections.
n.1: Awareness that the firm acts for the other side is not the same as informed consent to the arrangement.
n.2: The conflict exists because of the competing objectives, regardless of whether loss has yet occurred.
n.4: A conflict of interest is not limited to clients in litigation; competing bids for the same contract create a conflict.

Legal Services.q: A firm is approached by a prospective new client who wishes to instruct it to bring a claim against a company which was, until quite recently, itself a client of the same firm on a closely related matter. From having acted for that former client, the firm still holds confidential information about the former client's affairs which is material to the new client's proposed claim and would be of real tactical value in pursuing it. The former client has not consented to the firm acting against it, and no measures have been put in place to protect its confidential information. The firm considers whether it may take on the new instruction. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm must not act against the former client where it holds confidential information material to the new matter.
The firm may act, provided the fee-earner who acted for the former client is different from the one now instructed.
The firm may act, provided it promises the new client that it will not actually use the confidential information it holds.
The firm may act in any event, because a former client has no say in who the firm chooses to act for later.
The firm may act freely against the former client, because the duty of confidentiality ended when that retainer concluded.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code prohibits acting for a client against a former client where the firm holds confidential information from the former retainer that is material to the new matter, unless the former client gives informed consent or effective safeguards (such as information barriers) protect that information.

n.1: Simply using a different fee-earner is not, by itself, an effective safeguard within the same firm.
n.2: A mere promise not to use the information does not satisfy the requirement for consent or effective safeguards.
n.3: The former client's interest in its confidential information does constrain who the firm may act against.
n.4: Confidentiality survives the end of the retainer, so it does not free the firm to act against the former client.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is representing the defendant in a contested civil trial due to be heard next week. Shortly before the defendant is due to give evidence, the client tells the solicitor privately that they intend to lie under oath about a central factual issue in the case, in order to improve their chances of winning, and instructs the solicitor to carry on regardless and to put that false account to the court in cross-examination and submissions. The solicitor is quite certain, from the documents, that the account is untrue. The solicitor considers how they must respond to the client's stated intention to give false evidence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must not put forward evidence they know to be false, and must cease acting if the client insists on giving it.
The solicitor may present the client's account as instructed, because the solicitor must always follow the client's instructions.
The solicitor must immediately inform the judge that the client intends to lie about the central factual issue.
The solicitor may present the account, provided the solicitor privately warns the client that lying is a criminal offence.
The solicitor may continue to act and simply avoid asking the client any question about the disputed issue.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must not knowingly or recklessly mislead the court, and must not adduce evidence they know to be false. If the client insists on giving false evidence, the solicitor cannot participate and must cease to act; they cannot, however, breach privilege by telling the court why.

n.1: The duty to follow instructions does not extend to helping the client deceive the court.
n.2: The solicitor must not disclose the client's privileged confidence to the judge.
n.3: A private warning does not make it proper to put forward evidence known to be false.
n.4: Carrying on while steering around the issue still misleads the court and is not permitted.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor becomes aware of facts which they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the SRA's regulatory requirements by another solicitor within the same firm, involving the deliberate misuse of money held in the client account. The solicitor is reluctant to become involved, hoping that the firm will quietly deal with the matter internally without any outside scrutiny, and is genuinely unsure whether they are obliged to take the matter beyond the firm at all. The solicitor considers what the regulatory framework requires of them in these circumstances. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor need do nothing, because reporting the conduct of a colleague is always a purely voluntary matter.
The solicitor may stay silent, provided they personally had no involvement in the misuse of the client money.
The solicitor must report the matter to the SRA, as there is a duty to report facts capable of amounting to a serious breach.
The solicitor may wait indefinitely to see whether the firm chooses to deal with the matter internally first.
The solicitor must report the matter only to the firm's managers, and never directly to the regulator itself.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires a solicitor to report promptly to the SRA (or another approved regulator) any facts or matters they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the regulatory arrangements, including breaches by others.

n.0: Reporting a serious breach is a duty, not a purely voluntary matter.
n.1: The duty to report does not depend on the solicitor having been personally involved.
n.3: The obligation is to report promptly, not to wait indefinitely for the firm to act.
n.4: The duty is to report to the SRA, not merely to raise it internally with managers.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is acting for a client in a dispute in which the opposing party is known to be represented by their own firm of solicitors throughout. Growing frustrated by what they see as slow, obstructive and unhelpful responses from the other side's solicitors, the solicitor decides that it would be quicker and altogether more effective to telephone and write to the opposing party directly, going over the heads of their solicitors, in order to press hard for an early settlement. The solicitor considers whether they may properly deal with the opposing party in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may contact the opposing party directly whenever it would be quicker than going through their solicitors.
The solicitor may contact the opposing party directly, because parties are always free to speak to one another.
The solicitor may contact the opposing party directly, provided a copy of each message is later sent to their solicitors.
The solicitor must not communicate directly with an opposing party who is legally represented, but must deal through their solicitors.
The solicitor may contact the opposing party directly, provided nothing said to them is actually untrue.
Legal Services.w: Where the opposing party is known to be legally represented, a solicitor should not communicate with that party directly about the matter without the consent of their solicitor. Doing so risks taking unfair advantage and cutting across the other party's representation.

n.0: Speed and frustration do not justify by-passing the other side's solicitors.
n.1: Although the parties themselves may talk, the solicitor must not initiate direct contact with a represented party.
n.2: Copying the messages to the solicitors afterwards does not make the direct approach proper.
n.4: Even if nothing untrue is said, direct contact with a represented party is improper.

Legal Services.q: A client with a strong but by no means certain civil claim asks a solicitor how the litigation might be funded and what the financial risks of bringing it will actually be. The solicitor discusses entering into a conditional fee agreement, but says nothing at all about what will happen to costs if the claim fails, and in particular never mentions that the client could be ordered to pay the opponent's legal costs, or that insurance against that very risk is available to buy. The client later loses at trial and is shocked to be facing the opponent's costs. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor breached only the rules on client money by failing to warn about the opponent's costs.
The solicitor acted properly, because the risk of paying an opponent's costs is common knowledge among litigants.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor need only ever explain the firm's own fees to the client.
The solicitor breached the duty to explain the funding options and the risk of paying the opponent's costs on losing.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, because the risk of an adverse costs order only arises after trial in any event.
Legal Services.w: To act in the client's best interests and give the best possible information, the solicitor must explain the available funding options and the associated risks, including the possibility of an adverse costs order if the claim fails and the availability of insurance against that risk.

n.0: The failing concerns funding and costs information, not the client money rules.
n.1: The solicitor cannot assume the client already understands the adverse costs risk.
n.2: The duty to inform is not limited to the firm's own fees; it includes the risk of paying the opponent's costs.
n.4: The client needs to understand the adverse costs risk before deciding to litigate, not only after trial.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is defending a client on a criminal charge that is due to go to trial. In a private conference the client admits to the solicitor that they did in fact commit the offence, but instructs the solicitor that they nonetheless wish to plead not guilty and to require the prosecution to prove its case against them at trial. The client does not ask the solicitor to put forward any positive account of innocence, but simply to hold the prosecution to proof. The solicitor considers carefully what they may and may not properly do at the trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may continue only if the client agrees to plead guilty to the offence charged.
The solicitor may put the prosecution to proof, but must not advance a positive case of innocence known to be false.
The solicitor must disclose the client's admission of guilt to the court before the trial begins.
The solicitor must refuse to act at all, because a client who has admitted guilt cannot plead not guilty.
The solicitor may run any defence the client wishes, including asserting facts the solicitor knows to be untrue.
Legal Services.w: A defendant who admits guilt to their solicitor may still require the prosecution to prove its case, and the solicitor may test and challenge the prosecution evidence. The solicitor must not, however, assert a positive case they know to be false or call the client to give evidence of innocence.

n.0: The client is entitled to require proof, so continuing does not depend on a guilty plea.
n.2: The solicitor must not disclose the client's privileged admission to the court.
n.3: An admission to the solicitor does not prevent a not-guilty plea putting the prosecution to proof.
n.4: The solicitor may not advance facts they know to be untrue, whatever the client wishes.

Legal Services.q: A firm is temporarily short of funds on one particular client's matter, because a payment that is due from that client has not yet arrived. A fee-earner proposes to cover the shortfall for the time being by using money that is held in the client account for a different, wholly unconnected client, fully intending to put the money back as soon as the awaited payment finally comes in. On this plan, the fee-earner insists, no client would ultimately lose out, and the borrowing would only ever be short-lived. The firm's compliance officer is asked whether this may be done. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm must not use one client's money for another, and a client's ledger must never be allowed to go overdrawn.
The firm may borrow one client's money for another, provided no client actually ends up out of pocket.
The firm may borrow from the client account, provided the amount involved is relatively small.
The firm may borrow one client's money for another, provided the affected client is not told about it.
The firm may borrow one client's money for another, provided it is repaid within a short period of time.
Legal Services.w: Client money is held for each client separately. A firm must not use one client's money to meet another client's, or the firm's own, obligations, and a client's ledger must never become overdrawn. The intention to repay does not make the use of the money permissible.

n.1: That no client ends up out of pocket does not excuse the improper use of client money.
n.2: The size of the sum does not make the misuse of client money acceptable.
n.3: Keeping the client uninformed makes matters worse, not permissible.
n.4: A short repayment period does not make using one client's money for another permissible.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is asked to deal with funds and becomes aware that the money is, or is likely to be, the proceeds of crime, and considers doing an act that would help another retain or use those proceeds. The solicitor is concerned about committing a substantive money laundering offence. The money appears to be criminal property. The solicitor is considering the principal offences. The solicitor has become aware that the money they are being asked to deal with is very likely the proceeds of crime, and is contemplating steps that would help someone else hold onto or use it, which brings squarely into view the substantive money laundering offences rather than merely the duty to report. Which of the following best describes the principal money laundering offences under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?
o: Money laundering offences apply only to banks, never to solicitors.
The only offence is failing to submit an annual compliance return.
An offence is committed only where the sums involved exceed a fixed statutory threshold on these facts as a general rule.
Concealing, arranging, and acquiring/using/possessing criminal property are the principal offences under sections 327 to 329.
There are no substantive money laundering offences, only a duty to report.
Legal Services.w: The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 creates the principal money laundering offences: concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removing criminal property (s.327); entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement facilitating the acquisition, retention, use or control of criminal property by another (s.328); and acquiring, using or possessing criminal property (s.329). These apply to solicitors as to others.

n.0: The offences apply to solicitors, not only banks.
n.1: The offences are not limited to failing to file a compliance return.
n.2: There is no general de minimis threshold for the principal offences.
n.4: There are substantive offences, not merely a reporting duty.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is found, following a full investigation and a contested hearing, to have deliberately taken money from the client account for their own personal use and to have created a series of false ledger entries over many months in order to conceal what they had been doing. The matter comes before the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, which finds as a fact that the solicitor acted dishonestly. In mitigation, the solicitor points to their previously unblemished record, the severe personal financial pressures they were under at the time, and the fact that the money has since been repaid in full. The tribunal considers the appropriate sanction. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome?
o: The tribunal has no power to strike off a solicitor and can only refer the matter back to the firm.
The solicitor will receive no more than a written rebuke, given their previously unblemished record.
A finding of dishonesty will ordinarily lead to the solicitor being struck off, save in exceptional circumstances.
The solicitor will simply be fined, because repaying the money in full cures the dishonesty entirely.
The solicitor cannot be struck off unless a criminal court has first convicted them of theft.
Legal Services.w: Proven dishonesty is treated with the utmost seriousness. Following the approach in Bolton v Law Society, a solicitor who has acted dishonestly will almost invariably be struck off the roll, save in exceptional circumstances, to maintain public confidence in the profession.

n.0: The SDT does have power to strike a solicitor off the roll.
n.1: A rebuke is not an adequate response to proven dishonesty of this kind.
n.3: Repayment mitigates loss but does not undo the dishonesty or avoid striking off.
n.4: The tribunal's jurisdiction does not depend on a prior criminal conviction.

Legal Services.q: A firm receives settlement funds on behalf of a client following the conclusion of a hard-fought dispute. A paralegal, dealing with the incoming payment, mistakenly pays the money into the firm's office account rather than into the separate client account. The error is not spotted at the time and is only discovered several weeks later, during a routine internal audit of the firm's accounts. The money has not been spent or otherwise touched and remains fully available. The firm's compliance officer is asked to explain exactly what rule has been breached and why. Which of the following best states the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The settlement funds became the firm's own office money the moment they were received, so paying them into that account was correct.
Client money may be mixed with the firm's own money, provided the two are properly separated again at the end of the retainer.
Client money must be held in a separate client account, so paying it into the office account was a breach to correct promptly.
Discovery of the error on the internal audit retrospectively excuses the breach, provided the money is later moved across.
Only a qualified solicitor, and never a paralegal, may handle client money, so the payment had no legal effect at all.
Legal Services.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, client money (which includes settlement monies held for a client) must be kept in a client account, separate from the firm's own money, and any breach must be remedied promptly on discovery.

n.0: Settlement monies held on behalf of the client are client money, not the firm's office money.
n.1: Client money must be kept separate from office money at all times, not merely reconciled at the end.
n.3: Discovery on audit does not excuse the breach; it triggers the duty to put it right promptly.
n.4: Staff may handle client money under proper supervision; the rule breached concerns the account it is held in.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is preparing a witness statement, which is to be verified by a statement of truth, on behalf of a client in ongoing civil proceedings. The client wants the statement to include a particular assertion of fact which the solicitor already knows, from the contemporaneous documents on the file, to be untrue, and the client asks the solicitor to draft and put forward the statement in exactly that form so that it can be signed and served on the other side. The solicitor considers whether they may properly do as the client asks. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may include the assertion, provided the client is willing personally to sign the statement of truth.
The solicitor must not put forward a statement of truth containing an assertion the solicitor knows to be untrue.
The solicitor may include the assertion, provided the other side is unlikely ever to discover that it is false.
The solicitor may include the assertion, because drafting a statement is a purely mechanical task.
The solicitor may include the assertion, because the client, not the solicitor, takes responsibility for the statement.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must not draft or put forward a statement of truth, or any document, that contains an assertion the solicitor knows to be false. To do so would be to mislead the court and to fail to act with integrity.

n.0: The client signing the statement does not cure the solicitor's knowing participation in a false statement.
n.2: The likelihood of discovery is irrelevant; advancing a knowingly false statement is improper regardless.
n.3: Drafting is not merely mechanical where the solicitor knows the content to be untrue.
n.4: The client's willingness to take responsibility does not permit the solicitor to advance what they know is false.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor who holds a current practising certificate is asked to administer an oath and take a sworn statement. In one situation the person swearing the statement is a stranger who has simply come in off the street for that purpose; in another, the person is the solicitor's own client, and the statement is to be used in the very matter in which the solicitor is acting for that client. The solicitor is unsure in which of these situations it is proper for them to administer the oath. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor may administer oaths only for their own clients, and never for members of the public.
A solicitor may administer oaths, but not in a matter in which they are acting for a party.
A solicitor may administer oaths in any matter, including one in which they act, without any restriction.
A solicitor may never administer oaths at all, because that function is reserved exclusively to the courts.
A solicitor may administer oaths only if separately appointed as a notary public to do so.
Legal Services.w: The administration of oaths is a reserved legal activity which solicitors holding a practising certificate are authorised to carry out. However, to preserve independence, a solicitor must not administer an oath or take a statement in a matter in which they, or their firm, are acting for a party.

n.0: The function is not limited to the solicitor's own clients; the restriction is the opposite way round.
n.2: A solicitor must not administer the oath in a matter in which they are acting, so it is not unrestricted.
n.3: Administering oaths is not reserved to the courts; solicitors may do it.
n.4: A solicitor need not be a notary public to administer oaths.

Legal Services.q: A client wishes to make a substantial gift to their solicitor (or to a member of the solicitor's family) in a will or transaction the solicitor is instructed to prepare. The gift is significant in size relative to the client's estate. The solicitor stands to benefit personally from the gift. The solicitor considers the conduct implications. The client wants to leave, or transfer, something of substantial value to the very solicitor advising them, or to that solicitor's family, in a document the solicitor is being asked to prepare, so the solicitor plainly stands to gain personally and must consider what conduct requires in that situation. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor must do?
o: The solicitor may accept the gift provided it is recorded in writing.
The solicitor must report the client to the SRA for attempting the gift.
The solicitor may simply prepare the gift, as clients are free to benefit their solicitors on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor may proceed provided the gift is shared with the whole firm.
The solicitor must advise the client to take independent legal advice, and decline to act on the gift if the client does not.
Legal Services.w: Where a client proposes to make a significant gift to the solicitor or the solicitor's family, there is an own-interest conflict and a risk to the solicitor's independence. The solicitor should advise the client to take independent legal advice about the gift and, unless the client does so, should not act in relation to it. Small gifts of modest value are treated differently.

n.0: Merely recording the gift in writing does not address the own-interest conflict.
n.1: The step is to require independent advice, not to report the client to the SRA.
n.2: The solicitor cannot simply prepare a significant gift benefiting themselves without safeguards.
n.3: Sharing the gift with the firm does not cure the conflict; independent advice is required.

Legal Services.q: A firm is asked to act for both the seller and the buyer in the same conveyancing transaction. The firm considers whether it may act for both parties given their opposing interests in the transaction. The two clients are on opposite sides of the same transaction. Their interests conflict. The firm is asked to handle the same conveyancing transaction for both the seller and the buyer at once, two clients whose interests in the deal are directly opposed, and it must decide whether it can properly act for both of them or whether the conflict rules stand in the way. Which of the following best describes the firm's position?
o: The firm may act for both only if neither party is legally represented elsewhere.
There is a conflict of interest, so the firm generally must not act for both, unless a recognised exception with safeguards applies.
The firm may act for both provided it charges only one set of fees.
The firm may always act for both buyer and seller to save costs.
The firm may act for both because conveyancing is administrative rather than adversarial on these facts as a general rule.
Legal Services.w: Acting for both the seller and buyer in the same transaction generally involves a conflict of interest, because their interests conflict, so the firm must not act for both unless one of the conflict exceptions applies (substantially common interest or competing for the same objective) with the required safeguards, including informed consent. Even then, acting must be reasonable.

n.0: Whether the parties are represented elsewhere does not, by itself, permit acting for both.
n.2: Charging a single fee does not resolve the conflict of interest.
n.3: The firm cannot always act for both merely to save costs; a conflict generally prevents it.
n.4: Conveyancing can involve genuinely conflicting interests; it is not merely administrative.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is appearing as the advocate for a client at a hearing in the county court. While preparing the night before, the solicitor becomes aware of a binding decision of a higher court which is directly relevant to the very legal issue that will be before the judge, but which is distinctly unhelpful to the client's argument and which the opposing advocate has plainly overlooked. The solicitor would much prefer to say nothing at all about it, in the hope that neither the judge nor the other side will happen to find it. The solicitor considers what their duty as an advocate actually requires. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The advocate may withhold the authority, because the duty to the client outweighs any duty to the court.
The advocate may stay silent about the authority, because it is for the other side to find and cite it.
The advocate may stay silent, provided they do not positively deny that any such authority exists.
The advocate must draw the court's attention to relevant adverse binding authority, even if it harms the client's case.
The advocate must cite the authority only if the judge specifically asks whether there is any against them.
Legal Services.w: An advocate owes a duty to the court not to mislead it, which includes a positive obligation to draw the court's attention to relevant binding authority, even where it is adverse to the client's case. The duty to the court takes precedence over the client's interests here.

n.0: The duty to the court prevails over the client's interests in this respect.
n.1: The advocate cannot leave it to the other side; the duty to cite adverse binding authority is the advocate's own.
n.2: Silence that allows the court to overlook binding authority is itself misleading.
n.4: The duty is not contingent on the judge happening to ask.

Legal Services.q: A firm is approached by two entirely separate would-be buyers who each, quite independently of the other, want the firm to act for them in trying to buy the very same house, which has only just come onto the market and is expected to attract several competing offers. Each buyer wants the firm's help to secure the property ahead of the other, and their interests in doing so are directly and obviously opposed. A fee-earner, seeing the prospect of two fees rather than one, wonders whether the firm can simply act for both buyers at the same time. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act for both buyers, because whichever of them succeeds will be perfectly satisfied with the outcome.
The firm may act for both buyers, provided each buyer instructs a different fee-earner within the firm.
The firm may act for both buyers, provided it does not tell either of them the amount the other is offering.
There is a conflict, as the buyers compete for the same property, so the firm should not act for both.
The firm may act for both buyers, because acting on a house purchase is only routine conveyancing work.
Legal Services.w: Two clients competing to buy the same property have directly conflicting interests, so there is a conflict of interest. The firm should not act for both unless a recognised exception applies with informed consent and safeguards; merely withholding information or using separate fee-earners does not cure it.

n.0: The eventual satisfaction of the winner does not remove the conflict at the time of acting.
n.1: Using different fee-earners in the same firm does not, by itself, cure a conflict between the clients.
n.2: Withholding each buyer's offer from the other does not resolve the underlying conflict.
n.4: The competing bids create a genuine conflict; this is not merely routine work.

Legal Services.q: A firm is dealing with two entirely separate clients at the same time. It needs to pay a disbursement of several hundred pounds on behalf of Client A, but the firm currently holds no money at all in the client account for Client A. It does, however, hold ample funds in the client account for a wholly unconnected Client B. A fee-earner, wanting to get the disbursement paid on time, proposes to pay it out of the client account anyway, in effect drawing on the money held for Client B, and to sort matters out later. The firm's compliance officer reviews the proposal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The disbursement may be paid from the client account, because all client money is pooled together anyway.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account only if sufficient funds are held for that particular client.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided Client B is unlikely to need the money soon.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided the shortfall is made good within a month.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided the sum involved is comparatively small.
Legal Services.w: Client money is held for each client separately, and a client's ledger must never become overdrawn. A payment out for a client must not exceed the funds actually held for that client, so paying Client A's disbursement from Client B's money is not permitted.

n.0: Client money is not pooled; each client's money is held and accounted for separately.
n.2: Whether Client B needs the money soon is irrelevant; using it for Client A is improper.
n.3: An intention to make good the shortfall later does not permit overdrawing a client ledger.
n.4: The size of the disbursement does not make the improper use of another client's money acceptable.

Legal Services.q: While acting for a client on the purchase of a business, a solicitor comes into possession of information that is plainly material to the client's decision whether to proceed with the purchase, having learned it in the ordinary course of that same matter. There is no legal restriction preventing the solicitor from passing it on, the information is not subject to any other client's confidentiality, it is not privileged, and the client has never asked to be kept in ignorance of anything. The solicitor wonders whether they are actually obliged to pass this material information on to the client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must disclose all information material to the matter of which they have knowledge, subject to limited exceptions.
The solicitor must never disclose information learned during a matter, as all such information is confidential.
The solicitor need only disclose information which the client has specifically asked the solicitor to obtain.
The solicitor has a discretion whether to disclose material information, depending on whether it helps the client's case.
The solicitor need only disclose the information if doing so is likely to increase the fees on the matter.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires a solicitor to make the client aware of all information material to the matter of which the solicitor has knowledge, subject to defined exceptions (such as legal restrictions on disclosure, another client's confidentiality, privilege, or the client's own instruction not to be told).

n.1: Information learned in the matter is not, for that reason alone, confidential from the client it concerns.
n.2: The duty is not limited to information the client asked the solicitor to obtain.
n.3: Disclosure of material information is a duty, not a discretion turning on whether it helps.
n.4: The duty to disclose does not depend on any effect on fees.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is acting for a client in financial remedy proceedings following a divorce. During a conference the client admits, in strict confidence, that they hold substantial assets in an undisclosed offshore bank account which they have deliberately kept out of the figures filed with the court, and firmly instructs the solicitor to say nothing whatever about those assets and to proceed on the basis of the figures already before the court. The solicitor knows that the court is being asked to decide the case on the footing that those figures are complete and accurate. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's duty under the SRA Standards and Regulations?
o: The duty of confidentiality entitles the solicitor to disregard the undisclosed assets entirely and simply carry on.
The solicitor must immediately report the client to the police for the non-disclosure of the offshore assets.
The solicitor may rely on the client's instructions and present the case exactly as the client wishes it to be put.
The solicitor must follow the client's instructions in full, including the instruction not to disclose the assets.
The solicitor must not knowingly mislead the court and must cease to act if the client refuses to correct the position.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must not knowingly or recklessly mislead the court. In financial remedy proceedings there is a duty of full and frank disclosure, so the solicitor cannot advance a case they know to be materially incomplete, and must cease acting if the client refuses to put the position right.

n.0: Confidentiality does not permit the solicitor to continue advancing a knowingly incomplete case.
n.1: An immediate report to the police is not the primary professional duty here; the duty is not to mislead the court and to cease acting if necessary.
n.2: The client's instructions cannot require the solicitor to mislead the court.
n.3: A solicitor must not follow an instruction that would result in the court being misled.

Legal Services.q: A firm concluded a client's matter some time ago and rendered its final bill, which the client duly paid in full. A modest balance of the client's own money nonetheless remains sitting in the firm's client account, and there is now no outstanding work, unpaid disbursement or any other proper reason for the firm to continue holding on to it. The money simply stays in the client account, month after month, without ever being dealt with. The firm's compliance officer reviews the client ledger and raises the outstanding balance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may simply transfer the residual balance to its own office account to tidy up the ledger.
The firm must return the residual balance to the client promptly once there is no longer any proper reason to hold it.
The firm may retain the balance permanently, provided it pays the client a small amount of interest.
The firm may keep the residual balance in its client account indefinitely, as it belongs to the client anyway.
The firm need only return the balance if and when the former client actually asks for it back.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be returned promptly to the client (or the person entitled to it) as soon as there is no longer any proper reason to hold it. Leaving residual balances sitting in the client account indefinitely is a breach.

n.0: The residual balance is the client's money and must not be moved into office account.
n.2: Paying some interest does not entitle the firm to keep money it has no reason to hold.
n.3: The money cannot simply be left in the client account indefinitely; it must be returned promptly.
n.4: The duty to return does not wait for the former client to ask.

Legal Services.q: A firm currently acts for a company on an ongoing commercial matter which is still very much live. A prospective new client then approaches the very same firm and asks it to bring an entirely unrelated contractual claim against that company. The new matter has nothing factually to do with the existing retainer, and no confidential information from the existing matter would need to be used in pursuing it. The company has neither been asked for, nor given, any consent to the firm acting against it. A fee-earner, seeing a chance to win extra work, wonders whether the firm may take on the new client and act against the company on the unrelated claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act against the company, provided a different fee-earner is put in charge of the new claim.
The firm may act against the company, provided the new client is charged a separate and higher fee.
The firm may freely act against the company, because the two matters are completely unrelated to each other.
The firm may act against the company, provided no confidential information from the existing matter is used.
The firm must not act against a person who is currently its own client, even on an entirely unrelated matter.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor owes a duty of loyalty to a current client. Acting against a person who is at the same time the firm's own client gives rise to a conflict and is not permitted, even where the two matters are unrelated, unless a recognised exception applies with informed consent.

n.0: Using a different fee-earner does not overcome the duty of loyalty owed to the current client.
n.1: Charging a higher fee is irrelevant to the conflict of acting against a current client.
n.2: Loyalty to a current client is engaged even where the new matter is unrelated.
n.3: The absence of shared confidential information does not cure the conflict of acting against a current client.

Legal Services.q: A prospective client of modest means wishes to bring a personal injury claim which the solicitor, after an initial assessment, considers has strong prospects of success. The client explains frankly that they simply cannot afford to pay the firm's fees on a private, hourly-rate basis as the case proceeds through the courts, and asks whether there is any lawful way in which the firm can act for them so that the firm's fee depends instead on the outcome of the claim. The solicitor considers the various funding options that are lawfully available for a claim of this kind. Which of the following best states the position?
o: The solicitor may enter a conditional fee agreement, which is lawful for such a claim if the statutory requirements are met.
