The solicitor must act free of charge, because a client who cannot pay privately is entitled to free representation.
The solicitor may act only if the client first obtains legal aid, which is available for all personal injury claims.
The solicitor cannot lawfully offer any arrangement under which the firm's fee depends upon the outcome of the case.
The solicitor may agree to buy the client's claim outright and keep whatever damages are ultimately recovered in it.
Legal Services.w: Conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') are lawful for claims of this kind under the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 (as amended), subject to statutory requirements on form and success-fee caps. Buying the claim outright would be champertous and is not permitted.

n.1: There is no rule requiring a solicitor to act free of charge for a client who cannot pay privately.
n.2: Legal aid is not generally available for personal injury claims, so this is not a precondition to acting.
n.3: Outcome-dependent fees are permitted through CFAs (and DBAs in some cases); they are not prohibited.
n.4: A solicitor may not purchase the client's cause of action and take the damages; that is champerty.

Legal Services.q: A firm is instructed to act for a private limited company on a substantial commercial matter. One of the company's directors, who happens to give the firm its day-to-day instructions on the matter, privately approaches the solicitor and asks them to structure the transaction in a particular way that would benefit that director personally, at the direct expense of the company itself. The solicitor is uneasy and is unsure to whom their professional duties are actually owed in this situation, and how they ought to respond to the director's personal request. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client is the board and all the shareholders jointly, so the solicitor needs every shareholder's consent to each step.
The client is whichever director gives the instructions, so the solicitor must act on that director's personal wishes here.
The client is the company, a separate legal person, so the solicitor must act in its interests, not a director's personal interests.
There is no identifiable client at all, because a company cannot itself be the client of a firm of solicitors.
The client is the majority shareholder, whose personal interests the solicitor must prefer to those of the company itself.
Legal Services.w: A company is a separate legal person and is itself the client. Instructions are given through its authorised officers, but the solicitor's duties are owed to the company, not to individual directors or shareholders in their personal capacities.

n.0: The solicitor takes instructions through authorised officers and need not obtain every shareholder's consent to each step.
n.1: A director gives instructions on the company's behalf, but is not personally the client.
n.3: A company can be, and here is, the client of the solicitor.
n.4: Duties are owed to the company, not to the majority shareholder personally.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor, acting entirely outside their professional practice and in their private life, is convicted of a serious criminal offence of dishonesty which involved deceiving other people over a sustained period for their own personal financial gain. The conduct had nothing directly to do with any client of the firm, or with the solicitor's day-to-day work. The solicitor now argues that, because the whole matter arose purely in their private life and away from the office, it is simply no concern of the SRA and cannot amount to any breach of their professional obligations. A colleague is asked whether that argument is correct. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The SRA has no interest in a solicitor's private life, so purely private conduct can never be a breach.
Private conduct is relevant only where the solicitor is actually sent to prison for the offence.
Private conduct can be acted on only if a client happens to complain about it to the SRA.
Private conduct is a matter for the police alone and is never within the SRA's remit.
Conduct outside practice can breach the duty to uphold public trust in the profession and lead to regulatory action.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Principles require solicitors to act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the profession and in legal services. Serious misconduct, including dishonesty, in a solicitor's private life can undermine that trust and so fall within the regulator's remit.

n.0: Private conduct is not beyond the SRA's reach where it affects public trust in the profession.
n.1: Regulatory action does not depend on the solicitor receiving a custodial sentence.
n.2: The SRA can act on serious private misconduct whether or not a client complains.
n.3: Criminal liability and professional regulation operate in parallel; both can apply.

Legal Services.q: A firm has finished acting for a client on a matter and has delivered its bill, but the client has failed to pay the firm's proper costs despite reminders. The client now demands that the firm immediately hand over the entire file of papers relating to the matter, which remains in the firm's possession, so that the client can take the matter elsewhere. The firm has done nothing wrong in the conduct of the matter and its fees are properly due and owing. The firm considers whether it may hold on to the papers until it is paid. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may keep the papers only if the client agreed, in writing at the outset, to such an arrangement.
The firm has no right to keep any papers, but may instead simply sue the client for the unpaid fees.
The firm must hand over all of the papers at once, because a client is always entitled to their file on demand.
The firm may exercise a retaining lien over the client's papers until its proper outstanding fees are paid.
The firm may keep the papers permanently, whether or not the client ever pays the outstanding fees.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor generally has a common-law retaining lien over a client's papers and property in the firm's possession as security for the firm's properly incurred and unpaid costs. The lien must not be exercised inconsistently with the solicitor's other duties, but it does entitle the firm to withhold the papers pending payment.

n.0: The retaining lien arises at common law and does not depend on a prior written agreement.
n.1: Suing for the fees is an additional remedy; it does not mean the firm has no lien over the papers.
n.2: A client is not automatically entitled to the file on demand where proper fees remain unpaid.
n.4: The lien secures payment; it is not a right to keep the papers permanently regardless of payment.

Legal Services.q: Acting for a buyer in a residential conveyancing transaction, a solicitor gives the seller's solicitor a written undertaking, in the firm's name, to discharge the buyer's existing mortgage over the property out of the sale proceeds immediately after completion. Completion duly takes place and the sale proceeds are received into the firm's client account. Before the mortgage is redeemed, however, the client instructs the solicitor not to pay off the existing mortgage after all, as the client now wishes to use that money for an entirely different purpose. The solicitor is unsure whether the undertaking must still be honoured in the face of the client's contrary instruction. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?
o: The solicitor may disregard the undertaking, because a client's instruction always overrides an undertaking given to a third party.
The undertaking is not binding, because undertakings given between solicitors carry no professional or legal force at all.
The solicitor may withdraw the undertaking at any time simply by writing to the recipient to say it no longer applies.
The undertaking binds only the firm as a whole, so no individual solicitor can ever be held responsible for it.
The solicitor is personally bound to honour the undertaking, and the client's later instruction does not release them from it.
Legal Services.w: A professional undertaking is binding on the solicitor who gives it, is enforceable (including by the court's supervisory jurisdiction), and must be performed. A client's subsequent contrary instruction does not release the solicitor from an undertaking already given to a third party.

n.0: A client's instruction cannot release the solicitor from an undertaking already given to a third party.
n.1: Undertakings between solicitors are binding and enforceable, not without force.
n.2: An undertaking cannot be unilaterally withdrawn once given; it must be performed or released by the recipient.
n.3: The individual who gives an undertaking is personally responsible for it, as well as the firm.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is representing a client in ongoing court proceedings. The client instructs the solicitor to take a particular step which would clearly advance the client's immediate interests in the case, but which the solicitor knows would have the effect of misleading the court about a matter that is material to the issues it has to decide. The client is adamant that their own interests must come first, and insists that the solicitor is simply there to do the client's bidding whatever it may be. The solicitor must decide how to resolve the clash between the duty owed to the client and the duty owed to the court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The duty to the client always comes first, because the client is the person the solicitor is retained to serve.
The solicitor may prefer the client's interests, provided the court does not actually discover that it was misled.
The duty to the court applies only to barristers acting as advocates, and not to solicitors at all.
The solicitor may simply choose whichever of the two duties seems more convenient in the circumstances.
Where the duties conflict, the duty to the court and the administration of justice takes precedence over the client's wishes.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor owes duties both to the client and to the court, but these are not equal. Where they conflict, the duty to the court and to the proper administration of justice prevails, so the solicitor must not take a step that would mislead the court, whatever the client instructs.

n.0: The duty to the client does not always come first; it yields to the duty to the court.
n.1: Whether the court discovers the deception is irrelevant; misleading it is impermissible.
n.2: The duty to the court applies to solicitors as well as barristers.
n.3: The resolution is not a matter of convenience; the court duty governs.

Legal Services.q: A firm takes on a new client and begins substantive work on the matter almost straight away. The client is never given any written information about how the firm's charges will be worked out, about what they should do if they become unhappy with the service they receive, or about the regulatory protections that apply to them as a client. Some months later the client, who by now has a serious grievance, complains that they were told nothing at all about their position at the very outset of the retainer. The firm's compliance officer reviews what information should have been provided. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm need only tell the client the firm's hourly rate, and nothing about complaints or regulation.
The firm need only provide information about complaints if and when the client actually raises one.
At the outset the client must be told about costs, complaints handling and the right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman.
The firm need give no information, because clients are taken to understand how solicitors' firms operate.
The firm need give the client no information at the outset, provided a full bill is delivered at the very end.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code requires clients to be given, at the outset and in an accessible way, the information they need to make informed decisions — including the likely costs, the firm's complaints procedure, and their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman and to whom the firm is regulated.

n.0: The required information goes well beyond the hourly rate; it covers complaints and regulation.
n.1: Complaints information must be given at the outset, not only once a complaint is made.
n.3: Clients cannot be assumed to know their position; the information must be provided.
n.4: Information must be given at the outset, not deferred until the final bill.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is acting for an elderly client on the sale of the client's home. The client's adult son, who is not himself a client of the firm and holds no power of attorney or other authority, telephones the solicitor and purports to give instructions to reduce the agreed sale price and to redirect the sale proceeds into a bank account held in the son's own name. The solicitor has not been able to speak to the client directly to confirm any of this, and the son is pressing hard for the changes to be actioned at once. The solicitor considers whether they may act on the son's instructions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must act on the son's instructions, since the son is evidently looking after the elderly client's affairs.
The solicitor may act on the son's instructions, provided the son confirms them to the firm in writing.
The solicitor may act only on instructions from the client, or someone with the client's authority.
The solicitor may act on the son's instructions, because the changes would in any case speed the matter up.
The solicitor may act on the son's instructions, because a close family member may always instruct on a client's behalf.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor must take instructions from the client, or from a person the client has properly authorised to give them. A family member without authority cannot give binding instructions, and the redirection of sale proceeds should in any event alert the solicitor to a serious risk of financial abuse.

n.0: An assumption that the son manages the client's affairs is not the same as proper authority.
n.1: The son putting his instructions in writing does not supply the missing authority from the client.
n.3: Speeding the matter up does not justify acting without the client's authority.
n.4: Family relationship alone does not give a person authority to instruct on the client's behalf.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is instructed by a long-standing client to act on the sale of the client's house, which is being marketed in the ordinary way. Unknown to the client at first, the solicitor privately wishes to buy the house themselves, at the full asking price, as a personal investment, and would like to go on advising the client about the conduct of the sale at the same time as being the purchaser. The solicitor is confident that they would treat the client entirely fairly throughout, but is unsure whether it is proper to advise the client on a transaction in which the solicitor is personally the buyer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may act for the client, provided the solicitor genuinely believes they will treat the client fairly.
The solicitor may act for the client, provided the purchase is approved in advance by another partner in the firm.
The solicitor may act for the client and buy the house, provided the solicitor pays the full asking price for it.
There is an own-interest conflict, so the solicitor must not act for the client on a sale to the solicitor themselves.
There is no difficulty at all, because a solicitor is free to buy property from a client like any other buyer.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Code prohibits acting where the solicitor's own interest conflicts, or there is a significant risk it may conflict, with the client's interest. A solicitor buying the very asset they are advising the client to sell has a clear own-interest conflict and must not act for the client on it.

n.0: A subjective belief in fair treatment does not cure an own-interest conflict.
n.1: Another partner's approval does not cure the individual solicitor's own-interest conflict in acting for the client.
n.2: Paying the asking price does not remove the own-interest conflict inherent in advising on a sale to oneself.
n.4: The problem is not the purchase itself but acting for the client while being the buyer.

Legal Services.q: An elderly client comes to a solicitor to give instructions about disposing of their property during their lifetime, but attends the meeting accompanied throughout by a much younger relative who happens to stand to benefit very substantially from the arrangement the client is proposing. During the meeting the relative does almost all of the talking, repeatedly answers questions on the client's behalf, and appears distinctly anxious to ensure that the client is never left alone with the solicitor at any point. The solicitor becomes concerned that the client's instructions may not genuinely be their own. Which of the following best describes how the solicitor should proceed?
o: The solicitor should ask the relative to confirm in writing that the instructions represent the client's wishes.
The solicitor may simply take the instructions as relayed by the relative, since the relative knows the client's wishes.
The solicitor may proceed without further enquiry, provided the client nods in agreement with what is said.
The solicitor must refuse to act altogether whenever a client attends with a relative who will benefit.
The solicitor should see the client alone, to satisfy themselves that the instructions are genuinely the client's own free wishes.
Legal Services.w: Where there is a risk that a client is being influenced by a third party, particularly one who stands to benefit, the solicitor should take instructions from the client alone and in private, so as to satisfy themselves that the instructions are genuinely those of the client and freely given.

n.0: Written confirmation from the benefiting relative does not establish the client's free will.
n.1: The solicitor must not simply rely on the benefiting relative to relay the client's wishes.
n.2: A nod of agreement in the relative's presence does not resolve the concern about influence.
n.3: An outright refusal to act is not required; seeing the client alone is the appropriate step.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor gives another party's solicitor a professional undertaking, in the course of a transaction, to send certain title documents once the transaction has completed. The undertaking as given does not specify any particular date, or any period, within which the documents are to be provided. After completion, the solicitor then takes no steps at all for a long period to fulfil the undertaking, taking the convenient view that, because no deadline was ever written down, there is no time by which they are actually obliged to perform it. The recipient eventually complains about the delay. The solicitor considers their obligation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Because no time was specified, the solicitor is under no obligation to perform the undertaking at any particular point.
The solicitor may choose any timescale they like, however long, since none was written into the undertaking.
The undertaking lapses automatically if it is not performed immediately upon completion of the transaction.
Where no time is specified, the undertaking must still be performed within a reasonable time.
The undertaking need only be performed if and when the recipient formally demands performance of it.
Legal Services.w: An undertaking is binding according to its terms, and where it does not specify a time for performance, the law implies that it must be carried out within a reasonable time. The absence of a stated deadline does not mean there is no obligation to perform.

n.0: The absence of a stated time does not remove the obligation; a reasonable time is implied.
n.1: The solicitor cannot take an unlimited time; performance must be within a reasonable period.
n.2: An undertaking does not lapse merely because it is not performed the instant the transaction completes.
n.4: Performance is not contingent on a formal demand by the recipient.

Legal Services.q: In the course of negotiating the terms of a commercial deal for a client, a solicitor is dealing directly with the representatives on the other side of the transaction. In order to gain an advantage in the negotiation, the solicitor is sorely tempted to make a statement to the other side about the client's position and intentions which the solicitor knows perfectly well to be false, calculating that the misrepresentation will help to secure noticeably better terms for their own client. The statement would be made to the other party, and not to any court. The solicitor considers whether making it would be proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided the other side has its own solicitors to protect it.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided the statement is made orally rather than in writing.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, because the duty of honesty is owed only to the court, not to opponents.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided doing so secures a genuine advantage for their own client.
A solicitor must not mislead or attempt to mislead anyone, including third parties, in the course of practice.
Legal Services.w: The duty of honesty and the requirement not to mislead are not confined to dealings with the court. A solicitor must not mislead, or attempt to mislead, clients, the court, or third parties such as the other side in a negotiation.

n.0: The other side being represented does not license misleading them.
n.1: An oral misrepresentation is no more permissible than a written one.
n.2: The duty not to mislead extends beyond the court to third parties.
n.3: Advancing the client's interests does not permit making a statement known to be false.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is instructed by the owner of a small business in a dispute with a supplier over an unpaid invoice. Without discussing any alternative, the solicitor immediately issues court proceedings, which substantially increases the costs the client will incur. The solicitor never mentions to the client that mediation or another form of alternative dispute resolution might resolve the matter more cheaply and quickly, and the client only learns of this later from an accountant. The client complains about the way the matter was handled. Which of the following best explains the solicitor's regulatory position under the SRA Standards and Regulations?
o: The solicitor breached the duty to act in the client's best interests by not advising on the realistic options, including mediation.
The solicitor breached confidentiality by disclosing details of the dispute to the opposing supplier without the client's consent.
The solicitor breached the conflict rules, because acting against a supplier in a commercial dispute always creates a conflict.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, provided the client ultimately succeeds in the litigation commenced on their behalf.
The solicitor acted properly, as choosing litigation over mediation was a tactical matter within the solicitor's own discretion.
Legal Services.w: SRA Principle 7 and the Code require a solicitor to act in each client's best interests, which includes advising on the realistic options for resolving a dispute — including ADR and its costs consequences — so the client can give informed instructions.

n.1: No confidential information was disclosed on these facts; the breach is the failure to advise, not a confidentiality breach.
n.2: Acting against a supplier in a dispute does not, without more, create a conflict of interest.
n.3: Success in the litigation does not cure the failure to advise the client of cheaper, quicker options at the outset.
n.4: The course of action is not unfettered: the client must first be advised of the realistic options, including ADR, before instructions are taken.

Legal Services.q: A firm is asked to act for two clients on the same transaction: a group of investors who together wish to buy and then jointly develop a single commercial property, all of them pursuing exactly the same commercial objective and wanting the deal structured in the same way. There is nonetheless a technical conflict of interest between them, because their individual positions are not quite identical. The clients all want the one firm to act for the whole group in order to save time and cost, and are content to be told how their information will be handled. The firm considers whether it may act. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act provided it simply charges each investor a separate fee for the work done.
The firm may never act for two clients where any conflict of interest exists between them, whatever the circumstances.
The firm may act only if the SRA gives its prior approval to the joint retainer between the investors.
The firm may act only under the substantially-common-interest exception, with informed consent and appropriate safeguards.
The firm may act for the group without any consent, because the investors all want the same outcome.
Legal Services.w: Although there is a conflict, the SRA Code permits acting where the clients have a substantially common interest in relation to the matter, provided each gives informed consent (generally in writing) and appropriate safeguards are put in place. It is not an absolute bar.

n.0: Charging separate fees does not address the conflict; informed consent and safeguards do.
n.1: A conflict is not an absolute bar; the substantially-common-interest exception can apply.
n.2: There is no requirement for prior SRA approval of such a retainer.
n.4: A shared desired outcome does not remove the need for informed consent and safeguards.

Legal Services.q: A prospective client who is profoundly deaf contacts a firm and asks it to arrange a British Sign Language interpreter for their first appointment, so that they can understand the advice and give proper instructions. The fee-earner is reluctant, regarding the request as inconvenient and an unwelcome additional cost to the firm, and wonders whether the firm can instead simply insist that the client bring along a friend or relative to interpret, or else decline to take the client on at all. The firm seeks advice on its obligations towards this prospective client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may decline to act for the client, because a firm is free to choose its clients for any reason it likes.
The firm must not discriminate and must make reasonable adjustments, such as arranging an interpreter.
The firm need only make adjustments if the client can show that the disability was caused by another's fault.
The firm may insist that the client bring their own interpreter, as the cost of adjustments always falls on the client.
The firm has no obligations until a retainer is formally agreed, so it need do nothing for a prospective client.
Legal Services.w: Under the Equality Act 2010 and the SRA's requirements, a firm must not unlawfully discriminate and must make reasonable adjustments for disabled clients, which can include arranging and paying for measures such as a sign language interpreter.

n.0: A firm's freedom to choose clients does not extend to unlawful discrimination on protected grounds.
n.2: The duty does not depend on how or why the client came to be disabled.
n.3: The duty to make reasonable adjustments means the cost cannot simply be shifted onto the disabled client.
n.4: Obligations not to discriminate and to make adjustments apply to prospective clients, not just existing ones.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is instructed by an adult client on a contentious family matter, but the whole of the client's legal fees is being paid by the client's wealthy parent. The parent, who is not themselves a client of the firm, begins contacting the solicitor directly and repeatedly, giving instructions about how the matter should be conducted and pressing the solicitor to take steps that suit the parent's own wishes rather than the objectives the client has actually set. The solicitor must decide whose instructions and interests are to govern the conduct of the matter. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must follow the parent's instructions, because the person who pays the fees is entitled to direct the matter.
The solicitor must cease acting at once, because a matter can never be funded by anyone other than the client.
The solicitor may follow the parent's instructions, provided the client is kept informed of what is being done.
The solicitor must give equal weight to the client's and the parent's wishes, since the parent is funding the work.
The solicitor's duties remain owed to the client, so the solicitor must act on the client's instructions and interests, not the payer's.
Legal Services.w: Where a third party funds the client's fees, the solicitor's professional duties are still owed to the client. The solicitor must act on the client's instructions and in the client's best interests, must not allow the payer to influence the matter improperly, and must be alert to any conflict.

n.0: Paying the fees does not entitle the payer to direct how the client's matter is run.
n.1: Third-party funding is permitted; it does not require the solicitor to cease acting.
n.2: Merely keeping the client informed does not justify acting on the payer's instructions.
n.3: The client's instructions govern; the payer's wishes are not given equal weight.

Legal Services.q: A firm decides, in order to cut its costs, to outsource part of its legal work — the drafting of certain documents and some file review — to an external provider that is not part of the firm. The outsourced work will involve the external provider having access to confidential client information. A partner assumes that, once the work has been handed over to the external provider, responsibility for it, and for anything that goes wrong, passes entirely to that provider. The firm seeks advice on its obligations when outsourcing work in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may outsource the work with no need to consider client confidentiality, as that duty ends on outsourcing.
The firm may outsource the work only if every client individually approves the particular provider chosen.
Once the work is outsourced, all responsibility for it and for any confidentiality breach passes to the external provider.
The firm may not outsource any legal work at all, because such work must always be done in-house.
The firm may outsource the work but remains responsible for it and must ensure the client's confidentiality is protected.
Legal Services.w: A firm may outsource work, but it remains responsible for compliance with its regulatory obligations in relation to that work, must ensure that client confidentiality is protected by the arrangement, and should inform clients where appropriate. Responsibility is not simply transferred to the provider.

n.0: The duty of confidentiality continues and must be protected in the outsourcing arrangement.
n.1: Individual client approval of the specific provider is not the governing requirement; responsibility and confidentiality are.
n.2: Responsibility for regulatory compliance and confidentiality does not pass wholly to the provider.
n.3: Outsourcing of legal work is permitted; it is not prohibited.

Legal Services.q: Part way through a retainer, a solicitor wishes to stop acting for a client. The solicitor is aware that they cannot simply abandon the client without justification. The retainer is ongoing and the client still needs representation. The solicitor is considering when and how they may cease to act. Midway through the matter the solicitor would prefer to bow out, but is conscious that the client still needs representation and that simply dropping the client could leave them badly exposed, so the solicitor needs to know on what basis and with what notice they may properly stop acting. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may cease to act only where there is good reason and on reasonable notice to the client.
The solicitor may cease to act only with the permission of the court in every case on these facts.
The solicitor may never cease to act once a retainer has begun.
The solicitor may cease to act only if the client has failed to pay any fee at all.
The solicitor may cease to act at any time for any reason without notice.
Legal Services.w: A solicitor should not cease acting for a client without good reason and without giving reasonable notice, so as not to prejudice the client. Good reasons may include a conflict of interest, the client's failure to give proper instructions or to pay, or being asked to act improperly. The solicitor must still protect the client's position when withdrawing.

n.1: Court permission is not required in every case to cease acting.
n.2: A solicitor can cease acting for good reason, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Non-payment is one possible good reason, but not the only one.
n.4: A solicitor cannot simply cease acting at any time without reason or notice.

Legal Services.q: A firm decides to try to drum up new personal injury work by having its marketing staff telephone, and approach in person in the street, members of the public with whom the firm has no existing connection whatsoever, encouraging them there and then to bring accident claims through the firm. The individuals contacted have not asked to be approached, have never dealt with the firm before, and have no prior relationship with it of any kind. A partner questions whether this particular method of winning new business is actually permitted under the conduct rules. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may make unsolicited approaches, provided the people contacted are not required to pay anything upfront.
The firm may make unsolicited approaches, provided each person contacted is told the call is marketing.
The firm may make unsolicited approaches, provided it does not misstate the strength of any potential claim.
Making unsolicited approaches in person or by telephone to members of the public to win work is not permitted.
The firm may make unsolicited approaches to anyone it likes, because marketing by solicitors is unrestricted.
Legal Services.w: The SRA rules restrict how firms may seek work, and prohibit making unsolicited approaches in person or by telephone to members of the public in order to win instructions. Such cold-calling of the public is not a permitted method of publicity.

n.0: The absence of an upfront charge does not make cold-calling of the public permitted.
n.1: Labelling the call as marketing does not make an unsolicited approach to the public permissible.
n.2: Not overstating the claim does not cure the impropriety of the unsolicited approach itself.
n.4: Solicitors' marketing is subject to conduct rules; it is not unrestricted.

Legal Services.q: A junior solicitor, newly qualified and employed in a busy litigation team, discovers that the senior partner supervising a particular case is deliberately withholding a document that plainly must be disclosed, in order to mislead the court about a key issue in the proceedings. The junior is acutely anxious about the consequences of speaking up against a senior colleague on whom their career and reputation depend, and is sorely tempted simply to say nothing and to let the partner deal with the matter as they see fit. The junior seeks advice on their professional duty. Which of the following best states the junior solicitor's position under the SRA Standards and Regulations?
o: The junior may remain silent unless and until there is conclusive proof of the partner's intention to mislead the court.
The junior owes an overriding duty to the administration of justice and must not let the court be misled, whatever their seniority.
The junior must give priority to the firm's commercial interests, which outweigh the conduct of any individual case.
The junior's primary duty is to avoid reputational damage to the firm, so simply remaining silent is the correct course here.
The junior owes a duty of confidentiality to the partner that prevents any disclosure of the partner's conduct at all.
Legal Services.w: The SRA Principles require solicitors to uphold the rule of law and the proper administration of justice, and the Code prohibits knowingly or recklessly misleading the court. This duty to the court overrides duties owed to an employer or colleague, and applies to solicitors at every level of seniority.

n.0: The junior cannot wait for conclusive proof once they know the court is being misled; they must act on that knowledge.
n.2: Commercial interests do not outweigh the overriding duty to the court.
n.3: Avoiding reputational damage does not justify allowing the court to be misled.
n.4: There is no duty of confidentiality that requires or permits a solicitor to conceal another's attempt to mislead the court.

Legal Services.q: Several years ago a solicitor acted for a client on a private matter which has long since concluded, and the retainer between them came to an end at that time. The former client has since died. A relative of the deceased now approaches the solicitor and asks to be told confidential information about the deceased's financial affairs that the solicitor had learned while acting on that old matter. The relative argues that, because the client is now dead and the matter has been closed for years, the duty of confidentiality can no longer apply to any of it. The solicitor considers their position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The information may be disclosed to a relative of the deceased, because family members are always entitled to it.
The duty of confidentiality ends on the client's death, so the information may now be freely disclosed to relatives.
The duty of confidentiality ends automatically as soon as the retainer between the solicitor and client comes to an end.
The information may be disclosed once a fixed number of years has passed since the matter was concluded.
The duty of confidentiality continues after the retainer ends and after death, so the information must not be disclosed.
Legal Services.w: The duty of confidentiality is a continuing one: it survives the ending of the retainer and continues after the client's death. The solicitor may not disclose the former client's confidential information to a relative simply because the client has died or the matter is closed.

n.0: Relatives have no automatic entitlement to a deceased client's confidential information.
n.1: The duty continues after death; it is not extinguished by it.
n.2: Confidentiality does not end when the retainer ends.
n.3: There is no fixed period after which the confidential information may simply be released.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor holds confidential information about a client which, in the ordinary course, the solicitor would be strictly bound to keep secret and not to reveal to anyone. The solicitor is then served with a court order, made in entirely separate proceedings, which requires the solicitor to disclose that very information; there is no proper basis on which the order can be challenged and the information is not protected by privilege. The client does not want the information revealed at all. The solicitor must reconcile the duty of confidentiality with the terms of the court order. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The duty of confidentiality is absolute, so the solicitor must refuse to comply with the court order in every case.
The solicitor may disclose the information only after the client has had a final opportunity to remove it.
The solicitor must ignore the order, because a solicitor's duty to the client always overrides any court order.
The solicitor may comply with the order only if the client first gives express consent to the disclosure.
Confidentiality must yield where disclosure is required by law, such as under a valid court order or a statutory duty.
Legal Services.w: The professional duty of confidentiality is not absolute. It gives way where disclosure is required or permitted by law — for example under a valid court order, or a statutory obligation such as those under the anti-money-laundering regime — and the solicitor must then comply.

n.0: Confidentiality is not absolute; it yields to a legal obligation to disclose.
n.1: The client has no right to strip out the information before a required disclosure is made.
n.2: A solicitor may not simply ignore a valid court order in reliance on the duty to the client.
n.3: Compliance with a valid court order does not depend on the client's consent.

Legal Services.q: A person who is not a solicitor, and who holds no professional authorisation of any kind, sets up a business offering, for a fee, to conduct litigation on behalf of members of the public in the county court and to stand up and address the court on their behalf at hearings. They genuinely believe that, because the market for legal services is open to competition, anyone at all is free to offer these services. A qualified solicitor is asked whether these particular activities may lawfully be carried on by an unauthorised person in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Conducting litigation and exercising rights of audience are reserved legal activities that may only be carried on by an authorised person.
Only exercising rights of audience is restricted; conducting litigation may be carried on by any person for reward.
These activities may be carried on by anyone, provided no fee above a fixed statutory maximum is charged for them.
These activities may be carried on by anyone, provided the client is told in writing that the provider is not a solicitor.
Anyone may conduct litigation and exercise rights of audience, because no legal activity is restricted to authorised persons.
Legal Services.w: Under the Legal Services Act 2007, certain activities are 'reserved legal activities' — including the exercise of a right of audience and the conduct of litigation — which may only be carried on by a person authorised to do so; doing so while unauthorised is a criminal offence.

n.1: Both the conduct of litigation and rights of audience are reserved, not just rights of audience.
n.2: There is no fee ceiling that permits an unauthorised person to carry on reserved activities.
n.3: A disclosure that the provider is not a solicitor does not permit carrying on a reserved activity.
n.4: Some legal activities are reserved and restricted to authorised persons.

Legal Services.q: A solicitor is asked to act for both the buyer and the seller in the same residential conveyancing transaction. The two parties have agreed a price directly between themselves and wish to save money by instructing a single solicitor to handle the whole matter for them. They are not related or otherwise connected in any way, they have been negotiating at arm's length, and each of them plainly has their own distinct interests in the price, the contract terms and the timing of the sale and completion. The solicitor asks whether it is proper to act for both parties to this transaction. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may act for both, provided the agreed price is confirmed to be a fair market value.
The solicitor may always act for both buyer and seller, because a conveyancing sale involves only routine paperwork.
There is a conflict, so the solicitor should not act for both buyer and seller on the same sale unless a narrow exception applies.
The solicitor may act for both, provided the buyer and seller each pay half of the solicitor's fee.
The solicitor may act for both, because the parties have already agreed the price between themselves.
Legal Services.w: Acting for both buyer and seller in the same transaction gives rise to a conflict of interest, because their interests in the price and terms differ. The solicitor should not act for both unless one of the limited exceptions (such as a substantially common interest) applies with appropriate safeguards.

n.0: A fair price does not cure the conflict inherent in acting for both sides.
n.1: Conveyancing is not merely routine; buyer and seller have opposing interests in the deal.
n.3: Splitting the fee does not remove the conflict between the parties' interests.
n.4: Agreeing the price between themselves does not eliminate the conflict over the terms and conduct of the sale.

Legal Services.q: A private client is dissatisfied with the service they have received from their solicitor on a matter and makes a formal, written complaint to the firm about it. The firm investigates the complaint fully under its own internal complaints procedure and sends the client a detailed final written response, but the client remains unhappy with both the way the matter was handled and the outcome of the complaint itself. The client now asks the solicitor what further avenue is open to them to have their complaint about the firm's service considered independently by someone outside the firm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client must complain directly to the Solicitors Regulation Authority, which resolves all client service complaints.
The client has no further route available, because the firm's final response on the complaint is conclusive.
The client must be informed of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman, and of the time limits for doing so.
The client may only escalate the matter if the amount in dispute exceeds a fixed financial threshold set by the firm.
The client's only remaining option is to bring a claim in the civil courts against the firm for its poor service.
Legal Services.w: Firms must operate a complaints procedure and inform clients, in writing at the outset and again if a complaint is not resolved, of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman (which handles service complaints) and of the applicable time limits for doing so.

n.0: The SRA regulates conduct; service complaints go to the Legal Ombudsman, not the SRA.
n.1: The firm's final response is not the end of the road; the client may go to the Legal Ombudsman.
n.3: Access to the Legal Ombudsman is not gated behind a firm-set financial threshold.
n.4: Litigation is not the only route; the Legal Ombudsman deals with service complaints.

Legal Services.q: A client tells a solicitor, in confidence during a meeting at the office, that they intend to carry out a serious act of violence against a named individual, giving enough detail that the solicitor forms the genuine belief that there is a real and imminent risk to that person's life. The information was plainly given in confidence, and the solicitor is acutely conscious of the strict duty of confidentiality that is ordinarily owed to a client. The solicitor now has to decide whether they may disclose what they have been told, to the police or the intended victim, in order to try to prevent the threatened harm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may disclose the threat only after the intended victim has already come to serious harm.
The solicitor may disclose the threat only if the client first gives express permission to do so.
Confidentiality may be overridden where disclosure is necessary to prevent serious harm, such as a risk to a person's life.
The solicitor must disclose every confidence a client shares, whether or not any harm is threatened.
The duty of confidentiality is absolute, so the solicitor may not disclose the threat in any circumstances at all.
Legal Services.w: The duty of confidentiality is not absolute. Disclosure may be justified, exceptionally, where it is necessary to prevent serious harm — for example where the solicitor reasonably believes disclosure is needed to prevent death or serious physical harm to a person.

n.0: The point of the exception is to prevent the harm, not to wait until after it occurs.
n.1: The exception applies precisely because the client will not consent; consent is not required.
n.3: There is no duty to disclose ordinary confidences; the exception is narrow and harm-based.
n.4: Confidentiality is not absolute; a serious-harm exception can apply.

Legal Services.q: A prospective client telephones a firm to ask it to act on a perfectly straightforward matter that is well within the firm's ordinary expertise and capacity. On working out the prospective client's religion from their name and their manner of speaking, the fee-earner tells them, quite untruthfully, that the firm is simply too busy to be able to help them, when in reality the fee-earner has decided that they do not wish to act for someone of that particular religion. The prospective client suspects the real reason for the refusal and complains to the firm. The firm considers its position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The firm must not refuse to act, or provide a worse service, because of a client's protected characteristic.
The firm may refuse on this basis, provided it does not tell the client the real reason for the refusal.
The firm may refuse to act for anyone it chooses, for any reason, because it is a private business.
The firm may refuse on this basis, provided another local firm is available to take the client on.
The firm has no obligations to a mere prospective client who has not yet been formally taken on.
Legal Services.w: Under the Equality Act 2010 and the SRA's requirements, a firm must not discriminate against a person because of a protected characteristic (such as religion), including by refusing to act or by offering a lesser service. This applies to prospective clients as well as existing ones.

n.1: Concealing the real reason does not make discriminatory refusal lawful.
n.2: A firm's freedom to choose clients does not extend to unlawful discrimination.
n.3: The availability of another firm does not excuse discriminatory treatment.
n.4: Anti-discrimination duties apply to prospective clients, not only those already retained.

Property Law & Practice.q: A local planning authority discovers that a building operation was carried out some years ago without the required planning permission. The authority is considering whether it may still take enforcement action against the breach. A period of time has elapsed since the unauthorised building operation was substantially completed. The authority is considering enforcement. During the buyer's investigations it comes to light that an extension was built some years back without the planning permission it needed, and the parties are now weighing whether, given the time that has passed, the local authority could still take steps against the unauthorised work. Which of the following best describes the position on time limits for enforcement?
o: Enforcement may be time-barred once the relevant statutory period since the breach has expired.
There is no time limit, so enforcement can always be taken however long ago the breach occurred.
Enforcement depends solely on whether the neighbours object.
Enforcement is possible only within 6 months of the breach in every case.
Enforcement is barred as soon as the building is occupied.
Property Law & Practice.w: Planning enforcement is subject to time limits: after the relevant statutory period has elapsed since the breach (historically four years for building operations and certain changes of use to a single dwelling, and ten years for other breaches, though these limits have been reformed), the development generally becomes immune from enforcement and lawful. A buyer's solicitor should check for immunity or a certificate of lawfulness.

n.1: There is a time limit; enforcement is not always available regardless of when the breach occurred.
n.2: Time limits, not merely neighbour objections, determine whether enforcement can be taken.
n.3: The limitation period is measured in years, not a flat six months.
n.4: Enforcement is not barred simply by occupation; the statutory period governs.

Property Law & Practice.q: The buyer's and seller's solicitors have agreed all the terms and are ready to make the contract legally binding. They intend to exchange contracts by telephone using a recognised Law Society formula rather than meeting in person. The buyer asks at what point the parties become legally committed to the transaction, and what exchange achieves. The solicitor considers the effect of exchange of contracts in a conveyancing transaction. Both parties had been treating the deal as provisional and could still have walked away until now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Exchange transfers legal ownership of the property to the buyer immediately.
The parties are legally bound from the moment terms are first agreed, long before exchange.
Exchange of contracts has no legal effect, and either party may still withdraw freely afterwards on these facts.
On exchange the parties become legally bound to complete, and neither can withdraw without being in breach of contract.
The parties become bound only once completion has actually taken place, not on exchange.
Property Law & Practice.w: Before exchange, either party may withdraw without liability ('subject to contract'). On exchange of contracts, a binding contract comes into existence and both parties are committed to completing on the agreed date; a party who then fails to complete is in breach.

n.0: Exchange does not transfer legal ownership; that happens on completion and registration.
n.1: The parties are not bound merely by agreeing terms subject to contract before exchange.
n.2: Exchange is precisely what makes the contract binding; it is not without effect.
n.4: The binding commitment arises on exchange, before completion.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor is checking the seller's capacity to sell, because the property is not being sold by a single individual absolute owner but by two co-owners holding on trust, one of whom has since died. The solicitor is concerned to ensure the buyer takes free of any beneficial interests. The solicitor considers how a buyer takes free of the beneficial interests of co-owners. The property had been in the joint names of a couple, one of whom had recently died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer can never take free of the beneficial interests of co-owners in any circumstances.
The buyer must obtain the written consent of every beneficiary before completing the purchase.
The buyer takes free of beneficial interests automatically, whoever the money is paid to.
The buyer takes free of beneficial interests only if the purchase price is paid to a single surviving co-owner on these facts as a general rule.
The buyer should ensure the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) so that beneficial interests are overreached.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where land is held on a trust of land by co-owners, a buyer overreaches the beneficiaries' interests (which are swept off the land onto the proceeds) by paying the purchase money to at least two trustees or a trust corporation. Where one of two co-owners has died, a second trustee may need to be appointed to achieve overreaching.

n.0: The buyer can take free by overreaching through payment to two trustees.
n.1: Overreaching, not each beneficiary's written consent, is the mechanism.
n.2: Overreaching is not automatic regardless of who is paid; two trustees are required.
n.3: Payment to a single surviving co-owner does not overreach beneficial interests behind a trust.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor has investigated the title and searches and is ready to advise the client before exchange of contracts. The solicitor prepares to summarise the key features, rights, burdens and any issues affecting the property for the client. The solicitor has completed the investigation of title and searches. The client is about to be committed on exchange. Having worked through the official copies, the contract and the results of the searches, the solicitor is at the point where the client must decide whether to go ahead, and needs to put the findings before the buyer in a digestible form before the buyer is locked in by exchanging contracts. Which of the following best describes the step the solicitor should take?
o: Provide the buyer with a report on title summarising the position, so the buyer can make an informed decision before exchange.
Advise the buyer only if the buyer specifically asks for information.
Send the buyer the raw official copies and searches with no explanation.
Leave all advice on title to the buyer's mortgage lender.
Exchange contracts first and inform the buyer of any problems only after completion on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Before exchange, the buyer's solicitor should report to the client on the results of investigating the title and searches (a report on title), explaining the property, the rights it benefits from, the burdens on it, and any problems, so that the client can make an informed decision before being committed on exchange. This is central to acting competently for the buyer.

n.1: The solicitor should advise proactively, not only if asked.
n.2: Sending raw documents without explanation does not discharge the solicitor's duty to advise.
n.3: The buyer's solicitor, not the lender, must advise the buyer on the title.
n.4: Problems should be reported before exchange, not left until after completion.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer of registered land has completed the purchase by deed of transfer and paid the price, but has not yet applied to register the transfer at the Land Registry. The buyer believes that, having completed, they are already the legal owner. The transfer is a registrable disposition of registered land that has not yet been registered. The buyer assumes legal ownership passed on completion. Completion has taken place, the deed of transfer has been signed and the money has changed hands, and the buyer, assuming that is the end of the matter, has not yet lodged any application at the Land Registry, believing the legal estate already sits with them by virtue of completion alone. Which of the following best describes the effect of registration on a registrable disposition?
o: Registration is required only for first registration of unregistered land.
Legal title passes on completion of the deed, and registration is merely optional.
The disposition does not operate at law until the registration requirements are met.
Legal title passes only when the purchase money is paid, regardless of registration.
The transfer is void unless registered within seven days of completion.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under s.27 of the Land Registration Act 2002, a registrable disposition of a registered estate (such as a transfer, or the grant of a legal charge or a lease over seven years) does not operate at law until the relevant registration requirements are met. Until registration, the buyer holds only an equitable interest, so registration is essential, not optional.

n.0: Registration of dispositions is required for dealings with already-registered land too, not only first registration.
n.1: Legal title does not pass on completion alone for registered land; registration is required and not optional.
n.3: Payment of the money does not pass legal title without registration.
n.4: The transfer is not void if not registered within seven days; but it does not operate at law until registered.

Property Law & Practice.q: A landlord grants a new lease of premises to a tenant for a fixed term of 15 years. The tenant's solicitor must ensure that the tenant's leasehold estate is properly protected and given legal effect. The tenant asks whether the new lease needs to be registered at the Land Registry. The solicitor considers the registration of a newly granted lease. The tenant was paying a substantial premium for the new lease and wanted it properly protected. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A lease is registered only if the landlord's own title is unregistered.
Only leases granted for more than 21 years need to be registered at the Land Registry on these facts as a general rule.
A newly granted lease for a term of more than seven years must be registered with its own title at the Land Registry.
No lease ever needs to be registered at the Land Registry, whatever its length.
A newly granted 15-year lease takes effect purely orally without any registration.
Property Law & Practice.w: The grant of a lease for a term of more than seven years is a registrable disposition (or, out of unregistered land, triggers compulsory registration). Such a lease must be registered with its own leasehold title at the Land Registry, and a note entered against the landlord's title.

n.0: Registration of a >7-year lease is required whether or not the landlord's title is registered.
n.1: The threshold is more than seven years, not 21.
n.3: Longer leases (over seven years) do require registration.
n.4: A 15-year lease must be granted by deed and registered, not made orally.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor is preparing to complete a purchase and must ensure that, on completion, the buyer will actually be able to take physical occupation of the property, free of the seller and any occupiers, unless the contract provides otherwise. The contract is for the sale with vacant possession. The buyer asks what vacant possession means and what the seller must do. The solicitor considers the obligation to give vacant possession on completion. The buyer was relying on moving into an empty house on the day of completion itself. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Vacant possession requires the seller to leave all their furniture for the buyer to use.
Vacant possession means the buyer takes the property with the seller and their belongings still in it on these facts.
Vacant possession means the buyer must vacate their own current home before completion.
The seller must give up the property empty of people and possessions so the buyer can take undisturbed occupation on completion.
Vacant possession is only relevant where the property is being sold subject to a tenancy.
Property Law & Practice.w: An obligation to give vacant possession requires the seller to hand over the property on completion free of people, chattels and legal interests entitling anyone to possession, so that the buyer can take actual, undisturbed possession. It does not apply where the property is sold subject to (rather than with vacant possession free of) a tenancy.

n.0: The seller must remove their belongings, not leave furniture for the buyer.
n.1: Vacant possession means the property is empty for the buyer, not still occupied by the seller.
n.2: Vacant possession concerns the property being sold, not the buyer's current home.
n.4: Vacant possession applies precisely where the property is not sold subject to a tenancy.

Property Law & Practice.q: The solicitors acting for a buyer and a seller in a residential transaction are preparing the contract and, as is usual in conveyancing practice, propose to base it on a widely used standard set of contractual terms rather than drafting every provision from scratch, adapting them with any special conditions the transaction requires. The buyer asks what these standard terms are and their role in the contract. The solicitor considers the use of the Standard Conditions of Sale in a residential conveyancing contract. The solicitors wanted a reliable, well-understood framework rather than reinventing every clause. Which of the following best describes their role?
o: The Standard Conditions of Sale replace the need for any written contract between the parties.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are commonly incorporated as the contract's general terms, supplemented by special conditions for the particular deal.
The Standard Conditions of Sale apply only to commercial property and never to residential sales.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are drafted afresh by the parties for every individual transaction.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are imposed by statute and cannot be varied by the parties in any way on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Property Law & Practice.w: Residential conveyancing contracts commonly incorporate the Standard Conditions of Sale as their general terms (with the Standard Commercial Property Conditions used for commercial deals). These standard terms are then adapted and supplemented by special conditions tailored to the particular transaction.

n.0: They form part of, rather than replace, the written contract.
n.2: The residential Standard Conditions of Sale are for residential deals (commercial deals use the SCPC).
n.3: They are pre-drafted standard terms, not written afresh each time.
n.4: The Standard Conditions are contractual terms the parties adopt and can vary, not statutory rules.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor acting for a buyer is carrying out pre-contract searches on a residential property. The solicitor wishes to discover matters recorded by the local authority, such as planning permissions and enforcement notices, financial charges, and whether the road serving the property is publicly maintained. The solicitor considers which search reveals local authority matters affecting the property. The buyer wanted to be sure there were no planning problems or road-adoption issues affecting the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is no way to discover local authority matters before contracts are exchanged.
A bankruptcy search against the buyer reveals planning permissions affecting the property.
A local search (local land charges search and enquiries of the local authority) reveals such local authority matters.
The register of title at the Land Registry reveals all local authority planning and highways matters on these facts.
An environmental search is the only search that reveals whether a road is publicly maintained.
Property Law & Practice.w: A local search — comprising a search of the local land charges register (LLC1) and enquiries of the local authority (CON29) — reveals local authority matters such as planning permissions and refusals, enforcement and other notices, financial charges, and whether roads and drains serving the property are publicly maintained.

n.0: Local authority matters can and should be discovered pre-contract via the local search.
n.1: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not planning permissions.
n.3: The Land Registry title does not reveal all local authority planning/highways matters; the local search does.
n.4: The local search, not the environmental search, reveals adopted-highway status.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor acting for a buyer sends detailed pre-contract enquiries to the seller's solicitor to find out about the practical and legal position of the property — for example disputes with neighbours, guarantees, alterations, and rights and arrangements affecting the property. The buyer relies on the answers in deciding whether to proceed. The solicitor considers the purpose and status of pre-contract enquiries of the seller. The buyer wanted to learn as much as possible about the property before deciding whether to proceed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Pre-contract enquiries obtain information from the seller, whose replies must not be misleading and may found a misrepresentation claim if untrue.
Pre-contract enquiries are pointless, because the seller is under no obligation to answer honestly on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Pre-contract enquiries replace the need for the buyer to investigate title at all.
Pre-contract enquiries transfer to the seller the entire risk of any defect in the property.
Pre-contract enquiries are answered by the local authority rather than the seller.
Property Law & Practice.w: Pre-contract enquiries (for example the TA6 property information form or CPSE) are used to obtain information from the seller about the property. While the buyer cannot rely on the seller to volunteer everything, the seller's replies must not be misleading, and a false reply on which the buyer relies may give rise to a misrepresentation claim.

n.1: Replies are not free of consequence; misleading answers can found a misrepresentation claim.
n.2: Enquiries do not replace investigation of title.
n.3: Enquiries do not transfer all risk of defects to the seller.
n.4: Pre-contract enquiries are answered by the seller, not the local authority.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor reviews the proprietorship register of the registered title and notes the class of title with which the seller is registered. The buyer wants the best possible title. The solicitor explains that different classes of registered title exist, offering different levels of guarantee. The property is registered with the highest class. The solicitor considers the classes of registered title. The buyer was paying a substantial sum and wanted the strongest guarantee of the seller's ownership. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Absolute title is the best class, giving the fullest state guarantee of the proprietor's ownership.
Good leasehold title is the best class available for a registered freehold estate.
Qualified title is the highest class, guaranteeing the whole of the proprietor's ownership.
Possessory title is the best class of title available to a registered proprietor.
There is only one class of registered title, with no variation between properties.
Property Law & Practice.w: Absolute title is the best class of registered title, giving the fullest guarantee: the proprietor holds the estate subject only to entries on the register and to overriding interests. Possessory and qualified titles are inferior classes with limitations, and good leasehold applies only to leases.

n.1: Good leasehold is a class for leases, not the best class for a freehold.
n.2: Qualified title is a lesser class with a specified defect, not the highest.
n.3: Possessory title is an inferior class, not the best.
n.4: There are several classes of registered title.

Property Law & Practice.q: A developer wishes to grant a would-be buyer the right, exercisable in the future, to buy a plot of land at a set price if the buyer chooses to do so within a stated period. The buyer wants to be sure this right will bind the land even if the developer sells to someone else first. The buyer asks how such a right can be protected against third parties. The solicitor considers the protection of an option to purchase over registered land. The developer was actively marketing the surrounding land and might sell before the option was used. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An option to purchase cannot be protected on the register and can never bind a later buyer.
An option to purchase must be registered as a local land charge with the local authority.
An option to purchase binds all future owners automatically without any need to protect it.
An option to purchase is protected only by the buyer taking physical possession of the land on these facts.
An option to purchase is an estate contract which should be protected by entering a notice on the register.
Property Law & Practice.w: An option to purchase land is an estate contract (an interest in land). To bind a later purchaser of registered land, it should be protected by entering a notice on the charges register of the burdened title; if not protected, it may be lost against a subsequent registered disposition for value.

n.0: An option can be protected by a notice; it is not incapable of binding a later buyer.
n.1: An option over registered land is protected at the Land Registry, not as a local land charge.
n.2: An option does not bind future owners automatically; it needs protection.
n.3: Protection is by a register notice, not merely by taking possession.

Property Law & Practice.q: Having completed the purchase of registered land, the buyer's solicitor must now deal with the Land Registry so that the buyer becomes the registered proprietor. The solicitor had obtained a priority search before completion. The buyer asks what must be done after completion to perfect the buyer's legal title, and within what period. The solicitor considers the post-completion registration of a transfer of registered land. The solicitor had a limited priority window in which to secure the buyer's registration. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's solicitor must apply to register the transfer, ideally within the priority period given by the pre-completion search.
No application to the Land Registry is needed, because legal title passed on completion on these facts as a general rule.
Only the seller's solicitor can apply to register the change of ownership.
The buyer becomes registered proprietor automatically 12 years after completion.
Registration is optional and has no effect on the buyer's legal title to the land.
Property Law & Practice.w: A transfer of registered land must be completed by registration: the buyer's solicitor applies to the Land Registry to register the buyer as proprietor. The application should be made within the priority period conferred by the pre-completion official search (OS1) to preserve priority; legal title only vests on registration.

n.1: Registration is required; legal title does not fully vest until the buyer is registered.
n.2: The buyer's solicitor (the transferee's side) applies to register the transfer.
n.3: Registration is not automatic after 12 years; the solicitor must apply.
n.4: Registration is not optional for a registrable disposition; it is essential to legal title.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer and seller have agreed the sale of a house and their solicitors are drawing up the contract for sale of the land. The parties want to be sure that the contract they enter into will be valid and enforceable as a contract for the disposition of an interest in land. One party assumes an oral agreement, or an exchange of emails without signatures, will suffice. The solicitor advises on the formalities required for a valid contract for the sale of land under the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989. The parties wanted certainty that their agreement to buy and sell the house would actually hold. Which of the following best describes the requirements?
o: The contract need only be signed by the seller, and the buyer's signature is not required.
The contract must be in writing, incorporate all the agreed terms in one document (or by reference), and be signed by or on behalf of both parties.
The contract must be made by deed and witnessed, or it has no effect at all.
The contract may be made orally, provided both parties clearly intend to be bound by it.
The contract is valid as soon as the price is agreed, whether or not anything is written down on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under s.2 Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, incorporate all the expressly agreed terms in one document (or where contracts are exchanged, in each), and be signed by or on behalf of each party.

n.0: Both parties (not just the seller) must sign the contract or their part of it.
n.2: A land contract requires writing under s.2 but need not be made by deed; the transfer is by deed.
n.3: An oral land contract does not satisfy s.2, whatever the parties' intentions.
n.4: Agreeing the price without a compliant written contract is not enough.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer has purchased a piece of land which turns out to be unregistered, this being the first sale of it for many years so that first registration is now compulsory. The buyer's solicitor must ensure the buyer is registered for the first time at the Land Registry within the statutory period. The buyer asks about the obligation to register unregistered land following the purchase. The solicitor considers compulsory first registration. The land had not been registered before and this sale was the first for a great many years. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: First registration must be applied for within 12 years of completion of the purchase.
First registration is the seller's responsibility, not the buyer's, after completion.
Unregistered land can never be registered at the Land Registry in any circumstances.
There is no obligation to register unregistered land after a purchase; it may remain unregistered forever on these facts.
The buyer must apply for first registration within two months of completion, or the transfer of the legal estate becomes void.
Property Law & Practice.w: A conveyance on sale of unregistered land is a trigger for compulsory first registration. The buyer must apply to register the estate within two months of completion; if they fail to do so, the transfer of the legal estate becomes void and the estate reverts to the transferor to hold on a bare trust.

n.0: The period is two months, not 12 years.
n.1: It is the buyer/transferee who must apply for first registration.
n.2: Unregistered land is registered on first registration.
n.3: There is an obligation to register following a triggering event; it cannot simply stay unregistered.

Property Law & Practice.q: On completion of the assignment of a lease part-way through a rent period, the outgoing tenant (assignor) has already paid rent (and service charge) in advance for the whole period, part of which relates to the time after completion when the incoming tenant (assignee) will hold the lease. The parties need to deal fairly with these outgoings. The buyer asks how such payments are dealt with on completion. The solicitor considers the apportionment of rent and outgoings on the assignment of a lease. The assignment was completing midway through a quarter for which the rent had already been paid. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The landlord refunds the whole period's rent to the assignor and re-charges the assignee.
Rent and outgoings are apportioned at completion so each party bears them for the period during which they hold the lease.
The assignee must reimburse the landlord directly for the assignor's earlier rent payments.
The assignor bears the full rent for the whole period, and the assignee pays nothing towards it on these facts.
Rent and outgoings are never apportioned and simply fall wherever they happen to lie.
Property Law & Practice.w: On completion of a leasehold assignment part-way through a payment period, rent and other outgoings are apportioned between assignor and assignee so that each bears them for the portion of the period during which they respectively hold the lease, with a balancing payment made on completion.

n.0: The landlord does not refund and re-charge; the parties apportion between themselves.
n.2: The apportionment is between assignor and assignee, not a direct reimbursement of the landlord.
n.3: The rent is apportioned; the assignor does not bear the whole period alone.
n.4: Apportionment is standard practice; outgoings are not simply left where they lie.
