Property Law & Practice.q: On completion of a purchase, the seller has an existing mortgage over the property which must be discharged so the buyer takes free of it. The seller's solicitor undertakes to use the completion money to redeem the mortgage and to send the buyer's solicitor evidence of discharge. The buyer's solicitor relies on this arrangement. The buyer asks how the seller's mortgage is dealt with on completion. The solicitor considers the discharge of the seller's mortgage. The buyer had to be sure of taking the property free of the seller's existing lender's charge. Which of the following best describes the usual practice?
o: The seller's mortgage is automatically discharged the moment contracts are exchanged.
The seller's solicitor gives an undertaking to discharge the mortgage from the proceeds and to forward evidence of discharge.
The seller's mortgage can never be discharged, so the buyer must simply accept it remains.
The buyer's solicitor must pay off the seller's mortgage in addition to the purchase price.
The buyer must take the property subject to the seller's existing mortgage and repay it themselves on these facts.
Property Law & Practice.w: On completion, the seller's outstanding mortgage is redeemed from the sale proceeds. In practice the seller's solicitor gives the buyer's solicitor an undertaking to discharge the mortgage and to send evidence of discharge (such as the electronic DS1/e-DS1), allowing the buyer to complete safely and take free of the charge.

n.0: The mortgage is discharged on completion, not automatically on exchange.
n.2: The mortgage is discharged so the buyer takes free of it.
n.3: The seller's mortgage is redeemed from the seller's proceeds, not paid extra by the buyer.
n.4: The buyer does not normally take subject to and repay the seller's mortgage.

Property Law & Practice.q: The buyer of a residential property is proceeding to completion. The buyer's solicitor holds the mortgage advance and the balance of the purchase money, and the seller's solicitor holds the executed transfer. The buyer asks what actually happens on completion day to pass the transaction from a binding contract to the buyer taking the property. The solicitor considers what occurs on completion of a conveyancing transaction. The buyer's funds were in place and the parties were ready to move the deal to its conclusion. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Completion transfers only the deposit, with the balance payable months later.
The purchase money is transferred to the seller's solicitor and the executed transfer and documents are released to the buyer.
Completion simply means the parties sign the contract for the first time.
The buyer becomes the registered proprietor automatically without any transfer of money.
The seller keeps both the money and the property until the buyer later applies to court on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: On completion, the balance of the purchase price (together with the mortgage advance) is transferred to the seller's solicitor, and in return the executed transfer deed and the title documents are released to the buyer's solicitor, so that the buyer becomes entitled to the property and can apply to register the transfer.

n.0: On completion the balance of the price is paid, not merely the deposit.
n.2: Signing the contract is exchange, not completion.
n.3: Registration follows completion; it is not automatic without the transfer of money.
n.4: On completion the seller is paid and gives up the property and documents.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer intends to rely on the physical condition of the property when deciding whether to proceed and at what price. The buyer's solicitor advises the buyer about protecting themselves against the risk of hidden physical problems with the building. The property is an older house. The solicitor considers the buyer's protection regarding the physical state of the property. The house was over a hundred years old and the buyer had not yet had it inspected. Which of the following best describes the appropriate advice?
o: The buyer may rely entirely on the seller's estate agent's description of the property's condition on these facts.
The buyer need not obtain any survey, because the seller guarantees the condition of the property.
The buyer is fully protected by the local land charges search against physical defects.
The buyer should obtain an appropriate survey of the property, as the seller is not obliged to disclose physical defects.
The buyer's solicitor's investigation of title will reveal all physical defects in the building.
Property Law & Practice.w: Because caveat emptor applies to the physical condition of the property, the buyer should commission an appropriate survey (its level depending on the property's age and type) to identify physical defects. The seller is not obliged to volunteer them, and title investigation and searches do not reveal building condition.

n.0: The estate agent's description is not a reliable substitute for a survey.
n.1: The seller does not guarantee the property's condition.
n.2: The local land charges search does not reveal physical defects.
n.4: Investigation of title concerns ownership and burdens, not the physical state of the building.

Property Law & Practice.q: After investigating title and before completion, a buyer's solicitor of registered land wishes to protect the buyer against the risk of the seller making some further disposition, or a new entry appearing on the register, in the gap between the final search and registration of the buyer. The solicitor considers the pre-completion search of the register that confers a priority period. Completion was a few weeks away and the buyer wanted protection in the interim period. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An official search of the register with priority (Form OS1) gives a priority period within which the buyer must apply to register.
The buyer obtains priority automatically on exchange of contracts, with no search needed on these facts as a general rule.
A bankruptcy search of the register gives the buyer priority over later dispositions.
A local land charges search gives the buyer a priority period against later entries.
There is no way to protect a buyer against entries made after the final search.
Property Law & Practice.w: A pre-completion official search of the whole register with priority (Form OS1) confers a priority period (currently 30 working days) during which any application to register the buyer's disposition takes priority over other entries, provided the buyer completes and applies to register within that period.

n.1: Priority is obtained via the OS1 search, not automatically on exchange.
n.2: A bankruptcy search does not confer priority over dispositions.
n.3: The local land charges search does not give a Land Registry priority period.
n.4: There is a mechanism (OS1) to protect the buyer against later entries.

Property Law & Practice.q: A commercial landlord is granting a lease of commercial premises and is considering the VAT position, in particular whether VAT will be charged on the rent and on any premium. The default position for most supplies of interests in land is that they are exempt from VAT, but there is a mechanism by which the landlord can choose to charge VAT. The landlord asks about VAT on the commercial property. The solicitor considers the option to tax for VAT purposes. The landlord wanted to be able to recover the VAT it incurred on refurbishing the premises. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only residential property can ever be subject to an option to tax.
VAT is always charged at the standard rate on every supply of land, with no exemption on these facts as a general rule.
Supplies of land are generally exempt from VAT, but the owner may 'opt to tax', making its supplies standard-rated.
VAT on land is charged only where the buyer is an individual rather than a business.
Land can never be subject to VAT under any circumstances at all.
Property Law & Practice.w: Most supplies of interests in land are exempt from VAT by default. However, the owner of commercial property can elect to 'opt to tax' (waive the exemption), which makes its supplies of that property standard-rated for VAT, allowing it to recover related input VAT. Residential property largely remains exempt.

n.0: The option to tax applies to commercial, not residential, property.
n.1: Land supplies are generally exempt by default, not always standard-rated.
n.3: The VAT position turns on the option to tax, not on whether the buyer is an individual.
n.4: Land can be subject to VAT, for example following an option to tax.

Property Law & Practice.q: After exchange of contracts, and having investigated the seller's title, the buyer's solicitor identifies certain queries and outstanding matters relating to the title that need to be resolved before completion — for example confirming the discharge of an existing mortgage. The solicitor raises formal written queries with the seller's solicitor. The buyer asks what these queries are called and their purpose in the conveyancing process. The solicitor considers requisitions on title. The seller still had an outstanding mortgage that would need to be discharged on completion. Which of the following best describes them?
o: Requisitions on title are the seller's demands that the buyer pay the price early.
Requisitions on title are the buyer's application to the Land Registry for first registration.
Requisitions on title are searches carried out with the local authority before exchange.
Requisitions on title are formal queries raised on the seller's title, typically to clear up outstanding matters before completion.
Requisitions on title are enquiries answered by the buyer's surveyor about the building's condition on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Requisitions on title are formal questions raised by the buyer's solicitor with the seller's solicitor, in practice used mainly after exchange to deal with completion arrangements and to ensure outstanding matters (such as discharge of the seller's mortgage and completion mechanics) are resolved before completion.

n.0: Requisitions are the buyer's queries, not the seller's demand for early payment.
n.1: Requisitions are not the application for first registration.
n.2: Requisitions are queries on title, not local authority searches.
n.4: Requisitions concern title, not the surveyor's report on physical condition.

Property Law & Practice.q: On completion of the purchase of registered land, legal ownership is to be transferred from the seller to the buyer. The buyer's solicitor prepares the document that will transfer the legal estate, to be executed by the seller (and, where relevant, the buyer). The buyer asks what form this document takes and how it must be executed to be effective. The solicitor considers the transfer deed used to transfer registered land. The buyer needed to become the registered owner and take good legal title to the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer of legal ownership requires no document at all once the price is paid on these facts.
The transfer is effective as soon as it is signed, whether or not it is witnessed.
The transfer is made by the buyer alone, and the seller need not execute anything.
The transfer is made by deed (e.g. Form TR1), which must be signed as a deed, witnessed, and delivered.
The transfer of registered land may be made by a simple unsigned written note.
Property Law & Practice.w: The legal estate in land is transferred by deed. In registered conveyancing this is usually a Land Registry transfer (Form TR1), which must be executed as a deed — signed by the transferor (and transferee where it contains their covenants), witnessed, and delivered — and then submitted to the Land Registry to register the buyer.

n.0: A deed of transfer is required; payment alone does not pass legal title.
n.1: Execution as a deed requires witnessing, not merely signature.
n.2: The transfer is executed by the transferor (seller), not the buyer alone.
n.4: A transfer of a legal estate cannot be made by a mere unsigned note.

Property Law & Practice.q: A leaseholder of a flat receives a demand from the landlord for a large service charge to cover major works to the building. The leaseholder considers that the amount is excessive and that they were not properly consulted about the works. The leaseholder asks about the protections that apply to residential service charges. The solicitor considers the statutory controls on residential service charges. The bill ran to thousands of pounds and the leaseholder had heard nothing about the works in advance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The leaseholder can never challenge a service charge once a demand has been issued.
Service charges are payable only if the leaseholder personally approved every item of work.
Residential service charges must be reasonable and reasonably incurred, and statutory consultation is required for qualifying works.
A landlord may charge whatever service charge it wishes, and the leaseholder must simply pay it on these facts as a general rule.
There are no controls at all on the level of residential service charges in England.
Property Law & Practice.w: Residential service charges are regulated: charges are payable only to the extent they are reasonably incurred and the works or services are of a reasonable standard, and landlords must carry out statutory consultation before undertaking qualifying works (or qualifying long-term agreements) above the prescribed thresholds, failing which recovery is capped.

n.0: Leaseholders can challenge unreasonable service charges (for example at the tribunal).
n.1: Payability does not require the leaseholder's personal approval of every item, but reasonableness and consultation apply.
n.3: A landlord cannot charge whatever it wishes; reasonableness controls apply.
n.4: There are statutory controls on residential service charges.

Property Law & Practice.q: A seller of a commercial building has exercised the option to tax the property, and the sale would otherwise be an exempt supply for VAT purposes. The buyer's solicitor is advising on the VAT treatment of the purchase price. The seller has opted to tax the commercial property. The transaction is a sale of commercial land. The property being sold is a commercial building on which the seller has exercised the option to tax, and the buyer's solicitor is working through what that election does to the price the buyer must find, given that sales of land would ordinarily be exempt from the tax. Which of the following best describes the effect of the option to tax on the sale?
o: The option to tax applies only to residential property sales.
The option to tax exempts the buyer from paying any SDLT.
VAT becomes chargeable on the sale price, converting what would be an exempt supply into a taxable one.
The option to tax has no effect on the VAT treatment of the sale.
The option to tax makes the sale zero-rated, so no VAT is charged on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Supplies of land are generally exempt from VAT, but a seller may exercise an option to tax (waiving the exemption) in respect of commercial property. Once opted, VAT at the standard rate becomes chargeable on the sale (and on rents), which affects the buyer's cash flow and, because SDLT is charged on the VAT-inclusive price, the SDLT payable.

n.0: The option to tax applies to commercial, not residential, property.
n.1: The option to tax does not exempt the buyer from SDLT; indeed SDLT is charged on the VAT-inclusive price.
n.3: The option to tax changes an exempt supply into a taxable one, so it does have an effect.
n.4: The option to tax makes the supply standard-rated, not zero-rated.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer is purchasing registered land. A person other than the seller is living at the property and is in actual occupation of it, but no entry protecting any interest they may have appears on the register. The buyer's solicitor is concerned about whether any interest of that occupier could bind the buyer. The occupier is in actual occupation and has an interest, but nothing is noted on the register. On a pre-completion inspection it becomes clear that someone other than the seller is actually living in the property, yet a search of the register turns up no notice or restriction hinting at any interest that person might hold, which leaves the buyer's solicitor uneasy about what the buyer might unwittingly take subject to. Which of the following best describes the risk to the buyer under the Land Registration Act 2002?
o: The buyer takes free of all interests simply by registering the transfer.
The buyer is never bound by anything unless it is registered as a notice.
Occupiers can never have interests capable of binding a purchaser of registered land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Any interest not entered on the register is automatically void against the buyer.
An interest of a person in actual occupation may be an overriding interest that binds the buyer despite not being on the register.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under Schedule 3 to the Land Registration Act 2002, the interest of a person in actual occupation can be an overriding interest that binds a purchaser even though it is not protected by an entry on the register, subject to exceptions (for example, where enquiry was made and the interest not disclosed, or the occupation was not reasonably discoverable). Hence the need to inspect and enquire.

n.0: Registering the transfer does not defeat overriding interests.
n.1: Some interests bind without being registered as notices, notably overriding interests.
n.2: Occupiers can have interests capable of overriding, contrary to this option.
n.3: Not every unregistered interest is void; overriding interests can still bind.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer of registered land is about to complete, and the buyer's solicitor is aware that certain interests can bind a buyer even though they do not appear on the register. In particular, someone other than the seller appears to be living at the property. The solicitor is concerned about interests of persons in actual occupation. The buyer asks what step should be taken before completion in relation to occupiers. The solicitor considers overriding interests and occupiers on a purchase of registered land. An adult relative of the seller appeared to be living at the property and paying towards it. Which of the following best describes the appropriate step?
o: The buyer takes free of all interests of occupiers automatically on registration.
The solicitor should simply ignore any occupier who is not named as the registered proprietor.
The solicitor should ask the local authority whether anyone is in occupation of the property.
The solicitor should inspect the property and enquire about occupiers, as a person in actual occupation may have an overriding interest.
The solicitor need not consider occupiers at all, because only registered interests can ever bind a buyer on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Certain interests of persons in actual occupation can override a registered disposition and bind a buyer even without being on the register. The buyer's solicitor should therefore inspect the property and make enquiries of any occupiers, obtaining consents or releases where necessary, to avoid taking subject to an undisclosed occupier's interest.

n.0: The buyer does not automatically take free of occupiers' overriding interests.
n.1: An occupier who is not the registered proprietor may still have an overriding interest.
n.2: Enquiries about occupation are made of the seller/occupiers, not the local authority.
n.4: Unregistered overriding interests can bind a buyer; not only registered interests matter.

Property Law & Practice.q: Two people are buying a property together and intend that, if one dies, their share should pass under their will rather than automatically to the survivor. They wish to hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common. The buyers want to hold as tenants in common and to alert future dealings to the trust. The conveyancer is completing the transfer and Land Registry forms. The two purchasers want to make sure that if one of them dies their share goes under their will and not automatically to the other, so they are buying as tenants in common, and the conveyancer must reflect that choice on the register so future dealings account for the trust behind the legal title. Which of the following best describes what should be done on the register to reflect this?
o: A Form A restriction should be entered, reflecting that the survivor cannot give a valid receipt for capital money alone.
Nothing need be done, as co-owners always hold as beneficial joint tenants.
The property must be registered with two separate title numbers, one per owner.
The legal estate should be transferred into the name of one owner only.
A notice should be entered protecting each owner's beneficial share as a burden on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where co-owners hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common, a Form A restriction is entered on the proprietorship register. It reflects that a sole surviving registered proprietor cannot give a valid receipt for capital money (so a second trustee is needed to overreach), signalling that the survivorship rule does not apply to the beneficial interests.

n.1: Co-owners do not always hold as beneficial joint tenants; they may choose a tenancy in common.
n.2: Co-owned property has a single title; it is not split into separate titles per owner.
n.3: The legal estate is held jointly by the co-owners as trustees, not in one name only.
n.4: Beneficial shares under a trust of land are not protected by a notice; a restriction is used.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer discovers that the seller carried out building works to the property some years ago, and the buyer's solicitor is concerned about whether the works had the necessary approvals confirming they meet construction standards for safety and quality, separately from any planning permission. The buyer asks about the approval regime concerned with the standard of building work itself. The solicitor considers building regulations approval. The earlier works had no paperwork, and the buyer's lender was likely to ask questions about them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There are no standards governing the safety and quality of building work in England.
Building Regulations compliance is confirmed by the local land charges search alone.
Building Regulations apply only to entirely new houses and never to alterations of existing ones.
Building Regulations approval is the same thing as planning permission and need not be checked separately on these facts as a general rule.
Building work must generally comply with the Building Regulations, and the buyer should check that approval or a completion certificate was obtained.
Property Law & Practice.w: Building work must comply with the Building Regulations, which govern the safety and quality of construction. This is separate from planning permission. A buyer's solicitor should check that any relevant works had Building Regulations approval and a completion (or final) certificate, and consider indemnity insurance or regularisation if not.

n.0: There are construction standards governing building work.
n.1: Building Regulations compliance is evidenced by certificates, not simply the local land charges search.
n.2: Building Regulations apply to many alterations, not only new houses.
n.3: Building Regulations are distinct from planning permission and must be checked separately.

Property Law & Practice.q: A borrower has defaulted on a legal mortgage over registered land, and the lender wishes to sell the property to recover the debt. The lender is considering how it may sell and what duty it owes in doing so. The lender's power of sale has arisen and become exercisable following the borrower's default. The lender proposes to sell the mortgaged property. The borrower has fallen badly into arrears, the lender wants to realise its security by selling the house, and it is weighing up how it may go about the sale and, in particular, what obligation if any it owes to the borrower when it comes to the price it achieves. Which of the following best describes the lender's position on sale?
o: The lender may keep any surplus proceeds of sale over the debt for itself.
The lender must always sell the property at a public auction and never by private treaty on these facts as a general rule.
The lender may sell under its power of sale but must take reasonable care to obtain a proper price for the property.
The lender cannot sell without first obtaining a court order in every case.
The lender may sell at any price it chooses, owing no duty at all to the borrower.
Property Law & Practice.w: A mortgagee exercising its power of sale must take reasonable care to obtain the true market value (a proper price) for the property. It need not necessarily obtain a court order to sell (though possession may require one), it cannot sell at an undervalue with impunity, and any surplus after discharging the debt and prior charges is held for the borrower or subsequent chargees.

n.0: Surplus proceeds are held for the borrower/subsequent chargees, not kept by the lender.
n.1: The lender may sell by private treaty; auction is not compulsory.
n.3: A court order is not invariably required to exercise the power of sale.
n.4: The lender owes a duty to obtain a proper price; it cannot sell at any price with impunity.

Property Law & Practice.q: A landlord grants a new lease of registered land for a term of 15 years. The tenant's solicitor is advising on what must be done for the tenant to obtain the legal estate in the lease. The lease is granted out of a registered freehold for a term exceeding seven years. The tenant wishes to acquire the legal leasehold estate. The landlord is carving a fifteen-year lease out of its registered freehold, and the incoming tenant's solicitor is working out what step is needed for the tenant actually to hold the legal leasehold estate, given that the term runs well beyond the short-lease threshold. Which of the following best describes the requirement?
o: The lease must be registered only if it exceeds 21 years.
The lease must be completed by registration with its own title, as a lease over seven years is a registrable disposition.
The lease cannot be registered at all because the freehold is already registered.
The lease takes effect at law on completion of the deed, with no registration required.
The lease need only be noted on the landlord's title and requires no separate registration on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: The grant of a lease for a term of more than seven years out of registered land is a registrable disposition under the Land Registration Act 2002. To take effect at law, it must be completed by registration, and the tenant will be registered as proprietor of its own leasehold title (with a notice also entered against the landlord's title).

n.0: The registration threshold is more than seven years, not 21 years.
n.2: A lease over seven years is registered with its own title even though the freehold is registered.
n.3: A lease over seven years does not take effect at law on completion alone; registration is required.
n.4: A lease over seven years requires its own registered title, not merely a note on the landlord's title.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer discovers that previous building works at the property, which required building regulations approval, were carried out without a completion certificate ever being obtained. The buyer's solicitor considers the risk this poses and how it may be addressed. Works subject to building regulations were done but no completion certificate exists. The buyer is concerned about the lack of compliance evidence. The buyer's enquiries reveal that earlier works which plainly needed building regulations approval were carried out but no completion certificate was ever issued, and the solicitor must advise on the risk this creates and the practical ways of putting the buyer in a safe position before committing. Which of the following best describes an appropriate way to deal with this?
o: Ignore the issue, as building regulations compliance is irrelevant to a purchaser.
Seek a regularisation certificate or building regulations indemnity insurance to address the lack of a completion certificate.
Refuse to complete, as a missing completion certificate makes the purchase impossible on these facts as a general rule.
Rely on the local search alone, which guarantees full building regulations compliance.
Require the seller to demolish and rebuild the works before completion in every case.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where works subject to building regulations lack a completion certificate, the buyer may face enforcement risk or difficulty on resale. Practical solutions include obtaining a regularisation certificate from the local authority, or building regulations indemnity insurance to cover the risk of enforcement. The issue should be investigated, not ignored.

n.0: Building regulations compliance is relevant to a purchaser and should not be ignored.
n.2: A missing certificate does not make the purchase impossible; it can be managed by regularisation or insurance.
n.3: The local search does not guarantee building regulations compliance for all works.
n.4: Demolition and rebuilding is not the routine or required solution.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor is investigating title and comes across an old restrictive covenant burdening the registered land, entered on the charges register, which restricts the use the buyer intends to make of the property. The buyer wishes to proceed but is concerned about the covenant. The solicitor considers how the buyer might deal with the risk of an enforceable restrictive covenant on the title. The covenant restricted the property to residential use, but the buyer planned to run a business. Which of the following best describes an appropriate practical step?
o: The buyer should simply ignore the covenant, as covenants on the register are never enforceable.
The buyer must abandon the purchase entirely, as nothing can be done about a restrictive covenant.
The buyer is automatically freed from the covenant once they are registered as proprietor.
The buyer can remove the covenant unilaterally by applying to the Land Registry to delete the entry on these facts.
The buyer may seek to obtain restrictive covenant indemnity insurance, or a release or modification, to address the risk.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where an enforceable restrictive covenant affects the title and threatens the buyer's intended use, practical solutions include obtaining restrictive covenant indemnity insurance, seeking a release or variation from the person with the benefit, or applying to the Upper Tribunal to discharge or modify the covenant.

n.0: Registered covenants can be enforceable; they should not simply be ignored.
n.1: The purchase need not be abandoned; there are ways to manage the risk.
n.2: Registration as proprietor does not free the buyer from a binding covenant.
n.3: The buyer cannot unilaterally delete a valid covenant entry.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer of a property intends to carry out significant works, including building an extension and changing the use of part of the property. The buyer's solicitor advises that certain permissions may be needed before the works can lawfully go ahead, to avoid enforcement action. The buyer asks what permission is generally required for development of land. The solicitor considers the requirement for planning permission. The proposed extension was large and the change of use was likely to attract the council's attention. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Planning permission is needed only for commercial and never for residential property on these facts as a general rule.
No permission is ever required to build on or change the use of one's own land.
Planning permission is granted automatically once the buyer completes the purchase.
Planning permission is generally required for development, which includes building works and material changes of use.
Planning permission is required only where the property is a listed building.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under planning legislation, planning permission is generally required to carry out 'development', which includes building, engineering and other operations, and material changes in the use of land or buildings (subject to permitted development rights and exceptions). Carrying out development without permission may lead to enforcement action.

n.0: Planning control applies to residential as well as commercial development.
n.1: Development generally needs permission; owners cannot always build or change use freely.
n.2: Permission is not granted automatically on completion of a purchase.
n.4: Planning control is not limited to listed buildings (which have additional controls).

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor is asked to act for both the buyer and the buyer's mortgage lender in a residential purchase, on the basis that their interests in obtaining good title are the same. During the transaction the solicitor becomes aware of something about the property or the borrower that the lender would want to know but the buyer would prefer to keep from the lender. The solicitor considers their position when acting for both buyer and lender. The borrower had asked the solicitor to keep a particular matter from the lender's knowledge. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The solicitor may always act for both, and may keep the borrower's confidences from the lender whatever happens on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor may act for both, but need not disclose anything material to the lender at all.
The solicitor may never act for both a buyer and a lender in the same transaction.
The solicitor may act for both while their interests coincide, but must cease to act if an actual conflict arises that cannot be reconciled.
The solicitor must always prefer the lender's interests over those of the buyer client.
Property Law & Practice.w: A solicitor may usually act for both buyer and lender in a standard residential purchase because their interests coincide, but must not continue if a conflict of interest arises between them (for example information material to the lender that the buyer will not allow to be disclosed); the solicitor would then have to cease acting for one or both.

n.0: The solicitor cannot simply withhold material information from the lender client while continuing to act for both.
n.1: The solicitor cannot act for the lender while concealing material information from it.
n.2: Acting for both is permissible where interests coincide; it is not always prohibited.
n.4: The solicitor owes duties to both clients and must not simply prefer the lender.

Property Law & Practice.q: A landlord of business premises protected by the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 wishes to oppose the tenant's application for a new tenancy, because the landlord genuinely intends to demolish and reconstruct the premises (or to occupy them for its own business). The tenancy is protected and the landlord opposes renewal. The landlord relies on a statutory ground. The tenant has applied for a new tenancy of its protected business premises, but the landlord wants to resist, saying it genuinely means to knock the building down and rebuild, or to move into the premises for its own business, and the question is on what footing the landlord may oppose renewal. Which of the following best describes the landlord's ability to oppose renewal?
o: The landlord may oppose renewal only on statutory grounds, some of which (redevelopment or own occupation) entitle the tenant to compensation.
The landlord may oppose renewal for any reason it chooses, without needing a statutory ground on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The landlord may oppose renewal only with the consent of the tenant.
The landlord may oppose renewal only by obtaining permission from the SRA.
The landlord can never oppose renewal of a protected business tenancy.
Property Law & Practice.w: A landlord may oppose the grant of a new business tenancy only on one or more of the grounds set out in s.30(1) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, such as breaches by the tenant, suitable alternative accommodation, or the landlord's genuine intention to redevelop or to occupy the premises. Where opposition succeeds on certain 'no-fault' grounds (such as redevelopment or own occupation), the tenant is entitled to statutory compensation.

n.1: The landlord cannot oppose for any reason; a statutory ground is required.
n.2: Opposition does not depend on the tenant's consent.
n.3: SRA permission is irrelevant to opposing a business lease renewal.
n.4: The landlord can oppose on statutory grounds, so 'never' is wrong.

Property Law & Practice.q: During a conveyancing transaction, one solicitor gives the other solicitor a professional undertaking — for example to discharge a mortgage from the completion proceeds, or to send documents after completion. The recipient relies on the undertaking to complete safely. A question arises about the status of undertakings given between solicitors in conveyancing. The solicitor considers the effect of a conveyancing undertaking. Completion could not safely take place without relying on the other side's promise to act. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor's undertaking binds only if it is also converted into a formal deed.
A solicitor's undertaking is enforceable only against the client, never the solicitor on these facts as a general rule.
A solicitor's undertaking can be withdrawn at will at any time before performance.
A solicitor's undertaking is a mere courtesy with no binding effect whatsoever.
A solicitor's undertaking is binding and enforceable, and must be performed; conveyancing relies heavily on such undertakings.
Property Law & Practice.w: Professional undertakings are a cornerstone of conveyancing practice: they are personally binding on the solicitor who gives them, enforceable (including through the court's supervisory jurisdiction), and must be performed. This allows solicitors to complete transactions safely in reliance on each other's undertakings.

n.0: An undertaking is binding without being made a deed.
n.1: An undertaking is enforceable against the solicitor personally, not only the client.
n.2: An undertaking cannot be withdrawn at will; it must be performed or released.
n.3: An undertaking is binding, not a mere courtesy.

Property Law & Practice.q: A long leaseholder of a flat, having held the lease for some years, wishes to obtain greater security by extending the term of their lease, or by joining with other leaseholders to acquire the freehold of the building. The leaseholder asks whether the law gives long residential leaseholders any such rights against the landlord. The solicitor considers leasehold enfranchisement and lease extension rights. The leaseholder had a long lease but was worried about its diminishing value as the years passed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Long leaseholders have no rights at all to extend their lease or acquire the freehold.
Only commercial leaseholders, and never residential ones, have any enfranchisement rights.
A leaseholder may extend the lease only by paying the landlord whatever sum the landlord demands on these facts as a general rule.
A leaseholder can acquire the freehold only if the landlord freely chooses to sell it.
Qualifying long residential leaseholders have statutory rights to extend their lease or (collectively for flats) to acquire the freehold.
Property Law & Practice.w: Statute gives qualifying long residential leaseholders important rights: a leaseholder of a flat may claim an individual lease extension, and leaseholders of flats may collectively enfranchise (acquire the freehold of their building); leaseholders of houses have their own enfranchisement rights. The price is determined by statutory valuation, not simply the landlord's demand.

n.0: Long residential leaseholders do have statutory enfranchisement/extension rights.
n.1: These rights are for residential, not commercial, leaseholders.
n.2: The price is set by statutory valuation, not an arbitrary landlord demand.
n.3: Enfranchisement does not depend solely on the landlord choosing to sell.

Property Law & Practice.q: On exchange of contracts for the sale of a property incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale, the buyer pays a 10% deposit to the seller's solicitor. A question arises as to the capacity in which the seller's solicitor holds the deposit pending completion. The Standard Conditions of Sale apply and the deposit has been paid to the seller's solicitor. The parties want to know how the deposit is held. On exchange the buyer hands over the customary ten per cent, and the parties, having incorporated the standard conditions, want to be clear whether the seller's solicitor may release that money to the seller straight away or must instead hold it until the deal actually completes. Which of the following best describes the usual position under the Standard Conditions?
o: The seller's solicitor holds the deposit as stakeholder, releasing it only on completion.
The deposit is forfeited to the seller immediately on exchange in every case.
The deposit belongs to the buyer's solicitor until completion.
The deposit must be paid directly to the Land Registry on exchange.
The seller's solicitor holds the deposit as agent for the seller, who may use it at once.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the deposit is generally held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder, meaning it is held for both parties and released to the seller only on completion (subject to the buyer being able to use a deposit received on a related sale). Holding as agent, allowing the seller to use it before completion, is the alternative but not the default position.

n.1: The deposit is not forfeited on exchange; forfeiture arises only on the buyer's default in completing.
n.2: The deposit is held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder, not by the buyer's solicitor.
n.3: The deposit is not paid to the Land Registry on exchange.
n.4: Holding as agent (with immediate use) is not the default under the Standard Conditions; stakeholder is.

Property Law & Practice.q: A tenant of commercial premises wishes to assign the lease to a buyer, and the lease contains a covenant not to assign without the landlord's consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. The tenant applies to the landlord for consent, but the landlord is slow to respond and appears to be withholding consent without good reason. The tenant asks about the landlord's obligations. The solicitor considers the landlord's duties on an application for consent to assign under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988. The proposed assignee was financially sound and the tenant was anxious to complete the sale. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The tenant may assign the lease freely without ever seeking the landlord's consent.
The landlord must give consent within a reasonable time except where it is reasonable to withhold it, and give written reasons for any refusal.
The landlord must always consent to any proposed assignment without exception.
The landlord has no time limit and may take as long as it wishes to consider the application.
The landlord may refuse consent for any reason at all, however arbitrary, and need not explain on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where a lease requires the landlord's consent to assign, not to be unreasonably withheld, the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988 imposes duties on the landlord to give consent within a reasonable time (unless it is reasonable to refuse), to give the tenant written notice of the decision, and to state reasons for any refusal, with the burden of showing reasonableness on the landlord.

n.0: The tenant must seek consent where the lease requires it.
n.2: The landlord may reasonably refuse in some cases; it need not always consent.
n.3: The 1988 Act requires a decision within a reasonable time, not unlimited delay.
n.4: The landlord cannot refuse for any arbitrary reason where consent is not to be unreasonably withheld.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor is acting for a buyer of unregistered land. To investigate the seller's title, the solicitor is provided with an epitome of title and must identify a good root of title from which to trace ownership. The buyer asks how far back the title must be traced and what makes a document a good root of title. The solicitor considers the requirements for a good root of title in unregistered conveyancing. The land had never been registered and the seller produced only a bundle of old title deeds. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A good root of title is simply the seller's own statement that they own the property.
There is no need to investigate title at all for unregistered land.
A good root of title is a document at least 15 years old that deals with the whole legal and equitable estate and adequately identifies the property.
A good root of title need only be the most recent conveyance, however recently it was made on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A good root of title must be a document at least 100 years old to be acceptable.
Property Law & Practice.w: For unregistered land, the buyer traces title from a good root of title: a document at least 15 years old that deals with (or shows who owns) the whole legal and equitable interest in the property, contains an adequate description of it, and casts no doubt on the title.

n.0: The seller's assertion of ownership is not a root of title.
n.1: Title must be investigated for unregistered land.
n.3: The most recent conveyance is not necessarily a good root; it must be at least 15 years old and meet the criteria.
n.4: The requirement is at least 15 years, not 100.

Property Law & Practice.q: A tenant of a commercial lease (a new tenancy) wishes to assign the lease, and the landlord, as a condition of giving consent, requires the outgoing tenant to guarantee the performance of the incoming assignee. The outgoing tenant asks whether such a guarantee is lawful and what it involves, given that they would otherwise be released on assignment. The solicitor considers the authorised guarantee agreement under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995. The landlord was cautious about the assignee and wanted the outgoing tenant to stand behind them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The landlord can require the outgoing tenant to guarantee every future assignee indefinitely down the chain on these facts as a general rule.
An authorised guarantee agreement makes the outgoing tenant liable even after a lawful further assignment.
The landlord may require an authorised guarantee agreement, under which the outgoing tenant guarantees the immediate assignee's performance.
The outgoing tenant remains automatically liable for the whole term regardless of any guarantee.
No guarantee of any kind may lawfully be required from an outgoing tenant on assignment.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the LTCA 1995, although an outgoing tenant of a new tenancy is released on a lawful assignment, the landlord may (where reasonable or required by the lease) require the outgoing tenant to enter an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA), guaranteeing the performance of the immediate assignee only, until that assignee itself lawfully assigns.

n.0: An AGA can guarantee only the immediate assignee, not every future assignee.
n.1: AGA liability ends when the assignee lawfully assigns onward.
n.3: The outgoing tenant is released on lawful assignment, subject only to an AGA; it is not automatically liable for the whole term.
n.4: A guarantee (AGA) can lawfully be required in appropriate circumstances.

Property Law & Practice.q: A person has an estate contract (a contract to buy registered land) and wishes to protect it against the possibility that the seller might sell to someone else before completion, so that a later buyer would be bound by it. The interest is a third-party interest in registered land that the holder wishes to protect on the register. The holder wants a later purchaser to be bound. Some weeks will pass between contract and completion, during which the buyer worries the seller could be tempted to sell the same land to a higher bidder, and the buyer wants to put something on the register now so that any later purchaser would take the land bound by the buyer's contract. Which of the following best describes the appropriate method of protection?
o: Doing nothing, as estate contracts bind later buyers automatically.
Applying for first registration of the seller's title.
Lodging a caution against first registration of the land.
Entering a restriction that prevents any dealing with the land at all.
Entering a notice on the register in respect of the estate contract.
Property Law & Practice.w: A third-party interest such as an estate contract is protected in registered land by entering a notice on the charges register. A notice preserves the priority of the interest so that a later registered disposition takes subject to it. A restriction, by contrast, regulates whether and how a disposition may be registered (for example, requiring a certificate), rather than protecting the priority of a burden.

n.0: Estate contracts do not automatically bind later buyers of registered land; protection is needed.
n.1: First registration relates to bringing unregistered land onto the register, not protecting this interest.
n.2: A caution against first registration applies to unregistered land, not registered land.
n.3: A restriction controls how dispositions may be registered; it does not itself protect the priority of a burden like an estate contract.

Property Law & Practice.q: On the agreed completion date, the buyer's solicitor fails to complete the purchase because the buyer's funds are not ready, and the seller wishes to force the issue. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale, under which time is not automatically of the essence for completion. The seller asks how they can make time of the essence and put pressure on the buyer to complete. The solicitor considers the service of a notice to complete. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The seller may serve a notice to complete, making time of the essence and requiring completion within the notice period.
The seller may treat the contract as automatically discharged the instant completion does not occur on these facts.
The seller must apply to the court for an order compelling completion before taking any other step.
The seller can do nothing at all and must simply wait indefinitely for the buyer to complete.
The seller may immediately rescind and keep the deposit the moment completion is a day late.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where completion does not take place on the agreed date and time is not of the essence, the innocent party may serve a notice to complete under the Standard Conditions of Sale, which makes time of the essence and requires completion within the notice period (usually 10 working days); failure to comply then allows the innocent party to pursue their remedies.

n.1: The contract is not automatically discharged the instant completion is missed.
n.2: A notice to complete, not necessarily a court application, is the usual first step.
n.3: The seller has a remedy (a notice to complete); it need not wait indefinitely.
n.4: The seller cannot rescind and keep the deposit immediately for a short delay where time is not of the essence.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor is dealing with a first purchase of land which appears to be unregistered, and wishes to confirm whether the land is in fact registered or unregistered, and whether any pending applications or cautions against first registration affect it. The solicitor considers which Land Registry search is used to check the registration position of land thought to be unregistered. The seller's deeds were incomplete and it was not entirely clear whether the land was registered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is no means of checking whether apparently unregistered land is in fact registered on these facts as a general rule.
A bankruptcy search reveals whether the land is registered or unregistered.
An index map search (SIM) at the Land Registry reveals whether the land is registered and any caution against first registration.
A drainage and water search reveals the registration status of the land.
A local land charges search reveals whether the land is registered at the Land Registry.
Property Law & Practice.w: A search of the index map (SIM) at the Land Registry reveals whether the land (or any part of it) is already registered, whether there is a pending application for first registration, and whether there is any caution against first registration, which is important when dealing with apparently unregistered land.

n.0: The index map search checks the registration position.
n.1: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not registration status.
n.3: A drainage and water search does not reveal registration status.
n.4: The local land charges search does not reveal Land Registry registration status.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor wishes to find out whether the property is connected to mains water and drainage, whether the public sewer runs within its boundaries, and who is responsible for the water and sewerage services. The solicitor considers which pre-contract search provides this drainage and water information. The property was in a rural area and the buyer was unsure whether it was on mains drainage at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Drainage and water information cannot be obtained before completion of the purchase.
The local land charges search alone provides all drainage and water connection information.
A drainage and water search (CON29DW) provides information about mains water and sewerage connections.
The buyer must physically dig up the garden to establish the drainage position.
A bankruptcy search reveals whether the property is connected to mains drainage.
Property Law & Practice.w: A drainage and water search (CON29DW) is made with the relevant water and sewerage undertaker and reveals whether the property is connected to mains water and to the public sewer, the location of public sewers, and who is responsible for the services.

n.0: Drainage and water information is obtained pre-contract via the CON29DW search.
n.1: The local land charges search does not cover drainage and water connections in this way.
n.3: A formal search, not excavation, provides the information.
n.4: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not drainage.

Property Law & Practice.q: A purchaser of registered land buys for valuable consideration and completes the registrable disposition by registration. Before the purchase there was a third-party interest that was not protected by any notice or restriction on the register and was not an overriding interest. The buyer took a registered disposition for value; the third-party interest was unprotected. The buyer wants to know the effect on that interest. The buyer is paying full market value and will complete the transfer by registration, and it has emerged that a third party held some interest in the land beforehand which was never entered on the register and does not fall within any category of overriding interest, so the buyer wants to know where that leaves it. Which of the following best describes the position under the Land Registration Act 2002?
o: The unprotected interest is converted into an overriding interest on completion.
The buyer takes subject to every prior interest whether protected or not.
The unprotected interest automatically binds the buyer regardless of registration on these facts.
The registered disposition for value postpones (takes priority over) the unprotected interest.
Priority is decided solely by which interest was created first in time.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under s.29 of the Land Registration Act 2002, on the registration of a registrable disposition made for valuable consideration, the priority of any interest affecting the estate is postponed to the disposition unless it was protected (by notice or as an overriding interest) at the time of registration. So an unprotected, non-overriding interest is postponed to the buyer.

n.0: An unprotected interest is not converted into an overriding interest by completion.
n.1: The buyer for value does not take subject to unprotected interests that are not overriding.
n.2: An unprotected, non-overriding interest does not automatically bind the buyer for value.
n.4: For registered dispositions for value, the s.29 priority rule, not simply first in time, governs.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer is purchasing a house with the assistance of a mortgage, and the buyer's solicitor is also instructed to act for the mortgage lender in the same transaction, as is common where their interests are aligned. Before completion the solicitor must satisfy the lender about the title. The buyer asks what the solicitor must provide to the lender confirming the property is good security. The solicitor considers the report or certificate given to the lender in a residential purchase with a mortgage. The lender would only release the mortgage advance once it was satisfied about the title. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor gives the lender a certificate of title confirming the title is good and marketable and complies with the lender's requirements.
The solicitor gives the lender a copy of the local authority's planning file.
The solicitor gives the lender a physical survey report on the condition of the building.
The solicitor gives the lender nothing, because the lender makes its own independent title investigation on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor gives the lender the buyer's personal bank statements as security.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where the buyer's solicitor also acts for the lender, the solicitor investigates title on the lender's behalf and provides a certificate of title (typically in the form required by the lender/UK Finance Handbook) confirming that the title is good and marketable and meets the lender's requirements, so that the mortgage advance is released.

n.1: The certificate confirms the title position, not merely a copy of the planning file.
n.2: The certificate of title concerns title, not a physical survey.
n.3: The solicitor does report to the lender; the lender relies on the certificate of title.
n.4: The solicitor provides a certificate of title, not the buyer's bank statements.

Property Law & Practice.q: A property owner wishes to carry out a modest development, such as a small extension, that falls within the categories the general planning legislation treats as permitted without a specific application. The owner asks whether express planning permission is needed. The works fall within the scope of permitted development rights and any conditions and limits are met. The owner wants to avoid an unnecessary application. The owner wants only a modest addition to the house, the sort of works the general development order treats as already permitted so long as the stated limits and conditions are respected, and is keen not to spend time and money on a formal application if none is actually needed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Express planning permission is always required for any works to a building without exception on these facts.
The works require permission only if they cost above a fixed monetary threshold.
Permitted development rights remove the need for building regulations approval as well.
Express planning permission may not be required because the works fall within permitted development rights.
Planning permission is never required for works to residential property.
Property Law & Practice.w: Certain classes of development are granted planning permission by a general development order (permitted development rights), so that no express application is needed provided the works fall within the specified classes and comply with the relevant conditions and limitations. Where the works exceed those limits, express permission is required.

n.0: Express permission is not always required; permitted development rights can apply.
n.1: The test is the class and limits of development, not a monetary cost threshold.
n.2: Permitted development addresses planning permission, not building regulations, which are separate.
n.4: Permission can be required for residential works that exceed permitted development limits.

Property Law & Practice.q: A contract for the sale of a residential property requires the seller to give the buyer vacant possession on completion. Shortly before completion, the buyer's solicitor is concerned that other people may be living at the property who could remain after completion. The contract requires vacant possession on completion. The buyer's solicitor is checking the position on occupiers. The contract obliges the seller to hand the property over with vacant possession, but the buyer's solicitor has picked up hints that other people may be living there, and is anxious to establish exactly what the seller must deliver and why the presence of any occupier could matter to the buyer. Which of the following best describes what vacant possession requires and why the occupier check matters?
o: The seller must give up the property empty of people, possessions and legal occupiers, so occupiers with rights must be dealt with before completion.
Vacant possession requires only that the furniture be removed, not the people.
Occupiers are irrelevant because their rights end automatically on completion.
Vacant possession merely requires the seller to hand over the keys, whoever is living there on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Vacant possession is satisfied so long as the seller personally has moved out.
Property Law & Practice.w: An obligation to give vacant possession requires the seller to hand over the property free of people, chattels and any legal right of occupation, so that the buyer can take actual, unimpeded possession on completion. Occupiers with interests could be overriding interests binding the buyer, so the solicitor must ensure any such occupiers are dealt with (for example, by obtaining releases) before completion.

n.1: Vacant possession requires the removal of people and their right to occupy, not merely furniture.
n.2: Occupiers' rights do not automatically end on completion; they may bind the buyer.
n.3: Vacant possession is more than handing over keys; the property must be free of occupiers and possessions.
n.4: It is not enough that the seller alone has moved out if others with rights remain.

Property Law & Practice.q: Between exchange and completion of a purchase of registered land, the buyer holds a contract but is not yet the registered proprietor. The buyer's solicitor is concerned to protect the buyer's interest under the contract against the risk of the seller attempting to sell or mortgage the property to someone else before completion. The solicitor considers how the buyer's contractual (estate contract) interest can be protected on the register. The seller was known to be in financial difficulty, raising a risk of a competing dealing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer is automatically registered as proprietor on exchange, so no protection is needed.
The buyer can only protect the interest by taking physical possession of the property.
The buyer protects the interest by lodging the deposit with the Land Registry.
The buyer's contractual interest cannot be protected on the register in any way before completion.
The buyer may protect the estate contract by entering a notice against the seller's registered title.
Property Law & Practice.w: On exchange the buyer acquires an equitable interest (an estate contract) in the land. For registered land this can be protected by entering a notice on the charges register of the seller's title, which protects the buyer's priority against a subsequent purchaser or chargee.

n.0: The buyer is not registered as proprietor on exchange; protection may be prudent.
n.1: The interest is protected by a register entry, not merely by taking possession.
n.2: Protection is by entering a notice, not by lodging the deposit at the Land Registry.
n.3: The buyer's estate contract can be protected by a notice; it is not unprotectable.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer has completed the purchase of a residential property for a price above the relevant threshold. The buyer's solicitor must deal with the tax payable on the purchase and file the necessary return with HMRC within the statutory time limit, or penalties will arise. The buyer asks about the tax on the purchase and the deadline. The solicitor considers stamp duty land tax on the acquisition of land in England. The price was well above the tax threshold and the deadline for filing was fast approaching. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Stamp duty land tax is payable by the seller out of the sale proceeds, not by the buyer.
Stamp duty land tax is payable by the buyer, and an SDLT return must generally be filed within 14 days of completion.
The SDLT return may be filed at any time within six years of completion without penalty.
No tax is ever payable on the purchase of residential property in England.
Stamp duty land tax is payable only where the buyer is a company and never an individual on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Stamp duty land tax (SDLT) on the acquisition of land in England is payable by the buyer. The buyer's solicitor must submit an SDLT return and pay the tax due generally within 14 days of the effective date (usually completion), with penalties and interest for late filing or payment.

n.0: SDLT is payable by the buyer, not the seller.
n.2: The return must be filed within 14 days, not any time within six years.
n.3: SDLT can be payable on residential purchases above the threshold.
n.4: SDLT applies to individuals as well as companies.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor is acting for both the buyer and the buyer's mortgage lender in a purchase, as is commonly permitted where their interests are not in conflict. After investigating title, the solicitor must confirm to the lender that the property is good security for the loan. The solicitor acts for both buyer and lender, whose interests currently coincide. The solicitor is reporting to the lender before completion. The same solicitor is acting for the buyer and for the mortgage lender, whose interests presently pull in the same direction, and having investigated the title the solicitor must now give the lender the formal confirmation it needs about the property before the advance is released for completion. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor provides to the lender?
o: A guarantee that the borrower will repay the mortgage in full.
A valuation of the property in place of any confirmation about the title.
A certificate of title confirming that the title is good and marketable and the property is suitable security.
An undertaking to indemnify the lender against any fall in the property's value.
A report on title addressed only to the buyer, with nothing provided to the lender on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where a solicitor acts for both buyer and lender, the solicitor gives the lender a certificate of title confirming that the title is good and marketable and that the property provides adequate security for the advance, in the standard form required by the lender. This is distinct from a valuation and does not guarantee repayment or property values.

n.0: The solicitor does not guarantee the borrower's repayment.
n.1: A valuation is separate; the lender needs confirmation about the title via the certificate.
n.3: The solicitor does not indemnify the lender against falls in value.
n.4: The lender requires its own certificate of title; a report to the buyer alone is insufficient.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer and seller have exchanged contracts for a residential sale and need to fix the completion date. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale and contains no special condition altering the default completion timetable. The buyer asks when completion will take place if nothing else is agreed. The solicitor considers the default completion date under the Standard Conditions of Sale. The parties had not written any specific completion date into the contract they had signed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Under the Standard Conditions, completion takes place 20 working days after exchange unless a different date is agreed.
There is no default completion date, so completion may occur at any time the buyer chooses.
Completion always takes place on the same day as exchange under the Standard Conditions.
Completion takes place only once the buyer has obtained planning permission for the property on these facts.
Completion takes place exactly six months after exchange under the Standard Conditions.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, in the absence of an agreed date the completion date is 20 working days after the date of the contract (exchange). In practice the parties usually agree a specific completion date as a special condition to fit the chain.

n.1: There is a default date under the SCS; completion is not simply at the buyer's whim.
n.2: Completion is not on the same day as exchange by default; there is a 20-working-day default.
n.3: Completion does not depend on obtaining planning permission.
n.4: The default is 20 working days, not six months.

Property Law & Practice.q: A first mortgage of unregistered land was granted without the lender taking the title deeds (for example, a second charge, or a legal mortgage where deeds are held elsewhere). The lender wishes to protect its mortgage against a later buyer or lender. The mortgage is of unregistered land and is not protected by deposit of the title deeds. The lender wants its security to bind third parties. A lender advanced money on the security of unregistered land but, because the title deeds are held elsewhere, could not take them as security, and it is anxious that its charge should still bind anyone who later buys the land or lends against it rather than being quietly defeated. Which of the following best describes how the mortgage should be protected?
o: It should be protected by a notice on the seller's registered title.
It should be registered as a puisne mortgage (a land charge) against the estate owner's name.
It is automatically protected without any registration because it is a legal mortgage.
It requires no protection because mortgages always bind later buyers.
It should be protected by an official search with priority.
Property Law & Practice.w: A legal mortgage of unregistered land that is not protected by a deposit of the title deeds (a puisne mortgage) is registrable as a land charge (Class C(i)) against the estate owner's name. If not registered, it will be void against a later purchaser of the land for value, so registration is essential to bind third parties.

n.0: A notice on a registered title is the method for registered land, not this unregistered mortgage.
n.2: A puisne mortgage is not automatically protected; it must be registered as a land charge.
n.3: An unprotected puisne mortgage can be void against a later purchaser, so protection is required.
n.4: An official search with priority is a registered-land search, not a method of protecting an unregistered mortgage.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer complains after completion that the property has a physical defect (such as damp) which the seller did not mention, and argues that the seller should have disclosed it. The seller says the buyer should have investigated the property's physical condition themselves. There was no misrepresentation. The solicitor considers the principle of caveat emptor in the sale of land. The damp had been present for years but was not obvious on a casual inspection of the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The seller is under a general duty to disclose every physical defect in the property to the buyer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Under caveat emptor the buyer bears the risk of the physical condition, so the buyer should survey the property; the seller need not volunteer physical defects.
The buyer may always rescind after completion for any physical defect discovered later.
The seller must guarantee that the property is free from all physical defects.
Caveat emptor requires the seller to arrange and pay for the buyer's survey.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the principle of caveat emptor ('let the buyer beware'), the risk of the physical condition of the property lies with the buyer. The seller is not generally obliged to disclose physical defects (as opposed to certain latent defects in title), so the buyer should commission a survey and raise enquiries before exchange.

n.0: There is no general duty on the seller to disclose all physical defects.
n.2: The buyer cannot generally rescind after completion for a physical defect absent misrepresentation.
n.3: The seller does not guarantee the property is defect-free.
n.4: Caveat emptor puts the onus on the buyer to survey, not the seller.

Property Law & Practice.q: Two solicitors are ready to exchange contracts by telephone, each holding their client's signed part of the contract, with the buyer's deposit held by the buyer's solicitor. They wish to exchange in a way that creates a binding contract at the moment of the telephone call, using an established professional procedure. The solicitors are exchanging by telephone under a recognised professional protocol. They want certainty about the moment of exchange. Both solicitors are poised to exchange over the telephone, each holding their own client's signed part of the contract and the buyer's deposit held ready, and they want to use the recognised professional procedure that pins down the precise instant at which a binding contract springs into existence. Which of the following best describes the mechanism they will use?
o: Exchange by the buyer registering a notice at the Land Registry.
Exchange by simply posting the contracts to each other without more.
Exchange by completing the Land Registry transfer form TR1.
Exchange only becomes effective once completion has taken place.
Exchange under one of the Law Society formulae (for example Formula A, B or C).
Property Law & Practice.w: Solicitors commonly exchange contracts by telephone using the Law Society formulae (Formula A where one solicitor holds both signed parts, Formula B where each holds their own client's part, and Formula C for chains). The formula records undertakings and fixes the precise moment a binding contract comes into existence on the call.

n.0: Registering a notice does not effect exchange of contracts.
n.1: Postal exchange is a different method; telephone exchange uses the Law Society formulae.
n.2: Form TR1 is the transfer deed used at completion, not the exchange mechanism.
n.3: A binding contract arises on exchange, not only on completion.

Property Law & Practice.q: A person is buying an existing leasehold flat from the current leaseholder, taking over the remainder of an existing long lease rather than being granted a brand new lease by the landlord. The buyer's solicitor must appreciate the nature of the transaction and the additional matters that arise because the interest is leasehold. The buyer asks how taking over an existing lease differs from being granted a new one. The solicitor considers the distinction between the assignment and the grant of a lease. The flat was held on a long lease with many years still left to run at a modest ground rent. Which of the following best describes it?
o: There is no legal difference between taking over an existing lease and being granted a new one on these facts as a general rule.
This is a freehold purchase, because the buyer is paying a capital sum for the flat.
This cannot be done at all, because existing leases can never be transferred to a new person.
This is an assignment of the existing lease, transferring the current leaseholder's interest, rather than the grant of a new lease.
This is the grant of a new lease directly by the landlord to the buyer.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where a buyer takes over the unexpired term of an existing lease from the current tenant, this is an assignment of the lease (the assignor transfers their leasehold interest to the assignee). It is distinct from the grant of a new lease, where the landlord creates a fresh leasehold estate in favour of the tenant.

n.0: Assignment and grant differ significantly in their legal mechanics and consequences.
n.1: A leasehold flat is a leasehold, not a freehold, interest.
n.2: Existing leases can be assigned to a new person, subject to the lease terms.
n.4: The landlord is not granting a new lease; the existing lease is being assigned.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor is investigating title to registered land before exchange. The solicitor needs to obtain evidence of the seller's ownership and of the entries affecting the title. The land is registered at the Land Registry. The solicitor is deducing and investigating title. Ahead of exchange the buyer's solicitor needs to satisfy itself that the seller really owns what is being sold and to see every entry that burdens or benefits the title, and since the land is registered it must obtain the right form of official evidence from the Land Registry rather than sifting old deeds. Which of the following best describes how title to registered land is deduced?
o: By carrying out a full-title indemnity insurance policy in place of investigation.
By providing official copies of the register and title plan (and any referred-to documents).
By handing over the original paper title deeds going back 30 years.
By providing an epitome of title with a good root of title at least 15 years old.
By obtaining a statutory declaration of ownership from the seller.
Property Law & Practice.w: Title to registered land is deduced by supplying official copies of the register (showing the property, proprietorship and charges registers) and the title plan, together with copies of any documents referred to. This differs from unregistered land, where title is deduced by an epitome of title tracing ownership from a good root of title at least 15 years old.

n.0: Indemnity insurance does not replace deducing title; it addresses specific defects.
n.2: Registered title is deduced from official copies, not by handing over old paper deeds.
