n.3: An epitome and good root of title are used for unregistered, not registered, land.
n.4: A statutory declaration is not the ordinary means of deducing registered title.

Property Law & Practice.q: A tenant took an assignment of a commercial lease that was granted in 2010 (a 'new' tenancy for the purposes of the relevant legislation). After the assignment, the assignee tenant fails to pay the rent, and the landlord considers who is liable. The lease covenants bind the current tenant while they hold the lease. The landlord asks about the assignee's liability for the lease covenants. The solicitor considers the liability of an assignee of a new tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995. The assignee had taken over a lease with many years still to run and substantial rent obligations. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assignee is never liable for any of the lease covenants after taking the assignment.
The assignee, as the current tenant, is bound by the tenant covenants of the lease while it holds the lease (privity of estate).
Only the original tenant remains liable for the covenants, whoever currently holds the lease on these facts as a general rule.
The assignee is liable only for covenants it expressly agrees to in a separate document.
The landlord can enforce the covenants only against the freeholder, not the tenant.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, for a 'new' tenancy (granted on or after 1 January 1996) the tenant covenants pass to the assignee, who is bound by them while they hold the lease (privity of estate). The outgoing tenant is generally released on a lawful assignment, subject to any AGA.

n.0: The current assignee tenant is bound by the tenant covenants while it holds the lease.
n.2: For a new tenancy the original tenant is generally released on assignment, so it is not solely liable.
n.3: The assignee is bound by the lease covenants generally, not only those separately agreed.
n.4: The landlord enforces tenant covenants against the tenant, not the freeholder.

Property Law & Practice.q: Shortly before completion, a buyer's solicitor carries out an official search of the register with priority against the seller's registered title. The search reveals no adverse entries. The solicitor wants to understand the effect of the priority conferred by the search. The search is an official search with priority (OS1). The solicitor is planning completion and registration. With completion imminent, the solicitor lodges the official pre-completion search against the seller's title, gets a clear result showing no adverse entries, and now wants to understand exactly what protection that clear search buys the buyer in the run-up to registering the purchase. Which of the following best describes the protection the priority search confers?
o: It transfers legal title to the buyer immediately on the date of the search on these facts as a general rule.
It confers a priority period during which the buyer's application to register is protected against later entries.
It removes the need ever to register the transfer at all.
It provides indemnity insurance against any defect in the seller's title.
It permanently prevents the seller from ever dealing with the land again.
Property Law & Practice.w: An official search of the register with priority (OS1) gives the buyer a priority period (of 30 working days) during which the buyer's application to register the disposition takes priority over any other application, so entries made by others in that window do not affect the buyer. The buyer must complete and apply to register within the priority period.

n.0: It does not transfer legal title on the search date.
n.2: The transfer must still be registered; the search does not remove that requirement.
n.3: It is not indemnity insurance against title defects.
n.4: It does not permanently prevent the seller dealing with the land; it protects a limited priority period.

Property Law & Practice.q: A borrower already has a first mortgage over their property in favour of Bank A, and now wishes to borrow further from Bank B, which will take a second charge over the same property. Both charges are registered. The borrower defaults, and the property is sold, but the proceeds are insufficient to pay both lenders in full. The lenders dispute priority. The solicitor considers the priority of two registered charges over the same property. Both banks had lent substantial sums and the sale proceeds would not cover them both. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The later charge always takes priority over the earlier charge in every case.
Registered charges generally rank in the order in which they are entered on the register, so the earlier-registered charge has priority.
The two charges always share the proceeds equally, whatever the order of registration.
A second charge can never validly be created over a property that already has a first charge on these facts as a general rule.
Priority between charges depends solely on which lender advanced the larger sum.
Property Law & Practice.w: The priority of registered charges over the same registered estate is generally determined by the order in which they are entered on the register. So a first registered charge (Bank A) ranks ahead of a later registered charge (Bank B), and is paid first from the proceeds of sale.

n.0: The later charge does not automatically take priority.
n.2: The charges do not share equally; registration order governs priority.
n.3: A second charge can validly be created behind a first charge.
n.4: Priority is by registration order, not the size of the advance.

Property Law & Practice.q: A person is buying their first home and has heard that they may qualify for a reduction in the tax normally payable by buyers, while another buyer purchasing an additional residential property (on top of one they already own) may have to pay more. The client asks how stamp duty land tax varies according to the buyer's circumstances. The solicitor considers SDLT reliefs and surcharges. The client was weighing up the true cost of the purchase once the tax was taken into account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: First-time buyers may qualify for SDLT relief, while buyers of additional residential properties may pay a higher-rate surcharge.
Buyers of additional properties are entirely exempt from SDLT on the extra property.
SDLT reliefs and surcharges depend only on whether the property is registered or unregistered.
First-time buyers always pay double the ordinary rate of SDLT on their purchase.
SDLT is a single flat amount that is identical for every buyer regardless of their circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: SDLT varies with circumstances: first-time buyers may claim first-time buyers' relief (paying reduced or no SDLT up to certain limits), whereas a buyer purchasing an additional residential property (such as a second home or buy-to-let) may be liable to the higher-rate surcharge on top of the standard rates.

n.1: Buyers of additional properties pay more (a surcharge), not nothing.
n.2: Reliefs/surcharges turn on the buyer's circumstances, not the registration status of the land.
n.3: First-time buyers receive relief, not a doubled rate.
n.4: SDLT is not a single flat amount for everyone; rates and reliefs vary.

Property Law & Practice.q: Contracts have been exchanged for the purchase of a house, with completion due in a few weeks. Between exchange and completion, before the buyer has taken possession, the property is seriously damaged by fire through no fault of either party. The buyer assumes the seller bears the loss until completion. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale. The solicitor considers where the risk in the property lies between exchange and completion, and the buyer's insurance position. The buyer had not yet arranged buildings insurance, assuming the seller remained responsible. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Risk is shared equally between buyer and seller between exchange and completion in every case.
Risk remains with the seller until completion, so the buyer need not insure until completion day on these facts.
Risk generally passes to the buyer on exchange, so the buyer should insure the property from exchange of contracts.
Risk passes to the buyer only once the buyer has physically moved into the property.
Risk never passes to the buyer at all, and the seller must always bear any damage.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the risk in the property generally passes to the buyer on exchange of contracts. The buyer is therefore well advised to insure the property from exchange (and lenders typically require it), since damage occurring before completion is generally the buyer's risk.

n.0: Risk is not shared equally; it generally passes to the buyer on exchange.
n.1: Risk does not remain with the seller until completion under the standard position.
n.3: Risk passes on exchange, not on taking physical possession.
n.4: Risk does pass to the buyer on exchange under the SCS.

Property Law & Practice.q: On completion of a sale, the contract for sale and the transfer deed contain overlapping provisions, and a question arises about whether the buyer can still rely on the terms of the contract after completion, or whether those terms are subsumed into the transfer. Some contractual obligations were intended to continue after completion. The buyer asks about the effect of completion on the contract terms. The solicitor considers the doctrine of merger on completion. Some obligations in the contract had been intended to carry on being enforceable after completion. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Contract terms generally merge in the transfer on completion, except those the parties intend to survive completion.
The contract is automatically rescinded on completion, extinguishing every obligation.
The transfer deed has no effect, and only the contract governs the parties after completion on these facts.
All contract terms always survive completion in full and can be relied on indefinitely.
Completion has no effect at all on the enforceability of the contract terms.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the doctrine of merger, on completion the terms of the contract generally merge in the transfer deed, so that the buyer's rights derive from the transfer. However, contractual obligations not covered by the transfer, and terms expressed to survive completion (non-merger provisions), continue to be enforceable.

n.1: Completion does not automatically rescind the contract; merger applies to its terms.
n.2: The transfer deed is effective; it is what conveys the estate.
n.3: Not all contract terms survive; many merge in the transfer.
n.4: Completion does affect the contract terms through merger.

Property Law & Practice.q: A commercial lease was granted before 1 January 1996 (an 'old' tenancy). The original tenant lawfully assigned the lease some years ago, and the current tenant has now defaulted on the rent. The landlord seeks to recover the arrears from the original tenant. The lease is an old tenancy and the original tenant assigned it before the current default. The landlord pursues the original tenant. The lease dates from well before the 1996 reforms, the person who originally took it assigned it on some years ago and has had nothing to do with the property since, yet the current tenant has now stopped paying and the landlord, looking for someone solvent to pursue, has turned its attention back to that first tenant. Which of the following best describes the original tenant's position?
o: The original tenant is liable only if they gave an authorised guarantee agreement.
The original tenant can never be pursued once a new tenant is in occupation.
The original tenant is liable only for defaults occurring within six months of the assignment on these facts as a general rule.
The original tenant was automatically released from all liability on assigning the lease.
Under privity of contract, the original tenant of an old lease generally remains liable on the covenants for the whole term.
Property Law & Practice.w: For 'old' tenancies (granted before 1996), privity of contract means the original tenant generally remains liable on the leasehold covenants for the whole term, even after assigning, because they contracted directly with the landlord. This contrasts with 'new' tenancies under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, where an assigning tenant is generally released (often subject to an authorised guarantee agreement).

n.0: An authorised guarantee agreement is a feature of new tenancies; old-lease liability rests on privity of contract.
n.1: On an old lease the original tenant can be pursued despite a new tenant being in occupation.
n.2: The original tenant's liability on an old lease is not limited to six months after assignment.
n.3: Automatic release on assignment applies to new tenancies, not old ones.

Property Law & Practice.q: Before completing a purchase, the buyer's solicitor wishes to check whether the seller is subject to any bankruptcy proceedings that could affect their ability to deal with the property, particularly where a mortgage lender is also being acted for. The solicitor considers which search is made to check the insolvency position of an individual seller or borrower. A lender was funding the purchase and wanted to be sure the borrower was not insolvent. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A drainage and water search reveals the seller's insolvency position on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The Land Registry title plan reveals the seller's bankruptcy status.
A local land charges search reveals whether the seller is bankrupt.
There is no way to check whether an individual seller is bankrupt.
A bankruptcy search (Form K16 at the Land Charges Department) is made against the individual to check for insolvency entries.
Property Law & Practice.w: A bankruptcy search (Form K16) is made at the Land Charges Department against the name of an individual (for example a borrower, on behalf of a lender) to reveal any bankruptcy petitions or orders that would affect the person's capacity to deal with the property.

n.0: A drainage and water search does not reveal insolvency.
n.1: The title plan does not show bankruptcy status.
n.2: The local land charges search does not reveal an individual's bankruptcy.
n.3: Insolvency can be checked by a bankruptcy search.

Property Law & Practice.q: A tenant of premises has committed a breach of a covenant in the lease (other than non-payment of rent), and the landlord wishes to forfeit the lease and recover possession. Before taking steps to forfeit, the landlord's solicitor advises that a particular statutory notice must first be served on the tenant. The tenant asks what the landlord must do before forfeiting for such a breach. The solicitor considers the procedure for forfeiture for breach of a non-rent covenant. The tenant had altered the premises in serious breach of covenant and refused to put matters right. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The landlord may forfeit immediately for any breach without giving the tenant any notice at all on these facts as a general rule.
The landlord may forfeit only by physically evicting the tenant without any legal process.
The landlord must first serve a notice under s.146 Law of Property Act 1925 specifying the breach and allowing time to remedy it.
The landlord must obtain the tenant's written consent before forfeiting the lease.
The landlord must apply to the Land Registry to cancel the tenant's leasehold title.
Property Law & Practice.w: To forfeit a lease for breach of a covenant other than payment of rent, the landlord must first serve a notice under s.146 Law of Property Act 1925 specifying the breach, requiring it to be remedied (if capable of remedy) and, where appropriate, requiring compensation, giving the tenant a reasonable time to comply before forfeiture is pursued (and the tenant may seek relief).

n.0: A s.146 notice is required first; the landlord cannot forfeit immediately without notice for a non-rent breach.
n.1: Forfeiture must follow the proper legal process, not self-help eviction of residential tenants.
n.3: The tenant's written consent is not the requirement; a s.146 notice is.
n.4: Forfeiture is not effected by cancelling the leasehold title at the Land Registry.

Property Law & Practice.q: An individual sells a property which has been their only or main home throughout their period of ownership, making a gain on the sale. They are concerned about whether they must pay tax on that gain. The property was not used for any business and has always been their residence. The seller asks about the capital gains tax position on the sale of their home. The solicitor considers private residence relief from capital gains tax. The seller had lived in the house as their home for the whole of the time they had owned it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gain on a person's home is taxed as income under income tax rules.
Capital gains tax is always payable in full on any sale of a person's home, with no relief on these facts.
Private residence relief generally exempts the gain on a person's only or main home from capital gains tax.
Private residence relief applies only to properties owned by companies.
No tax of any kind can ever arise on the disposal of residential property.
Property Law & Practice.w: A gain on the disposal of a dwelling that has been the individual's only or main residence throughout the period of ownership is generally exempt from capital gains tax under private residence relief (with some final-period and other rules), so no CGT is typically payable on the sale of a main home.

n.0: The gain is a capital gain, not income taxed under income tax.
n.1: CGT is generally not payable on a main home due to private residence relief.
n.3: Private residence relief is for individuals' homes, not company-owned property.
n.4: Tax can arise on some property disposals (e.g. investment property); the relief is specific to the main home.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer's solicitor is considering additional pre-contract searches beyond the standard ones, depending on the location and nature of the property. The property is near a river and in an area historically used for industry, so there is concern about the risk of flooding and of land contamination. The solicitor considers which search addresses these particular environmental risks. The house stood close to a river and on the site of a long-closed industrial works. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A bankruptcy search against the seller reveals the property's flood risk.
The local land charges search is the only search that reveals contamination and flood risk.
A Land Registry official copy reveals whether the land is contaminated or at risk of flooding.
An environmental search reveals risks such as land contamination and flooding affecting the property.
Environmental risks cannot be investigated before exchange of contracts.
Property Law & Practice.w: An environmental search reports on environmental risks affecting the property, including whether the land is or may be contaminated (and the risk of liability under the contaminated land regime) and the risk of flooding, drawing on databases of past land uses and flood data.

n.0: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not flood risk.
n.1: The local land charges search does not provide the detailed environmental risk data.
n.2: Official copies of the register do not report contamination or flood risk.
n.4: Environmental risks can be investigated pre-exchange via an environmental search.

Property Law & Practice.q: On exchange of contracts for a residential purchase, the buyer is required to pay a deposit to the seller's solicitor. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale, and the buyer asks how much the deposit will usually be and on what basis the seller's solicitor holds it pending completion. The buyer is concerned about whether the money is at risk if the transaction does not complete. The solicitor considers the usual deposit and the basis on which it is held. The buyer was funding the deposit from savings and was nervous about handing the money over. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The deposit is usually 10% of the price and is generally held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder until completion.
The deposit is held by the buyer's own solicitor and never released to the seller's side.
No deposit is ever payable on exchange of a residential conveyancing contract.
The deposit is usually the full purchase price and is paid directly to the seller personally on these facts as a general rule.
The deposit is always 50% of the price and is spent immediately by the seller.
Property Law & Practice.w: The deposit is customarily 10% of the purchase price, payable on exchange. Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the seller's solicitor generally holds the deposit as stakeholder, meaning it is held on behalf of both parties and released to the seller only on completion.

n.1: The deposit is held by the seller's solicitor (as stakeholder), not retained by the buyer's solicitor.
n.2: A deposit is payable on exchange; it is not the case that none is ever payable.
n.3: The deposit is not the full price, nor paid to the seller personally in the ordinary case.
n.4: The usual deposit is 10%, not 50% spent immediately.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer has completed the purchase of a property that attracts stamp duty land tax. The buyer's solicitor must deal with the tax and the associated return promptly after completion. SDLT is chargeable on the transaction. The solicitor is attending to post-completion steps. Completion of the purchase has just taken place on a transaction that attracts the tax, and the buyer's solicitor, mindful that registration of the buyer's title depends on the tax position being dealt with, is checking exactly how soon the return must be submitted and the tax paid. Which of the following best describes the deadline for the SDLT return and payment?
o: An SDLT return must be filed and the tax paid within 14 days of the effective date of the transaction.
An SDLT return must be filed within 12 months of completion.
The SDLT return must be filed before exchange of contracts.
SDLT is payable only when the buyer later sells the property on these facts as a general rule.
No return is required where the buyer instructs a solicitor.
Property Law & Practice.w: A land transaction return for SDLT must generally be filed, and the tax paid, within 14 days of the effective date of the transaction (usually completion). Registration of the buyer's title at the Land Registry cannot proceed without evidence that the SDLT position has been dealt with, so this is a key post-completion step.

n.1: The deadline is 14 days, not 12 months.
n.2: The return follows the effective date (completion), not exchange.
n.3: SDLT is payable on the purchase, not deferred until a later sale.
n.4: A return is required regardless of whether a solicitor is instructed (the solicitor usually files it).

Property Law & Practice.q: An owner of a house wishes to raise money by borrowing against the property and grants a mortgage to a bank. The bank wants its security to be legally effective and to be protected against later buyers or lenders. The owner's solicitor advises on how a mortgage of registered land is created and protected. The client asks how the bank's mortgage takes effect as a legal charge and secures priority. The solicitor considers the creation and registration of a legal mortgage of registered land. The owner needed the loan quickly and the bank wanted watertight security over the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A mortgage of registered land can only ever be created by physically depositing the title deeds.
A mortgage of registered land need not be in writing and may be created orally.
A mortgage of registered land is protected only by the lender taking possession of the property.
A legal mortgage of registered land is created by a charge, which must be registered against the title to take effect as a legal charge.
A mortgage of registered land takes effect legally as soon as it is signed, with no need to register it on these facts as a general rule.
Property Law & Practice.w: A mortgage of registered land is created by a legal charge, which is a registrable disposition. It must be completed by registration against the registered title (entry in the charges register) to take effect as a legal charge and to secure its priority; until registered it takes effect only in equity.

n.0: Deposit of deeds is not how a legal mortgage of registered land is created.
n.1: A mortgage must be by deed/charge in writing, not oral.
n.2: The charge is protected by registration, not by the lender taking possession.
n.4: A legal charge of registered land must be registered to take effect at law, not merely signed.

Property Law & Practice.q: After completion, a buyer discovers that a pre-contract statement made by the seller about the property was false and had induced the buyer to enter the contract, causing the buyer loss. The buyer wishes to know what remedy might be available for the seller's false pre-contract statement, given that completion has already taken place. The solicitor considers the remedies for misrepresentation in a conveyancing transaction. The false statement had concerned an important feature that had influenced the buyer's decision. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's sole remedy is to apply to the Land Registry to reverse the registration.
The buyer may only sue the local authority that carried out the searches.
The buyer may reclaim the SDLT paid to HMRC as compensation for the misrepresentation on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The buyer has no remedy at all once completion has taken place, whatever was said.
The buyer may have a claim for misrepresentation, potentially for rescission and/or damages, depending on the type of misrepresentation.
Property Law & Practice.w: A false pre-contract statement of fact that induced the contract may give rise to a misrepresentation claim, with remedies of rescission and/or damages depending on whether the misrepresentation was fraudulent, negligent or innocent (subject to the effect of completion and any contractual terms limiting liability).

n.0: Reversing the registration is not the remedy for misrepresentation.
n.1: The claim lies against the seller who made the statement, not the local authority.
n.2: Reclaiming SDLT is not a misrepresentation remedy.
n.3: Completion does not necessarily extinguish a misrepresentation claim.

Property Law & Practice.q: On exchange of contracts incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale, the buyer's solicitor advises the buyer about insuring the property. The buyer assumes the seller remains responsible for the property until completion. Under the Standard Conditions, risk in the property passes to the buyer on exchange. The buyer wrongly assumes the seller bears the risk until completion. Contracts have just been exchanged on the sale, the standard conditions apply, and the buyer, assuming the seller will look after the building right up to completion, is surprised when the solicitor raises the question of insurance, given how the standard conditions allocate the risk between the parties from exchange onwards. Which of the following best describes the buyer's position on insurance?
o: The property is automatically insured by the Land Registry between exchange and completion.
The buyer need not insure until completion, as the seller bears all risk until then.
Neither party need insure because the contract allocates all loss to the seller.
Insurance is unnecessary because any damage entitles the buyer to rescind automatically.
The buyer should insure the property from exchange, as risk generally passes to the buyer on exchange.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, risk in the property generally passes to the buyer on exchange of contracts, and the seller is not obliged to insure after exchange. The buyer should therefore insure the property from exchange (or ensure it is covered), because if it is damaged between exchange and completion the buyer generally must still complete.

n.0: The Land Registry does not insure property between exchange and completion.
n.1: The seller does not bear all risk until completion under the Standard Conditions; risk passes on exchange.
n.2: The contract does not allocate all loss to the seller; risk passes to the buyer.
n.3: Damage does not automatically entitle the buyer to rescind; the buyer generally must still complete.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer who already owns a home is purchasing a second residential property (an additional dwelling) which will not replace their main residence. The buyer's solicitor is calculating the stamp duty land tax and considers whether a higher charge applies. The purchase is of an additional residential dwelling, not a replacement of the only or main home. The solicitor is computing the SDLT due. The buyer already owns and is keeping their existing home and is now buying a further residential property as well, rather than replacing their main residence, and the solicitor working out the tax on the second purchase needs to know whether an additional charge bites on a transaction of this kind. Which of the following best describes the SDLT position?
o: No SDLT is payable on any residential purchase under the current rules.
SDLT is charged at a flat rate regardless of the number of properties owned on these facts.
The lower first-time buyer rates apply to the additional dwelling.
Higher rates of SDLT generally apply to the purchase of an additional residential dwelling.
The purchase is exempt from SDLT because the buyer already owns a home.
Property Law & Practice.w: The purchase of an additional residential dwelling (such as a second home or buy-to-let), where the buyer is not replacing their only or main residence, generally attracts higher rates of SDLT, an additional percentage on top of the standard residential rates. The higher rates do not apply where the purchase replaces the buyer's only or main home.

n.0: SDLT is payable on residential purchases above the relevant thresholds.
n.1: SDLT is charged on a banded basis, and additional dwellings attract a surcharge, not a single flat rate.
n.2: First-time buyer relief does not apply to someone already owning a home buying an additional dwelling.
n.4: Owning a home does not exempt the additional purchase; higher rates generally apply.

Property Law & Practice.q: A tenant occupies commercial premises for the purposes of its business under a lease that has not been excluded from statutory protection. As the contractual term approaches its end, the tenant is concerned about whether it can be required to leave. The tenancy is a business tenancy to which the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 applies. The tenant occupies for business purposes. The tenant runs its business from the premises under a lease that was never contracted out of the statutory protection, and as the fixed term nears its end the tenant is worried about whether the landlord can simply require it to pack up and leave once the contractual term expires. Which of the following best describes the tenant's position on security of tenure?
o: The tenant's rights depend entirely on whatever the lease says, with no statutory protection on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The tenant may remain indefinitely and the landlord can never recover the premises.
The tenancy ends automatically on the contractual term date and the tenant must leave.
The tenant has security of tenure only if the premises are residential.
The tenancy does not end automatically; the tenant has security of tenure and a right to apply for a new tenancy, resisted only on statutory grounds.
Property Law & Practice.w: Under Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, a tenant occupying premises for the purposes of a business has security of tenure: the tenancy does not determine automatically at the end of the contractual term but continues until ended by a statutory procedure, and the tenant has the right to apply for a new tenancy. The landlord can oppose renewal only on one of the statutory grounds. Parties may contract out by the prescribed procedure before the lease is granted.

n.0: There is statutory protection under the 1954 Act, not merely whatever the lease says.
n.1: The landlord can recover possession on statutory grounds, so the tenant cannot always remain.
n.2: A protected business tenancy does not end automatically at the term date.
n.3: The 1954 Act protects business, not residential, tenancies.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer is purchasing unregistered land. To discover whether any registrable third-party interests (such as restrictive covenants, estate contracts or certain mortgages) affect the land, the buyer's solicitor must carry out the appropriate central search. The land is unregistered, so interests are recorded against names rather than a title number. The solicitor is investigating incumbrances before completion. The title to this land has never been registered, so incumbrances are not tied to a title number but recorded against the names of successive owners, and the buyer's solicitor needs to run the correct central search to flush out any registered burdens before the buyer commits to completion. Which of the following best describes the search that should be carried out?
o: A local land charges search only, which reveals all private incumbrances.
An index map search, which lists all restrictive covenants affecting the land.
An official search of the register with priority against the title number.
A land charges search (Form K15) against the names of the estate owners.
No search is needed because unregistered land carries no third-party interests.
Property Law & Practice.w: For unregistered land, many third-party interests are registered as land charges against the name of the relevant estate owner. The buyer's solicitor must therefore carry out a Central Land Charges search (Form K15) against the names of the estate owners for their periods of ownership to reveal registered land charges such as restrictive covenants, estate contracts and puisne mortgages.

n.0: A local land charges search reveals public/local matters, not private land charges against names.
n.1: An index map search checks whether land is registered; it does not list covenants.
n.2: An official search of the register with priority applies to registered, not unregistered, land.
n.4: Unregistered land can be affected by third-party interests; searches are needed.

Property Law & Practice.q: A buyer is purchasing a newly built flat 'off-plan' from a developer before it has been completed, and the buyer's solicitor must consider matters that do not arise on the purchase of an existing, completed property. The buyer asks what additional issues arise when buying a new-build property from a developer. The solicitor considers new-build conveyancing. The block was still a building site and completion would not occur for many months yet. Which of the following best describes an issue particular to new-build purchases?
o: New-build purchases raise no different issues from the purchase of an existing house.
New-build purchases can never be bought with the aid of a mortgage.
New-build purchases raise particular issues such as a new-build warranty, roads and services adoption, and the developer's construction obligations.
New-build purchases never require any planning permission or building regulations approval on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
New-build purchases require no investigation of title because the property is brand new.
Property Law & Practice.w: New-build purchases raise particular issues, including obtaining a new-home warranty (such as NHBC cover), checking arrangements for adoption of roads and sewers (and any bonds), confirming planning and building regulations compliance, and dealing with the developer's obligations to complete construction and any long-stop/backstop dates.

n.0: New-build purchases do raise additional, distinct issues.
n.1: New-builds can be, and often are, bought with a mortgage.
n.3: New-builds still require planning permission and building regulations compliance.
n.4: Title (including the newly created title/lease) still requires investigation.

Property Law & Practice.q: A solicitor acting for a buyer of registered land needs to investigate the seller's title before exchange of contracts. The solicitor obtains up-to-date official copies of the register of title and the title plan from the Land Registry. The solicitor is checking the entries to understand what the buyer will acquire and what burdens affect the property. The solicitor considers the structure of the register of title. The buyer wanted to know exactly what rights and burdens the registered title carried before committing. Which of the following best describes how the register is organised?
o: The register is made up only of the title plan, with no written entries at all.
The register comprises the property register, the proprietorship register and the charges register.
The register comprises a single continuous narrative with no separate parts or divisions.
The register comprises a list of every previous owner going back at least fifteen years.
The register consists solely of a record of the mortgages secured on the property.
Property Law & Practice.w: A registered title is made up of three parts: the property register (describing the land and estate and noting benefiting rights), the proprietorship register (naming the registered proprietor, class of title and any restrictions), and the charges register (recording burdens such as mortgages, covenants and easements affecting the land).

n.0: The register includes written entries as well as the title plan.
n.2: The register is divided into parts, not a single narrative.
n.3: Registered title does not require a 15-year chain of owners; that concerns unregistered title.
n.4: The register records more than mortgages; it has three parts.

Property Law & Practice.q: A client is simultaneously selling their existing home and buying a new one, with the sale proceeds needed to fund the purchase, and both transactions form part of a chain with other buyers and sellers. The client's solicitor must manage the timing so that the client is not left having sold their home without a new one, or vice versa. The client asks how the two transactions are coordinated. The solicitor considers the synchronisation of a related sale and purchase in a chain. The client could not afford to buy the new home without the proceeds of selling the old one. Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach?
o: The solicitor should complete the sale and purchase on entirely unrelated dates without coordination on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor should exchange on the purchase first and worry about selling the existing home later.
The solicitor should exchange on the sale weeks before even finding a property to buy.
The solicitor should synchronise exchange (and completion) of the sale and purchase so the client is not committed to one without the other.
The solicitor should treat the two transactions as wholly independent, ignoring the chain.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where a client's sale and purchase are dependent (a chain), the solicitor must synchronise the transactions — exchanging (and completing) on the sale and the purchase on the same day or in a coordinated sequence — so the client is never contractually bound to buy without having sold, or to sell without having secured the purchase.

n.0: Uncoordinated completion dates risk leaving the client without a home or double-committed.
n.1: Exchanging on the purchase alone risks the client being unable to fund it if the sale fails.
n.2: Exchanging on the sale before finding a purchase risks having nowhere to move to.
n.4: The chain must be managed, not ignored.

Property Law & Practice.q: Following the assignment of a lease, the lease requires that the landlord be formally notified of any dealing with the lease, such as an assignment or a mortgage, within a specified time after completion. The incoming tenant's solicitor must attend to this post-completion step. The buyer asks what must be done to notify the landlord of the assignment. The solicitor considers giving notice of assignment to the landlord where the lease so requires. The lease was strict about being told of any change in the identity of the tenant. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Notice of the assignment is given to the Land Registry instead of the landlord.
The assignee's solicitor must give notice of the assignment (and any charge) to the landlord as required by the lease, usually paying a fee.
The outgoing tenant, not the incoming tenant, must give notice of the assignment to the buyer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The landlord must be notified only if the rent is being increased on the assignment.
There is never any need to tell the landlord that the lease has changed hands.
Property Law & Practice.w: Where the lease contains a covenant requiring notice of dealings, the assignee's solicitor must, after completion, serve notice of the assignment (and of any mortgage) on the landlord (or its solicitor) within the time the lease specifies, usually accompanied by the fee the lease provides for, and obtain a receipted copy.

n.0: Notice is given to the landlord, not (for this purpose) the Land Registry.
n.2: The incoming tenant/assignee's side gives the notice to the landlord.
n.3: Notice is required regardless of whether the rent changes.
n.4: Where the lease requires it, the landlord must be notified of the assignment.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person made a potentially exempt transfer (an outright lifetime gift to an individual) but then died four years later, so that the gift becomes chargeable to inheritance tax because the donor did not survive the full seven years. The personal representatives consider whether the tax on the failed PET is reduced because the donor survived for several years after making it. The court considers taper relief for inheritance tax. The gift had been made to help a grandchild, and the donor had seemed in good health then. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Taper relief may reduce the IHT payable on a failed PET where the donor survived more than three years after the gift.
Taper relief increases the tax payable the longer the donor survived after the gift.
Taper relief is available only for gifts made to charities during the donor's lifetime on these facts as a general rule.
Taper relief applies only where the donor survived less than one year after the gift.
Taper relief reduces the value of the gift itself so that no tax is ever payable.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a donor dies within seven years of a PET (or LCT) so that it becomes chargeable, taper relief may reduce the amount of IHT payable on that transfer on a sliding scale where the donor survived more than three years, with the reduction increasing the closer the death is to the seven-year point.

n.1: Taper relief reduces, not increases, the tax as survival lengthens.
n.2: Taper relief is not confined to charitable gifts.
n.3: Taper relief operates where more than three years have passed, not under one year.
n.4: Taper relief reduces the tax, not the value of the gift, and does not always eliminate the tax.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator wishes to appoint a partner in a firm of solicitors as their executor, and intends that the solicitor should be able to charge the estate for the professional work of administering it. The will is being drafted. The testator wants the professional executor to be paid for their services. The executor is a professional acting in the course of their profession. The testator is keen to appoint an experienced solicitor to shoulder the administration and expects that professional to be paid for the work involved, so the person drafting the will needs to know what has to be included if the solicitor is lawfully to charge the estate for their time. Which of the following best describes what is required for the professional executor to be remunerated?
o: The executor may charge whatever they wish without any authority, as executors are always paid on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The executor may charge only if appointed by the court rather than by the will.
The executor can never be paid for administering an estate in any circumstances.
The will should contain a charging clause (or statutory provision must apply) authorising the professional executor to charge for their services.
The executor may charge only if the residuary beneficiaries later agree in writing.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: An executor is not automatically entitled to remuneration for time and trouble; authority is needed. This is usually given by a charging clause in the will permitting a professional executor to charge for their services, and there is also statutory provision allowing a trust corporation or professional PR to charge reasonable remuneration where others consent, subject to conditions.

n.0: Executors are not automatically entitled to be paid; authority such as a charging clause is required.
n.1: Court appointment is not the basis for a professional executor's charging entitlement.
n.2: A professional executor can be paid where properly authorised, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Remuneration usually rests on a charging clause, not merely on later beneficiary agreement.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will names a sole executor who is a child aged 15 at the date of the testator's death. A grant of probate is needed to administer the estate promptly, but the named executor is a minor. The only named executor has not yet reached 18. A grant is required without delay. The will names just one executor, but that person is only fifteen years old at the date of death, and the estate needs administering without waiting years, so the question is how a grant can be obtained when the sole named executor has not yet come of age. Which of the following best describes the position on the grant?
o: The minor's parents automatically become the executors in the minor's place permanently on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A minor cannot take a grant while under 18; a grant may be taken by others on the minor's behalf, with the minor's own right reserved.
The estate cannot be administered at all until the minor turns 18.
The 15-year-old may take the grant of probate immediately as the named executor.
The will is invalid because it names a minor as executor.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A minor cannot take a grant of probate while under 18. Where the only executor is a minor, a grant (for example letters of administration with will annexed for the minor's use and benefit) may be taken by others, such as the minor's parents or guardians, with the minor's own right to a grant reserved until they reach 18.

n.0: Those who act do so for the minor's use, with the minor's right reserved, not as permanent executors displacing the minor.
n.2: Administration need not wait until the minor turns 18; others may act meanwhile.
n.3: A 15-year-old cannot take the grant while a minor.
n.4: Naming a minor as executor does not invalidate the will.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: During their lifetime, a person makes an outright gift of a large sum of money to their adult child. The donor survives for several years after making the gift. The personal representatives, after the donor's later death, must consider the inheritance tax treatment of that lifetime gift to an individual. The court considers potentially exempt transfers (PETs) for inheritance tax. The gift had been a generous one made to help the child buy their first home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A lifetime gift to an individual is a potentially exempt transfer, becoming fully exempt if the donor survives seven years.
A lifetime gift to an individual is never subject to inheritance tax in any circumstances.
A lifetime gift to an individual becomes exempt only if the donor survives for three years.
A lifetime gift to an individual is always immediately chargeable to inheritance tax when made on these facts as a general rule.
A lifetime gift to an individual is exempt only up to the amount of the annual exemption.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: An outright lifetime gift to another individual is a potentially exempt transfer (PET). It is not charged to IHT when made, and becomes wholly exempt if the donor survives seven years; if the donor dies within seven years, it becomes chargeable (with taper relief potentially reducing the tax after three years).

n.1: A PET can become chargeable if the donor dies within seven years.
n.2: The survival period is seven years, not three.
n.3: A PET is not immediately chargeable when made.
n.4: A PET is not limited to the annual exemption; the seven-year rule governs its exemption.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person who is not a personal representative, and has no authority to act, nonetheless intermeddles in a deceased's estate — for example by taking possession of and dealing with the deceased's assets as though entitled to administer them. Creditors and beneficiaries seek to hold that person responsible. The court considers the position of an executor de son tort. The person had moved into the deceased's home and begun selling off the contents. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Such a person automatically becomes the validly appointed executor of the estate.
A person who intermeddles in an estate without authority may be liable as an executor de son tort for their dealings.
A person who deals with a deceased's assets without authority incurs no liability of any kind on these facts.
Such a person is liable only if they were a beneficiary named in the deceased's will.
Only a validly appointed executor can ever incur any liability in relation to an estate.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A person who, without a grant or lawful authority, intermeddles with a deceased's estate and does acts characteristic of an executor may be treated as an executor de son tort ('of his own wrong') and become liable to account to the estate, creditors and beneficiaries for their dealings.

n.0: Intermeddling does not make the person a validly appointed executor.
n.2: Unauthorised intermeddling does attract liability, contrary to this option.
n.3: Liability as executor de son tort does not depend on being a named beneficiary.
n.4: Liability is not confined to validly appointed executors; an intermeddler can be liable.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: An estate is solvent but the debts and liabilities must be paid out of the various parts of the estate in the correct order. The will disposes of some property specifically and leaves a residue, and there is also property that is undisposed of by the will. The personal representatives must apply assets to pay the unsecured debts in the statutory order. The court considers the order of application of assets to pay debts under the Administration of Estates Act 1925. The estate was solvent but the debts had to be met from somewhere before the gifts were paid. Which of the following best describes the general starting point?
o: Property undisposed of by the will, and then the residue, is generally applied before resorting to specific gifts.
Specific gifts are always applied first to pay debts, before any residue or undisposed-of property on these facts.
Debts are paid only out of specific legacies and never out of the residue.
The personal representatives may choose any order they like for applying assets to debts.
All assets are applied rateably at once, regardless of how the will disposes of them.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the statutory order in the Administration of Estates Act 1925 (for a solvent estate), unsecured debts are met first from property undisposed of by the will, then from residue, before recourse to property specifically given, with pecuniary legacies and specific gifts being progressively more protected (subject to any contrary provision in the will).

n.1: Specific gifts are among the last resorted to, not the first.
n.2: Debts are met from undisposed-of property and residue before specific legacies, not only from legacies.
n.3: The PRs must follow the statutory order, not choose freely.
n.4: Assets are applied in a set order, not all rateably at once.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Personal representatives are about to distribute an estate, but are concerned that there may be unknown creditors or claimants who could later come forward and hold them personally liable if the estate has already been distributed. They wish to protect themselves before distributing. The court considers the statutory protection available to personal representatives before distribution. The deceased had run a business and there might be creditors the PRs did not yet know about. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The PRs can protect themselves only by obtaining the consent of every possible claimant first.
The PRs have no way to protect themselves and must simply distribute and hope no claimant appears on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The PRs are automatically protected against all unknown claimants without taking any step.
The PRs may distribute free of liability provided they act honestly and in good faith.
The PRs may advertise for claimants under s.27 Trustee Act 1925 and, after the notice period, distribute without personal liability to unknown claimants.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.27 Trustee Act 1925, personal representatives may give statutory notice by advertisement (for example in the London Gazette and a local newspaper) for creditors and claimants. Having waited the required period (at least two months), they may distribute without being personally liable to claimants of whom they had no notice.

n.0: Obtaining every possible claimant's consent is not the mechanism; advertisement is.
n.1: There is a protective step; PRs are not left without protection.
n.2: Protection is not automatic; the s.27 procedure must be followed.
n.3: Honest good faith alone does not give the s.27 protection.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person gives away their house to their child during their lifetime, hoping to reduce inheritance tax, but continues to live in the house rent-free until death, so that they never truly gave up the benefit of the property. On the death, the personal representatives consider the inheritance tax treatment of the earlier gift. The court considers the rules on gifts with reservation of benefit. The parent carried on living in the house exactly as before, paying nothing for the privilege. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift is valid for IHT provided the child pays a market rent to the donor for the property.
The gift removes the house from the estate provided the donor survived three years.
The gift is fully effective for IHT, because the house was given away during the donor's lifetime on these facts.
The house is generally treated as remaining part of the deceased's estate for IHT, as a gift with reservation of benefit.
The gift is ignored entirely, and the house passes under the donor's will as if never given.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the gift with reservation of benefit rules, where a person gives away property but reserves a benefit (such as continuing to live in the house rent-free), the property is generally treated as still forming part of their estate for inheritance tax purposes on death, negating the tax advantage.

n.0: Only paying a full market rent (removing the reservation) could avoid the rule; a rent-free arrangement does not.
n.1: The three/seven-year rules do not save a gift with a continuing reserved benefit.
n.2: The reservation of benefit means the gift is not effective to remove the house for IHT.
n.4: The gift is not simply ignored; it is treated as part of the estate for IHT.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator leaves a substantial part of their net estate to a registered charity, and the executors are told that this may reduce the rate of inheritance tax on the rest of the estate, not merely provide an exemption for the charitable gift itself. The charitable gift is large in proportion to the net estate. The executors are considering the reduced rate of inheritance tax. The testator directed a sizeable slice of the estate to a registered charity, and the executors have been told this may do more than exempt the charitable gift itself, potentially lowering the rate of tax on what is left, so they want to know the threshold that triggers that lower rate and what the rate becomes. Which of the following best describes when the reduced rate applies and what it is?
o: Where at least 25% of the estate passes to charity, the rate is reduced to 20%.
The reduced rate reduces the tax to 0% regardless of the size of the charitable gift.
The reduced rate applies only to lifetime gifts, never on death.
Where at least 10% of the net estate passes to charity, the rate of inheritance tax on the rest is reduced to 36%.
Where any gift at all is made to charity, the whole estate becomes exempt from inheritance tax on these facts.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where at least 10% of a defined 'net estate' is left to charity, the rate of inheritance tax on the remainder of that component of the estate is reduced from 40% to 36%. The charitable gift itself is also exempt. This is separate from the general charity exemption, which applies to any charitable gift.

n.0: The threshold is 10% of the net estate for the reduced rate of 36%, not 25% for 20%.
n.1: The reduced rate is 36%, not 0%.
n.2: The reduced rate applies to the death estate, not only lifetime gifts.
n.4: Any charitable gift is exempt, but it does not make the whole estate exempt.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: An adult child of the deceased, who was not adequately provided for by the deceased's will, wishes to claim against the estate. The child is not a spouse or civil partner of the deceased and was financially independent as an adult, though now in some need. The applicant is an adult child, not a surviving spouse. The claim is under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975. The claimant is a grown-up child of the deceased who was left little or nothing by the will and, though long financially independent, is now facing real need, and the court must decide what yardstick applies to a claim of this kind brought by someone who is not the deceased's surviving spouse. Which of the following best describes the standard of provision the court may order for such an applicant?
o: No provision at all, because only spouses may claim under the Act.
Such financial provision as would be reasonable for the applicant's maintenance.
Such financial provision as would be reasonable in all the circumstances, whether or not for maintenance.
An equal share of the estate with all other children of the deceased.
Whatever sum the applicant requests, provided the estate can afford it.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, for applicants other than a surviving spouse or civil partner, the standard is such financial provision as it would be reasonable for the applicant to receive for their maintenance. The higher 'reasonable in all the circumstances' standard, not limited to maintenance, applies only to a surviving spouse or civil partner.

n.0: Children, cohabitants and others may claim, not only spouses.
n.2: The non-maintenance standard is reserved for surviving spouses/civil partners, not an adult child.
n.3: There is no automatic equal share among children; the court assesses maintenance provision.
n.4: The court does not simply award whatever the applicant requests; it applies the maintenance standard and the statutory factors.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: An estate includes land which is to be held on trust for beneficiaries, one of whom is a minor with a life interest arising. A single individual proposes to take out the grant and act alone as the only personal representative. A question arises about the minimum number of personal representatives required in these circumstances. The court considers the number of personal representatives needed where there is a minor beneficiary or a life interest. The estate's main asset was a house held for the family, including a young grandchild. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only a trust corporation, and never individuals, may act where there is a life interest.
At least four personal representatives are always required to administer any estate.
No personal representative is needed where a minor is a beneficiary of the estate.
A single personal representative can always act alone, whatever interests arise under the estate on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Where a minority or life interest arises, at least two personal representatives (or a trust corporation) are required.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Although a sole personal representative can generally act, where there is a minority interest or a life interest arising under a will or intestacy, at least two personal representatives (or a trust corporation) are required to give a valid receipt for capital money arising from land, to protect the beneficiaries.

n.0: Two individuals can act; a trust corporation is an alternative, not the only option.
n.1: The maximum is four PRs, but two is not always required unless such interests arise.
n.2: PRs are needed to administer the estate even where a minor benefits.
n.3: A sole PR cannot give a valid receipt for capital from land where a minority or life interest arises.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will leaves a substantial gift to their spouse and appoints the spouse as executor. The couple later divorce (the marriage is dissolved), but the testator never changes the will before dying. The former spouse claims the gift and the right to act as executor. The court considers the effect of divorce on gifts and appointments in an existing will under the Wills Act 1837. The couple had gone through a bitter divorce a year or so before the testator died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The divorce has no effect at all on the will and its provisions remain fully in force.
The former spouse takes the gift and acts as executor exactly as if the divorce had not happened.
The former spouse still acts as executor but loses only the gift left to them.
The whole will is revoked automatically by the divorce, so the testator dies intestate.
The former spouse is treated as having died before the testator, so the gift and appointment to them fail.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.18A Wills Act 1837, where a marriage is dissolved or annulled after the will, any appointment of the former spouse as executor and any gift to the former spouse take effect as if the former spouse had died on the date the marriage ended (the rest of the will remaining valid).

n.0: Divorce does affect the will's provisions for the former spouse.
n.1: The former spouse does not take the gift or act as executor as before.
n.2: Both the gift and the executor appointment to the ex-spouse are affected, not just the gift.
n.3: Divorce does not revoke the whole will; only the provisions for the ex-spouse are affected.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A deceased owned a house as a tenant in common with another person, each owning a half share, and lived in it with that co-owner. The executors are valuing the deceased's half share for inheritance tax and consider whether the fact of co-ownership affects the value. The deceased owned an undivided share, not the whole, of the co-owned property. The executors are valuing the share for inheritance tax. The deceased and another person had each owned an equal share of the home as tenants in common and lived there together, and the executors, valuing only the deceased's half for tax, are wondering whether the reality that a part share is harder to sell than the whole affects the figure they should use. Which of the following best describes the valuation of the deceased's share?
o: A discount may be applied to the value of the undivided share to reflect co-ownership, subject to the related property rules.
The whole property is included in the deceased's estate regardless of the co-ownership.
The deceased's share is always valued at exactly half the vacant possession value of the whole on these facts as a general rule.
The share is valued at double its proportionate value because of the co-ownership.
The share has no value for inheritance tax because it cannot be sold alone.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: An undivided share in co-owned land is generally valued at less than a simple proportion of the whole, so a discount (commonly around 10-15%) may be applied to reflect the difficulty of selling a part share. However, the related property rules can restrict the discount where the other share is held by a spouse or civil partner.

n.1: Only the deceased's share, not the whole property, is included in the estate.
n.2: A part share is not automatically valued at an exact proportion; a discount may apply.
n.3: The share is discounted, not increased, to reflect co-ownership.
n.4: The share does have value; it is not disregarded merely because it is a part share.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A surviving spouse makes a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, arguing that the will (or intestacy) did not make reasonable provision for them. The estate argues that a spouse should only receive what they need for their maintenance. The court must apply the correct standard of provision for a surviving spouse. The court considers the standard of reasonable financial provision under the 1975 Act. The surviving spouse argued the will had left them far less than was fair after a long marriage. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A surviving spouse can never make a claim under the Act if there was a valid will.
A surviving spouse is automatically entitled to the whole of the estate under the Act.
For a surviving spouse the standard is such provision as is reasonable in all the circumstances, not limited to maintenance.
The standard for a surviving spouse is the same as for a distant dependant.
A surviving spouse is limited to provision reasonably required for their maintenance only on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: The 1975 Act applies a higher 'surviving spouse standard' to a spouse or civil partner: reasonable financial provision means such provision as it would be reasonable in all the circumstances for them to receive, whether or not required for maintenance. Other applicants are generally limited to the 'maintenance standard'.

n.0: A spouse can claim under the Act despite a valid will.
n.1: The spouse is not automatically entitled to the whole estate; the court exercises discretion.
n.3: The spouse standard is more generous than that for other dependants.
n.4: A spouse is not limited to the maintenance standard.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator dies leaving a will that makes no provision, or inadequate provision, for a person who was financially dependent on them or closely connected to them, such as a surviving spouse, a child, or a cohabitee of the last two years. That person wishes to challenge the distribution and claim provision from the estate. The court considers who may apply for reasonable financial provision under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975. The person left out had depended on the deceased for support and felt badly let down by the will. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No one can challenge a will that has been validly executed by the testator.
Certain categories, including spouses, children, cohabitees of two years and dependants, may apply for reasonable financial provision.
Only a surviving spouse may ever apply for provision from a deceased's estate.
Only creditors of the estate may make a claim against the deceased's assets.
Anyone at all may apply for provision from the estate, whatever their connection to the deceased on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, defined categories of applicant — including the deceased's spouse or civil partner, former spouse (not remarried), a cohabitee for the two years before death, a child, a person treated as a child of the family, and a person maintained by the deceased — may apply for reasonable financial provision from the estate.

n.0: A validly executed will can still be challenged under the 1975 Act.
n.2: Applicants are not limited to the surviving spouse.
n.3: The 1975 Act concerns family and dependants, not creditors' claims.
n.4: Only defined categories may apply, not anyone at all.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate. They leave no surviving spouse or civil partner and no children or other issue. They are survived by both of their parents. A question arises as to who is entitled to the estate under the intestacy rules. There is no spouse or civil partner and no issue. The deceased's parents survive. The deceased died without leaving a will, was neither married nor in a civil partnership, and had no children or remoter descendants, but both of their parents are still living, so the estate has to be distributed under the statutory rules that apply when there is neither spouse nor issue. Which of the following best describes who takes the estate?
o: The estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia.
The estate is divided among the deceased's more remote relatives, bypassing the parents.
The estate passes automatically to the deceased's closest friend.
The deceased's parents take the estate in equal shares.
The estate passes to the deceased's siblings in priority to the parents.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the intestacy rules, where there is no surviving spouse or civil partner and no issue, the estate passes to the deceased's parents (in equal shares if both survive). Only if there are no parents does the estate pass to siblings of the whole blood, and so on down the statutory order.

n.0: The estate passes to the Crown only if there are no qualifying relatives at all.
n.1: Parents take before more remote relatives, not the other way round.
n.2: An intestate estate does not pass to a friend; the statutory order governs.
n.4: Parents take in priority to siblings under the statutory order.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A deceased owned shares in an unquoted trading company and business assets used in a trading business they carried on. The executors are considering whether relief may reduce the value of these business assets for inheritance tax purposes. The assets are relevant business property held for the requisite period. The executors are computing the inheritance tax on the estate. Among the deceased's assets are shares in an unquoted trading company and equipment used in a business the deceased ran, all held for long enough to qualify, and the executors want to know whether a relief exists that could strip out much or all of the value of those business assets before tax is charged. Which of the following best describes the relief that may apply to the business assets?
o: Business property relief may reduce the value transferred, potentially by up to 100% for qualifying business property.
No relief is available for business assets under any circumstances.
Business assets are always charged to inheritance tax at double the normal rate on these facts as a general rule.
The business assets are entirely exempt from inheritance tax in every case.
Relief applies only if the business assets are sold before death.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Business property relief can reduce the value transferred of qualifying relevant business property (such as an interest in an unincorporated business or unquoted trading company shares) held for the requisite period, at rates of up to 100% (or 50% for some assets), subject to conditions and exclusions (for example, businesses that are wholly or mainly investment).

n.1: Relief is available for qualifying business property, so 'no relief' is wrong.
n.2: Business assets are not charged at double the normal rate.
n.3: Business property is not automatically wholly exempt; relief depends on conditions and rates.
n.4: Relief applies to qualifying property held at death, not only to assets sold beforehand.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: During the administration of an estate, the personal representatives wish to transfer the deceased's freehold house to a beneficiary who is entitled to it under the will. The PRs need to vest the legal estate in the beneficiary. The property to be transferred is land. The PRs are giving effect to the beneficiary's entitlement. Administration has reached the point of handing the deceased's freehold house to the beneficiary entitled to it under the will, and the personal representatives want to be sure they use the correct formality to pass the legal estate rather than relying on some informal handover. Which of the following best describes the requirement for vesting the land in the beneficiary?
o: The PRs may vest the land by simply handing over the keys to the beneficiary on these facts.
The PRs must use a written assent to vest the legal estate in the land in the beneficiary.
The PRs must obtain a court order to transfer the land to the beneficiary.
The land vests automatically in the beneficiary on the testator's death.
The land can be vested only by the beneficiary purchasing it from the estate.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Personal representatives vest a beneficiary's entitlement in estate assets by an assent. For land, the assent must be in writing, signed by the PRs, and name the person in whose favour it is given. An oral or informal transfer is not effective to vest the legal estate in land.

n.0: Handing over keys does not vest the legal estate in land; a written assent is required.
n.2: A court order is not generally required for the PRs to assent land to a beneficiary.
n.3: Legal title to the deceased's land does not vest automatically in the beneficiary; it passes via the PRs and an assent.
n.4: The beneficiary is entitled under the will; they need not purchase the land from the estate.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies leaving the whole of their estate to their surviving spouse (who is UK domiciled). The personal representatives are considering the inheritance tax position of the gift to the spouse. They understand that transfers between spouses attract a particular exemption. The court considers the spouse (inter-spouse) exemption from inheritance tax. The couple had been married for decades and everything was left to the survivor outright. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is no exemption for transfers between spouses under the inheritance tax rules.
Transfers between spouses are exempt only up to the amount of the nil rate band.
Transfers between spouses are exempt only where the couple have children together.
Transfers between UK-domiciled spouses are generally exempt from inheritance tax without limit.
Transfers between spouses are taxed at the full 40% rate like any other gift.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: The spouse (or civil partner) exemption means that transfers of value between spouses or civil partners are generally exempt from inheritance tax, without limit, where the recipient spouse is UK domiciled (a capped exemption applies where the recipient is non-domiciled).

n.0: There is a spouse exemption from IHT.
n.1: The exemption is not capped at the nil rate band for a UK-domiciled spouse.
n.2: The exemption does not depend on the couple having children.
n.4: Spouse transfers are exempt, not taxed at 40%.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A member of the armed forces, while in actual military service on operations, expresses their testamentary wishes informally, without the usual formalities of writing, signature and two witnesses. They later die. A question arises whether these informal wishes can take effect as a will. The person was in actual military service when the wishes were expressed. The usual Wills Act formalities were not observed. The service member spoke their wishes plainly to comrades while deployed on active operations, with no opportunity to sit down and prepare a formal signed and witnessed document, and after their death the family want to know whether those informally expressed wishes can govern the estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The wishes take effect only as a lifetime gift, not as a will.
The wishes are effective only if later reduced to a signed and witnessed document.
The wishes are wholly ineffective, because no will can ever dispense with the statutory formalities on these facts.
The wishes are valid only if a commanding officer countersigned them.
A privileged will may be valid despite the lack of formalities, because the testator was in actual military service.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A privileged will may be made by a soldier in actual military service (and by certain seamen), without the usual formalities: it may be informal, even oral, and can dispose of the testator's estate. This is an exception to the Wills Act formalities, reflecting the position of those on active service.

n.0: A privileged will operates as a will, not merely as a lifetime gift.
n.1: A privileged will need not later be reduced to signed, witnessed writing.
n.2: The formalities can be dispensed with for a privileged will, so the wishes are not automatically ineffective.
n.3: No countersignature by a commanding officer is required for a privileged will.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator prepares a document intended to be their will. A dispute later arises about whether it was validly executed as a will. The document is in writing and was signed by the testator, but there is a question about the involvement of witnesses at the time of signing. The executor needs to know the formal requirements for a valid will. The court considers the formalities for a valid will under the Wills Act 1837. The document had been prepared at home and the family disagreed about who had actually been present. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The will must be registered at a government registry before it can take effect as valid.
The will is valid provided it is typed and signed, whether or not anyone witnessed the signature.
