The will must be signed by the testator before a single independent witness, such as a solicitor.
The will need only be in the testator's own handwriting, with no requirement for any witnesses at all on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The will must be in writing, signed by the testator, whose signature is made or acknowledged before two witnesses present at the same time, who then sign.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.9 Wills Act 1837, a valid will must be in writing and signed by the testator (or by someone in their presence and at their direction), the testator must intend by the signature to give effect to the will, and the signature must be made or acknowledged in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time, who each then sign (or acknowledge) in the testator's presence.

n.0: There is no requirement to register a will for it to be valid.
n.1: Witnessing is required; a typed and signed document alone is not enough.
n.2: A single witness is not sufficient; two witnesses are required.
n.3: Two witnesses are generally required; a handwritten will is not exempt from that.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator makes a will shortly before marrying their partner, and the will is expressly stated to be made in expectation of that forthcoming marriage to that named person, with the intention that it should not be revoked when the marriage takes place. The marriage then goes ahead. After the testator's death, a relative argues the will was automatically revoked by the marriage. The court considers the exception to revocation by marriage under the Wills Act 1837. The will named the future spouse and said in terms that it was made in view of the coming marriage. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The will is revoked because a will can never anticipate a future marriage.
The will is revoked by the marriage regardless of any contemplation of it.
The exception applies only where the will leaves everything to the new spouse.
The will is not revoked by the marriage, because it was made in contemplation of that marriage.
The will is revoked unless it was made on the actual day of the wedding itself on these facts.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.18 Wills Act 1837, where it appears from the will that at the time it was made the testator was expecting to marry a particular person and intended that the will should not be revoked by that marriage, the will is not revoked when the marriage takes place.

n.0: A will can be made in contemplation of a future marriage.
n.1: The contemplation-of-marriage exception prevents revocation here.
n.2: The exception is not limited to wills leaving everything to the spouse.
n.4: The will need not be made on the wedding day itself.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person has died leaving a valid will which appoints a named executor who is willing and able to act. The executor needs formal authority to deal with the deceased's assets, such as to sell property and collect in bank accounts. The executor asks what document confers that authority where there is a valid will and a willing executor. The court considers the appropriate grant of representation in these circumstances. The executor was ready and willing to act and needed authority to sell the deceased's house. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The executor obtains a grant of probate, which confirms their authority to administer the estate under the will.
The executor needs no grant at all and may deal with every asset without any authority on these facts.
The executor obtains letters of administration with the will annexed.
The executor must apply to the Court of Protection for authority to act.
The executor obtains letters of administration, as used where there is no valid will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where the deceased left a valid will appointing an executor who is willing and able to act, the appropriate grant is a grant of probate, which confirms the executor's authority (deriving from the will) to administer the estate.

n.1: A grant is generally needed to deal with many assets; the executor cannot ignore it.
n.2: Letters of administration with the will annexed are used where there is a will but no proving executor.
n.3: The Court of Protection deals with living persons lacking capacity, not deceased estates.
n.4: Letters of administration are for cases without a proving executor, e.g. intestacy.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person owned a house as a beneficial joint tenant with another person. The deceased's will purports to leave 'my share of the house' to a third party. On the death, a question arises as to whether the deceased's interest in the jointly owned house passes under the will, or in some other way. The court considers the effect of a beneficial joint tenancy on death. The couple had bought the house together years earlier as joint owners of the whole. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The deceased's share passes under the will to the third party named to receive it.
The deceased's share passes on intestacy because the will cannot deal with jointly owned property.
The deceased's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant by survivorship, outside the will.
The whole house passes to the third party named in the deceased's will.
The deceased's share is held by the personal representatives for the estate's creditors first.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Property held as beneficial joint tenants passes on death to the surviving joint tenant(s) by the right of survivorship, outside the will and the intestacy rules. A gift in the will of the deceased's 'share' is ineffective unless the joint tenancy had been severed before death.

n.0: An unsevered joint tenant's interest does not pass under the will.
n.1: It does not pass on intestacy either; survivorship takes it.
n.3: The survivor takes the deceased's interest by survivorship; the third party takes nothing of it.
n.4: It passes to the surviving joint tenant, not to the estate for creditors, subject to any claims.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: After a testator's death, it becomes clear that the will, owing to a clerical error or a failure to understand the testator's instructions, does not carry out the testator's actual intentions — for example a figure or name was mistyped. A beneficiary wishes to have the will corrected to reflect what the testator truly intended. The court considers the power to rectify a will under the Administration of Justice Act 1982. A legacy figure had plainly been mistyped, giving a result the testator could never have intended. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court may rewrite the will freely to achieve whatever result seems fairest to the family on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may rectify a will only if every beneficiary consents to the change.
A will can never be corrected once the testator has died, whatever the error.
Rectification is available only where the whole will was forged or fraudulently made.
The court may rectify the will where it fails to carry out the testator's intentions due to a clerical error or a failure to understand instructions.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.20 Administration of Justice Act 1982, the court may order rectification of a will if satisfied that it fails to carry out the testator's intentions in consequence of a clerical error, or a failure to understand the testator's instructions. Applications are generally subject to a time limit from the grant.

n.0: Rectification corrects specific errors; it does not permit free rewriting for fairness.
n.1: Rectification does not require every beneficiary's consent.
n.2: A will can be rectified in the defined circumstances after death.
n.3: Rectification is not confined to forgery or fraud.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Having obtained a grant, personal representatives are administering the estate. They need to carry out various tasks, such as selling estate property to raise money, appropriating assets to satisfy legacies, and running the deceased's business briefly. The PRs ask about the scope of their powers to deal with the estate assets. The court considers the powers of personal representatives under the Administration of Estates Act 1925 and the Trustee Act 2000. The estate held a mix of property, investments and a small business the deceased had run. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: PRs have no powers to deal with the estate and must obtain a court order for every step.
PRs have wide statutory powers, including to sell, mortgage, appropriate and invest estate assets in the course of administration.
PRs may only distribute the estate exactly as directed and may never sell any asset.
PRs may deal with the estate only with the written consent of every beneficiary for each act on these facts as a general rule.
PRs may exercise powers only over land, and never over any other kind of estate asset.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Personal representatives have extensive statutory powers to administer the estate — including powers to sell, mortgage or lease assets, to appropriate assets towards a beneficiary's entitlement, to invest, and to postpone distribution — under the Administration of Estates Act 1925, the Trustee Act 2000 and related legislation (supplemented by the will).

n.0: PRs have wide powers and need not obtain a court order for every step.
n.2: PRs can sell assets; they are not confined to distributing them in specie.
n.3: PRs do not need every beneficiary's written consent for each act.
n.4: PRs' powers extend to all estate assets, not only land.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator made a valid will some years ago. They have now executed a new, later will which is validly made and which deals with the whole of their estate, and which contains a clause expressly revoking all former wills. A relative argues that the earlier will still has some effect. The court considers the revocation of an earlier will by a later will under the Wills Act 1837. The later will had been drawn up carefully by a solicitor and dealt with the entire estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The earlier will remains fully effective, because a will can never revoke an earlier one.
The earlier will prevails, because it was made first in time.
The later valid will, containing an express revocation clause, revokes the earlier will.
The later will is invalid, because a person may only ever make one will in their lifetime.
Both wills take effect together in full, whatever the later will says.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.20 Wills Act 1837, a will may be revoked by a later will or codicil. A later validly executed will containing an express revocation clause revokes the earlier will; even without an express clause, a later will revokes an earlier one to the extent it is inconsistent with, or effectively disposes of the whole estate dealt with by, the earlier one.

n.0: A later will can and here does revoke the earlier will.
n.1: The later will, not the earlier, prevails once the earlier is revoked.
n.3: A person may make successive wills; the later valid will governs.
n.4: The wills do not both take effect where the later revokes the earlier.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A sole executor named in a will proves the will and obtains probate, then dies before completing the administration of the estate. That executor had themselves appointed an executor of their own will who has proved it. A question arises about who is now entitled to complete the administration of the first estate. The court considers the chain of representation. The first executor had died only part-way through winding up the original estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executor of the last surviving executor becomes executor of the original estate by the chain of representation.
The original estate is left with no personal representative and simply cannot be administered.
The beneficiaries of the original estate automatically become its executors.
The chain of representation applies equally to administrators as it does to executors.
A fresh grant of probate to the original estate is always required, and the chain never applies on these facts.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the chain of representation, where a sole or last surviving executor who has proved the will dies having appointed an executor who proves their will, that executor automatically becomes executor of the original testator's estate too, and so on down the chain. The chain is broken by an intestacy or failure to appoint/prove an executor.

n.1: The original estate is not left without a PR where the chain operates.
n.2: Beneficiaries do not automatically become executors.
n.3: The chain of representation applies to executors, not administrators.
n.4: A fresh grant is not always required; the chain can continue the representation.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will makes a gift 'to my grandchildren', a class of beneficiaries which could in principle continue to grow as more grandchildren are born. The executors need to know at what point the class of beneficiaries is fixed, so that the estate can be distributed without waiting indefinitely for further grandchildren to be born. The court considers the class-closing rules for a class gift. Further grandchildren might still be born, and the executors could not wait forever to distribute. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only grandchildren alive at the date the will was made can ever take under the gift.
The class closes at the testator's death and excludes any grandchildren born afterwards in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Under the class-closing rules, the class generally closes when the first member becomes entitled to their share, including those alive at that point.
The class closes only on the death of the last surviving member of the class.
The class never closes, and distribution must wait until it is impossible for more members to be born.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the class-closing rules (the rule in Andrews v Partington), a class gift generally closes when the first member becomes entitled to call for their share (for example on the testator's death for an immediate vested gift, or when the first member satisfies a contingency), including all members alive at that point but excluding those born later, so the estate can be distributed.

n.0: Grandchildren born after the will but before the class closes can take.
n.1: The closing point is the class-closing rule, not invariably the testator's death excluding all later-born members.
n.3: The class does not close only on the death of the last member.
n.4: The class does close under the class-closing rules; distribution need not wait indefinitely.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A will refers to a separate document, already in existence at the date the will is executed and clearly identified in the will, which the testator wishes to be treated as part of the will (for example a list of specific gifts). The separate document is not itself executed as a will. The document existed and was identified at the time the will was made. The testator intends it to form part of the will. The will points to a separate list of specific gifts, a document that was already in existence and clearly identified when the will was signed but which was never itself executed with will formalities, and the question is whether that list can nevertheless be treated as forming part of the will. Which of the following best describes when such a document may be incorporated into the will?
o: It may be incorporated only if it is deposited with the court before death.
It may be incorporated even if created after the will, provided the testator later approves it on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It can never be incorporated unless it is itself signed and witnessed as a will.
It may be incorporated by reference if it existed at the date of the will and is clearly identified in and referred to as existing by the will.
It is incorporated automatically whenever a will mentions any other document.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A document may be incorporated by reference into a will if it already exists at the date the will is executed, the will refers to it as an existing document, and it is clearly identified. If so, it is treated as part of the will even though not itself executed with will formalities. A document created after the will cannot be incorporated.

n.0: Deposit with the court is not a requirement for incorporation by reference.
n.1: A document created after the will cannot be incorporated, even with later approval.
n.2: Incorporation is precisely a way of giving effect to an unexecuted document, so it need not itself be signed and witnessed.
n.4: Mere mention is not enough; the existence, identification and reference conditions must be met.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator signs their will in the presence of one friend, who signs as a witness. Later the same day, a second friend, who was not present when the testator signed, adds their signature as a second witness without the testator signing again in their presence. A question arises whether the will has been validly executed. The two witnesses were not both present together when the testator signed or acknowledged the signature. The formalities of the Wills Act 1837 are in issue. The testator signed while only the first friend looked on, and it was not until later that day that the second friend, who had been elsewhere at the moment of signing, added a signature, with the testator neither signing afresh nor acknowledging the earlier signature in front of both together. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The will is valid only if the second witness was a qualified solicitor.
The will is validly executed, because the witnesses signed on the same day as the testator.
The will is validly executed, because only one witness need ever be present with the testator on these facts as a general rule.
The will is validly executed, because two witnesses signed it in total.
The will is not validly executed, as both witnesses must be present together when the testator signs or acknowledges the signature.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.9 of the Wills Act 1837, the testator's signature must be made or acknowledged in the presence of two witnesses present at the same time, each of whom then signs (or acknowledges) in the testator's presence. Because the two witnesses were not present together when the testator signed or acknowledged, the will is not validly executed.

n.0: There is no requirement that a witness be a solicitor.
n.1: Signing on the same day does not cure the failure to have both witnesses present together.
n.2: The two witnesses must be present at the same time; one is not sufficient.
n.3: It is not enough that two witnesses signed in total; they must be present together at the key moment.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator executed a will which, on its face, was properly signed and witnessed. After the testator's death a beneficiary under an earlier will alleges that the testator did not actually know and approve the contents of the later will — for example because it was prepared by someone who benefited and there are suspicious circumstances. The court must decide whether the testator knew and approved the will's contents. The court considers the requirement of knowledge and approval. The later will had been drawn up by a relative who took the largest share under it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Knowledge and approval are irrelevant once a will has been signed and witnessed.
The testator is always presumed to know and approve the contents, and this can never be challenged on these facts as a general rule.
The testator must have known and approved the contents of the will, and suspicious circumstances may require the propounder to prove this.
The will fails automatically wherever the person who drafted it takes any benefit under it.
Knowledge and approval need only be shown where the testator could not read the will themselves.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A valid will requires that the testator knew and approved its contents. Normally this is presumed where the will was duly executed by a capable testator, but where there are circumstances exciting suspicion (such as the preparation of the will by a substantial beneficiary), the burden is on the person propounding the will to prove positive knowledge and approval.

n.0: Knowledge and approval remain a requirement even where the will is signed and witnessed.
n.1: The presumption can be displaced where suspicious circumstances arise.
n.3: A benefit to the drafter raises suspicion but does not automatically invalidate the will.
n.4: Knowledge and approval must be shown generally, not only where the testator cannot read.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: After executing their will, a testator makes handwritten alterations to it — crossing out one legacy and writing in a different amount — but these alterations are not signed or witnessed in any way. After the testator's death, a beneficiary relies on the altered figures. The court considers the effect of unattested alterations to a will under the Wills Act 1837. The changes were scrawled in ink in the margin at some point after the will was first signed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Unattested alterations are always fully effective as written by the testator.
Any alteration, however made, automatically revokes the whole will.
Unattested alterations are generally invalid, and the will takes effect in its original form if the original wording is apparent.
The altered figures always prevail over the original wording of the will.
Alterations are valid provided the testator initials them, without any need for witnesses on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.21 Wills Act 1837, an alteration made after execution is generally invalid unless it is executed like a will (signed by the testator and witnessed, often by initials in the margin). If the original wording remains apparent, the will takes effect as originally written; if the original is obliterated so it cannot be read, that gift may fail.

n.0: Unattested alterations are not generally effective as written.
n.1: An alteration does not automatically revoke the whole will.
n.3: The altered figures do not prevail where the alteration is unattested.
n.4: Alterations require attestation (execution) to be valid, not merely initials without witnesses.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A solicitor is instructed to prepare a will for an elderly client whose age and medical condition give rise to a real risk that their testamentary capacity could later be challenged. The solicitor wishes to take a sensible precaution to guard against a future dispute about capacity. The solicitor considers the recognised good practice for such cases. The court considers the 'golden rule' in will drafting for testators whose capacity may be in doubt. The client was frail and there was a real chance a relative would later dispute the will. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The solicitor should simply refuse to act for any client who is elderly or unwell.
The will should be witnessed or approved by a medical practitioner who has assessed and recorded the testator's capacity.
The solicitor should ask the beneficiaries to confirm in writing that the testator had capacity.
The solicitor should delay preparing the will until the testator has fully recovered their health on these facts.
The solicitor should have the will signed without witnesses to speed matters up.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: The 'golden rule' of good practice is that, where a testator is aged or seriously ill so that capacity may later be doubted, the will should be witnessed or approved by a medical practitioner who satisfies themselves of, and records, the testator's capacity, to provide contemporaneous evidence should the will be challenged.

n.0: The golden rule does not require refusing to act for the elderly or unwell.
n.2: Beneficiaries confirming capacity is not the recognised safeguard.
n.3: Delaying indefinitely is not the answer; a medical assessment is the recognised step.
n.4: A will still requires proper witnessing; omitting witnesses is wrong.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will leaves a gift to their own child. That child dies before the testator, but the child leaves children of their own (the testator's grandchildren) who survive the testator. The will contains no express substitution provision. The executors must decide who takes the gift. The court considers the statutory exception to lapse for gifts to the testator's issue under the Wills Act 1837. The child had died in an accident a year before the testator, leaving young children behind. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift passes to the deceased child's own issue who survive the testator, under s.33 Wills Act 1837.
The gift fails entirely and passes to the Crown as ownerless property.
The gift passes to the deceased child's estate to be distributed under their own will on these facts.
The gift lapses and falls into residue, because the child predeceased the testator.
The gift is shared equally among all the other beneficiaries named in the will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.33 Wills Act 1837, where a will leaves a gift to the testator's child or remoter issue who predeceases the testator leaving issue of their own who survive the testator, those issue take the gift in place of the deceased beneficiary (unless a contrary intention appears in the will).

n.1: The gift does not pass to the Crown; the statutory substitution applies.
n.2: The gift passes to the deceased child's issue, not into the child's estate.
n.3: Section 33 prevents lapse where the beneficiary is the testator's issue leaving issue.
n.4: The gift is not shared among the other beneficiaries; s.33 substitutes the issue.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will makes a specific gift of 'my shares in ABC Ltd' to a named beneficiary. Before the testator dies, however, the testator sold all of those shares and no longer owns any shares in ABC Ltd at the date of death, and the will was not updated. The beneficiary claims the value of the shares, or other assets in substitution. The court considers the doctrine of ademption. The testator had sold the shareholding to fund their retirement and never replaced it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executors must buy equivalent shares so that the beneficiary receives the gift in specie.
The gift takes effect over whatever the testator bought with the proceeds of sale.
The gift is unaffected, because a specific gift can never fail once it is written in the will.
The specific gift adeems and fails, because the subject matter no longer forms part of the estate at death.
The beneficiary is entitled to the cash value of the shares out of the general estate instead on these facts.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A specific gift adeems (fails) if the specific asset given no longer forms part of the testator's estate at the date of death — for example because it has been sold or otherwise disposed of. The beneficiary receives nothing in its place, absent a contrary provision.

n.0: The executors are not required to buy replacement shares.
n.1: The gift does not automatically attach to substituted assets.
n.2: A specific gift can fail by ademption despite being written in the will.
n.4: The beneficiary is not entitled to the cash value out of the general estate.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's estate turns out to be insufficient to pay all the debts and give effect to all the gifts in the will in full. Some gifts will have to be reduced or will fail. The executors must decide the order in which the different kinds of gift (specific, general/pecuniary, and residuary) are reduced to meet the shortfall. The court considers the doctrine of abatement of gifts. The debts were heavy and there was plainly not enough to satisfy every gift in full. Which of the following best describes the general order?
o: Specific gifts abate first, before any general or residuary gifts are touched.
Gifts abate in the order in which they happen to appear in the wording of the will.
General legacies abate last, after both specific and residuary gifts have been exhausted.
Residuary gifts abate first, then general (pecuniary) legacies, and specific gifts abate last.
All gifts abate equally and proportionately at the same time, whatever their type.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where an estate is insufficient, gifts abate to meet liabilities in a set order: the residuary gift is used first, then general (pecuniary) legacies abate rateably, and specific gifts abate last (with the subject matter of specific gifts being the most protected), subject to any contrary provision in the will.

n.0: Specific gifts abate last, not first.
n.1: Abatement follows the type of gift, not the order of appearance in the will.
n.2: General legacies abate before specific gifts, not last.
n.4: Gifts do not all abate equally at once; the order depends on their type.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person named as executor in a will does not wish to take on the role of administering the estate, and wants to step back so that someone else can obtain the grant, without ever intermeddling in the estate. The executor asks how they can formally decline the appointment. The court considers renunciation of the office of executor. The named executor had a demanding job and simply did not want the burden of the estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An executor who has not intermeddled may renounce probate, giving up the right to act, by a formal renunciation.
An executor may simply ignore the estate, with no formal step required to decline the role on these facts.
An executor named in a will can never decline the appointment and must always act.
An executor may renounce only after they have already obtained the grant of probate.
An executor who renounces automatically forfeits any gift left to them in the will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: An executor who has not intermeddled in the estate may renounce their right to probate by signing a formal renunciation, which is filed at the Probate Registry. Once they have intermeddled, however, they may lose the right to renounce.

n.1: A formal renunciation is required; simply ignoring the estate is not the proper step and risks intermeddling.
n.2: An executor is not forced to act; they may renounce if they have not intermeddled.
n.3: Renunciation occurs before taking the grant, not after obtaining probate.
n.4: Renouncing the office does not automatically forfeit a gift under the will.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate and is survived by their spouse, but they had no children or other issue, and no other closer relatives who take priority. The estate is substantial. The spouse and more distant relatives dispute how the estate is distributed. The court considers the entitlement of a surviving spouse on intestacy where the intestate leaves no issue. The intestate had never had children and had outlived most of their wider family. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate is shared equally between the spouse and the intestate's parents and siblings.
The surviving spouse takes the whole of the estate absolutely where the intestate leaves no issue.
The spouse takes only a statutory legacy, with the rest passing to more distant relatives.
The whole estate passes to the intestate's parents, and the spouse receives nothing.
The estate passes to the Crown because the intestate left no children.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the current intestacy rules, where an intestate is survived by a spouse or civil partner but leaves no issue, the spouse takes the whole of the estate absolutely (the previous entitlement of parents and siblings in that situation having been removed).

n.0: The estate is not shared with parents and siblings where there is a spouse and no issue.
n.2: The spouse takes the whole estate, not just a statutory legacy.
n.3: The estate does not pass to the parents ahead of the spouse.
n.4: The estate does not pass to the Crown where there is a surviving spouse.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate, leaving no will and therefore no appointed executor. A close relative wishes to take on the administration of the estate and obtain formal authority to deal with the assets and distribute them under the intestacy rules. The relative asks what grant of representation is appropriate where the deceased left no valid will. The court considers the appropriate grant on intestacy. The deceased had left no will at all, and a son wished to sort out the estate for the family. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The estate passes automatically to the Crown because there is no will.
No grant is required on intestacy, and any relative may distribute the estate freely.
The relative must be appointed as an executor by the court before administering the estate.
A grant of probate is obtained, as for a person who left a valid will and executor.
A grant of letters of administration is obtained by an entitled applicant under the intestacy rules.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where there is no valid will (or no proving executor), the appropriate grant is a grant of letters of administration, obtained by a person entitled to apply under the rules of priority (broadly following the order of those entitled to the estate on intestacy).

n.0: The estate does not pass to the Crown merely because there is no will, if there are relatives.
n.1: A grant is generally required; relatives cannot simply distribute freely.
n.2: On intestacy an administrator is appointed via letters of administration, not an executor.
n.3: A grant of probate applies where there is a will and a proving executor, not on intestacy.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Personal representatives have finished paying the debts and are ready to transfer estate property to the beneficiaries entitled under the will, including transferring the deceased's house to a beneficiary. They need to know the mechanism by which estate property is vested in a beneficiary. The court considers the use of an assent in the administration of an estate. The debts had all been paid and the beneficiary was waiting to have the house put in their name. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An assent is required only for personal chattels and never for land.
Property automatically vests in beneficiaries the moment the testator dies, with no further step.
The PRs must sell all estate property and can only ever distribute cash to beneficiaries.
The PRs vest property in a beneficiary by an assent, which for land must be in writing.
Property can be transferred to a beneficiary only by a court order in every case.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: When ready to distribute, personal representatives transfer estate property to the entitled beneficiary by an assent. An assent of a legal estate in land must be in writing, signed by the PRs and naming the person in whose favour it is given, in order to pass the legal estate.

n.0: An assent of land must be in writing; the requirement is not confined to chattels.
n.1: Property does not vest in beneficiaries automatically at death; the PRs must assent or transfer it.
n.2: PRs are not obliged to sell everything and distribute only cash; they may assent assets in specie.
n.4: A court order is not required for an ordinary assent.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate leaving no spouse or civil partner. They are survived by various relatives, including children, parents, and siblings, and the family needs to know the order in which relatives inherit on intestacy where there is no surviving spouse. The court considers the statutory order of entitlement on intestacy in the absence of a spouse. The intestate had died suddenly with no will and a scattering of relatives of varying closeness. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate passes immediately to the Crown whenever there is no surviving spouse.
The estate passes to the intestate's parents first, ahead of any children of the intestate.
The estate is always shared equally among all surviving relatives regardless of their relationship on these facts as a general rule.
The estate passes to the issue first; only if there are none does it pass to parents, then siblings, and so on down the statutory order.
The estate passes to the most distant surviving relative, in reverse order of closeness.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where there is no surviving spouse or civil partner, the estate passes under the statutory order to the issue on the statutory trusts; if there are no issue, then to parents; then to brothers and sisters of the whole blood (on statutory trusts); and so on down the prescribed order, with the Crown taking only as a last resort (bona vacantia).

n.0: The estate passes to the Crown only if no qualifying relatives exist.
n.1: Issue take before parents, not the other way round.
n.2: The estate is not shared equally among all relatives; a strict order applies.
n.4: Closer relatives take before more distant ones, not in reverse.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: During their lifetime, a person transfers a substantial sum into a discretionary trust for the benefit of their family. This is not an outright gift to an individual. The personal representatives, and the settlor's advisers, consider the immediate inheritance tax treatment of a lifetime transfer into such a trust. The court considers lifetime chargeable transfers into trust for inheritance tax. The sum settled was well above the available tax-free threshold at the time it was made. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A transfer into a discretionary trust is a lifetime chargeable transfer, potentially attracting IHT at the lifetime rate when made.
A transfer into a discretionary trust is taxed only when the trust eventually ends.
A transfer into a discretionary trust is a potentially exempt transfer, exactly like a gift to an individual on these facts.
A transfer into a discretionary trust is always entirely free of inheritance tax.
A transfer into a discretionary trust is chargeable only if the settlor dies within seven years.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A lifetime transfer into a relevant property trust (such as most discretionary trusts) is a lifetime chargeable transfer (LCT), not a PET. To the extent it exceeds the available nil rate band, it may attract IHT at the lifetime rate (broadly 20%) when made, with a further charge if the settlor dies within seven years.

n.1: The immediate charge arises when made, not only when the trust ends.
n.2: A transfer into such a trust is an LCT, not a PET.
n.3: It is not always free of IHT; it can be immediately chargeable above the NRB.
n.4: It can be chargeable when made, not only on death within seven years.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies leaving a substantial legacy to a registered charity. The personal representatives are considering the inheritance tax treatment of the gift to the charity, and whether leaving a large proportion to charity affects the rate of tax on the rest of the estate. The court considers the charity exemption and the reduced rate of inheritance tax. A large slice of the estate had been left to a well-known national charity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Gifts to charity are exempt only up to the amount of the nil rate band.
Gifts to charity are exempt from inheritance tax, and leaving at least 10% of the net estate to charity can reduce the rate on the rest to 36%.
Gifts to charity are exempt only where the charity is based within the United Kingdom and nowhere else on these facts as a general rule.
There is no inheritance tax advantage of any kind in leaving money to charity.
Gifts to charity are taxed at the full 40% rate like any other legacy.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Gifts to qualifying charities are exempt from inheritance tax. In addition, where at least 10% of the net estate is left to charity, the rate of IHT on the remainder of the chargeable estate is reduced from 40% to 36%.

n.0: The charity exemption is not capped at the nil rate band.
n.2: The exemption is not limited only to UK-only charities in the way stated.
n.3: There are clear IHT advantages to charitable giving.
n.4: Charitable gifts are exempt, not taxed at 40%.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Two testators, a couple, make wills in agreed, mirror terms, and expressly agree with each other that neither will alter their will after the first of them dies, intending the survivor to be bound. After the first dies leaving their estate accordingly, the survivor then makes a new will departing from the agreement. The disappointed beneficiaries under the original arrangement seek a remedy. The court considers the doctrine of mutual wills. They had promised each other faithfully that the survivor would leave everything as agreed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The agreement is enforceable only if it was made in a formal deed separate from the wills.
The survivor is completely free to change their will, and the agreement has no effect at all.
The survivor's later will is automatically void, because mirror wills can never be changed.
The doctrine applies only where the two wills were contained in a single document.
Equity may impose a constructive trust binding the survivor to the agreed terms, despite the later will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where two people make mutual wills on the basis of a binding agreement not to revoke them, and one dies having kept to the agreement, equity may impose a constructive trust on the survivor's estate to give effect to the agreed dispositions, notwithstanding that the survivor later makes a different will.

n.0: A separate formal deed is not required; the binding agreement is the key.
n.1: Mutual wills can bind the survivor; the agreement is not without effect.
n.2: The later will is not automatically void; equity imposes a constructive trust instead.
n.3: The doctrine does not require the wills to be in a single document.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person who believes they are dying makes a gift of an asset to another, in contemplation of their imminent death, and hands over the asset (or the means of control of it) on the condition that the gift is to take effect only if they die. They then die of the contemplated cause. The recipient claims the asset as a valid gift, although it was not left to them by will. The court considers the doctrine of donatio mortis causa (deathbed gift). The donor, gravely ill in hospital, handed over the keys and documents to the recipient. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A deathbed gift is valid only if the donor in fact recovers from their illness.
A deathbed gift takes effect immediately and unconditionally when the words are spoken on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A valid deathbed gift may take effect where it was made in contemplation of imminent death, conditional on death, with delivery of the subject matter.
A deathbed gift is valid only where it is witnessed by two independent witnesses.
A deathbed gift is never valid unless it is also set out in a properly executed will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A donatio mortis causa is a valid gift made in contemplation of the donor's impending death, conditional upon death (so it is revocable if the donor recovers), and completed by delivery of the subject matter or the means of controlling it, taking effect on death outside the will.

n.0: The gift takes effect on death; if the donor recovers, it is revoked.
n.1: The gift is conditional on death, not immediate and unconditional.
n.3: Two witnesses are not required for a donatio mortis causa.
n.4: A donatio mortis causa does not require a will; that is its point.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Personal representatives wish to distribute an estate but are concerned that there may be unknown creditors or beneficiaries who could later come forward and hold the PRs personally liable. They want to protect themselves before distributing. The PRs wish to guard against claims from persons of whom they are unaware. They intend to distribute after taking protective steps. The personal representatives are ready to wind up the estate but are worried that some creditor or beneficiary they know nothing about could surface later and hold them personally to account, so before paying everything out they want to take a recognised step that shields them from claims by people of whom they are unaware. Which of the following best describes a step that protects the PRs against unknown claimants?
o: Obtaining a Part 36 offer from the beneficiaries before distributing.
Paying the entire estate to the Crown as a precaution.
Retaining the whole estate indefinitely so that nothing is ever distributed.
Advertising for claimants under section 27 of the Trustee Act 1925 and distributing after the notice period expires.
Distributing immediately without any notice, as PRs are never personally liable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Personal representatives may protect themselves against claims by unknown creditors and beneficiaries by advertising for claimants under s.27 of the Trustee Act 1925 (in the Gazette and appropriate publications) and waiting the specified period (at least two months) before distributing. They are then not personally liable to claimants of whom they had no notice, though such claimants may pursue the assets in the beneficiaries' hands.

n.0: A Part 36 offer is a litigation settlement device, irrelevant to protecting against unknown claimants.
n.1: Paying the estate to the Crown is not a protective step and would be a breach of duty.
n.2: Retaining the estate indefinitely is not a proper discharge of the PRs' duties.
n.4: PRs can be personally liable, so distributing without notice is not safe.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: After a testator's death, a family member argues that the will should be set aside because the testator was pressured into making it by another relative who stood to benefit, amounting to undue influence. There is evidence of a close relationship of trust between the testator and that relative, but no direct evidence of coercion. The court considers the doctrine of undue influence as it applies to wills. The relative had grown very close to the testator and managed much of their day-to-day affairs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Undue influence applies to lifetime gifts but can never affect the validity of a will.
Undue influence is established simply by showing the testator was elderly and unwell.
Undue influence need not be proved at all; mere persuasion is always enough to set aside a will.
Undue influence is presumed wherever a will benefits a person in a relationship of trust with the testator on these facts as a general rule.
Undue influence in the case of a will must be positively proved, as coercion overpowering the testator's own volition; it is not presumed.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Unlike undue influence affecting lifetime transactions, there is no presumption of undue influence in relation to wills. It must be positively proved that the testator's own volition was overborne by coercion (not merely persuasion or influence), and the burden lies on the person alleging it.

n.0: Undue influence can affect the validity of a will, not only lifetime gifts.
n.1: Age and ill-health alone do not establish undue influence.
n.2: Mere persuasion is not enough; coercion overpowering the will is required.
n.3: There is no presumption of undue influence for wills; it must be proved.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: On an intestacy, part of the estate is to be held for the intestate's issue. One of the intestate's children has already died, leaving children of their own (the intestate's grandchildren). The estate must be divided among the issue. The family asks how the share for that branch of the family is dealt with, and whether minor beneficiaries take immediately. The court considers the statutory trusts for issue on intestacy. One of the intestate's children had died young, leaving two children of their own who survived. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate is divided equally per capita among all descendants of every generation at once.
The issue take per stirpes, with a deceased child's share passing to their own children, contingent on reaching 18 (or marrying earlier).
Minor grandchildren take their share outright and immediately, whatever their age.
Grandchildren can never take any share on intestacy while any child of the intestate survives.
A deceased child's share simply lapses, and the surviving children take everything between them on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: On the statutory trusts, the issue take per stirpes: the estate is divided between the branches, and the share of a child who has predeceased passes to that child's own issue equally. Interests of issue are contingent on attaining 18 (or marrying or forming a civil partnership earlier).

n.0: Division is per stirpes by branch, not per capita across all generations.
n.2: Minor beneficiaries' interests are contingent on reaching 18, not taken outright at any age.
n.3: Grandchildren take their deceased parent's share even while other children survive.
n.4: A deceased child's share does not simply lapse; it passes to their issue.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate leaving a spouse. The spouse survives the intestate, but by only a few days, dying shortly after the intestate. A question arises about whether the spouse must survive the intestate by a particular period in order to inherit on the intestacy, which affects whether the estate passes through the spouse's estate or to the intestate's other relatives. The court considers the survivorship requirement for a spouse on intestacy. The spouse had clung on for only a matter of days after the intestate's sudden death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The spouse must survive the intestate by a full calendar year to take on the intestacy.
The spouse must survive the intestate by 28 days to take on the intestacy; otherwise the estate is distributed as if the spouse had not survived.
The spouse must survive by six months to inherit any part of the estate.
There is no survivorship requirement of any kind for a spouse on an intestacy.
The spouse takes on the intestacy however briefly they survive the intestate, even by a moment on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the intestacy rules, a surviving spouse or civil partner must survive the intestate by 28 days in order to take their entitlement on the intestacy. If they do not, the estate is distributed as if the spouse had not survived the intestate.

n.0: The period is 28 days, not a full year.
n.2: The period is 28 days, not six months.
n.3: There is a 28-day survivorship requirement for a spouse on intestacy.
n.4: A brief survival is not enough; the 28-day rule applies.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A deceased person's estate is insolvent: the debts and liabilities exceed the assets available to meet them. The personal representative must pay the debts in the correct order and cannot simply pay favoured creditors first. The estate cannot pay all the deceased's debts in full. The PR must apply the statutory order for an insolvent estate. It has become clear that the deceased owed more than the estate is worth, so not every creditor can be paid in full, and the personal representative, pressed by various creditors each wanting to be paid, needs to know the order in which the limited funds must lawfully be applied. Which of the following best describes how the PR must deal with the debts?
o: The PR must pay the debts in the statutory order of priority for insolvent estates, secured creditors and expenses, then preferential, then unsecured debts.
The PR must pay the residuary beneficiaries before any creditors.
The PR may pay whichever creditors the PR chooses, in any order.
The PR must distribute the estate equally between beneficiaries and creditors alike on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances on these facts.
The PR must pay all creditors in full regardless of the shortfall.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where an estate is insolvent, the personal representative must administer it according to the statutory order of priority for insolvent estates: reasonable funeral, testamentary and administration expenses and secured creditors are dealt with, then preferential debts, then ordinary unsecured debts (which abate rateably if insufficient), and deferred debts last. The PR cannot simply prefer chosen creditors.

n.1: Beneficiaries take nothing until creditors are paid; they do not come before creditors.
n.2: The PR cannot pay creditors in any order of their choosing; the statutory order binds them.
n.3: Creditors are paid in priority to beneficiaries, not equally with them.
n.4: An insolvent estate cannot pay all creditors in full; the shortfall is shared by rateable abatement within a class.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator made a first will, then revoked it by making a second will, and later destroyed the second will intending to bring back the first. The testator believes the original first will is automatically restored. After death, a dispute arises about which will (if any) is effective. The court considers the revival of a revoked will under the Wills Act 1837. The testator had believed, wrongly, that tearing up the second will would bring the first back to life. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A revoked will can be revived only by re-execution or by a codicil showing an intention to revive it, not merely by destroying the later will.
Both the first and second wills take effect together once the second is destroyed.
Destroying the later will automatically revives the earlier will in every case.
The earlier will revives provided the testator tells someone they wish to revive it on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A revoked will can never be revived under any circumstances at all.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.22 Wills Act 1837, a will once revoked is not revived merely by revoking the instrument that revoked it. It can be revived only by re-executing it with will formalities, or by a duly executed codicil showing an intention to revive it.

n.1: The two wills do not both take effect; revival requires the proper steps.
n.2: Destroying the later will does not automatically revive the earlier one.
n.3: An oral statement of intention does not revive a revoked will.
n.4: A revoked will can be revived by re-execution or codicil, so 'never' is wrong.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A personal representative administers an estate carelessly and in breach of duty — for example paying legacies before settling debts, or misapplying estate assets — causing loss to the estate and the beneficiaries. The disappointed beneficiaries wish to make the PR personally responsible for the loss. The court considers the liability of a personal representative for maladministration (devastavit). The PR had paid out legacies to friends before settling what the estate owed its creditors. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A personal representative is liable only if they acted dishonestly rather than merely carelessly.
A personal representative is liable only up to the amount of any fee they received for acting.
A personal representative's only sanction is removal from office, never any personal liability.
A personal representative may be personally liable for a devastavit where loss is caused by their breach of duty in administering the estate.
A personal representative can never be personally liable for anything done in administering the estate on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A personal representative who causes loss to the estate through a breach of duty — a devastavit, such as maladministration, misapplication of assets, or paying beneficiaries before creditors — may be personally liable to make good the loss to the estate and beneficiaries.

n.0: Liability for devastavit does not require dishonesty; carelessness in breach of duty suffices.
n.1: Liability is measured by the loss caused, not capped at any fee.
n.2: Personal liability, not merely removal, can follow a devastavit.
n.4: PRs can be personally liable for maladministration.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A deceased's death estate exceeds the available nil rate band, and inheritance tax is payable on the excess. The executors are calculating the tax due on the chargeable estate passing on death (with no reduced-rate charity provision applying). No special reliefs or the reduced charity rate are in issue. The executors need the rate of inheritance tax on the taxable death estate. The value of the estate comfortably exceeds the nil rate band available to it, no gift to charity attracts the reduced rate and no special reliefs bite on the excess, so the executors simply need the ordinary percentage at which tax falls due on the part of the death estate that is chargeable. Which of the following best describes the rate of inheritance tax on the chargeable death estate above the nil rate band?
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Inheritance tax on the chargeable death estate above the available nil rate band is generally charged at 40%. (A reduced rate of 36% applies where at least 10% of the net estate is left to charity, and lifetime chargeable transfers into trust are taxed at 20% during life, but the standard death rate is 40%.)

n.0: 45% is not the inheritance tax death rate (it echoes an income tax additional rate).
n.1: 50% is not the inheritance tax death rate.
n.3: 20% is the lifetime rate for chargeable transfers into trust, not the death rate.
n.4: 10% is the proportion of the estate to charity needed for the reduced 36% rate, not the tax rate.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies without leaving a valid will, and is therefore intestate. They are survived by their spouse and by children (issue). The estate exceeds the statutory legacy figure. The family need to know how the estate is distributed between the surviving spouse and the children under the intestacy rules. The court considers the entitlement of a surviving spouse where the intestate leaves issue. The estate comfortably exceeded the fixed statutory legacy figure set for a surviving spouse. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The children take the entire estate, and the surviving spouse receives nothing at all.
The estate is divided equally between the spouse and each of the children in equal shares on these facts.
The spouse takes only the personal chattels, with everything else passing to the children.
The spouse takes the entire estate absolutely, and the children receive nothing at all.
The spouse takes the personal chattels, a statutory legacy, and half the residue, with the other half to the issue.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the intestacy rules, where the intestate leaves a spouse (or civil partner) and issue, the spouse takes the personal chattels, a fixed statutory legacy (with interest), and one half of the residuary estate absolutely; the other half of the residue is held on the statutory trusts for the issue.

n.0: The spouse does take a substantial entitlement; the children do not take everything.
n.1: The division is not simply equal shares among spouse and each child.
n.2: The spouse takes more than just the chattels where there is issue.
n.3: Where there is issue, the spouse does not take the whole estate.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A widow dies. Her late husband died some years earlier leaving his entire estate to her, so that none of his nil rate band was used on his death. The personal representatives of the widow's estate wish to know whether the husband's unused nil rate band can be used against the widow's estate. The court considers the transferable nil rate band between spouses. The husband's whole estate had passed to his wife, using none of his own allowance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transferable nil rate band is available only where the spouses had made mirror wills.
The survivor's estate can only ever use a single nil rate band, whatever happened on the first death on these facts.
The first spouse's unused nil rate band is simply lost and can never be used again.
The nil rate band can be transferred only between parents and children, not between spouses.
The unused proportion of the first spouse's nil rate band may be transferred and claimed against the survivor's estate.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a spouse or civil partner dies without using all of their nil rate band (for example because their estate passed exempt to the survivor), the unused proportion can be transferred to and claimed on the death of the survivor, potentially giving the survivor's estate up to two nil rate bands.

n.0: The transfer does not depend on mirror wills having been made.
n.1: The survivor's estate may use more than a single nil rate band via the transfer.
n.2: The unused nil rate band is not lost; it can be transferred.
n.3: The transferable nil rate band operates between spouses/civil partners, not parent to child.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A potential applicant wishes to bring a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, but a grant of representation to the estate was taken out some time ago, and time has been passing. The applicant is concerned about a time limit for bringing the claim. The court considers the time limit for a claim under the 1975 Act. The applicant had only recently learned of the death, with the grant taken out months earlier. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim must be brought within six years of the date of the deceased's death.
A claim must generally be brought within six months of the grant of representation, though the court may permit a late claim.
There is no time limit at all for bringing a claim under the 1975 Act.
A claim must be brought before the grant of representation is ever taken out.
A claim may be brought at any time until the estate has been fully distributed on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: An application under the 1975 Act must generally be made within six months of the date on which the grant of representation was first taken out. The court has a discretion to allow an application to be made after that period in appropriate cases.

n.0: The period runs from the grant (six months), not six years from death.
n.2: There is a time limit; it is not open-ended.
n.3: The claim is made after the grant, within six months of it, not before it.
n.4: The general limit is six months from the grant, not merely until distribution.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator has a valid will, and later wishes to make some changes to it without making an entirely new will. They execute a separate document, properly signed and witnessed, which amends certain provisions of the existing will while leaving the rest in place. The executor asks about the status and effect of this supplementary document. The court considers codicils and their effect on a will. The testator wanted only to tweak a couple of legacies rather than rewrite the whole will. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A codicil is a supplementary testamentary document that amends the will and, on execution, republishes it as at the codicil's date.
A codicil can only reduce gifts in a will and can never add new ones.
A codicil has no legal effect unless it is written on the same piece of paper as the will on these facts as a general rule.
A codicil need not be signed or witnessed, unlike a will.
A codicil automatically revokes the entire existing will and replaces it in full.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A codicil is a testamentary document, executed with the same formalities as a will, which adds to, varies or partially revokes an existing will. It leaves the rest of the will in force, and on execution it 'republishes' the will as at the date of the codicil.

n.1: A codicil can add, vary or revoke provisions, not only reduce gifts.
n.2: A codicil need not be on the same paper as the will.
n.3: A codicil must be executed with will formalities (signed and witnessed).
n.4: A codicil amends rather than automatically revokes the whole will.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will leaves a gift to a named charity. By the time the testator dies, that charity has ceased to exist as a separate body, having merged with or transferred its assets to a successor charity carrying on the same charitable work. The executors must decide what happens to the gift. The court considers the effect of a gift to a charity that has ceased to exist in its original form. The charity's work was still being carried on, now under the banner of a larger organisation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executors may keep the gift for the estate's own general purposes.
The gift is void and the money passes to the Crown as ownerless property.
The gift may pass to the successor charity carrying on the work, or be applied cy-pres, rather than simply failing.
The gift automatically lapses and falls into residue in every case.
The gift passes to the testator's next of kin because the charity no longer exists on these facts as a general rule.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a charitable gift is made and the named charity has ceased to exist but its work continues (for example through a successor or merged charity), the gift can often be given effect to that successor, or applied cy-pres to a similar charitable purpose, particularly where a general charitable intention is shown, rather than lapsing.

n.0: The executors cannot simply keep the gift for the estate.
n.1: It does not pass to the Crown as bona vacantia in these circumstances.
n.3: A charitable gift does not automatically lapse where the work continues; cy-pres or a successor may take it.
n.4: It does not necessarily pass to the next of kin.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A will leaves a general pecuniary legacy of a fixed sum of money to a beneficiary, without specifying when it is to be paid. The executors do not pay it until well over a year after the death. The beneficiary asks whether they are entitled to interest on the delayed legacy, and from when. The legacy is a general pecuniary legacy with no special payment date. Payment was delayed beyond a year from death. The will left a fixed cash sum to the beneficiary but said nothing about when it should be paid, and the executors did not in fact pay it until well over a year had gone by, prompting the beneficiary to ask whether interest is due on the delayed legacy and, if so, from what date it starts to run. Which of the following best describes the position on interest?
o: Interest generally runs on a general pecuniary legacy from the first anniversary of death (the end of the executor's year).
Interest runs only from the date the beneficiary first demands payment.
No interest is ever payable on a pecuniary legacy however long payment is delayed on these facts as a general rule.
Interest runs from the date the grant of probate is issued.
Interest runs on the legacy from the date of death in every case.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: A general pecuniary legacy that is not paid within the executor's year generally carries interest from the first anniversary of the death (the date by which it ought to have been paid), at the rate applicable to legacies, unless the will provides otherwise or an exception applies (such as a legacy to a minor child of the testator, which may carry interest from death).

n.1: Interest does not depend on the beneficiary demanding payment.
n.2: Interest can be payable if the legacy is paid late, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Interest runs from the first anniversary of death, not the date of the grant.
n.4: Interest on a general legacy generally runs from the end of the executor's year, not from death.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A will contains a gift described in words that are ambiguous or unclear, and the executors must work out what the testator meant, for example which of two possible people or assets was intended. They wish to know how the court approaches the interpretation of the words used in a will. The court considers the interpretation (construction) of wills, including the 'armchair' principle. The wording could point to either of two people the testator had known by the same name. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court refuses to interpret any will that contains an ambiguous or unclear expression.
The court interprets the will solely by reference to what the beneficiaries say the testator meant on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court ignores the words of the will entirely and simply gives effect to what seems fair.
The court must always give the words their most literal meaning, whatever the resulting absurdity.
The court seeks the testator's intention from the words used, read in light of the surrounding circumstances known to the testator (the armchair principle).
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: In construing a will the court seeks the testator's intention as expressed in the words used, read in their ordinary sense but in the light of the circumstances known to the testator when the will was made (placing itself in the testator's 'armchair'). Extrinsic evidence is admissible in limited circumstances under s.21 AJA 1982.

n.0: The court does interpret ambiguous wills rather than refusing to do so.
n.1: Interpretation is not governed by the beneficiaries' assertions of intention.
n.2: The court does not ignore the words and simply do what seems fair.
n.3: The court avoids an absurd literal reading where the context shows another meaning.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate, leaving a surviving spouse and adult children. There is no will and so no executor. A grant is needed to administer the estate, and a question arises as to who has the right to apply for the grant of letters of administration. There is no will appointing an executor. Several relatives could potentially apply. With no will and therefore no executor named, the family need someone formally authorised to gather in and distribute the estate, and a dispute has arisen about which of the various relatives has the right to step forward and take out the grant that will allow the administration to proceed. Which of the following best describes who is entitled to apply for the grant?
o: The grant is issued automatically to the eldest child in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The persons entitled to the estate on intestacy, in the priority order set by the Non-Contentious Probate Rules, spouse first.
Only the deceased's solicitor may apply for the grant.
Any member of the public who wishes to administer the estate.
Only a creditor of the estate may apply for the grant.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a person dies intestate, the right to apply for a grant of letters of administration follows the order of priority in the Non-Contentious Probate Rules, broadly tracking entitlement to the estate: the surviving spouse or civil partner first, then children, and so on. A person with a beneficial entitlement generally has priority.

n.0: The grant does not automatically go to the eldest child; the NCPR order governs.
n.2: The solicitor does not have priority to apply merely as the deceased's solicitor.
n.3: Not any member of the public may apply; entitlement follows the NCPR order.
n.4: A creditor may apply only in limited circumstances, not in priority to those entitled.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person inherited assets on which inheritance tax was paid, and then died a relatively short time afterwards, so that the same assets are, in effect, taxed twice within a short period. The executors are considering whether any relief mitigates this double charge. Inheritance tax was charged on the first death and again on the second, close in time. The executors seek to reduce the second charge. The deceased had themselves inherited substantial assets on which inheritance tax had already been paid only a short time before, and now those same assets are being taxed again on this second death, so the executors are looking for a relief that softens the blow of the same property being hit twice in quick succession. Which of the following best describes the relief that may apply?
o: Quick succession relief may reduce the inheritance tax on the second death where the deaths are close in time.
The relief applies only where the two deceased were married to each other.
There is no relief; the assets are simply taxed in full on each death.
The relief eliminates all inheritance tax on any estate within ten years of another on these facts.
The second estate is wholly exempt because tax was paid on the first death.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Quick succession relief reduces the inheritance tax payable on a death where the deceased's estate includes property on which inheritance tax was charged on an earlier death within the preceding five years. The relief is tapered according to the time between the two deaths, mitigating the double charge on the same property in quick succession.

n.1: Quick succession relief does not require the two deceased to have been married.
n.2: Relief does exist for this situation, so it is not simply taxed in full each time.
n.3: The relief tapers and applies within five years, not a blanket ten-year elimination.
n.4: The second estate is not wholly exempt; the relief tapers a partial reduction.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: Personal representatives are pressed by residuary beneficiaries to distribute the estate very soon after the death, before the PRs have been able to ascertain the full extent of the assets and liabilities. The PRs are concerned about distributing too early. Only a few months have passed since the death. The PRs wish to know whether they are obliged to distribute so soon. Barely a few months after the death the residuary beneficiaries are pressing hard to be paid out, but the personal representatives have not yet pinned down all the assets and liabilities, and they want to know whether they can be forced to distribute so soon or whether they are entitled to more time. Which of the following best describes the 'executor's year'?
o: The PRs must distribute the entire estate within 28 days of the death.
The PRs must distribute as soon as the grant is issued, whatever the state of the estate.
The PRs are not bound to distribute the estate before the expiry of one year from the death.
The PRs may never distribute until at least six years have passed.
The PRs must distribute immediately on demand by any residuary beneficiary.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: By the 'executor's year', personal representatives are not bound to distribute the estate before the expiry of one year from the death. They may need longer where the estate is complex, and distributing prematurely risks personal liability if further liabilities emerge, but beneficiaries generally cannot compel distribution within the first year.

n.0: There is no 28-day distribution requirement.
n.1: PRs need not distribute the moment the grant issues, regardless of the estate's state.
n.3: The executor's year is one year, not a six-year bar on distribution.
n.4: PRs are not compelled to distribute immediately on a beneficiary's demand within the year.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person made a chargeable lifetime transfer into a trust and also made a potentially exempt transfer to an individual, and then died within seven years. The executors must work out how the nil rate band is applied to these lifetime transfers when computing the inheritance tax. Several lifetime transfers were made within the seven years before death. The executors must apply the cumulation principle. In the seven years before death the deceased had made a chargeable transfer into a trust and a potentially exempt gift to an individual, and the executors, now bringing those failed and chargeable transfers into account, must apply the nil rate band across them in the correct sequence. Which of the following best describes how the nil rate band is applied?
o: The nil rate band is applied to the largest transfer first, whenever it was made.
The nil rate band is applied only to the death estate and never to lifetime transfers on these facts as a general rule.
The nil rate band is shared equally between all the transfers regardless of date.
The nil rate band is applied to the transfers in chronological order, earlier transfers using it up first (cumulation).
Each lifetime transfer has its own separate full nil rate band.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Inheritance tax on lifetime transfers operates on a cumulative basis: the nil rate band is set against transfers in chronological order, so earlier transfers use it up first, and later transfers (and ultimately the death estate) have the benefit only of any remaining band. This is the principle of cumulation.

n.0: The band is applied chronologically, not to the largest transfer first.
n.1: The band is applied to lifetime transfers too, not only the death estate.
n.2: It is not shared equally regardless of date; order matters.
n.4: Each transfer does not get its own full separate band; cumulation applies.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator, intending to revoke their existing will, deliberately tears it up and throws it away, doing so with the settled intention of revoking it. In another scenario the will is accidentally destroyed in a fire without any intention to revoke it. The executor asks whether the will has been revoked in each case. The court considers revocation of a will by destruction under the Wills Act 1837. In each case the will could no longer be found in the place where it had been kept. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A will can never be revoked by destruction, only by making a later will.
Any destruction of a will revokes it, whether or not the testator intended to revoke it on these facts as a general rule.
A will is revoked only if it is destroyed in the presence of two witnesses.
Intention alone revokes a will, even without any act of destruction at all.
