Revocation by destruction requires both the act of destruction and the intention to revoke; accidental destruction does not revoke.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.20 Wills Act 1837, a will is revoked by burning, tearing or otherwise destroying it by the testator (or by someone in their presence and at their direction), with the intention of revoking it. Both the physical act and the intention are required, so accidental destruction without intention does not revoke the will.

n.0: Revocation by destruction is a recognised method under s.20.
n.1: Destruction without the intention to revoke does not revoke the will.
n.2: Witnesses are not required for revocation by destruction.
n.3: Intention alone, without the act of destruction, does not revoke by this method.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies leaving an estate whose value is well above the tax-free threshold. The personal representatives must work out the inheritance tax payable on the death estate. They understand that a certain amount of the estate is taxed at a nil rate before tax is charged on the excess. The PRs ask about the basic operation of the nil rate band. The court considers the charge to inheritance tax on death and the nil rate band. The estate was worth well over a million pounds and the family faced a large tax bill. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Inheritance tax is charged only on the part of the estate below the nil rate band.
Inheritance tax is charged on the whole estate at 40% with no tax-free amount at all on these facts.
Inheritance tax is charged on the death estate above the available nil rate band, broadly at 40% on the excess.
Inheritance tax is never payable on a deceased person's estate in any circumstances.
Inheritance tax is charged at a flat 20% on the entire value of every estate.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: On death, inheritance tax is charged on the value of the death estate. A nil rate band (a threshold) is taxed at 0%, and the value of the estate above the available nil rate band is charged to IHT, broadly at 40% (subject to reliefs and exemptions).

n.0: Tax is charged on the excess above the nil rate band, not the part below it.
n.1: There is a nil rate band, so not the whole estate is taxed.
n.3: IHT can be payable on estates above the threshold.
n.4: The death rate is broadly 40% on the excess, not a flat 20% on everything.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will leaves a legacy to a named friend. The friend dies before the testator, and is not related to the testator. The will contains no substitution provision saying who should take if the friend predeceases. After the testator's death, the executors must decide what happens to the gift. The friend left children of their own. The court considers the doctrine of lapse. The friend had been named for a modest legacy and had no family connection to the testator. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift is simply void and the whole will fails as a result.
The gift takes effect in favour of the friend's estate as though the friend had survived.
The gift is held on trust indefinitely until the friend's estate can claim it.
The gift passes automatically to the deceased friend's own children instead.
The gift lapses because the beneficiary predeceased the testator, and it falls into residue.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the doctrine of lapse, a gift to a beneficiary who predeceases the testator generally fails (lapses). Unless there is a substitution clause or a statutory exception applies, the lapsed gift falls into residue (or, if it is the residuary gift, passes on intestacy).

n.0: The lapse of one gift does not make the whole will fail.
n.1: A lapsed legacy falls into residue, not the friend's estate.
n.2: The gift does not vest in the friend's estate; it lapses.
n.3: The gift does not automatically pass to the friend's children (no statutory exception applies to a mere friend).

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator's will leaves a legacy to a beneficiary, and that same beneficiary (or the beneficiary's spouse) acts as one of the two witnesses to the execution of the will. After the testator's death a question arises about the effect of the beneficiary having witnessed the will. The will is otherwise validly executed. The court considers the witness-beneficiary rule under the Wills Act 1837. The beneficiary had stepped in as a witness when the testator signed the will at home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The whole will is void because a beneficiary witnessed it.
The gift is valid provided there was a third, independent witness in addition on these facts.
The gift to the witnessing beneficiary is valid and takes effect in full.
The gift to the witnessing beneficiary (or their spouse) is void, but the will itself remains valid.
The beneficiary keeps the gift but is disqualified from acting as an executor.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.15 Wills Act 1837, a gift to a person who witnesses the will (or to that witness's spouse or civil partner) is void, though the witness remains a competent witness and the will itself is validly executed. The rest of the will stands.

n.0: The whole will is not void; only the gift to the witness fails.
n.1: If there are already two other independent witnesses the gift may be saved, but with the beneficiary as a necessary witness the gift is void; witnessing itself voids the gift under s.15.
n.2: The gift to the witnessing beneficiary is void, not valid in full.
n.4: The consequence is that the gift is void, not merely disqualification from being executor.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A will leaves a legacy to a beneficiary. The will is witnessed by two people, one of whom is the spouse (married partner) of that beneficiary. The remainder of the will is validly executed. The gift is to a beneficiary whose spouse acted as one of the two witnesses. The validity of the gift, rather than of the will, is in question. The will was properly drawn up and attested by two people, but one of those two witnesses happens to be married to the very person to whom the will leaves a legacy, which puts in doubt not the validity of the will as a whole but whether that particular beneficiary may keep the gift. Which of the following best describes the effect on the gift?
o: The gift is reduced by half rather than failing entirely.
The gift to the beneficiary fails, because a gift to the spouse of an attesting witness is void.
The whole will is invalid because a beneficiary's spouse witnessed it.
The gift is valid, because the rule only affects a witness who is personally the beneficiary.
The gift is valid, because the will had a second, independent witness.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.15 of the Wills Act 1837, a gift to an attesting witness, or to the spouse or civil partner of an attesting witness, is void, although the will itself remains validly executed and the witness's attestation is still effective. So the gift to this beneficiary (whose spouse witnessed the will) fails, but the will stands.

n.0: The gift fails entirely; it is not merely halved.
n.2: The will itself is not invalidated; only the gift fails.
n.3: The rule extends to the spouse or civil partner of a witness, not only the witness personally.
n.4: The presence of another witness does not save the gift under s.15.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: An adult who lacks the mental capacity to make a valid will has assets that would, on intestacy, pass in a way that does not reflect their known wishes or best interests. A relative wishes a will to be made on the person's behalf. The person cannot make a valid will themselves due to lack of capacity. A will reflecting their best interests is desired. The person's condition means they can no longer understand what making a will involves, yet the way their property would devolve on intestacy would cut across what everyone knows they would have wanted, and a relative is asking how, if at all, a will reflecting the person's best interests might still be made. Which of the following best describes how a will may be made for such a person?
o: No will can ever be made for a person who lacks testamentary capacity.
A relative may simply sign a will on the person's behalf without any court involvement on these facts.
The Court of Protection may authorise a statutory will to be made on behalf of the person who lacks capacity.
The intestacy rules must always apply, as a will is impossible in this situation.
The person's attorney under a lasting power of attorney may make a will for them.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a person lacks testamentary capacity, the Court of Protection may, under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, authorise the execution of a statutory will on their behalf, making provision in their best interests. This is distinct from an ordinary will and requires the court's involvement.

n.0: A statutory will can be made, so it is not true that no will is ever possible.
n.1: A relative cannot simply sign a will for the person without court authority.
n.3: Intestacy is not inevitable; a statutory will can be authorised.
n.4: An attorney under an LPA cannot make a will for the donor; that requires the Court of Protection.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person took out a life assurance policy and, during their lifetime, wrote the policy in trust for their children, so that the policy proceeds are held on trust for the children rather than forming part of the person's own estate. On the person's death, a question arises about how the policy proceeds are dealt with. The court considers the treatment of a life policy written in trust. The policy had been set up years ago specifically to provide for the children on death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The policy proceeds pass on intestacy regardless of the terms of the trust.
The policy proceeds can only ever be paid to the deceased's surviving spouse.
The policy proceeds pass to the beneficiaries under the trust, outside the estate and generally free of the deceased's IHT.
The policy proceeds pass to the personal representatives to be used to pay the estate's debts on these facts as a general rule.
The policy proceeds always form part of the deceased's estate and pass under the will.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where a life policy is written in trust, the policy proceeds do not form part of the deceased's estate; they pass directly to the beneficiaries under the trust, outside the will and intestacy, and are generally outside the deceased's estate for inheritance tax purposes.

n.0: The proceeds pass under the trust, not on intestacy.
n.1: The beneficiaries are those named in the trust, not necessarily the spouse.
n.3: The proceeds pass to the trust beneficiaries, not to the PRs for debts.
n.4: A policy in trust does not form part of the estate or pass under the will.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies intestate leaving no surviving spouse or civil partner, no issue, no parents, no siblings or their issue, no grandparents, and no uncles or aunts or their issue. Diligent enquiries reveal no relatives entitled under the statutory order at all. There is no one entitled under the intestacy rules. The deceased left no qualifying relatives. Careful enquiries into the family tree have turned up no surviving spouse or civil partner, no children, no parents, no brothers or sisters or their descendants, and no more distant relatives entitled under the statutory order, leaving the estate with no one to take it under the intestacy rules. Which of the following best describes what happens to the estate?
o: The estate is divided equally among the deceased's friends and neighbours.
The estate passes to the Crown (or the Duchy of Lancaster or Cornwall) as bona vacantia.
The estate passes to the deceased's most recent employer.
The estate escheats to the local authority for the area where the deceased lived.
The estate is held indefinitely by the personal representatives until a relative appears.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Where an intestate leaves no person entitled under the statutory order of entitlement, the estate passes to the Crown (or to the Duchy of Lancaster or the Duke of Cornwall for those areas) as bona vacantia ('ownerless goods'). The Crown has a discretion to make provision for dependants or others the deceased might have provided for.

n.0: The estate does not pass to friends and neighbours on intestacy.
n.2: There is no entitlement in a former employer.
n.3: The estate goes to the Crown as bona vacantia, not to the local authority by escheat.
n.4: The PRs do not hold it indefinitely awaiting a relative; it passes as bona vacantia.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A married couple die in circumstances where it is uncertain which of them died first — for example in a common accident — and the order of their deaths affects who inherits under their wills and the intestacy rules. There is no evidence to establish who survived whom. The court considers the presumption of order of death (commorientes) under the Law of Property Act 1925. The couple were found together and nothing could show which of them had died first. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Where the order of deaths is uncertain, they are presumed to have died at exactly the same instant.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the estates are simply pooled and divided equally.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the elder is presumed to have survived the younger.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, both estates pass automatically to the Crown.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the younger is presumed to have survived the elder.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.184 Law of Property Act 1925, where two or more people die in circumstances making it uncertain who survived whom, for the purposes of succession the deaths are presumed to have occurred in order of seniority, so the younger is presumed to have survived the elder.

n.0: They are not presumed to die simultaneously; s.184 applies the seniority presumption.
n.1: The estates are not simply pooled and divided equally.
n.2: It is the younger, not the elder, who is presumed to have survived.
n.3: The estates do not automatically pass to the Crown.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A beneficiary named in a testator's will unlawfully kills the testator and is convicted of the killing. The beneficiary then seeks to inherit under the will. The other beneficiaries and the estate object to the killer taking any benefit from the death. The court considers the forfeiture rule as it applies to a beneficiary who unlawfully kills the testator. The killer stood to inherit the bulk of the estate under the very will they were named in. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The killer takes the gift as normal, because the will is valid and names them as beneficiary on these facts as a general rule.
The killer takes the gift but must pay a fine equal to its value to the estate.
The forfeiture rule generally prevents the killer from taking any benefit, and the gift passes as if the killer had predeceased.
The killer takes the gift provided the killing was manslaughter rather than murder.
The whole will is revoked by the killing, so the estate passes on intestacy to the killer.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the forfeiture rule, a person who unlawfully kills another is generally precluded from taking any benefit in consequence of the death. The killer is treated as having predeceased the testator (so any substitution or gift over may take effect), though the court has a limited power to modify the rule in some manslaughter cases.

n.0: The killer does not take the gift as normal; forfeiture applies.
n.1: The killer forfeits the benefit; they do not simply pay a fine and keep it.
n.3: Forfeiture applies to unlawful killing generally, not only where relief is refused in manslaughter cases.
n.4: The killing does not revoke the will or pass the estate to the killer on intestacy.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A deceased owned agricultural land and farm buildings that had been occupied for the purposes of agriculture for the required period before death. The executors are considering whether a specific relief may reduce the value of this agricultural property for inheritance tax. The property is qualifying agricultural property occupied for the requisite period. The executors are calculating the inheritance tax. The deceased had farmed the land and buildings for many years up to death, meeting the ownership and occupation conditions, and the executors are keen to establish whether a specific relief can reduce, perhaps to nothing, the agricultural value of that property when the inheritance tax bill is worked out. Which of the following best describes the relief that may apply?
o: Agricultural property is charged to inheritance tax at a special higher rate.
Relief applies only to land that has never been farmed.
Agricultural property relief may reduce the agricultural value of the property, potentially by up to 100%.
Agricultural land is always entirely outside the scope of inheritance tax.
No relief is available for agricultural property under the inheritance tax rules on these facts.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Agricultural property relief can reduce the agricultural value of qualifying agricultural property (land, pasture and certain buildings occupied for agricultural purposes) by up to 100% (or 50% in some cases), where the ownership and occupation conditions are met. It applies to the agricultural value, with any excess (such as development value) potentially relieved separately.

n.0: There is no special higher rate for agricultural property.
n.1: Relief applies to property occupied for agriculture, not land never farmed.
n.3: Agricultural land is not automatically outside inheritance tax; relief has conditions.
n.4: Relief is available for qualifying agricultural property, so 'no relief' is wrong.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A testator made a valid will leaving their estate to various beneficiaries. Some time later the testator marries. The will was not expressed to be made in contemplation of that marriage. After the testator's death, the beneficiaries under the will and the new spouse dispute whether the will still stands. The court considers the effect of marriage on an existing will under the Wills Act 1837. The testator had married a new partner some years after first making the will. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The testator's marriage revokes the earlier will, unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage.
Marriage has no effect at all on a will made before the marriage.
Marriage suspends the will temporarily but it revives automatically on any later divorce.
Marriage revokes only the gifts to persons other than the new spouse, leaving the rest intact.
Marriage revokes the will only if the testator has children with the new spouse.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under s.18 Wills Act 1837, a will is revoked by the testator's subsequent marriage (or civil partnership), unless it appears the will was made in expectation (contemplation) of that particular marriage and the testator intended it not to be revoked.

n.1: Marriage does have an effect: it generally revokes the earlier will.
n.2: Marriage revokes the will; it does not merely suspend it pending a divorce.
n.3: Marriage revokes the whole will, not only gifts to others.
n.4: Revocation by marriage does not depend on there being children.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A person dies owning their home, which they leave to their children (direct descendants). The personal representatives are considering whether an additional inheritance tax allowance, beyond the ordinary nil rate band, is available because the home is passing to descendants. The court considers the residence nil rate band. The family home was worth a substantial sum and was being left to the deceased's two children. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The residence nil rate band applies to any gift of any property to anyone at all.
The residence nil rate band exempts the whole of the home from inheritance tax in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An additional residence nil rate band may be available where a home is left to direct descendants, subject to conditions and a taper for large estates.
The residence nil rate band is available only where the home is left to a spouse.
There is no additional allowance for a home; only the ordinary nil rate band applies.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: The residence nil rate band is an additional nil rate band available, subject to conditions, where a residence (or its value) is left to direct descendants. It is subject to a maximum amount and is tapered away for estates above a high value threshold.

n.0: The RNRB applies to a residence left to descendants, not any gift to anyone.
n.1: It is a capped additional band, not a complete exemption of the whole home.
n.3: It applies where the home passes to descendants, not (for the RNRB) to a spouse.
n.4: There is an additional residence nil rate band beyond the ordinary NRB.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: An elderly testator makes a will, and after their death a disappointed relative challenges it on the ground that the testator lacked the mental capacity to make a will at the time. The court must decide whether the testator had the requisite testamentary capacity when the will was made. The relative points to the testator's age and some confusion. The court considers the test for testamentary capacity. The relative pointed to episodes of confusion in the months before the will was signed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The testator must have a perfect memory and full physical health when making the will.
The testator need only be able to sign their name at the time the will is executed.
The testator must obtain a doctor's certificate of capacity, or the will is automatically void on these facts as a general rule.
The testator must understand the nature of making a will, the extent of their property, and the claims to which they ought to give effect.
The testator must simply be over the age of eighteen at the time the will is made.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Under the test in Banks v Goodfellow, a testator has testamentary capacity if they understand the nature of the act of making a will and its effects, understand the extent of the property being disposed of, and can comprehend and appreciate the claims to which they ought to give effect, with no disorder of the mind perverting their judgement.

n.0: Perfect memory and full physical health are not required.
n.1: Ability to sign is not enough; the testator must have the requisite understanding.
n.2: A doctor's certificate is prudent (the golden rule) but not a legal precondition to validity.
n.4: Being over eighteen is necessary but not sufficient; the Banks v Goodfellow test must be met.

Wills & Administration of Estate.q: A court is considering a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 and must decide whether the will (or intestacy) makes reasonable financial provision for the applicant, and if not, what provision to order. The court is directed to weigh a range of matters. The court must exercise its discretion by reference to statutory guidelines. The applicant qualifies to claim. The court has accepted that the applicant is entitled to bring the claim and must now decide whether the estate makes reasonable provision for them and, if not, what to award, weighing the competing interests of the applicant and the beneficiaries rather than looking at any single consideration in isolation. Which of the following best describes the matters the court takes into account?
o: Only the size of the estate, regardless of anyone's needs.
A range of statutory factors, including the needs and resources of the applicant and beneficiaries, the deceased obligations, and the estate size.
Only the applicant's conduct towards the deceased during their lifetime.
Only the express wishes stated by the deceased in the will, and nothing else on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances on these facts.
Only whether the applicant is a blood relative of the deceased.
Wills & Administration of Estate.w: Section 3 of the 1975 Act sets out the factors the court must consider, including the financial needs and resources of the applicant and of any beneficiary, any obligations the deceased had towards them, the size and nature of the estate, any disability, and the conduct of the parties. The deceased's wishes are relevant but not decisive.

n.0: The estate's size is one factor among many, not the sole consideration.
n.2: Conduct is only one of several statutory factors.
n.3: The deceased's wishes are one factor, not the only consideration.
n.4: Being a blood relative is not the sole factor; needs and resources are central.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds money for many clients in its general client account. During a compliance review it emerges that the firm has not carried out any reconciliation comparing its client cash account, the client ledger balances and the bank statement for several months. The COFA is asked how often such a reconciliation must be performed under the SRA Accounts Rules. The compliance review has already flagged that client ledger totals have not been checked against the bank statements for some time, and the COFA is anxious to put a proper timetable in place so that any discrepancy between the firm's records and the bank would be caught and investigated quickly. Which of the following best describes the requirement for reconciling the client account?
o: The firm need only reconcile the client account when a discrepancy is suspected.
The firm must reconcile the client account at least every five weeks.
There is no set frequency, provided reconciliations are done from time to time.
The firm must reconcile the client account at least every six months.
The firm must reconcile the client account only once each financial year.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require a firm, at least every five weeks, to obtain statements for all client accounts, reconcile the bank balance with the client cash account and the total of the client ledger balances, and to promptly investigate and resolve any differences. The reconciliation must be signed off by the COFA or a manager.

n.0: Reconciliations must be regular, not only when a discrepancy is suspected.
n.2: There is a specific maximum interval of five weeks.
n.3: Six-monthly reconciliation does not meet the five-week requirement.
n.4: Annual reconciliation is far less frequent than the rules require.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's cashier prepares the periodic client account reconciliation, comparing the bank statement, the client cash account and the total of the client ledger balances. A junior member of staff asks whether the cashier can simply file the completed reconciliation once it balances, or whether anyone else must review it. The firm is an authorised body. The firm wants to be confident its client money controls are robust and that responsibility for oversight does not rest solely with the person who compiles the figures, so the question of who must review and approve each completed reconciliation has become a live governance point in the review. Which of the following best describes the requirement about approving the reconciliation under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The reconciliation must be approved by the firm's external accountant each time.
The reconciliation must be signed off by the COFA or a manager of the firm.
The reconciliation may be filed by the cashier alone once it balances.
The reconciliation must be sent to the SRA for approval each time.
The reconciliation must be signed off by the client whose money is held.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that each client account reconciliation is signed off by the COFA or a manager of the firm. This provides independent oversight of client money, so that discrepancies are identified and investigated by someone with responsibility, rather than the reconciliation resting solely with the person who prepared it.

n.0: The external accountant reports periodically but need not approve each reconciliation.
n.2: The reconciliation cannot simply be filed by the cashier who prepared it.
n.3: Reconciliations are not routinely sent to the SRA for approval.
n.4: The client does not sign off the firm's internal reconciliation.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives various sums of money in the course of its work, and the bookkeeper must decide which sums count as 'client money' for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules, because that determines how they must be handled. The firm holds money for clients and third parties, as well as its own money. The bookkeeper considers the definition of client money under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm acts on a conveyancing purchase, a probate matter and a personal injury claim, and in each it holds different sums whose correct handling turns on whether they are client money or the firm's own money, so the classification matters at the point of receipt. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Client money means only cash physically handed over by a client in person.
Client money means only money held for a client in a matter involving litigation.
Client money means any money at all that passes through the firm, including its own profit costs already billed on these facts as a general rule.
Client money includes money held or received for a client or third party, and money held on account of costs or for disbursements not yet incurred.
Client money means only money belonging to the firm itself.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, client money is money held or received by a firm relating to regulated services delivered to a client, including money held on account of costs or for disbursements not yet incurred, money held for a third party, and money as trustee or in a fiduciary capacity.

n.0: Client money is not limited to cash handed over in person.
n.1: Client money is not confined to litigation matters.
n.2: The firm's own money (such as billed profit costs) is office money, not client money.
n.4: Client money is not the firm's own money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm delivers a bill to a client for £2,000. In error, the client pays £2,200, £200 more than the amount billed. The firm identifies the overpayment when the receipt is processed. The client did not intend the extra £200 to be held on account of any future work. The cashier considers how the £200 overpayment should be treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The client's payment plainly exceeded the sum demanded in the bill, there is nothing in the correspondence to suggest the extra was meant as money on account of any further work, and the cashier wants to deal with the surplus correctly rather than leaving it to swell the firm's income. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £200?
o: The £200 may be transferred to another client whose ledger is short.
The £200 may be kept in the office account until the client asks for it.
The £200 may be retained by the firm as a goodwill credit.
The £200 is office money because it was paid together with the firm's fees.
The £200 is client money and must be returned to the client promptly.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Only the £2,000 matching the bill is office money. The £200 overpaid does not belong to the firm; it is client money. The firm must pay it into the client account and return it to the client promptly, since there is no proper reason to hold it, rather than retaining it or leaving it in the office account.

n.0: It cannot be applied to another client's shortfall.
n.1: It must not be held in the office account awaiting a request; it is client money to be returned promptly.
n.2: The firm cannot keep the overpayment as a goodwill credit.
n.3: Being paid with the fees does not make the overpayment office money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's cashier is about to make a payment from the general client account that would take the overall balance on the client bank account itself into debit (overdrawn), not merely one client's ledger. The cashier queries whether this is permitted. The proposed payment would overdraw the client bank account as a whole. The firm operates a general client account. A payment is queued up that, once it goes out, would take not just one client's ledger but the whole client bank account below zero, and the cashier pauses, unsure whether letting the client account itself slip into an overdrawn position is something the rules will tolerate. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The client account may be overdrawn with the bank's consent to an overdraft facility.
The client account may be overdrawn provided it is brought back into credit within a month.
There is no restriction on the client account being overdrawn.
The client account may be overdrawn if the firm's office account is in credit.
The client account must not be overdrawn; a payment that would overdraw it must not be made.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm must not make a payment from a client account if it would result in the client account being overdrawn. Client money must always be available, and overdrawing the client account (or an individual client's ledger) would mean paying out money the firm does not hold for clients, which breaches the SRA Accounts Rules.

n.0: An agreed bank overdraft facility does not make overdrawing the client account permissible.
n.1: Restoring the position within a month does not permit overdrawing the client account.
n.2: There is a clear rule against overdrawing the client account.
n.3: The state of the office account does not license overdrawing the client account.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm acting for a client in a transaction receives £1,000 from a third party, the money being intended for the client in connection with the matter the firm is handling. The cashier is unsure how to classify money that has come from someone other than the firm's own client, and whether the usual client account protections apply to it. The money relates to the firm's delivery of regulated services. The payment arrived from someone other than the firm's own client but was clearly earmarked for the client in connection with the matter the firm is handling, and the cashier is unsure whether money that did not come from the client still attracts the full protection of the client account rules. Which of the following best describes the treatment of the £1,000 under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £1,000 is office money because it came from a third party.
The £1,000 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
The £1,000 must be returned to the third party regardless of the client's interest.
The £1,000 may be held in cash outside any account as third-party money.
The £1,000 falls outside the rules because the payer is not the firm's client.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Client money includes money held or received for a third party in the course of delivering regulated services, not only money received from the firm's own client. Money received from a third party for the client is client money and must be paid into the client account and dealt with in accordance with the rules.

n.0: Money from a third party for the client is client money, not office money.
n.2: It is held for the client's benefit and dealt with under the rules, not automatically returned to the payer.
n.3: It cannot be held in cash outside a client account.
n.4: The rules apply to money held for third parties too, not only the firm's client.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm incurs £20 in postage sending letters in the ordinary course of running a client's matter, and pays it out of the office petty cash. The cashier asks whether this £20 can be charged to the client as a disbursement and recovered from client money, or whether it is simply part of the firm's own running costs. The postage is general office correspondence. The letters were routine correspondence about the client's matter rather than anything paid to an outside party, and the cashier is trying to draw the line between the firm's own general running expenses and genuine disbursements incurred on the client's behalf that can be met from client money. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £20?
o: The postage may be deducted from any client's ledger to spread the cost.
The postage must be reported to the SRA as a client account transaction.
The postage must be met from client money held for the client.
The postage is part of the firm's own overheads and is office money expenditure.
The postage must be paid directly from the client account as a disbursement.
Solicitor Accounts.w: General running costs of the firm, such as ordinary postage and office overheads, are office money expenditure and are met from the office account. They are not disbursements paid to third parties on the client's behalf out of client money, so they are not charged to the client account (though the firm may recover them through its bill as part of its charges).

n.0: It cannot be deducted from clients' ledgers to spread the cost.
n.1: It is a routine office expense, not something reported to the SRA as a client account transaction.
n.2: Ordinary office postage is not met from client money.
n.4: It is not a client account disbursement.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's bookkeeper is classifying the various receipts of the firm and needs to identify which money counts as the firm's own 'office money', as distinct from client money, because office money is handled differently under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has billed some clients for its fees. The bookkeeper considers the meaning of office money. The firm has delivered bills to several clients for completed work, holds sums to meet its own office overheads such as rent and salaries, and also holds money for ongoing matters, and the bookkeeper needs to isolate which of these belongs to the firm itself. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Office money is the firm's own money, such as money to pay the firm's own expenses or billed profit costs.
Office money means any money held for a client on account of future costs.
Office money means client money that has not yet been paid into the client account on these facts.
Office money means money held for a third party in a transaction.
Office money means money held by the firm as trustee for a beneficiary.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Office money is money that belongs to the firm itself — for example money to meet the firm's own running costs, and money the firm is entitled to for costs once a bill has been delivered. It is kept in the office account, separate from client money.

n.1: Money held on account of a client's future costs is client money, not office money.
n.2: Client money remains client money even before it is banked.
n.3: Money held for a third party is client money.
n.4: Money held as trustee is client money (held in a fiduciary capacity).

Solicitor Accounts.q: During a reconciliation a firm discovers £100 in its general client account that it cannot attribute to any client or matter, having been paid in some time ago with no identifying reference. The bookkeeper wants to deal with it correctly and asks whether the firm can simply transfer it to the office account to tidy the ledgers. The firm has records of its receipts. The payment carried no client name, matter reference or narrative when it reached the bank, none of the firm's fee-earners recognises it, and it has been sitting unallocated in the general client account, so the cashier wants to know how to treat it while its true owner is investigated. Which of the following best describes the correct approach to the unidentified funds under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may keep the money in a suspense office ledger and treat it as profit on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may ignore the money because it is a small sum below any threshold.
The firm must pay the money to the SRA as soon as it is discovered.
The firm may transfer the money to the office account immediately as unclaimed.
The firm must take reasonable steps to identify the owner and, meanwhile, keep the money in the client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Unidentified money received into the client account is treated as client money until its owner is established. The firm must take reasonable steps to identify the correct recipient and, in the meantime, keep the money safe in the client account. It cannot simply be swept into the office account or treated as the firm's profit.

n.0: The money is not the firm's profit and must be kept as client money.
n.1: There is no threshold that allows unidentified client money simply to be ignored.
n.2: The money is kept in the client account while its owner is sought, not paid to the SRA on discovery.
n.3: Unidentified funds cannot be transferred to the office account as unclaimed.

Solicitor Accounts.q: During an internal review it becomes clear that a firm has committed a serious breach of the SRA Accounts Rules: client money has been used improperly and a significant shortfall existed on the client account for a period. The COFA is considering what, beyond correcting the position, the firm must do about the breach itself. The breach is serious rather than trivial. The improper use of client money went undetected for a period before the review uncovered it, the shortfall has now been made good from office money, and the COFA is turning to the question of what the firm must do about the breach itself beyond simply restoring the missing funds. Which of the following best describes the COFA's obligation under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The COFA must report the breach only if a client suffers a permanent loss.
The COFA need only record the breach internally and take no further step.
The COFA must report the breach to the firm's bank rather than the SRA.
The COFA must report every breach, however trivial, to the SRA immediately.
The COFA must ensure a serious breach is reported to the SRA.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The COFA must ensure the firm records breaches of the Accounts Rules and reports serious breaches to the SRA. A serious breach, such as improper use of client money causing a significant shortfall, must be reported; less serious breaches are recorded and dealt with internally but reported to the SRA on request or as part of the wider picture.

n.0: Reporting a serious breach does not depend on the client suffering permanent loss.
n.1: A serious breach cannot simply be recorded internally with no report.
n.2: The report goes to the SRA, not the bank.
n.3: Not every trivial breach must be reported immediately; seriousness is the trigger.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has carried out work for a client and wishes to take payment of its fees from money it holds for that client in the client account. The bookkeeper is asked what must happen before the firm can transfer money from the client account to the office account in respect of its costs. The bookkeeper considers the transfer of costs from client to office account under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has completed a discrete piece of work and wishes to be paid for it from the money it already holds for the client in the client account, and the bookkeeper needs to know what step must come first before that money can move to the office account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may transfer money for its costs at any time, before or without any bill.
The firm may transfer its costs only with the prior written approval of the SRA.
The firm may transfer its costs provided the amount taken is reasonable, without a bill on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm may never transfer client money to the office account for its own costs.
The firm may transfer money for its costs from client to office account only after a bill or written notification of costs has been given to the client.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money held for a client becomes office money, capable of transfer to the office account for the firm's costs, only once the firm has delivered a bill of costs or other written notification of the costs incurred. Only then, and only up to the amount notified, may the transfer be made.

n.0: A transfer for costs cannot be made before or without a bill.
n.1: SRA approval is not required for a proper costs transfer.
n.2: Reasonableness of the amount does not dispense with the need for a bill.
n.3: The firm can take its properly billed costs from client money, so 'never' is wrong.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm must arrange for its compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules to be examined and an accountant's report obtained. The firm proposes to have the report prepared by its own in-house bookkeeper who prepares the day-to-day accounts. The compliance officer questions whether this is appropriate. The person preparing the report must be suitably qualified and independent. The report is required for the SRA regime. Looking to keep costs down, the firm suggests that the very bookkeeper who writes up its day-to-day client account entries should also prepare the accountant's report for the SRA, and the compliance officer is uneasy about whether that person is the right one to sign it off. Which of the following best describes the requirement for the reporting accountant?
o: The report may be prepared by any person the firm chooses without qualification on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The report must be prepared by an accountant who is qualified and independent (a registered auditor), not the firm's own bookkeeper.
The report may be prepared by the firm's COFA regardless of qualification.
Any member of the firm's staff may prepare the accountant's report.
The report must be prepared by the SRA itself on the firm's behalf.
Solicitor Accounts.w: An accountant's report must be prepared by an independent accountant who is a member of a recognised professional body and (for these purposes) a registered auditor. The firm's own bookkeeper who prepares the accounts lacks the required independence, so cannot prepare the report; the reporting accountant must be suitably qualified and independent of the firm's routine bookkeeping.

n.0: The reporting accountant must be qualified; not just anyone the firm chooses.
n.2: The COFA (an internal officer) is not the independent reporting accountant.
n.3: Not any staff member may prepare the report; independence and qualification are required.
n.4: The SRA does not prepare firms' accountant's reports.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds client money for many different clients in its general client account. The bookkeeper is setting up the accounting records and wants to ensure that the firm can, at any time, show how much is held for each individual client and on what matter. The firm must keep records of its dealings with client money. Many clients' funds are pooled in one bank account. The firm handles matters for dozens of clients whose money all sits in the one general client account at the bank, and the bookkeeper wants the system built so that, if asked at any moment, the firm can say precisely how much of that pooled balance belongs to a given client on a given matter. Which of the following best describes the record-keeping requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm need only record the total balance held across all clients.
The firm need not keep ledgers provided the bank statement is retained.
The firm must keep a separate client ledger for each client, identifying the client and the matter and showing a running balance.
The firm may record client money only once a year in its annual accounts.
The firm may keep a single combined ledger for all clients with no individual breakdown on these facts as a general rule.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require accurate, contemporaneous records, including a separate client ledger account for each client (and matter), recording all receipts and payments of that client's money and showing a current balance. This enables the firm to demonstrate at any time how much it holds for each client, even though the money is pooled in one bank account.

n.0: Recording only the total across all clients does not meet the requirement for individual ledgers.
n.1: Retaining the bank statement does not replace the requirement to keep client ledgers.
n.3: Records must be contemporaneous, not compiled only once a year.
n.4: A single combined ledger with no individual client breakdown is not sufficient.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm needs to pay a disbursement (such as a court fee or expert's fee) on behalf of a client, and the bookkeeper must decide whether it can be paid from the client account and how it is recorded. The firm holds sufficient money for that client. The bookkeeper considers the payment of disbursements from the client account under the SRA Accounts Rules. The disbursement is a court issue fee that must be paid to progress the client's claim, the firm holds ample funds for this client in the client account, and the bookkeeper wants to confirm whether the payment can properly be met from those client funds. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A disbursement may be paid from the client account without recording it in the ledgers.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account only if sufficient client money is held for that particular client.
A disbursement may be paid from money held for a different client if convenient.
A disbursement may never be paid from the client account and must always come from office money on these facts.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account even if no money is held for that client.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A disbursement may be paid out of the client account on a client's behalf only where sufficient client money is held for that client (so that the client's ledger is not overdrawn). Otherwise it must be met from office money, and the payment must be properly recorded in the accounts.

n.0: All payments must be recorded in the ledgers.
n.2: Another client's money must not be used to pay the disbursement.
n.3: Disbursements can be paid from client money where held, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: A disbursement cannot be paid from the client account if no money is held for that client.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm is reviewing the controls around payments out of its client account. At present, any fee-earner can instruct the bank to release client money without further sign-off. The COFA is concerned that withdrawals of client money should be properly controlled so that money is only ever paid out for a proper purpose. The firm is an authorised body. An internal review has revealed that the firm has no real controls over who can move money out of the client account, with individual fee-earners able to trigger payments unchecked, and the COFA is determined to establish who must be involved in authorising a withdrawal before any client money leaves the account. Which of the following best describes the requirement about authorising withdrawals of client money under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Only the SRA may authorise a withdrawal of client money from the client account.
A withdrawal of client money must be appropriately authorised and supervised by the firm.
Any member of staff may authorise a withdrawal of client money without oversight.
Withdrawals of client money need no authorisation provided they are reconciled later.
Only the client personally may authorise each withdrawal of client money.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that withdrawals from the client account are appropriately authorised and supervised, and may only be made for a proper purpose and to the extent of funds held for the client. Firms must have systems ensuring a suitably responsible person authorises payments, rather than leaving withdrawals uncontrolled.

n.0: The SRA does not authorise individual routine withdrawals.
n.2: Uncontrolled withdrawals by any member of staff are not permitted.
n.3: Later reconciliation does not remove the need for proper authorisation at the time.
n.4: The client need not personally authorise each withdrawal; the firm must have proper internal authorisation.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds £1,200 in the client account for a client, provided to cover an anticipated disbursement. When the disbursement is finally incurred it costs only £900, leaving £300 of the client's money in the client account with no remaining purpose on the matter. The cashier considers what should happen to the £300. The matter is otherwise concluded. The client had put the firm in funds generously to be sure the disbursement could be met, the actual cost came in lower than expected, and with the work now finished the firm is left holding money that has served its purpose and has no further role to play on the matter. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £300 surplus may be retained by the firm against possible future costs.
The £300 surplus becomes office money once the disbursement is paid.
The £300 surplus may be kept in the client account indefinitely.
The £300 surplus may be transferred to the office account as a handling charge.
The £300 surplus is client money and must be returned to the client promptly.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The £300 not needed for the disbursement remains client money. With the matter concluded and no proper reason to hold it, the firm must return the surplus to the client promptly. It does not become office money, and cannot be retained against speculative future costs or taken as a charge.

n.0: The firm cannot retain it against possible future costs.
n.1: Paying the disbursement does not convert the surplus into office money.
n.2: It cannot be left in the client account indefinitely once there is no reason to hold it.
n.3: It cannot be taken to the office account as a handling charge.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm acting for a client in a personal injury claim receives a settlement of £2,500 paid to the firm on the client's behalf. The firm considers that £500 of the sum represents costs it is entitled to, but it has not yet delivered any bill to the client for those costs. The cashier must decide how the £2,500 is classified when it is received. No bill or written notification of costs has yet been given. The settlement cheque has been paid to the firm rather than to the client directly, the client is expecting to receive the balance after the firm's charges, and the cashier is conscious that the firm cannot help itself to its costs simply because it believes it is owed them. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the receipt?
o: The whole £2,500 is office money because the firm is owed costs.
The £500 is office money and only £2,000 is client money on receipt.
The £500 may be paid straight into the office account before any bill.
The £2,500 may be split at the firm's discretion whenever convenient.
The whole £2,500 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money received on behalf of a client, such as damages, is client money in its entirety and must be paid into the client account. The firm cannot treat any part as office money for its costs until it has delivered a bill or other written notification of costs; only then may it transfer the billed amount to the office account.

n.0: The firm is owed costs but cannot treat the money as office money without a bill.
n.1: No part is office money yet, because no bill has been delivered.
n.2: The £500 cannot go to the office account before any bill.
n.3: The receipt is client money and must be banked as such promptly, not apportioned at will.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm needs to pay a Land Registry fee of £300 on a client's behalf. To avoid delay, the firm pays the £300 from its office account before it has received any money from the client to cover it. The firm later expects to be reimbursed for the disbursement. The cashier considers how this is treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The fee was payable to a third party to progress the registration without delay, the client had not yet put the firm in funds for it, and the firm chose to advance the cost itself, meaning the cashier must decide how the payment and its later recovery are correctly recorded. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment?
o: The firm must treat the £300 as client money even though it came from the office account.
The firm may recover the £300 from client money without ever notifying the client of the cost on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may pay the disbursement from office money and later recover it from the client by a bill or from client money held.
The firm must never pay a client's disbursement from office money in any circumstances.
The firm may reimburse itself from another client's money in the client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm may meet a client's disbursement out of its own office money if it wishes, effectively advancing the cost. It then recovers the sum from the client, either by including it in a bill or by reimbursing itself from client money held for that client once available, with the disbursement properly notified to the client.

n.0: Money paid out of the office account is office money, not client money.
n.1: The disbursement must be properly notified to and recoverable from the client, not taken silently.
n.3: Paying a disbursement from office money is permitted, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Another client's money cannot be used to reimburse the firm.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives a single payment that comprises both client money (money on account of a disbursement not yet incurred) and office money (the firm's billed fees), paid together in one sum. The bookkeeper must decide how to deal with this mixed receipt under the SRA Accounts Rules. The bookkeeper considers the treatment of a mixed receipt. The single cheque arrives with a covering letter that does not separate the two elements, and the bookkeeper must decide how to route it so that the client's protected money is not left sitting in the office account while the firm's fees are extracted. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?
o: The client money must reach the client account promptly, for example by banking the whole sum and transferring the office money out promptly.
The client money element may be ignored because it was paid together with office money on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The mixed receipt need not be split and may be spent as the firm sees fit.
The whole receipt may simply be paid into the office account and left there.
The whole receipt may be kept in cash and allocated later whenever convenient.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where a receipt is mixed client and office money, the firm must ensure the client money is paid promptly into the client account. In practice the whole sum may be paid into the client account and the office money element then transferred promptly to the office account (or the sum allocated appropriately), so client money is properly protected.

n.1: The client money element cannot be ignored.
n.2: The receipt must be dealt with under the rules, not spent as the firm sees fit.
n.3: The whole receipt cannot simply be left in the office account.
n.4: It cannot be kept in cash and allocated whenever convenient.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives a sum of money from a client on account of costs for future work, which is client money under the SRA Accounts Rules. The bookkeeper must decide where this money should be held. The firm operates a general client account. The bookkeeper considers the requirement as to where client money must be kept under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has a single general client account at its bank and no separate designated deposit account for this client, and the fee-earner asks the bookkeeper for confirmation of where the money should sit while the work is carried out over the coming weeks. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Client money may be kept in the personal account of the fee-earner handling the matter.
Client money may be kept in the firm's office account with its own money.
Client money must be kept in cash in the firm's safe rather than in any bank account.
Client money need not be kept in any particular account, so long as it is spent on the client.
Client money must be kept in a client account, separate from the firm's own money.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be kept in a client account (an account at a bank or building society in the firm's name that includes the word 'client'), separate from the firm's own (office) money.

n.0: Client money must not be held in a fee-earner's personal account.
n.1: Client money must not be kept in the office account.
n.2: Client money is held in a client bank account, not as cash in a safe.
n.3: Client money must be held in a client account, not merely spent appropriately.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives £800 from a client, made up of £500 in respect of a bill already delivered and £300 paid on account of future work not yet billed. The cashier accepts that the £500 is office money and the £300 is client money, and now needs to deal with the receipt physically. The firm operates a general client account and an office account. The cashier is satisfied about how the two elements are classified and is now focused on the mechanics of banking the single cheque, wanting to be sure that whichever route is chosen the client money element does not end up sitting in the office account even briefly. Which of the following best describes an acceptable way to handle this mixed receipt under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Pay the whole £800 into the office account and leave it there.
Hold the whole £800 in cash and allocate it once the next bill is raised.
Pay the whole £800 into the client account and promptly transfer the £500 to the office account.
Pay the whole £800 into the office account and transfer £300 to client account next month.
Pay the £500 into the client account and the £300 into the office account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: With a mixed receipt the firm must ensure the client money element reaches the client account. An acceptable method is to pay the whole sum into the client account and promptly transfer the office money element (£500) to the office account. Splitting the receipt, paying £500 to office and £300 to client, is also acceptable; leaving client money in the office account is not.

n.0: Leaving the whole receipt in the office account leaves client money unprotected.
n.1: Holding it all in cash to allocate later does not get the client money into the client account promptly.
n.3: Delaying the client money to the office account for a month is not prompt handling.
n.4: This reverses the split: the £500 is office money and the £300 is client money, not the other way round.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm delivers a bill to a client that includes the firm's professional fees plus VAT charged on those fees. The client pays the bill in full. The cashier is classifying the VAT element the firm has charged on its own fees, and asks whether that VAT is client money or office money for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules. The VAT is output tax on the firm's own services. The bill separated out the firm's professional charges and the VAT chargeable on them, the client has now settled the whole amount, and the cashier is working through which elements of the payment are the firm's own money and which, if any, must be treated as belonging to the client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The VAT must be paid into a separate designated client account.
The VAT belongs to the client and must be returned to them.
The VAT must be held in the client account until it is paid to HMRC.
The VAT charged on the firm's own fees is office money.
The VAT charged on the firm's own fees is client money.
Solicitor Accounts.w: VAT the firm charges on its own professional fees is part of the firm's billed charges and is office money once the bill is delivered and paid. The firm accounts for that output VAT to HMRC as part of its own tax affairs; it is not client money held for the client.

n.0: It need not go into a designated client account.
n.1: It does not belong to the client to be returned; it is part of the firm's charge.
n.2: It is office money, not client money held pending payment to HMRC.
n.4: VAT on the firm's own fees is not client money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's periodic client account reconciliation reveals a difference between the balance shown by the client cash account, the total of the client ledger balances, and the bank statement, which cannot immediately be explained. The bookkeeper is unsure what to do about the discrepancy. A difference has emerged on the client account reconciliation. The cause is not yet identified. The latest reconciliation has thrown up a mismatch between the client cash account, the total of the client ledgers and the bank statement that the bookkeeper cannot immediately account for, and the firm must decide how to respond to an unexplained difference of this kind on the client account. Which of the following best describes what the firm must do under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may carry the discrepancy forward indefinitely until it resolves itself.
The firm must immediately close the client account.
The firm must report the discrepancy to the police before investigating.
The firm must promptly investigate and correct any differences shown by the reconciliation.
The firm may ignore small discrepancies as immaterial.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require the firm to carry out reconciliations at least every five weeks and, crucially, to investigate and correct promptly any differences the reconciliation reveals. A discrepancy between the cash account, ledger totals and bank statement must be resolved, as it may indicate an error or a shortfall in client money.

n.0: The firm cannot carry an unexplained discrepancy forward indefinitely.
n.1: Closing the client account is not the required response to a discrepancy.
n.2: Prompt investigation and correction, not police reporting, is the prescribed step.
n.4: Discrepancies must be investigated, not ignored as immaterial.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm acting for the seller in a conveyancing transaction receives a deposit of £4,000 from the buyer's solicitor, expressed to be held by the firm as stakeholder pending completion. Before completion, the seller asks the firm to release the deposit to the seller straight away. The firm holds the money as stakeholder. The transaction has exchanged but not yet completed, the seller is keen to get its hands on the money early, and the firm must weigh the seller's request against the terms on which the deposit was handed over and the protections those terms are designed to give the other side. Which of the following best describes how the firm may deal with the deposit under the SRA Accounts Rules and its stakeholder role?
o: The firm may release the deposit to the seller on the seller's instruction alone on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may keep the deposit as security for its own costs on the sale.
The firm may release the deposit to the buyer at any time before completion.
As stakeholder the firm must hold the deposit and not release it before completion without both parties' authority.
The firm may pay the deposit into the office account as it acts for the seller.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A deposit held as stakeholder is client money held for both parties: the firm holds it in the client account and may only release it in accordance with the stakeholder terms, generally on completion. It cannot pay it out on the seller's instruction alone, treat it as office money, or apply it to its own costs.

n.0: As stakeholder the firm cannot release it on the seller's instruction alone.
n.1: The firm cannot apply a stakeholder deposit to its own costs.
n.2: It cannot simply be released to the buyer before completion either; the stakeholder terms govern.
n.4: A stakeholder deposit is client money and must not go into the office account.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm delivered a bill to a client for £1,000 and duly transferred that sum from client money to the office account. The client queries the charges, and the firm agrees to reduce (abate) its bill to £700, accepting it over-charged by £300. At the point of the reduction the firm still holds other client money for this client. The firm considers how to deal with the £300. The firm had already moved the billed amount across to its office account in the ordinary way, but the client's complaint about the level of the charges has been upheld to the extent of £300, and the firm must now work out the accounts consequences of having taken money it has agreed it should not have charged. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £300 may be retained by the firm as a contribution to its costs.
The £300 need not be repaid because the client agreed to continue instructing the firm on these facts.
The £300 remains office money because it was validly billed at the time.
The £300 over-charged is client money again and must be returned to the client or the client account.
The £300 may be kept in the office account until the client requests repayment.
Solicitor Accounts.w: When a firm abates (reduces) a bill after transferring the billed sum to the office account, the amount of the reduction was never properly the firm's money. The over-charged £300 must be treated as client money once more and repaid to the client, or returned to the client account, promptly.

n.0: The firm cannot retain the over-charged amount as a contribution to costs.
n.1: Continued instructions do not entitle the firm to keep the over-charge.
n.2: The reduction means the £300 was not validly the firm's after all.
n.4: It must be repaid promptly, not held pending a request.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has delivered a bill to a client and, applying the money it held for the client, is entitled to £600 of costs. That £600 has therefore become office money, but it remains sitting in the general client account some time after the bill was delivered, mixed with genuine client money. The cashier queries whether this is acceptable. The money is now properly due to the firm. The bill was delivered to the client several weeks ago, the entitlement to the £600 is not in doubt, and yet the sum has never been moved across to the office account, so it continues to swell the client account balance alongside money that genuinely belongs to other clients. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £600 may remain in the client account indefinitely once it is due to the firm.
The £600 must be paid to the SRA because it is mixed with client money.
The £600 may remain in the client account until the client next instructs the firm.
The £600 must be transferred out of the client account to the office account promptly.
The £600 need not be moved provided the client account is reconciled each month.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Once money the firm holds has become office money (here, billed costs the firm is entitled to), it should not be left in the client account. Retaining office money in the client account is itself a breach, so the firm must transfer the £600 to the office account promptly after the entitlement arises.

n.0: Office money must not be left in the client account indefinitely.
n.1: The money is the firm's; it is transferred to the office account, not paid to the SRA.
n.2: There is no basis for leaving it until the client next gives instructions.
n.4: Reconciliation does not cure the retention of office money in the client account.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm is given authority to operate a client's own personal bank account (in the client's name) under a power of attorney or mandate, for example to manage the affairs of a client who is unwell. The money in the account belongs to and is in the name of the client, not the firm. The firm operates the client's own account under a mandate. The bookkeeper asks about the applicable duties. To help a client who has become too unwell to manage their own affairs, the firm has been authorised under a power of attorney to run the client's personal bank account, which stays in the client's name, and the bookkeeper is unsure what obligations the Accounts Rules place on the firm in operating it. Which of the following best describes the firm's obligations under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm must treat the account as office money belonging to the firm.
The firm must transfer the money into its own general client account first.
The firm must obtain the SRA's authority before operating any client's own account on these facts as a general rule.
The firm has no obligations because the money is in the client's own name.
The firm must keep records of its dealings on the client's own account, though it is not the firm's client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where a firm operates a client's own account (in the client's name) under a mandate or power of attorney, the money is not client money held by the firm and does not go into the firm's client account. However, the SRA Accounts Rules require the firm to keep records of its dealings on that account, so its operation of the account can be reviewed.

n.0: The money is the client's, not office money belonging to the firm.
n.1: The firm does not move the client's own-account money into its general client account.
n.2: Prior SRA authority is not required to operate a client's own account under a proper mandate.
n.3: The firm does have record-keeping obligations even though the account is in the client's name.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm is opening a new account at its bank in which to hold client money and is completing the paperwork with the bank. A partner asks what requirements the SRA Accounts Rules impose on the nature and naming of an account used to hold client money. The firm carries on its activities in England and Wales. The bank has offered the firm a choice of account types and asked how the account should be styled, and the partner wants to be sure the account the firm opens will actually qualify as a client account under the rules rather than an ordinary business account that happens to hold client money. Which of the following best describes the requirement for a client account under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: It must be an account held in the name of the client rather than the firm.
It must be an account at a bank or building society, in the firm's name, whose name includes the word 'client'.
It must be an account held outside England and Wales for tax reasons.
It may be any account the firm chooses, with no particular name required.
It must be an account held personally in the name of an individual solicitor on these facts as a general rule.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A client account must be an account at a bank or building society at which the firm carries on its activities (in practice in England and Wales), held in the name of the firm, and its name must include the word 'client'. This ensures client money is clearly identifiable and segregated from the firm's own money.

n.0: It is in the firm's name (including 'client'), not the client's own name.
n.2: It is held where the firm carries on business, not offshore for tax reasons.
n.3: The account cannot be any account with no required name; 'client' must appear.
n.4: It is held in the firm's name, not an individual solicitor's personal name.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm agrees to operate a joint bank account together with a third party (for example, holding money jointly with another party's representative in a transaction). The account is not the firm's own client account but is operated jointly. The firm has some control over a joint account holding money in a matter. The bookkeeper considers the record-keeping duties. In the course of a transaction the firm ends up operating a bank account jointly with a third party, an account that is plainly not the firm's own client account but over which the firm shares control, and the bookkeeper wants to know what, if anything, the rules require the firm to record about it. Which of the following best describes the firm's obligations regarding a joint account under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm must keep records of transactions on the joint account, even though the usual client account rules do not fully apply.
The firm has no record-keeping obligations at all in respect of a joint account.
The firm must pay all money in the joint account to the SRA.
The firm must treat the joint account as its own general client account in every respect on these facts as a general rule.
The firm must close the joint account because such accounts are prohibited.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where a firm operates a joint account with another party, the money in it is not held solely by the firm and the full client account regime does not apply, but the SRA Accounts Rules still require the firm to keep appropriate records of its dealings on the joint account (for example, statements and a record of transactions), so that its handling of the money can be checked.

n.1: The firm is not free of all record-keeping duties for a joint account.
n.2: Money in a joint account is not paid to the SRA.
n.3: A joint account is not treated as the firm's own general client account in every respect.
n.4: Joint accounts are not prohibited; they are specifically provided for.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has a designated individual responsible for compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules, ensuring the firm's systems keep client money safe and that breaches are recorded and reported. A question arises about who bears this specific responsibility within the firm. The firm is an authorised body. The compliance team considers the role responsible for accounts compliance. The firm is an authorised body regulated by the SRA, and during a review of its governance the compliance team wants to confirm exactly which named role carries responsibility for the systems that keep client money safe and for recording and reporting breaches of the rules. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Every fee-earner is individually the compliance officer for their own client money.
There is no requirement for any particular person to be responsible for accounts compliance on these facts as a general rule.
The firm must have a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA) responsible for compliance with the Accounts Rules.
The firm's external bank is responsible for ensuring compliance with the Accounts Rules.
Only the SRA itself is responsible for a firm's compliance with the Accounts Rules.
Solicitor Accounts.w: An authorised firm must have a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA), who must take reasonable steps to ensure the firm and its people comply with the SRA Accounts Rules, and to record and (where serious) report breaches.
