(A COLP is separately responsible for wider regulatory compliance.)

n.0: Individual fee-earners are not each the firm's COFA.
n.1: A specific officer (the COFA) is required for accounts compliance.
n.3: The bank is not responsible for the firm's Accounts Rules compliance.
n.4: The SRA regulates but does not act as the firm's internal compliance officer.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives a cheque that is made payable not to the firm but to a third party, counsel, in settlement of counsel's fee. The firm simply forwards the cheque, unaltered, to counsel and does not pay it through any of its own accounts. The cashier queries whether this cheque is client money that must be paid into the client account. The firm never has access to the funds itself. The cheque never entered the firm's banking system at all; it arrived drawn in favour of counsel, was checked, and was placed straight back in the post to counsel, so the cashier must decide whether something the firm merely handled but never banked counts as client money for the rules. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The cheque must be endorsed by the firm and banked in the client account first.
A cheque payable to a third party and merely forwarded is not client money passing through the firm's accounts.
The cheque must be paid to the SRA as third-party money.
The cheque is client money and must be paid into the client account before forwarding on these facts.
The cheque is office money and must be recorded in the office account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money is client money where the firm holds or receives it. A cheque made payable to a third party, which the firm merely passes on without banking, is not money the firm holds or receives into its accounts, so it is not client money to be paid into the client account, though the firm should record having handled it.

n.0: There is no need to endorse and bank a cheque payable to a third party in the client account.
n.2: It is forwarded to the payee, not paid to the SRA.
n.3: The firm does not hold or receive these funds, so they are not client money to bank.
n.4: It is not the firm's office money either.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds £900 in the client account for a client's disbursement. The fee-earner needs to pay a disbursement of £1,100 on that client's behalf and asks the cashier to pay the full amount from the client account. Only £900 of client money is held for this client. The cashier considers how the payment may properly be made under the SRA Accounts Rules. The disbursement is due to a third party and cannot be delayed without prejudicing the client's matter, yet the client has provided only part of the sum required, so the cashier must find a way to make the full payment without allowing this client's ledger to fall into a debit balance. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?
o: The firm may pay the £1,100 and correct the resulting debit balance within five weeks.
The firm may pay £900 from the client's funds and must fund the £200 excess from office money.
The firm may pay the whole £1,100 from the client account despite holding only £900.
The firm may pay the whole £1,100 by using another client's money in the account.
The firm must refuse to pay the disbursement until the client provides more money.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm must not make a payment from the client account that exceeds the money held for that client, as that would overdraw the client's ledger and use other clients' money. It may pay out the £900 held and must meet the £200 excess from office money (or wait for further client funds), keeping the client ledger from going into debit.

n.0: An overdrawn client ledger is a breach even if corrected within five weeks.
n.2: Paying the whole £1,100 from client funds would overdraw the client's ledger.
n.3: Using another client's money for this payment is prohibited.
n.4: The firm can lawfully pay by funding the excess from office money, so outright refusal is not required.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives £600 from a client specifically to pay a search fee that the firm has already incurred but not yet paid to the search provider. Instead of ensuring the money is used for that purpose, the cashier posts the £600 to the office account and the search fee remains unpaid for some time. The COFA reviews the entry. The money was provided for a specific disbursement. The client handed over the money for the express purpose of clearing a search fee the firm had already run up on the matter, but instead of that money reaching the provider the fee stayed outstanding while the receipt sat in the office account, and the COFA is examining how the sum should have been handled. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The money need not be applied to the search fee at all, as the firm chooses how to use it on these facts.
The money may be used for the firm's general expenses until the fee falls due.
The money should be held as client money and used to pay the disbursement, or the disbursement paid promptly.
The money may remain in the office account indefinitely once the fee is eventually paid.
The money is office money the moment it is received for a disbursement already incurred.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money received from a client to meet a specific disbursement is client money and must be dealt with accordingly: held in the client account and applied to the disbursement, or used to pay the disbursement promptly. Posting it to the office account and leaving the disbursement unpaid misapplies the client's money and breaches the rules.

n.0: The firm cannot treat it as free to use as it chooses; it is earmarked client money.
n.1: It must not be used for the firm's general expenses.
n.3: It cannot remain in the office account indefinitely.
n.4: It does not automatically become office money simply because the disbursement was already incurred; it is the client's money for that purpose.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has held client money during its accounting period and has obtained an accountant's report which is qualified, indicating a significant risk to client money arising from the firm's compliance failures. The firm must deal with the qualified report. The report has been qualified by the reporting accountant. The firm holds client money and is not exempt. The reporting accountant has examined the firm's handling of client money and returned a report that is qualified, flagging a significant risk to client money arising from compliance failings, and the firm now has to decide what it must do with a report in that state and by when. Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation regarding a qualified accountant's report?
o: The firm must deliver every report, qualified or not, to the SRA in all cases.
The firm must deliver the qualified report to the SRA within six months of the end of the accounting period.
The firm may keep a qualified report internally and never send it to the SRA.
The firm must deliver the report to the SRA within one month of the period end on these facts as a general rule.
The firm need not deliver even a qualified report to the SRA unless asked.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm that has held client money must obtain an accountant's report within six months of the end of the accounting period. Where the report is qualified (identifying a significant risk to client money), the firm must deliver it to the SRA within that six-month period. An unqualified report generally need not be sent to the SRA unless requested.

n.0: Not every report must be delivered; it is qualified reports that must be sent (unqualified generally need not be).
n.2: A qualified report cannot simply be kept internally; it must go to the SRA.
n.3: The period is six months, not one month.
n.4: A qualified report must be delivered to the SRA, not withheld until asked.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm proposes to agree with a commercial client, in writing at the outset of the retainer, that the firm will not account to the client for interest on client money held during the matter, or will account on a specified different basis. The client is a sophisticated commercial party willing to agree this. The arrangement is recorded in a written agreement. At the very start of the retainer the firm wants to record in writing, with a commercial client well able to understand the point, that interest on any client money held will either not be paid or will be dealt with on some agreed alternative footing rather than the usual default. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules on interest?
o: The firm may vary the interest arrangement only with the SRA's approval.
The firm can never contract out of accounting for interest in any circumstances.
The firm and client may agree in writing to a different arrangement for interest, provided it is fair and the client agrees.
The firm must always pay the exact bank interest regardless of any agreement.
The firm may keep all interest without any agreement or disclosure to the client on these facts as a general rule.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The default position is that a firm must account to the client for a fair sum of interest on client money. However, the firm and client may agree a different arrangement, including that no interest (or a different amount) will be accounted for, provided this is agreed (typically in writing) and is fair, with the client having sufficient information to give informed agreement.

n.0: Varying the interest arrangement is a matter for agreement with the client, not SRA approval.
n.1: The firm can contract out by fair written agreement, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: A fair agreed arrangement can displace the default; the exact bank interest is not always payable.
n.4: The firm cannot simply keep all interest with no agreement or disclosure.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives client money and, rather than paying it into the client account without delay, the fee-earner holds the cheque in the file for some time before banking it. The firm's compliance officer is concerned about the timing. The money is undoubtedly client money. The compliance officer considers the requirement for prompt banking of client money under the SRA Accounts Rules. The cheque was received a fortnight ago in respect of a client's ongoing matter, remained clipped inside the paper file over that period, and only came to light when the compliance officer reviewed unbanked receipts during a routine file audit of open matters. Which of the following best describes it?
o: There is no requirement about when client money must be banked.
Client money need only be banked once the related matter has been completed.
Client money must be banked within exactly 30 days and never sooner.
Client money may be held outside a client account indefinitely, provided it is eventually banked.
Client money must be paid promptly into a client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that client money is paid promptly into a client account. Holding a cheque or other client money without banking it promptly is a breach of the rules, even if the money is not misapplied.

n.0: There is a clear promptness requirement.
n.1: Banking must be prompt, not deferred until the matter completes.
n.2: The requirement is prompt banking, not a fixed 30-day period.
n.3: Client money cannot be held outside a client account indefinitely.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A partner instructs a cashier to transfer £3,000 from the general client account into the office account, describing it as an advance against fees the firm expects to bill later. No bill or written notification of costs has been delivered for that sum, and the money is currently held for a client. The cashier is uneasy about carrying out the instruction. The cashier considers the position under the SRA Accounts Rules. The partner is under pressure to improve the firm's month-end figures and has framed the movement as a routine advance, but the cashier knows no bill has gone out for the sum and that the money still belongs to a client, and must decide whether it is proper to act on the instruction. Which of the following best describes the correct response?
o: The cashier may make the transfer because the firm expects to bill the fees later.
The cashier may make the transfer provided it is reversed within five weeks.
The cashier should not make the transfer, as taking the money without a bill would breach the rules.
The cashier must carry out any transfer a partner instructs without question.
The cashier may make the transfer if the partner confirms the instruction in writing on these facts.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Client money may become office money capable of transfer only once a bill or written notification of costs has been delivered. Transferring client money to the office account as an unbilled 'advance' against future fees would be an improper withdrawal in breach of the Accounts Rules, so the cashier should not make the transfer merely on the partner's say-so.

n.0: An expectation of billing later does not make the money office money now.
n.1: Reversing it later does not make an improper withdrawal permissible.
n.3: A partner's instruction does not authorise a transfer that breaches the rules.
n.4: A written instruction does not cure the absence of a bill.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has been holding client money for a client, but the matter has now concluded, all bills have been paid, and there is no longer any proper reason for the firm to continue holding the balance. The money simply remains in the client account. The bookkeeper considers what must happen to client money once there is no longer any reason to hold it, under the SRA Accounts Rules. The transaction completed some months ago, the firm's final bill has been settled in full, and a modest balance simply remains in the client account with no outstanding disbursements or further steps for the firm to take on the client's behalf. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Client money may be transferred to the firm's office account once the matter is over.
Client money must be paid to the SRA once the matter has been completed.
Client money may be kept in the client account indefinitely after the matter has ended.
Client money must be returned to the client (or the person entitled) promptly once there is no longer any proper reason to hold it.
Client money left over automatically becomes the firm's office money at the end of the matter on these facts as a general rule.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that client money is returned promptly to the client (or other person entitled to it) as soon as there is no longer any proper reason to hold it. Leaving residual balances in the client account is a breach.

n.0: It must be returned to the client, not transferred to the office account.
n.1: It is returned to the client, not paid to the SRA.
n.2: Client money cannot be kept indefinitely after the matter ends.
n.4: Leftover client money does not become the firm's office money automatically.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives £5,000 from a client on account of anticipated legal fees, for which no bill has yet been delivered, so the money is client money and is paid into the general client account. The firm operates a conventional double-entry bookkeeping system with a cash account (client side) and a client ledger for each client. The bookkeeper is asked to record the receipt correctly in the firm's accounts. The firm's client ledger for this client currently shows a nil balance, the cheque has cleared into the general client account at the bank, and the cashier is entering the transaction into the accounting system, mindful that every entry must have an equal and opposite counter-entry to keep the records in balance. Which of the following best describes the double-entry required to record this receipt?
o: Credit the client cash account and credit the client's ledger, with no debit entry.
Record the receipt on the office side only, as the money will later fund the firm's fees.
Debit the office cash account and credit the client's ledger on the office side.
Debit the client's ledger and credit the client cash account, both on the client side.
Debit the client cash account and credit the client's ledger, both on the client side.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A receipt of client money increases the client bank balance and creates a liability to the client. In double entry that is recorded by debiting the client cash account (money in) and crediting the client's ledger account (the firm owes it to the client), both entries on the client side.

n.0: Every entry needs an equal and opposite entry; two credits do not balance.
n.1: Money received on account before a bill is client money and is recorded on the client side.
n.2: Client money is recorded on the client side, not the office side.
n.3: This reverses the entries; a receipt is a debit to cash, not a credit.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives £2,000 from a client at the outset of a matter, paid in advance to cover both the firm's anticipated legal fees and potential disbursements as the work progresses. No bill has yet been delivered and no disbursements have yet been incurred. The cashier must classify the £2,000 on receipt for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules. The money is a general payment on account. The client handed over the money as a single general payment at the start of the retainer to keep things moving, without allocating it between fees and specific disbursements, and the cashier must classify the whole sum correctly at the point it is received rather than waiting to see how it is later spent. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £2,000?
o: The £2,000 need not be banked until a disbursement is actually incurred.
The £2,000 may be retained in the office account until the first bill.
The whole £2,000 is office money because it will fund the firm's fees.
The whole £2,000 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
Half is office money for fees and half is client money for disbursements.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money paid in advance generally on account of costs and disbursements, before any bill is delivered or disbursement incurred, is client money in its entirety. It must be paid promptly into the client account. It becomes office money, in whole or part, only as bills are delivered or the firm is entitled to reimbursement.

n.0: It must be banked promptly, not held unbanked until a disbursement arises.
n.1: It cannot be retained in the office account pending a bill.
n.2: None of it is office money yet, as no bill has been delivered.
n.4: There is no automatic half-and-half split; the whole sum is client money on account.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm delivers a bill to a client for £800 in respect of completed work. The client sends a single cheque for £1,000, intending £800 to settle the bill and £200 to be held on account of future work not yet billed. The bookkeeper must decide how the £1,000 is classified and dealt with under the SRA Accounts Rules. The covering letter with the cheque makes clear the client's intention that part settles the outstanding bill and part is a payment in advance for further work the firm will carry out later, and the cashier must record and route the two elements correctly rather than treating the whole payment as one. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £1,000 receipt?
o: The £1,000 may be retained in the office account and apportioned at the year end.
The £200 is office money because it exceeds the amount of the bill.
The whole £1,000 is office money because a bill has been delivered.
The whole £1,000 is client money because it arrived in one cheque.
The £800 is office money and the £200 is client money, which must reach the client account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The £800 matching the delivered bill is office money the firm is entitled to; the £200 paid on account of unbilled future work is client money. The client money element must be paid promptly into the client account, whether by splitting the receipt or banking the whole sum into client account and transferring the £800 out.

n.0: The client money element must reach the client account promptly, not await a year-end apportionment.
n.1: The £200 on account of future costs is client money, not office money.
n.2: Only the billed £800 is office money; the £200 on account is client money.
n.3: The £200 relating to unbilled work is client money, not client money merely because of one cheque; the whole is not client money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds money for several different clients in its general client account. The bookkeeper is asked whether money held for one client can be used to make a payment on behalf of a different client, on the basis that all the money is in the same bank account. The bookkeeper considers whether client money may be used across different clients under the SRA Accounts Rules. All the clients' funds sit together in the firm's general client account at the bank, and a fee-earner suggests that, because the pooled balance is more than enough overall, a payment for one client could be met even though little is held for that particular client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money held for one client must not be used for another client; each client's money is accounted for separately.
Money held for one client may be used for another provided it is replaced within a week.
Money in the general client account may be used freely for any client, as it is all pooled together.
Money held for one client may be used for another if the two clients are related.
Money held for one client may be used for another with the firm's own authorisation.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Although client money for different clients may be held in one general client account, the firm must account for each client's money separately (through client ledgers) and must not use one client's money for the benefit of another. Doing so is a breach of the SRA Accounts Rules.

n.1: Replacing it quickly does not make using another client's money permissible.
n.2: Money in the general client account is not a free pool; it is held for individual clients.
n.3: The clients being related does not permit it.
n.4: The firm cannot authorise using one client's money for another.

Solicitor Accounts.q: After a matter concludes, a firm is left holding a residual balance of £900 for a former client whom it cannot trace despite reasonable efforts. The firm wishes to withdraw the money from the client account and pay it to charity. The residual balance exceeds £500 and the client cannot be found. The firm wants to clear the balance in a compliant way. Long after the matter ended the firm is still holding a leftover balance of £900 for a client who has vanished despite genuine efforts to trace them, and the firm would like to clear it by giving it to charity, mindful that the sum is above the level at which it could act on its own. Which of the following best describes what the firm must do under the SRA Accounts Rules for a balance of this size?
o: The firm may pay any residual balance to charity without the SRA's authority whatever its size on these facts.
The firm must obtain the SRA's prior authority before withdrawing a residual balance exceeding £500 to pay to charity.
The firm may simply transfer the balance to its own office account as unclaimed.
The firm must keep the balance in the client account indefinitely and take no step.
The firm must pay the balance to the former client's bank despite being unable to trace them.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The Accounts Rules allow residual client balances to be withdrawn and paid to charity where the firm has taken reasonable steps to return the money and keeps records. For balances of £500 or less per client matter this may be done without SRA authority; for larger balances (such as £900) the firm must obtain the SRA's prior authority before withdrawing.

n.0: Larger residual balances (over £500) require the SRA's authority; it is not unrestricted.
n.2: The firm cannot simply take the residual balance to its own office account.
n.3: Leaving it indefinitely with no step is not the compliant route.
n.4: The client cannot be traced, so payment to their bank is not possible; the charity route with SRA authority applies.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm undertaking publicly funded work receives a payment from the Legal Aid Agency in respect of the firm's costs on a matter. The cashier is used to the rule that money received for the firm's costs is client money until a bill is delivered, and asks whether this Legal Aid Agency payment must go into the client account or may be paid into the office account. The payment is for the firm's own costs. The firm does a good deal of publicly funded work and receives regular payments from the Legal Aid Agency covering its costs on such matters, and the cashier wants to apply the correct treatment to this receipt rather than assuming it must follow the ordinary route for money received in respect of costs. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Payments from the Legal Aid Agency for the firm's costs may be paid into the office account.
The payment must be split equally between the client and office accounts.
The payment must be held in cash until the matter is finally assessed.
The payment must be paid into a separate designated deposit account for the client.
The payment must always be paid into the client account like any other receipt.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules make specific provision for legal aid work: payments received from the Legal Aid Agency for the firm's costs may be paid into the office account, even though they include sums that would otherwise be client money, reflecting the way legal aid funding operates. The firm must still deal with any client money element appropriately.

n.1: There is no automatic equal split rule for such payments.
n.2: The payment is not held in cash pending assessment.
n.3: A designated deposit account is not required for a Legal Aid Agency costs payment.
n.4: Legal aid payments for costs need not be routed through the client account like ordinary receipts.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A person who is a client of a firm, but has no active matter requiring legal services, asks the firm to receive a sum into its client account and pay it out later to third parties the client will nominate, purely to move the money. No underlying legal transaction or service by the firm is connected with the payments. The firm's compliance officer considers whether this is permitted. The compliance officer considers the prohibition on providing banking facilities under the SRA Accounts Rules. The client explains that the firm's client account would simply be a convenient staging point for moving the money to associates abroad, and the compliance officer notes there is no retainer, transaction, or piece of legal work to which any of the proposed payments relates. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The firm may pass any money the client wishes through the client account without restriction on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may do this provided each payment is under a fixed statutory limit.
The firm may do this provided it charges the client a fee for handling the money.
The firm must not use the client account to provide banking facilities for payments unconnected with a legal service or transaction.
The firm may do this provided the source of the money is recorded on the file.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules prohibit using a client account to provide banking facilities through the firm: payments into and out of the client account must relate to the delivery of regulated services or an underlying legal transaction. Passing unconnected funds through the account is a breach and a money laundering risk.

n.0: The client account cannot be used freely to move any money.
n.1: There is no payment threshold that permits banking facilities.
n.2: Charging a fee does not make a prohibited banking facility permissible.
n.4: Recording the source does not make it permissible.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm arranges for a client's money in a transaction to be held not by the firm but through a third-party managed account operated by a regulated payment provider, so that payments in and out are handled by that provider rather than through the firm's own client account. The bookkeeper asks how money handled in this way is treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm never itself holds or receives the money. Under the arrangement the payment provider receives the funds and makes payments on the agreed terms, the firm gives instructions but never itself receives or controls the money, and the bookkeeper wants to understand how, if at all, this money features in the firm's own client account obligations. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money held through a compliant third-party managed account is not client money held by the firm.
The firm must still pay the money into its own client account before it can be used.
Use of a third-party managed account is prohibited under the SRA Accounts Rules.
The firm must reconcile the third-party managed account as if it were its own client account.
The firm must treat the money as office money because a payment provider holds it.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The Accounts Rules permit a firm to use a third-party managed account (TPMA). Because the firm does not itself hold or receive the money, it is not client money held by the firm, and the usual client account obligations (such as reconciliations) do not apply to it, though the firm must take steps to satisfy itself the arrangement is appropriate and inform the client.

n.1: The point of a TPMA is that the money is not routed through the firm's own client account.
n.2: TPMAs are expressly permitted, not prohibited.
n.3: Because the money is not the firm's client money, the firm does not reconcile the TPMA as its own client account.
n.4: Money in a TPMA is not office money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A client asks a firm to receive a very large sum into the client account from an unexplained overseas source and then to pay it out quickly to third parties, with the legal work involved being minimal and disproportionate to the sums moving through the account. The cashier and the firm's compliance officer are uneasy. The transactions show classic warning signs of money laundering. The account activity is disproportionate to the underlying legal work. The client wants the firm to take in a very large and unexplained sum from abroad and shunt it straight out again to third parties, while the actual legal work is trivial and wholly out of proportion to the money involved, and the cashier and compliance officer both sense that something is badly wrong. Which of the following best describes the correct response consistent with the Accounts Rules and wider obligations?
o: The firm should not allow the client account to be used in this way and should consider its anti-money-laundering obligations, including any reporting duty.
The firm may pass the funds through the client account freely as the client has requested on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm must simply return the money to the overseas source without further thought.
The firm may proceed provided the money leaves the account within 48 hours.
The firm may proceed provided it charges a higher fee for handling the money.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Using the client account to pass funds through with little or no connected legal work is prohibited (no banking facilities) and is a classic money-laundering red flag. The firm should not facilitate it, must consider its anti-money-laundering duties (including customer due diligence and any obligation to make a suspicious activity report), and should not simply move the money as instructed.

n.1: The firm must not pass such funds through the client account freely.
n.2: Simply returning the money without considering AML reporting duties may itself be inappropriate (tipping off/failure to report).
n.3: A quick turnaround does not cure the banking-facilities prohibition or AML concerns.
n.4: Charging a higher fee does not make facilitating suspicious transactions permissible.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's client account ledger for a particular client shows that a payment out on behalf of that client would exceed the money actually held for them, so that the client's ledger would show a debit balance — in effect, using other clients' money. The bookkeeper is asked whether such a payment may be made. The bookkeeper considers the rule against overdrawn client ledgers under the SRA Accounts Rules. The proposed payment is a disbursement the fee-earner wishes to make on behalf of the client, but the client's ledger shows only a small credit balance, so meeting the payment in full would push that individual ledger into a debit position for a time. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A client ledger may be overdrawn provided the firm records the reason on the file.
A client ledger may be overdrawn if no client ends up out of pocket overall.
A payment must not be made that would result in a debit balance on the client's ledger, as this would use other clients' money.
There is no restriction on a client ledger showing a debit balance.
A client ledger may be overdrawn provided the shortfall is made good within a month on these facts as a general rule.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm must only ever pay out of the client account money held for the particular client on whose behalf the payment is made. A payment that would overdraw an individual client's ledger (a debit balance) would in effect use other clients' money and is a breach of the SRA Accounts Rules.

n.0: Recording a reason does not permit an overdrawn client ledger.
n.1: Overall neutrality does not permit using one client's money for another.
n.3: There is a clear restriction against a debit balance on a client ledger.
n.4: A short repayment period does not permit overdrawing the ledger.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's cashier mistakenly pays £700 of one client's money out of the client account to settle a search fee that should have been met from office money, so that a shortfall now exists on the client side and another client's ledger is effectively affected. The error is discovered during a routine check. The COFA considers what the firm must do about the shortfall under the SRA Accounts Rules. The mistaken payment has already left the client account and reached the payee, the affected client's ledger now shows less than it should, and the COFA is focused on what the firm must do to restore the position and put right the breach as soon as it has come to light. Which of the following best describes the correct action?
o: The firm must correct the breach promptly and promptly replace any shortfall from its own money.
The firm must report the breach to the police before taking any corrective action.
The firm may correct the shortfall only if the affected client complains.
The firm may leave the shortfall until the end of the accounting period.
The firm need take no action provided the overall client account balance is positive.
Solicitor Accounts.w: On discovering a breach of the Accounts Rules, the firm must put it right promptly. Where client money is improperly withdrawn or a shortfall arises, the firm must replace the missing money promptly from its own (office) money, so that clients' funds are restored. The breach should also be recorded and, if serious, reported.

n.1: The rules require prompt correction; police reporting is not the prescribed step here.
n.2: Correction is required regardless of whether the client complains.
n.3: The shortfall must be replaced promptly, not left to the period end.
n.4: A positive overall balance does not cure the shortfall on an individual client's funds.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's cashier tends to write up the client ledgers in batches some weeks after transactions occur, so at any given time the ledgers do not reflect recent receipts and payments and do not show an accurate current balance for each client. The COFA is concerned about this practice. The firm holds client money for many clients. The delay means that at any moment the ledgers understate or overstate what is really held for each client, so a fee-earner checking a balance before making a payment cannot rely on the figure shown, and the COFA is worried the practice falls short of what the rules require of the firm's records. Which of the following best describes the requirement for accounting records under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The records must be accurate and contemporaneous and show the current balance on each client ledger.
The records may be written up whenever convenient, provided they eventually balance.
The records need not show a running balance, only the total client account balance.
The records need only be written up once a year before the accountant's report.
The records may omit individual client ledgers if a global client account is reconciled on these facts.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The Accounts Rules require accurate and contemporaneous records of dealings with client money, including a separate client ledger for each client showing all receipts and payments and the current balance. Writing up ledgers weeks late means the records are neither contemporaneous nor able to show accurate current balances, which is a breach.

n.1: Records must be contemporaneous, not written up whenever convenient.
n.2: Each client ledger must show a running/current balance, not only the global total.
n.3: Annual write-up is not contemporaneous record-keeping.
n.4: Individual client ledgers are required; a global reconciliation does not replace them.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm delivers numerous bills to clients throughout the year and needs to be able to demonstrate, and readily locate, all the bills and other written notifications of costs it has given. The bookkeeper is designing the record-keeping systems. The firm must be able to show its costs notifications on request. The records must be readily accessible. The firm issues a steady stream of bills and other costs notifications to clients across the year, and, knowing that money can only move from client to office account once such a notification has gone out, the bookkeeper wants a system that lets the firm find and demonstrate all of them quickly. Which of the following best describes the requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules regarding bills?
o: The firm need not keep any record of the bills it has delivered.
The firm may rely solely on the individual client files with no central record on these facts as a general rule.
The firm must keep a central record of all bills and other written notifications of costs given to clients.
The firm must send a copy of every bill to the SRA as it is issued.
The firm must keep bills only for matters that are still ongoing.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require a firm to keep a central record (readily accessible) of all bills and other written notifications of costs given to clients. This allows the firm and any reviewer to check the basis on which money has been transferred from client to office account, since costs may only be transferred once a bill or notification has been delivered.

n.0: The firm cannot dispense with keeping a record of bills delivered.
n.1: A central record is required, not merely reliance on scattered individual files.
n.3: Bills are not routinely sent to the SRA as issued.
n.4: Records of bills are not confined to ongoing matters; the central record covers bills generally.

Solicitor Accounts.q: Facing a temporary shortage in the office account, a solicitor uses £2,000 of client money from the client account to pay the firm's rent, intending to replace the money a week later, which the firm does. No client authorised the use of their money for this purpose. The COFA discovers what has happened. The COFA considers the position under the SRA Accounts Rules. The office account was temporarily short of funds when the rent fell due, the solicitor dipped into the client account to cover it and topped the client account back up a week later, and the COFA must assess whether the temporary and fully-reimbursed nature of the borrowing makes any difference. Which of the following best describes it?
o: There is no breach provided no individual client's ledger went into debit on these facts.
There is no breach because the money was replaced within a week.
Using client money to meet the firm's expenses is a serious breach even if it is replaced.
The use is acceptable if the firm records its reason on the file.
The use is acceptable because it was a short-term, temporary measure.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Client money may only be used for the purpose for which it is held. Using it to meet the firm's own expenses, such as rent, is an improper withdrawal and a serious breach of the Accounts Rules — potentially raising integrity issues — even where the firm intends to and does replace the money shortly afterwards.

n.0: The breach lies in the improper use, not only in whether a ledger went into debit.
n.1: Replacing the money does not undo the breach of misusing client money.
n.3: Recording a reason does not authorise using client money for the firm's expenses.
n.4: Being short-term or temporary does not make misuse of client money acceptable.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives money from a client on account of costs for work the firm has not yet done and for which no bill has yet been delivered. The bookkeeper must classify this money for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules, as it affects which account it goes into. The bookkeeper considers how money on account of costs is treated before a bill is raised. The client has paid the sum in advance to fund forthcoming work on the matter, the firm has not yet carried out that work, and no bill or other written notification of costs has been sent, so the bookkeeper must decide how to treat the payment on receipt. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Money on account of costs is always office money and goes straight into the office account on these facts.
Money on account of costs belongs to the firm immediately and may be spent at once.
Money on account of costs is treated as a gift to the firm from the client.
Money on account of costs, before a bill is delivered, is client money and must go into the client account.
Money on account of costs need not be banked at all until the bill is raised.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money received from a client generally on account of costs for work not yet billed is client money and must be paid into the client account. It becomes office money (which may be transferred to the office account) only once the firm has delivered a bill or other written notification of costs.

n.0: It is client money until a bill is delivered, not immediately office money.
n.1: It does not belong to the firm to spend before a bill is raised.
n.2: It is the client's money on account, not a gift to the firm.
n.4: It must be banked promptly in the client account, not held unbanked.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm needs to make a payment out of the client account on behalf of a client — for example to pay a disbursement or to return money to the client. The bookkeeper is asked when withdrawals from the client account are permitted under the SRA Accounts Rules. The payment relates to the client for whom the money is held. The bookkeeper considers the permitted withdrawals from a client account. The firm holds a credit balance for the client on that matter, the intended payment is a disbursement due to be met from those funds, and the bookkeeper wants to confirm the circumstances in which money may properly leave the client account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Client money may be withdrawn only for the purpose it is held, on the client instructions or as permitted, and only up to funds held for that client.
Client money may never be withdrawn from the client account for any reason at all.
Client money may be withdrawn freely provided the total client account balance stays positive on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Client money may be withdrawn from the client account for any purpose the firm chooses.
Client money may be withdrawn only after the SRA has approved each individual payment.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, client money may be withdrawn from the client account only for the purpose for which it is being held, following the client's instructions or as otherwise permitted by the rules, and only to the extent of the money held for that particular client (so as not to overdraw the client's ledger).

n.1: Client money can be withdrawn for proper purposes; it is not frozen entirely.
n.2: A positive overall balance does not permit overdrawing an individual client's ledger.
n.3: Withdrawals cannot be for any purpose the firm chooses.
n.4: Routine withdrawals do not need individual SRA approval.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm's bank levies charges relating to the operation of the general client account, and the firm also incurs charges on its office account. The cashier is unsure how the bank charges on the client account should be met and recorded, and asks whether they can be deducted from the client money in the account. No client has agreed to bear the firm's bank charges. The bank has debited the charges directly, and the cashier is deciding which side of the firm's books should bear them and from which pot of money they should ultimately be met, conscious that anything taken from client money would leave the clients' funds short. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the client account bank charges?
o: The bank charges may be left as a debit on the client cash account until year end.
The firm's bank charges are the firm's own expense and must be met from office money.
The bank charges must be paid to the SRA rather than the bank.
The bank charges may be deducted proportionately from the client money held.
The bank charges may be deducted from the ledger of the client last paid in.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Bank charges on the operation of the firm's accounts are the firm's own running costs and are office money expenses. They must be met from office money and must not be deducted from client money, which would reduce the funds held for clients and create a shortfall on the client account.

n.0: Leaving a debit on the client cash account would mean client money bears the firm's costs.
n.2: Bank charges are paid to the bank, not the SRA; the point is that they are office money.
n.3: Client money must not be reduced to pay the firm's bank charges.
n.4: The charges cannot be taken from an individual client's ledger.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has held and dealt with client money throughout its accounting period. As the period ends, the COFA is arranging for an independent accountant to examine the firm's compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm is not exempt from the requirement. The COFA considers the deadline for obtaining the accountant's report under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has operated a busy client account throughout the year with numerous receipts and payments across many matters, it does not fall within any exemption, and the COFA is now planning the year-end compliance steps and needs to know the deadline that applies to the independent accountant's examination. Which of the following best describes the requirement?
o: The firm must obtain an accountant's report within six months of the end of the accounting period.
The firm must obtain an accountant's report only once every three years.
The firm need not obtain an accountant's report unless the SRA requests one.
The firm must obtain an accountant's report within two years of the end of the period on these facts.
The firm must obtain an accountant's report within one month of the end of the period.
Solicitor Accounts.w: A firm that has held client money in an accounting period must obtain an accountant's report within six months of the end of that period. Where the report is qualified (identifying a significant risk to client money), the firm must deliver it to the SRA within that same six-month period.

n.1: The report is obtained for each accounting period, not once every three years.
n.2: The obligation is automatic for firms that have held client money, not dependent on an SRA request.
n.3: Two years is longer than the six-month requirement.
n.4: One month is far shorter than the six-month period allowed.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has held client money for a client in its general client account and has determined that a fair sum of interest of £25 is due to the client for the period the money was held. The general client account itself pools many clients' money and the bank pays interest to the firm on the whole balance. The cashier must decide from which of the firm's funds the £25 interest paid to the client is met. The firm has calculated a fair sum of interest for the period the client's money was held, the money sat in the pooled general client account rather than a separate designated account, and the cashier now needs to identify which of the firm's funds should bear the payment to the client. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment?
o: The £25 must be taken from other clients' money in the general client account.
The £25 need not be paid because it was earned on a pooled account.
The £25 interest paid to the client is met from the firm's office money.
The £25 must be paid to the client from the SRA compensation fund.
The £25 must be deducted from the client's own capital held in the account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where client money is held in a general client account, the interest the bank pays belongs to the firm, and the firm's obligation to account to the client for a fair sum of interest is met out of the firm's own office money. It is not taken from other clients' funds, nor from the client's own money held in the account.

n.0: Interest due to a client is not taken from other clients' money.
n.1: The firm must account for a fair sum of interest even on a pooled account.
n.3: It is paid by the firm from office money, not from the compensation fund.
n.4: It is not deducted from the client's own capital; it is additional, from office money.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives £2,000 of client money but, through a posting error, the cashier pays it into the firm's office account instead of the client account. The mistake comes to light during the next reconciliation, by which time the money has been sitting in the office account for a period. The firm wants to put matters right. The money is undoubtedly client money. The receipt was correctly identified as client money at the outset, but a keying error sent it to the wrong ledger and the wrong bank account, and it was only when the balances were checked that the misplacement came to light, leaving the firm to decide how quickly and by what route to put it right. Which of the following best describes the correct action under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may leave the money in the office account until the matter concludes on these facts.
The firm must report the error to the police before correcting it.
The firm may leave the money in the office account as the error was innocent.
The firm must transfer the money into the client account promptly on discovering the error.
The firm need do nothing provided the office account is never overdrawn.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Client money paid into the office account in error must be transferred into the client account promptly once the error is discovered, so that the client money is properly protected. The mistake is a breach that must be corrected without delay, and recorded; an innocent cause does not excuse leaving the money misplaced.

n.0: It cannot be left in the office account until the matter concludes.
n.1: Police reporting is not the prescribed step; prompt correction is.
n.2: An innocent error does not permit leaving client money in the office account.
n.4: The breach must be corrected regardless of whether the office account stays in credit.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm has held only a very small amount of client money during its accounting period, and the average and maximum client account balances have remained low throughout. The COFA queries whether the firm is nonetheless obliged to obtain and deliver an accountant's report, given the cost involved. The firm holds no Legal Aid Agency money. The COFA considers the exemption from the accountant's report requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm's client account activity has been minimal, with only occasional small balances passing through during the period, and the COFA is weighing the cost of an accountant's report against whether the firm's limited handling of client money brings it within one of the exemptions in the rules. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A firm is exempt whenever it employs a qualified in-house accountant.
A firm may be exempt where the client money held stays within the low thresholds set by the rules.
Every firm that holds any client money at all must always obtain an accountant's report.
A firm is exempt from the report requirement only if it has never held any client money.
A firm is exempt from the report requirement simply by notifying the SRA in advance.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The Accounts Rules exempt a firm from obtaining an accountant's report where the only client money held is money from the Legal Aid Agency, or where the average client account balance does not exceed a low prescribed figure and the maximum balance stays within a prescribed cap during the period. Otherwise the report is required.

n.0: Employing an in-house accountant is not the basis of the exemption.
n.2: There are exemptions, so it is not the case that every firm holding client money must always obtain a report.
n.3: Firms that hold small amounts within the thresholds can be exempt even though they have held some client money.
n.4: Mere notification to the SRA does not create the exemption; the threshold conditions must be met.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm is reviewing its record-keeping and asks how long it must retain its accounting records, such as client ledgers, records of bills, and statements and reconciliations, once they have been created. A member of staff suggests they can be destroyed after a year to save storage. The firm holds client money in the ordinary course of its work. The firm generates a large volume of ledger cards, bills, bank statements and reconciliations each year, storage space is at a premium, and a member of staff has proposed a routine clear-out to reduce the archive, prompting the COFA to check exactly how long the accounting records must be preserved. Which of the following best describes the requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: There is no minimum period for which accounting records must be kept.
The firm may destroy its accounting records after one year.
The firm must keep its accounting records for at least twelve months only.
The firm need only keep records until the next accountant's report is obtained.
The firm must keep its accounting records for at least six years.
Solicitor Accounts.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require a firm to keep, and retain for at least six years, accurate and contemporaneous accounting records showing its dealings with client money, including client ledgers, records of bills, and reconciliations. Destroying them after a year would breach the retention requirement.

n.0: There is a specific minimum retention period.
n.1: Records cannot be destroyed after only one year.
n.2: Twelve months is well short of the six-year requirement.
n.3: Retention is not tied to the next accountant's report; a minimum of six years applies.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A solicitor receives a cheque for £1,500 of client money but, wishing to smooth the firm's own cash position, deliberately holds it for four days before paying it into the client account, even though it could have been banked at once. The delay is a conscious choice rather than an administrative oversight. The COFA reviews the incident. The COFA considers its seriousness under the SRA Accounts Rules. The solicitor could have banked the cheque the same day but chose not to, using the firm's temporary hold on the money to ease its own cash position, and the COFA is weighing how seriously the rules treat a delay that was a conscious decision rather than a mere oversight. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The delay is acceptable provided no client suffers actual financial loss.
The delay is a matter for the firm's internal policy and not the rules.
Deliberately delaying the banking of client money is a serious breach of the rules.
A delay of only four days is never a breach of the rules.
The delay is acceptable because the money was eventually banked in full.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Client money must be paid promptly into the client account. A deliberate decision to withhold client money from the client account to benefit the firm's cash flow is a serious breach, and the deliberate nature aggravates it; it may also raise integrity concerns, regardless of whether the money is later banked in full or a client suffers loss.

n.0: Breach does not depend on a client suffering actual loss.
n.1: Prompt banking is a rule requirement, not merely internal policy.
n.3: A short delay can still breach the promptness requirement, especially if deliberate.
n.4: Eventual banking does not excuse a deliberate failure to bank promptly.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm holds a substantial sum of client money in its general client account for some months while a transaction proceeds, and the account earns interest. The client asks whether they are entitled to any of that interest. The firm has no separate agreement with the client varying the position. The bookkeeper considers the firm's obligations as to interest on client money under the SRA Accounts Rules. Interest rates over the period have been such that the account earned a meaningful sum, the client has now asked about it on completion of the matter, and the firm wants to be sure it meets its obligations rather than simply absorbing the interest into its own income without consideration. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm must account to the client for a fair sum of interest on the client money held.
The firm need not consider interest unless the client expressly demands it.
The firm must pay all interest earned to the SRA compensation fund.
The firm may keep all interest earned on client money as its own office money.
The firm must pay the client the exact interest the bank credited, never more or less.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules the firm must account to clients for a fair sum of interest on client money held, unless a different arrangement has been agreed in writing. What is fair depends on the amount and the period held; it need not be the precise sum the bank paid, but the firm cannot simply retain the interest.

n.1: The obligation arises regardless of whether the client demands interest.
n.2: Interest is accounted for to the client, not paid to the compensation fund.
n.3: The firm cannot simply keep the interest as its own.
n.4: The obligation is to account for a fair sum, not necessarily the exact bank interest.

Solicitor Accounts.q: A firm receives money from a client specifically to pay a professional disbursement, such as counsel's fee, that has already been incurred but not yet paid. The cashier is deciding whether the money is client money or may be treated as office money on receipt. The money is earmarked for a specific professional disbursement already incurred but unpaid. The cashier must classify and handle it correctly. The client has sent money specifically so that a particular professional disbursement, counsel's fee, can be settled, a fee that has already been run up but not yet paid, and the cashier must decide whether that earmarked money is the client's or can be treated as the firm's on receipt. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment?
o: It is automatically office money the moment it is received because the disbursement was already incurred on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It need not be banked at all provided the disbursement is paid eventually.
It must be paid directly to the SRA pending payment of the disbursement.
It is client money to be paid into the client account, unless and until it is properly used to pay the disbursement or otherwise becomes office money.
It may be spent on the firm's general expenses because it relates to an incurred cost.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Money received from a client to pay a specific professional disbursement is client money and must be paid into the client account and applied to that disbursement (or otherwise dealt with under the rules). It does not automatically become office money simply because the disbursement has already been incurred; the firm must handle it as the client's money for the intended purpose.

n.0: It does not automatically become office money on receipt merely because the cost was incurred.
n.1: It must be banked promptly in the client account, not left unbanked.
n.2: It is not paid to the SRA; it is held as client money and applied to the disbursement.
n.4: It cannot be spent on the firm's general expenses.

Solicitor Accounts.q: Rather than holding a client's substantial sum in the pooled general client account, a firm opens a separate designated deposit account in the firm's name for that particular client, into which the money is paid and on which the bank pays interest. The client asks who is entitled to the interest that the designated account earns. The account holds only this client's money. The firm decided that the size of the sum and the length of time it would be held justified a separate account rather than pooling it with other clients' funds, and the client, aware that interest rates make the sum meaningful, now wants to know precisely how the interest on that dedicated account is to be dealt with. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The interest belongs to the firm because the account is in the firm's name.
The interest is shared equally between the firm and the client.
All the interest actually earned on the designated deposit account belongs to that client.
The firm keeps the interest and pays the client only a fair sum from office money.
The interest must be paid to the SRA because it arises on a designated account.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where client money is held in a separate designated deposit account holding only that client's money, the interest the account actually earns belongs to that client and must be accounted for to them in full. This differs from a general client account, where the firm keeps the bank interest but must account to the client for a fair sum.

n.0: The account being in the firm's name does not make the interest the firm's.
n.1: The interest is not shared; it all belongs to the client.
n.3: The 'fair sum from office money' approach applies to a general client account, not a designated deposit account.
n.4: The interest belongs to the client, not the SRA.

Solicitor Accounts.q: After a matter completes, a firm is left holding a residual balance of £50 in the client account for a former client. Despite reasonable efforts over a period, the firm cannot trace the client to return the money, and the balance simply remains in the client account. The COFA wants to clear the balance properly. The sum is small and the client cannot be found. The firm has written to the client's last known address more than once, made other reasonable enquiries to locate them, and kept a record of those efforts, but the money still cannot be returned, and the COFA wants to clear the small balance from the client account in a compliant way. Which of the following best describes how the firm may deal with this residual balance under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may pay the balance to a charity, having taken reasonable steps to trace the client and kept records.
The firm must pay the balance to the client's bank even though the client cannot be traced.
The firm may transfer the balance to its own office account as unclaimed profit.
The firm may keep the balance indefinitely in the client account and take no further step.
The firm must obtain the SRA's prior written authority before paying away any residual balance on these facts.
Solicitor Accounts.w: Where a firm holds a residual client balance and, despite reasonable steps, cannot return it to the client, the Accounts Rules permit the money to be withdrawn and paid to a charity, provided the firm has taken reasonable steps to trace and return it and keeps appropriate records. For small balances, SRA prior authority is not required.

n.1: The client cannot be traced, so paying it to the client's bank is not possible.
n.2: The residual balance cannot be taken as the firm's own profit.
n.3: Leaving it indefinitely with no further step is not the prescribed route.
n.4: For a small balance like this, prior SRA authority is not required if the conditions are met.

Land Law.q: A landlord granted a 20-year headlease of a commercial building. The head tenant later breached a covenant in the headlease, and the landlord has now forfeited the headlease for that breach. A sub-tenant, who occupies the second floor of the building under a sub-lease granted out of the headlease, was in no way responsible for the head tenant's breach and has always complied with its own obligations. The forfeiture of the headlease would ordinarily bring the sub-lease to an end as well, leaving the innocent sub-tenant without any premises from which to run its business. The sub-tenant wishes to protect its position and remain in occupation of its part. Which of the following best describes the sub-tenant's position?
o: The sub-tenant has no remedy, because forfeiture of the headlease automatically ends all sub-leases with no relief.
The sub-tenant may prevent the forfeiture of the headlease altogether by paying the head-rent.
The sub-tenant may apply for relief from forfeiture and, if granted, be vested with a new lease of their part.
The sub-tenant may only claim damages from their immediate landlord and cannot keep possession.
The sub-tenant becomes the freeholder's direct tenant automatically on the same terms.
Land Law.w: Forfeiture of a headlease destroys sub-leases derived from it, but a sub-tenant (or mortgagee) may apply for relief under s.146(4) LPA 1925. The court may vest a new lease of the sub-tenant's part in them, usually for no longer than the original sub-term.

n.0: Relief is available to sub-tenants under s.146(4); forfeiture is not the automatic end of their rights.
n.1: A sub-tenant cannot simply prevent forfeiture of the headlease by paying the head-rent.
n.3: Relief can restore possession by a new lease, so the sub-tenant is not confined to damages.
n.4: There is no automatic direct tenancy with the freeholder on forfeiture.

Land Law.q: Immediately after granting a legal mortgage over their home to a bank, the borrower fell into arrears with the monthly mortgage payments. The bank wishes to take possession of the property with a view to selling it. The borrower argues that the bank has no right to possession unless and until it first obtains a court order establishing that the borrower is in default, and that the right to possession cannot arise merely from the grant of the mortgage itself. The bank seeks advice on the nature and timing of its right to possession of the mortgaged home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A legal mortgagee may never take possession of a mortgaged dwelling in any circumstances.
A legal mortgagee has no right to possession until the borrower has defaulted for at least six months. in the absence of any contrary agreement
A legal mortgagee has a right to possession that arises as soon as the mortgage is made, subject to statutory and equitable restrictions for dwellings.
A legal mortgagee acquires a right to possession only after exercising its power of sale.
A legal mortgagee must first obtain the borrower's written consent before taking possession.
Land Law.w: A legal mortgagee's right to possession arises from the grant of the mortgage itself, 'before the ink is dry' (Four-Maids v Dudley Marshall). In practice, for a dwelling the right is subject to statutory controls (s.36 Administration of Justice Act 1970) allowing the court to postpone possession where the borrower can remedy the default.

n.0: A mortgagee can take possession of a dwelling, subject to the AJA 1970 protections.
n.1: The right to possession does not depend on a fixed period of default.
n.3: The right to possession is independent of, and precedes, exercise of the power of sale.
n.4: The borrower's consent is not required for a legal mortgagee to seek possession.

Land Law.q: The owner of a house has the benefit of an express legal right of way, granted by deed, over a strip of a neighbour's land, giving vehicular access to the public road. The neighbour, who owns the land burdened by the right of way, has recently erected a locked gate across the route and refuses to provide a key, physically preventing the dominant owner from getting through to the road. The dominant owner needs the access restored and seeks advice on the appropriate remedy against the neighbour for this substantial interference with the right of way. Which of the following best describes the remedy available?
o: The dominant owner must apply to modify the easement before the gate can be removed.
The dominant owner may seek an injunction requiring removal of the obstruction to the right of way.
The dominant owner has no remedy, because an easement gives no right to unobstructed passage, on these facts.
The dominant owner may only claim damages and cannot compel removal of the gate.
The easement is extinguished as soon as the servient owner obstructs it in any way.
Land Law.w: Substantial obstruction of an easement is an actionable interference. The dominant owner may seek an injunction requiring removal of the obstruction (and damages), so long as the interference is substantial rather than trivial.

n.0: No modification application is required to object to an unlawful obstruction.
n.2: An easement carries the right to use the way substantially unobstructed.
n.3: The dominant owner is not limited to damages; an injunction to remove the obstruction is available.
n.4: Obstruction does not extinguish the easement; it is an interference to be restrained.

Land Law.q: A brewery lent money to the owner of a pub, taking a mortgage over the pub as security for the loan. A term of the mortgage provides that, even after the loan has been repaid in full and the mortgage redeemed, the owner of the pub must continue to buy all of the pub's beer exclusively from the brewery for a further period of 20 years. The owner has now repaid the loan in full and wishes to be free to buy beer from wherever they choose, but the brewery insists that the 20-year tie continues to bind them notwithstanding redemption of the mortgage. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The continuing tie is fully binding, because parties may agree any terms they wish in a mortgage.
The tie is enforceable because a lender is always entitled to a collateral commercial benefit.
The continuing tie is void as a collateral advantage that survives redemption and clogs the equity.
The tie is enforceable only for as long as any part of the loan remains outstanding, and here it ends.
The whole mortgage is void, so the borrower need never have repaid the loan at all.
Land Law.w: A collateral advantage that continues after redemption and is not a fair, independent bargain can be struck down as a clog on the equity of redemption: on redemption the borrower is entitled to have the property returned unencumbered by continuing fetters (cf Kreglinger, Noakes v Rice).

n.0: A tie continuing after redemption is not simply binding as agreed; equity controls clogs on redemption.
n.1: A collateral advantage is not always enforceable; one that outlasts redemption may be void.
n.3: Answering that the tie ends with the loan misstates the reason: the tie here is expressed to continue after redemption and is struck down as a clog.
n.4: Only the offending collateral term is affected; the mortgage and repayment obligation stand.

Land Law.q: By a deed made some years ago, the owner of Plot A was granted a legal easement, a right of way, to use a driveway over the neighbouring Plot B in order to reach the road. Plot A has since been sold and transferred to a new owner, who now wishes to use the driveway to get to and from their property in the ordinary way. The owner of Plot B refuses to allow this, arguing that the right of way was personal to the original owner of Plot A in whose favour it was granted, and did not pass to the new owner when Plot A was sold. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The new owner may use the driveway only if a fresh deed of grant is executed.
The new owner may use the driveway only with the express consent of Plot B's owner.
The easement benefits Plot A, so it passes to the new owner and can be used by them.
The easement lapsed when Plot A changed hands and must be re-created to continue.
The easement was personal to the original grantee and did not pass on the sale of Plot A.
Land Law.w: An easement is a property right attached to the dominant land, not a personal right. The benefit runs with Plot A automatically on a transfer, so the new owner of Plot A takes the benefit of the easement over Plot B.

n.0: No fresh deed is needed; the benefit passes with the dominant land.
n.1: The new owner does not need Plot B owner's consent to exercise an existing easement.
n.3: The easement does not lapse on a sale of the dominant land.
n.4: A validly granted easement is proprietary, not personal to the first grantee.

Land Law.q: Rather than exercising its power of sale, a mortgagee took possession of a tenanted investment property from a defaulting borrower and began collecting the rents from the tenants itself. The borrower later challenges the way the mortgagee has handled the property while in possession, alleging that it failed to be diligent in collecting all of the rent that was due, allowed some units to stand empty, and left part of the income uncollected. The borrower seeks advice on the standard to which a mortgagee in possession is held in dealing with the income from the mortgaged property. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The mortgagee must transfer the property back to the borrower before collecting any rent.
The mortgagee may keep all the rents as compensation for the borrower's default.
The mortgagee must account strictly, including for rents it did receive and those it should have received with due diligence.
The mortgagee need only account for rents it actually chose to collect, and nothing more.
The mortgagee owes no duties at all once it has lawfully taken possession of the property. in the circumstances
Land Law.w: A mortgagee in possession is accountable on a strict basis: it must account not only for what it actually receives but also for what it would have received but for its own default or want of due diligence (the doctrine of 'wilful default').

n.0: The mortgagee can take possession without first re-transferring the property.
n.1: Rents collected must be applied to the debt and accounted for, not simply kept.
n.3: The mortgagee must account for rents it ought to have received, not only those it collected.
n.4: Taking possession brings duties; the mortgagee is not free of obligation.

Land Law.q: A metalworking workshop operates immediately next door to Mr Barlow's house in a residential street. In recent months the workshop has begun running noisy cutting and hammering machinery late into the night, often continuing until the early hours of the morning, well beyond ordinary working hours. The noise regularly wakes Mr Barlow's household, prevents them from sleeping, and seriously disturbs their ordinary use and enjoyment of their home. Mr Barlow has complained to the workshop's owner, who refuses to change the hours, saying it is entitled to run its business on its own premises exactly as it sees fit. Which of the following best describes Mr Barlow's claim?
o: No claim, because a landowner may always use their own land as they wish.
Trespass to land, because the noise physically enters the homeowner's property.
Breach of a restrictive covenant implied into every conveyance of neighbouring land. as a general rule in most cases
Private nuisance, for unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of the home, giving rise to an injunction and damages.
Adverse possession, because the noise interferes with the homeowner's occupation.
Land Law.w: Unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land, such as excessive night-time noise, is an actionable private nuisance. Remedies include an injunction to restrain the nuisance and damages.

n.0: The right to use one's land is limited by the duty not to cause an actionable nuisance.
n.1: Noise is an interference with enjoyment (nuisance), not a direct physical trespass.
n.2: No restrictive covenant is implied into every conveyance; this is a nuisance claim.
n.4: Nuisance does not create or defeat title by adverse possession.

Land Law.q: A neighbour has carried out building work close to the boundary that substantially and permanently reduces the natural light that has long been enjoyed through the claimant's windows, causing a real and lasting loss of amenity and making the affected rooms noticeably darker and less usable throughout the day. The claimant has an established right to that light, acquired over many years of uninterrupted enjoyment, and objects strongly to the interference now that the new building is in place. The claimant seeks advice on the most effective remedy available to deal with the neighbour's obstruction of the light. Which of the following best describes the remedy available?
o: Damages only, because interference with a right to light can never be restrained by injunction.
An injunction to restrain the interference. on the facts of this case
Nothing, unless the claimant proves the exact financial loss caused by the reduced light.
An order that the claimant sell their house to the neighbour at a price the court fixes.
Nothing, because a neighbour may always build on their own land however they wish.
Land Law.w: Substantial interference with an acquired right to light is normally restrained by injunction. The court may award damages in lieu only where the injury is small, quantifiable and adequately compensated by a small sum, and an injunction would be oppressive (Shelfer; Coventry v Lawrence).

n.0: An injunction can be granted for substantial interference with a right to light.
n.2: A claim for interference with an amenity right does not require proof of exact financial loss.
