n.3: The court does not compel the innocent claimant to sell to the wrongdoer.
n.4: The right to build is limited by the neighbour's acquired right to light.

Land Law.q: A borrower mortgages their property to a lender. The mortgage contains a term that would prevent the borrower from ever redeeming (getting the property back free of the mortgage) even after repaying the loan, or that imposes an oppressive collateral advantage on the lender. The term fetters the borrower's ability to redeem. The borrower challenges the term. The mortgage the borrower signed contains a term that would stop them ever getting the property back clear of the mortgage even after paying everything off, or saddles them with an oppressive extra advantage in the lender's favour, and the borrower now challenges that term. Which of the following best describes how equity treats such a term?
o: Equity always enforces any advantage the lender bargains for.
The term converts the mortgage into an outright sale of the property on these facts as a general rule.
The term is fully enforceable because the borrower agreed to it.
Equity will not permit clogs or fetters on the equity of redemption, so such a term may be struck down.
The term is enforceable provided it was in writing.
Land Law.w: Equity protects the borrower's equity of redemption and will not allow 'clogs or fetters' on the right to redeem: a term that prevents redemption altogether, or is otherwise oppressive or an unconscionable collateral advantage, may be struck down. The essential right to redeem the property on repaying the debt must be preserved.

n.0: Equity does not enforce oppressive or unconscionable collateral advantages.
n.1: A mortgage is security, not an outright sale; the borrower retains the equity of redemption.
n.2: The borrower's agreement does not make an unlawful clog on redemption enforceable.
n.4: Being in writing does not save a clog on the equity of redemption.

Land Law.q: A registered proprietor discovers that the register contains a mistake which understates the extent of the land included in their registered title, so that a strip that should form part of their title is not shown as belonging to them and appears in a neighbour's title instead. The proprietor is not in possession of the disputed strip. They wish to have the register put right so that it accurately reflects the true extent of their title. The proprietor seeks advice on whether, and by what means, the position can be corrected. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The register may be altered to correct the mistake. on these facts
Alteration is available only where the mistake benefits a squatter in adverse possession.
The proprietor must instead claim damages, as the register itself cannot be changed.
The register can never be altered once a title has first been registered.
Alteration is impossible unless every affected party first agrees to it in writing.
Land Law.w: The register can be altered to correct a mistake. Where alteration would prejudice a registered proprietor in possession there are restrictions (it is then 'rectification'); but where the proprietor is not in possession, correction is more freely available under the LRA 2002.

n.1: Alteration to correct mistakes is not confined to adverse-possession cases.
n.2: The remedy is correction of the register, with indemnity for loss, not merely damages in place of it.
n.3: The register is not immutable; the LRA 2002 provides for alteration to correct mistakes.
n.4: Unanimous written consent is not a precondition to alteration.

Land Law.q: Before completion, a seller and buyer wish to enter into a binding contract for the sale of land. They want to be sure the contract is validly made so that it can be enforced. The agreement concerns the sale of an interest in land. The parties are recording their contract. Ahead of completion the seller and buyer want a binding commitment locking each of them into the sale, and, aware that agreements about land are not made like ordinary contracts, they are anxious to record their bargain in a way that the law will actually recognise and enforce. Which of the following best describes the formalities for a valid contract for the sale of land?
o: It requires no particular formality and may be inferred from conduct alone on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It must be in writing, incorporate all the expressly agreed terms in one document, and be signed by or for both parties.
It must be made by deed, like the transfer itself.
It need only be signed by the seller, not the buyer.
It may be made orally provided the price is agreed.
Land Law.w: Under s.2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, incorporate all the expressly agreed terms in one document (or, where contracts are exchanged, in each), and be signed by or on behalf of each party. Failure to comply generally renders the contract void.

n.0: A land contract requires signed writing; it cannot rest on conduct alone.
n.2: The contract need not be by deed; the deed is used for the transfer, the contract needs signed writing.
n.3: Both parties must sign, not only the seller.
n.4: An oral contract for the sale of land is not valid, even if the price is agreed.

Land Law.q: The owner of a dominant field enjoys a right of way, granted by deed for agricultural access, along a track over a neighbour's land. In recent months the dominant owner has occasionally led a small number of additional animals along the track on the way to market, causing only a trivial increase in the overall amount of use and no real additional wear, damage or inconvenience to the servient land. The servient owner, who has come to dislike the arrangement, wishes to treat this as an excessive use of the easement and to stop the dominant owner from using the track at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Excessive user converts the easement into a profit à prendre over the servient land.
Any change at all in the pattern of use automatically extinguishes the easement.
A minor increase in use within the nature of the easement is not actionable as excessive user.
The dominant owner must pay compensation to the servient owner for any increase in use.
The servient owner may block the way entirely because the dominant owner altered the use, on these facts.
Land Law.w: Whether use is 'excessive' is a question of degree. A trivial or minor increase that remains within the character of the easement granted is not actionable; only use that goes materially beyond the scope of the right is restrained.

n.0: Excessive user does not transform an easement into a profit.
n.1: A minor change within the nature of the right does not extinguish the easement.
n.3: There is no general obligation to compensate for a minor increase in permitted use.
n.4: The servient owner cannot block a validly used easement for a trivial increase.

Land Law.q: Owing to an error made by the Land Registry when titles in the area were first registered, a strip of land that in fact belongs to Mr Vaughan's registered title was mistakenly included within the registered title of his neighbour, Ms Ward. Relying on her title, Ms Ward has since fenced the strip into her garden and treated it as her own. Mr Vaughan has now discovered the mistake and wishes both to have the register corrected so that the strip is shown as his, and to be compensated for any loss he has suffered as a result. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The true owner must claim in the tort of deceit against the Land Registry for the error.
The register may be altered to correct the mistake. on the facts of this case
The true owner's only remedy is to buy the strip back from the neighbour at market value.
The neighbour keeps the strip automatically, because the register is conclusive as to ownership.
The register can never be altered once a title has been registered, whatever the mistake.
Land Law.w: The register can be altered to correct a mistake (rectification where it prejudices a registered proprietor in possession). Where a person suffers loss by reason of a mistake in the register or its rectification, a statutory indemnity may be payable under the LRA 2002.

n.0: The route is statutory alteration plus indemnity, not a deceit claim against the registry.
n.2: The remedy is correction of the register, not a forced purchase by the true owner.
n.3: Registration is not indefeasible against a mistake; the register can be rectified.
n.4: The register is not immutable; the LRA 2002 provides for alteration and rectification of mistakes.

Land Law.q: The owner of land benefited by a restrictive covenant became aware of a neighbour's breach of it but did not take any steps to enforce the covenant for a period of a few years. During that time the benefited owner did nothing to encourage the breach, made no representation that the breach would be tolerated, and the neighbour did not rely on the owner's inaction or change their position because of it in any way. When the benefited owner finally seeks to enforce the covenant, the neighbour argues that the delay in itself now defeats the claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant is unenforceable, because any delay in enforcing a covenant destroys it.
The covenant is enforceable, but only in damages and never by way of injunction once there has been any period of delay.
The covenant remains enforceable, because mere delay without reliance or acquiescence does not bar it.
The covenant is unenforceable, because delay always amounts to acquiescence in law.
The covenant is unenforceable, because covenants must be enforced within one year of breach.
Land Law.w: Delay alone does not defeat a covenant. Equitable relief may be barred by laches or acquiescence, but that generally requires prejudicial reliance or conduct making enforcement unconscionable; mere lapse of time, without more, does not.

n.0: Delay by itself does not destroy a covenant.
n.1: Delay without reliance does not automatically confine the claimant to damages.
n.3: Delay is not the same as acquiescence; acquiescence needs more than the passage of time.
n.4: There is no fixed one-year limit for enforcing a restrictive covenant.

Land Law.q: An owner sold off a plot in the middle of their land to a buyer, keeping the surrounding land, and the conveyance of the plot said nothing whatever about any right of access to it. As a result the plot is now completely landlocked: there is no way of reaching it from the public road except by passing over the seller's retained land, and the buyer cannot otherwise get to or use the plot at all. The buyer of the landlocked plot needs access and asserts a right to cross the retained land. Which of the following best describes the basis of any such right?
o: A profit à prendre over the retained land, permitting the buyer to take its produce.
An easement of necessity implied into the conveyance. on these facts
A right arising only after the buyer has crossed the retained land as of right for 20 years.
A bare licence to cross the retained land, revocable by the seller at any time.
No right can arise, because access must always be granted expressly in the conveyance.
Land Law.w: Where land is left landlocked on a sale of part, an easement of necessity is implied into the conveyance to give the only access, because the land cannot be used at all without it. The right is implied from the circumstances, not the parties' express words.

n.0: Access is an easement, not a profit to take produce from the retained land.
n.2: Necessity gives an immediate implied easement, without waiting 20 years.
n.3: The buyer's right is a proprietary easement of necessity, not a revocable licence.
n.4: An easement of necessity can be implied; express words are not always required.

Land Law.q: A developer built a small single-storey extension in clear breach of a restrictive covenant benefiting a neighbouring house. The breach causes the benefited neighbour only modest harm to their outlook, which can readily be valued in money, and taking the extension down again would be highly wasteful and expensive, out of all proportion to that limited harm. The neighbour has applied promptly to the court for an injunction requiring the extension to be demolished. The developer accepts that there has been a breach, but argues that a modest money payment would fully compensate the neighbour and that ordering demolition would be oppressive. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome of the application?
o: The court must always grant an injunction to enforce a restrictive covenant, whatever the effect.
The court may award damages in lieu of an injunction, given the small and quantifiable nature of the harm.
The neighbour has no remedy of any kind at all, because a restrictive covenant cannot be enforced once the breach is already complete.
The court will order the developer to buy out the neighbour's land at a price it fixes.
Damages are never available for breach of a restrictive covenant; only an injunction lies.
Land Law.w: Although an injunction is the usual remedy, the court has a discretion to award damages in lieu (in equity) where the injury is small, capable of being estimated in money and adequately compensated by a small payment, and an injunction would be oppressive (Shelfer; Coventry v Lawrence).

n.0: An injunction is not automatic; the court may award damages in lieu in an appropriate case.
n.2: A completed breach does not bar a remedy; damages in lieu remain available.
n.3: The court does not force the neighbour to sell their land to the wrongdoer.
n.4: Damages in lieu of an injunction can be awarded for breach of a restrictive covenant.

Land Law.q: Before completing the sale of a house, and after contracts had been exchanged, the seller removed two items and took them away with them. The first was an ornate mirror that had been screwed into a purpose-built recess built into the wall of the sitting room. The second was a large free-standing wardrobe which simply rested on the floor under its own weight and was not attached to the structure of the house in any way. On moving in, the buyer discovered both had gone and claims that they should have been left behind as part of the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Both items are chattels, so the seller was entitled to remove each of them before completion.
Whether the items pass depends solely on what the seller privately intended to keep.
Neither item passes, because only the land itself passes on a sale and never any objects.
Both items are fixtures, so each of them should have been left for the buyer.
The mirror is likely a fixture and passes with the house; the wardrobe is a chattel the seller may remove.
Land Law.w: Fixtures pass with the land; chattels do not. Whether an item is a fixture depends on the degree and, principally, the purpose of annexation. A mirror screwed in to fit a recess is annexed to enhance the building (a fixture); a wardrobe resting by its own weight is a chattel.

n.0: An item annexed to fit and enhance the building is a fixture, not a chattel.
n.1: The test is objective (degree and purpose of annexation), not the seller's private intention.
n.2: Objects can pass with land as fixtures; it is not true that only bare land passes.
n.3: A free-standing item resting by its own weight is a chattel, not a fixture.

Land Law.q: A person entered a unilateral notice against the register of a registered title, claiming to have a proprietary interest in the property. The registered proprietor disputes that the person has any interest at all and regards the claim as baseless and damaging, because the notice is interfering with a sale of the property that is due to complete shortly. The proprietor wants the entry removed as quickly as possible so that the sale can proceed. A trainee solicitor is asked to advise on the correct step for the proprietor to take to have the unilateral notice removed and to require the claimant to justify the interest claimed. Which of the following is correct?
o: Apply to the court for an order that the notice was fraudulently entered before it can be removed, on these facts.
Enter a competing unilateral notice to override the first one on the register.
Do nothing, because a unilateral notice automatically lapses after 12 months.
Apply to the registrar to cancel the unilateral notice, requiring the beneficiary to substantiate the claim.
Apply for first registration of the title afresh to clear all existing entries.
Land Law.w: The registered proprietor may apply to cancel a unilateral notice. The beneficiary of the notice is warned and must substantiate the claimed interest; if they do not, the notice is cancelled.

n.0: A court finding of fraud is not the mechanism; the proprietor uses the registry's cancellation procedure.
n.1: Entering another notice does not remove the first; cancellation is the route.
n.2: A unilateral notice does not automatically lapse; it must be cancelled.
n.4: The title is already registered; there is no re-registration to clear entries.

Land Law.q: A landlord purports to grant a lease, but the maximum duration of the term is not certain and cannot be ascertained at the outset; the arrangement is to last for an indefinite or uncertain period. The parties intend a leasehold interest. The duration of the term is not ascertainable at the start. The landlord has purported to grant what the parties call a lease, but the arrangement is expressed to last for an indefinite or open-ended period whose maximum length simply cannot be worked out at the start, casting doubt on whether a valid fixed-term lease has been created at all. Which of the following best describes the effect of the uncertainty of term?
o: There is generally no valid fixed-term lease, because a lease requires a term of certain maximum duration.
The lease is valid because certainty of term is not a requirement on these facts as a general rule.
The uncertainty is cured automatically once rent is first paid.
The uncertainty converts the lease into a freehold estate.
The lease is valid and simply lasts forever.
Land Law.w: Certainty of term is an essential requirement of a valid lease: the maximum duration of the term must be certain or ascertainable at the outset. An agreement for an uncertain or indefinite term does not create a valid fixed-term lease (though a periodic tenancy, which is certain because it can be ended by notice, may arise where rent is paid on a periodic basis).

n.1: Certainty of term is required for a lease.
n.2: Payment of rent may create a periodic tenancy, but does not cure an uncertain fixed term as such.
n.3: Uncertainty does not convert a lease into a freehold.
n.4: An uncertain-term lease is not saved by lasting forever; that is not what the parties granted.

Land Law.q: For over 12 years a man occupied a paddock belonging to a neighbour, fencing it off, grazing his own animals on it and otherwise using it entirely as his own, and intending throughout to possess it. The land is unregistered. Each year, while the man took a two-week summer holiday away, the paddock was left empty and unattended, but on each return he resumed exactly the same use as before. The paper owner, hoping to defeat any claim, now argues that these annual two-week gaps mean that the man's possession was not truly continuous and that time never ran in his favour. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails, because an intention to possess can never be shown for open land such as a paddock, on these facts.
Any period, however short, in which the land is left empty restarts the limitation period from zero.
The claim fails, because the paper owner's continuing legal title prevents time from running.
Adverse possession is not defeated by short interruptions where possession and the intention to possess continue.
Adverse possession requires the squatter to remain physically present every single day.
Land Law.w: Adverse possession requires factual possession and an intention to possess. Brief, ordinary interruptions do not defeat continuity where the squatter deals with the land as an occupying owner would and intends to continue possessing it (JA Pye v Graham).

n.0: An intention to possess can be shown over open land such as a paddock.
n.1: Short absences do not automatically reset the limitation clock if possession and intention continue.
n.2: The owner's paper title is exactly what the limitation period runs against.
n.4: Constant physical presence is not required; the test is dealing with the land as an owner would.

Land Law.q: A tenant of shop premises carried out significant structural alterations, knocking through an internal wall, without the landlord's consent, in breach of a covenant in the lease prohibiting alterations without consent. The landlord wishes to forfeit the lease for this breach. Before taking any step to forfeit, the landlord served on the tenant a notice under section 146 of the Law of Property Act 1925, specifying the breach and requiring the tenant to remedy it within a reasonable time. The tenant, who wants to keep the lease and continue trading, has responded by applying to the court. Which of the following best describes the tenant's position?
o: The tenant may apply for relief from forfeiture. on the facts of this case
The tenant has no remedy, because forfeiture for breach of covenant is always final.
The tenant may ignore the notice, because a s.146 notice has no legal effect on a tenant.
The tenant can only claim damages and cannot keep the lease once a s.146 notice is served.
The tenant is automatically entitled to keep the lease once a s.146 notice is served.
Land Law.w: For breaches other than non-payment of rent, the landlord must first serve a s.146 LPA 1925 notice specifying the breach and (if remediable) requiring it to be remedied. The tenant may then apply for relief from forfeiture, which the court can grant on appropriate terms.

n.1: Forfeiture for breach of covenant is not final; the tenant can seek relief.
n.2: A s.146 notice is a legal prerequisite to forfeiture and cannot simply be ignored.
n.3: Relief can restore the lease, so the tenant is not confined to damages.
n.4: Service of a s.146 notice does not automatically preserve the lease; the tenant must obtain relief.

Land Law.q: A solicitor acts for Mr Farrell, who is buying a registered freehold house from Mr Grant for £420,000 with the aid of a mortgage. Mr Grant is the sole registered proprietor. He lives in the house with his adult sister, who contributed £80,000 towards the original purchase price and has lived there ever since; she is not named on the register and nothing is entered to protect any interest of hers. When asked, Mr Grant states that his sister has no interest in the property. Mr Farrell does not inspect the house before completion, and completes the purchase. After completion the sister refuses to leave and claims a beneficial share. Is Mr Farrell bound by the sister's interest?
o: No, because Mr Farrell had no actual knowledge of her interest and chose not to inspect the property.
Yes, because a person in actual occupation with a beneficial interest has an overriding interest.
No, because her interest was not protected by the entry of a notice or restriction on the register.
Yes, because the sister's contribution to the purchase price was disclosed to Mr Grant before completion.
No, because only interests belonging to the registered proprietor can bind a buyer of registered land.
Land Law.w: Under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 LRA 2002, the interest of a person in actual occupation is an overriding interest binding a buyer even if it is unprotected on the register. The exception for occupation that was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection does not assist a buyer who did not inspect, where the sister plainly lives in the house.

n.0: A buyer cannot rely on not inspecting; the exception requires that the occupation was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection.
n.2: Actual occupation is precisely the mechanism by which an unprotected interest can override, so the lack of a notice does not defeat it.
n.3: Disclosure to the seller is irrelevant; what matters is the sister's actual occupation of the property.
n.4: Interests of occupiers other than the registered proprietor can and do bind buyers of registered land under Schedule 3.

Land Law.q: A restrictive covenant benefits Plot A and burdens Plot B, restricting building on Plot B. Plot A has since been sold, and in the conveyance to the buyer the seller expressly assigned to the buyer the benefit of the restrictive covenant, at the same time as transferring the land itself. The owner of Plot B has now begun building work in clear breach of the covenant. The new owner of Plot A, relying on the express assignment of the benefit contained in their own conveyance, wishes to enforce the covenant against the owner of Plot B and bring the building work to a halt. Which of the following best describes the new owner of Plot A's position?
o: The new owner of Plot A cannot enforce it, because the benefit of a covenant can never be assigned.
The new owner of Plot A can enforce the covenant. in the circumstances
The new owner can enforce it only by first obtaining the burdened owner's agreement.
Only the original covenantee can enforce the covenant, whatever the conveyance said.
The covenant lapsed on the sale of Plot A and can no longer be enforced by anyone.
Land Law.w: The benefit of a restrictive covenant can pass to a successor by express assignment (as well as by annexation or under a building scheme). Here the conveyance assigned the benefit, so the new owner of the benefited land can enforce it against the burdened owner.

n.0: The benefit of a restrictive covenant can be assigned, so enforcement is not confined to the original parties.
n.2: Enforcement does not require fresh agreement from the burdened owner.
n.3: Successors can enforce where the benefit has passed to them by assignment or annexation.
n.4: The covenant did not lapse; its benefit was carried to the new owner by assignment.

Land Law.q: An unmarried couple bought a home that was registered in one partner's sole name. Over the following 15 years both of them contributed, in differing amounts at different times, to the mortgage instalments, the household bills and a series of improvements, and they ran their money largely as a joint venture. There was never any express agreement or declaration about the size of each party's beneficial share. The relationship has now ended and, although it is accepted that the non-owning partner has some beneficial interest, the parties cannot agree how large that share should be. How will the court most likely determine the size of the beneficial shares?
o: Equally in every case, because cohabitation automatically creates a 50:50 beneficial split.
In proportion only to each party's direct contribution to the original purchase price.
By treating the non-owner as having no interest, absent a written declaration of trust.
By awarding the entire beneficial interest to the sole legal owner in whose name the registered title happens to stand.
By inferring or imputing shares from the parties' whole course of dealing in relation to the property.
Land Law.w: Where a common intention constructive trust is established but the shares are not declared, the court quantifies the beneficial interests by inferring, or where necessary imputing, the parties' intentions from their whole course of dealing (Jones v Kernott; Stack v Dowden).

n.0: There is no automatic equal split; the shares depend on the parties' dealings.
n.1: Quantification is not limited to purchase-price contributions once a constructive trust is established.
n.2: A constructive trust does not require a written declaration to give the non-owner a share.
n.3: The sole legal owner does not necessarily take the whole beneficial interest where a trust is found.

Land Law.q: A bank agreed to lend Mr Bianchi £180,000 against his registered freehold shop as security. Mr Bianchi signed a document intended to create a legal charge over the shop in the bank's favour, and the loan was advanced to him in full. Owing to an oversight at the bank, the document was signed but never validly executed as a deed. Mr Bianchi has now defaulted on the loan, and a dispute has arisen about the bank's rights over the shop. The bank is concerned that, because the charge was not made by deed, it may have no security at all. Which of the following best describes the bank's position?
o: The bank has an equitable charge, as a valid agreement for value to grant a charge can take effect in equity.
The bank has a fully legal mortgage, because signing the document is enough to create one.
The bank has no security of any kind and ranks only as an unsecured creditor for the debt.
The bank has a profit a prendre over the land until the loan has been repaid in full.
The bank acquires a fully legal mortgage as soon as it takes possession of the property from the borrower in person.
Land Law.w: A legal mortgage or charge must be made by deed (s.52 LPA 1925). Without a valid deed there is no legal charge, but a written agreement for value to grant a charge can be specifically enforceable and take effect as an equitable charge (United Bank of Kuwait v Sahib).

n.1: A legal charge requires a validly executed deed, which is missing, so it is not a legal mortgage.
n.2: The bank is not left wholly unsecured; equity can recognise an equitable charge from the agreement.
n.3: A profit a prendre is a right to take produce from land; it is not a form of security for a loan.
n.4: Taking possession does not convert a defective charge into a legal mortgage.

Land Law.q: For more than 25 years the owner of Meadow Farm has drawn water for the farmhouse and its livestock through a pipe running from a natural spring on the neighbouring land at Hill House. This has been done openly, without ever asking permission and without any interruption or objection from the successive owners of Hill House. Hill House has recently been sold to Mr Underwood, who has now capped the spring and cut off the supply, saying that the farm has no right to his water. The owner of Meadow Farm seeks advice on whether a continuing right to take the water can be established, and how. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A restrictive covenant obliging the neighbour not to interfere with the farm's supply of water.
No right at all, because a right to take water can only ever be granted expressly by deed.
An easement acquired by prescription, since taking water from another's land is an easement.
A natural right of drainage that every landowner automatically enjoys over neighbouring land.
A profit a prendre acquired by prescription, as taking water is a right to take produce from the land.
Land Law.w: A right to take water from another's land is classified as an easement, not a profit a prendre, because water is not owned as part of the soil (Race v Ward). Such an easement can be acquired by prescription through at least 20 years' use as of right, and binds a successor such as Mr Underwood.

n.0: A restrictive covenant is a promise restricting use of land; it is not the mechanism for a right to take water.
n.1: Express grant by deed is one route, but prescription can create the easement without any deed.
n.3: A natural right of drainage concerns water leaving land naturally, not a positive right to take a neighbour's water.
n.4: A profit is a right to take something capable of ownership that forms part of the land (game, fish, minerals, grazing); water does not qualify.

Land Law.q: A commercial lease contains a covenant by the tenant not to assign the lease without the landlord's consent, 'such consent not to be unreasonably withheld'. The tenant has found a proposed assignee that is financially sound, has excellent references, and would plainly be a satisfactory tenant of the premises. When the tenant duly applies in writing for consent to the assignment, the landlord refuses — not because of any concern about the assignee at all, but because the landlord would rather bring the lease to an end and re-let the premises to someone else at a higher rent. The tenant challenges the refusal. Which of the following best describes the landlord's position?
o: The landlord may refuse consent for any reason it wishes, because it owns the reversion.
The landlord may withhold consent indefinitely without giving the tenant any reasons at all.
The landlord may refuse consent only if the proposed assignee has a poor financial record.
The landlord must not unreasonably withhold consent. on the facts of this case
The tenant may assign freely, because a covenant against assignment is void as a restraint on alienation.
Land Law.w: Where consent is not to be unreasonably withheld, the landlord must act reasonably and (under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988) give consent within a reasonable time unless it is reasonable to refuse, with written reasons. Refusing simply to recover the premises is not a reason connected with the assignment and is likely unreasonable.

n.0: A qualified covenant imports a duty not to withhold consent unreasonably; the landlord is not free to refuse for any reason.
n.1: The 1988 Act requires the landlord to respond within a reasonable time and give reasons.
n.2: Reasonableness is judged on the facts; financial concerns are one possible ground, but here there are none.
n.4: A covenant against assignment is not void; it is a valid, common restriction.

Land Law.q: A seller wishes to transfer the legal freehold estate in a property to a buyer. The parties have agreed terms, and the seller now needs to carry out the transfer itself in the correct form to pass the legal estate. The transfer of the legal estate is being effected. The parties are executing the transfer document. Terms have been agreed and the moment has come to pass the freehold from seller to buyer, so the parties are executing the document that actually transfers ownership, and they need to be sure it takes the correct form required for a legal estate to change hands. Which of the following best describes the formality required to convey a legal estate in land?
o: The conveyance must be approved by the court before it takes effect.
The conveyance must be made by deed, which must be signed, witnessed and delivered as a deed.
The conveyance may be made by a simple oral agreement between the parties.
The conveyance requires only that the price be paid, with no document at all on these facts.
The conveyance requires only an exchange of emails between the parties.
Land Law.w: A legal estate in land must be conveyed by deed (s.52 Law of Property Act 1925). To be a valid deed, the instrument must make clear on its face that it is a deed, and be signed by the person making it in the presence of a witness who attests it, and be delivered (Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s.1). Registration is then required to perfect the legal title.

n.0: Court approval is not required to convey a legal estate.
n.2: An oral agreement cannot convey a legal estate; a deed is required.
n.3: Payment alone does not convey the legal estate; a deed is required.
n.4: An exchange of emails does not satisfy the deed formalities.

Land Law.q: A solicitor acts for Mr Frost, who is buying a registered house from Ms Gill. Mr Frost knows that a lodger occupies one of the upstairs rooms. Before completion, Mr Frost's solicitor asks Ms Gill, but does not ask the lodger, whether anyone other than the seller has any interest in the house. Ms Gill replies that no one else has any interest. In fact the lodger has a beneficial interest in the house and remains in actual occupation. After completion the lodger asserts that interest against Mr Frost, who says he cannot be bound because he was told there was no other interest. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer is bound, because inquiry must be made of the occupier, not merely the seller.
The buyer is not bound, because the buyer already knew that the lodger was living in the property.
The buyer is bound only if the lodger's interest was entered as a notice on the register.
The buyer is not bound, because the seller was asked and stated that no one else had an interest.
The buyer is not bound, because a lodger can never have an interest capable of overriding.
Land Law.w: Under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 LRA 2002, the interest of a person in actual occupation overrides. The exception for failure to disclose applies only where inquiry was made of the person entitled to the interest. Inquiry of the seller alone does not trigger it, so the lodger's interest binds Mr Frost.

n.1: The buyer's knowledge does not defeat the interest; if anything, it reinforces that the buyer is bound.
n.2: Actual occupation makes the interest override without any need for a notice on the register.
n.3: The seller's denial is irrelevant; the relevant inquiry must be made of the occupier who holds the interest.
n.4: An occupier such as a lodger can hold a beneficial interest capable of overriding through actual occupation.

Land Law.q: Three siblings own a house together, holding it as beneficial joint tenants. Over a number of years they came to a clear understanding among themselves, and consistently acted on the basis, that each of them owned a distinct one-third share which they were each free to dispose of by will. No formal written notice of severance was ever served by any of them on the others. One of the siblings has now died, having left a will purporting to deal with their share of the house. The question arises how the beneficial interest in the house is now held. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The joint tenancy was severed by their mutual conduct. on the facts of this case
The joint tenancy is intact, so the deceased's share passes by survivorship to the other two.
The beneficial ownership reverted to the person who originally provided the purchase money.
The deceased's third passes to the state, because informal severance is legally ineffective.
Severance is impossible without a signed written notice served on all the other joint tenants.
Land Law.w: A beneficial joint tenancy can be severed not only by written notice under s.36(2) LPA 1925 but also by mutual agreement or a course of dealing showing all treat their shares as held in common (Williams v Hensman). Severance defeats survivorship, so the deceased's share passes under their estate.

n.1: Survivorship does not apply once the joint tenancy has been severed by mutual conduct.
n.2: Severance does not send the interest back to whoever paid the purchase money.
n.3: Informal severance by agreement or course of dealing is effective in equity.
n.4: Written notice is one method; mutual agreement or a course of dealing also severs.

Land Law.q: Ms Yates and Mr Zaman bought a house together as an unmarried couple, taking the legal title in both their names as trustees and holding the beneficial interest as tenants in common in equal shares. Their relationship has since broken down. Ms Yates has moved out and wants the house sold so that she can realise her share, which she needs for a deposit on somewhere new. Mr Zaman has remained living in the house and refuses to agree to a sale. Ms Yates applies to the court under the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 for an order for sale. Which of the following best describes the court's powers on the application?
o: The court has no power to intervene in a dispute between co-owners of land.
The court must physically partition the house and the land between the two co-owners, dividing it into separate parcels.
The court may order a sale, refuse it, or regulate occupation, weighing the statutory factors.
The court may only award financial compensation to the co-owner who wishes to sell.
The court must order an immediate sale whenever any co-owner asks for one.
Land Law.w: Under s.14 TOLATA 1996 the court may make such order as it thinks fit relating to the trustees' functions, including ordering or refusing a sale and regulating occupation. Section 15 lists the factors to weigh (the intentions and purpose of the trust, the welfare of any minor occupier, and the interests of any secured creditor).

n.0: The court plainly has jurisdiction to resolve co-ownership disputes under s.14.
n.1: Physical partition is not the remedy the court must impose; it exercises the s.14 discretion.
n.3: The court's powers are not limited to compensation; it can order sale or regulate occupation.
n.4: A sale is not automatic; the court weighs the s.15 factors and may refuse it.

Land Law.q: For more than 30 years the owner of a farm has grazed their sheep on a neighbouring landowner's meadow, doing so openly, as of right, and without the neighbour's permission, and the neighbour never objected at any time throughout that long period. The meadow has now been sold to a new owner, who wishes to put a stop to the grazing and argues that the farmer has no right to continue turning animals out on the land. The farmer seeks advice on the nature of any right they have acquired over the meadow, and whether it binds the new owner. Which of the following best describes it?
o: No right at all, because a right to graze can only be granted expressly by deed, on these facts.
A licence to graze, which ended automatically when the meadow changed hands.
An easement of grazing, which cannot bind a successor to the servient land.
A profit à prendre of pasture acquired by prescription, binding the new owner of the meadow.
An overriding interest in the meadow arising from the presence of the sheep.
Land Law.w: A right to take the produce of another's land, such as grazing (pasture), is a profit à prendre. It can be acquired by long use as of right (prescription) and, once acquired as a legal profit, binds successors to the servient land.

n.0: A profit can be acquired by prescription, not only by express deed.
n.1: Use as of right is not a mere licence and does not end on a sale of the servient land.
n.2: Grazing is a right to take produce and so is a profit, not an ordinary easement, and a legal profit binds successors.
n.4: A profit is not an interest that overrides simply because animals are present; it binds as a legal profit acquired by prescription.

Land Law.q: Ms Everett holds a flat under a long lease that requires her to pay an annual service charge to the landlord, which is meant to fund the cleaning, lighting and maintenance of the common parts of the building. For the past year the landlord has largely failed to provide those services: the common parts have been left dirty, and the lighting has often not worked. Ms Everett is angry about this and has refused to pay the latest service charge at all, taking the view that, because the landlord has not provided the services, she owes nothing. She seeks advice on her position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The tenant is automatically released from the service charge because the landlord has not performed its side.
The tenant may withhold the service charge indefinitely until every service has been provided in full.
The tenant must pay the charge and has no remedy of any kind for the landlord's failure to provide services.
The tenant owes nothing, because covenants in a lease are always mutually dependent on one another.
The tenant remains liable to pay, but may claim, or sometimes set off, for the landlord's failure to provide the services.
Land Law.w: Leasehold covenants are generally independent, so the landlord's failure to provide services does not by itself discharge the tenant's covenant to pay. The tenant's route is a claim for breach (and, where the conditions are met, equitable set-off); service charges are also controlled for reasonableness by s.19 Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

n.0: Covenants are not automatically discharged by the other party's breach; the obligation to pay continues.
n.1: Simply withholding the charge indefinitely is not permitted and risks the tenant's own breach.
n.2: The tenant is not without a remedy; she can sue for the breach and may have statutory protection on reasonableness.
n.3: Lease covenants are generally independent, not mutually dependent, so non-provision does not cancel the charge.

Land Law.q: For more than 30 years the members of the Okafor household have fished a stretch of a neighbouring landowner's private lake, doing so openly, as of right, and without the landowner's permission, and the previous landowner never objected at any point during that period. The land around the lake has now been sold to a new owner, who has put up notices and wishes to stop the fishing altogether. The household wishes to continue fishing and seeks advice on what right, if any, they have acquired over the lake through their long and uninterrupted use, and whether that right is binding on the new owner. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A profit à prendre of fishing (piscary) acquired by prescription.
No right at all, because a right to fish can only be granted expressly by deed.
An easement of fishing, which cannot bind any successor to the servient land.
A licence to fish, which ended automatically when the lake was sold.
An overriding interest in the lake arising from the act of fishing itself.
Land Law.w: A right to take fish from another's water is a profit à prendre (a profit of piscary). It can be acquired by long use as of right (prescription), and once acquired as a legal profit it binds successors to the servient land.

n.1: A profit can be acquired by prescription, not only by express deed.
n.2: Fishing is the taking of produce, so it is a profit, and a legal profit binds successors.
n.3: Use as of right is not a mere licence and does not end on a sale of the servient land.
n.4: The right is a profit acquired by prescription; it does not depend on overriding through occupation.

Land Law.q: A man lives with his partner in a house of which she is the sole registered owner. On several occasions she expressly assured him that 'half of this is yours'. Relying on those repeated assurances, he paid for and personally project-managed a large two-storey extension to the house, and he gave up the tenancy of his own flat in order to move in and commit fully to the relationship. The couple have now separated, and the partner denies that he has acquired any beneficial interest in the house at all. On which basis is he most likely to establish a beneficial share?
o: A resulting trust, measured strictly and only by the amount of his direct financial contribution to the original purchase price.
An easement over the home, arising from the money he spent on the extension.
No interest, because the assurance was not put into a signed written declaration of trust.
A licence, revocable by the legal owner on giving him reasonable notice to leave.
A common intention constructive trust, based on the express assurance and his detrimental reliance.
Land Law.w: An express assurance of a share, coupled with detrimental reliance (paying for the extension and giving up his flat), gives rise to a common intention constructive trust (Grant v Edwards; Stack v Dowden).

n.0: His interest is not confined to purchase-price contributions once a common intention trust is shown.
n.1: Spending on the property founds a trust interest, not an easement.
n.2: A constructive trust does not require a signed written declaration.
n.3: He has a beneficial interest, not a mere revocable licence.

Land Law.q: A buyer, Mr Naylor, purchased a registered freehold property for £500,000. Some years earlier the land had been made subject to a restrictive covenant, in favour of a neighbouring owner, prohibiting any use other than as a private dwelling. That covenant had never been protected by the entry of a notice on the register of the property's title. Mr Naylor, who knew nothing of the covenant, completed the purchase and was registered as proprietor. He has now opened a shop on the ground floor. The neighbouring owner, who has the benefit of the covenant, seeks to enforce it against Mr Naylor and stop the commercial use. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant does not bind the new owner: an unprotected covenant loses priority to a buyer for value.
The covenant binds the new owner, because opening a shop is a serious breach of its terms.
The covenant binds the new owner, because restrictive covenants automatically run with the land in equity.
The covenant does not bind, because the burden of a covenant can never pass to a successor in title.
The covenant binds the new owner, because it was created before the new owner bought the land.
Land Law.w: In registered land a restrictive covenant must be protected by a notice to bind a later purchaser. An unprotected covenant is postponed to a registered disposition made for valuable consideration (s.29 LRA 2002), so it does not bind the buyer (though it may still bind the original covenantor personally).

n.1: The seriousness of the breach does not make an unprotected covenant enforceable against a purchaser.
n.2: The burden can run in equity, but only if protected; without a notice it loses priority to a buyer for value.
n.3: The burden of a restrictive covenant can pass in equity (Tulk v Moxhay); it fails here only for want of protection.
n.4: Priority in registered land turns on protection by notice, not merely on when the covenant was created.

Land Law.q: Thirteen years ago a man took exclusive possession of a plot of unregistered land, fenced it, cultivated it and otherwise used it as his own, intending to possess it, and he has continued to do so without interruption ever since. The plot belongs on paper to a company that had bought a larger site including this plot but never used this particular part and did nothing at all about the man's occupation. The company has now realised what has happened and wishes to recover the plot, arguing that its documented paper ownership must prevail over a mere squatter, whatever the length of his occupation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The owner's title is extinguished, because 12 years' adverse possession bars the owner's right to recover unregistered land.
The squatter acquired title after 10 years, once the limitation period expired.
The owner keeps title, because a squatter needs 20 years' possession of unregistered land.
The squatter must apply to be registered before the owner's title can be affected.
The owner may recover the land at any time, because adverse possession does not apply to unregistered land, in these circumstances.
Land Law.w: For unregistered land the Limitation Act 1980 bars the paper owner's right to recover after 12 years of adverse possession (factual possession plus intention to possess), and the owner's title is then extinguished.

n.1: The period is 12 years, not 10; the 10-year notice regime applies to registered land under LRA 2002.
n.2: The unregistered-land limitation period is 12 years, not 20.
n.3: For unregistered land no registration is needed; the owner's title is extinguished by the passage of time.
n.4: Adverse possession applies to unregistered land; this is the classic limitation regime.

Land Law.q: Two people take a transfer of land to hold as joint tenants. For a joint tenancy of the legal (and beneficial) estate to exist, four characteristics must be present in their ownership. The co-owners hold together rather than in distinct shares. The question concerns the requirements for a joint tenancy. The two co-owners have taken a transfer of the property intending to hold it together as joint tenants rather than in distinct shares, and, to be sure a joint tenancy has genuinely arisen, they want to know the set of conditions their co-ownership must satisfy. Which of the following best describes the 'four unities' required for a joint tenancy?
o: Unity of price, purpose, place and person.
Unity of registration, occupation, payment and intention.
Unity of possession, interest, title and time.
Unity of survivorship, severance, shares and sale.
Unity of possession alone, the other unities being irrelevant.
Land Law.w: A joint tenancy requires the four unities: unity of possession (each is entitled to possession of the whole), unity of interest (their interests are identical in nature, extent and duration), unity of title (they derive title from the same document or act), and unity of time (their interests vest at the same time). A tenancy in common requires only unity of possession.

n.0: 'Price, purpose, place and person' are not the four unities.
n.1: 'Registration, occupation, payment and intention' are not the four unities.
n.3: 'Survivorship, severance, shares and sale' are not the four unities.
n.4: A joint tenancy needs all four unities, not just unity of possession.

Land Law.q: For more than ten years a landowner has occupied a narrow strip of land on the wrong side of a boundary fence, in the genuine and reasonable belief that the strip formed part of their own registered title. The land on both sides is registered. The true registered proprietor of the strip has recently commissioned a survey, noticed the position, and objects to the landowner's continued occupation. The landowner has nonetheless applied to the Land Registry to be registered as proprietor of the strip on the basis of their long occupation. Which of the following best describes the landowner's prospects on that application?
o: The application succeeds automatically, because ten years' occupation always confers title.
The application must fail, because any objection by the registered proprietor always defeats it, on these facts.
The applicant must show 12 years' possession before any application can be considered.
The application must fail, because adverse possession cannot ever apply to registered land.
The application may still succeed under the reasonable-belief-of-boundary condition, despite the objection.
Land Law.w: Although a registered proprietor's objection usually defeats a Schedule 6 application, one of the three exceptions is that the applicant reasonably believed the land belonged to them for ten years and it adjoins their own land. On these facts that condition may be satisfied.

n.0: Ten years' occupation does not confer title automatically; the conditions must be met.
n.1: An objection does not always defeat the application; the boundary condition is an exception.
n.2: For registered land the relevant period under Schedule 6 is ten years, not twelve.
n.3: Adverse possession can apply to registered land under the Schedule 6 regime.

Land Law.q: A squatter acquired a strip of unregistered land by 12 years' adverse possession, with the effect that the paper owner's title to the strip was extinguished under the Limitation Act 1980. Throughout that period the strip had been subject to a legal right of way benefiting a neighbouring property, which had been created by deed many years before the squatter arrived. The owner of the neighbouring property wishes to continue using the right of way over the strip, but the squatter argues that their adverse possession has swept away all earlier rights over the land. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The squatter takes the land free of the easement, because adverse possession clears all prior rights.
The easement is automatically extinguished after 12 years, along with the paper owner's title.
The squatter takes the land subject to the existing legal easement.
The squatter takes free of the easement unless the neighbour objected during the 12 years.
The neighbour must re-grant the right of way to the squatter for it to continue.
Land Law.w: Adverse possession extinguishes the dispossessed paper owner's title, but the squatter takes the land subject to third-party proprietary rights such as an existing legal easement. The neighbour's right of way is not defeated by the squatter's possession of the servient strip.

n.0: Adverse possession does not sweep away third-party rights like easements; it defeats only the paper owner's title.
n.1: The easement is not extinguished merely because the servient owner's title is.
n.3: The neighbour need not have objected; their easement survives regardless.
n.4: No re-grant is needed; the legal easement continues to bind the land.

Land Law.q: A wife agreed to charge the family home, which she co-owns with her husband, to a bank as security for the debts of her husband's struggling business. She entered into the charge only after her husband pressured her and seriously misled her about the nature and extent of what she was signing, and she received no independent legal advice about the transaction. The business has since failed, and the bank, which took no steps to ensure that she understood the transaction or obtained advice, now seeks to enforce the charge and take possession of the home. The wife seeks advice on her position against the bank. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The charge may be set aside against her. as a general rule in most cases
The lender's position is unaffected, because undue influence is only relevant between the spouses.
The charge is automatically void, because a spouse can never validly charge a jointly owned home.
The charge binds her only for half of the debt, reflecting her share of the home.
The charge is fully enforceable against her, because she signed the security documents.
Land Law.w: Where a person offers their home as surety for another's debts in a non-commercial relationship, the lender is put on inquiry as to undue influence. If it fails to take reasonable steps (such as ensuring she received independent advice), the charge may be set aside as against her (RBS v Etridge).

n.1: Undue influence affects the lender where it was put on inquiry and did nothing.
n.2: Such a charge is not automatically void; it may be set aside in the circumstances described.
n.3: If set aside for undue influence, the charge fails against her, not merely as to half.
n.4: Her signature does not save the charge where the lender was on notice and took no steps.

Land Law.q: A separated couple own the family home together on trust for themselves as beneficial joint tenants. One of them has since moved out and now wants the house to be sold so that they can realise their share of the value. The other still lives in the house with the couple's two young children and strongly opposes any sale. The party seeking a sale has applied to the court for an order for sale of the property under the trusts of land legislation. In deciding whether to order a sale, the court must weigh a number of statutory factors. Which of the following is a factor the court must take into account in these circumstances?
o: The conduct of the applicant in the breakdown of the relationship between the parties, on these facts.
Whether the occupying co-owner has anywhere cheaper that they could move to instead.
The tax consequences for each co-owner of ordering, or refusing to order, a sale.
The welfare of any minor who occupies, or might reasonably be expected to occupy, the home.
The market value of the property at the exact date the application is issued.
Land Law.w: Section 15 TOLATA 1996 lists the factors on a s.14 application, which include the intentions and purpose of the trust, the welfare of any minor who occupies or might be expected to occupy the land, and the interests of any secured creditor.

n.0: The parties' conduct in the relationship breakdown is not a listed s.15 factor.
n.1: Whether a cheaper alternative exists is not a listed statutory factor.
n.2: Tax consequences are not among the specified statutory factors.
n.4: The precise market value on the issue date is not a s.15 factor.

Land Law.q: A buyer of registered land carried out a reasonably careful inspection of the property before completion. A person who held a beneficial interest in the property was not, at the time of that inspection, living there in any way that was apparent, and there was nothing on a reasonably careful inspection to alert the buyer to their presence or to the existence of their interest. The buyer had no actual knowledge of the interest and completed the purchase in good faith. The occupier now asserts their beneficial interest against the buyer as an overriding interest. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer takes free, because the occupation was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the buyer had no knowledge.
The buyer takes free only if the occupier had expressly disclaimed the interest in writing.
The buyer is bound, because a buyer is always fixed with knowledge of anyone with an interest. in the circumstances
The buyer is bound, because any beneficial interest automatically overrides on a sale.
The buyer is bound, because the occupier's interest existed before the buyer purchased.
Land Law.w: Under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 LRA 2002, an interest of a person in actual occupation does not override where the occupation was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the buyer did not actually know of the interest. On these facts the exception applies and the buyer takes free.

n.1: No written disclaimer is required; the exception operates on non-obvious occupation without knowledge.
n.2: A buyer is not fixed with knowledge of hidden interests; the exception turns on obviousness and knowledge.
n.3: A beneficial interest does not override automatically; the para 2 exception can defeat it.
n.4: Mere pre-existence of the interest does not make it bind where the exception applies.

Land Law.q: Two people own land as beneficial joint tenants. One of them dies. The survivor and the deceased's family dispute what happens to the deceased's interest, the family arguing it passes under the deceased's will. The co-owners held as joint tenants, not tenants in common, and no severance occurred. One joint tenant has died. The couple held the property as beneficial joint tenants with no severance ever having taken place, and now that one of them has died a dispute has erupted between the survivor and the deceased's relatives, who insist the deceased's share should pass under the will. Which of the following best describes the effect of the death?
o: The deceased's interest passes on the deceased's intestacy to their next of kin.
The deceased's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant by the right of survivorship.
The deceased's interest passes to the Crown as ownerless property.
The deceased's interest passes under the deceased's will to their chosen beneficiary on these facts.
The deceased's interest is divided equally between the survivor and the estate.
Land Law.w: Under a joint tenancy the right of survivorship (jus accrescendi) applies: on the death of a joint tenant, their interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), outside the deceased's will or intestacy. Survivorship takes precedence over any testamentary gift, so the deceased cannot leave their joint-tenancy interest by will (unless they severed it before death).

n.0: It does not pass on intestacy; survivorship takes it to the co-owner.
n.2: It passes to the surviving joint tenant, not to the Crown.
n.3: A joint tenant's interest does not pass under their will; survivorship applies.
n.4: It is not split between survivor and estate; the whole passes by survivorship.

Land Law.q: A house is held by two trustees, Mr Price and Mrs Quinn, on trust for several adult beneficiaries in defined shares. One of those beneficiaries lives in the house and has a beneficial interest under the trust. A buyer agrees to purchase the house from the trustees and, on completion, pays the whole of the purchase price to Mr Price and Mrs Quinn together as the two trustees. After completion, the beneficiary who lives in the house refuses to leave, claiming that, because she was in occupation and had a beneficial interest, her interest binds the buyer and entitles her to remain. The buyer seeks advice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer takes subject to the interests, because a buyer of a trust property is always bound by them.
The buyer takes subject to the occupier's interest, because actual occupation always binds a buyer.
The buyer takes free only if the occupying beneficiary consented in writing to the sale.
The buyer takes free of the beneficial interests. on the facts of this case
The buyer takes free only if the beneficial interests were protected by a notice on the register.
Land Law.w: Payment of capital money to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) overreaches the beneficiaries' interests, which are swept off the land onto the proceeds of sale. The buyer therefore takes free, even of an occupier's interest (City of London BS v Flegg).

n.0: A buyer is not automatically bound; overreaching is the mechanism that frees the title.
n.1: Actual occupation does not save an interest that has been overreached by proper payment to two trustees.
n.2: The occupier's written consent is not required where the interest is overreached by two-trustee payment.
n.4: Overreaching operates regardless of any notice; a notice is neither needed nor effective against it.

Land Law.q: A landlord forfeited a commercial lease by peaceably re-entering the premises and changing the locks, after the tenant had fallen three months behind with the rent. The tenant's business depends entirely on the premises, and the tenant now urgently wants the lease restored. The tenant has offered to pay the landlord all of the rent arrears in full, together with interest and the landlord's reasonable costs of the forfeiture, and is able to pay these sums immediately. The landlord, however, would prefer to keep the premises and re-let them to someone else at a higher rent. The tenant applies to the court. Which of the following best describes the tenant's position?
o: The tenant may claim damages but cannot recover possession of the premises.
The tenant can obtain relief only if the arrears were caused by circumstances beyond their control.
The tenant may recover the lease only if the landlord agrees to grant a new one.
The tenant is likely to obtain relief from forfeiture on paying the arrears, interest and costs.
The tenant has no remedy, because forfeiture for rent arrears is always final once re-entry occurs.
Land Law.w: Where a lease is forfeited for non-payment of rent, the court will generally grant the tenant relief from forfeiture if the tenant pays the arrears, interest and costs, restoring the lease. Equity treats the right of re-entry as security for the rent.

n.0: Relief can restore possession, so the tenant is not limited to damages.
n.1: Relief on payment of arrears does not require the tenant to prove the cause of the default.
n.2: Relief restores the existing lease; it does not depend on the landlord agreeing to a new one.
n.4: Forfeiture for rent arrears is not final; the tenant has a right to seek relief.

Land Law.q: A landlord agreed to let a flat to a tenant for a fixed term of two years, at the full market rent of £1,200 a month, with no premium or fine taken, the tenancy to take effect in possession immediately. Instead of using a deed, the parties simply recorded the letting in a written tenancy agreement, which each of them signed. A dispute has since arisen between them about the tenant's rights, and the tenant needs to know whether they hold a valid legal lease of the flat, given that no deed was ever executed to create it. Which of the following best describes the status of the lease?
o: It is a valid legal lease, because a lease for three years or less at a market rent may be created without a deed.
It is void, because every lease must be created by deed to have any effect.
It is a mere licence, because it was not made by deed.
It is valid only if the tenant also registers it as a notice against the landlord's title.
It is only an equitable lease, because it was not completed by registration at the Land Registry. on these facts
Land Law.w: A lease for a term not exceeding three years, taking effect in possession at the best rent reasonably obtainable without a fine, is an exception to the deed requirement (s.54(2) LPA 1925) and can be a legal lease even if made only in writing or orally.

n.1: Not every lease needs a deed; short leases within s.54(2) are excepted.
n.2: A validly granted short legal lease is not a mere licence.
n.3: A short legal lease within s.54(2) does not require a notice to be valid.
n.4: The lease is legal under the short-lease exception, not merely equitable, and short legal leases are not registrable dispositions.

Land Law.q: A seller and a buyer signed a valid written contract for the sale of a house, the contract complying with the formalities required for a contract for the disposition of an interest in land, with completion fixed for a date some weeks later. Before completion, and without any lawful justification, the seller changed their mind and refused to go ahead with the sale, telling the buyer that the deal was off. The buyer, who very much wants the house and has already incurred survey and legal costs, seeks advice on what claim arises against the seller from the refusal to complete. Which of the following best describes it?
o: No claim at all, because a contract for land is unenforceable until completion takes place. on these facts
An overriding interest in the house that binds the new purchaser automatically.
A restrictive covenant claim, because the seller promised not to sell to anyone else.
Breach of the contract for sale, for which the buyer may seek damages (and, in principle, specific performance).
A claim in the tort of deceit, because the seller misled the buyer about completing.
Land Law.w: A contract for sale that satisfies s.2 LP(MP)A 1989 is binding. If the seller refuses to complete, the buyer may sue for breach of contract, seeking damages and (as land is unique) potentially specific performance.

n.0: A valid land contract is enforceable before completion, not only at completion.
n.1: An estate contract may be protected, but the buyer's primary claim against the seller is for breach of contract.
n.2: The seller's promise is contractual, not a restrictive covenant on the land.
n.4: The claim lies in contract, not deceit, on these facts.

Land Law.q: A married couple, Mr and Mrs Hale, live together in a house which is registered in the sole name of Mr Hale. Mrs Hale made no financial contribution to the purchase and has no beneficial interest in the property, but she is concerned that Mr Hale, with whom relations have become strained, might try to sell or mortgage the home over her head without telling her. She wishes to protect her right to occupy the matrimonial home so that it is binding on any buyer or lender who deals with Mr Hale in the future. Which of the following is the correct way for her to do so?
o: By registering a notice of home rights under the Family Law Act 1996 against the title.
It cannot be protected at all, because the spouse has no beneficial interest in the home.
By relying on an overriding interest, which arises automatically from the marriage.
By registering a restriction that prevents the owning spouse from ever selling the home.
By lodging a caution, which is the only route open to a non-owning spouse.
Land Law.w: A non-owning spouse or civil partner has statutory home rights (a right of occupation) under the Family Law Act 1996. To bind a purchaser these must be protected by entry of a notice on the register; they are not an overriding interest and marriage alone does not bind a buyer.

n.1: Home rights exist independently of any beneficial interest and can be protected.
n.2: Home rights are not overriding and do not bind a buyer automatically from the marriage.
n.3: Home rights are protected by a notice; they do not entitle the spouse to a restriction barring any sale.
n.4: Protection is by a notice of home rights, not a caution.

Land Law.q: A lender is exercising its power of sale over a defaulting borrower's home. Rather than marketing and selling the property on the open market, the lender wishes to sell it directly to a company that the lender itself owns and controls. The borrower has heard of the proposed sale and is worried that the price paid by the connected company will be well below what the home is really worth, leaving a large shortfall for which the borrower would remain personally liable. The borrower seeks advice on whether the lender is entitled to sell the home to its own company at all, and on what terms. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The lender may sell to a connected company only if it proves it took reasonable care to obtain the true market value.
The sale to a connected company is automatically void and cannot be completed.
The lender cannot sell the property at all while it has any connection with the buyer.
The lender owes no duty as to price once it has decided to sell to a connected buyer.
The lender may sell to its own company on any terms, because it controls the power of sale, on the facts described above.
Land Law.w: A mortgagee cannot sell to itself, and a sale to a connected company is closely scrutinised: the burden is on the mortgagee to show it took reasonable care to obtain the true market value (Tse Kwong Lam v Wong Chit Sen). If it cannot, it is liable for any shortfall.

n.1: Such a sale is not automatically void; the issue is whether a proper price was obtained.
n.2: A sale to a connected buyer is permitted but heavily scrutinised, not outright prohibited.
n.3: The duty as to price applies with particular force where the buyer is connected to the lender.
n.4: Control of the power of sale does not free the lender from the duty to obtain a proper price.

Land Law.q: A plot of land is subject to an old restrictive covenant that limits its use to residential purposes only. Over the years, however, the surrounding neighbourhood has changed completely and is now wholly commercial in character, so that the covenant has become obsolete and no longer secures any real practical benefit to the land it was originally meant to protect. The owner of the plot wishes to use it for commercial purposes and wants the covenant formally removed or modified so that it no longer stands in the way of that use. Which of the following is the correct route to achieve that?
o: Bring a claim in the county court for damages in place of the covenant.
Apply to the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under s.84 LPA 1925 to discharge or modify the covenant.
Apply to the Land Registry to delete the covenant from the register as of right.
Simply ignore the covenant, because a covenant automatically ends once the area changes character, on these facts.
Obtain the consent of the original covenantee, who alone can release the covenant.
Land Law.w: A person interested in freehold land affected by a restrictive covenant may apply to the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under s.84 LPA 1925 to discharge or modify it, for example where it is obsolete or no longer secures any practical benefit.

n.0: A damages claim does not remove the covenant; discharge is via s.84.
n.2: The Land Registry does not delete covenants as of right on the owner's say-so.
n.3: A covenant does not automatically end because the neighbourhood changes; a discharge must be obtained.
n.4: The original covenantee is often not the current beneficiary; the statutory route is the Upper Tribunal.

Land Law.q: A landowner claims to have an easement over neighbouring land. To be capable of existing as an easement at all, the right must satisfy the essential characteristics of an easement. There is a dominant and a servient piece of land. The court applies the established test. The owner insists they enjoy an easement over the neighbouring land, and, with a benefited plot and a burdened plot in the picture, the court must test the claimed right against the established requirements before it can be recognised as an easement rather than some lesser or invalid right. Which of the following best describes the characteristics required for a right to be an easement?
o: There must be a dominant and servient tenement in different ownership, the right must accommodate the dominant land, and be capable of grant.
The dominant and servient land must always be owned by the same person.
The right must be registered as a company charge to be valid.
The right must give the dominant owner exclusive possession of the servient land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There need only be a dominant tenement, with no servient land required.
Land Law.w: Under Re Ellenborough Park, a right can be an easement only if: there is a dominant and a servient tenement; the right accommodates (benefits) the dominant tenement; the dominant and servient tenements are owned or occupied by different persons; and the right is capable of forming the subject matter of a grant (sufficiently definite, within the general nature of easements, and not amounting to exclusive possession).

n.1: The tenements must be owned/occupied by different persons, not the same person.
n.2: Registration as a company charge is not a characteristic of an easement.
n.3: An easement must not give exclusive possession of the servient land.
n.4: Both a dominant and a servient tenement are required.

Land Law.q: One of two beneficial joint tenants wishes to bring the joint tenancy to an end and hold as tenants in common, so that their share can pass under their will. They are considering the ways in which a beneficial joint tenancy may be severed during their lifetime. The co-owners currently hold as beneficial joint tenants. One wishes to sever. One of the beneficial joint tenants no longer wants the survivorship rule to apply to their share, preferring that it pass under their will as a distinct share, and is asking what steps are open to them, during their lifetime, to turn the joint tenancy into a tenancy in common. Which of the following best describes how severance may be effected?
o: Only by obtaining a court order in every case.
Only with the consent of all the other joint tenants in writing.
Only on the death of one of the joint tenants.
By written notice to the other joint tenant(s), or by an act operating on one's own share, mutual agreement, or a course of dealing.
Severance of a beneficial joint tenancy is not possible during the joint tenants' lifetimes on these facts as a general rule.
Land Law.w: A beneficial joint tenancy may be severed during the joint tenants' lives in several ways: by giving written notice of severance to the other joint tenant(s) under s.36(2) of the Law of Property Act 1925, or by one of the methods in Williams v Hensman, namely an act of a joint tenant operating on their own share (such as selling or mortgaging it), mutual agreement, or a course of dealing. Severance creates a tenancy in common.

n.0: A court order is not required; written notice or the Williams v Hensman methods suffice.
n.1: Written notice under s.36(2) does not require the others' consent.
n.2: Severance occurs during life; death triggers survivorship, not severance.
n.4: Severance is possible during the joint tenants' lifetimes.
