Land Law.q: A document drawn up between a landlord and a tenant purports to grant the tenant a lease of shop premises 'for the duration of the war', and fixes no other date, event or maximum period by reference to which the term is to come to an end. A rent is reserved and paid monthly, and the tenant has gone into occupation and traded from the premises. A dispute has now arisen between the parties over the status of the arrangement, and in particular whether a valid lease for a term of years was ever created by a grant framed in this open-ended way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A valid lease arises, because the end of the war provides a sufficiently certain end date.
No valid term of years arises, because a lease must have a certain maximum duration.
A fee simple arises, because an uncertain lease is automatically upgraded to freehold.
An easement arises, giving the tenant a right to occupy until the war ends.
A valid lease arises, because the parties clearly intended a tenancy to exist between them.
Land Law.w: A lease must have a certain maximum duration, ascertainable at the outset. A term 'for the duration of the war' is uncertain and does not create a valid term of years (Lace v Chantler; Prudential Assurance v London Residuary Body), although a periodic tenancy may arise from entry and payment of rent.

n.0: The end of the war is not ascertainable in advance, so the term is uncertain.
n.2: An uncertain lease is not converted into a freehold estate.
n.3: A right to exclusive possession for a term is a lease question, not an easement.
n.4: Intention to create a tenancy cannot cure the lack of certainty of maximum duration.

Land Law.q: When rebuilding a garden wall along the boundary with the neighbouring registered property, Mr Croft built the new wall several feet over the boundary, so that it now stands on a strip of his neighbour Ms Dalby's registered land. The wall has been up for only a few months. Ms Dalby wants the wall taken down and the strip restored to her, but Mr Croft argues that she has suffered no real financial loss and that, at most, she should be paid a small sum and leave the wall where it is. Ms Dalby seeks advice on the most appropriate remedy. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An injunction requiring removal of the encroaching wall, with damages in lieu available at the court's discretion.
Nothing, because the neighbour acquired title to the strip by adverse possession the very moment the encroaching wall was built.
Damages only, because an injunction is never available for a boundary encroachment.
Nothing, unless the claimant can prove a specific financial loss caused by the wall.
An order transferring the encroached strip to the neighbour on payment of its market value.
Land Law.w: An encroachment is a continuing trespass to land. The primary remedy is an injunction to remove it, though the court has a discretion to award damages in lieu (Jaggard v Sawyer). Trespass is actionable without proof of loss.

n.1: Adverse possession requires long possession and, for registered land, the LRA 2002 procedure; it is not instant.
n.2: An injunction is available and usual for encroachment; damages are not the only remedy.
n.3: Trespass is actionable per se, so the claim does not depend on proving financial loss.
n.4: The court does not force the claimant to sell the strip to the trespasser.

Land Law.q: An owner of land enjoys, by permission, a right to use a driveway over adjoining land also owned by the same seller. The seller then sells the benefited land to a buyer by conveyance, without expressly mentioning the driveway right, which was in use at the time. A right in use at the time of the conveyance was not expressly granted. The conveyance is silent about the right. When the two plots were in common ownership the buyer's plot was enjoyed with the informal use of a driveway across the retained land, and when the seller later conveyed the benefited plot without mentioning that right, which was in use at the time, the buyer wants to know whether a legal easement passed anyway. Which of the following best describes how a legal easement may nonetheless arise on the conveyance?
o: An easement arises only if the buyer pays an additional sum for it.
The right is automatically extinguished by the conveyance.
Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 may operate to convert the right into a legal easement passing with the conveyance.
An easement can arise only by twenty years' prescription.
No easement can ever arise unless expressly granted in the conveyance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Land Law.w: Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 implies into a conveyance of land all rights, privileges and easements enjoyed with the land, and can operate to upgrade a permission or informal right (such as use of a driveway) into a full legal easement passing to the buyer, even though the conveyance does not expressly mention it, where the conditions are met.

n.0: No additional payment is required for s.62 to operate.
n.1: The right is not extinguished; s.62 can carry it forward as an easement.
n.3: Prescription is one route, but s.62 provides another without needing twenty years' use.
n.4: An easement can arise without express grant, for example via s.62.

Land Law.q: An owner of a house and garden sold off the rear part of the garden to a buyer, keeping for themselves the front part next to the road. Across the retained front part there was a visible, well-worn path which the owner had regularly used, before the sale, to get from the rear part of the garden out to the road. The conveyance to the buyer said nothing at all about any right to use that path. The buyer of the rear part now wishes to use the path for access to the road and asserts a right to do so. Which of the following best describes the basis of that right?
o: A right arising only if the buyer registers a notice against the retained land.
A bare licence to use the path, which the seller may withdraw at any time.
No right can arise, because the seller's earlier use over their own land cannot become an easement. on these facts
An implied easement under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows, over the continuous and apparent quasi-easement used before the sale.
A profit à prendre entitling the buyer to take gravel from the path.
Land Law.w: On a sale of part, the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows can imply, in the buyer's favour, an easement over a quasi-easement that was continuous and apparent, and necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the part sold, and used by the seller for its benefit before the sale. The worn path meets that description.

n.0: An implied easement under Wheeldon v Burrows arises on the conveyance without registering a notice.
n.1: The buyer's right is a proprietary easement, not a revocable bare licence.
n.2: A quasi-easement used by the common owner can crystallise into an easement on a sale of part.
n.4: Using a path for access is an easement, not a profit to take material from the land.

Land Law.q: A house has enjoyed daylight through a particular ground-floor window, continuously and without interruption, for more than 20 years. The owner of the neighbouring land now proposes to erect a tall building close to that window, in a position that would substantially reduce the amount of light reaching the room behind it and leave the room noticeably darker. The house owner, alarmed at the prospect of the room becoming dark and unusable, wishes to establish and protect a right to that light so as to resist the proposed building. On what basis is such a right to light most likely to exist?
o: No right at all, because rights to light can only be granted expressly by deed.
A natural right to light that every landowner automatically enjoys over neighbouring land.
An overriding interest in the neighbour's land arising from the flow of light.
An easement of light acquired by prescription through 20 years' uninterrupted enjoyment.
A restrictive covenant implied into the conveyance of the neighbouring plot.
Land Law.w: A right to light can be acquired as an easement by prescription where light has been enjoyed through a defined aperture for at least 20 years without interruption (Prescription Act 1832). Substantial interference can then be restrained.

n.0: Rights to light commonly arise by prescription, not only by express deed.
n.1: There is no general natural right to light; it must be acquired, usually by prescription.
n.2: A right to light is an easement, not an interest that overrides through occupation.
n.4: No restrictive covenant is implied into a conveyance to give a right to light.

Land Law.q: A neighbour built a garage that encroaches slightly onto the adjoining landowner's land. The neighbour did so openly, over several weeks, while the landowner stood by and, by both words and conduct, actively encouraged the neighbour to believe that they would be allowed to keep the garage where it was. Relying on that encouragement, the neighbour spent substantial sums of money completing the garage. The landowner has since fallen out with the neighbour, changed position, and now demands that the garage be removed. The neighbour seeks advice on the basis on which they might resist removal and assert a right. Which of the following is that basis?
o: Adverse possession, because building the garage gave them immediate title to the strip.
A resulting trust, because the money spent on building the garage is treated as a contribution to the purchase of the land.
A restrictive covenant, because the landowner impliedly promised not to object.
An easement, because the garage now needs access over the landowner's remaining land.
Proprietary estoppel, because they relied to their detriment on the landowner's encouragement.
Land Law.w: Where an owner encourages or acquiesces in another's detrimental reliance such that it would be unconscionable to deny them a right, proprietary estoppel arises. The court then satisfies the equity, which may allow the encroachment to remain or require compensation.

n.0: Building the garage does not give instant title by adverse possession.
n.1: Spending on the garage does not create a resulting trust of the neighbour's land.
n.2: There is no restrictive covenant; the neighbour's protection, if any, is estoppel.
n.3: The issue is the encroachment itself, not a need for access amounting to an easement.

Land Law.q: A first mortgagee exercised its power of sale over a defaulting borrower's property and sold it at auction for £320,000. After discharging its own loan, interest and the costs of the sale, together amounting to £250,000, a surplus of £70,000 remained in the mortgagee's hands. A second mortgagee is registered against the title of the property and is owed £40,000. The borrower says that, as the property was theirs, the whole of the surplus should simply be paid over to them. The first mortgagee seeks advice on how, in law, it must deal with the surplus proceeds of sale. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: It may set the surplus off against unrelated debts the borrower owes it.
It may keep the entire surplus as compensation for the borrower's default.
It must pay the surplus into court in every case before anyone can claim it.
It must pay the whole surplus straight back to the borrower, ignoring the second mortgagee.
It holds the surplus on trust: for any later mortgagee next, then for the borrower.
Land Law.w: A selling mortgagee holds the proceeds on statutory trust: pay prior incumbrances, its own debt and costs, then account for the surplus to any subsequent mortgagee of whom it has notice, and finally to the borrower (s.105 LPA 1925).

n.0: The surplus cannot be applied to unrelated debts; it is held on the statutory trust.
n.1: The mortgagee cannot keep the surplus; it must account for it.
n.2: Payment into court is not required in every case; the mortgagee accounts under s.105.
n.3: A later mortgagee's claim ranks ahead of the borrower for the surplus.

Land Law.q: Two business associates decided to buy a commercial investment property together, purely as a money-making venture and with no domestic or family relationship between them. For convenience the legal title was taken in the sole name of one of them, but the other associate provided half of the £400,000 purchase price from their own funds. There was no written declaration of trust, and nothing was said about how the beneficial interest would be held. The associates have now fallen out, and the one who contributed half the price wants to know what interest, if any, they have in the property. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An equal 50:50 beneficial share, applying the presumption used for a shared family home, in these circumstances.
A charge over the property for the money advanced, enforceable as a mortgage.
A beneficial share under a resulting trust, reflecting the proportion of the purchase price they provided.
No interest at all, because the legal title is in the other associate's sole name.
A licence to use the property, revocable by the legal owner at any time.
Land Law.w: Outside the family-home context, a contribution to the purchase price of property vested in another's name gives rise to a presumed resulting trust in favour of the contributor in proportion to their contribution.

n.0: The Stack v Dowden family-home approach does not apply to an arm's-length commercial purchase.
n.1: The contribution creates a trust interest, not a mortgage charge, absent an agreement for security.
n.3: Sole legal ownership does not defeat a resulting trust arising from a purchase-price contribution.
n.4: A purchase-money contribution creates a beneficial interest, not a mere revocable licence.

Land Law.q: Two neighbours are in dispute about the precise line of the boundary between their two registered titles, where their gardens meet. One of them argues that the red edging shown on the official title plan for the registered title fixes, precisely and conclusively, where the legal boundary runs, and that the other neighbour's fence has therefore been put up in the wrong place. The other neighbour disputes that the title plan can be relied on in that way. They seek advice on what weight the title plan actually carries in fixing the exact line of the boundary. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Boundary disputes can only be resolved by the neighbours buying out one another.
The red edging on the title plan always fixes the precise legal boundary between titles, on these facts.
The register is conclusive as to the exact boundary and cannot be questioned at all.
The title plan usually shows only general boundaries and does not fix the exact legal boundary line.
The boundary is wherever the current fence stands, regardless of the registered titles.
Land Law.w: Under the general boundaries rule (LRA 2002), a registered title plan shows general boundaries only and does not determine the exact line, unless the boundary has been formally 'determined'. The precise line is a matter of evidence.

n.0: Boundary disputes are resolved on the evidence, not only by a buy-out.
n.1: The red edging indicates general, not exact, boundaries.
n.2: The register is not conclusive as to the exact boundary under the general boundaries rule.
n.4: A fence line does not automatically fix the legal boundary.

Land Law.q: A landlord owns two adjoining industrial units. It let the first unit to a tenant under a lease that expressly permitted, and was clearly granted for, use as a restaurant, and the tenant fitted it out at considerable expense for that purpose. The landlord then carried out extensive works to the second, retained unit, installing equipment that generates fumes and vibration which make it impossible in practice to run a restaurant from the first unit. The tenant, unable to trade, seeks a remedy against the landlord for the loss of the use for which the unit was let. Which of the following best describes the tenant's claim?
o: Breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment only, entitling the tenant to forfeit the landlord's reversion.
No claim, because a landlord owes no obligations in relation to neighbouring land it owns.
Trespass, because the landlord has physically entered the demised premises without consent.
Nuisance, which requires the landlord's activity to interfere with the tenant's personal health and comfort rather than their business use.
Derogation from grant, because the landlord has substantially deprived the tenant of the use the lease was granted for.
Land Law.w: A landlord must not derogate from its grant: having let the unit for a particular purpose, it must not use its retained land so as to make that purpose substantially impossible. The tenant can claim for derogation from grant (and often breach of quiet enjoyment).

n.0: A tenant cannot forfeit the landlord's reversion; forfeiture is a landlord's remedy.
n.1: A landlord's use of retained land can breach the non-derogation obligation.
n.2: There is no need for physical entry to the demised premises for derogation from grant.
n.3: Derogation from grant does not require interference with health, unlike some nuisance claims.

Land Law.q: Ms Adeyemi has lived for the last 14 years with her partner, Mr Doyle, in a house that was bought in, and remains registered in, Mr Doyle's sole name. There is no express declaration of trust. Throughout that time Ms Adeyemi paid roughly half of every monthly mortgage instalment from her own earnings, paid for a large rear extension, and the couple ran their finances jointly and always spoke of the house as belonging to them both. The relationship has now broken down and Mr Doyle asserts that, as the sole registered owner, the entire beneficial interest is his. Ms Adeyemi wishes to claim a beneficial share of the house. On which basis is she most likely to establish an interest?
o: A common intention constructive trust, from the parties' shared intention and her detrimental reliance.
No interest, because the legal title is in Mr Doyle's sole name and there is no written declaration of trust.
An overriding interest, binding Mr Doyle irrespective of any shared intention between them.
A resulting trust, giving her a share fixed solely by the proportion of the purchase price she provided.
A proprietary estoppel, giving her the entire beneficial ownership of the home.
Land Law.w: For a family home in one party's sole name, a beneficial share is normally established through a common intention constructive trust: a shared intention (express or inferred) that the claimant have an interest, coupled with detrimental reliance (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott).

n.1: Absence of a written declaration does not defeat a constructive trust, which is expressly exempt from the writing requirement.
n.2: An overriding interest concerns whether an interest binds a third-party purchaser, not how the interest is created between the couple.
n.3: The resulting-trust approach based purely on purchase-price contributions is not the modern route for a family home dispute of this kind.
n.4: Estoppel might give some remedy but would not automatically give her the entire beneficial interest, and is not the primary basis here.

Land Law.q: When selling off part of their garden, an owner extracted from the buyer a covenant to contribute to the cost of maintaining a private road shared by both plots. That buyer has since sold their plot on to a successor in title. The successor now regularly uses the shared road but refuses to pay any contribution towards its upkeep, arguing that the obligation to pay was personal to the original buyer and did not pass to them on the sale. The owner of the retained land, faced with mounting repair bills, seeks advice on whether the maintenance obligation can be enforced against the successor. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The obligation binds the successor, because positive and restrictive covenants are treated identically. on the facts of this case
The obligation is not directly enforceable against the successor, because the burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land.
The obligation binds the successor, because the burden of any freehold covenant runs with the land.
The obligation is void, because covenants to pay money can never be created over land.
The obligation binds the successor, because it was protected by a notice on the register.
Land Law.w: The burden of a positive covenant (here, to pay towards upkeep) does not run with freehold land at law or in equity (Rhone v Stephens). It cannot be enforced directly against a successor, though indirect devices (such as a chain of indemnity covenants or the benefit-and-burden principle) may assist.

n.0: Positive and restrictive covenants are treated differently as to whether the burden runs.
n.2: Only the burden of restrictive covenants can run in equity; positive burdens do not run.
n.3: Covenants to pay money are valid; the difficulty is enforcing the burden against a successor.
n.4: Entry of a notice cannot make a positive burden run where the law does not allow it.

Land Law.q: A landlord and a tenant entered into a written agreement, signed by both and complying with the formalities for a contract for the disposition of an interest in land, for the grant of a seven-year lease of business premises at a stated rent. On the strength of that agreement the tenant went into possession of the premises and has paid the agreed rent ever since. No lease was ever completed by deed as the agreement had envisaged. A dispute has now arisen between them, and it has become important to determine whether the tenant holds a lease for the full seven-year term or merely some lesser interest. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The tenant has no interest of any kind, because a seven-year lease must be by deed to exist.
The tenant has an equitable lease, because equity treats a specifically enforceable agreement for a lease as a lease.
The tenant has a legal seven-year lease, because taking possession dispenses with the need for a deed. on these facts
The tenant has a mere licence, revocable by the landlord on reasonable notice.
The tenant has only a periodic tenancy at law and no rights under the seven-year agreement.
Land Law.w: A seven-year lease requires a deed to be legal, but a specifically enforceable written agreement for the lease takes effect as an equitable lease (Walsh v Lonsdale), so the tenant holds on the agreed terms in equity.

n.0: Absence of a deed does not leave the tenant with no interest; equity recognises the agreement.
n.2: Taking possession does not create a legal seven-year lease without a deed.
n.3: An enforceable agreement for a lease is more than a revocable licence.
n.4: The agreement gives an equitable lease on its terms, not merely an implied periodic tenancy.

Land Law.q: Two trustees hold registered land on trust for beneficiaries and sell it to a buyer, who pays the purchase money to both trustees. The beneficiaries had equitable interests under the trust. The buyer wishes to take the land free of those beneficial interests, which should attach to the proceeds. The purchase money is paid to two trustees. The beneficiaries hold behind the trust. Two trustees holding registered land on trust for beneficiaries have sold it, taking care that the buyer paid the purchase money to both of them, and the buyer wants to be confident it takes the land clear of the beneficiaries' interests, which should instead fasten onto the sale money. Which of the following best describes the effect of overreaching?
o: Overreaching is impossible where the land is registered.
Overreaching requires payment to a single trustee only.
The buyer takes subject to the beneficial interests despite paying two trustees on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Overreaching requires the personal consent of every beneficiary to the sale.
The beneficiaries' equitable interests are overreached and transfer to the proceeds of sale, so the buyer takes free of them.
Land Law.w: Where trustees of land sell and the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation), the beneficiaries' equitable interests are overreached: they are detached from the land and transfer to the proceeds of sale in the trustees' hands, so the buyer takes the land free of those interests, even if a beneficiary was in actual occupation.

n.0: Overreaching operates for registered land through payment to two trustees.
n.1: Overreaching requires payment to two trustees (or a trust corporation), not a single trustee.
n.2: Paying two trustees overreaches the interests, so the buyer does not take subject to them.
n.3: Overreaching does not require each beneficiary's personal consent.

Land Law.q: For more than 25 years Mrs Kelso, the owner of a house, has walked every day across an adjoining field to reach a lane, using a well-worn path. She has never asked permission to do so, and neither the previous owners of the field nor anyone else has ever objected or tried to stop her. The field has recently been sold to Mr Lang, who has now put up a fence blocking the path and has told Mrs Kelso that she has no right to cross his land. Mrs Kelso seeks advice on whether she can continue to use the path to reach the lane. Which of the following best describes her position?
o: She has no right at all, because a right of way over open land can only ever arise by necessity.
She has a personal licence only, which was personal to the old owner and ended when the field was sold.
She has an overriding interest in the field that binds the new owner however the use first began.
She has an easement, but only if it had been expressly granted to her by deed at some earlier time.
She may have acquired an easement by prescription, from using the way as of right for over 20 years.
Land Law.w: Long use of a right of way as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for at least 20 years can give rise to an easement by prescription. Once acquired as a legal easement, it binds a successor to the servient land such as Mr Lang.

n.0: Necessity is a separate, narrow route; it is not the only way to acquire a right of way.
n.1: Nothing indicates the use was permissive; use as of right is the basis for prescription, not a mere licence.
n.2: A right of way is an easement; it is not an interest that overrides through occupation of the servient land.
n.3: Express grant by deed is one way to create an easement, but prescription creates one without any deed.

Land Law.q: A landowner wants to understand which interests in land are capable of existing as legal estates, as distinct from those that can only be equitable. They hold what they describe as ownership of their house and also grant various rights over it. The question concerns the categories recognised by the Law of Property Act 1925. The landowner asks about legal estates in land. The landowner regards themselves as simply owning their house outright and has also handed out assorted rights over it to others, and wants to understand which of these various interests the law will recognise as capable of being legal, as opposed to merely equitable, interests in the land. Which of the following best describes the position under section 1 of the Law of Property Act 1925?
o: Only the freehold can be a legal estate; leases are always equitable.
Only two legal estates are capable of existing: the freehold (fee simple absolute in possession) and the leasehold (term of years absolute).
There are five legal estates capable of existing in land.
Any interest in land whatsoever may exist as a legal estate.
Legal estates were abolished, so all interests in land are now equitable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Land Law.w: Under s.1(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925, only two estates in land are capable of subsisting or being conveyed at law: the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold). Section 1(2) lists the interests capable of being legal (such as legal easements and charges); all other interests take effect in equity.

n.0: Leases (terms of years absolute) can be legal estates, not only the freehold.
n.2: There are two legal estates, not five.
n.3: Not any interest can be legal; only the two estates and the s.1(2) interests can be.
n.4: Legal estates were not abolished; the 1925 Act rationalised them into two.

Land Law.q: A borrower took out a mortgage over her home to fund her business. A term of the mortgage provides that the borrower may not redeem the mortgage — that is, repay the loan and have the charge removed from the title — for a period of 40 years, effectively tying her to this particular lender, on onerous terms, for the entire likely life of the loan. The borrower's financial circumstances have since improved and she wishes to repay the loan early and remortgage elsewhere on much better terms, but the lender insists that she is bound by the 40-year restriction on redemption. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The borrower may redeem early only by paying the lender all the interest that would have accrued over 40 years.
The postponement is fully binding, because parties are free to agree any redemption date they choose.
The mortgage is entirely void, so the borrower owes nothing and keeps the property free of charge.
The postponement is likely void as a clog on the equity of redemption, so the borrower may redeem.
The borrower may redeem only if the lender is shown to have acted dishonestly in taking the mortgage.
Land Law.w: Equity protects the borrower's right to redeem. A term that postpones or fetters redemption so as to render the equity of redemption illusory or is otherwise oppressive is void as a clog on the equity, allowing the borrower to redeem.

n.0: Redemption on such an onerous fetter does not require paying all future interest.
n.1: A postponement that makes the right to redeem illusory is not simply binding as agreed.
n.2: Only the offending term is struck down; the mortgage debt itself remains.
n.4: Dishonesty is not required; the clog doctrine invalidates oppressive fetters on redemption.

Land Law.q: A landowner, doing a friend a favour, gave the friend oral permission to keep a caravan on a corner of the landowner's field while the friend looked for somewhere permanent to live. Nothing was ever put in writing and no rent or other payment was charged. Some months later the landowner sold and transferred the whole field to a buyer, who intends to develop it. The buyer now wants the caravan removed, but the friend insists that, having been given permission to keep the caravan there, they have a right to remain which binds the new owner of the field. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The permission is an overriding interest binding the buyer because the friend is in occupation.
The permission is a restrictive covenant preventing the buyer from removing the caravan.
The permission is a bare licence, which is personal and does not bind the buyer of the land.
The permission is a lease, which gives the friend a proprietary right against the buyer.
The permission is an easement, which automatically binds the buyer as a legal interest.
Land Law.w: A bare licence is mere permission to be on land. It is personal to the parties, creates no proprietary interest, and does not bind a purchaser of the land; the buyer can require the caravan's removal (subject to reasonable notice).

n.0: A personal licence is not an interest capable of overriding under Schedule 3, so occupation does not make it bind.
n.1: A licence is not a restrictive covenant and imposes no burden running with the land.
n.3: There is no grant of exclusive possession for a term, so it is not a lease.
n.4: Parking/keeping a caravan by permission is not an easement, and a bare licence is not a legal interest.

Land Law.q: A landowner has used a right of way over a neighbour's land openly, without permission and without force or secrecy, for well over twenty years, and now claims a legal easement by long use. The use has been as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for the requisite period. The landowner claims a prescriptive easement. For well over twenty years the landowner has openly driven across the neighbour's land to reach their own, doing so without asking permission, without any secrecy and without force, and now, relying on that long and uninterrupted use, claims to have acquired a legal right of way. Which of the following best describes how such an easement may be acquired by prescription?
o: By long use as of right, which may be claimed under common law prescription, lost modern grant, or the Prescription Act 1832.
By a single year's use of the right of way.
By any use at all, even if it was with the owner's permission.
Only by an express deed of grant from the servient owner.
By registering the right as a company charge at Companies House on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Land Law.w: An easement may be acquired by prescription where the claimant has used the right 'as of right' (without force, without secrecy and without permission, nec vi, nec clam, nec precario) for the requisite long period. There are three routes: common law prescription, the doctrine of lost modern grant, and the Prescription Act 1832 (typically requiring twenty years' use).

n.1: A single year's use is far short of the period required.
n.2: Use with permission is not 'as of right' and cannot found prescription.
n.3: Prescription arises from long use, not an express deed of grant (which would be express grant, not prescription).
n.4: Registration as a company charge is irrelevant to acquiring an easement by prescription.

Land Law.q: A large, mature tree stands in Mr Sharpe's garden, close to the boundary with Ms Turner's house next door. Over several years the tree's roots have spread under the boundary and beneath Ms Turner's house, and they are now causing subsidence that has cracked the walls and damaged the foundations, requiring costly repairs. Ms Turner has asked Mr Sharpe to deal with the tree, but he has refused, saying the tree is on his own land and its natural growth is not his responsibility. Ms Turner wants both to recover for the damage and to stop further encroachment. Which of the following best describes her claim?
o: Trespass to land, which requires the tree owner to have personally entered onto the neighbour's property without any permission.
Breach of an implied easement of support owed by the tree owner.
Adverse possession, because the roots have occupied part of the neighbour's land.
No claim, because a landowner is never liable for the natural growth of trees.
Private nuisance, for which the neighbour may seek an injunction and damages for the encroaching roots.
Land Law.w: Encroachment by tree roots that causes damage is an actionable private nuisance. The neighbour may abate the nuisance, and may seek damages for the harm and an injunction to restrain continuing encroachment.

n.0: Trespass requires a direct physical intrusion by a person or thing placed by the defendant, not natural root growth, which is dealt with in nuisance.
n.1: This is not a support easement question; the cause of action is nuisance.
n.2: Roots spreading underground do not give the tree owner title by adverse possession.
n.3: A landowner can be liable in nuisance for encroaching roots that cause damage.

Land Law.q: A seller of registered land, Delia, entered into an estate contract in January agreeing to sell the land to a first buyer. The first buyer paid a deposit but did not protect the estate contract by entering a notice against the title on the register. In March, before the sale to the first buyer had been completed, Delia transferred the same land to a second buyer for valuable consideration, and the second buyer was duly registered as the new proprietor. The first buyer has now discovered the second sale and asserts the estate contract against the second buyer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The second buyer is bound, because a prior estate contract always binds a later purchaser of the land.
The second buyer takes free only if the first buyer was not in occupation of the land.
The second buyer is bound if the first buyer can show the second buyer ought to have discovered the contract. on these facts
The second buyer takes free of the estate contract, because an unprotected interest is postponed to a registered disposition for value.
The first buyer prevails, because the estate contract was created before the second sale.
Land Law.w: On a registered disposition for valuable consideration, priority is governed by s.29 LRA 2002: interests not protected by an entry on the register (and not overriding) are postponed to the disposition. An unprotected estate contract of vacant land therefore does not bind the registered second buyer.

n.0: A prior estate contract does not automatically bind a later registered purchaser for value.
n.1: Occupation could raise an overriding interest, but on these facts the unprotected contract is postponed; occupation is not stated.
n.2: Notice is generally irrelevant in registered land; priority turns on protection and the s.29 rules.
n.4: Mere priority in time does not preserve an unprotected interest against a registered disposition for value.

Land Law.q: A borrower and a lender entered into a written agreement, signed by both parties, under which the borrower agreed to grant the lender a charge over the borrower's registered property as security for a loan of £120,000; and, on the strength of that agreement, the lender advanced the whole of the £120,000 to the borrower. Through an oversight on both sides, no formal legal charge was ever executed by deed. The borrower has since defaulted on the loan, and the lender is anxious to know what security, if any, it now holds over the property. Which of the following best describes the lender's security?
o: The lender has no security of any kind and is merely an unsecured creditor.
The lender automatically has a full legal charge once the loan money is advanced.
The lender has a lien over the property that arises only if it takes physical possession. in the circumstances
The lender has an equitable charge, because a specifically enforceable agreement to grant a charge takes effect in equity.
The lender has a profit à prendre over the property until the loan is repaid.
Land Law.w: An agreement for value to grant a charge, satisfying s.2 LP(MP)A 1989 and specifically enforceable, creates an equitable charge in the lender's favour, even though no legal charge has been executed (United Bank of Kuwait v Sahib).

n.0: The lender is not left unsecured; equity recognises an equitable charge from the enforceable agreement.
n.1: Advancing the loan does not by itself create a legal charge; a deed is needed for that.
n.2: An equitable charge does not depend on the lender taking possession.
n.4: A profit à prendre is a right to take produce from land, not a form of security.

Land Law.q: A co-owner of a house has become bankrupt, and their trustee in bankruptcy has applied to the court for an order for sale of the house so that the bankrupt's share can be realised for the benefit of the creditors. The bankrupt's spouse still lives in the house with the family and strongly opposes the sale. More than one year has now passed since the bankrupt's estate first vested in the trustee. The court must decide how to weigh the competing interests on the trustee's application for sale. Which of the following best describes the position once this length of time has passed?
o: The trustee has no power to seek a sale of a co-owned family home at all.
The welfare of the creditors is irrelevant once a family occupies the property.
The court must always refuse a sale while the bankrupt's family remain living in the home. in the circumstances
After one year, the interests of the creditors generally outweigh other considerations save in exceptional circumstances.
The court must order an immediate sale on the day the bankruptcy is declared.
Land Law.w: On a trustee in bankruptcy's application, s.335A Insolvency Act 1986 applies: after one year from the vesting of the estate, the court assumes that the creditors' interests outweigh all other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional.

n.0: The trustee can seek a sale of the co-owned home under the statutory scheme.
n.1: The creditors' interests are central, not irrelevant, on a trustee's application.
n.2: The court is not required to refuse a sale while the family remains; after a year the creditors usually prevail.
n.4: A sale is not ordered automatically on the day of bankruptcy; the s.335A framework applies.

Land Law.q: For more than 20 years the owner of a house has driven a car across a neighbouring farmer's private track to get from the house to the public road, doing so openly whenever needed, without ever asking the farmer's permission and without the farmer or any predecessor objecting or trying to stop it. The farm has recently been sold to a new owner, who has installed a locked barrier across the track and told the house owner that they have no right to drive across the land. The house owner seeks advice on whether the right can be continued. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An easement exists, but only if the house owner first registers it against the farm's title.
No right exists, because an easement can only ever be created by express grant in a deed.
No right exists, because easements over agricultural land cannot arise by prescription.
A vehicular easement may have arisen by prescription, from long use as of right.
A licence exists that ended automatically when the farm was sold to the new owner.
Land Law.w: Long use of a right of way as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for at least 20 years can give rise to an easement by prescription, which is a legal easement binding successors to the servient land.

n.0: A prescriptive legal easement binds successors without the dominant owner registering it.
n.1: Easements can arise by prescription or implication, not only by express grant.
n.2: There is no bar on prescriptive easements over agricultural land.
n.4: Use as of right is not a licence; nothing indicates permission was given.

Land Law.q: A restrictive covenant, taken when neighbouring plots were sold off, restricts the use of one plot (the burdened plot) to residential purposes only, and was expressed to be for the benefit of the other plot. Both plots have since been sold on to new owners. The new owner of the burdened plot has now begun converting the building on it into offices, in clear breach of the covenant. The new owner of the benefited plot, who was not the original person in whose favour the covenant was first made, wishes to enforce the covenant and put a stop to the office use. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant is enforceable only if the burdened owner expressly agreed to be bound on purchase.
The covenant is enforceable only if it was created within the last 20 years.
The covenant is unenforceable, because covenants can only ever be enforced by the original parties.
The covenant is enforceable at common law, because the burden of covenants runs with the land at law. on these facts
The covenant is enforceable in equity if the benefit passed to the claimant and the Tulk v Moxhay conditions are met.
Land Law.w: The burden of a restrictive covenant can run in equity where the Tulk v Moxhay conditions are satisfied and it is protected against the burdened land, and the benefit can pass to a successor of the benefited land (by annexation, assignment or a building scheme), who may then enforce it.

n.0: The burden can bind a successor in equity without a fresh agreement, if properly protected.
n.1: There is no 20-year limit on the enforceability of a restrictive covenant.
n.2: Successors, not just original parties, can enforce and be bound by restrictive covenants in equity.
n.3: The burden of a covenant does not run at common law; it runs, if at all, in equity.

Land Law.q: A tenant's lease contains the landlord's usual covenant for quiet enjoyment of the premises. Wanting to force the tenant out so that the flat can be re-let at a higher rent, the landlord has repeatedly entered the flat without notice, deliberately disconnected services to the flat, and otherwise harassed the tenant so as to make continued occupation intolerable. The tenant, who has done nothing wrong and is up to date with the rent, wishes to remain in the flat and to obtain a remedy for the landlord's conduct. The tenant seeks advice on the claim available against the landlord. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Adverse possession, because the landlord has interfered with the tenant's occupation.
Breach of a repairing covenant only, limited to the cost of restoring the services.
Breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment, for which the tenant may claim damages and an injunction.
Forfeiture of the landlord's reversion, ending the landlord's interest in the property, in these circumstances.
No claim, because a landlord may enter and manage its own property whenever it wishes.
Land Law.w: The covenant for quiet enjoyment protects the tenant's lawful possession from substantial interference by the landlord. Repeated unlawful entry, cutting off services and harassment breach it, entitling the tenant to damages and an injunction (and such conduct may also amount to unlawful eviction/harassment under statute).

n.0: The landlord's interference does not give the tenant title by adverse possession.
n.1: This is not a repairing-covenant claim confined to service costs; it is breach of quiet enjoyment.
n.3: A tenant cannot forfeit the landlord's reversion; forfeiture is a landlord's remedy.
n.4: The landlord's right to manage does not extend to substantially interfering with the tenant's possession.

Land Law.q: In 2016 a landlord granted a 10-year commercial lease of office premises. Some years into the term, with the landlord's written consent, the tenant assigned the lease to an assignee; and, as a lawful condition of giving that consent, the landlord required the outgoing tenant to enter into an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA) guaranteeing the assignee's performance of the covenants. The assignee has since fallen several months into arrears with the rent, and the landlord wishes to recover the unpaid sums. The landlord seeks advice on which party or parties it can pursue for the arrears. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assignee alone, because the outgoing tenant gave no continuing liability.
Any former tenant in the chain, as all remain liable for the life of the lease.
The outgoing tenant alone, under the principle of privity of contract.
The assignee as current tenant, and the outgoing tenant under its AGA.
Only the landlord's managing agent, who approved the assignment.
Land Law.w: Under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, on a lawful assignment of a post-1995 lease the outgoing tenant is released from the tenant covenants, but may be required to guarantee the immediate assignee by an AGA. So the landlord can pursue the current tenant (assignee) and the outgoing tenant under its AGA, but not earlier tenants.

n.0: The outgoing tenant remains liable under its AGA for the assignee, so it is not the assignee alone.
n.1: Former tenants are released under the 1995 Act; the old privity-of-contract liability for the life of the lease does not apply.
n.2: For post-1995 leases the outgoing tenant is released on assignment, subject only to any AGA.
n.4: An agent authorising the assignment does not become liable for the rent.

Land Law.q: A buyer takes a transfer of registered freehold land and is duly registered as the new proprietor. It later emerges that a tenant holds a legal lease of part of the property, granted for a term of five years at a market rent, which was neither noted on the register nor mentioned to the buyer at any time before completion. The tenant is in actual occupation of their part and now asserts the lease against the new owner, who had expected to take the whole of the land free of any such lease. The buyer seeks advice on whether the lease is binding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The lease binds the buyer only if the buyer inspected the property before completion.
The lease does not bind the buyer, because only leases granted for more than seven years can bind.
The lease binds the buyer, because a legal lease of seven years or less is an overriding interest.
The lease does not bind the buyer, because it was not noted on the register before completion.
The lease binds the buyer only if the tenant also had a beneficial interest in the freehold.
Land Law.w: A legal lease granted for a term of seven years or less is an overriding interest under Schedule 3 paragraph 1 LRA 2002 and binds a buyer of the registered estate even though it is not noted on the register and cannot be separately registered.

n.0: The overriding status of a short legal lease does not depend on the buyer inspecting.
n.1: Leases of seven years or less bind as overriding interests; longer leases are registrable dispositions.
n.3: A short legal lease does not need to be noted to bind; it overrides under Schedule 3 para 1.
n.4: A legal lease binds regardless of whether the tenant also has a freehold interest.

Land Law.q: A developer bought a plot of land subject to a restrictive covenant limiting the plot to no more than two houses. In clear and deliberate breach of that covenant, the developer has begun constructing a block of flats on the plot. The neighbour who has the benefit of the covenant, and whose own property's value and outlook depend directly upon it, has acted promptly on learning of the works and wishes to stop the development before the block of flats is completed. The neighbour seeks advice on the most effective remedy available to enforce the covenant. Which of the following is that remedy?
o: Damages only, because an injunction can never be granted to enforce a covenant.
An order that the neighbour sell their own land to the developer at a fixed price.
Nothing, because a developer may always build as it wishes on its own land.
An injunction restraining the breach and the continued construction of the flats.
A declaration that the covenant is valid, but no order stopping the building work.
Land Law.w: Where a restrictive covenant is breached and the benefited owner acts promptly and suffers real harm, the primary remedy is an injunction to restrain the breach. Damages in lieu are the exception, awarded only in limited circumstances.

n.0: An injunction can be, and usually is, granted to enforce a restrictive covenant.
n.1: The court does not compel the innocent neighbour to sell to the wrongdoer.
n.2: The right to build is limited by an enforceable restrictive covenant.
n.4: A bare declaration would be an inadequate remedy where an injunction is appropriate.

Land Law.q: A squatter in adverse possession of registered land applied in 2023 under Schedule 6 of the Land Registration Act 2002 to be registered as proprietor. That application was rejected because the registered proprietor objected to it in time. Over the following two years the registered proprietor took no steps at all to evict the squatter or otherwise to regularise the position, and the squatter has remained in open and undisturbed adverse possession of the land throughout that period. The squatter now wishes to make a further application to be registered as proprietor. Which of the following best describes the squatter's position on a second application?
o: The squatter must instead purchase the land from the registered proprietor to obtain title.
The registered proprietor's title was automatically extinguished when the first application was rejected, on these facts.
The squatter can never apply again once the first application has been rejected.
The squatter must start a fresh ten-year period of possession before applying again.
The squatter may make a further application and this time is generally entitled to be registered as proprietor.
Land Law.w: If a Schedule 6 application is rejected after objection but the proprietor does not, within the following two years, evict the squatter or otherwise regularise the position, the squatter (still in adverse possession) may reapply and is then generally entitled to be registered as proprietor.

n.0: The squatter is not required to buy the land; registration can follow under the two-year rule.
n.1: Title is not automatically extinguished on rejection; the two-year mechanism must operate.
n.2: Rejection is not the end; the two-year rule can entitle the squatter to reapply successfully.
n.3: The squatter need not start a fresh ten-year period; the further application follows the two years.

Land Law.q: A landlord granted a five-year lease of commercial premises at a rent of £18,000 a year, payable quarterly in advance. The lease contains a clause allowing the landlord to re-enter and forfeit if the rent is unpaid. The tenant has now failed to pay the rent for the last two quarters, amounting to £9,000, despite the landlord having made formal demand for it. The landlord has taken no step, such as demanding or accepting further rent, that would amount to waiving the breach, and wishes to bring the lease to an end and recover the premises. Which of the following best describes the landlord's position?
o: The landlord may forfeit the lease by peaceable re-entry or court proceedings, subject to the tenant's right to relief.
The landlord must first serve a notice under s.146 of the Law of Property Act 1925.
The landlord may forfeit only if the lease has less than seven years left to run.
The landlord may forfeit only after obtaining the consent of the court to end the lease early, as a matter of general law.
The landlord cannot forfeit for non-payment of rent, which is recoverable only as a debt.
Land Law.w: A forfeiture clause lets the landlord re-enter for non-payment of rent, by court proceedings (or, for commercial premises, peaceable re-entry), subject to the tenant's right to apply for relief from forfeiture. A s.146 notice is required for breaches other than non-payment of rent.

n.1: A s.146 notice is required for breaches other than non-payment of rent, so it is not needed here.
n.2: Forfeiture for rent arrears does not depend on the length of the residue of the term.
n.3: No prior court consent is needed to exercise a contractual right of re-entry; the court's role is on any relief application.
n.4: Rent arrears are a debt, but a forfeiture clause additionally allows the lease to be ended.

Land Law.q: By a deed made when he sold off part of his yard, Mr Voss granted the buyer, Ms Wren, an easement to park up to two cars on a clearly defined area of the retained yard. For the first two years Ms Wren used the area only for parking. She has now begun using the same area to store business stock, a shipping container and pallets of goods, so that it is often impossible to park there at all. Mr Voss objects that this goes well beyond what he granted. Ms Wren maintains that, having been given rights over the area, she may put it to any reasonable use. Which of the following best describes Ms Wren's rights?
o: The neighbour may store goods there, provided it does not increase the overall burden on the servient land.
The neighbour may use the area for any purpose, because an express easement allows all reasonable uses.
The neighbour may use the area only for the parking the deed permits; storage exceeds the grant.
The neighbour has lost the easement entirely by exceeding it, and may no longer park cars there at all.
The neighbour may store goods there, because storage is naturally incidental to a right to park cars.
Land Law.w: An express easement is confined to the purpose for which it was granted. Using the land for storage goes beyond a right to park and is actionable, but exceeding the scope does not automatically extinguish the easement itself.

n.0: The test is the scope of the grant, not merely whether the burden increases; storage is outside the grant.
n.1: An express easement is limited to its granted purpose; it does not authorise all reasonable uses.
n.3: Excessive use is restrained, but it does not destroy the validly granted right to park.
n.4: Storage is a distinct use, not something inherently incidental to parking vehicles.

Land Law.q: A landowner granted a neighbour a right of way over the landowner's registered land. The grant was made only in a written contract signed by both parties, and was never completed by deed as a legal easement. No notice in respect of the right was entered on the register. The landowner has since sold and transferred the registered land to a buyer for value. The neighbour wishes to continue using the right of way and asserts it against the new owner, who says they took the land free of it. The neighbour seeks advice on the nature of the right and whether it binds the buyer. Which of the following best describes it?
o: It is an equitable easement, which will only bind a buyer if it is protected by a notice on the register.
It is void, because an easement can never be created otherwise than by statute.
It is a profit à prendre, binding a buyer once the neighbour registers a caution.
It is a bare licence, which can never bind a buyer of the land in any circumstances. on these facts
It is a legal easement, which binds any buyer of the servient land automatically.
Land Law.w: A legal easement must be granted by deed. A signed written contract to grant an easement, for value, takes effect only as an equitable easement, which in registered land binds a buyer of the servient land only if protected by a notice on the register.

n.1: Easements can be created by grant; the point is that without a deed the grant is equitable.
n.2: An easement is not a profit, and protection is by notice, not a caution.
n.3: An equitable easement is more than a bare licence and can bind if protected.
n.4: Without a deed the easement is equitable, not legal, so it does not bind automatically.

Land Law.q: Twelve years ago Mr Quirke asked his neighbour whether he could store building materials on a narrow strip of the neighbour's land that runs alongside his own. The neighbour agreed, and since then Mr Quirke has kept materials there continuously, treating the strip as a useful extension of his yard. Nothing further has ever been said about the arrangement, and the neighbour has never withdrawn permission or objected. Mr Quirke now claims that, having used the strip for so long, he has acquired title to it by adverse possession and that it belongs to him. The land is unregistered. Which of the following best explains whether his claim can succeed?
o: His claim succeeds, but only because the neighbour never physically removed the stored materials.
His claim succeeds, because twelve years of continuous use of the strip is enough to acquire title to it.
His claim fails, because the right to acquire land by adverse possession has been abolished in England.
His claim succeeds, because storing goods on another's land confers ownership after ten years' use.
His claim fails, because possession with the owner's permission is not adverse, so time never ran.
Land Law.w: Adverse possession requires factual possession and an intention to possess, and crucially the possession must be without the owner's consent (JA Pye (Oxford) v Graham). Because the neighbour gave permission, the use is not adverse and time does not begin to run.

n.0: The claim fails because the use was permissive, not because of anything the neighbour did or did not do physically.
n.1: Length of use alone is not enough; the possession must be adverse, which permission prevents.
n.2: Adverse possession still exists, although the LRA 2002 changed the procedure for registered land.
n.3: Storing goods with permission is not adverse possession, and there is no automatic acquisition of ownership.

Land Law.q: A property is subject to a first registered charge in favour of Bank A and a later, second, registered charge in favour of Bank B. Bank A's charge secures an initial loan and, by its express terms, also secures any further advances that Bank A may later choose to make to the same borrower. Bank A now wishes to make a further advance to the borrower and to have that further advance rank ahead of Bank B's second charge in order of priority. Bank A seeks advice on whether, and in what circumstances, it can achieve priority for the further advance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Bank B's charge is void, because a property can carry only one registered charge at a time.
Bank A always ranks first for all sums, regardless of when advances were made or notice received.
The two charges rank equally and share the proceeds of sale rateably in all cases.
Bank B always ranks first for everything it is owed, because its own charge was registered before Bank A made the further advance.
Bank A's further advance may still rank ahead of Bank B where the tacking rules under the LRA 2002 are satisfied.
Land Law.w: Priority of registered charges generally follows the order of registration, but a prior chargee may 'tack' further advances so they rank with its original charge in defined circumstances under s.49 LRA 2002 (for example where it had no notice of the subsequent charge, or was obliged to make the advance).

n.0: A property can carry more than one registered charge; the later charge is not void.
n.1: The first chargee does not automatically rank first for further advances in all cases; tacking is subject to conditions.
n.2: Registered charges do not simply share rateably; they rank by priority.
n.3: A prior chargee can, within the tacking rules, gain priority for a further advance over an intervening charge.

Land Law.q: A tenant of commercial premises breached a covenant in the lease to keep the premises in good repair, allowing the roof and guttering to fall into disrepair. The landlord served a valid notice under section 146 of the Law of Property Act 1925 specifying the breach, and then began court proceedings to forfeit the lease. Since the proceedings began, the tenant has carried out all of the outstanding repairs, paid the landlord's reasonable costs, and fully remedied the position complained of. The tenant wishes to keep the lease and has applied to the court for relief from forfeiture. Which of the following best describes the tenant's position?
o: The court may grant relief only if the tenant proves the breach was not their fault.
The court must grant relief automatically once the tenant has remedied the breach.
The court must refuse relief, because forfeiture for breach of a repairing covenant is always final. on these facts
The court has no power to grant relief once a s.146 notice has been served.
The court has a discretion to grant relief, and is likely to do so where the breach has been remedied and relief is just.
Land Law.w: Relief from forfeiture is discretionary. Where the tenant has remedied the breach, compensated the landlord and the breach was not serious or lasting, the court will usually grant relief on terms, restoring the lease, as forfeiture is regarded as security for performance rather than a windfall.

n.0: The tenant need not prove absence of fault to obtain relief.
n.1: Relief is discretionary, not automatic, even where the breach is remedied.
n.2: Forfeiture for breach of covenant is not final; relief is available in the court's discretion.
n.3: The court retains power to grant relief after a s.146 notice; indeed that is when relief is sought.

Land Law.q: A solicitor acts for Ms Bright, who is buying a house with unregistered title from Mr Coombes for £310,000. Mr Coombes is registered on the title deeds as sole legal owner, but unknown to Ms Bright he in fact holds the house on trust and there is a beneficiary entitled to a share. That beneficiary is not living in the property, and nothing in the deeds, on a reasonably careful inspection, or in Ms Bright's pre-contract enquiries suggests that anyone other than Mr Coombes has an interest. Ms Bright pays the whole price to Mr Coombes and takes a conveyance of the legal estate. Several months after completion the beneficiary comes forward and asserts that their interest binds Ms Bright. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because a payment to a single owner can never overreach a beneficial interest.
Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because the beneficiary could in principle have been discovered on enquiry.
Ms Bright takes free of the beneficial interest, as a bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice of it.
Ms Bright takes free of the interest, because beneficial interests in unregistered land are void unless registered as land charges.
Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because a purchaser of unregistered land is always bound by beneficial interests.
Land Law.w: A beneficial interest under a trust is not registrable as a land charge, so in unregistered land it is governed by the doctrine of notice. A bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice (actual, constructive or imputed) takes free of it. Here nothing could be discovered on reasonable enquiry, so Ms Bright had no notice.

n.0: Overreaching is not the issue here; the point is the buyer's lack of notice, which defeats the interest regardless of overreaching.
n.1: The facts show the interest could not be discovered on reasonable enquiry, so no constructive notice is fixed on Ms Bright.
n.3: The land charges regime does not apply to beneficial interests under a trust, so non-registration does not make the interest void.
n.4: A purchaser is not bound by every beneficial interest; the doctrine of notice governs interests outside the land charges system.

Land Law.q: A buyer of registered land completed the purchase of a house. Living in the house at the time of the purchase, in plainly obvious day-to-day occupation, was a person who had contributed a substantial part of the purchase price when the house was first bought and who had acquired a beneficial interest as a result. That person's interest was not entered anywhere on the register, and neither the seller nor the buyer's solicitor ever asked the occupier whether they claimed any interest in the property. After completion the occupier asserts their beneficial share against the buyer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer is bound only if they actually knew the occupier claimed an interest before completion.
The buyer is bound only if the occupier had lodged a caution against the title before completion.
The buyer takes free, because a person who merely contributed to the purchase price can never acquire an interest in the land itself.
The buyer is bound, because a person in actual occupation with a beneficial interest has an overriding interest.
The buyer takes free, because interests not entered on the register never bind a purchaser.
Land Law.w: Under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 LRA 2002, the interest of a person in actual occupation binds a buyer of registered land, subject to the exceptions. Where occupation is obvious and no inquiry was made of the occupier, the interest overrides even though unregistered.

n.0: Actual knowledge is not required; actual occupation is the key.
n.1: No caution is needed; the overriding interest arises from occupation itself.
n.2: A purchase-price contribution can give a beneficial interest under a trust.
n.4: Actual occupation is the very mechanism by which an unregistered interest can bind a buyer.

Land Law.q: A neighbour has built a large timber garden structure close to the boundary between two registered properties. Part of the structure's roof projects across the boundary line and physically overhangs the claimant's land by around half a metre, intruding into the airspace above the claimant's garden. The claimant never consented to this and objects to the intrusion, wishing to have the offending part of the structure taken down so that nothing projects over their land. The claimant seeks advice on the remedy available for this encroachment into the airspace above their registered land. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An injunction requiring removal of the overhanging structure. on these facts
Nothing, unless the claimant can show the overhang caused measurable financial loss.
Damages only, because an overhang above the surface is never a trespass to land.
Nothing, because ownership of land does not extend to the airspace above it at all.
An order transferring the airspace to the neighbour on payment of a fair sum.
Land Law.w: A landowner's rights extend to the airspace at a height necessary for ordinary use and enjoyment. A structure overhanging that airspace is a trespass, and the usual remedy is an injunction to require its removal (with damages in lieu at the court's discretion).

n.1: Trespass is actionable without proof of financial loss.
n.2: An overhang into the usable airspace is a trespass, so relief is not confined to damages.
n.3: Ownership extends to the airspace needed for ordinary use, so an overhang can trespass.
n.4: The court does not force the claimant to transfer the airspace to the trespasser.

Land Law.q: Two friends, Ms Hollis and Ms Iqbal, bought a house together several years ago. They hold the legal estate on trust for themselves, and in equity they hold as beneficial joint tenants, so that on the death of either the survivor would take the whole by survivorship. Following a disagreement, Ms Hollis decides she no longer wishes to share ownership in that way. She signs a written notice stating that she wishes to sever the joint tenancy with immediate effect, and posts it to Ms Iqbal at the house, where it is duly delivered. Ms Iqbal does not agree to the change. Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice?
o: It has no effect, because a joint tenancy can be severed only by the agreement of all of the joint tenants.
It ends the co-ownership altogether, so the property is then owned solely by the severing friend.
It has no effect, because severance of a joint tenancy must be made by deed rather than by written notice.
It severs both the legal and the beneficial joint tenancy, so each of the friends holds a distinct legal share.
It severs the beneficial joint tenancy, so the friends hold the equitable interest as tenants in common.
Land Law.w: A written notice under s.36(2) LPA 1925 severs the joint tenancy in equity, converting the beneficial interest into a tenancy in common in equal shares. The notice takes effect when delivered and does not require the other joint tenant's agreement. The legal estate cannot be severed and remains held on a joint tenancy.

n.0: Section 36(2) allows unilateral severance by written notice; the agreement of all is only one of several methods.
n.1: Severance changes how the beneficial interest is held; it does not extinguish the other co-owner's share.
n.2: Written notice is itself a valid method of severance; no deed is required.
n.3: The legal estate cannot be held as a tenancy in common and is not severed; only the equitable joint tenancy is affected.

Land Law.q: By a deed, a landowner granted the owner of the neighbouring house 'a right of way on foot' over a lane running across the landowner's field. For years the neighbour used the lane only to walk to and from the road. The neighbour has now built a garage beside the house and wishes to drive cars along the lane to reach it, which would involve regular vehicular use of the lane. The landowner objects that the grant was for access on foot only, while the neighbour argues that a right of way permits any reasonable means of access. Which of the following best describes the neighbour's rights?
o: The right is limited to access on foot, and driving vehicles falls outside the express grant.
The right extends to any reasonable use, including vehicular access to the garage.
The right is void for uncertainty, because it did not specify the type of vehicles allowed.
The right entitles the neighbour to vehicular access, provided it does not increase the burden.
The right automatically expands to vehicular use once the dominant land is developed.
Land Law.w: An express easement is construed by its grant. A right of way 'on foot' is confined to pedestrian access; using it for vehicles exceeds the grant and is actionable, regardless of later development of the dominant land.

n.1: An express easement does not confer all reasonable uses; it is limited to what was granted.
n.2: A pedestrian right of way is certain; it is simply limited to access on foot.
n.3: The test is the scope of the grant, not merely whether the burden increases.
n.4: Development of the dominant land does not automatically enlarge the scope of an express right.

Land Law.q: A conveyance of part of a seller's land imposed a restrictive covenant on the land sold, the covenant being expressed to be 'for the benefit of the retained land' of the seller. That retained land has since been sold on to a new owner. The later conveyance of the retained land did not expressly mention the restrictive covenant or purport to assign its benefit to the new owner. The current owner of the burdened land is now acting in breach, and the new owner of the retained land nevertheless wishes to enforce the covenant against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The benefit is likely annexed to the retained land and passes with it, so the new owner can enforce it.
Only the original covenantee may enforce the covenant, regardless of who owns the land.
The new owner can enforce it only if the benefit was expressly assigned in their conveyance.
The covenant lapsed when the retained land was sold without mentioning it.
The benefit is personal to the original seller and cannot pass to a later owner of the retained land, on these facts.
Land Law.w: Where a covenant is expressed to benefit identified retained land, the benefit is annexed to that land (and s.78 LPA 1925 assists annexation). It then passes automatically to successors of the benefited land, who can enforce it without an express assignment.

n.1: Successors to the benefited land can enforce, not only the original covenantee.
n.2: Express assignment is unnecessary where the benefit is annexed to the land.
n.3: The covenant does not lapse merely because the benefited land is sold.
n.4: A covenant taken for the benefit of retained land is not merely personal to the seller.

Land Law.q: Mrs Pryce fell into arrears on the mortgage over her home, and the lender exercised its power of sale. Wanting a quick sale, the lender put the property on the market for only a few days, did not obtain a proper valuation, and sold it to a company connected with the lender for £250,000, a figure well below the £310,000 that a proper marketing campaign would realistically have achieved. Mrs Pryce, who is left owing the shortfall on her loan, complains that the property was effectively given away and that the sale price was far too low. She seeks advice on the lender's duty and any remedy she may have. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The sale is automatically void, and the property must be returned to the borrower free of the mortgage.
The lender must take reasonable care to obtain the proper price, and any shortfall sounds in damages.
The borrower's only remedy is to repay the connected buyer and recover the property by way of redemption.
The lender owes no duty at all as to the price once the borrower has defaulted, so there is no remedy.
The lender need only act in good faith, so the price actually obtained is legally irrelevant.
Land Law.w: A mortgagee exercising its power of sale must act in good faith and take reasonable care to obtain the true market value at the time of sale (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance). A sale at an undervalue, particularly to a connected party, can found a claim in damages for the difference.

n.0: The sale to a purchaser is not usually set aside; the remedy is damages, so the sale is not automatically void.
n.2: Once the power of sale is validly exercised the equity of redemption is overreached, so redemption is not the remedy.
n.3: Default does not free the lender of any duty as to price; it must take reasonable care to obtain the proper value.
n.4: Good faith is necessary but not sufficient; there is a distinct duty of reasonable care as to price.

Land Law.q: Ms Jarvis holds a flat under a seven-year lease. The lease contains a covenant by the landlord to keep the roof and exterior of the building in repair. Over the winter the roof falls into serious disrepair and rainwater repeatedly enters the flat, damaging Ms Jarvis's furniture and decorations. She has told the landlord about the problem in writing on several occasions and given access, but the landlord has refused to carry out any repairs. Ms Jarvis wishes to know what she can do to make the landlord repair the roof and to recover for the damage she has already suffered. Which of the following best describes the remedy most likely available to her?
o: Forfeiture of the lease, which is the tenant's only remedy against a landlord in breach of covenant.
Damages for breach of the repairing covenant, and possibly specific performance to compel the repairs.
An indefinite withholding of rent, which automatically discharges the landlord's repairing covenant.
No remedy, because a landlord's repairing obligations cease to be enforceable once the lease is granted.
A declaration that a constructive trust of the reversion has arisen in the tenant's favour.
Land Law.w: A landlord's repairing covenant is enforceable by the tenant. The usual remedy is damages for breach, and specific performance may be ordered against a landlord to compel the repairs (s.17 Landlord and Tenant Act 1985).

n.0: Forfeiture is a landlord's remedy for a tenant's breach; it is not the tenant's remedy against the landlord.
n.2: Any rent set-off is limited and does not discharge the landlord's covenant; simply withholding rent risks the tenant's own breach.
n.3: Covenants in a lease remain enforceable between landlord and tenant throughout the term.
n.4: A constructive trust of the reversion is irrelevant; this is an ordinary leasehold covenant claim.

Land Law.q: A developer laid out an estate of similar houses, dividing the land into plots and selling each plot subject to identical covenants restricting use to a single private dwelling. The developer's clear and common intention, understood by all the buyers when they bought, was that the plots should be mutually bound by, and mutually able to enforce, the covenants against one another. One current owner is now acting in breach of the covenant, and another owner within the estate, who bought a different plot from the developer, wishes to enforce the covenant against them. Which of the following best describes the basis on which they can do so?
o: The covenants are unenforceable, because identical covenants on many plots cancel each other out.
The owner can enforce it only against the original buyer of the offending plot, not a successor.
The owner cannot enforce it, because only the developer who imposed the covenants can enforce them.
