The owner can enforce it under a building scheme. in the absence of any contrary agreement
The owner can enforce it only if the benefit was expressly assigned to them in their conveyance.
Land Law.w: Where the conditions for a building (or letting) scheme are met, the covenants are mutually enforceable between the owners of plots within the scheme, so any plot owner can enforce against any other, including successors (Elliston v Reacher).

n.0: Identical covenants across plots are the hallmark of a scheme, not a reason they fail.
n.1: Scheme covenants bind and benefit successors, not just original buyers.
n.2: Under a building scheme, enforcement is not confined to the developer.
n.4: A building scheme provides mutual enforceability without needing express assignment.

Land Law.q: For many years the owner of land benefited by a restrictive covenant stood by and watched the neighbouring owner of the burdened land openly breach it, saying nothing at all. The benefited owner went further still, positively encouraging the neighbour to carry on and to spend substantial sums on building work, in reliance on the shared understanding that no objection would ever be taken. Only now, once the building work has been completed at great cost, has the benefited owner abruptly changed position and applied for an injunction to enforce the covenant and require the works to be pulled down. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant is automatically extinguished after a period of any breach, whatever the owner did.
The owner can enforce fully, because covenants can never be affected by the parties' conduct.
An injunction must always be granted as of right, because acquiescence can never be a defence to breach of a restrictive covenant.
The owner loses only the right to damages, but keeps the right to an injunction as of course.
Equitable relief may be refused, because the owner's acquiescence makes it unconscionable to enforce now.
Land Law.w: Equitable remedies are discretionary. Long acquiescence in a known breach, especially where the defendant relied on it to their detriment, can make it unconscionable to grant an injunction, so relief may be refused even though the covenant subsists.

n.0: Mere breach for a time does not automatically extinguish a covenant.
n.1: The parties' conduct is highly relevant to whether equity will assist.
n.2: Acquiescence can bar equitable relief; an injunction is not granted as of right.
n.3: Acquiescence more naturally affects the equitable injunction than a common-law damages claim.

Land Law.q: A borrower has repaid the mortgage loan in full slightly after the contractual redemption date stated in the mortgage. The lender argues that, the legal date for redemption having passed, the borrower has lost the right to get the property back. The borrower has repaid the debt after the legal redemption date. The borrower wishes to recover the property. The borrower has finally cleared the whole debt, but only a little after the contractual date fixed in the mortgage for redemption, and the lender is now arguing that, because that legal date has gone by, the borrower has forfeited any right to have the property back. Which of the following best describes the borrower's right to redeem?
o: The borrower loses all right to the property once the legal redemption date passes on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The borrower may redeem only with the lender's fresh consent after that date.
The property automatically becomes the lender's on the legal redemption date.
The borrower may redeem only by taking court proceedings within 24 hours.
The borrower retains an equitable right to redeem (the equity of redemption) even after the legal date for redemption has passed.
Land Law.w: Although a mortgage historically fixed a legal date for redemption, equity recognises the borrower's continuing right to redeem after that date, the equity of redemption. On repaying the debt (with interest and costs), the borrower is entitled to have the property back and the mortgage discharged, notwithstanding that the contractual redemption date has passed.

n.0: The borrower does not lose the property merely because the legal date passed; equity allows redemption.
n.1: Redemption after the legal date does not require the lender's fresh consent.
n.2: The property does not become the lender's automatically on the legal date.
n.3: There is no 24-hour court-proceedings requirement to redeem.

Land Law.q: An elderly farmer, Mr Iremonger, repeatedly assured his niece, Ms Jones, over many years that the farm 'will be yours one day' and that she should regard her future as tied to it. Relying on those assurances, Ms Jones worked long hours on the farm for well below a market wage for 15 years, turned down other employment and did not move away to build a separate career. When Mr Iremonger died, his will left the farm to a charity and made no provision for Ms Jones. She seeks advice on any claim she may have to an interest in the farm. Which doctrine is most likely to assist her?
o: No claim, because a promise to leave property by will can never give rise to any interest in land.
A resulting trust, because her years of unpaid labour count as a contribution to the purchase price.
A binding contract, because the repeated assurances amounted to an enforceable promise to leave her the farm.
An express trust, because the farmer's repeated statements declared a trust of the farm in her favour.
Proprietary estoppel, because she relied to her detriment on assurances it is unconscionable to deny.
Land Law.w: Proprietary estoppel arises from a clear assurance, detrimental reliance and unconscionability (Gillett v Holt; Thorner v Major). Ms Jones's long, underpaid work and lost opportunities in reliance on the assurance are classic estoppel; the court then decides how to satisfy the equity.

n.0: Such a promise can found a proprietary estoppel, so Ms Jones is not without a claim.
n.1: A resulting trust turns on purchase-price contributions, not on labour given in reliance on an assurance.
n.2: Assurances about the future are not a contract, and a contract to leave property would need to satisfy formalities.
n.3: Loose statements of intention do not declare an express trust of identified property.

Land Law.q: The windows of Mrs Tomlin's house have received daylight across a neighbouring plot, without interruption, for more than 20 years. The plot has been bought by a developer, which has begun putting up a large extension only a short distance from Mrs Tomlin's windows. When finished, the extension would substantially reduce the light to two of her main rooms, making them noticeably dark for ordinary use. Mrs Tomlin wants the offending part of the extension taken down, but the developer says that at most it should have to pay her a sum of money and can otherwise build as it likes on its own land. Mrs Tomlin seeks advice on the remedy she is most likely to obtain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Nothing, unless Mrs Tomlin first registers the right of light as a notice on the developer's title.
An injunction requiring removal, the usual remedy for substantial interference with a right of light.
Nothing, because a right of light cannot be acquired over a neighbour's land in any circumstances.
Damages only, because an injunction can never be granted for interference with an easement of light acquired by prescription.
An order that the developer purchase Mrs Tomlin's house at its full market value.
Land Law.w: A right of light can be acquired by long enjoyment, and substantial interference with it is usually restrained by injunction (Shelfer). Damages in lieu may be awarded in exceptional cases (Coventry v Lawrence), but the injunction is the primary remedy.

n.0: A right of light acquired by prescription does not depend on the claimant entering a notice to be enforceable.
n.2: A right of light can be acquired, commonly by prescription, so relief is available.
n.3: An injunction is the usual remedy; damages in lieu are the exception, not an absolute rule.
n.4: The court does not force the claimant to sell; it restrains or compensates the interference.

Land Law.q: An occupier is granted the right to occupy residential premises. The agreement is labelled a 'licence', but in substance the occupier has exclusive possession of the premises for a fixed term at a rent, and the owner has no genuine right to share or control occupation. The label used and the substance of the arrangement differ. The occupier has exclusive possession for a term at a rent. Although the document the parties signed is headed a licence, in reality the occupier has been given exclusive possession of the premises for a fixed period at a rent, with the owner retaining no genuine right to come and go or share the space, so substance and label appear to diverge. Which of the following best describes how the arrangement is characterised?
o: It is neither a lease nor a licence and creates no rights at all.
It is likely a lease (tenancy), because the substance (exclusive possession for a term at a rent) prevails over the label.
It is an easement over the premises.
It is a licence, because the parties labelled it a licence.
It is a freehold estate because the occupier has exclusive possession on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Land Law.w: Following Street v Mountford, the grant of exclusive possession of premises for a term at a rent creates a tenancy (lease), whatever label the parties use; the court looks at the substance of the arrangement, not merely its description. If the occupier truly has exclusive possession for a term, it is a lease even if called a licence.

n.0: Exclusive possession for a term at a rent does create rights (a lease).
n.2: An easement is a right over another's land, not exclusive possession of premises.
n.3: The label 'licence' does not govern where the substance is a tenancy.
n.4: Exclusive possession for a term is characteristic of a leasehold, not a freehold estate.

Land Law.q: A landowner sold off a plot of land and, on the sale, took from the buyer a covenant restricting building on the plot. The covenant was expressed to be for the benefit of other land; but that other land was land which the seller did not own at all and which was situated several miles away from the plot that had been sold. A successor in title now wishes to enforce the covenant against the current owner of the burdened plot, who has begun building on it. The successor seeks advice on whether the covenant is enforceable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant is enforceable, because restrictive covenants always bind successors to the burdened plot. on the facts of this case
The covenant is not enforceable against the successor, because a restrictive covenant must accommodate (touch and concern) the benefited land.
The covenant is enforceable, because the burden of any covenant runs with the land in equity.
The covenant is enforceable only if it was also protected by a notice on the register.
The covenant is enforceable, because it was expressed to benefit some land, wherever situated.
Land Law.w: For the burden of a restrictive covenant to run in equity, the covenant must accommodate (touch and concern) the benefited land — it must relate to and benefit that land, which normally requires proximity. A covenant benefiting distant, unconnected land does not satisfy this and is not enforceable against successors.

n.0: Restrictive covenants bind successors only where the running conditions, including accommodation, are satisfied.
n.2: Not every covenant burden runs in equity; the touch-and-concern requirement must be met.
n.3: Protection by notice is necessary but not sufficient; the covenant must first be one whose burden can run.
n.4: Merely being expressed to benefit some land is insufficient; the land must be accommodated.

Land Law.q: A buyer purchased unregistered land from a seller for value and duly completed. Unknown to the buyer, the seller had, some months before, entered into an estate contract agreeing to sell the same land to a third party. That estate contract was capable of registration as a land charge but was never registered against the seller's name in the Land Charges Register. The buyer completed the purchase in good faith and had no actual knowledge of the earlier contract. The third party has now come forward, relying on the estate contract, and claims that it binds the buyer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer takes subject to the estate contract, because a purchaser of unregistered land is bound by all prior contracts.
The buyer takes free of the estate contract, because an unregistered land charge is void against a purchaser for value.
The buyer takes free only if they registered their own purchase as a land charge first.
The buyer takes subject to the estate contract, because estate contracts always override later sales.
The buyer takes subject to the estate contract if the third party can prove the buyer ought to have discovered it.
Land Law.w: An estate contract is a registrable land charge (Class C(iv)) in unregistered land. If not registered, it is void against a purchaser of a legal estate for money or money's worth, regardless of the purchaser's notice (Land Charges Act 1972; Midland Bank v Green).

n.0: A purchaser is not bound by every prior contract; an unregistered land charge is void against them.
n.2: The purchaser does not need to register their own purchase to take free of the unregistered charge.
n.3: An estate contract does not override; if unregistered it loses to a purchaser for value.
n.4: Actual or constructive notice is irrelevant to a registrable-but-unregistered land charge.

Land Law.q: Mr Reeves orally agreed with a neighbouring landowner, Mrs Sandhu, that he would buy a strip of her paddock for £15,000 to extend his garden. No written contract was ever drawn up or signed. Relying on the agreement, Mr Reeves paid Mrs Sandhu a £3,000 deposit in cash, took possession of the strip, removed the old fence and spent a further £6,000 laying a patio and planting the area. Some months later, after the value of the land rose, Mrs Sandhu told Mr Reeves that there was no binding deal and demanded that he leave the strip. Mr Reeves seeks advice on any claim he may have. On which basis is he most likely to obtain relief?
o: A resulting trust, because the buyer provided the money used to acquire the land from the owner.
Proprietary estoppel, because the buyer relied to their detriment on the landowner's assurance.
No relief at all, because an agreement to sell land that is not in writing has no legal effect for any purpose.
Specific performance of the oral contract, because taking possession satisfies the formalities for a land contract.
Breach of a binding sale contract, because payment of the deposit created an enforceable agreement for the land.
Land Law.w: A contract for the sale of land must be in a signed written document (s.2 LP(MP)A 1989), so the oral agreement is void and there is no contractual claim or specific performance. However, proprietary estoppel (and a constructive trust, expressly preserved by s.2(5)) can give relief where there is an assurance, detrimental reliance and unconscionability (Cobbe; Thorner v Major).

n.0: A resulting trust is not the natural analysis where the claim rests on assurances and reliance rather than a purchase-price contribution to co-ownership.
n.2: Section 2 makes the oral contract void, but equity can still intervene through estoppel or constructive trust, so relief is not excluded.
n.3: Specific performance needs a valid contract; taking possession does not satisfy the s.2 writing requirement.
n.4: Paying a deposit does not create a contract for land; s.2 requires a signed written agreement, which is missing.

Land Law.q: Two people owned a house together as beneficial joint tenants, so that on the death of one of them the survivor would ordinarily take the whole of the beneficial interest in the house by right of survivorship. One of the two then unlawfully killed the other. If the ordinary rule of survivorship were simply applied, the killer would take the entire house as the surviving joint tenant, benefiting directly from the killing. The personal representatives of the deceased dispute that the killer should be permitted to profit in this way from the death. Which of the following best describes the effect on the beneficial ownership of the house?
o: The killer keeps their own half but must sell the house and pay the proceeds into court.
Survivorship applies as normal, so the killer takes the whole house outright.
The forfeiture rule prevents the killer taking by survivorship, so the deceased's share passes under their estate.
The house passes automatically to the deceased's next of kin free of the killer's interest entirely, in these circumstances.
The joint tenancy is unaffected, but the killer holds the house on trust for the state.
Land Law.w: The forfeiture rule prevents a person who unlawfully kills another from benefiting from the death. It stops the survivorship that would have given the killer the deceased's share, which instead passes as part of the deceased's estate; the killer retains only their own original share.

n.0: There is no rule requiring a sale into court; the point is the destination of the deceased's share.
n.1: Survivorship is displaced by the forfeiture rule; the killer does not take the whole.
n.3: The killer retains their own existing beneficial share; the whole does not pass to next of kin.
n.4: The killer does not hold on trust for the state; the deceased's share passes under their estate.

Land Law.q: In March last year a property developer, Hartwell Developments Ltd, agreed to let a neighbouring occupier, Mr Okafor, use a plot at the edge of one of its building sites. The arrangement was recorded in a document signed by both of them. It was expressed to give Mr Okafor 'the right to occupy the plot for as long as he wishes', with no fixed end date and no provision allowing either party to bring it to an end. Hartwell Developments Ltd intended the right to take effect as a legal estate that would bind any future owner of the site. A trainee solicitor is asked to advise whether that is possible under the Law of Property Act 1925. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: It cannot be a legal estate, because a legal estate must first be substantively registered before it can exist.
It can be a legal estate, because a right to occupy for an uncertain period is a term of years absolute.
It can be a legal estate, because the developer intends the right to bind the land permanently and indefinitely.
It can be a legal estate, because any interest in land will become legal once it is granted to the neighbour by deed.
It cannot be a legal estate, as only a fee simple absolute in possession or a term of years absolute is legal.
Land Law.w: Section 1(1) LPA 1925 recognises only two legal estates: a fee simple absolute in possession and a term of years absolute. A right for an uncertain or indefinite period is neither, so it cannot exist as a legal estate (at most it takes effect in equity).

n.0: Registration affects how a legal estate is dealt with, but it is s.1(1) that limits which estates can be legal at all.
n.1: A term of years absolute requires a certain maximum duration; a right lasting 'as long as he wishes' lacks that certainty.
n.2: Intention to bind the land does not create a legal estate outside the two categories fixed by s.1(1).
n.3: Creation by deed is a formality; it cannot turn an interest that is not one of the two permitted estates into a legal estate.

Land Law.q: A developer sells part of their land and imposes a restrictive covenant on the buyer not to build on the land sold, to protect the developer's retained land. The land is later sold on to a new owner who wishes to build. The covenant is restrictive (negative) and was intended to benefit the retained land. The burdened land has changed hands. When selling off part of the land the developer made the buyer promise not to build on it, so as to protect the land the developer kept, and now that the burdened plot has passed into new hands the new owner wants to build, raising the question whether that negative promise still binds them. Which of the following best describes when the burden of the restrictive covenant runs to bind the new owner in equity?
o: The burden runs in equity under Tulk v Moxhay if the covenant is restrictive, touches and concerns the land, and there is notice.
The burden binds the new owner only if they paid less than market value.
The burden runs only if the new owner personally re-covenants with the developer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The burden of a restrictive covenant never binds a successor to the land.
The burden runs at law automatically like any positive obligation.
Land Law.w: Under Tulk v Moxhay, the burden of a restrictive covenant can run in equity to bind successors where the covenant is negative (restrictive) in substance, it touches and concerns (benefits) the covenantee's retained land, the parties intended the burden to run, and the successor has notice (in registered land, protected by a notice on the register). Positive covenants do not run in this way.

n.1: Being bound does not depend on paying below market value; notice is the relevant factor.
n.2: A fresh covenant by the new owner is a separate device; Tulk v Moxhay makes the original burden run in equity.
n.3: The burden of a restrictive covenant can bind successors in equity; it is positive covenants that do not run.
n.4: The burden does not run at law like a positive obligation; it runs in equity under Tulk v Moxhay.

Land Law.q: A mortgage of a commercial property contains a term giving the lender an option to purchase the mortgaged property itself, at a fixed price set at the outset, exercisable at the lender's choice at any time during the mortgage. The borrower has since repaid, or now wishes to repay, the loan in full and to recover the property free of the mortgage; but the lender says it intends to exercise the option and take the property at the fixed price instead. The borrower seeks advice on whether the option is valid and enforceable against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The option binds the borrower only after the borrower has first defaulted on the loan.
The option is fully valid, because a lender may always negotiate an option to buy as part of its security. on these facts
The option is void, because an option for the lender to buy the mortgaged property is a clog on the equity of redemption.
The whole mortgage is void, so the borrower keeps the property free of any charge.
The option is valid only if the borrower had independent legal advice before signing.
Land Law.w: An option granted to the mortgagee to purchase the mortgaged property is repugnant to the equity of redemption and void as a clog: the borrower must be able to get the property back on redemption, free of any right in the lender to acquire it (Samuel v Jarrah Timber).

n.0: Default does not validate the option; it is void as a clog whenever exercisable.
n.1: Such an option is not simply valid; it is struck down as inconsistent with redemption.
n.3: Only the offending option is void; the mortgage and debt remain.
n.4: Independent advice does not save an option that clogs the equity of redemption.

Land Law.q: A house is held on a trust of land for two adult beneficiaries, each of whom is entitled to an interest in possession under the trust and neither of whom has any other home. One of the two beneficiaries now wishes to move into the house and live there. The other beneficiary objects, arguing that the first has no right to occupy the trust property and should not be permitted to do so. The beneficiary who wishes to live there seeks advice on whether they are entitled to occupy the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A beneficiary with an interest in possession has a statutory right to occupy.
Both beneficiaries must occupy jointly at all times or neither may occupy.
The trustees have no power to regulate or exclude a beneficiary's occupation of the land.
No beneficiary of a trust of land has any right to occupy the trust property at all.
Only a beneficiary who provided the purchase money has any right to occupy the property.
Land Law.w: Under ss.12–13 TOLATA 1996 a beneficiary who is beneficially entitled to an interest in possession has a right to occupy trust land (where the purposes include occupation and it is available and suitable), and the trustees may reasonably regulate occupation, including by imposing conditions or compensation.

n.1: Joint occupation at all times is not required; trustees may regulate occupation.
n.2: Trustees do have powers under s.13 to regulate and, where appropriate, restrict occupation.
n.3: Beneficiaries with an interest in possession do have a statutory right to occupy under s.12.
n.4: The right to occupy is not confined to those who contributed the purchase money.

Land Law.q: A right of way granted by deed benefited a dominant plot of land. For a period of over 40 years the right of way was never used at all by the dominant owner or anyone else. During that long period the dominant owner built a permanent brick structure squarely over the access point and otherwise acted consistently, and unequivocally, as though the right of way was no longer needed or wanted. The servient owner now argues that the right of way has long since been lost. The dominant owner, whose circumstances have changed, seeks advice on whether the easement still exists. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The easement is extinguished automatically by any period of non-use, whatever the owner intended.
The easement may be treated as abandoned, because prolonged non-use together with an intention to abandon can extinguish it.
The easement is extinguished only if the servient owner pays compensation for its release.
The easement is suspended during non-use but revives the moment the dominant owner wishes to use it, as a matter of general law.
The easement can never be lost once it has been granted by deed, however long it is unused.
Land Law.w: An easement can be extinguished by abandonment, but this requires more than mere non-use: there must be a fixed intention never to assert the right again, which may be inferred from long non-use coupled with conduct such as building over the access point.

n.0: Non-use alone, without an intention to abandon, does not extinguish an easement.
n.2: No compensation payment is required; extinguishment turns on abandonment, not payment.
n.3: Abandonment, once established, extinguishes the easement; it does not merely suspend it pending revival.
n.4: An expressly granted easement can be lost by abandonment, though the threshold is high.

Land Law.q: A squatter has been in open adverse possession of a plot of registered land for 15 years. The registered proprietor has taken no steps during that time to remove the squatter or to assert any claim to the land. The squatter argues that, because more than the old 12-year limitation period has now passed, the registered proprietor's title has automatically been extinguished in the squatter's favour and the land has become theirs without more. The squatter seeks advice on their true position under the current law governing adverse possession of registered land. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The proprietor's title was extinguished but the squatter must pay compensation to be registered.
The squatter became the registered proprietor automatically after 10 years of possession.
The registered proprietor's title was automatically extinguished after 12 years, as with unregistered land, as a matter of general law.
The registered proprietor's title is not automatically extinguished; the squatter must use the LRA 2002 procedure to be registered.
Adverse possession has no application at all to registered land in any circumstances.
Land Law.w: For registered land the automatic extinguishment rule does not apply. Time does not bar the registered proprietor; instead the squatter must apply under Schedule 6 LRA 2002 (after 10 years), and the proprietor can object, so title is not lost by mere lapse of time.

n.0: There is no scheme of paying compensation to be registered; the proprietor's objection generally defeats the application.
n.1: There is no automatic registration of the squatter after 10 years; an application and the Schedule 6 process are needed.
n.2: Registered land is not subject to the 12-year automatic extinguishment of unregistered land.
n.4: Adverse possession does apply to registered land, but under the Schedule 6 regime.

Land Law.q: A developer laying out a new residential estate wishes to grant each house-buyer, as a right appurtenant to their house, a right to wander at will, for general recreation, over the whole of a large and undefined area of parkland and woodland that the developer intends to retain. The developer wants this right to take effect as a legal easement benefiting each house on the estate and binding future owners of the retained land. The developer seeks advice on whether a right framed in this broad and general way can properly exist as an easement at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: It is a valid easement, because any right that benefits a buyer's house can be an easement.
It is a profit à prendre, because the buyers take the benefit of the land's amenity.
It is unlikely to be an easement, because a right to wander generally over undefined land is too wide.
It is a valid easement, because a right of recreation over land is always inherently capable of existing as an easement.
It is a valid easement, provided only that the developer grants it by deed.
Land Law.w: To be an easement a right must satisfy the Re Ellenborough Park requirements, including being capable of forming the subject-matter of a grant. A right to roam at large over undefined land is too wide and indefinite (a mere ius spatiandi). A right to use a defined recreational area can be an easement, but a general right to wander cannot.

n.0: Not every right benefiting a house is an easement; it must meet the Ellenborough Park criteria.
n.1: A profit is a right to take produce; wandering for recreation takes nothing from the land.
n.3: Recreational rights are not automatically easements; the right must be sufficiently defined.
n.4: Granting by deed cannot cure a right that is too wide to be an easement at all.

Land Law.q: A restrictive covenant imposed in 1965 restricts a plot of land to use for a single dwelling only. The covenant has never been formally discharged or modified, and it remains registered against the burdened land. The current owner of the plot now wishes to build a second house on it, and a neighbouring owner who has the benefit of the covenant objects to the proposal. The plot owner argues that the covenant is by now so old, dating back some sixty years, that it can no longer be relied upon or enforced against them. The neighbour seeks advice on the position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The covenant is automatically discharged once the plot owner decides to build.
The covenant is unenforceable, because covenants made before 1970 are no longer valid.
The covenant remains enforceable, because a restrictive covenant is not lost by mere age.
The covenant is enforceable, but only for damages and never by injunction after so long.
The covenant is unenforceable, because restrictive covenants expire after a fixed number of years.
Land Law.w: A restrictive covenant does not lapse merely through the passage of time. It remains enforceable unless discharged or modified (for example by the Upper Tribunal under s.84 LPA 1925) or defeated by conduct such as acquiescence.

n.0: A covenant is not discharged simply because the burdened owner wishes to breach it.
n.1: Covenants made before 1970 are not automatically invalid.
n.3: Age alone does not confine the claimant to damages instead of an injunction.
n.4: There is no fixed expiry period for restrictive covenants.

Land Law.q: A squatter has been in adverse possession of a piece of registered land for 11 years, occupying it openly as their own throughout that period. The squatter applies under Schedule 6 to the Land Registration Act 2002 to be registered as the proprietor of the land in place of the current registered proprietor. The registered proprietor is duly notified of the application by the Land Registry and, within the time allowed for doing so, objects to it. None of the three special statutory conditions that can override such an objection applies on these facts. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome of the application?
o: The squatter is registered immediately, because a registered proprietor cannot object to such an application, on these facts.
The application is rejected permanently, because adverse possession cannot affect registered land at all.
The application is rejected initially, because the registered proprietor objected and no statutory exception applies.
The squatter must instead show 12 years' possession before any application can be made.
The application succeeds automatically, because 10 years' adverse possession of registered land gives title.
Land Law.w: Under Schedule 6 LRA 2002 a squatter may apply after 10 years, but the registered proprietor is notified and, if they object, the application is generally rejected unless one of the three limited conditions applies. The proprietor then usually has a further period to evict or regularise.

n.0: The registered proprietor is entitled to object; the squatter is not registered as of right.
n.1: Adverse possession can affect registered land, but through the Schedule 6 notice regime.
n.3: For registered land the trigger is 10 years under Schedule 6, not 12.
n.4: Ten years' possession does not automatically give title to registered land; the proprietor can object.

Land Law.q: A tenant of commercial premises has, on more than one occasion, sublet part of the premises without the landlord's consent, in breach of a covenant in the lease prohibiting subletting without consent. The breaches do not concern the payment of rent. The landlord, having lost patience, now wishes to forfeit the lease and recover possession of the premises because of the unauthorised subletting. Before the landlord can lawfully proceed to forfeit the lease for a breach of this kind, there is a step that the law requires the landlord to take first. Which of the following is that step?
o: Simply re-enter the premises, because no notice is required for any type of breach.
Give the tenant six months to buy the freehold before forfeiture can proceed.
Apply to the Land Registry to remove the tenant's lease from the register.
Obtain a court order authorising the landlord to end the lease before taking any step, in these circumstances.
Serve a notice under s.146 LPA 1925 specifying the breach and, if remediable, requiring it to be remedied.
Land Law.w: For a breach other than non-payment of rent, forfeiture requires the landlord first to serve a s.146 notice specifying the breach and, where the breach is capable of remedy, requiring the tenant to remedy it and (usually) pay compensation, before proceeding to forfeit.

n.0: A s.146 notice is required for non-rent breaches; re-entry without it is not permitted.
n.1: There is no right for the tenant to buy the freehold as a precondition of forfeiture.
n.2: Forfeiture is not carried out by an application to the Land Registry.
n.3: No separate court authorisation to end the lease is needed before serving the s.146 notice.

Land Law.q: Three friends own a house together as beneficial joint tenants. One of the three, without telling the other two, grants a mortgage over their own beneficial interest in the house to a lender as security for a personal loan. That friend has now died. The two surviving friends assume that, under the right of survivorship, the deceased's interest in the house simply passes to them by operation of law and that the lender's mortgage falls away with the death. The question arises how the deceased friend's beneficial interest in the house is now held and dealt with. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The whole beneficial ownership passed to the lender on the grant of the mortgage.
Nothing changed, so the deceased's share passes by survivorship to the other two friends. in the circumstances
The mortgage is void, because a joint tenant cannot deal with their share at all.
The joint tenancy continued and the lender's charge simply disappeared on the death.
Mortgaging the share severed that friend's joint tenancy, so their share is held in common and passes under their estate.
Land Law.w: A joint tenant who deals with their own equitable share — for example by mortgaging it — severs the joint tenancy as to that share, converting it into a tenancy in common. Survivorship no longer applies to it, so on death it passes under the deceased's estate (subject to the mortgage).

n.0: Mortgaging one share does not transfer the whole beneficial ownership to the lender.
n.1: Survivorship does not operate on a share that has been severed by the owner dealing with it.
n.2: A joint tenant can deal with their own share; doing so severs the joint tenancy.
n.3: The lender's charge over the severed share survives the death; it does not disappear.

Land Law.q: The owner of a house and an adjoining field had, while owning both together, regularly used a track running across the field in order to reach the house from the lane. The owner then sold the house to a buyer but kept the field for themselves. The conveyance of the house to the buyer said nothing at all about any right to use the track across the retained field. The buyer of the house now wishes to continue using the track for access, as the seller had always done, and asserts a right to do so. Which of the following best describes the basis of any such right?
o: A bare licence, personal to the buyer, which the seller may revoke at will.
An easement implied into the conveyance in the buyer's favour, for example under s.62 LPA 1925 or Wheeldon v Burrows.
A profit à prendre over the field, allowing the buyer to take produce from it.
A right arising only if the buyer later uses the track as of right for 20 years.
No right can arise, because an easement can only ever be created by an express grant in the conveyance.
Land Law.w: On a sale of part, an easement may be implied in favour of the buyer over the retained land, for example under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows (continuous and apparent quasi-easements necessary for reasonable enjoyment) or by s.62 LPA 1925 operating on prior use.

n.0: The buyer's right, if any, is a proprietary easement, not a revocable bare licence.
n.2: Using a track for access is an easement, not a profit to take produce.
n.3: An implied easement can arise immediately on the conveyance without 20 years' later use.
n.4: Easements can be implied on a conveyance, not only expressly granted.

Land Law.q: A registered plot of land is subject to a restrictive covenant, imposed when it was first sold off, that no building on it may exceed two storeys. The plot has since been sold by the original covenantor to Mr Nunez, who has now built a third storey on his house. The covenant was taken for the benefit of the neighbouring plot, which is now owned by Ms Osei; she was not the original person in whose favour the covenant was made, but the benefit passed to her when she bought the neighbouring plot. Ms Osei wishes to stop the breach and have the third storey removed. Which of the following best describes whether she can enforce the covenant against Mr Nunez?
o: She can enforce it, but the only remedy available is damages, as an injunction is never granted for a covenant.
She can enforce it, because the burden of a restrictive covenant runs with the land at common law.
She cannot enforce it, because the burden of a covenant can never bind a successor to the original covenantor.
She cannot enforce it, because only the original covenantee is ever able to enforce a restrictive covenant.
She can enforce it, because the burden of a restrictive covenant can run in equity to bind a successor.
Land Law.w: The burden of a restrictive covenant can run in equity where the Tulk v Moxhay conditions are met and it is protected against the burdened land, and the benefit can pass to a successor of the benefited land, who may then enforce it, typically by injunction.

n.0: An injunction is the usual remedy for breach of a restrictive covenant; damages are not the only option.
n.1: The burden of a covenant does not run at common law; it runs, if at all, in equity.
n.2: The burden of a restrictive covenant can bind successors in equity, so it is not unenforceable against Mr Nunez.
n.3: The benefit of a restrictive covenant can pass to a successor of the benefited land, who may enforce it.

Land Law.q: Ms Ackroyd fell behind with the payments on the mortgage over her flat, and the lender decided to exercise its power of sale. Anxious to recover its money quickly, the lender put the flat on the market for only a few days over a public holiday, did not obtain a professional valuation, and accepted an early offer of £190,000. A proper marketing campaign would realistically have achieved around £230,000. Ms Ackroyd, who is left owing the shortfall to the lender, complains that the flat was effectively sold off cheaply and that the lender made no real effort to obtain a proper price. Which of the following best describes the lender's duty?
o: The lender owes a duty only to later mortgagees, and none at all to the borrower.
The lender may sell at any price it chooses, because the borrower has lost all rights on default.
The lender must take reasonable care to obtain the true market value.
The lender must obtain the borrower's consent to the sale price before completing the sale.
The lender must always sell by public auction to discharge its duty to the borrower.
Land Law.w: A mortgagee exercising its power of sale must act in good faith and take reasonable care to obtain the true market value / proper price at the time of sale (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance). A negligent sale exposes it to damages for the shortfall.

n.0: The duty is owed to the borrower (and others interested in the equity), not only to later mortgagees.
n.1: Default does not free the lender to sell at any price; the duty of reasonable care as to price remains.
n.3: The lender need not obtain the borrower's consent to the price, but must take reasonable care.
n.4: There is no rule requiring sale by auction; the duty is as to obtaining a proper price.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees of a trust wish to hand over certain administrative and investment functions to a professional agent, because they lack the time and expertise to carry out all the day-to-day management themselves. A beneficiary objects, arguing that trustees must always act personally and can never delegate any of their functions to anyone else. The trustees seek advice on whether, and how, they may delegate functions to an agent under the modern statutory framework. The day-to-day management had become time-consuming and technically demanding for the trustees involved. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Trustees may never delegate any of their functions and must always act personally in everything.
Trustees may delegate only if all the beneficiaries consent in signed writing beforehand.
Trustees may delegate every function including the distribution of the trust, without any limit.
Trustees may delegate certain functions to an agent under the Trustee Act 2000, subject to safeguards.
Trustees may delegate only to another trustee, and never to an outside professional agent.
Trusts Law.w: The Trustee Act 2000 permits trustees to delegate certain of their functions (such as investment and administration) to agents, subject to safeguards including acting within the duty of care, giving any necessary policy statement, and keeping the arrangement under review. Certain core functions cannot be delegated.

n.0: The old strict rule against delegation has been relaxed by statute.
n.1: General beneficiary consent in writing is not the statutory precondition.
n.2: Some functions (such as distribution decisions) cannot be delegated, so 'every function' is wrong.
n.4: Delegation may be to an outside agent, not only to another trustee.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees of a substantial trust fund wish to invest the trust money. They are considering putting the entire fund into a single asset. A beneficiary questions whether the trustees are entitled to invest as they propose, and whether there are statutory criteria they must apply when exercising their power of investment. The trustees seek advice on the scope of their power of investment and the criteria that govern how it must be exercised. The fund was large and the beneficiaries' financial security depended heavily on how it was invested. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Trustees have a wide power of investment but must apply the standard investment criteria of suitability and diversification.
Trustees must always place the entire fund into a single asset for simplicity.
Trustees may only ever invest trust money in government bonds and nothing else.
Trustees may not invest trust money at all without first obtaining a court order.
Trustees may invest the fund in any way they personally please, with no criteria to apply on these facts as a general rule.
Trusts Law.w: Under the Trustee Act 2000, trustees have a general power to invest as if absolutely entitled, but in exercising it they must have regard to the standard investment criteria — the suitability of investments and the need for diversification appropriate to the trust.

n.1: Diversification points against putting the whole fund into a single asset.
n.2: Trustees are no longer confined to a narrow list such as government bonds.
n.3: A court order is not generally required before trustees may invest.
n.4: The power of investment is not unfettered; the statutory criteria must be applied.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee mixes trust money with their own in a bank account, spends the balance down to a low point (below the amount of trust money), and then later pays in fresh money of their own from an unconnected source. The beneficiaries seek to claim the later deposits as trust money. The account balance had dropped below the level of trust money before the new, unconnected deposits were made. After paying in the trust money the trustee ran the mixed account almost dry, so that at one point the balance fell well below the sum taken from the trust, and only afterwards did the trustee top it up again with money of their own from a wholly separate source. Which of the following best describes the position under the lowest intermediate balance rule?
o: The trust may claim the highest balance the account ever reached at any time.
The trust claim cannot exceed the lowest intermediate balance, so later unconnected deposits are not automatically trust money.
The trust may always claim the full amount originally paid in, regardless of intervening withdrawals on these facts.
The trust may claim all later deposits because any money in the account belongs to the trust.
The trust loses all claim to the account the moment any withdrawal is made.
Trusts Law.w: Under the lowest intermediate balance rule, the beneficiaries' traceable claim to a mixed account cannot exceed the lowest balance to which the account fell after the trust money was paid in. Later deposits from an unconnected source are not treated as trust money, absent an intention to make good the trust, so the claim is capped at that lowest intermediate balance.

n.0: The claim is limited by the lowest, not the highest, balance reached.
n.2: The claim is capped at the lowest intermediate balance, not the full amount originally paid in.
n.3: Later unconnected deposits do not automatically become trust money.
n.4: A withdrawal does not necessarily destroy the entire claim; the claim survives up to the lowest balance.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees are choosing investments for a trust fund. They are considering putting the entire fund into a single high-risk asset. A beneficiary questions whether the trustees are approaching the investment decision correctly under the Trustee Act 2000. The trustees have a general power of investment but must apply the statutory criteria. They are considering concentrating the whole fund in one asset. Tempted by the prospect of a large return, the trustees are contemplating sinking the whole fund into one speculative asset, and a beneficiary who has got wind of the plan wants to know what factors the trustees are actually obliged to weigh before committing the fund in that way. Which of the following best describes the standard investment criteria the trustees must apply?
o: The personal investment preferences of the trustees themselves.
The suitability of investments to the trust and the need for diversification of investments so far as appropriate.
The requirement to invest only in government-backed securities.
The maximisation of returns regardless of risk to the trust fund.
The need to obtain the prior approval of the court for each investment on these facts as a general rule.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.4 of the Trustee Act 2000, in exercising the power of investment trustees must have regard to the standard investment criteria: the suitability of the proposed investment to the trust (including the suitability of that kind of investment and of the particular investment), and the need for diversification of investments in so far as is appropriate to the circumstances of the trust.

n.0: The criteria are objective statutory factors, not the trustees' personal preferences.
n.2: Trustees have a wide power of investment; they are not confined to government securities.
n.3: Trustees must consider risk and suitability, not maximise return regardless of risk.
n.4: Court approval is not required for each investment under the standard criteria.

Trusts Law.q: A professional trust corporation is appointed as trustee of a substantial trust and is paid for acting. It holds itself out as having specialist expertise in trust administration and investment. When a beneficiary later alleges that the trustee fell below the required standard, the trustee argues that it should be judged by the same standard as an ordinary lay person acting as trustee. The beneficiary disputes this. The court considers the standard of care applicable to a professional trustee. The corporation charged substantial fees and marketed itself widely as a specialist in trust work. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A professional trustee owes no enhanced duty, provided it charges reasonable fees.
A professional trustee is judged only by whether it acted honestly and in good faith.
A higher standard of care is expected of a professional trustee holding itself out as having special expertise.
A professional trustee is judged by exactly the same standard as an unpaid lay trustee.
A professional trustee is judged by a lower standard, because it takes on difficult trusts on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: The statutory duty of care in the Trustee Act 2000 is calibrated to the trustee: a person acting as a professional trustee, or holding themselves out as having special knowledge or experience, is held to a correspondingly higher standard of care and skill than a lay trustee.

n.0: Charging reasonable fees does not remove the enhanced duty.
n.1: Honest good faith is not the measure; reasonable professional care is.
n.3: A professional trustee is not judged by the lay standard.
n.4: Professional trustees are held to a higher, not a lower, standard.

Trusts Law.q: A testator leaves a legacy in their will to a named charitable institution which, unknown to the testator, had already ceased to exist by the time the testator died, so that the specific gift cannot take effect as intended. It is established that the testator had a general charitable intention rather than an intention to benefit only that one particular institution. The executors seek advice on what happens to the failed charitable gift. The institution had merged into other bodies some years before the testator made the will in question. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift passes to the testator's next of kin, because the named charity no longer exists.
The gift passes to whichever charity the executors personally prefer, without any restriction on these facts.
The gift is void, because a charitable gift can never be redirected to a different charity.
The gift may be applied cy-près to another charity with similar purposes, given the general charitable intention.
The gift simply fails and falls back into the testator's residuary estate in every case.
Trusts Law.w: Where a charitable gift fails at the outset (initial failure) but the testator had a general charitable intention, the doctrine of cy-près allows the property to be applied to another charitable purpose as near as possible to the original, rather than failing altogether.

n.0: It does not pass to the next of kin where cy-près applies.
n.1: Redirection is to similar charitable purposes under court/Commission scheme, not the executors' free choice.
n.2: Charitable gifts can be redirected cy-près; they are not incapable of redirection.
n.4: With a general charitable intention, the gift does not simply fail into residue.

Trusts Law.q: A trust provides for a beneficiary to receive capital 'on attaining the age of 25'. The beneficiary is currently 20 years old. A question arises about the nature of the beneficiary's interest before reaching that age, and what happens if the beneficiary were to die before 25. The gift is expressed to take effect only on the beneficiary reaching a stated age. The beneficiary has not yet reached that age. The trust document ties the gift of capital to the beneficiary reaching a particular age, the beneficiary is still some years short of it, and the family want to understand both what the beneficiary presently owns and what would happen to the entitlement were the beneficiary to die before getting there. Which of the following best describes the nature of the interest?
o: It is a contingent interest that automatically passes to the estate if the beneficiary dies at 22.
It is a vested interest that the beneficiary owns absolutely from the outset.
It is a contingent interest, which does not vest unless and until the beneficiary reaches 25.
It is no interest at all, because future interests are not recognised in trusts.
It is a vested interest defeasible only on the beneficiary's marriage.
Trusts Law.w: An interest expressed to arise 'on attaining' a stated age is contingent on the beneficiary satisfying that condition. It does not vest unless and until the beneficiary reaches 25; if the beneficiary dies before then, the contingency is not met and the interest generally fails, rather than passing to the beneficiary's estate.

n.0: A contingent interest that fails does not automatically pass to the estate; the contingency was not met.
n.1: The interest is contingent, not vested absolutely from the outset.
n.3: Future (contingent) interests are recognised in trusts.
n.4: The interest is contingent on age, not a vested interest defeasible on marriage.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee has committed a technical breach of trust which has caused loss, but the trustee acted honestly throughout, took what they reasonably believed to be a proper course, and the breach arose from an understandable mistake rather than any want of probity. The trustee asks the court to relieve them from personal liability for the breach in these circumstances. The beneficiaries argue that any breach must result in liability. The court considers its power to relieve a trustee from liability. The loss was significant, but the trustee had genuinely tried to do the right thing throughout. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court may relieve the trustee from liability if they acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused.
The court has no power to relieve a trustee from liability for any breach of trust whatsoever on these facts.
The court may relieve the trustee only if the beneficiaries all consent to the relief.
The court must relieve any trustee who simply asserts that they acted in good faith.
The court may relieve the trustee only where the breach caused no loss to the trust at all.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.61 of the Trustee Act 1925, the court has a discretion to relieve a trustee, wholly or partly, from personal liability for a breach of trust if it appears that the trustee acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused for the breach and for omitting to obtain directions.

n.1: The court does have a statutory power to relieve trustees in appropriate cases.
n.2: Beneficiary consent is not a precondition to s.61 relief.
n.3: Relief is discretionary and requires honesty and reasonableness, not a bare assertion of good faith.
n.4: Relief is available even where loss was caused, provided the statutory conditions are met.

Trusts Law.q: A person who is not a trustee helps a trustee to commit a breach of trust, for example by helping to channel misapplied trust funds, though that person never receives the trust property for their own benefit. The beneficiaries seek to hold the helper personally liable. The claim is one of accessory liability for assisting the breach. The helper did not receive trust property beneficially. The outsider never kept any of the trust money for themselves but played an active part in moving it along and putting the breach into effect, and the beneficiaries are seeking to hold that helper personally accountable as an accessory to what the trustee did. Which of the following best describes what must be shown for dishonest assistance?
o: That the person received trust property beneficially with knowledge of the breach.
That the person was a trustee or fiduciary of the property in question.
That the person genuinely believed their conduct was honest, whatever the objective standard on these facts.
That the person dishonestly assisted in a breach of trust, dishonesty being assessed objectively by ordinary standards.
That the person was negligent in failing to detect the breach of trust.
Trusts Law.w: Dishonest assistance imposes personal liability on an accessory who dishonestly assists a breach of trust, even without receiving trust property. Dishonesty is judged by the objective standards of ordinary honest people, applied to the defendant's actual knowledge of the facts; the defendant's own view that they were honest is not the test.

n.0: Beneficial receipt with knowledge is knowing receipt, a different claim.
n.1: The defendant need not be a trustee or fiduciary to be liable as an accessory.
n.2: The defendant's own belief in their honesty does not determine liability; the standard is objective.
n.4: Mere negligence is insufficient; dishonesty is required.

Trusts Law.q: A trust fund produces income and is also capable of capital growth. Some beneficiaries are entitled to the income now (life tenants), while others are entitled to the capital in due course (remaindermen). The trustees must decide how to manage and invest the fund, balancing the competing interests of these different classes of beneficiary. One class complains that the trustees have favoured the other. The trustees seek advice on the duty they owe as between the different beneficiaries. The fund was expected to last for many years, spanning the lifetimes of several different beneficiaries. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The trustees must always prefer the interests of the income beneficiaries over the remaindermen.
The trustees owe a duty of impartiality to hold an even hand between the different classes of beneficiary.
The trustees must always prefer the interests of the capital beneficiaries over the life tenants.
The trustees owe no duty to balance interests and may favour whichever class they like.
The trustees must distribute the entire fund immediately to end the competing claims.
Trusts Law.w: Trustees owe a duty to act impartially (fairly) between the beneficiaries, holding an even hand between those entitled to income and those entitled to capital, and must not favour one class of beneficiary at the expense of another.

n.0: Trustees must not automatically prefer the income beneficiaries.
n.2: Trustees must not automatically prefer the capital beneficiaries.
n.3: Trustees do owe a duty to balance the competing interests fairly.
n.4: Impartiality does not require immediate distribution of the whole fund.

Trusts Law.q: A trust instrument directs trustees to divide a fund equally among 'all of my employees and former employees', and the trust is a fixed trust under which each beneficiary is to receive an equal, defined share. To carry out an equal division, the trustees need to be able to draw up a complete list of every beneficiary. On the facts it is impossible to compile a complete list of all the former employees. The trustees seek advice on whether the trust is valid. The business had employed a great many people over many years, and its old personnel records were seriously incomplete. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The fixed trust fails, because a complete list of all the beneficiaries cannot be drawn up.
The trust is valid, because the class of beneficiaries is described in general terms.
The trust is valid, because certainty of objects never applies to fixed trusts.
The trust is valid, and the trustees may simply divide the fund among those they can find.
The trust is valid, provided the trustees can identify at least one beneficiary.
Trusts Law.w: For a fixed trust, certainty of objects requires that a complete list of all the beneficiaries can be compiled (the 'complete list' test in IRC v Broadway Cottages), because each is entitled to a defined share. If a complete list cannot be made, the fixed trust fails.

n.1: A general description is not enough where a complete list cannot be compiled.
n.2: Certainty of objects does apply to fixed trusts.
n.3: The trustees cannot simply divide among those found where an equal fixed division requires a full list.
n.4: Identifying one beneficiary does not satisfy the complete-list test for a fixed trust.

Trusts Law.q: Trust property is misapplied in breach of trust and comes into the hands of a third party who was not a trustee. The beneficiaries seek to make that third party personally liable for having received the property. The third party received trust property traceable to the breach and their state of knowledge is in issue. The claim is one of knowing receipt rather than dishonest assistance. Funds taken from the trust in breach ended up in the hands of an outsider who used them for their own benefit, and the beneficiaries, focusing on that outsider's awareness of where the money had come from, want to fix them with personal liability for having taken it. Which of the following best describes the basis of liability for knowing receipt?
o: The recipient is liable only if they dishonestly assisted in the breach of trust.
The recipient is liable only if they still retain the specific property received.
The recipient is liable only if they acted as a trustee of the property.
The recipient is strictly liable merely for having received trust property, regardless of knowledge on these facts.
The recipient must have received trust property for their own benefit with knowledge making retention unconscionable.
Trusts Law.w: Liability for knowing receipt requires that the defendant received trust property (or its traceable proceeds) beneficially, that the receipt was in breach of trust, and that the defendant had knowledge such that it would be unconscionable for them to retain the benefit. It is a fault-based personal liability, distinct from the strict proprietary tracing claim.

n.0: That describes dishonest assistance, which is a separate head of liability.
n.1: Personal liability for knowing receipt does not require the defendant still to retain the property.
n.2: The recipient need not have acted as a trustee; beneficial receipt suffices.
n.3: Knowing receipt is not strict; a sufficient degree of knowledge is required.

Trusts Law.q: A discretionary trust exists under which trustees may distribute income among a class of potential beneficiaries. One member of the class, before any distribution has been made to them, purports to deal with their supposed 'share' as though they already owned a defined part of the fund. A dispute arises about the nature of that member's interest. No distribution has yet been made in that member's favour. The member has run into financial difficulty and is trying to raise money against what they assume is their entitlement, but the trustees have made no decision in their favour, and the other potential beneficiaries dispute that this member owns anything they can deal with at all. Which of the following best describes the interest of an object of a discretionary trust before any distribution?
o: The object has no proprietary interest in any particular part of the fund, only a hope of being selected.
The object holds the legal title to a proportionate part of the trust property.
The object may compel the trustees to pay them an equal share on demand.
The object owns a fixed and defined share of the fund from the outset.
The object's interest vests automatically after a fixed period regardless of selection on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: An object of a discretionary trust has no proprietary interest in any specific part of the fund unless and until the trustees exercise their discretion in that object's favour. Before then the object has only a hope (a mere expectancy) of benefiting, and cannot claim a defined share or compel payment.

n.1: The object holds no legal title to any part of the trust property.
n.2: The object cannot compel an equal payment on demand.
n.3: The object does not own a fixed share before any distribution.
n.4: The interest does not vest automatically after a period; it depends on the trustees' selection.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor wishes to create a valid express private trust during their lifetime, transferring assets to trustees to hold for a group of beneficiaries. A dispute later arises as to whether a valid trust was created at all. The court examines whether the fundamental requirements for the creation of an express trust are satisfied on the facts. The settlor's adviser is asked to explain what must be established for a valid express private trust to exist. The assets were substantial, and several people claimed to be entitled under the arrangement the settlor had described. Which of the following best describes the requirements?
o: There must be a professional trustee appointed, or no valid trust can arise at all.
There must be certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter and certainty of objects.
There must simply be a signed document, whatever its contents happen to say.
There must be consideration provided by the beneficiaries to the settlor for the trust.
There must be approval of the arrangement by the court before any trust can exist.
Trusts Law.w: An express private trust requires the 'three certainties' (Knight v Knight): certainty of intention to create a trust, certainty of the subject matter of the trust, and certainty of the objects (beneficiaries), together with the relevant formalities and constitution.

n.0: A professional trustee is not required for a valid trust.
n.2: A signed document is not enough; the three certainties must be present.
n.3: A trust is not a bargain; beneficiaries need give no consideration.
n.4: No prior court approval is required to create a trust.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee wrongfully pays trust money into the trustee's own personal bank account, which already contains the trustee's own money, and then makes various withdrawals from the mixed account, some of which are dissipated. The beneficiaries seek to trace into what remains. The account contains a mixture of trust money and the trustee's own money. The beneficiaries wish to identify the trust's share of the balance. Instead of keeping the trust money separate, the trustee funnelled it into their own current account alongside their personal funds and then drew on the account for various purposes, some of the money simply frittered away, leaving the beneficiaries to work out how much of what is left they can claim. Which of the following best describes a rule applied when a trustee mixes trust money with their own in a bank account?
o: The trustee is generally presumed to have spent their own money first, preserving the trust money so far as possible.
The beneficiaries may claim the whole account including the trustee's own contributions.
The beneficiaries can never trace into a mixed bank account of this kind.
The balance is always divided equally between the trustee and the beneficiaries.
The trust money is always presumed to have been spent first, defeating the beneficiaries' claim on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: Where a trustee mixes trust money with their own money in a bank account, equity applies rules favourable to the beneficiaries. Under the rule in Re Hallett, the trustee is generally presumed to have dissipated their own money first, so far as possible preserving the trust money in the account for the beneficiaries (subject to refinements such as Re Oatway).

n.1: The beneficiaries trace the trust's share, not the trustee's own contributions in addition.
n.2: Beneficiaries can trace into a mixed bank account using equity's rules.
n.3: The account is not simply divided equally by default; the tracing rules favour the beneficiaries.
n.4: Trust money is not presumed spent first against the beneficiaries; the opposite presumption favours them.

Trusts Law.q: Two lay trustees administer a trust together. They disagree about a particular decision: one trustee wishes to take a certain course, and the other does not. The first trustee purports to act alone, on the basis that a majority or even a single trustee should be able to bind the trust. A beneficiary questions whether one of two trustees can act unilaterally in this way. The trustees seek advice on how decisions must be taken where there is more than one trustee of a private trust. The proposed course would have committed a significant part of the fund to a single course of action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Any decision is valid provided at least one trustee supports it.
Trustees of a private trust must generally act unanimously, so one trustee cannot act alone.
The trustee who was appointed first has the casting vote on any disagreement.
A single trustee may always act alone and bind the trust, whatever the others think.
Decisions are always taken by a simple majority of the trustees in every private trust.
Trusts Law.w: Trustees of a private trust must generally act unanimously; decisions require the agreement of all the trustees, and one trustee cannot bind the trust by acting alone (unless the trust instrument or statute provides otherwise, as for some charitable and pension trusts where majority decisions may apply).

n.0: Support from only one trustee does not make a decision valid.
n.2: There is no casting vote for the first-appointed trustee.
n.3: A single trustee cannot generally act alone to bind a private trust.
n.4: Private trustees act unanimously, not by simple majority.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee wishes to buy an asset which forms part of the trust property, paying what they say is a fair market price for it. The purchase is not authorised by the trust instrument, the beneficiaries or the court. A beneficiary later objects to the trustee having bought trust property, even though the price paid was fair. The trustee argues that, as the price was fair and honestly arrived at, the sale to themselves should stand. The asset was an attractive one that the trustee had long wanted to acquire for their own portfolio. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The purchase is valid, because a trustee is always free to buy trust property.
The purchase is voidable by the beneficiaries under the self-dealing rule, regardless of the fairness of the price.
The purchase is valid, provided the trustee genuinely believed the price to be fair.
The purchase is void only if the trustee paid less than the market value of the asset on these facts as a general rule.
The purchase is valid and unimpeachable, because the trustee paid a fair market price.
Trusts Law.w: Under the self-dealing rule, a trustee who purchases trust property may have the transaction set aside (it is voidable) at the instance of a beneficiary, however fair the price and however honest the trustee, unless the purchase was authorised. The rule is strict and applies irrespective of fairness.

n.0: A trustee is not free to buy trust property without authority.
n.2: The trustee's honest belief in fairness does not validate the purchase.
n.3: The rule applies regardless of whether the price was below market value.
n.4: A fair price does not save a self-dealing purchase from being voidable.

Trusts Law.q: A trust has two continuing trustees. One of the original trustees has died, and the continuing trustees wish to appoint a replacement so that the administration can proceed smoothly. The trust instrument contains no special provision about appointing new trustees, and no person is nominated for that purpose. The trustees rely on the statutory power to appoint. The death has left the trust with a vacancy the two remaining trustees are keen to fill quickly so that decisions can continue to be taken properly, and, finding nothing in the trust document nominating anyone to make appointments, they turn to the general statutory machinery for bringing in a replacement. Which of the following best describes how a new trustee may be appointed under the Trustee Act 1925?
o: The deceased trustee's personal representatives automatically become the new trustees.
The continuing trustees may appoint a replacement in writing under the statutory power of appointment.
No replacement may be appointed unless the trust instrument expressly allows it.
Only the court may ever appoint a new trustee in these circumstances.
A new trustee can be appointed only if all the beneficiaries personally sign the appointment.
Trusts Law.w: Section 36 of the Trustee Act 1925 provides a statutory power to appoint new trustees, for example where a trustee has died. In the absence of a nominated person, the surviving or continuing trustees may appoint a replacement, and the appointment must be in writing. Court appointment is available but not necessary here.

n.0: The deceased trustee's personal representatives do not automatically become trustees.
n.2: The statutory power applies even without express provision in the trust instrument.
n.3: Court appointment is not the only route; s.36 gives the continuing trustees power to appoint.
n.4: The beneficiaries need not all sign the appointment under s.36.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees are about to distribute the trust fund but are concerned that there may be beneficiaries or claimants of whom they are not currently aware, and they do not want to be personally liable if an unknown claimant later comes forward after the distribution. They wish to protect themselves before distributing. The trustees seek advice on a statutory step they can take to guard against personal liability to unknown claimants. The estate was complex, with dealings going back many years and records that were far from complete. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees are automatically protected against all unknown claimants without taking any step.
The trustees can only protect themselves by obtaining the consent of every possible claimant first on these facts.
The trustees may advertise for claimants under s.27 Trustee Act 1925 to protect themselves before distributing.
The trustees may distribute free of any liability provided they act honestly and in good faith.
The trustees have no way to protect themselves and must simply distribute and hope for the best.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.27 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees may give statutory notice by advertisement for claimants, and, having waited the required period, may then distribute the estate/trust fund without being personally liable to claimants of whom they had no notice at the time of distribution.

n.0: Trustees are not automatically protected without taking the statutory step.
n.1: Obtaining every possible claimant's consent is not the mechanism; advertisement is.
n.3: Honest good faith alone does not give the s.27 protection.
n.4: There is a protective step available; trustees are not left with no protection.

Trusts Law.q: A person makes what is intended to be an outright gift of registered land to a donee, but fails to complete the necessary transfer and registration formalities, so that the legal title never passes and the gift is imperfect. The donee is a volunteer. The donee argues that, because the donor plainly intended to benefit them, the court should treat the failed gift as taking effect as a declaration of trust in the donee's favour instead. The land was valuable, and the donee had spent money in the expectation that the intended gift would go through. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will not treat a failed gift as a declaration of trust merely to give effect to the donor's intention.
The court will perfect the gift because the donee is a volunteer who relied on it.
The failed gift takes effect as a charitable trust for the donee's benefit.
The failed gift automatically creates a resulting trust in the donee's favour.
The court will always save a failed gift by treating it as a self-declaration of trust on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: Equity will not perfect an imperfect gift, and it will not construe an intended outright gift as a declaration of trust simply to give effect to the donor's intention where the transfer has failed (Milroy v Lord; Jones v Lock). The court does not save the gift by reinterpreting it as a trust.

n.1: Volunteer status and reliance do not lead equity to perfect the imperfect gift.
n.2: There is no charitable element; this is a private intended gift.
n.3: A failed gift does not create a resulting trust for the intended donee.
n.4: The court does not routinely rescue failed gifts as self-declarations of trust.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees receive a substantial sum of money into the trust and then simply leave it sitting idle in a non-interest-bearing account for a long period, making no attempt to invest it or otherwise make it productive for the beneficiaries. A beneficiary complains that the trustees have failed in their duties by allowing the trust money to lie unproductive. The trustees argue that keeping the money in cash was the safest thing to do. The sum involved was large and remained idle for well over a year without earning anything at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
