o: The trustees are likely in breach, as they must invest trust money and not leave it lying idle and unproductive.
The trustees are in breach only if a beneficiary can prove the exact profit that was lost.
The trustees owe no duty to invest and may leave trust money uninvested indefinitely.
The trustees have acted properly, provided the money was held in a reputable bank.
The trustees have acted properly, because keeping trust money in cash is always the safest course on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: Trustees are under a duty to invest trust money so as to make it productive for the beneficiaries, applying their power of investment and the standard investment criteria. Leaving substantial sums lying idle and uninvested for a prolonged period is a breach of that duty.

n.1: Breach does not depend on the beneficiary proving the precise lost profit.
n.2: Trustees do owe a duty to invest; they cannot leave money idle indefinitely.
n.3: Using a reputable bank does not discharge the duty to invest productively.
n.4: Holding trust money in cash is not automatically the proper or safest course.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor transfers a fund to trustees to be applied for a stated purpose, and claims that the trust is a valid charitable trust so that it does not need identifiable beneficiaries and can last indefinitely. The purpose is said to benefit the community. When the status of the trust is challenged, the court must decide whether it qualifies as charitable. The settlor's adviser is asked to explain the essential requirements a trust must meet to be charitable. The fund was substantial and the settlor wanted the arrangement to endure well beyond an ordinary lifetime. Which of the following best describes the requirements?
o: It must benefit the settlor's own family and friends as its primary object.
It must have identifiable individual beneficiaries who can enforce it in court on these facts.
It must be registered as a company before it can be treated as charitable.
It must simply be intended by the settlor to do some good in the world.
It must be for a recognised charitable purpose, for the public benefit, and exclusively charitable.
Trusts Law.w: To be charitable, a trust must be for a purpose within the descriptions of charitable purposes in the Charities Act 2011, must be for the public benefit, and must be exclusively charitable. Charitable trusts are an exception to the beneficiary principle and are enforced by the Attorney General/Charity Commission.

n.0: A trust primarily for the settlor's family and friends is not charitable.
n.1: Charitable trusts need no identifiable individual beneficiaries; that is the point of the exception.
n.2: Incorporation as a company is not required for a charitable trust.
n.3: A general intention to do good is not enough; the purpose must be legally charitable.

Trusts Law.q: A professionally drafted trust instrument contains a clause purporting to exempt the trustees from liability for loss to the trust caused by their own negligence, however serious, but not for loss caused by their own fraud or dishonesty. A beneficiary who has suffered loss through the trustees' careless (but honest) administration challenges the clause, arguing that a trustee can never exclude liability for failing to take proper care. The clause had been drawn carefully to cover even serious carelessness, but stopped short of dishonesty. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A trustee exemption clause may validly exclude liability for fraud as well as for negligence.
A trustee exemption clause may validly exclude liability for negligence, but not for fraud or dishonesty.
A trustee exemption clause is valid only in trusts administered by lay, unpaid trustees.
A trustee exemption clause is always void, because trustees can never limit their liability at all.
A trustee exemption clause is valid only where every beneficiary consented to it in writing.
Trusts Law.w: A trustee exemption clause can validly exclude liability for breaches of trust committed negligently, and even with gross negligence, but cannot exclude liability for the trustee's own fraud or dishonesty (Armitage v Nurse).

n.0: Liability for fraud or dishonesty cannot be excluded.
n.2: Such clauses are not confined to lay or unpaid trustees.
n.3: Such clauses are not always void; they can exclude liability for negligence.
n.4: Validity does not depend on every beneficiary's written consent.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees are ready to distribute the estate but are unsure whether a particular potential beneficiary is still alive or has died, having made reasonable enquiries without resolving the question. They are anxious to distribute without risk of personal liability if the missing person later appears. The trustees cannot be certain whether a beneficiary is alive or dead despite reasonable enquiry. They wish to protect themselves before distributing. The trustees have chased every lead to establish whether the potential beneficiary is alive but drawn a blank, they are ready to wind up the estate and pay out to the others, and they are looking for a way to do so that will not leave them personally answerable if the missing person later surfaces. Which of the following best describes a step the trustees can take for protection?
o: Retain the entire fund indefinitely and never distribute to anyone.
Pay the whole fund to the Crown as if it were ownerless property.
Distribute the fund on their own assumption without any protection, accepting personal liability.
Apply to the court for a Benjamin order permitting distribution on a stated assumption about the missing beneficiary.
Distribute equally among the known beneficiaries and ignore the missing person entirely without any order.
Trusts Law.w: Where trustees cannot establish whether a beneficiary is alive or dead, they may apply to the court for a Benjamin order, authorising distribution on a specified assumption (for example that the missing person predeceased). This protects the trustees from personal liability if the assumption later proves wrong, while the missing beneficiary's claim (if any) survives against the recipients.

n.0: Retaining the fund indefinitely is not a proper discharge of the trustees' duties.
n.1: The fund is not paid to the Crown merely because one beneficiary cannot be traced.
n.2: Distributing on their own assumption without protection leaves the trustees personally exposed.
n.4: Simply ignoring the missing person without an order or other protection risks personal liability.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees commit a breach of trust by making an unauthorised investment that loses value, so that the trust fund is now worth less than it would have been had the trustees acted properly. The beneficiaries seek a remedy requiring the trustees to make good the loss to the fund. The breach has caused a shortfall in the value of the trust fund. The beneficiaries seek equitable compensation. The unauthorised investment has fallen sharply in value, leaving the fund worth considerably less than it would have been had the trustees kept to their proper powers, and the beneficiaries now want a remedy that puts the trust back where it should have stood. Which of the following best describes the measure of the trustees' liability?
o: The trustees are liable only for a fixed statutory penalty regardless of the loss.
The trustees have no liability provided they acted in good faith throughout.
The trustees must restore the fund to the position it would have been in had the breach not occurred.
The trustees are liable only for losses that were reasonably foreseeable at the date of the breach.
The trustees are liable only to return the specific unauthorised investment as it now stands.
Trusts Law.w: A trustee in breach is liable to restore the trust fund, or compensate it, so as to put it in the position it would have been in had the breach not been committed, subject to questions of causation. The focus is on restoring the fund's value, not on foreseeability in the tortious sense or a fixed penalty.

n.0: Liability is measured by the loss to the fund, not a fixed statutory penalty.
n.1: Good faith does not automatically excuse liability for breach (though s.61 relief may be sought separately).
n.3: Equitable compensation focuses on restoring the fund, not on tortious foreseeability.
n.4: The remedy is to restore the value, not merely to hand back the depreciated investment.

Trusts Law.q: One person provides the purchase money for a property but the legal title is put into the name of another, unconnected, person, with no evidence of any gift or loan intended. The person who provided the money later claims a beneficial interest. There is no relationship between them giving rise to any presumption of advancement. The purchase money came wholly from the claimant, and title was taken in the other's name. The claimant funded the entire purchase price out of their own resources but, for convenience, allowed the property to be conveyed into the sole name of an unrelated acquaintance, and there is nothing to suggest the money was ever meant as a gift or a loan to that person. Which of the following best describes the likely beneficial ownership?
o: A resulting trust is presumed in favour of the person who provided the purchase money.
The person who provided the money has no interest unless there was a written declaration of trust.
The legal owner is beneficially entitled because legal title always determines beneficial ownership.
The property is automatically held on a constructive trust for both equally.
A presumption of advancement means the money was a gift to the legal owner.
Trusts Law.w: Where a person provides the purchase money for property but title is taken in another's name, a presumed (purchase money) resulting trust arises in favour of the provider, absent evidence of a gift or loan or an applicable presumption of advancement. The legal owner is presumed to hold the beneficial interest on resulting trust for the person who paid.

n.1: A resulting trust can arise without a written declaration; the provider is not left with no interest.
n.2: Legal title does not conclusively determine beneficial ownership; equity may presume a resulting trust.
n.3: It is a resulting trust for the provider, not an automatic equal constructive trust.
n.4: No presumption of advancement arises between unconnected parties, so the money is not presumed a gift.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee of a private trust wishes to retire from the trusteeship. There will remain, after the retirement, two trustees who will continue to administer the trust, and all the other trustees consent to the retirement by deed. The retiring trustee wants to be properly discharged without a new appointment being made. At least two trustees will remain and all co-trustees consent by deed. The trustee has grown elderly and wishes to step back, the remaining trustees are content to carry on between them and are willing to formalise matters, and everyone wants the departure handled in a way that leaves the retiring trustee properly discharged rather than exposed to lingering responsibility. Which of the following best describes how the trustee may retire under the Trustee Act 1925?
o: The trustee may retire only if all the beneficiaries consent in writing.
The trustee may retire simply by informing the beneficiaries orally.
The trustee may retire only if a new trustee is appointed to replace them on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The trustee cannot retire without a court order in any circumstances.
The trustee may retire by deed, provided at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) remain and the co-trustees consent.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.39 of the Trustee Act 1925, a trustee may retire without a replacement being appointed if, after the retirement, there will remain at least two trustees or a trust corporation, the retirement is by deed, and the co-trustees (and anyone empowered to appoint trustees) consent by deed. Those conditions are met here.

n.0: It is the co-trustees' consent by deed that is required, not that of all beneficiaries.
n.1: Retirement requires a deed and consents, not merely oral notice to beneficiaries.
n.2: A replacement need not be appointed if two trustees will remain (s.39).
n.3: A court order is not required where the s.39 conditions are satisfied.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor establishes a trust that pursues a mixture of aims, some charitable and some that are not charitable at all, and the trust funds may be applied to either kind of purpose at the trustees' discretion. The trust seeks recognition as a charity. The funds could lawfully be applied to non-charitable as well as charitable purposes. The trust deed lists a range of aims side by side, some plainly charitable and others not charitable at all, and leaves the trustees free to spend the fund on either sort, so the question is whether an arrangement drawn so widely can attract charitable status and its advantages. Which of the following best describes the effect on the trust's charitable status?
o: The trust is charitable so long as the non-charitable purposes are lawful.
The trust is charitable because it pursues at least one charitable purpose.
The trust is not charitable because it is not established exclusively for charitable purposes.
The trust is charitable provided most of the funds are in fact used for charity.
The trust is charitable if the trustees promise to prefer the charitable purposes on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: To be charitable a trust must be established exclusively for charitable purposes. Where trust funds may be applied to non-charitable as well as charitable purposes, the trust is not exclusively charitable and generally fails to qualify as a charity, even if some of the purposes are charitable.

n.0: Lawfulness of the non-charitable purposes does not make the trust exclusively charitable.
n.1: Pursuing one charitable purpose does not cure the presence of permitted non-charitable purposes.
n.3: It is not enough that most funds are in fact used for charity; the purposes must be exclusively charitable.
n.4: A promise to prefer charity does not satisfy the exclusivity requirement.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor transfers property to trustees on an express trust which then fails, or which disposes of only part of the beneficial interest so that a surplus remains undisposed of after the trust purposes have been carried out. There is no provision in the trust instrument dealing with what should happen to the undisposed-of beneficial interest. The question arises as to where the beneficial interest in the surplus goes. A significant sum was left over once the express purposes had been fully carried out by the trustees. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The undisposed-of beneficial interest is shared equally among all the original beneficiaries.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest is applied by the trustees to any purpose they choose.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest passes automatically to the Crown as ownerless property on these facts.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest results back to the settlor (or their estate) on an automatic resulting trust.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest passes to the trustees beneficially as a windfall.
Trusts Law.w: Where an express trust fails or does not exhaust the beneficial interest, the undisposed-of interest is held on an automatic resulting trust for the settlor (or their estate), because the settlor did not effectively dispose of that part of the beneficial interest.

n.0: It results to the settlor, not shared among beneficiaries who were not given it.
n.1: Trustees cannot apply the surplus to purposes of their own choosing.
n.2: The surplus goes back to the settlor, not to the Crown as bona vacantia in the ordinary case.
n.4: Trustees do not take the surplus beneficially; they hold on resulting trust.

Trusts Law.q: Before making their will, a testator agrees with a friend that the testator will leave property to the friend absolutely on the face of the will, but that the friend will in fact hold it on trust for a third party. The friend accepts this during the testator's lifetime. The will itself gives the property to the friend outright, with nothing on its face to indicate any trust. After the testator's death, the intended third party seeks to enforce the arrangement. The property was significant, and the friend had expressly promised the testator to carry out the arrangement. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The friend takes the property absolutely, because the will contains no mention of any trust on these facts as a general rule.
The arrangement fails, because a trust of this kind can never be enforced after death.
The arrangement is valid only if the third party gave consideration to the testator.
A fully secret trust may be enforced, as the terms were communicated to and accepted by the friend in the testator's lifetime.
The arrangement fails, because secret trusts are not recognised in English law.
Trusts Law.w: A fully secret trust arises where a will leaves property to a person apparently absolutely, but the testator has communicated the terms of a trust to that person and they have accepted them during the testator's lifetime. It is then enforced against the apparent legatee (Ottaway v Norman).

n.0: The absence of any trust on the face of the will is the very hallmark of a fully secret trust.
n.1: Such arrangements can be enforced after death if the requirements are met.
n.2: Secret trusts do not depend on consideration from the beneficiary.
n.4: Secret trusts are recognised in English law.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor transfers property to trustees to be used to provide and maintain sports facilities primarily for the benefit of the employees of a particular company and their families. Although expressed as a purpose, the arrangement directly benefits an ascertainable group of individuals who could enforce it. The trust is for a purpose but a class of persons stands to benefit and could enforce it. The settlor's evident aim was to give the company's workforce somewhere to play sport, the individuals who would use and benefit from the facilities can readily be identified, and any of them could come to court to insist the trustees carry the arrangement out as intended. Which of the following best describes the likely validity of this arrangement?
o: It is valid only if it is expressed to last no longer than 21 years.
It may be valid because the purpose is for the benefit of ascertainable individuals who can enforce it.
It is valid only if it qualifies as a charitable trust for the advancement of amateur sport.
It is void because all purpose trusts without a charitable purpose are invalid without exception.
It is void because sports facilities can never be the subject of a trust.
Trusts Law.w: Following Re Denley, a trust expressed as a purpose may be valid as a private trust where the purpose is sufficiently clear and directly or indirectly benefits ascertainable individuals who have standing to enforce it. Because identifiable people benefit and can enforce the trust, the beneficiary principle is satisfied.

n.0: Validity here rests on the ascertainable beneficiaries, not on a fixed 21-year limit (though perpetuity must still be satisfied).
n.2: The trust can be valid as a private Re Denley trust even if it is not charitable.
n.3: Not all non-charitable purpose trusts are void; Re Denley recognises those benefiting ascertainable individuals.
n.4: Sports facilities can be the subject of a valid trust.

Trusts Law.q: A settlement gives a person the ability to distribute a fund among a class, but expressed so that the person may distribute if they choose, and is not obliged to distribute at all, with the fund passing elsewhere in default. A question arises whether this is a trust imposing a duty or a mere power. The person is under no obligation to distribute and there is a gift over in default. The drafting leaves it genuinely open whether the person named was meant to be obliged to hand the fund out or merely permitted to do so if they saw fit, and because the fund goes elsewhere if nothing is done, the characterisation matters for whether anyone can compel a distribution. Which of the following best describes the key distinction between a trust and a mere power in this context?
o: A power always imposes a stricter duty to act than a trust.
A trust imposes a duty to distribute, whereas a mere power confers a discretion that need not be exercised.
A trust and a mere power are legally identical and produce the same obligations on these facts as a general rule.
A power, unlike a trust, can never be exercised in favour of a class.
A trust never allows any discretion as to who benefits.
Trusts Law.w: The essential distinction is that a trust imposes an obligation: the trustee must carry out the distribution. A mere (bare) power confers a discretion that the donee may choose whether or not to exercise; if it is not exercised, the property passes under any gift over in default. The presence of a duty, not merely a discretion, marks a trust.

n.0: A power imposes a less onerous obligation than a trust, not a stricter one.
n.2: Trusts and powers are not identical; one imposes a duty, the other a discretion.
n.3: A power can be exercised in favour of a class; that is not the distinction.
n.4: A discretionary trust does allow discretion as to who benefits, though the duty to distribute remains.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor creates a trust directing trustees to distribute a fund among such of a wide class of people as the trustees select, giving the trustees a discretion as to who benefits and in what shares. A question arises whether the class of objects is sufficiently certain for the trust to be valid. The trust is a discretionary trust rather than a fixed trust. The trustees have a discretion to choose among the class. The class the settlor chose is broad and loosely defined, the trustees want to know before they start distributing whether the trust is even valid, and their solicitor explains that the certainty test for a trust of this discretionary kind is not the same as for one giving fixed shares. Which of the following best describes the test for certainty of objects of a discretionary trust?
o: Whether the settlor named at least one specific member of the class.
Whether the trustees can agree unanimously on who should benefit.
Whether the class is small enough for the trustees to know each member personally on these facts as a general rule.
Whether it can be said with certainty of any given individual that they are or are not a member of the class.
Whether a complete list of every member of the class can be drawn up.
Trusts Law.w: For a discretionary trust the test for certainty of objects is the 'is or is not' (given postulant) test from McPhail v Doulton: the trust is valid if it can be said with certainty whether any given individual is or is not a member of the class. A complete list is not required; that stricter test applies to fixed trusts.

n.0: Naming one specific member is not the test for certainty of a class.
n.1: Unanimity on who benefits is not the test for conceptual certainty of the objects.
n.2: There is no requirement that the class be small enough to know each member personally.
n.4: The complete list test applies to fixed trusts, not discretionary trusts.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee misappropriates trust money and uses it to buy an identifiable asset in the trustee's own name, so that the original trust money can no longer be recovered as money but the asset bought with it still exists and has been kept separate. The beneficiaries wish to claim the asset itself, rather than merely suing the trustee personally, because the asset has risen in value. The beneficiaries seek advice on their proprietary remedy. The asset had since risen sharply in value, which was why the beneficiaries wanted it rather than mere compensation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiaries may claim only the original sum of money, and never any increase in value.
The beneficiaries may trace the trust money into the asset and claim it in equity.
The beneficiaries have no claim at all, because the money has changed its form.
The beneficiaries may claim the asset only if the trustee is insolvent at the time.
The beneficiaries have only a personal claim against the trustee and can never claim the asset.
Trusts Law.w: Equity allows a beneficiary to trace misapplied trust money into an identifiable substitute asset and to assert a proprietary claim to that asset (or a charge over it). This can allow the beneficiaries to claim the asset and any increase in its value.

n.0: Tracing into an appreciating asset can capture the increase in value.
n.2: A change in form does not defeat tracing where the substitute is identifiable.
n.3: Tracing does not depend on the trustee's insolvency, though it is especially valuable then.
n.4: The beneficiaries are not confined to a personal claim; a proprietary tracing claim may lie.

Trusts Law.q: A landowner orally declares that they hold a piece of land on trust for another person, intending to create a valid trust of the land. Nothing about the declaration is ever put into or evidenced by any signed writing. Later, a dispute arises and the beneficiary seeks to enforce the trust of the land, while the landowner denies that any enforceable trust of land was ever created because of the absence of writing. The land was valuable, and the intended beneficiary had made arrangements in the expectation of receiving it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust of land is void, because trusts of land can never be created by an individual on these facts.
The trust of land is unenforceable, because a declaration of trust of land must be evidenced in signed writing.
The trust of land is fully valid and enforceable despite the absence of any writing.
The trust of land is valid, because oral declarations of trust are always sufficient.
The trust of land is valid, provided the beneficiary has taken possession of the land.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925, a declaration of trust respecting land or any interest in land must be manifested and proved by some signed writing. An oral declaration of a trust of land is unenforceable (though not necessarily void) for want of the required written evidence.

n.0: Individuals can create trusts of land; the issue is the writing requirement.
n.2: A trust of land is not enforceable on an oral declaration alone; written evidence is needed.
n.3: Oral declarations are not always sufficient; land trusts require signed writing.
n.4: Taking possession does not satisfy the s.53(1)(b) writing requirement.

Trusts Law.q: A father transfers property into the sole name of his young child, or a husband transfers property into his wife's sole name, without any express declaration of trust and without any evidence one way or the other about his intention. A dispute later arises as to whether the child or wife holds the property on resulting trust for the transferor, or takes it beneficially. The transferor argues a resulting trust arises in his favour. The property was valuable, and years later the transferor sought to recover it from the transferee. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A presumption of advancement may apply, so the transfer is presumed to be a gift, though this can be rebutted.
The property passes to the Crown, because the intention behind the transfer is unclear.
A resulting trust automatically arises in the transferor's favour and cannot be displaced on these facts.
The transferee always holds on trust for the transferor, whatever their relationship.
The transfer is always an outright gift, and no presumption can ever be rebutted.
Trusts Law.w: In certain relationships (such as father to child, or husband to wife) equity presumes advancement — that a gift was intended — which displaces the ordinary presumption of a resulting trust. The presumption of advancement is itself rebuttable by evidence of a contrary intention.

n.1: The property does not pass to the Crown for uncertainty of intention.
n.2: A resulting trust does not automatically arise where the presumption of advancement applies, and presumptions can be rebutted.
n.3: The transferee does not hold on trust in every case; advancement may apply.
n.4: The presumption of advancement is rebuttable, not conclusive.

Trusts Law.q: An adult beneficiary of full capacity is absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest in a trust fund, with no other person having any interest in it. The trust was set up to pay the fund to the beneficiary at a later age, but the beneficiary now wishes to bring the trust to an end immediately and have the fund transferred to them straight away, against the wishes of the trustees who point to the age condition. The fund was substantial and the beneficiary had a pressing personal reason for wanting it released now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiary may require the trustees to transfer the fund and end the trust under the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The beneficiary has no power to interfere with how the trustees choose to administer the trust.
The beneficiary may end the trust only if a court first approves the early distribution.
The beneficiary may end the trust only with the consent of the settlor who created it.
The beneficiary must wait until the stated age, because the terms of the trust are binding come what may on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier, a beneficiary (or beneficiaries together) who is of full age and capacity and absolutely entitled to the whole beneficial interest may direct the trustees to transfer the trust property and bring the trust to an end, overriding a mere postponement of enjoyment.

n.1: An absolutely entitled adult beneficiary can indeed call for the fund.
n.2: Court approval is not needed where a single adult is absolutely entitled.
n.3: The settlor's consent is not required to invoke Saunders v Vautier.
n.4: An age condition merely postponing enjoyment does not prevent a sole absolutely-entitled adult ending the trust.

Trusts Law.q: A lender advances money to a company for a specific, identified purpose (to pay a particular class of the company's creditors), on terms that the money is to be used only for that purpose and not mixed with the company's general funds. Before the purpose can be carried out, the company becomes insolvent. The lender argues that the money did not become part of the company's general assets available to all creditors, but was held on trust. The money was paid into a separate account and was never mixed with the company's ordinary trading funds. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The money may be held on a Quistclose-type trust for the lender, as it was advanced for a specific purpose that failed.
The money is held on a charitable trust because it was to pay creditors.
The money automatically belongs to the company's general creditors on its insolvency.
The money is the company's absolutely, because a loan always transfers full ownership.
The money is held on trust only if the loan agreement expressly created a trust in those words on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: Where money is lent for a specific, exclusive purpose and is not to be at the borrower's free disposal, a Quistclose trust may arise: the money is held on trust for that purpose, and if the purpose fails, it results to the lender rather than falling into the general estate (Barclays Bank v Quistclose; Twinsectra v Yardley).

n.1: There is no charitable element; it is a private purpose loan.
n.2: Such money does not necessarily fall to the general creditors; a trust may protect it.
n.3: A purpose-restricted loan does not transfer full beneficial ownership to the borrower.
n.4: The trust can arise from the purpose restriction without the word 'trust' being used.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee administering a family trust makes a number of decisions about the trust investments and the management of the trust property. A beneficiary later complains that the trustee did not act carefully enough. The trustee, who is a lay person, argues that they did their honest best. The court must decide the standard of care against which the trustee's conduct is measured under the modern statutory framework. The trustee's adviser explains the applicable statutory duty of care. The trust was substantial and the decisions the trustee took had a real impact on the value of the fund. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The trustee must guarantee that the trust suffers no loss of any kind whatsoever.
The trustee is judged by the standard of the most expert professional trustee available.
The trustee must exercise such care and skill as is reasonable in the circumstances, with more expected of a professional.
The trustee is judged purely by whether they personally acted in honest good faith.
The trustee owes no duty of care at all, provided they were unpaid and acting voluntarily on these facts as a general rule.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.1 of the Trustee Act 2000, a trustee must exercise such care and skill as is reasonable in the circumstances, having regard to any special knowledge or experience they have or hold themselves out as having. A higher standard is expected of professional trustees.

n.0: The duty is one of reasonable care, not a guarantee against all loss.
n.1: The standard is reasonable care in the circumstances, not that of the most expert trustee.
n.3: Honest good faith alone is not the standard; reasonable care and skill is required.
n.4: Even an unpaid lay trustee owes the statutory duty of care.

Trusts Law.q: A testator leaves a gift to a specific charitable institution, but by the date of death that institution has ceased to exist. It is argued that the gift should be applied cy-près to another charity with similar objects rather than failing. The gift has failed at the outset because the named charity no longer exists. The institution named in the will had already closed its doors by the time the testator died, so the gift cannot take effect as written, and those hoping to save it want it redirected to a similar cause rather than allowed to fall into residue. Which of the following best describes what must be shown for the gift to be applied cy-près on this initial failure?
o: Nothing further need be shown; cy-près always applies whenever a charitable gift fails.
The residuary beneficiaries must consent to the cy-près application.
The gift can never be saved once the named charity has ceased to exist.
A general charitable intention must be shown for the gift to be applied cy-près.
A general charitable intention is required only where the charity fails after the gift takes effect.
Trusts Law.w: Where a charitable gift fails at the outset (initial failure), it can be applied cy-près only if the testator had a general charitable intention (an intention to benefit charity generally rather than only the particular institution). Where failure occurs after the gift has taken effect (subsequent failure), cy-près applies without needing to show general charitable intention.

n.0: Cy-près does not apply automatically on initial failure; general charitable intention must be shown.
n.1: The consent of residuary beneficiaries is not the applicable requirement.
n.2: The gift can be saved by cy-près if a general charitable intention is established.
n.4: For initial failure general charitable intention is required; it is subsequent failure that does not require it.

Trusts Law.q: A person voluntarily transfers money to another, or contributes to the purchase price of an asset that is then put into the other's sole name, without any intention to make a gift and without any express trust being declared. Later a dispute arises about the beneficial ownership of the money or asset. The person who provided the funds argues that they retained a beneficial interest despite the legal title being in the other's name. The asset had appreciated significantly in value since it was first bought with the disputed contribution. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The person who provided the funds can never claim any beneficial interest at all.
The legal owner takes the entire beneficial interest, because they hold the legal title.
A constructive trust of the whole fund automatically arises in favour of the legal owner on these facts.
A resulting trust arises only where the parties signed a written declaration of trust.
A resulting trust may arise in favour of the person who provided the funds, absent an intention to give.
Trusts Law.w: Where a person voluntarily transfers property to another, or contributes to its purchase price, without intending a gift and without an express trust, equity presumes a resulting trust in favour of the person who provided the funds, in proportion to their contribution (unless the presumption is rebutted).

n.0: The contributor may well claim a beneficial interest via a resulting trust.
n.1: Holding legal title does not necessarily carry the beneficial interest here.
n.2: The resulting trust favours the contributor, not the legal owner.
n.3: A resulting trust arises by presumption and needs no written declaration.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor wishes to create a trust of land and proposes to appoint six individuals as trustees so that decisions can be shared widely. A solicitor advises that there is a statutory limit on the number of trustees who may hold legal title to land. The trust property consists of land held on trust. The settlor wants as many trustees as possible. The settlor is enthusiastic about spreading responsibility as widely as possible and has drawn up a list of six proposed trustees, but the solicitor warns that the law will not let all of them hold the legal estate in the land, whatever the settlor's wishes. Which of the following best describes the position on the number of trustees of land?
o: The maximum number of trustees of land is two in every case.
There is no limit on the number of trustees who may hold legal title to land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A trust of land must always have exactly three trustees.
The limit on trustees of land applies only to charitable trusts.
The number of trustees of land is limited to a maximum of four, being the first four named who are able and willing to act.
Trusts Law.w: Where land is held on trust, the number of trustees is limited to a maximum of four; if more are named, the first four named who are able and willing to act take the legal estate. This contrasts with trusts of pure personalty, where there is no statutory maximum number of trustees.

n.0: The maximum is four, not two.
n.1: There is a statutory maximum of four for trustees of land.
n.2: There is no fixed requirement of exactly three trustees.
n.3: The four-trustee limit for land is not confined to charitable trusts.

Trusts Law.q: A will leaves property to a named person 'to hold on trust for the purposes I have communicated to them', so that the existence of a trust is disclosed on the face of the will, but the actual beneficiaries and terms are not. The testator had told that person the terms of the trust before executing the will, and the person accepted them at that time. After death, a question arises as to whether this half-secret trust is enforceable. The property was substantial, and the trustee had written down the terms the testator gave before the will was signed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust fails, because a trust that is mentioned in a will can never be a secret trust.
The named person takes the property beneficially, because the terms were not set out in the will on these facts.
The trust fails, because half-secret trusts are not recognised in English law.
The half-secret trust may be enforced, as the terms were communicated and accepted before or at the time the will was made.
The trust is valid only if the terms were communicated after the will had been executed.
Trusts Law.w: A half-secret trust is disclosed on the face of the will but its terms are not. It may be enforced where the terms were communicated to, and accepted by, the trustee before or at the time the will was executed (Blackwell v Blackwell). Communication after the will is generally too late.

n.0: A trust mentioned in a will is precisely a half-secret trust.
n.1: The person does not take beneficially; the will shows they hold on trust.
n.2: Half-secret trusts are recognised in English law.
n.4: For half-secret trusts communication must be before or at the time of the will, not after.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees who have no particular expertise in investment matters are about to exercise their power to invest a large trust fund across a range of assets. They are considering simply making the investment decisions themselves, on the basis of their own general knowledge, without taking any external input. A beneficiary asks whether the trustees are required to take advice before investing. The trustees seek guidance on their obligations under the Trustee Act 2000. The sums to be invested were considerable and the range of possible investments was wide and complex. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may invest only through a stockbroker who takes over the decision entirely.
The trustees must ordinarily obtain and consider proper advice before exercising the power of investment.
The trustees must always follow whatever advice they receive without any independent thought on these facts.
The trustees never need to take any advice, because the decision is entirely theirs to make.
The trustees must obtain the consent of every beneficiary before making any investment.
Trusts Law.w: Under the Trustee Act 2000, before exercising the power of investment (and when reviewing investments) trustees must obtain and consider proper advice about how the power should be exercised, having regard to the standard investment criteria, unless it is reasonably concluded that advice is unnecessary.

n.0: Taking advice does not require handing the decision entirely to a broker.
n.2: They must consider advice, but they are not bound to follow it blindly.
n.3: Trustees generally must take proper advice; it is not simply their own decision.
n.4: Beneficiary consent to each investment is not required.

Trusts Law.q: A sole adult beneficiary is absolutely entitled to the whole of a trust fund under a trust that was intended to continue until the beneficiary reached a later age. The beneficiary, now of full age and mentally capable, wishes to bring the trust to an end and have the property transferred to them at once, despite the settlor's contrary wishes. The beneficiary is of full age, capacity, and absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest. The settlor had intended the fund to be kept back until the beneficiary was considerably older, but the beneficiary is now an adult of full capacity, solely and absolutely entitled to everything in the fund, and wants it handed over immediately rather than waiting as the settlor wished. Which of the following best describes the beneficiary's ability to end the trust?
o: The beneficiary cannot end the trust because the settlor's stated intention is binding on these facts as a general rule.
The beneficiary must wait until the age specified by the settlor in every case.
The beneficiary may require the trustees to transfer the property and end the trust under the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The beneficiary may end the trust only after obtaining the court's approval.
The beneficiary may end the trust only with the consent of the settlor.
Trusts Law.w: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier, a beneficiary who is of full age and capacity and absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest (or all such beneficiaries acting together) may direct the trustees to transfer the trust property and bring the trust to an end, notwithstanding the settlor's contrary intention or a specified later age.

n.0: The settlor's stated intention does not prevent a sui juris, absolutely entitled beneficiary ending the trust.
n.1: The beneficiary need not wait for the settlor's specified age if absolutely entitled and sui juris.
n.3: Court approval is not required where the Saunders v Vautier conditions are met.
n.4: The settlor's consent is not required.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor creates a trust of a fund to be used to maintain a specific animal belonging to the settlor, and for the upkeep of a particular tomb, for as long as the law allows. There are no human beneficiaries to enforce the trust, and the purpose is not charitable. The settlor's adviser considers whether such a non-charitable purpose trust can nonetheless be valid, given the general rule that private purpose trusts are void for want of a beneficiary. The settlor left detailed directions about how the particular animal and the tomb were each to be looked after. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Such trusts are valid only if they are for the public benefit like a charitable trust.
Such trusts are always void, because there are no beneficiaries who can enforce them.
Such trusts are always valid, because a settlor may create a trust for any purpose at all on these facts.
Such trusts are valid only if a charity agrees to take responsibility for enforcing them.
Such trusts may be valid as recognised anomalous exceptions, but only if they satisfy the perpetuity rules.
Trusts Law.w: Although non-charitable purpose trusts are generally void for lack of a beneficiary, there are recognised anomalous exceptions — including trusts for specific animals and for the maintenance of particular graves or monuments — which may be valid provided they comply with the perpetuity rules (Re Endacott; Re Dean).

n.0: These exceptions do not require public benefit; that is the charitable route.
n.1: These recognised exceptions are not always void.
n.2: A settlor cannot create a valid private trust for any purpose whatever.
n.3: A charity's willingness to enforce is not the basis of these exceptions.

Trusts Law.q: Two trustees jointly administer a trust. One of them commits a breach of trust which causes loss to the fund, and the other trustee, although not the prime mover, is also implicated in the breach through their conduct. The beneficiaries wish to recover the whole loss and ask whether they may pursue either trustee for the entire amount, and how liability is ultimately shared between the trustees themselves. The loss was large, and the beneficiaries wanted to pursue whichever trustee was best able to pay it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Neither trustee is liable, because the loss was caused by their joint decision rather than one of them.
The beneficiaries must sue both trustees together or they can recover nothing at all.
The trustees are jointly and severally liable to the beneficiaries, and may claim contribution between themselves.
Each trustee is liable to the beneficiaries only for their own precise share of the loss.
Only the trustee who was the prime mover of the breach can ever be liable to the beneficiaries.
Trusts Law.w: Trustees are jointly and severally liable to the beneficiaries for a breach of trust, so the beneficiaries may recover the whole loss from either. As between the trustees themselves, a trustee who has paid may seek contribution (or in some cases an indemnity) from a co-trustee under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978.

n.0: A joint decision does not exonerate the trustees; both may be liable.
n.1: The beneficiaries need not sue both together; either can be pursued for the whole.
n.3: Liability to the beneficiaries is joint and several, not limited to each trustee's share.
n.4: Liability is not confined to the prime mover; an implicated co-trustee is also liable.

Trusts Law.q: Trust property is misapplied in breach of trust and comes into the hands of a third party who is a stranger to the trust. That third party receives the trust property for their own benefit, and at the time of receipt (or later) they have knowledge that makes it unconscionable for them to retain it. A beneficiary seeks to make the recipient personally liable. The recipient argues that, as they were never a trustee, they owe the trust nothing. The recipient had taken the property in circumstances that plainly should have alerted them to the breach. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The recipient can never be liable, because they were not a trustee of the trust.
The recipient may be personally liable for knowing receipt of trust property received with the requisite knowledge.
The recipient is liable only if they also actively assisted in the breach of trust on these facts as a general rule.
The recipient is liable only if they physically still possess the trust property.
The recipient is liable only where they paid nothing at all for the trust property.
Trusts Law.w: A stranger who beneficially receives trust property transferred in breach of trust, with knowledge (such that retention is unconscionable), may be personally liable for 'knowing receipt', accounting as a constructive trustee, even though they were never an express trustee.

n.0: Non-trustees can incur liability for knowing receipt.
n.2: Knowing receipt is distinct from dishonest assistance; active assistance is not required.
n.3: Liability for knowing receipt does not require continued possession of the property.
n.4: Liability turns on knowledge and beneficial receipt, not simply on paying nothing.

Trusts Law.q: Trustees of a trust that owns land agree to sell the land to a buyer. The beneficiaries hold equitable interests under the trust. The buyer's solicitor is concerned to ensure the buyer takes the land free of those beneficial interests, which should instead attach to the sale proceeds. There are two trustees who will receive the purchase money. The buyer wishes to overreach the beneficiaries' equitable interests. The trust owns a valuable freehold that the trustees have agreed to sell, the beneficiaries have equitable interests behind the trust, and the buyer's solicitor is anxious to structure completion so that those interests lift off the land and attach instead to the money the trustees receive. Which of the following best describes how overreaching is achieved on the sale?
o: Overreaching is impossible where the land is subject to a trust.
The beneficial interests are overreached automatically whenever any single trustee sells the land on these facts.
The beneficial interests are overreached if the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees or a trust corporation.
Overreaching requires the personal consent of every beneficiary to the sale.
Overreaching occurs only if the buyer registers a notice against the beneficiaries.
Trusts Law.w: On a sale by trustees of land, the beneficiaries' equitable interests are overreached, transferring from the land to the proceeds of sale, if the buyer pays the capital money to at least two trustees or a trust corporation. The buyer then takes free of the beneficial interests, which attach to the money in the trustees' hands.

n.0: Overreaching is precisely the mechanism for selling trust land free of beneficial interests.
n.1: Payment to a single trustee does not overreach; at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) are needed.
n.3: Overreaching does not require every beneficiary's personal consent.
n.4: Overreaching turns on payment to two trustees, not on registering a notice against beneficiaries.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee spends a great deal of time and effort administering a complex trust and considers that they ought to be paid for their work. The trust instrument contains no charging clause authorising payment, the beneficiaries have not agreed to remunerate the trustee, and there is no statutory entitlement applicable to this lay trustee. The trustee nonetheless takes a sum from the trust fund as remuneration for their services. A beneficiary objects. The administration had been unusually burdensome, running to many hours of work over several months. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustee is always entitled to be paid a reasonable sum for the work they do.
The trustee may take whatever remuneration they consider fair for their efforts.
The trustee is generally not entitled to remuneration for their services without authorisation.
The trustee is entitled to payment because they spent a great deal of time on the trust.
The trustee may be paid provided the trust as a whole has increased in value.
Trusts Law.w: As a fiduciary, a trustee is generally not entitled to profit from the trust, including by way of remuneration, unless authorised — for example by a charging clause in the trust instrument, the consent of the beneficiaries, the court, or an applicable statutory provision (such as for professional trustees).

n.0: There is no general right to remuneration for a lay trustee acting without authority.
n.1: The trustee cannot simply take what they think is fair.
n.3: Effort and time spent do not create an entitlement to be paid.
n.4: An increase in the trust's value does not authorise unauthorised remuneration.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee, in breach of trust, makes an unauthorised investment which loses a substantial part of the trust fund's value, causing loss to the beneficiaries. The beneficiaries wish to hold the trustee personally responsible for the loss the breach has caused to the trust. The trustee accepts the investment was unauthorised but argues that they should not have to make good the loss out of their own pocket. The beneficiaries seek advice on the remedy available against the trustee. The unauthorised investment had been a large part of the fund and its collapse left the beneficiaries much worse off. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The trustee's only obligation is to apologise and to act more carefully in the future.
The trustee is liable only if the beneficiaries can prove the trustee acted dishonestly.
The trustee has no personal liability, because the loss was caused by a fall in the market.
The trustee is personally liable to compensate the trust for the loss caused by the breach.
The trustee is liable only up to the amount of any fee they received for acting.
Trusts Law.w: A trustee who commits a breach of trust is personally liable to restore the trust fund to the position it would have been in but for the breach, by way of equitable compensation for the loss caused. Liability does not depend on dishonesty.

n.0: An apology is no substitute for restoring the loss to the trust.
n.1: Liability for breach of trust does not require proof of dishonesty.
n.2: The trustee cannot escape liability by attributing the loss to the market where the investment was an unauthorised breach.
n.4: Liability is measured by the loss caused, not capped at any fee received.

Trusts Law.q: An organisation seeks charitable status for a trust whose purpose falls within a recognised charitable description. The regulator questions whether the trust provides sufficient benefit to the public, as the class who may benefit is defined by a personal connection to the settlor. The purpose is otherwise capable of being charitable. The concern is whether the benefit is genuinely available to a section of the public. The stated objects would ordinarily fall within a charitable description, but those who can benefit are confined to people connected to the settlor personally, and the regulator is focused on whether an arrangement so limited really delivers the kind of benefit the law demands of a charity. Which of the following best describes the public benefit requirement for a charitable trust?
o: The trust must benefit every member of the public without exception.
The trust satisfies public benefit if it benefits any group, however defined by personal ties on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The public benefit requirement was abolished by the Charities Act 2011.
A charitable trust need show no public benefit provided its purpose is worthwhile.
The trust must be for the public benefit, generally benefiting the public or a sufficient section of it, not a group defined by personal connection.
Trusts Law.w: A charitable trust must be for the public benefit: it must confer an identifiable benefit and be available to the public or a sufficient section of it. A class defined by a personal nexus, such as a relationship to a particular individual or employment by a particular employer, generally fails the requirement (subject to limited exceptions, notably for the relief of poverty).

n.0: It need not benefit literally everyone; a sufficient section of the public suffices.
n.1: A class defined by personal ties generally fails public benefit (outside the poverty exception).
n.2: The public benefit requirement was retained, not abolished, by the Charities Act 2011.
n.3: Public benefit is required; a worthwhile purpose alone is not enough.

Trusts Law.q: A beneficiary of a trust asks the trustees to provide information about the trust, including the trust accounts and documents recording how the trust property has been dealt with. The trustees are reluctant and question whether they are obliged to account to the beneficiary at all. The beneficiary insists they are entitled to be kept informed and to see the trust accounts. The trustees seek advice on their duties to account and to provide information to beneficiaries. The beneficiary had become suspicious about how the trust property was being managed by the trustees. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Trustees must disclose absolutely every document, including their confidential reasons for discretionary decisions.
Trustees must keep accounts and, in general, provide beneficiaries with trust accounts and information about the trust.
Trustees owe no duty to keep any accounts or to provide beneficiaries with any information at all.
Trustees need account only to the settlor, and never to the beneficiaries of the trust.
Trustees must provide information only if a beneficiary first obtains a court order compelling it.
Trusts Law.w: Trustees are under a duty to keep proper accounts and records and, on request, generally to provide beneficiaries with trust accounts and information about the administration of the trust, so that beneficiaries can hold them to account (subject to limits, e.g. confidential reasons for exercising discretions).

n.0: Trustees need not disclose their confidential reasons for discretionary decisions.
n.2: Trustees do owe duties to account and to inform beneficiaries.
n.3: The duty to account is owed to the beneficiaries, not only the settlor.
n.4: A beneficiary need not obtain a court order before receiving trust accounts in the ordinary case.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor purports to create a discretionary trust for the benefit of an enormous, effectively boundless class, such as 'all the residents of a large region', so vast that any sensible exercise of the trustees' discretion would be impossible even though the class concept is clear. A beneficiary challenges the trust's validity. Conceptually the class is certain, but it is so large that the trust cannot sensibly be carried out. The drafting is clear enough in the abstract, but the sheer number of potential objects runs into the millions, so the trustees protest that they could not begin to survey the class or make any rational choice between its members however hard they tried. Which of the following best describes why the trust may nonetheless fail?
o: It must be valid because the class concept is conceptually certain.
It fails for uncertainty of subject matter rather than of objects.
It fails only because the trustees have not yet been appointed.
It fails because discretionary trusts are not recognised in English law on these facts as a general rule.
It may fail for administrative unworkability, the class being so wide that the trust cannot be executed.
Trusts Law.w: Even where a class is conceptually certain, a discretionary trust may be void for administrative unworkability if the class is so hopelessly wide (for example, all the residents of a large area) that the trust cannot sensibly be executed. This is a distinct ground of invalidity from conceptual uncertainty.

n.0: Conceptual certainty does not guarantee validity; administrative unworkability can still defeat the trust.
n.1: The issue is the objects being unworkably wide, not uncertainty of subject matter.
n.2: The problem is the width of the class, not the absence of appointed trustees.
n.3: Discretionary trusts are recognised; the issue is the unworkable width of this class.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor is deciding between two arrangements for a fund. Under the first, each named beneficiary would be absolutely entitled to a fixed and defined share of the fund. Under the second, the trustees would have a discretion to decide which members of a class receive anything at all, and how much, so that no member has any entitlement unless the trustees choose in their favour. The settlor asks their adviser to explain the essential difference between these two kinds of trust. The fund was large, and the settlor wanted to understand the practical consequences of choosing each structure. Which of the following best describes the distinction?
o: A discretionary trust requires beneficiaries to give consideration, while a fixed trust does not on these facts as a general rule.
A fixed trust gives the trustees discretion, while a discretionary trust gives fixed shares.
There is no real difference; the two kinds of trust operate in exactly the same way.
A fixed trust need not satisfy any certainty of objects, unlike a discretionary trust.
In a fixed trust the beneficiaries' shares are defined, whereas in a discretionary trust distribution is at the trustees' discretion.
Trusts Law.w: Under a fixed trust the beneficiaries and their shares are determined by the trust instrument, so the trustees must simply give effect to those defined entitlements. Under a discretionary trust the trustees have a discretion as to which objects benefit and to what extent, and no object has an entitlement until the discretion is exercised.

n.0: Neither type requires beneficiaries to give consideration.
n.1: The description is reversed; fixed trusts have defined shares and discretionary trusts confer discretion.
n.2: The two differ significantly in how entitlements arise.
n.3: Both types must satisfy certainty of objects, by their respective tests.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor establishes a trust fund to relieve poverty among a defined group of poor people. A question arises about the requirement of public benefit, because the class of potential beneficiaries is relatively narrow and, in the ordinary way, a charitable trust must benefit a sufficient section of the public rather than a small private group. The trustees seek advice on whether the trust can be charitable despite the narrowness of the class it benefits. The defined group was small and known to the settlor, which is what prompted the concern about public benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is charitable only if the poor beneficiaries are complete strangers to the settlor on these facts.
The trust cannot be charitable, because it benefits too small a class of people.
The trust cannot be charitable, because relief of poverty is not a charitable purpose.
The trust is charitable only if it benefits the whole of the general public without limit.
Trusts for the relief of poverty are treated more generously, so a narrower class may still be charitable.
Trusts Law.w: Relief of poverty is a recognised charitable purpose, and the public benefit requirement is applied more leniently to poverty trusts, so a comparatively narrow class (even, historically, poor relations or poor employees) may still qualify as charitable.

n.0: There is no requirement that the poor beneficiaries be strangers to the settlor.
n.1: Poverty trusts are not defeated merely by a relatively narrow class.
n.2: Relief of poverty is a charitable purpose.
n.3: A charitable trust need not benefit the entire public without limit.

Trusts Law.q: A trust holds a fund for a minor beneficiary who is not yet entitled to the capital, and which produces income. The minor needs money for their education and maintenance. The trustees wish to apply some of the trust income for the minor's benefit but are unsure of their power to do so where the beneficiary is under age and not yet entitled to income as of right. The trustees seek advice on their statutory power to apply income for a minor beneficiary. The minor's school fees and living costs were mounting, and there was ample income available in the trust. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may never apply any trust money for a minor until the minor comes of age.
The trustees must accumulate all income and can never use it for the minor's benefit.
The trustees may apply income only with the prior approval of the court in every case.
The trustees may apply income only if the minor's parents formally consent in writing.
The trustees have a statutory power of maintenance to apply income for the minor's benefit.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.31 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees have a statutory power of maintenance to apply income (as they think fit) for the maintenance, education or benefit of a minor beneficiary, accumulating any surplus income, unless the trust instrument excludes or varies the power.

n.0: Trustees are not barred from applying money for a minor until majority.
n.1: Trustees need not accumulate all income; they may apply it for the minor's benefit.
n.2: Prior court approval is not required to exercise the statutory power of maintenance.
n.3: Parental written consent is not the statutory precondition.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor tells the intended beneficiary that they are giving them property on trust, but never actually transfers the legal title of the property to the intended trustees, and does everything as a gratuitous arrangement for which the beneficiary gives nothing in return. The trust is therefore never completely constituted by a transfer of the property. The intended beneficiary, a volunteer, seeks to compel the settlor to perfect the arrangement. The property remained registered in the settlor's sole name throughout, and no deed of transfer was ever executed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is incompletely constituted, and equity will not assist a volunteer to perfect it.
The court will compel the settlor to transfer the property to complete the trust.
The trust is fully constituted, because the settlor announced an intention to create it.
The trust is valid, because the beneficiary relied on the settlor's statement.
The trust is valid, because consideration is never required to create a trust.
Trusts Law.w: A trust must be completely constituted by vesting the trust property in the trustees (or a valid self-declaration of trust). Where it is not, and the intended beneficiary is a volunteer, equity will not perfect an imperfect gift or assist a volunteer to compel constitution (Milroy v Lord).

n.1: Equity will not compel the settlor to complete an imperfect gift for a volunteer.
n.2: An announced intention does not constitute the trust without vesting the property.
n.3: Reliance alone does not constitute the trust here.
n.4: Though consideration is not needed to create a trust, a volunteer cannot compel constitution of an incomplete one.

Trusts Law.q: A beneficiary who holds a subsisting equitable interest under an existing trust wishes to transfer that equitable interest to another person. The beneficiary simply gives oral instructions to that effect, without executing any signed writing to dispose of the equitable interest. A dispute later arises as to whether the equitable interest was validly transferred to the intended recipient. The recipient argues the oral instruction was enough. The equitable interest was worth a substantial sum, and the recipient had begun to treat it as their own. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The disposition is fully effective, because equitable interests can be transferred orally.
The disposition is effective, because the beneficiary clearly intended to transfer the interest on these facts.
The disposition is effective, provided the trustees were told about it verbally.
The disposition is ineffective, because a disposition of a subsisting equitable interest must be in signed writing.
The disposition is void, because equitable interests can never be transferred at all.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.53(1)(c) of the Law of Property Act 1925, a disposition of a subsisting equitable interest must be in writing signed by the person disposing of it (or their agent). An oral disposition of an existing equitable interest is ineffective.

n.0: A subsisting equitable interest cannot be disposed of by purely oral means.
n.1: Clear intention does not dispense with the s.53(1)(c) writing requirement.
n.2: Merely informing the trustees orally does not satisfy the signed-writing requirement.
n.4: Equitable interests can be transferred; the requirement is signed writing.

Trusts Law.q: An unmarried couple live in a house that is registered in the sole name of one partner. The other partner claims a beneficial share, relying on an express common intention that the property would be shared, together with conduct amounting to detrimental reliance on that understanding. There is no express declaration of trust and the non-owner made no direct contribution to the purchase price. The non-owning partner seeks advice on the basis of a claim to a beneficial interest. The couple had lived in the house for many years and organised their finances around the shared understanding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The non-owner may claim a share only if there was a signed written declaration of trust.
A resulting trust arises automatically in the non-owner's favour regardless of intention.
The legal owner is the sole beneficial owner, because a home is always owned by whoever is on the title.
A common intention constructive trust may arise from the shared intention together with detrimental reliance.
The non-owner can have no interest at all, because they did not contribute to the purchase price.
Trusts Law.w: A common intention constructive trust can arise where the parties shared an intention (express or inferred) that the beneficial interest be shared, and the claimant acted to their detriment in reliance on that intention. Direct financial contribution is not the only route (Lloyds Bank v Rosset; Stack v Dowden).

n.0: A constructive trust arises without a signed written declaration.
n.1: A common intention constructive trust turns on intention and reliance, not an automatic resulting trust.
n.2: Sole legal ownership does not always mean sole beneficial ownership.
n.4: A beneficial share is not confined to those who contributed to the purchase price.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor wishes to create a charitable trust and is considering purposes in the fields of education, religion and the provision of recreational facilities in the interests of social welfare. The settlor wants to be sure that each proposed purpose is capable of being charitable and satisfies the public benefit requirement. The settlor's adviser reviews the recognised descriptions of charitable purposes. The settlor intended each purpose to benefit the wider community rather than any private group of individuals. Which of the following best describes the position on these purposes?
o: Only the relief of poverty is capable of being a charitable purpose in English law.
The advancement of education and of religion, and certain recreational purposes for social welfare, can each be charitable.
The advancement of religion can never be charitable, because it benefits only believers on these facts as a general rule.
Education is charitable only where it is provided entirely free of any charge.
Recreational facilities can never be charitable in any circumstances whatsoever.
Trusts Law.w: The Charities Act 2011 lists recognised charitable purposes including the advancement of education and of religion, and the provision of recreational facilities in the interests of social welfare, each of which must also satisfy the public benefit requirement.

n.0: Charitable purposes are not limited to the relief of poverty.
n.2: Advancement of religion is a recognised charitable purpose.
n.3: Charitable education is not confined to free provision.
n.4: Recreational facilities for social welfare can be charitable.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor purports to declare a trust over 'the bulk of my estate' for certain beneficiaries, without in any way identifying which specific assets, or what proportion, are to be held on the trust. The remaining assets are to pass elsewhere. When the arrangement is challenged, the court has to decide whether the trust can take effect, given that it is impossible to identify with certainty the property that is supposed to be subject to it. The estate contained a wide range of assets of very different values, none earmarked for the beneficiaries. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is valid, and the court will simply decide what a fair 'bulk' should be.
The trust is valid, because the beneficiaries are identified even if the property is not.
The trust fails for uncertainty of subject matter, because the trust property cannot be identified.
The trust takes effect over the whole estate, since the property cannot be separated out.
The trust is valid, because the settlor clearly intended to benefit the beneficiaries.
Trusts Law.w: Certainty of subject matter requires the trust property to be identifiable. A description such as 'the bulk' of an estate is too vague to identify the property, so the trust fails for uncertainty of subject matter (Palmer v Simmonds).

n.0: The court will not fix a 'fair bulk' where the subject matter is uncertain.
n.1: Certain objects do not cure uncertainty as to the trust property.
n.3: The uncertainty defeats the trust; it does not extend it to the whole estate.
n.4: A clear intention cannot save a trust whose property is unidentifiable.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor purports to create a private trust of a fund to be used to maintain and promote a particular abstract purpose, rather than for the benefit of any identifiable people. The purpose is not charitable, and does not fall within any of the recognised exceptional categories of valid non-charitable purpose trust. There are no human beneficiaries who could go to court to enforce the trust. The validity of the arrangement is challenged. The settlor had set aside a considerable fund and appointed trustees willing to devote it entirely to the purpose. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is void, because a private trust must generally have beneficiaries who can enforce it.
The trust is valid, because the settlor's purpose is clearly and precisely defined.
The trust is valid, because the absence of beneficiaries makes it easier to administer.
The trust is valid, because any purpose a settlor chooses can be the object of a trust.
The trust is valid, provided the trustees are willing to carry the purpose out.
Trusts Law.w: Under the beneficiary principle, a private trust must generally have ascertainable beneficiaries who can enforce it. A non-charitable purpose trust with no beneficiaries is void, save for a few anomalous exceptions (such as trusts for specific animals or monuments) (Morice v Bishop of Durham; Re Astor).

n.1: Precision of the purpose does not cure the lack of a beneficiary to enforce it.
n.2: The absence of beneficiaries is fatal, not an advantage.
n.3: Not every purpose can be the object of a valid private trust.
n.4: Trustees' willingness does not supply the missing enforcer.

Trusts Law.q: A beneficiary discovers, some years after the event, that a trustee committed a breach of trust. In one scenario the breach was an ordinary (non-fraudulent) breach; in another, the trustee acted fraudulently or still retains trust property in their own hands. The beneficiary wishes to know whether a limitation period bars a claim against the trustee for the breach of trust, and whether the position differs depending on the nature of the breach. The beneficiary had only just uncovered the breach while going through some old trust papers. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A six-year period applies to every claim against a trustee without any exception at all.
The claim is barred after twelve years in every case, whatever the nature of the breach.
A six-year limitation period generally applies, but there is no period for fraud or where the trustee retains trust property.
A three-year period applies to all breach of trust claims, as for personal injury.
There is never any limitation period for any claim against a trustee for breach of trust on these facts as a general rule.
Trusts Law.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the general limitation period for a claim against a trustee for breach of trust is six years, but no limitation period applies to a claim in respect of fraud or fraudulent breach by the trustee, or to recover trust property (or its proceeds) still in the trustee's hands.

n.0: The six-year period is subject to exceptions for fraud and retained trust property.
n.1: There is no blanket twelve-year bar covering all breaches, including fraud.
n.3: The three-year personal injury period does not apply to breach of trust.
n.4: There is a limitation period for ordinary breaches, so 'never' is wrong.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee properly incurs expenses in the administration of the trust, for example paying for necessary professional advice and the upkeep of trust property, and now seeks to be reimbursed. A beneficiary queries whether the trustee is entitled to recover these sums from the trust. The expenses were properly incurred in carrying out the trust. The trustee seeks reimbursement rather than remuneration for their time. In the ordinary course of running the trust the trustee paid for necessary professional advice and met the running costs of trust property out of their own pocket, and now, entirely properly, wants those outlays met from the fund rather than being left personally out of pocket. Which of the following best describes the trustee's entitlement?
o: The trustee is entitled to be reimbursed out of the trust fund for expenses properly incurred in administering the trust.
The trustee can never recover any expenses from the trust in any circumstances.
The trustee may recover expenses only up to a fixed statutory cap per year.
The trustee may recover expenses only if the trust instrument expressly says so on these facts as a general rule.
The trustee may recover expenses only with the prior approval of the court.
Trusts Law.w: A trustee is entitled to be reimbursed from the trust fund, or to pay out of it, expenses properly incurred when acting on behalf of the trust (s.31 Trustee Act 2000). This right of indemnity for proper expenses is distinct from remuneration for the trustee's own time and services, which generally requires authority.

n.1: Trustees can recover properly incurred expenses; 'never' is wrong.
