n.2: There is no fixed annual statutory cap on recovering proper expenses.
n.3: The statutory right of indemnity applies without needing an express clause.
n.4: Court approval is not generally required to recover properly incurred expenses.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee (or other fiduciary) uses their position to obtain a benefit or profit for themselves, in circumstances where the opportunity came to them by reason of their fiduciary position. They act honestly and the trust suffers no loss, but they nonetheless retain a personal profit obtained through the position of trust. A beneficiary discovers this and complains. The trustee argues that, as they acted in good faith and the trust lost nothing, they should be allowed to keep the profit. The opportunity to make the profit had come to the trustee only because of information gained as trustee. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustee may keep the profit, provided the amount involved was relatively modest.
The trustee may keep the profit, because they acted honestly and the trust suffered no loss.
The trustee may keep the profit, because a fiduciary is entitled to be rewarded for their efforts.
The trustee may keep the profit, unless a beneficiary can prove the trustee acted dishonestly.
The trustee must account for the profit and may hold it on constructive trust, even if they acted honestly.
Trusts Law.w: A fiduciary must not profit from their position without authority. Any unauthorised profit obtained by reason of the fiduciary position must be accounted for and is held on constructive trust, regardless of good faith or the absence of loss to the trust (Keech v Sandford; Boardman v Phipps).

n.0: The size of the profit is irrelevant to the duty to account.
n.1: Honesty and absence of loss do not entitle the fiduciary to keep an unauthorised profit.
n.2: A fiduciary is not entitled to keep unauthorised profits as a reward.
n.3: Liability to account does not depend on proving dishonesty.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee of a trust is also a director of a company, and an opportunity arises in which the trustee's personal interests, or the interests of the company, come into conflict with the interests of the trust and its beneficiaries. The trustee proceeds to act in the matter without the authority of the trust instrument, the beneficiaries or the court. A beneficiary complains that the trustee has breached a fundamental fiduciary obligation. The opportunity was potentially very profitable, both for the company and for the trustee personally. Which of the following best describes the rule the trustee has broken?
o: A trustee may prefer their own interests provided the trust suffers no measurable loss.
A trustee owes no fiduciary duties at all where they are also a company director.
A trustee must not place themselves in a position where their duty and their interest conflict, without authority.
A trustee may act despite a conflict provided they act in what they think is good faith.
A trustee is free to act in any matter, even where their interest conflicts with the trust's on these facts.
Trusts Law.w: A core fiduciary duty of a trustee is the no-conflict rule: a trustee must not, without authority, place themselves in a position where their personal interest (or a duty to another) conflicts, or may conflict, with their duty to the trust and its beneficiaries.

n.0: The no-conflict rule applies regardless of whether loss results.
n.1: Being a company director does not remove the trustee's fiduciary duties.
n.3: Good faith does not authorise acting in a position of conflict.
n.4: A trustee is not free to act where their interest conflicts with the trust's.

Trusts Law.q: The beneficiaries of a trust would like to change the terms of the trust to make it work better for them, but some of the beneficiaries are minors or are unborn or unascertained, and so cannot give their own consent to the variation. The adult beneficiaries alone cannot bring about the change because not everyone with an interest can agree. They wish to know whether a variation can nonetheless be achieved. The proposed change would have improved the position of the whole family, including the youngest members. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust terms can never be varied once the trust has been created, in any circumstances.
Only the settlor may vary the trust, and only during the settlor's lifetime.
The trustees may vary the trust on their own initiative whenever they think it sensible.
The adult beneficiaries may simply vary the trust themselves, ignoring the minor and unborn interests.
The court may approve a variation on behalf of those who cannot consent under the Variation of Trusts Act 1958.
Trusts Law.w: Under the Variation of Trusts Act 1958, the court may approve an arrangement varying a trust on behalf of those who cannot consent for themselves — such as minors, unborn and unascertained beneficiaries — provided (for most categories) the variation is for their benefit.

n.0: Trusts can be varied, notably with the court's approval under the 1958 Act.
n.1: Variation is not confined to the settlor acting in their lifetime.
n.2: Trustees cannot unilaterally rewrite the beneficial terms of the trust.
n.3: The adult beneficiaries cannot simply override the interests of those who cannot consent.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee, faced with a difficult decision about how to exercise a discretionary power under the trust, is unsure whether the course they propose is proper and is worried about being personally liable if it later turns out to be wrong. Rather than simply going ahead and risking a breach, the trustee wants to protect their position by obtaining guidance before acting. The trustee seeks advice on what they can do to obtain protection when genuinely in doubt about the exercise of a power. The decision was finely balanced and the trustee did not want to expose themselves to a later claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustee has no option but to act on their own judgement and simply hope it is correct.
The trustee may act however they wish, because a trustee is never liable for an honest decision on these facts.
The trustee may resign, and doing so automatically discharges all past and future liability.
The trustee may apply to the court for directions and will be protected if they act in accordance with them.
The trustee must always obtain the consent of all the beneficiaries before exercising any power.
Trusts Law.w: A trustee who is genuinely in doubt about how to exercise a power or administer the trust may apply to the court for directions. If the trustee then acts in accordance with the court's directions, they are protected from a subsequent allegation of breach in respect of that action.

n.0: The trustee is not forced to act on their own judgement; they may seek court directions.
n.1: An honest decision does not automatically shield a trustee from liability.
n.2: Resignation does not discharge a trustee from liability for past breaches.
n.4: Unanimous beneficiary consent is not required to exercise a power, nor is it the protective route here.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor creates a discretionary trust under which trustees have discretion to distribute a fund among a wide class described as the settlor's 'relatives and dependants'. No beneficiary is entitled to any share unless and until the trustees exercise their discretion in their favour. A question arises as to the test for certainty of objects that applies to this discretionary trust, and whether the class is sufficiently certain for the trust to be valid. The class was potentially very large, and the trustees wanted to know whether they could validly administer it. Which of the following best describes the applicable test?
o: The trust is valid only if the trustees distribute equally among every member of the class.
The trust is valid only if the class contains no more than a fixed maximum number of people on these facts.
The trust is valid if it can be said with certainty whether any given person is or is not a member of the class.
The trust is valid only if a complete list of every possible beneficiary can be compiled.
The trust is valid only if all the beneficiaries can be personally identified in advance.
Trusts Law.w: For a discretionary trust, certainty of objects is governed by the 'is or is not' (given postulant) test: the trust is valid if it can be said with certainty whether any given individual is or is not a member of the class (McPhail v Doulton). A complete list is not required.

n.0: Equal distribution is not required; the trustees have a discretion.
n.1: There is no fixed numerical cap on the size of the class.
n.3: The complete-list test applies to fixed trusts, not discretionary trusts.
n.4: Advance identification of all beneficiaries is not required for a discretionary trust.

Trusts Law.q: In their will, a testator leaves all their property to their spouse absolutely, adding the words that they do so 'in the full confidence that she will do what is right' as regards the testator's children. After the testator's death, the children argue that these words created a binding trust in their favour over the property, so that the spouse holds it on trust for them rather than taking it outright. The spouse contends that the words were merely an expression of hope. The estate was large, and the spouse and children each held a very different understanding of what the words meant. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The words create a charitable trust for the benefit of the family.
The words create a trust because the testator expressed confidence in the spouse.
The words create a trust because they refer specifically to the testator's children on these facts.
The words are likely precatory only, so no trust arises and the spouse takes the property absolutely.
The words automatically create a binding trust in favour of the children.
Trusts Law.w: Certainty of intention requires an intention to impose a binding trust obligation. Precatory words expressing a hope, wish or 'confidence' generally do not create a trust (Lambe v Eames; Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry), so the spouse takes absolutely.

n.0: No charitable purpose is involved; this concerns a private gift.
n.1: Expressing confidence is a hope, not the imposition of a trust obligation.
n.2: Merely referring to the children does not turn precatory words into a trust.
n.4: Precatory words do not automatically create a binding trust.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee proposes to buy, from one of the beneficiaries, that beneficiary's equitable interest under the trust. The trustee approaches the beneficiary directly and offers to purchase the interest. A question arises as to whether such a purchase by a trustee of a beneficiary's interest is permissible, and on what conditions, given the trustee's fiduciary position and the information the trustee holds about the trust. The beneficiary was keen to realise their interest quickly and the trustee knew a great deal about its value. Which of the following best describes the position under the fair-dealing rule?
o: The purchase is always valid, because a beneficiary is free to sell their own interest to anyone on these facts as a general rule.
The purchase is valid only if approved by a majority of the other beneficiaries.
The purchase is permissible only if the trustee acts fairly, makes full disclosure and takes no advantage of their position.
The purchase is valid provided the trustee simply pays whatever the beneficiary first asks.
The purchase is automatically void, because a trustee can never deal with a beneficiary at all.
Trusts Law.w: Under the fair-dealing rule, a trustee may purchase a beneficiary's beneficial interest, but the transaction will be closely scrutinised and is liable to be set aside unless the trustee shows they acted honestly and fairly, made full disclosure, took no advantage of their position and gave a fair price.

n.0: The beneficiary's freedom to sell does not remove the scrutiny of dealings with their trustee.
n.1: Approval by other beneficiaries is not the governing condition of the fair-dealing rule.
n.3: Paying whatever is first asked does not satisfy the requirements of full disclosure and fairness.
n.4: The purchase is not automatically void; it is subject to the fair-dealing conditions.

Trusts Law.q: Trust money is misapplied and, after passing through various hands, ends up being received by a person who buys the relevant asset for full value, in good faith, and without any notice at all of the breach of trust or the beneficiaries' interest. The beneficiaries seek to trace the trust property into the hands of that person and to assert their equitable interest against them. The recipient relies on having bought in good faith for value without notice. The purchaser had paid the full market price and had no reason at all to suspect that anything was amiss. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiaries may always recover the property, whoever now holds it and however they acquired it.
Tracing is defeated only where the recipient paid more than the true value of the asset.
The recipient is liable in every case, because the property originally belonged to the trust.
The beneficiaries may recover unless the recipient can prove they were related to the trustee.
Tracing is defeated against a bona fide purchaser of the legal estate for value without notice.
Trusts Law.w: The equitable proprietary claim by tracing is defeated by the defence of the bona fide purchaser of a legal interest for value without notice ('equity's darling'). Such a purchaser takes free of the beneficiaries' equitable interest, so tracing against them fails.

n.0: Beneficiaries cannot recover against a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
n.1: The defence applies to a purchaser for value; it does not require overpayment.
n.2: Such a purchaser is not liable simply because the property came from the trust.
n.3: The defence turns on good faith, value and want of notice, not on any relationship to the trustee.

Trusts Law.q: A fiduciary, while acting for their principal in negotiating a contract, secretly accepts a bribe or secret commission from the other side in connection with that transaction. The principal discovers this and seeks to claim the bribe itself, not merely damages, arguing it is held on trust. The fiduciary received the bribe in breach of fiduciary duty. While handling a transaction for their principal, the fiduciary quietly took a payment from the counterparty as an inducement, the principal has since found out, and rather than settling for money damages the principal wants to lay claim to the very sum the fiduciary secretly pocketed. Which of the following best describes the principal's proprietary claim to the bribe?
o: The principal may claim the bribe only if it can be shown the principal suffered a loss.
The bribe belongs absolutely to the fiduciary as it came from a third party.
The bribe is forfeited to the state rather than held for the principal.
The principal has only a personal claim for an equivalent sum and no proprietary interest on these facts.
The fiduciary holds the bribe on constructive trust for the principal, who has a proprietary claim to it.
Trusts Law.w: A bribe or secret commission accepted by a fiduciary in breach of duty is held on constructive trust for the principal (FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital Partners). The principal therefore has a proprietary claim to the bribe and any traceable proceeds, in addition to any personal remedy, whether or not the principal suffered loss.

n.0: The proprietary claim does not depend on the principal proving a loss.
n.1: The bribe does not belong beneficially to the fiduciary despite coming from a third party.
n.2: The bribe is held for the principal, not forfeited to the state.
n.3: The principal has a proprietary claim, not merely a personal one.

Trusts Law.q: A settlor sets up a trust whose stated object is to promote and advance a particular political party's policies and to secure changes in the law that the party favours. The trust is said to be for the advancement of education and the public good. When registration as a charity is sought, a question arises as to whether a trust with an essentially political purpose of this kind can be charitable at all. The trustees seek advice on the position. The party's campaign literature would be funded from the trust, alongside efforts to lobby for the changes it wanted. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The trust is charitable, provided the political party it supports is lawfully registered.
The trust is charitable, because promoting political policies always advances public education.
The trust is charitable, because any trust that seeks to change the law benefits the public.
The trust is charitable, provided it also carries out some incidental educational activity.
A trust with a political purpose of promoting a party or changing the law is not charitable.
Trusts Law.w: A trust with a political purpose — promoting the interests of a political party, or procuring changes in the law or government policy — is not charitable, because the court cannot judge whether such changes are for the public benefit (McGovern v Attorney General; Bowman).

n.0: A party being lawfully registered does not make a trust to promote it charitable.
n.1: Promoting party politics is not treated as the charitable advancement of education.
n.2: Seeking to change the law is a political purpose, which is not charitable.
n.3: Incidental educational activity does not save a trust whose main purpose is political.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee wrongfully mixes trust money with the trustee's own money in a single bank account, and then makes various withdrawals and payments out of the mixed account, some for the trustee's own purposes. The beneficiaries wish to trace the trust money in the account and to do so on the basis most favourable to them, taking advantage of the equitable rules that apply where a wrongdoing trustee has mixed trust funds with their own. The account had seen many payments in and out, making it hard to say whose money funded which withdrawal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Equity applies rules favourable to the beneficiaries, generally treating the trustee as spending their own money first.
The mixed money is simply divided equally between the trustee and the beneficiaries in every case.
The beneficiaries may trace only if the trustee kept a precise record of every transaction.
The beneficiaries lose all rights to trace as soon as trust money is mixed with the trustee's own money on these facts.
The trustee is presumed to have spent the beneficiaries' money first, defeating the tracing claim.
Trusts Law.w: Where a trustee wrongfully mixes trust money with their own, equity resolves difficulties in the beneficiaries' favour: the trustee is generally presumed to spend their own money first (Re Hallett), but the beneficiaries may instead claim a purchased asset where that is more advantageous (Re Oatway).

n.1: The mixed fund is not simply split equally; the tracing rules favour the beneficiaries.
n.2: Tracing does not require the trustee to have kept precise records.
n.3: Mixing does not destroy the right to trace; equity assists the innocent beneficiaries.
n.4: The presumption operates against the wrongdoing trustee, not against the beneficiaries.

Trusts Law.q: A trust holds capital for a beneficiary who will become absolutely entitled to it in the future. Before that time arrives, the beneficiary has a pressing need for a capital sum, for example to help them buy a home or start a business. The trustees would like to advance part of the capital to the beneficiary now, ahead of the date of entitlement, but are unsure whether they have power to do so. The trustees seek advice on their statutory power to apply capital early for the beneficiary's benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may advance capital freely for any purpose, whether or not it benefits the beneficiary.
The trustees may never advance capital before the beneficiary becomes absolutely entitled to it.
The trustees have a statutory power of advancement to pay or apply capital early for the beneficiary's benefit.
The trustees may advance capital only with the consent of every other beneficiary of the trust.
The trustees may advance capital only if a court authorises the payment in advance.
Trusts Law.w: Under s.32 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees have a statutory power of advancement to pay or apply capital for the advancement or benefit of a beneficiary before they become absolutely entitled, subject to conditions and to any modification in the trust instrument.

n.0: Advancement must be for the beneficiary's benefit, not for any purpose at all.
n.1: Early advancement of capital is possible under the statutory power.
n.3: The consent of every other beneficiary is not the general statutory precondition.
n.4: Court authorisation is not generally required to exercise s.32.

Trusts Law.q: A person who is not a trustee dishonestly helps a trustee to commit a breach of trust, for example by knowingly assisting in the improper transfer or laundering of misapplied trust funds, although that person never receives any of the trust property for their own benefit. A beneficiary wishes to hold the assistant personally liable for the loss caused by the breach. The assistant argues that, since they never received any trust property, they cannot be liable. The assistant had helped route the misapplied funds through several accounts to disguise their origin. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assistant is liable only where the trustee who committed the breach cannot be found on these facts as a general rule.
The assistant can never be liable, because they did not receive any trust property.
The assistant is liable only if they acted carelessly rather than dishonestly.
The assistant may be personally liable for dishonest assistance in a breach of trust, though they received no property.
The assistant is liable only if they were themselves appointed as a trustee.
Trusts Law.w: A person who dishonestly assists in a breach of trust is personally liable to account for the resulting loss as an accessory, even though they never received any trust property. The touchstone is dishonesty judged by the objective standard (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan; Ivey v Genting).

n.0: Liability does not depend on the primary trustee being untraceable.
n.1: Receipt of property is not required for accessory (dishonest assistance) liability.
n.2: The basis of liability is dishonesty, not mere carelessness.
n.4: The assistant need not be a trustee to be liable.

Trusts Law.q: A donor executes a share transfer form and hands it, together with the share certificate, to the intended donee, having done everything within the donor's own power to transfer the shares. The only outstanding step is registration of the transfer by the company, which is a matter for the company and outside the donor's control. The donor dies before registration is completed. The intended donee argues the transfer should be treated as effective in equity despite the missing registration. The shares were valuable, and the donee had already lodged the transfer with the company before the donor died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer is effective at law, because handing over the certificate transfers legal title.
The transfer is wholly ineffective, because legal title had not been registered before death.
The transfer is effective only if the donee provided consideration for the shares.
The transfer may be effective in equity, because the donor did everything necessary for them to do.
The transfer is ineffective, because equity never perfects an imperfect gift in any circumstances.
Trusts Law.w: Where the donor has done everything within their own power to effect the transfer, leaving only steps for a third party (such as company registration), equity may treat the transfer as effective and the donor as holding on trust pending registration (Re Rose), even though legal title has not yet passed.

n.0: Handing over the certificate does not itself transfer legal title to shares.
n.1: The gift is not necessarily defeated by the absence of registration where the donor did all they could.
n.2: The Re Rose principle does not depend on the donee providing consideration.
n.4: The Re Rose principle is a recognised qualification to 'equity will not perfect an imperfect gift'.

Trusts Law.q: A trustee commits a breach of trust which, rather than causing a loss, actually results in a gain to the trust fund in one respect, while a separate, unrelated breach causes a loss in another respect. The trustee argues that the gain made on the first breach should be set off against, and so cancel out, the loss caused by the second, so as to reduce what the trustee must pay. The beneficiaries dispute that the two can be netted off against each other. The two breaches were quite separate events, arising from different decisions taken at different times. Which of the following best describes the general position?
o: Gains from one breach generally cannot be set off against losses from a separate, distinct breach.
The trustee may always keep any gain and pay only the balance after deducting it from the loss.
The beneficiaries must give the trustee credit for every gain the trustee ever makes.
The trustee is never liable at all where any of their breaches produced a gain.
Gains and losses from all the trustee's breaches are always netted off against one another.
Trusts Law.w: As a general rule, a trustee cannot set off a gain made in one breach of trust against a loss caused by a separate and distinct breach; each is treated separately. Set-off may exceptionally be allowed where the gain and loss arise from the same transaction or course of dealing (Bartlett v Barclays Bank).

n.1: The trustee cannot generally deduct an unrelated gain from the loss.
n.2: The beneficiaries need not credit gains from separate, distinct breaches.
n.3: A gain on one breach does not exonerate the trustee for a loss on another.
n.4: Gains and losses from distinct breaches are not automatically netted off.

Criminal Liability.q: During a fight, the defendant strikes the victim with a bottle, breaking the skin so that the victim bleeds, cutting through the whole skin (both the outer and inner layers). The prosecution considers a charge of unlawful wounding. The defendant intended or foresaw some harm. The injury broke the continuity of the whole skin. In the course of a brawl the defendant swung a bottle at the victim with enough force to split the skin so that blood flowed from the cut, the injury going right through both layers of skin rather than leaving a mere graze or a bruise beneath an intact surface. Which of the following best describes what amounts to a 'wound' for these offences?
o: A wound means only an injury caused by a bladed weapon.
A wound requires the victim to have been rendered unconscious.
A wound means any injury to the body, including internal bruising alone.
A wound requires the victim to suffer permanent disfigurement.
A wound requires a break in the continuity of the whole skin (both layers).
Criminal Liability.w: For the offences of wounding (under ss.20 and 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861), a 'wound' requires a break in the continuity of the whole skin, that is, both the outer layer (epidermis) and the inner layer (dermis). A mere graze or internal rupturing of blood vessels (bruising) is not a wound.

n.0: A wound is not confined to injuries from a bladed weapon.
n.1: Unconsciousness is not required for a wound.
n.2: Internal bruising alone, without breaking the whole skin, is not a wound.
n.3: Permanent disfigurement is not required; a break in the whole skin suffices.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant deliberately sets fire to a building, and does so either intending to endanger the life of another or being reckless as to whether the lives of others would be endangered by the fire. Damage by fire results. The defendant is charged with the aggravated form of criminal damage. The court considers arson being aggravated criminal damage endangering life under the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The fire spread quickly through the occupied building while several people were still inside at the time. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The offence is the same as basic criminal damage, with no additional element required.
The aggravated offence is committed where the damage is by fire and life is intended or recklessly endangered.
The offence requires the defendant to have intended to destroy the whole building completely on these facts.
The offence is committed only where the property destroyed belonged to another person.
The offence is committed only where a person was actually killed by the fire.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1(2) and s.1(3) Criminal Damage Act 1971, where criminal damage is caused by fire it is charged as arson, and it is aggravated where the defendant intends by the destruction/damage to endanger life, or is reckless as to whether life would be endangered. The aggravated offence can be committed even in respect of the defendant's own property.

n.0: The aggravated offence has the additional life-endangerment element.
n.2: Total destruction of the building is not required.
n.3: The aggravated offence can apply even to the defendant's own property, so ownership by another is not essential.
n.4: Actual death is not required; endangerment (intended or reckless) suffices.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant deliberately attacks the victim, intending to cause them really serious harm, and inflicts a grievous injury. The prosecution considers the most serious non-fatal offence against the person. The defendant acted with intent to cause really serious harm and caused grievous bodily harm. The issue is the required mental element for the gravest offence. The attack was deliberate and targeted, the defendant meaning to inflict really serious injury on the victim rather than merely to frighten or to cause a minor hurt, and a grievous injury duly resulted, so the prosecution is aiming at the most serious of the non-fatal offences against the person. Which of the following best describes the mens rea for the offence under section 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
o: The defendant must intend to kill the victim.
It suffices that the defendant was negligent as to causing harm.
It suffices that the defendant foresaw some harm might result.
The defendant must intend to cause grievous bodily harm (or intend to resist or prevent lawful apprehension).
The defendant need have no particular state of mind, as the offence is one of strict liability on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Section 18 (wounding or causing grievous bodily harm with intent) is a specific intent offence: the prosecution must prove the defendant intended to cause grievous bodily harm (or intended to resist or prevent lawful apprehension). Mere foresight of some harm suffices only for the lesser s.20 offence, not for s.18.

n.0: An intention to kill is the mens rea for murder/attempted murder, not what s.18 requires.
n.1: Negligence is insufficient for s.18.
n.2: Foreseeing some harm is the mens rea for s.20, not the intent required for s.18.
n.4: Section 18 requires a specific intent; it is not a strict liability offence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is alleged to have assisted a principal offender in committing a crime. However, the principal has been acquitted, or cannot be identified or convicted, at the time the alleged accessory is tried. It is nonetheless established that the offence was in fact committed by someone and that the defendant assisted or encouraged it. The principal has not been convicted, but the offence was committed and the defendant assisted it. By the time the alleged helper comes to trial the person who actually carried out the offence has walked free, or cannot be identified or convicted at all, yet the evidence still shows that the offence was committed by someone and that the defendant lent assistance or encouragement to its commission. Which of the following best describes the accessory's potential liability?
o: The accessory is liable only for a lesser offence than the principal in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The accessory can never be convicted unless the principal is first convicted.
The accessory's liability depends solely on whether the principal pleaded guilty.
The accessory may still be convicted if it is proved the offence was committed and they assisted or encouraged it with the required intent.
The accessory automatically takes the principal's place as the principal offender.
Criminal Liability.w: A secondary party's liability is derivative but does not depend on the principal actually being convicted. Provided it is proved that the offence was committed (by someone) and that the defendant aided, abetted, counselled or procured it with the required mental element, the accessory may be convicted even if the principal is acquitted, unidentified or not prosecuted.

n.0: The accessory can be convicted of the same offence, not necessarily a lesser one.
n.1: The principal need not first be convicted for the accessory to be liable.
n.2: Liability does not turn solely on the principal's plea.
n.4: The accessory is convicted as an accessory, not automatically recharacterised as the principal.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant receives goods from a friend, knowing or believing them to have been stolen, and dishonestly assists in disposing of them for the thief's benefit. The defendant was not the original thief. The goods were stolen and the defendant knew or believed this. The defendant dishonestly received or dealt with them. The defendant took no part in the original theft but later took delivery of the goods from the thief well aware that they were stolen, and then dishonestly lent a hand in getting rid of them so that the thief could turn them into cash. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Theft Act 1968?
o: Burglary under section 9.
Handling stolen goods under section 22.
No offence, because the defendant did not steal the goods.
Robbery under section 8.
Theft of the goods under section 1.
Criminal Liability.w: Handling stolen goods (s.22 Theft Act 1968) is committed where a person, otherwise than in the course of stealing, dishonestly receives stolen goods, or dishonestly undertakes or assists in their retention, removal, disposal or realisation by or for another, knowing or believing them to be stolen. The defendant's dishonest dealing with goods known to be stolen fits this offence.

n.0: There is no entry as a trespasser to a building, so it is not burglary.
n.2: Not being the original thief does not exonerate the defendant; handling is a distinct offence.
n.3: There is no use of force, so it is not robbery.
n.4: Theft is committed by the original appropriation; this defendant handled goods already stolen.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant becomes voluntarily intoxicated by alcohol and, while intoxicated, commits an offence of basic intent (one that can be committed recklessly), such as a basic assault. The defendant says they were too drunk to form any mens rea. The offence charged is a basic intent offence. The intoxication was voluntary. Having chosen to drink heavily, the defendant went on while intoxicated to commit an everyday offence of the kind that can be committed recklessly, and now protests that the drink had left them incapable of forming any guilty state of mind at the moment they acted. Which of the following best describes the effect of the voluntary intoxication?
o: Voluntary intoxication negates the mens rea of a basic intent offence and excuses the defendant.
Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence to any offence committed while drunk.
Voluntary intoxication is relevant only to offences of specific intent, never affecting the analysis of basic intent offences at all.
Voluntary intoxication reduces every offence to a lesser one automatically.
Voluntary intoxication is not a defence to a basic intent offence, as becoming intoxicated is itself reckless.
Criminal Liability.w: Under the rule in Majewski, voluntary intoxication is not a defence to a crime of basic intent: getting voluntarily intoxicated is itself regarded as a reckless course of conduct, supplying the recklessness needed. It may, however, negate the specific intent required for a specific intent offence (often leaving a basic intent fallback offence).

n.0: It does not excuse a basic intent offence; the recklessness in getting drunk suffices.
n.1: Voluntary intoxication is not a complete defence to any offence.
n.2: It is precisely for basic intent offences that voluntary intoxication provides no defence, so it is not irrelevant to their analysis.
n.3: It does not automatically reduce every offence to a lesser one.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, without any lawful justification or the victim's consent, deliberately pushes the victim, applying unlawful physical force to them, although the push causes no injury or lasting harm. The defendant is charged with a non-fatal offence based on the unlawful physical contact. The defendant argues that, because the victim was not hurt, no criminal offence can have been committed by a mere push. The court considers the offence of battery. The push was hard and entirely unwanted, though the victim was left without any lasting mark. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This can only be an assault, because assault covers all physical contact between people on these facts.
No offence is committed unless the victim apprehended the contact before it happened.
No offence is committed, because the push did not cause the victim any injury.
This is an offence only if the defendant used a weapon to push the victim.
This may amount to a battery, which requires the application of unlawful force, whether or not harm results.
Criminal Liability.w: The actus reus of battery is the application of unlawful force to another, however slight; injury is not required. The mens rea is intention or recklessness as to the application of unlawful force. A deliberate unlawful push is therefore capable of being a battery.

n.0: Assault is apprehension of force; the actual contact here is a battery.
n.1: Battery does not require the victim to have apprehended the contact in advance.
n.2: Battery does not require injury; any unlawful force suffices.
n.3: Battery does not require the use of a weapon.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant approaches the victim in the street and, in order to steal the victim's bag, threatens the victim with immediate force unless they hand it over, and then takes the bag. The force or threat is used at the time of, and in order to carry out, the stealing. The defendant is charged with an offence more serious than simple theft. The court considers the offence of robbery under the Theft Act 1968. The victim, badly frightened, let go of the bag rather than risk being attacked in the street. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Robbery is committed whenever force is used, even if no theft is involved at all.
Robbery requires the force to be used only after the property has already been taken away on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Robbery is theft where the defendant uses force, or threatens force, immediately before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal.
Robbery requires the victim to have suffered actual physical injury during the incident.
Robbery is simply any theft committed in a public place such as the street.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.8 Theft Act 1968, robbery is committed where a person steals and, immediately before or at the time of doing so and in order to do so, uses force on any person or puts or seeks to put any person in fear of being then and there subjected to force.

n.0: There must be a theft; force alone without stealing is not robbery.
n.1: The force must be immediately before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal.
n.3: Actual injury is not required; a threat of force suffices.
n.4: Robbery is not simply theft in a public place; force or threat of force is essential.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant receives money from another person on the express understanding that the defendant will use it only for a particular, specified purpose, and is obliged to deal with that money in that particular way. Instead, the defendant dishonestly spends the money on themselves. A question arises whether the money can be regarded as 'property belonging to another' for the purposes of theft, given that the defendant had physical possession of it. The court considers s.5 of the Theft Act 1968. The money had been handed over for one specific project and nothing else, but was spent elsewhere. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The money may be treated as belonging to another under s.5(3), as the defendant was obliged to deal with it in a particular way.
The money cannot belong to another unless it was physically kept separate from the defendant's own funds on these facts.
The money cannot be stolen, because a person cannot steal property that is already in their possession.
The money belonged solely to the defendant once received, so it cannot be stolen by them.
The money belongs to another only where the defendant received it by deception in the first place.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.5(3) Theft Act 1968, where a person receives property from another and is under an obligation to retain and deal with that property (or its proceeds) in a particular way, the property is regarded as belonging to the other. The defendant can therefore steal money they physically hold.

n.1: The property need not be physically segregated for s.5(3) to apply.
n.2: Property in the defendant's possession can still 'belong to another' for theft.
n.3: Receiving the money does not make it the defendant's own where s.5(3) applies.
n.4: Section 5(3) does not require the property to have been obtained by deception.

Criminal Liability.q: A person applying for a financial product is under a legal duty to disclose certain information to the other party, but dishonestly says nothing about a material matter they are obliged to reveal, intending to make a gain. No positive false statement is made; the wrong lies in the silence. There was a legal duty to disclose the information. The defendant dishonestly failed to disclose it, intending a gain. In completing the application the defendant was legally obliged to reveal a material fact but chose to stay silent about it, making no untrue statement of any kind, and did so dishonestly in the hope of securing a financial advantage that full disclosure would have denied them. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Fraud Act 2006?
o: No offence, because a mere failure to speak can never be fraud.
Theft, because information was withheld.
Fraud by failing to disclose information under section 3.
Fraud by abuse of position under section 4.
Fraud by false representation under section 2.
Criminal Liability.w: Fraud by failing to disclose information (s.3 Fraud Act 2006) is committed where the defendant dishonestly fails to disclose information which they are under a legal duty to disclose, intending to make a gain or cause a loss. It does not require a positive misstatement, which would instead be fraud by false representation.

n.0: A dishonest failure to disclose in breach of a legal duty can be fraud under s.3.
n.1: Withholding information is not theft; the Fraud Act governs this conduct.
n.3: Section 4 concerns abuse of a position of trust, not breach of a duty to disclose.
n.4: Section 2 requires a positive false representation, not merely a failure to disclose.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with unlawful act manslaughter. The 'unlawful act' relied on by the prosecution is said to be an act which, although perhaps careless or a breach of a civil obligation, does not in itself amount to any criminal offence. The defence argues that this cannot support a conviction for unlawful act manslaughter. The court considers whether the base act relied on is capable of founding the offence. The prosecution could point only to a careless breach of a civil obligation owed by the defendant. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A mere omission always suffices as the base act for unlawful act manslaughter.
The base act need not be unlawful at all, provided it caused the victim's death.
Unlawful act manslaughter requires the base act to be a criminal offence, not merely a civil wrong.
The base act must be an offence carrying a maximum of life imprisonment to qualify.
Any wrongful act at all, including a purely civil wrong, can found unlawful act manslaughter.
Criminal Liability.w: For unlawful act manslaughter the base 'unlawful act' must itself be a criminal offence; a mere civil wrong (such as a tort) or negligence is not sufficient (R v Franklin; R v Lamb). The criminal act must also be dangerous and cause death.

n.0: Unlawful act manslaughter is generally founded on an act, not a mere omission.
n.1: The base act must be unlawful in the criminal sense.
n.3: There is no requirement that the base offence carry a life maximum.
n.4: A purely civil wrong will not do; the base act must be a crime.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant attacks the victim intending to kill them, and carries out an act that would have killed the victim, but by chance the victim survives. The defendant is charged with attempted murder rather than murder, because death did not result. A question arises about the mental element required for attempted murder, which differs from that required for the full offence of murder. The court considers the mens rea for attempted murder. The victim survived only because of prompt emergency surgery, though the defendant had meant to kill. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Attempted murder requires only an intention to cause grievous bodily harm to the victim on these facts.
Attempted murder requires no mens rea because the victim did not in fact die.
Attempted murder requires an intention to kill; an intention to cause grievous bodily harm is not enough.
Attempted murder requires only recklessness as to whether the victim might die.
Attempted murder requires the same mens rea as the full offence of murder.
Criminal Liability.w: Although murder can be committed with intent to kill or to cause GBH, attempted murder requires a specific intention to kill; an intention merely to cause grievous bodily harm is insufficient for the attempt (R v Whybrow).

n.0: Intent to cause GBH suffices for murder but not for attempted murder.
n.1: A mens rea (indeed a heightened one) is required for the attempt.
n.3: Recklessness is insufficient for attempted murder.
n.4: The mens rea for the attempt is narrower than for the full offence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, at the time of the alleged offence, was suffering from a disease of the mind which gave rise to a defect of reason, such that they either did not know the nature and quality of their act, or did not know that what they were doing was wrong. The defendant raises a defence based on their mental state at the time. The court considers the defence of insanity. At the time the defendant was in the grip of a serious mental disorder affecting their reasoning. Which of the following best describes the applicable test?
o: Insanity applies only where the defendant was completely unconscious at the time of the act.
Insanity is established whenever the defendant acted irrationally or out of character.
Insanity requires a defect of reason, from a disease of the mind, so that the defendant did not know the nature and quality of the act, or that it was wrong.
Insanity requires the defendant to prove that they are still mentally ill at the date of trial.
Insanity requires only that the defendant was suffering from any diagnosed mental illness at the time on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Criminal Liability.w: Under the M'Naghten Rules, insanity requires that, at the time of the act, the defendant was labouring under a defect of reason, from a disease of the mind, such that they did not know the nature and quality of their act, or did not know that what they were doing was wrong. The defence bears the burden on the balance of probabilities.

n.0: The test does not require complete unconsciousness (that is closer to automatism).
n.1: Acting irrationally or out of character is not the legal test for insanity.
n.3: The test concerns the defendant's state at the time of the act, not at trial.
n.4: A diagnosed illness alone does not satisfy the specific M'Naghten test.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant performed the act constituting the offence while suffering a total loss of voluntary control caused by an external factor — for example a blow to the head, or a reaction to an anaesthetic — rather than by any internal disease of the mind. The defendant argues they were not acting voluntarily at all. The court considers the defence of (non-insane) automatism. The defendant had been knocked unconscious moments earlier and had no control over their movements. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Automatism requires a total loss of voluntary control caused by an external factor, negating the actus reus.
Automatism requires an internal disease of the mind and is treated as a form of insanity.
Automatism is a partial defence that merely reduces the offence to a lesser one.
Automatism applies whenever the defendant simply cannot remember committing the offence.
Automatism is available even where the defendant retained partial control over their actions on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Non-insane automatism arises where the defendant suffers a total loss of voluntary control due to an external cause (such as a blow, or an unexpected reaction to medication). It negates the voluntary act element of the actus reus and, if not self-induced, is a complete defence leading to acquittal.

n.1: An internal cause points to insane automatism (insanity), not non-insane automatism.
n.2: It is a complete defence (acquittal), not merely a partial one.
n.3: Mere loss of memory is not the same as a loss of voluntary control at the time.
n.4: Automatism requires a total, not partial, loss of voluntary control.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant damages another person's fence, honestly believing that the owner had consented, or would have consented, to the damage had they known of the circumstances. The defendant is charged with criminal damage and relies on a statutory lawful excuse. The defendant honestly believed in the owner's consent. The belief need not be reasonable, only honestly held. The defendant pulled down a neighbour's fence in the genuine belief that the owner had agreed, or at least would readily have agreed had they been asked in the circumstances, and now, charged with criminal damage, relies on that state of mind, the law being concerned with whether the belief was honestly held rather than whether it was reasonable. Which of the following best describes the lawful excuse under the Criminal Damage Act 1971?
o: A lawful excuse requires the belief in consent to be objectively reasonable in every case on these facts.
A defendant has a lawful excuse if they honestly believed the owner consented or would have consented to the damage.
A lawful excuse applies only to damage caused to the defendant's own property.
A lawful excuse arises only where the owner in fact expressly consented.
There is no lawful excuse based on belief in consent under the Act.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.5 of the Criminal Damage Act 1971, a person has a lawful excuse if at the time they believed the person entitled to consent to the damage had consented or would have consented had they known of the circumstances. The belief need only be honestly held; it need not be reasonable, and a further lawful excuse exists for acts done to protect property.

n.0: The belief need only be honest, not objectively reasonable.
n.2: The consent excuse concerns another's property (which the defendant believed the owner consented to damaging), not only the defendant's own.
n.3: Actual express consent is not required; an honest belief in consent suffices.
n.4: The Act does provide a lawful excuse based on belief in consent.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant claims they committed an offence only because a third party threatened to kill them or a family member unless they did so. The offence charged, however, is murder. The defendant seeks to rely on the defence of duress by threats. The threat was of death or serious injury. The offence charged is murder. The defendant says they took part only because a third party had threatened to kill them and their family unless they did as they were told, but the charge the defendant faces is the gravest of all, murder, which shapes whether a defence built on such threats is even open to them. Which of the following best describes the availability of duress by threats here?
o: Duress by threats is available to murder only if the threat was to the defendant personally.
Duress by threats reduces murder to manslaughter as a partial defence.
Duress by threats is available to murder provided the defendant was the secondary party.
Duress by threats is a complete defence to any offence, including murder.
Duress by threats is not available as a defence to murder (or attempted murder).
Criminal Liability.w: Duress by threats can be a defence to many offences where the defendant was compelled by a threat of death or serious injury and a sober person of reasonable firmness would have acted likewise. However, it is not available as a defence to murder or attempted murder (nor, generally, to a secondary party to murder), so it cannot assist this defendant.

n.0: Duress is unavailable to murder regardless of whom the threat targeted.
n.1: Duress does not operate as a partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter.
n.2: Duress is not available even to a secondary party to murder.
n.3: Duress is not a complete defence to murder.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits an offence not because a person expressly ordered them to, but because the objective circumstances they faced threatened death or serious injury, leaving them no reasonable alternative but to break the law — for example driving dangerously to escape an imminent threat. The defendant relies on a defence closely related to duress by threats. The court considers the defence of duress of circumstances. The defendant drove dangerously only to escape a group who were chasing them and threatening violence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Duress of circumstances applies only where the defendant sought and obtained police assistance first on these facts.
Duress of circumstances applies only where the danger was to the defendant's property.
Duress of circumstances may excuse an offence where objective circumstances of danger left no reasonable alternative.
There is no such defence; only an express threat from another person can ever excuse an offence.
Duress of circumstances is a complete defence to every offence, including murder.
Criminal Liability.w: Duress of circumstances operates on similar principles to duress by threats, but the compulsion arises from the objective circumstances of danger (threatening death or serious injury) rather than an express threat to commit a particular offence. Like duress by threats, it is not available to murder or attempted murder.

n.0: There is no requirement to have obtained police assistance first.
n.1: The danger must be to the person (death or serious injury), not merely property.
n.3: The defence exists and is not confined to express threats from a person.
n.4: It is not available to murder or attempted murder.

Criminal Liability.q: A statute makes it an offence to sell a particular regulated product to an underage buyer. A trader is charged after a sale to an underage buyer, even though the trader honestly and reasonably believed the buyer was of age. The offence is one that, on its proper construction, imposes liability without proof of mens rea as to the age element. The defendant was not at fault as to age. The trader made the sale in good faith, having checked as best they could and honestly and reasonably concluding the customer was old enough, yet the customer was in fact underage, and the offence as drafted says nothing about the seller needing to know or suspect the buyer's true age. Which of the following best describes the trader's liability?
o: The trader is liable only if the prosecution proves dishonesty.
The trader cannot be liable without proof of intention or recklessness as to the buyer's age on these facts.
The trader is liable only if they intended to break the law.
The trader may be liable because the offence is one of strict liability as to that element, requiring no mens rea.
The trader can never be convicted of an offence without full mens rea for every element.
Criminal Liability.w: Some statutory offences are offences of strict liability, requiring no mens rea as to one or more elements of the actus reus. Where, on its proper construction, an offence imposes strict liability (often regulatory offences protecting the public), the defendant may be convicted despite an honest and reasonable mistake, so the trader can be liable notwithstanding the belief as to age.

n.0: Dishonesty is not an element of such regulatory strict liability offences.
n.1: Strict liability offences do not require intention or recklessness as to the relevant element.
n.2: Liability does not depend on an intention to break the law.
n.4: Not every offence requires full mens rea; strict liability offences exist.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant unlawfully wounds the victim, who is taken to hospital and given ordinary, competent medical treatment. Despite that treatment the victim dies from the original wound, which was still an operating and substantial cause of death at the time. The defendant argues that it was the medical treatment, not the wound, that caused the death. The court considers whether ordinary medical treatment breaks the chain of causation in a homicide case. The wound was deep and, though treated, continued to threaten the victim's life until they died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The chain is broken because the victim died in hospital rather than at the scene.
The defendant is not liable, because the victim would have lived without any hospital treatment on these facts.
Ordinary competent medical treatment does not break the chain where the original wound remains an operating cause.
The chain is broken unless the defendant personally administered the treatment.
Any medical treatment given after the wound automatically breaks the chain of causation.
Criminal Liability.w: Medical treatment will only break the chain of causation in the most extraordinary cases (for example palpably wrong treatment that becomes the sole cause of death). Where the original wound is still an operating and substantial cause, ordinary treatment does not break the chain (R v Smith; R v Cheshire).

n.0: Dying in hospital does not break the chain of causation.
n.1: The wound remaining an operating cause means the defendant remains liable.
n.3: The chain is not broken merely because someone other than the defendant treated the victim.
n.4: Medical treatment does not automatically break the chain.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with theft and the only issue is dishonesty. The defendant claims they believed that what they did was in accordance with ordinary standards, and that they should be judged by their own view of honesty. The prosecution says a different, largely objective, test applies. The court must direct itself on the correct approach to dishonesty in the criminal law following recent authority. The defendant insisted their conduct was normal in their line of work and so could not be dishonest. Which of the following best describes the test for dishonesty?
o: The court decides what the defendant actually believed as to the facts, then applies the objective standard of ordinary decent people.
The defendant is dishonest whenever they took property belonging to someone else.
Dishonesty is judged purely by the defendant's own personal standards of honesty.
The defendant is dishonest only if they personally realised that ordinary people would regard their conduct as dishonest on these facts.
Dishonesty requires proof that the defendant intended to make a permanent gain for themselves.
Criminal Liability.w: Following Ivey v Genting Casinos (applied in criminal law in R v Barton and Booth), the court first ascertains the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decides whether their conduct was dishonest by the objective standards of ordinary decent people. There is no separate requirement that the defendant appreciated others would regard it as dishonest.

n.1: Taking another's property is not automatically dishonest.
n.2: Dishonesty is not judged purely by the defendant's own standards.
n.3: The old second (subjective) limb of Ghosh no longer applies.
n.4: Dishonesty does not require an intention to make a permanent gain.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant uses force against another person, claiming they did so to defend themselves from an attack. They honestly believed that force was necessary, and the degree of force they used was reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances as they believed them to be. The defendant relies on self-defence to a charge of assault. The court considers the elements of the defence of self-defence. The attacker had lunged first, and the defendant struck back only as hard as seemed necessary to fend them off. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Self-defence is available only where the defendant retreated as far as possible before using any force.
Self-defence requires that the defendant honestly believed force was necessary and used force that was reasonable in the circumstances as they believed them.
Self-defence is a partial defence that merely reduces the seriousness of the offence charged.
Self-defence requires only that the defendant honestly believed force was necessary, whatever force was used on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Self-defence requires the force used to be judged purely objectively, ignoring what the defendant believed.
Criminal Liability.w: Self-defence requires that the defendant honestly believed the use of force was necessary (judged on the facts as they believed them to be, even if mistaken) and that the degree of force used was reasonable in those circumstances. If made out, it is a complete defence.

n.0: There is no strict duty to retreat, though the possibility of retreat is a factor.
n.2: Self-defence is a complete defence, not merely a partial one.
n.3: The force used must also be reasonable; belief in necessity alone is not enough.
n.4: Necessity is judged on the facts as the defendant believed them, not purely objectively.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, during a heated argument, raises a fist and moves towards the victim in a threatening way, shouting that they are about to hit them, so that the victim genuinely and reasonably apprehends that unlawful force is about to be applied to them immediately. No blow is actually struck and no physical contact occurs. The defendant is charged with a non-fatal offence. The defendant argues that, as they never touched the victim, no offence was committed. The victim backed away in real fear, convinced that the blow was about to land at any moment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This can only be a battery, which requires the actual application of unlawful force.
This may amount to an assault, which requires the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful force.
No offence is committed unless the victim actually suffered some bodily harm.
This is an offence only if the defendant actually intended to kill the victim.
No offence is committed, because there was no physical contact between the parties.
Criminal Liability.w: The actus reus of assault (technical assault) is causing the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force. Physical contact is not required; the threatening conduct causing reasonable apprehension of immediate unlawful force is enough, coupled with intention or recklessness as to that apprehension.

n.0: Battery requires contact, but the threatening conduct here is an assault, which does not.
n.2: Assault does not require actual bodily harm.
n.3: Assault does not require an intention to kill.
n.4: Assault does not require physical contact.

Criminal Liability.q: A driver suffers a sudden and wholly unforeseeable event while driving — for example being attacked by a swarm of bees, or suffering an unexpected blackout — which causes them to lose all control of the vehicle, and the car strikes and injures a pedestrian. The driver did nothing voluntary that caused the loss of control. The prosecution nonetheless seeks to hold the driver criminally liable for the injury caused. The driver's adviser considers the requirement of voluntary conduct in the actus reus. The event was sudden and could not have been anticipated, and the driver had been driving normally until it struck. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The driver is liable, because the pedestrian was in fact injured by the driver's car.
The driver is liable, because a driver is always responsible for anything their vehicle does.
There is no liability, because the actus reus requires voluntary conduct, which was absent here.
The driver is liable, unless they can prove they had taken out motor insurance.
The driver is liable, because they were the person physically in control of the vehicle at the time.
Criminal Liability.w: The actus reus of an offence must generally be a voluntary act. Where the defendant's bodily movement is involuntary (automatism arising from an external cause, such as a swarm of bees or a blackout), the conduct element is not satisfied and there is no liability.

n.0: Mere causation of injury is not enough without a voluntary act.
n.1: A driver is not automatically liable for everything the vehicle does, absent voluntary conduct.
n.3: Insurance is irrelevant to criminal liability for the actus reus.
n.4: Being physically in the car does not supply a voluntary act where control was involuntarily lost.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant inflicts an injury on the victim, and the prosecution must decide whether it amounts to grievous bodily harm for the purposes of the serious non-fatal offences. The victim suffered very serious harm, and there is also evidence of a serious, medically recognised psychiatric condition caused by the incident. The harm was really serious in nature. The issue is the meaning of grievous bodily harm. The blow left the victim with very grave injuries, and in addition the incident brought on a serious, medically diagnosed psychiatric illness, so the court must be clear about what the law means by grievous bodily harm and whether harm of these kinds falls within it. Which of the following best describes 'grievous bodily harm'?
o: Any harm at all, however minor, provided some injury is caused.
Really serious harm, which can include serious psychiatric injury as well as serious physical injury.
Only harm that is permanent and irreversible.
Only physical injury, never psychiatric injury in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
Only a break in the continuity of the skin, and nothing else.
Criminal Liability.w: Grievous bodily harm means 'really serious harm'. It is not limited to physical injury: a serious, medically recognised psychiatric condition can amount to grievous bodily harm (and lesser psychiatric harm to actual bodily harm). It need not be permanent, and, unlike a 'wound', does not require a break in the skin.

n.0: Grievous bodily harm is really serious harm, not any minor injury.
n.2: The harm need not be permanent to be grievous bodily harm.
n.3: Serious psychiatric injury can amount to grievous bodily harm; it is not confined to physical injury.
n.4: A break in the skin is a 'wound'; grievous bodily harm is about the seriousness of harm.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits an offence after their drink was secretly spiked by someone else, so that they became intoxicated without knowing it and against their will. As a result of this involuntary intoxication they did not form the mens rea for the offence. The defendant relies on the involuntary nature of the intoxication. The court considers the effect of involuntary intoxication on criminal liability. Someone had secretly added a strong drug to the defendant's soft drink earlier that evening. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Involuntary intoxication may be a defence if, because of it, the defendant did not form the required mens rea.
Involuntary intoxication is treated in exactly the same way as voluntary intoxication.
Involuntary intoxication is never a defence, because the defendant still committed the act.
Involuntary intoxication is a defence only to offences of basic intent, and never specific intent on these facts.
Involuntary intoxication is a complete defence even where the defendant did form the mens rea.
Criminal Liability.w: Involuntary intoxication (for example a spiked drink) may be a defence where, because of it, the defendant did not form the mens rea of the offence. However, if the defendant did form the necessary mens rea despite the intoxication, the involuntary intoxication provides no defence (R v Kingston).

n.1: Involuntary intoxication is treated more favourably than voluntary intoxication.
n.2: It can be a defence where mens rea was not formed, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: It is not limited to basic intent offences in the way voluntary intoxication is.
n.4: If the mens rea was formed, intoxication (even involuntary) is no defence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits a criminal act — an unlawful assault — which, although not intended to kill or cause serious harm, is objectively dangerous in the sense that a sober and reasonable person would recognise it as carrying some risk of harm, and that act in fact causes the victim's death. The defendant is charged with manslaughter. The court considers the elements of unlawful act (constructive) manslaughter. The single blow the defendant struck unexpectedly proved fatal when the victim fell and hit their head. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is guilty only if a reasonable person would have foreseen a risk of death specifically.
The defendant is guilty only if the unlawful act was a civil wrong rather than a crime.
The defendant cannot be guilty, because they never intended to kill or cause serious harm.
The defendant is guilty of murder, because the unlawful act resulted in death.
The defendant may be guilty of unlawful act manslaughter, as a dangerous criminal act caused the death.
Criminal Liability.w: Unlawful act manslaughter requires an intentional criminal act which is objectively dangerous (a sober and reasonable person would recognise a risk of some harm) and which causes death. The defendant need not intend death or serious harm, nor foresee the risk (R v Church; DPP v Newbury).

n.0: The dangerousness test requires foresight of some harm, not specifically death.
n.1: The base act must be a crime, not merely a civil wrong.
n.2: Absence of intent to kill or cause serious harm does not preclude this form of manslaughter.
n.3: Without intent to kill or cause GBH it is manslaughter, not murder.

Criminal Liability.q: A person dishonestly obtains a service for which payment is, or would be, required, without paying for it, knowing that payment is expected, and intending to avoid paying. For example, they use a subscription service by dishonest means having decided never to pay. The service was one made available on the basis it would be paid for. The defendant obtained it dishonestly, intending not to pay. The defendant helped themselves to a service that is only ever provided on the footing that it will be paid for, using dishonest means to get it while having decided from the outset that they would never actually pay the charge that everyone knows attaches to it. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Fraud Act 2006?
o: Obtaining services dishonestly under section 11.
Fraud by false representation under section 2.
Theft of the service under the Theft Act 1968.
No offence, because services cannot be stolen.
Making off without payment under the Theft Act 1978.
Criminal Liability.w: Section 11 of the Fraud Act 2006 creates the offence of obtaining services dishonestly: obtaining services for which payment is required, by a dishonest act, knowing they are or might be chargeable and intending not to pay (or not to pay in full). Unlike the s.1 fraud offences, it is result-based (the services must actually be obtained).

n.1: Section 2 covers dishonest false representations; s.11 specifically covers obtaining services.
n.2: Services are not 'property' capable of being stolen under the Theft Act 1968.
n.3: Obtaining services dishonestly is an offence under s.11, so 'no offence' is wrong.
n.4: Making off without payment applies where payment on the spot is expected for goods/services already supplied and the defendant departs; s.11 fits obtaining the service dishonestly.

Criminal Liability.q: A person is overpaid by their employer due to a banking error and receives money to which they are not entitled. They are under an obligation to restore the overpayment but instead dishonestly keep and spend it, intending not to repay. The money was received by another's mistake and there was an obligation to restore it. The defendant dishonestly kept it. A payroll blunder meant the defendant was credited with far more than they were owed, they were plainly obliged to hand the surplus back, but instead they dishonestly treated the windfall as their own and spent it, with no intention of ever repaying the money that had reached them by mistake. Which of the following best describes how the Theft Act 1968 treats the overpayment?
o: Under section 5(4), the property is treated as belonging to the person entitled to restoration, so keeping it dishonestly can be theft.
The overpayment is a debt only, and non-repayment can never be a criminal offence.
The money belongs absolutely to the recipient once received, so it can never be theft on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The recipient commits burglary by retaining the funds.
The recipient commits robbery by keeping the money.
Criminal Liability.w: Section 5(4) of the Theft Act 1968 provides that where a person gets property by another's mistake and is under an obligation to make restoration, the property (and any proceeds) is treated as belonging to the person entitled to restoration. A dishonest failure to restore, with intention permanently to deprive, can therefore amount to theft.

n.1: It is not merely a civil debt; s.5(4) can make dishonest retention theft.
n.2: Section 5(4) prevents the money being treated as belonging absolutely to the recipient for theft purposes.
n.3: There is no entry as a trespasser to a building, so it is not burglary.
n.4: There is no force, so it is not robbery.

Criminal Liability.q: A professional owes the victim a duty of care and, by a grossly negligent breach of that duty, causes the victim's death. The breach involved a serious failure falling far below the standard reasonably expected, and there was an obvious and serious risk of death. The defendant is charged with manslaughter, though they committed no intentional unlawful act against the victim. The court considers gross negligence manslaughter. The victim had been in the defendant's professional care and died following the defendant's serious lapse. Which of the following best describes its elements?
o: There must be proof that the defendant foresaw the victim's death as a virtual certainty.
There must be evidence that the defendant acted with a dishonest motive of some kind.
There must be an intentional unlawful criminal act directed at the victim by the defendant.
There must be a duty of care, a grossly negligent breach, an obvious risk of death, and causation of death.
There must be proof that the defendant intended to kill or cause serious harm to the victim on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Gross negligence manslaughter (R v Adomako) requires a duty of care owed to the victim, a breach of that duty, an obvious and serious risk of death, that the breach caused the death, and that the negligence was so gross as to be criminal in the jury's view.

n.0: Foresight of virtually certain death is not the test; an objective risk of death is.
n.1: A dishonest motive is not an element of the offence.
n.2: It does not require an intentional unlawful act; it rests on negligence.
n.4: It does not require intent to kill or cause serious harm.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant charged with murder raises diminished responsibility, seeking to reduce the offence to manslaughter. A question arises at trial about who has to prove the elements of the partial defence, and to what standard, given that the prosecution ordinarily bears the burden of proving guilt. The court considers the burden and standard of proof for diminished responsibility. Two psychiatrists gave differing evidence about the extent of the impairment the defendant had suffered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Neither party bears any burden, because the judge decides the issue without proof.
The prosecution must disprove diminished responsibility beyond reasonable doubt.
The defence need only raise diminished responsibility, and the prosecution must then disprove it.
The defence must prove diminished responsibility on the balance of probabilities.
The defence must prove diminished responsibility beyond reasonable doubt.
Criminal Liability.w: Diminished responsibility is one of the exceptional situations where a legal burden rests on the defence: the defendant must prove the elements of the partial defence on the balance of probabilities.

n.0: There is a burden of proof; the judge does not simply decide without it.
n.1: The prosecution does not bear the burden of disproving diminished responsibility.
n.2: For diminished responsibility the defence bears a legal, not merely evidential, burden.
n.4: The defence standard is the balance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant takes another person's property intending to keep it, use it up, or otherwise treat it as their own to dispose of, so that the owner will not get it back in any meaningful form. In another version of the facts, the defendant borrows the property intending genuinely to return it in the same state very shortly. A dispute arises about the intention to permanently deprive. The court considers s.6 of the Theft Act 1968. The defendant had used the item up entirely, leaving nothing of value to return to the owner. Which of the following best describes the position?
