o: Treating property as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights can amount to intention permanently to deprive.
A genuine intention to return the very same property shortly can still be intention permanently to deprive on these facts.
Intention permanently to deprive is irrelevant to theft and need not be proved at all.
There is always an intention permanently to deprive whenever property is taken, even briefly.
Intention permanently to deprive requires the defendant to destroy the property completely.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.6 Theft Act 1968, a person may have the intention permanently to deprive if they intend to treat the property as their own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights. A genuine intention to return the very same property intact, by contrast, negates that intention.

n.1: A genuine intention to return the property shortly negates the required intention.
n.2: Intention permanently to deprive is an essential element of theft.
n.3: A brief taking with intention to return does not, in itself, show intention permanently to deprive.
n.4: Destruction is not required; treating the property as one's own to dispose of suffices.

Criminal Liability.q: A professional owes a duty of care to the victim, breaches that duty in a grossly negligent way, and the breach causes the victim's death. The prosecution considers gross negligence manslaughter. There was a duty, a grossly negligent breach, and a resulting death. The court must identify the further element required. The professional plainly owed the victim a duty of care and breached it in a way the prosecution says was grossly negligent, and that breach led to the victim's death, so the court must pin down the further ingredient that separates a criminal killing of this kind from ordinary civil negligence. Which of the following best completes the requirements for gross negligence manslaughter?
o: The defendant must have been reckless as to causing some property damage.
The breach must have given rise to a serious and obvious risk of death, and be so bad as to be criminal.
The defendant must have intended to kill or cause serious harm to the victim on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant must have foreseen the exact manner of the victim's death.
The breach need only give rise to a risk of some minor harm.
Criminal Liability.w: Under Adomako, gross negligence manslaughter requires a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation of death, a serious and obvious risk of death at the time of breach, and that the breach was so grossly negligent as to be criminal in the jury's view. A risk of merely some harm is insufficient; the risk must be of death.

n.0: Recklessness as to property damage is irrelevant to gross negligence manslaughter.
n.2: Intention to kill or cause serious harm is the mens rea of murder, not gross negligence manslaughter.
n.3: The defendant need not foresee the precise manner of death.
n.4: A risk of minor harm is not enough; the risk must be a serious and obvious risk of death.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, intending to commit a substantive offence, does an act which goes beyond mere preparation and is part of the actual carrying out of the intended crime, but is stopped before completing it. The defendant is charged with attempting to commit the offence. The prosecution must establish the conduct element of a criminal attempt. The court considers the actus reus of attempt under the Criminal Attempts Act 1981. The defendant had already begun putting their plan into action when the police intervened and stopped them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The defendant must have actually caused some harm before an attempt can be charged.
The defendant need only have formed the intention to commit the offence, without doing anything.
The defendant must do an act that is more than merely preparatory to the commission of the offence.
The defendant must have completed every step of the offence except the very last one.
Any act of preparation, however remote, is sufficient to amount to an attempt.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1(1) Criminal Attempts Act 1981, the actus reus of attempt is an act which is more than merely preparatory to the commission of the offence. The defendant must have moved beyond preparation into the execution of the intended crime.

n.0: An attempt does not require that harm was actually caused.
n.1: An intention alone, with no act beyond preparation, is not an attempt.
n.3: The defendant need not have completed all but the last act; more than merely preparatory suffices.
n.4: Merely preparatory acts, however remote, are not enough.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, reasonably anticipating an imminent attack, strikes the aggressor first, before any blow has actually landed on the defendant. The defendant did not attempt to run away before acting. The defendant is charged with an offence and relies on self-defence. The defendant struck pre-emptively and did not retreat. The issue is whether these facts defeat self-defence. Sensing that an attack was moments away, the defendant got their blow in first rather than waiting to be hit, and made no attempt to flee the scene beforehand, and the prosecution now argues that striking pre-emptively and standing their ground should rule out any reliance on self-defence. Which of the following best describes the law on retreat and pre-emptive force in self-defence?
o: The failure to retreat automatically defeats any claim of self-defence.
Self-defence is available only once the defendant has actually been struck.
There is no absolute duty to retreat, and a pre-emptive strike may be lawful, if the force is reasonable in the circumstances.
The defendant must always retreat as far as possible before using any force on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A pre-emptive strike can never be justified as self-defence.
Criminal Liability.w: In self-defence there is no absolute duty to retreat before using force, although the possibility of retreat is a factor in assessing the reasonableness of the force used. A person may also make a pre-emptive strike where they reasonably apprehend an imminent attack, provided the force used is reasonable in the circumstances as they believed them to be.

n.0: Failure to retreat is only a factor in reasonableness; it does not automatically defeat self-defence.
n.1: The defendant need not wait to be struck before defending themselves.
n.3: There is no absolute duty to retreat as far as possible.
n.4: A pre-emptive strike can be justified where an attack is reasonably apprehended.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant fails to act to prevent harm to a victim, and the victim is injured as a result of the defendant doing nothing. In general the criminal law imposes no liability for a mere failure to act, but the prosecution argues that this defendant was under a positive duty to act in the particular circumstances. The evidence is that the defendant had voluntarily assumed responsibility for the vulnerable victim's care and then neglected them. The court considers when an omission can give rise to liability. The victim was frail and wholly dependent on the defendant, who had taken them into their own household. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Liability for an omission arises only where the defendant is a qualified medical professional on these facts as a general rule.
There can never be criminal liability for a failure to act in any circumstances whatsoever.
Liability for an omission arises whenever the defendant simply could have prevented the harm.
Liability for an omission arises only where the defendant intended the victim to die.
Liability for an omission may arise where the defendant was under a recognised duty to act, such as an assumed duty of care.
Criminal Liability.w: Although there is no general duty to act, criminal liability for an omission arises where the defendant is under a recognised legal duty to act — for example by contract, a special relationship, the voluntary assumption of responsibility, or creating a dangerous situation — and fails to do so (R v Stone and Dobinson; R v Miller).

n.0: Duty situations are not confined to medical professionals.
n.1: There can be liability for omissions where a duty to act exists.
n.2: Mere ability to prevent harm does not create a duty to act.
n.3: Omissions liability does not require an intention that the victim die.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant intentionally inflicts bodily harm amounting to actual bodily harm on another person, who says they consented to what was done. The activity in question is not one of the recognised categories in which consent to such harm is treated as valid (such as properly conducted sport or reasonable surgery). The defendant relies on the victim's consent as a defence. The court considers the general rule on consent as a defence to offences against the person. The harm went well beyond the trivial, and the activity was nothing like sport or medical treatment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Consent is never a defence to any offence against the person in any circumstances at all.
Consent is generally not a defence to the intentional infliction of actual bodily harm, save in recognised exceptions.
Consent is a defence to actual bodily harm provided the victim was an adult who agreed.
Consent is always a complete defence to any offence against the person, however serious the harm on these facts.
Consent is a defence only where the harm was caused entirely by accident.
Criminal Liability.w: As a general rule, a person cannot validly consent to the intentional infliction of actual bodily harm or worse, so consent is no defence, except in recognised categories where public policy permits it (such as properly conducted sports, reasonable surgery, tattooing and the like) (R v Brown; A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980)).

n.0: Consent can be a defence to common assault/battery and within recognised exceptions, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Adult agreement does not make consent a defence to ABH outside the exceptions.
n.3: Consent is not a complete defence to all offences against the person.
n.4: Consent as a defence is not confined to accidental harm.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant honestly but mistakenly believes they are about to be attacked, and uses force in response that would have been reasonable had the situation been as they believed. In fact there was no real threat at all; the belief was genuine but wrong, and (in this scenario) was not caused by the defendant's voluntary intoxication. The defendant relies on self-defence. The court considers the effect of a mistaken belief on self-defence. In the dark the defendant genuinely thought the approaching figure was about to attack them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A mistaken belief can never be relied on, so the defence fails whenever the belief was wrong.
The defendant is judged only on the facts as they actually were, ignoring their honest belief.
The defendant may rely on the mistaken belief only if the mistake was a reasonable one to make.
The defendant may rely on the mistaken belief only where it was caused by voluntary intoxication.
The defendant is judged on the facts as they honestly believed them, even if the belief was mistaken.
Criminal Liability.w: For self-defence, the reasonableness of the force is judged on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them to be, even if that belief was mistaken; the belief need not be reasonable (though its reasonableness is relevant to whether it was genuinely held). A mistaken belief induced by voluntary intoxication, however, cannot be relied on.

n.0: A mistaken belief can be relied on; the defence does not automatically fail.
n.1: The defendant is judged on the facts as believed, not only as they actually were.
n.2: The mistake need not be reasonable, only genuinely held.
n.3: A drunken mistaken belief cannot be relied on, so this is the opposite of the rule.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, during an argument, shouts a threat at the victim who is standing close by, causing the victim to fear that unlawful force will be used against them then and there, although the defendant does not touch the victim. The victim apprehended immediate unlawful personal violence as a result of the words and situation. No physical contact occurred. Tempers flared and the defendant, standing only a pace or two from the victim, snarled a threat of immediate violence that left the victim genuinely fearing they were about to be struck, even though in the event the defendant never actually laid a finger on them. Which of the following best describes the offence of assault (technical assault) in these circumstances?
o: Assault is committed where the defendant causes the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence, which words alone can do.
Assault requires the defendant to intend to kill the victim.
Assault requires actual physical contact with the victim in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Assault requires the victim to suffer some physical injury.
Assault cannot be committed by words alone under any circumstances.
Criminal Liability.w: A technical assault is committed where the defendant intentionally or recklessly causes the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence. Physical contact is not required (that would be battery), and words alone (and even, in some cases, silence) can constitute an assault if they cause the requisite apprehension of immediate violence.

n.1: Assault does not require an intention to kill.
n.2: Physical contact is battery; assault requires apprehension of force, not contact.
n.3: Assault does not require actual injury; apprehension of force suffices.
n.4: Words alone can amount to assault if they cause apprehension of immediate violence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits an offence while voluntarily intoxicated through drink or drugs, and argues that, because of the intoxication, they did not form the mens rea for the offence. The offence is one of specific intent, and in the alternative the prosecution can prove a lesser offence of basic intent on the same facts. The court considers the effect of voluntary intoxication on liability. The defendant had drunk heavily before the incident and claimed to remember almost nothing of it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Voluntary intoxication automatically reduces every offence to a lesser included offence.
Voluntary intoxication may negate the mens rea of a specific intent offence, but is no defence to a basic intent offence.
Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence to any offence, whether of specific or basic intent.
Voluntary intoxication is never relevant to criminal liability in any circumstances at all.
Voluntary intoxication is a defence only to offences of basic intent, and never to specific intent on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Voluntary intoxication may be relevant to whether the defendant formed the mens rea of a specific intent offence (and so may reduce, e.g., murder to manslaughter). It is not a defence to offences of basic intent, because becoming voluntarily intoxicated is itself regarded as reckless (DPP v Majewski).

n.0: It does not automatically reduce every offence; the specific/basic distinction governs.
n.2: It is not a complete defence to all offences; basic intent offences remain.
n.3: It can be relevant to specific intent offences, so it is not always irrelevant.
n.4: The position is reversed: it may assist for specific intent, not for basic intent.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant stabs a victim, who is taken to hospital. The victim, for sincere reasons of their own, refuses a blood transfusion that would have saved their life, and dies from the wound as a result. The defendant argues that the victim's refusal of life-saving treatment broke the chain of causation, so that the defendant did not cause the death. The court considers whether the victim's refusal of treatment relieves the defendant of responsibility. The wound was still bleeding and untreated at the time the transfusion was refused by the victim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The refusal of treatment does not break the chain of causation, as the defendant must take the victim as found.
The defendant is liable only if the original wound was, by itself, immediately fatal.
The refusal of treatment breaks the chain of causation, so the defendant did not cause the death.
The refusal breaks the chain only if the victim's reason for refusing was medically irrational.
The defendant is not liable, because the victim could have chosen to survive by accepting treatment.
Criminal Liability.w: The 'thin skull' principle requires the defendant to take the victim as they find them, including their beliefs. A victim's refusal of medical treatment (for example on religious grounds) does not break the chain of causation, and the defendant remains liable for the death (R v Blaue).

n.1: The wound need not be immediately fatal by itself for the defendant to have caused death.
n.2: The refusal does not break the chain; the defendant takes the victim as found.
n.3: The rationality of the victim's reason for refusing treatment is not the test.
n.4: The victim's ability to have chosen treatment does not relieve the defendant.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant inflicts a non-fatal wound on a victim. Before the victim dies, an entirely free, deliberate and informed act of a third party (or of the victim), independent of the defendant's conduct, intervenes and is the immediate cause of the death. The defendant argues that this intervening act broke the chain of causation between the wound and the death. The court considers when a subsequent act will break the chain of causation. The later act was wholly independent of the defendant and was the immediate cause of the death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The chain is broken by any subsequent event at all, however minor or foreseeable.
The chain is broken only where the defendant intended the intervening act to occur.
Nothing that happens after the defendant's act can ever break the chain of causation on these facts.
The chain can be broken only by an act of the victim, and never by a third party.
A free, deliberate and informed intervening act may break the chain of causation, relieving the defendant.
Criminal Liability.w: The chain of causation may be broken by a novus actus interveniens: a free, deliberate and informed act of a third party (or the victim) that is sufficiently independent of the defendant's conduct can break legal causation and relieve the defendant of responsibility for the ultimate result.

n.0: Not every subsequent event breaks the chain; it must be free, deliberate and informed (or otherwise sufficiently independent).
n.1: The defendant's intention regarding the intervening act is not the test.
n.2: Subsequent events can break the chain in appropriate circumstances.
n.3: Both third-party and victim acts can, in principle, break the chain.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with gross negligence manslaughter. The defence argues that the defendant should be judged by reference to their own limited experience and personal shortcomings, rather than by any external standard, when deciding whether their conduct fell far below what was required. The prosecution says an objective standard applies. The court considers the standard by which the defendant's negligence is judged in gross negligence manslaughter. The defendant argued that their inexperience should excuse the seriousness of what they had done. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No standard of care applies, because gross negligence manslaughter is an offence of strict liability on these facts.
The defendant is judged by whether they personally realised their conduct was negligent.
The defendant is judged purely by their own subjective abilities and personal limitations.
The defendant is judged by the standard of the least experienced person in the field.
The defendant's conduct is judged against an objective standard of the reasonably competent person in their position.
Criminal Liability.w: Negligence in gross negligence manslaughter is assessed objectively: the defendant's conduct is measured against the standard of a reasonably competent person carrying out the relevant activity or occupying the relevant position, not by the defendant's own subjective abilities.

n.0: A standard of care applies; the offence is not one of strict liability.
n.1: The defendant's own realisation of negligence is not the test.
n.2: The test is objective, not based on the defendant's subjective abilities.
n.3: The standard is the reasonably competent person, not the least experienced.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant inflicts an injury on a victim, and the victim later dies. The defence argues that the defendant's act did not cause the death, because other factors also contributed. To establish causation, the prosecution must show both that the death would not have occurred without the defendant's act and that the act was a legally sufficient cause. The court considers the requirements for establishing causation in a result crime. Several factors had been present, and the defence pointed to each of them as a possible alternative cause. Which of the following best describes what the prosecution must prove?
o: Causation is established automatically once the defendant is shown to have acted unlawfully.
The defendant's act must be both a factual ('but for') cause and an operating and substantial legal cause of the result.
The prosecution need only show that the result would not have occurred but for the act, and nothing more on these facts.
The prosecution need only show that the defendant intended the result to occur.
It is enough that the defendant's act was one of many factors that happened to be present.
Criminal Liability.w: To establish causation the prosecution must prove factual causation (the result would not have occurred but for the defendant's act) and legal causation (the act was an operating and substantial cause of the result, more than minimal, and not overtaken by an intervening act).

n.0: Unlawfulness of the act does not by itself establish causation.
n.2: Factual causation alone is insufficient; legal causation is also required.
n.3: Intention goes to mens rea, not to whether the act caused the result.
n.4: Mere presence among many factors is not enough; the act must be a substantial operating cause.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant does not personally commit the substantive offence, but assists or encourages the principal offender to commit it — for example by acting as a lookout or supplying equipment — intending to assist or encourage and knowing the essential matters that make the principal's conduct an offence. The defendant is charged as a secondary party. The court considers the basis of accessorial (secondary) liability. The defendant had kept watch outside and had supplied the tools used to carry out the offence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A secondary party can never be convicted of the same offence as the principal offender.
A secondary party is liable only if they benefited financially from the principal's offence.
A secondary party is liable regardless of their intention, simply for being connected to the offender on these facts.
A person who aids, abets, counsels or procures an offence, intending to assist or encourage it, is liable as a secondary party.
A secondary party is liable only if they were physically present when the offence was committed.
Criminal Liability.w: A secondary party who aids, abets, counsels or procures the commission of an offence is liable to be tried and punished as a principal. The mens rea requires an intention to assist or encourage the principal's conduct, with knowledge of the essential matters constituting the offence (R v Jogee).

n.0: A secondary party can be convicted of the same offence as the principal.
n.1: Financial benefit is not a requirement of secondary liability.
n.2: Mens rea (intention to assist/encourage with knowledge) is required, not mere connection.
n.4: Physical presence is not always required (e.g. counselling or procuring).

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, with a view to gain for themselves or intending to cause loss to another, makes an unwarranted demand of the victim, reinforcing the demand with menaces — for example threatening to reveal damaging information unless the victim pays money. The demand is not one the defendant reasonably believes they have proper grounds to make in that way. The defendant is charged under the Theft Act 1968. The court considers the offence of blackmail. The defendant threatened to expose an embarrassing secret unless the victim paid over a large sum of money. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Blackmail requires the victim to have actually paid the money that was demanded.
Blackmail requires the defendant to have used physical violence against the victim.
Blackmail is committed only where the information threatened to be revealed was false on these facts.
Blackmail is committed by any demand for money, whether or not menaces were used.
Blackmail is making an unwarranted demand with menaces, with a view to gain or intent to cause loss.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.21 Theft Act 1968, blackmail is committed where a person, with a view to gain for themselves or another or with intent to cause loss to another, makes an unwarranted demand with menaces. A demand is unwarranted unless the defendant believes they have reasonable grounds for it and that the use of the menaces is a proper means of reinforcing it.

n.0: The offence is complete on the demand; the victim need not have paid.
n.1: Physical violence is not required; menaces suffice.
n.2: The truth or falsity of the information threatened is not the test.
n.3: Menaces are essential; a bare demand is not blackmail.

Criminal Liability.q: An organisation's activities cause a person's death, and the death was caused by the way in which the organisation's activities were managed or organised. That management amounted to a gross breach of a relevant duty of care owed to the deceased, and the way senior management managed the activities was a substantial element of the breach. The prosecution considers charging the organisation itself. The court considers corporate liability for a death of this kind. A safety failure running through the organisation's management had allowed the fatal accident to happen. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only an individual employee, and never the organisation, can be liable for such a death on these facts as a general rule.
The organisation is liable only if it intended the death to occur.
The organisation may be guilty of corporate manslaughter where a gross management failure by senior management caused death.
The organisation is automatically liable for any death connected to its activities.
An organisation can never be criminally liable for a death caused by its activities.
Criminal Liability.w: Under the Corporate Manslaughter and Corporate Homicide Act 2007, an organisation is guilty of corporate manslaughter if the way its activities are managed or organised causes death and amounts to a gross breach of a relevant duty of care, and the way senior management managed those activities is a substantial element of the breach.

n.0: The Act imposes liability on the organisation, not only individuals.
n.1: The offence does not require an intention that death occur.
n.3: Liability requires a gross management failure, not any connection to a death.
n.4: Organisations can be criminally liable under the 2007 Act.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, intending to steal from a particular safe, does everything necessary to open it, but unknown to them the safe is completely empty, so no theft could in fact be completed. The defendant is charged with attempted theft, and argues that as there was nothing to steal, they cannot be guilty. The defendant intended to steal and did acts more than merely preparatory. The offence was factually impossible to complete. The defendant had cased the target, brought the tools, and got as far as opening the safe fully intending to help themselves to the contents, only to find it standing completely empty, so that however hard they had tried there was in fact nothing there to be stolen. Which of the following best describes the position on attempts?
o: The defendant cannot be guilty, because the offence was impossible to complete.
The defendant is guilty only if they later succeed in a further attempt.
The defendant cannot be guilty unless property was actually taken.
The defendant may still be guilty of attempt, as factual impossibility is no defence.
The defendant is guilty of the full offence of theft despite the empty safe.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1(2) of the Criminal Attempts Act 1981, a person may be guilty of attempting to commit an offence even though the facts are such that the commission of the offence is impossible. So a defendant who intends to steal and does an act more than merely preparatory can be guilty of attempted theft even though the safe was empty.

n.0: Factual impossibility does not prevent liability for the attempt.
n.1: Liability for the attempt arises now; it does not depend on a later successful attempt.
n.2: Actual taking would be the full offence; the attempt does not require it.
n.4: The full offence is not committed where nothing is taken; the liability is for the attempt.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, intending to hit and injure one particular person, throws an object at them, but misses and instead strikes and injures a different, unintended victim who was standing nearby. The defendant is charged with an offence against the person actually injured. The defendant argues that they cannot be guilty, because they never intended to harm the person who was in fact hit. The court considers the doctrine that may apply where the intended and actual victims differ. The object flew past the intended target and struck a bystander who had been standing close by. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is guilty only of an attempt against the intended victim, and nothing more.
The doctrine of transferred malice allows the intent against the intended victim to transfer to the actual victim.
The defendant is guilty only if the two victims were committing the same kind of offence.
Malice can never transfer between different people in the criminal law.
The defendant is not guilty, because they had no intention to harm the person actually injured on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Under the doctrine of transferred malice, where a defendant has the mens rea for an offence against one victim and, by the same act, commits the actus reus of the same offence against another, the intent is transferred so that the defendant is guilty in respect of the actual victim (R v Latimer).

n.0: The defendant is not confined to liability for an attempt against the intended victim.
n.2: Transferred malice does not depend on the victims committing any offence.
n.3: Malice can transfer between people for the same type of offence.
n.4: The defendant can be guilty via transferred malice despite not intending to hit the actual victim.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant initially agrees to take part in a planned offence with others, but before the offence is carried out they change their mind and wish to avoid criminal liability as a secondary party. The defendant takes steps to distance themselves from the enterprise before it is carried out. The court considers the requirements for an effective withdrawal from participation in a joint criminal enterprise. The defendant had second thoughts and told the others plainly that they wanted nothing more to do with it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant avoids liability only if they physically prevent the offence from occurring.
Withdrawal may relieve the defendant of liability if they communicate it unequivocally, and timely, to the others.
A secondary party can never withdraw and avoid liability once they have agreed to take part.
The defendant avoids liability by privately deciding not to continue, without telling anyone on these facts.
The defendant automatically avoids liability simply by failing to turn up on the day.
Criminal Liability.w: A secondary party may escape liability by withdrawing before the offence is committed, but the withdrawal must generally be effective: communicated unequivocally to the other participants in time (and, for spontaneous violence or more advanced plans, may require more positive steps).

n.0: Physically preventing the offence is not always required, but mere non-attendance may be insufficient.
n.2: Withdrawal is possible; liability is not inevitable once agreement is made.
n.3: A private change of mind, uncommunicated, is not an effective withdrawal.
n.4: Merely failing to turn up may not be effective, unequivocal, communicated withdrawal.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant charged with murder relies on loss of control. The prosecution argues that the defence must fail because the defendant did not react instantly to the trigger but had a short period before acting, and because they acted partly out of anger. The defence points out that the defendant did genuinely lose self-control. The court considers the requirements of the loss of control defence, including the relevance of delay and of a desire for revenge. The defendant had waited a short while, still seething, before finally confronting and killing the victim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Any delay at all between the trigger and the killing automatically defeats the defence.
The defence succeeds even where the defendant acted in a considered desire for revenge.
The defence always fails unless the loss of self-control was completely sudden and immediate on these facts as a general rule.
The loss of self-control need not be sudden, but the defence fails if the defendant acted in considered desire for revenge.
The defence is available only where the defendant acted entirely without any emotion.
Criminal Liability.w: Under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, the loss of self-control need not be sudden, so some delay does not automatically defeat the defence. However, the defence does not apply if the defendant acted in a considered desire for revenge (s.54(4)).

n.0: Delay does not automatically defeat the defence.
n.1: A considered desire for revenge defeats the defence, so it does not succeed in that case.
n.2: Suddenness is not required, so the defence is not confined to instant reactions.
n.4: The defence does not require the absence of all emotion; it concerns loss of self-control.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant approaches a victim, uses force by pushing them, and at that moment and in order to do so takes the victim's bag. The prosecution charges robbery. Force was used on the victim at the time of the theft and in order to steal. The theft (appropriation) accompanied the use of force. The defendant came up to the victim in the street, shoved them hard, and in the very act of doing so snatched the bag from their grasp, the push being used precisely so that the defendant could get hold of the property and make off with it. Which of the following best describes the key requirements distinguishing robbery from theft?
o: Robbery requires the use of a weapon during the theft.
Robbery is theft where the defendant uses or threatens force on a person immediately before or at the time of stealing, and in order to steal.
Robbery requires entry into a building as a trespasser.
Robbery requires that the victim suffer actual bodily harm.
Robbery is committed only where force is used after the theft is complete on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Criminal Liability.w: Robbery (s.8 Theft Act 1968) is committed where a person steals and, immediately before or at the time of doing so and in order to steal, uses force on any person or puts or seeks to put any person in fear of being then and there subjected to force. All the elements of theft must be present, plus the force element used for the purpose of stealing.

n.0: A weapon is not required for robbery; any force (or threat of force) suffices.
n.2: Entry as a trespasser to a building is an element of burglary, not robbery.
n.3: Actual bodily harm is not required; even a small amount of force can suffice.
n.4: The force must be used before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal, not merely afterwards.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant acquires property in circumstances where the owner appears to have consented to the transfer, but the defendant then assumes the rights of an owner over that property. A question arises as to whether there can be an 'appropriation' for the purposes of theft where the owner consented to the defendant taking the property. The defence argues that consent by the owner prevents any appropriation. The court considers the meaning of appropriation under the Theft Act 1968. The owner had handed the property over, but the defendant then dealt with it entirely as their own. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There can be an appropriation even where the owner consented, as any assumption of an owner's rights suffices.
There can be no appropriation where the owner consented to the defendant taking the property.
Appropriation requires the owner to have been completely unaware that the property had been taken on these facts.
Appropriation occurs only where the defendant physically removes the property from the premises.
Appropriation requires the defendant to have used force to take the property from the owner.
Criminal Liability.w: Appropriation under s.3 Theft Act 1968 is any assumption of the rights of an owner. It can occur even where the owner has consented to the transfer of the property, so consent does not prevent an appropriation (R v Gomez; R v Hinks).

n.1: Owner consent does not prevent an appropriation.
n.2: The owner's awareness or otherwise is not the test for appropriation.
n.3: Appropriation does not require physical removal of the property.
n.4: Appropriation does not require force; that is robbery.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits a burglary while, at the time of the burglary, having with them a weapon of offence — for example a knife carried to threaten or injure — or a firearm or explosive. The defendant is charged with the most serious form of the burglary offences under the Theft Act 1968, reflecting the presence of the weapon. The court considers aggravated burglary. The defendant had brought the weapon along in case anyone tried to stop them during the break-in. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Aggravated burglary is committed only where the defendant stole items of high value.
Aggravated burglary applies only where more than one person took part in the burglary.
Aggravated burglary is any burglary committed at night rather than during the day.
Under s.10, aggravated burglary is burglary committed while the defendant has with them a weapon of offence, firearm or explosive.
Aggravated burglary requires the defendant actually to have used the weapon on a person on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.10 Theft Act 1968, aggravated burglary is committed where a person commits burglary and at the time has with them any weapon of offence, imitation firearm, firearm or explosive. It is the presence of the weapon at the relevant time, not its use, that aggravates the offence.

n.0: The value of items stolen is not the aggravating factor.
n.1: It does not depend on the number of participants.
n.2: Aggravated burglary is defined by the weapon, not by the time of day.
n.4: The weapon need only be had with the defendant; actual use is not required.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant enters a building as a trespasser without, at that point, any particular criminal intent. Having got inside, however, the defendant then steals property, or attempts to steal, or inflicts grievous bodily harm on someone within. The defendant is charged with burglary based on what they did after entering. The court considers the form of burglary under the Theft Act 1968 that turns on the defendant's conduct after entry. Once inside, the defendant helped themselves to items and struggled with an occupant who disturbed them. Which of the following best describes this form of the offence?
o: This is burglary only where the defendant entered a commercial rather than residential building on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
This is burglary only if the defendant was carrying a weapon when they entered the building.
Under s.9(1)(b), burglary is committed where, having entered as a trespasser, the defendant steals or attempts to steal or inflicts or attempts GBH.
This is burglary only if the defendant also caused damage to the building on entry.
This cannot be burglary, because the defendant had no criminal intent at the moment of entry.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.9(1)(b) Theft Act 1968, a person is guilty of burglary if, having entered a building (or part) as a trespasser, they steal or attempt to steal anything, or inflict or attempt to inflict grievous bodily harm. The relevant intent need only be formed after entry.

n.0: The offence is not confined to commercial buildings.
n.1: Carrying a weapon relates to aggravated burglary, not this offence.
n.3: Damage on entry is not required for s.9(1)(b).
n.4: Section 9(1)(b) does not require the intent at entry; conduct after entry suffices.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant commits an offence, claiming that they only did so because another person threatened them with death or serious injury unless they committed it, and a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing the defendant's characteristics might have responded in the same way, with no safe avenue of escape available. The defendant relies on duress by threats. The court considers the availability and requirements of that defence. The defendant said a gang had threatened to kill their family unless they carried out the offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Duress by threats may be a defence to most offences, but is not available to murder or attempted murder.
Duress by threats is available only where the threat was of minor harm to the defendant.
Duress by threats is available only where the defendant had a reasonable avenue of escape but chose not to use it.
Duress by threats is a complete defence to any offence, including murder, without exception.
Duress by threats is never a defence to any criminal offence in English law.
Criminal Liability.w: Duress by threats requires a threat of death or serious injury which a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing the defendant's relevant characteristics could not have resisted, with no safe avenue of escape. It is a complete defence to most crimes, but is not available to murder, attempted murder (or, generally, some forms of treason).

n.1: The threat must be of death or serious injury, not minor harm.
n.2: The defence requires the absence of a safe avenue of escape, not the presence of one.
n.3: Duress is not available to murder or attempted murder.
n.4: Duress is a recognised defence to many offences.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant occupies a position in which they are expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another person — for example as an employee or agent handling that person's affairs. The defendant dishonestly abuses that position, intending to make a gain for themselves or cause loss to the other, for example by secretly diverting the other's funds. The defendant is charged under the Fraud Act 2006. The court considers fraud by abuse of position. The defendant, an employee trusted with the accounts, quietly diverted company funds to themselves. Which of the following best describes the offence?
o: The offence can only be committed by a company director and by no one else.
The offence requires the defendant to have made an express false representation to the victim on these facts as a general rule.
The offence is committed only where the defendant used force against the victim.
Under s.4, the offence is committed by dishonestly abusing a position of financial trust, intending to gain or cause loss.
The offence requires the victim to have actually suffered a financial loss as a result.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.4 Fraud Act 2006, fraud by abuse of position is committed where a person occupies a position in which they are expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests, and dishonestly abuses that position intending to make a gain or cause loss. No false representation or actual loss is required.

n.0: It is not limited to company directors; many relationships qualify.
n.1: This form of fraud does not require an express false representation.
n.2: Force is not an element of the offence.
n.4: Actual loss to the victim is not required.

Criminal Liability.q: Two or more defendants agree together on a course of conduct which, if carried out in accordance with their intentions, will necessarily amount to the commission of a criminal offence by one or more of them. They are charged with an inchoate offence based on their agreement, even though the substantive offence has not yet been carried out. The court considers the offence of statutory conspiracy under the Criminal Law Act 1977. The two had agreed the plan in detail, though they were arrested before anything further could be done. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Conspiracy is committed only where the defendants also took a substantial step towards the crime on these facts.
Conspiracy requires the defendants to have signed a written agreement setting out the plan.
Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more people to pursue a course of conduct that will involve an offence.
Conspiracy requires the agreed offence to have actually been carried out and completed.
Conspiracy can be committed by a single person acting entirely alone.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1 Criminal Law Act 1977, statutory conspiracy is committed where a person agrees with one or more others on a course of conduct which, if carried out as intended, will necessarily amount to or involve the commission of an offence. The agreement itself is the offence; the substantive crime need not be carried out.

n.0: Unlike attempt, conspiracy does not require a substantial step towards the crime.
n.1: No written agreement is required; the agreement may be informal.
n.3: The agreed offence need not be carried out; the agreement is the offence.
n.4: Conspiracy requires at least two people; one person alone cannot conspire.

Criminal Liability.q: Two defendants set out together to commit a robbery. During it, one of them (the principal) inflicts serious harm on the victim. The prosecution seeks to hold the second defendant liable as an accessory to that further offence. The second defendant assisted or encouraged the principal in the venture. The issue is the mental element required of the accessory. The two set off together on the robbery, and in the middle of it the one who confronted the victim went further and inflicted serious injury, leaving the prosecution to work out on what mental footing the companion who merely helped and encouraged can be fixed with responsibility for that further violence. Which of the following best describes the mental element for secondary (accessorial) liability following the current law?
o: The accessory is liable on a strict liability basis regardless of their state of mind.
The accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal to commit the offence, with intention as to the essential matters, foresight being evidence of intent.
Mere foresight that the principal might commit the offence is automatically sufficient for liability on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The accessory is liable only if they physically carried out the offence themselves.
The accessory must have intended to kill the victim in every case.
Criminal Liability.w: Following R v Jogee, an accessory is liable where they assist or encourage the principal intending to do so and intending that the principal commit the offence (including any required mental element). Foresight that the principal might commit the offence is evidence from which intention may be inferred, but is not, by itself, the test for liability.

n.0: Secondary liability is fault-based, not strict.
n.2: Mere foresight is only evidence of intent, not automatically sufficient (correcting the former joint-enterprise approach).
n.3: An accessory need not personally carry out the offence; assisting or encouraging suffices.
n.4: An intention to kill is not required for accessorial liability to offences other than those needing that intent.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is attacked and uses force to defend themselves. In deciding whether the defendant has a defence, the court must consider both what the defendant believed the circumstances to be and whether the force used was proportionate. The defendant honestly believed force was necessary to defend themselves. The issue is the amount of force used. Set upon without warning, the defendant hit back to protect themselves, honestly convinced that force was needed to fend off the attack, and the court, accepting that belief, must now judge whether the amount of force the defendant actually used can be justified in the situation as they saw it. Which of the following best describes the test for the degree of force in self-defence?
o: The defendant must always retreat before any force can be justified.
The force is reasonable only if it caused no injury to the attacker.
The force is judged solely by what a trained expert would have done.
Any degree of force at all is permitted once the defendant is attacked on these facts.
The force must be reasonable in the circumstances as the defendant honestly believed them to be.
Criminal Liability.w: In self-defence, the defendant is judged on the facts as they honestly believed them to be (even if mistaken), and the force used must be reasonable (proportionate) in those circumstances. There is no absolute duty to retreat, and a pre-emptive strike may be lawful; grossly disproportionate force is not reasonable (with a modified test in householder cases).

n.0: There is no absolute duty to retreat before using force.
n.1: Reasonableness does not require that no injury be caused to the attacker.
n.2: The test is what was reasonable in the circumstances, not what a trained expert would do.
n.3: Not any degree of force is permitted; it must be reasonable/proportionate.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, dishonestly and intending to make a gain for themselves or to cause loss to another, makes a representation which they know to be untrue or misleading, in order to induce the victim to part with money. Whether or not the victim is in fact deceived or any gain is actually made, the defendant is charged under the Fraud Act 2006. The court considers fraud by false representation. The defendant sent the victim a convincing but wholly false demand for payment of a supposed debt. Which of the following best describes the offence?
o: The offence is committed by dishonestly making a false representation intending to gain or cause loss, whether or not a gain results.
The offence requires that the victim was actually deceived and in fact suffered a loss.
The offence requires that the defendant actually obtained property as a result of the representation on these facts as a general rule.
The offence requires the representation to have been made in writing rather than orally.
The offence is committed only where the defendant made a gain of more than a minimum amount.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.2 Fraud Act 2006, fraud by false representation is committed where a person dishonestly makes a false representation, knowing it is or might be untrue or misleading, intending thereby to make a gain for themselves or another or to cause loss to another. It is complete on the making of the representation with that intent; no gain, loss or deception need actually result.

n.1: Actual deception and loss are not required; the offence is conduct-based.
n.2: Obtaining property is not required; the offence is complete on the representation.
n.3: The representation may be oral, written or by conduct.
n.4: There is no minimum-gain threshold.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant unlawfully kills another human being. The prosecution charges murder. There is a dispute about the mental element that must be proved, because the defendant says they never actually wanted the victim to die. The evidence is capable of showing that the defendant at least intended to cause the victim really serious harm. The court considers the mens rea required for murder. The victim died from the injuries inflicted, and the defendant admitted meaning to cause them really serious harm. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Murder requires only that the defendant was reckless as to causing some harm.
Murder requires an intention to kill, and nothing less will ever suffice.
Murder requires an intention to kill or an intention to cause grievous bodily harm.
Murder requires premeditation and careful planning of the killing in advance.
Murder requires that the defendant foresaw a risk that death might possibly occur.
Criminal Liability.w: The mens rea for murder is 'malice aforethought', which means an intention to kill or an intention to cause grievous bodily harm (R v Vickers; R v Cunningham). An intention to cause GBH is sufficient even if the defendant did not intend to kill.

n.0: Recklessness is insufficient for murder.
n.1: An intention to cause GBH also suffices; intention to kill is not the only route.
n.3: Premeditation is not required; intention at the time of the act suffices.
n.4: Foresight of a mere risk of death does not establish the intention required for murder.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant takes an item of property belonging to another person. The prosecution charges theft, and there is a dispute about the elements that must be established. The defence accepts the item was taken but questions whether all the components of the offence are present. The court considers the definition of theft under the Theft Act 1968. The defendant's adviser explains what the prosecution must prove. The item was of some value and the defendant kept it, refusing to give it back to the owner. Which of the following best describes the elements of theft?
o: A taking of property with the intention of returning it to the owner later on.
Any taking of another person's property, whether or not it was dishonest.
A permanent taking of property, regardless of whether the defendant was dishonest.
A dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving them of it.
A dishonest taking of property, but only where force is also used against the owner on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1 of the Theft Act 1968, theft is the dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it. All five elements — appropriation, property, belonging to another, dishonesty and intention permanently to deprive — must be established.

n.0: An intention to return the property negates intent permanently to deprive.
n.1: A mere taking is not theft without dishonesty and intent permanently to deprive.
n.2: Dishonesty is an essential element; a permanent taking alone is not theft.
n.4: Force distinguishes robbery; it is not a requirement of theft.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant deliberately attacks a victim with the specific aim of causing them really serious harm, and does in fact inflict grievous bodily harm on the victim. The prosecution charges the most serious of the non-fatal offences against the person. The distinguishing feature of that offence, compared with the lesser wounding offence, lies in the mental element the defendant must be shown to have had. The court considers the mens rea required for the offence under s.18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The defendant had set out deliberately to cause the victim really serious and lasting harm. Which of the following best describes it?
o: It suffices that the defendant foresaw a risk of some minor harm to the victim.
The defendant must be shown to have intended to cause grievous bodily harm.
The defendant need only have applied unlawful force, with no particular intent.
The defendant must have intended to kill the victim, or the offence is not made out.
No mens rea is required, because s.18 is an offence of strict liability.
Criminal Liability.w: Section 18 OAPA 1861 (wounding or causing GBH with intent) is a specific intent offence: the prosecution must prove that the defendant intended to cause grievous bodily harm (or intended to resist/prevent lawful apprehension). Mere recklessness as to some harm is insufficient for s.18.

n.0: Foresight of minor harm suffices for s.20, not s.18.
n.2: Unlawful force with no particular intent does not satisfy s.18.
n.3: An intention to kill is not required; intention to cause GBH suffices.
n.4: Section 18 requires specific intent; it is not strict liability.

Criminal Liability.q: A diner eats a meal in a restaurant where payment is required on the spot before leaving. Knowing payment is expected there and then, the diner dishonestly leaves without paying and without any intention of returning to pay. Payment on the spot was required and expected for the meal supplied. The defendant left dishonestly, intending to avoid payment. The restaurant, like most, expected the bill to be settled before anyone left, the defendant knew perfectly well that payment on the spot was required, and having finished the meal they slipped out without paying and with no intention of ever coming back to make good the bill. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Theft Act 1978?
o: Theft of the meal under the Theft Act 1968.
Fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006.
No offence, because the meal had already been consumed.
Making off without payment under section 3.
Obtaining services dishonestly under the Fraud Act 2006.
Criminal Liability.w: Making off without payment (s.3 Theft Act 1978) is committed where a person, knowing that payment on the spot for goods supplied or services done is required or expected, dishonestly makes off without having paid as required and with intent to avoid payment. Leaving a restaurant without paying for a meal is the classic example.

n.0: The meal was supplied and consumed with payment expected on the spot; making off without payment fits better than theft here.
n.1: There need be no false representation; the offence is making off without payment.
n.2: Consuming the meal does not prevent the offence; the offence lies in making off without paying.
n.4: Obtaining services dishonestly focuses on dishonestly obtaining the service; the gist here is making off without paying for what was supplied.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant charged with murder relies on loss of control and points to a qualifying trigger. In one version of the facts the trigger is a genuine fear of serious violence from the victim; in another it is things said or done which constituted circumstances of an extremely grave character and gave the defendant a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged. The prosecution argues that the trigger relied on does not qualify. The court considers the qualifying triggers for loss of control. The defendant said the victim's conduct had left them feeling gravely and justifiably wronged in the moment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A fear of serious violence, or grave circumstances giving a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged, can qualify.
Only a fear of serious violence can ever be a qualifying trigger; words alone never suffice on these facts.
Sexual infidelity on its own is the paradigm qualifying trigger under the Act.
Any cause whatever of the loss of self-control is a qualifying trigger under the Act.
A qualifying trigger arises only where the victim had a weapon at the time.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009 the qualifying triggers are a fear of serious violence from the victim against the defendant or another, or things done or said (or both) which were of an extremely grave character and gave the defendant a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged. Sexual infidelity is expressly excluded as a trigger.

n.1: Grave things said or done can qualify, so words are not always excluded.
n.2: Sexual infidelity is expressly excluded as a qualifying trigger.
n.3: Not any cause qualifies; the trigger must fall within the statutory categories.
n.4: The victim possessing a weapon is not the statutory test.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant who kills the victim was, at the time, suffering from a recognised medical condition which gave rise to an abnormality of mental functioning that substantially impaired their ability to understand what they were doing, to form a rational judgement, or to exercise self-control, and which provides an explanation for the killing. The defendant is charged with murder and relies on a partial defence. The court considers diminished responsibility under the Homicide Act 1957 (as amended). Expert evidence confirmed the recognised condition and its effect on the defendant's functioning at the time. Which of the following best describes its effect?
o: If established, diminished responsibility results in a complete acquittal of the defendant on these facts.
Diminished responsibility is a general defence available to any criminal charge whatsoever.
Diminished responsibility applies only where the defendant was legally insane at the time.
Diminished responsibility reduces murder only to a charge of attempted murder.
If established, diminished responsibility is a partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter.
Criminal Liability.w: Diminished responsibility (s.2 Homicide Act 1957, as amended by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009) is a partial defence to murder. If the defendant proves the statutory elements on the balance of probabilities, the conviction is reduced from murder to voluntary manslaughter.

n.0: It is a partial defence, not a route to acquittal.
n.1: It is specific to murder, not a general defence to any charge.
n.2: It is distinct from insanity and does not require legal insanity.
n.3: It reduces murder to manslaughter, not to attempted murder.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant deliberately commits a criminal and dangerous act — throwing a heavy object from a height into a busy area below — without any intention to kill or seriously injure anyone, but a sober and reasonable person would plainly recognise the act as carrying a risk of some harm to those below. A passer-by is struck and killed. The defendant is charged with manslaughter. The court considers the dangerousness element of unlawful act manslaughter. The object was heavy and was thrown into a crowded street where people were plainly passing below. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The act is dangerous only if it was aimed directly at the particular victim who died.
The act is dangerous only if a reasonable person would foresee a risk of death specifically on these facts.
The act is dangerous if a sober and reasonable person would recognise it as risking some harm to another.
The act is dangerous only if it caused injury to more than one person.
The act is dangerous only if the defendant personally foresaw a risk of harm to others.
Criminal Liability.w: The dangerousness element of unlawful act manslaughter is objective: the act is dangerous if a sober and reasonable person would inevitably recognise that it carried a risk of some harm (not necessarily serious harm, and not necessarily death) to another (R v Church).

n.0: The act need not be aimed at the particular victim.
n.1: A risk of some harm suffices; foresight of death specifically is not required.
n.3: Harm to more than one person is not required.
n.4: Dangerousness is objective; the defendant's own foresight is not required.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with an offence which requires proof of intention. The defendant did not act with the aim or purpose of bringing about the prohibited result, but the prohibited result was a virtually certain consequence of what they deliberately did, and the defendant appreciated that it was virtually certain. The jury has to decide whether the defendant can be found to have intended the result. The defendant's adviser considers the meaning of intention, including oblique intention. The consequence was one the defendant had clearly seen coming as all but inevitable when they acted. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant automatically intended the result simply because it was a possible consequence.
The defendant cannot have intended the result, because it was not their aim or purpose.
Intention can never be inferred and must always be admitted by the defendant.
Intention is established whenever the defendant was merely careless as to the result.
The jury may find intention where the result was virtually certain and the defendant appreciated that.
Criminal Liability.w: Intention includes direct intent (aim or purpose) and oblique intent: where the result was a virtually certain consequence of the defendant's actions and the defendant appreciated that this was so, the jury is entitled to find that the defendant intended the result (R v Woollin).

n.0: A merely possible consequence does not establish intention.
n.1: Intention is not confined to aim or purpose; oblique intent may suffice.
n.2: Intention can be inferred from the circumstances; it need not be admitted.
n.3: Carelessness is not intention.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with attempting to commit an offence. The prosecution can show that the defendant did an act more than merely preparatory, but there is a dispute about the mental element required for the attempt. The defence argues that recklessness as to the consequences should be enough, while the prosecution says a higher mental element is needed. The court considers the mens rea of a criminal attempt. The defendant argued that they had only been reckless, not that they had actually intended the result. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The defendant must intend to bring about the consequences required for the full offence.
The defendant need only be reckless as to the consequences of their conduct.
The mens rea for an attempt is always lower than for the completed offence.
The defendant need have no mens rea at all, because the offence was not completed.
The defendant must merely have foreseen that the offence might possibly occur.
Criminal Liability.w: The mens rea of attempt generally requires an intention to commit the full offence; the defendant must intend to bring about the consequences that are the elements of the completed offence (for example, for attempted murder, an intention to kill). Recklessness as to the result is generally insufficient.

n.1: Recklessness as to the consequences is generally insufficient for attempt.
n.2: The mens rea for an attempt can be higher (e.g. attempted murder requires intent to kill), not always lower.
n.3: An attempt does require mens rea, notwithstanding non-completion.
n.4: Mere foresight of possibility is not the required intention.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with an offence that can be committed recklessly. The defendant did not intend the harmful result, but the question is whether they were reckless as to it. The evidence shows what the defendant themselves actually foresaw about the risk, and whether they went on to take it unreasonably. The court must apply the correct test for recklessness in criminal law. The defendant argues they should be judged only on what a reasonable person would have foreseen. The defendant had pressed on despite plainly appreciating the risk their conduct created for others. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Recklessness is judged purely by what a reasonable person would have foreseen, not the defendant.
Recklessness is established whenever any risk of harm objectively existed, whatever the defendant thought.
Recklessness applies only where the defendant was a professional who ought to have known better.
Recklessness requires the defendant to have intended the harmful result to occur.
Recklessness requires that the defendant themselves foresaw the risk and went on unreasonably to take it.
Criminal Liability.w: Recklessness in criminal law is subjective: the defendant must have foreseen the risk of the relevant result or circumstance and gone on unreasonably to take that risk (R v Cunningham; R v G). It is judged by what the defendant actually foresaw, not by the reasonable person.

n.0: The test is subjective, not what a reasonable person would have foreseen.
n.1: The mere objective existence of a risk is not enough; the defendant must have foreseen it.
n.2: Subjective recklessness applies generally, not only to professionals.
n.3: Recklessness is a lesser fault than intention and does not require intent.

Criminal Liability.q: Two people agree together on a course of conduct that will, if carried out as intended, necessarily amount to the commission of a criminal offence by one or more of them. They intend the agreement to be carried out. No steps beyond the agreement have yet been taken. The parties have agreed on a course of conduct amounting to an offence. The two of them sat down and agreed on a plan which, if carried through as they meant it to be, could only be achieved by committing a criminal offence, and although they fully intended to go ahead, nothing had yet been done to put the plan into effect beyond the agreement itself. Which of the following best describes the offence of statutory conspiracy?
o: Conspiracy requires the parties to have used threats against each other.
Conspiracy can be committed by a single person acting alone.
Conspiracy requires an act that is more than merely preparatory to the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An agreement between two or more people to pursue a course of conduct that will necessarily involve an offence, intending it be carried out.
Conspiracy requires that the substantive offence actually be committed.
Criminal Liability.w: Statutory conspiracy (Criminal Law Act 1977) is committed where a person agrees with one or more others on a course of conduct that, if carried out in accordance with their intentions, will necessarily amount to or involve the commission of an offence. The offence is complete on the agreement; the substantive offence need not be carried out.

n.0: Threats between the parties are not an element of conspiracy.
n.1: Conspiracy requires at least two people; one person alone cannot conspire.
n.2: An act more than merely preparatory is the actus reus of an attempt, not conspiracy.
n.4: The substantive offence need not actually be committed; the agreement is the offence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with attempting to commit an offence that requires a particular consequence (for example, attempted wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm). The defendant did an act more than merely preparatory. The issue is the state of mind required for the attempt. The defendant did a more-than-merely-preparatory act. The offence attempted requires a specified consequence. The defendant got well beyond mere preparation towards committing an offence that is defined by reference to a particular result, and the question for the court is not what they did but what they must be shown to have intended about that result before they can be convicted of the attempt. Which of the following best describes the mens rea for the attempt?
o: The defendant must intend to bring about the consequence required for the full offence.
It suffices that the defendant was negligent as to the consequence.
It suffices that the defendant was reckless as to the required consequence on these facts.
The defendant must intend an entirely different and more serious offence.
No mens rea is required once a more-than-merely-preparatory act is proved.
Criminal Liability.w: For an attempt under the Criminal Attempts Act 1981, the defendant must do an act more than merely preparatory with the intention of committing the full offence. In particular, the defendant must intend any consequence that is an element of the full offence, even where recklessness would suffice for the completed offence, so intention as to the consequence is required.

n.1: Negligence is insufficient for an attempt.
n.2: Recklessness as to the required consequence is insufficient for the attempt.
n.3: The defendant must intend the offence attempted, not a different, more serious offence.
n.4: Mens rea (intention) is essential to an attempt, not dispensed with by the act element.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant enters a building as a trespasser, and does so with the intention, at the moment of entry, of stealing property inside. The defendant is charged with burglary even though, in the event, they may not have managed to take anything. The court considers the form of burglary that is based on the defendant's intention at the point of entry, under the Theft Act 1968. The defendant had climbed in through an open window with the plan of taking whatever they could find. Which of the following best describes this form of the offence?
o: Burglary is committed only where the defendant was armed with a weapon on entry.
Burglary requires the defendant to have actually stolen something after entering the building.
Burglary is committed only where the defendant broke into the building by force.
Under s.9(1)(a), burglary is committed by entering a building as a trespasser with intent to steal, inflict GBH or cause damage.
Burglary requires the defendant to have entered a dwelling house, and never any other building on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.9(1)(a) Theft Act 1968, a person is guilty of burglary if they enter a building (or part) as a trespasser with intent to steal, inflict grievous bodily harm, or do unlawful damage. The offence is complete on entry with the relevant intent, whether or not the ulterior offence is carried out.

n.0: Being armed is relevant to aggravated burglary, not to basic burglary.
n.1: Section 9(1)(a) is complete on entry with intent; actual stealing is not required.
n.2: Breaking in by force is not required; trespassory entry suffices.
n.4: Burglary applies to buildings generally, not only dwellings.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant unlawfully attacks a victim and inflicts really serious harm — a deep wound and broken bones amounting to grievous bodily harm. The evidence shows that the defendant foresaw that their actions might cause some physical harm to the victim, but did not necessarily intend to cause serious harm. The defendant is charged under s.20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The court considers the mens rea required for the s.20 offence. The victim was left with lasting injuries requiring surgery, though the defendant had lashed out impulsively. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The defendant must have foreseen that death was a virtually certain consequence.
It suffices that the defendant intended or foresaw some harm; intention to cause serious harm is not required for s.20.
The defendant must have intended to kill the victim for the s.20 offence to apply.
The defendant must have intended to cause grievous bodily harm for the s.20 offence on these facts as a general rule.
No mens rea at all is required, because s.20 is an offence of strict liability.
Criminal Liability.w: For unlawful wounding or inflicting GBH under s.20 OAPA 1861, the mens rea is intention or recklessness (Cunningham) as to causing some harm; it is not necessary that the defendant intended or foresaw serious harm (R v Mowatt; R v Savage; Parmenter).

n.0: Foresight of virtually certain death is not the s.20 test.
n.2: An intention to kill is not required for s.20.
n.3: Intention to cause GBH is required for s.18, not for s.20.
n.4: Section 20 is not an offence of strict liability; a mens rea is required.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant persuades a vulnerable person to make them a substantial gift of money, which the donor, though perhaps unwise, was legally capable of making, so that ownership validly passes to the defendant. The prosecution alleges theft, arguing the defendant acted dishonestly in accepting the gift. Ownership of the money validly passed to the defendant by gift. The issue is whether accepting a valid gift can be an appropriation. The defendant cultivated the friendship of a lonely and vulnerable individual and steered them into handing over a large sum as an outright gift, a gift the donor had the legal capacity to make so that ownership genuinely passed, and the prosecution says the defendant's conduct in taking it was dishonest. Which of the following best describes the position on theft?
o: Theft is impossible because the donor consented to the transfer.
There can be no theft because a valid gift transfers full ownership to the defendant.
There can be no appropriation unless the property was taken without the owner's consent on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant is liable only in the civil courts for undue influence.
There can be an appropriation even where ownership passes by a valid gift, so theft may be committed if the taking was dishonest.
Criminal Liability.w: Following R v Hinks, an appropriation can occur even where the defendant receives property as an indefeasible gift and ownership validly passes. Appropriation is the assumption of the rights of an owner and does not require the absence of consent, so accepting even a valid gift dishonestly can amount to theft.

n.0: The donor's consent does not prevent theft where the other elements, including dishonesty, are present.
n.1: A valid gift does not preclude theft; there can still be an appropriation.
n.2: Appropriation does not require the absence of consent (Gomez, Hinks).
n.3: Criminal liability for theft can arise in addition to any civil remedy.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant, without any lawful excuse, deliberately or recklessly destroys or damages property belonging to another person — for example by smashing a neighbour's window. The property is not their own, and the defendant had no belief in any right to act as they did. The defendant is charged under the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The court considers the basic offence of criminal damage. The defendant smashed the window during an argument, knowing full well it was not theirs to damage. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Damaging another's property, provided the defendant honestly regretted the damage afterwards.
Damaging another's property, but only where the damage caused exceeds a fixed minimum value.
Destroying or damaging property belonging to another, intending to or being reckless as to that, without lawful excuse.
