Destroying or damaging any property at all, including the defendant's own, in every case.
Damaging another's property, but only where the defendant intended to endanger life by doing so on these facts.
Criminal Liability.w: Under s.1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971, the basic offence is committed where a person without lawful excuse destroys or damages property belonging to another, intending to destroy or damage such property or being reckless as to whether it would be destroyed or damaged.

n.0: Later regret does not affect whether the offence was committed.
n.1: There is no minimum value threshold for the offence.
n.3: The basic offence concerns property belonging to another, not the defendant's own.
n.4: Intent to endanger life is the aggravated offence under s.1(2), not the basic offence.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant unlawfully strikes a victim, and the blow causes the victim to suffer injuries that are more than merely transient and trifling — for example significant bruising, a black eye and a temporary loss of consciousness — although the injuries are not life-threatening or permanent. The defendant is charged with an offence under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 reflecting this level of harm. The court considers which offence is appropriate for actual bodily harm. The victim needed to rest for several days and had a badly swollen and painful face afterwards. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This can only be common assault, however serious the injuries the victim suffered.
This is an offence only if the defendant specifically intended to cause actual bodily harm on these facts as a general rule.
No offence is committed unless the injuries are permanent or life-threatening.
This may amount to assault occasioning actual bodily harm under s.47, requiring the mens rea for the assault or battery.
This must be grievous bodily harm with intent under s.18 in every case of injury.
Criminal Liability.w: Assault occasioning actual bodily harm (s.47 OAPA 1861) requires an assault or battery that causes actual bodily harm (harm more than transient and trifling). The mens rea is only that required for the underlying assault or battery; no additional intent as to the harm is needed.

n.0: Injury beyond the transient and trifling takes this above common assault.
n.1: No additional intent as to the ABH is required beyond the assault/battery mens rea.
n.2: ABH does not require permanent or life-threatening injury.
n.4: Section 18 requires intent to cause GBH; that is not established merely by ABH-level injury.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant carries out a series of acts against a victim as part of one connected episode: at the point when the defendant had the guilty mind (mens rea), the act that actually caused the prohibited result had not yet been completed, and by the time the fatal act occurred the defendant may have believed the victim was already dead. The defence argues that the guilty act and the guilty mind did not exactly coincide in time. The court considers the coincidence of actus reus and mens rea. The whole episode unfolded over a short, continuous period as part of a single connected course of events. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The coincidence requirement does not apply to offences against the person at all.
The defendant is liable only if the victim in fact died at the exact moment of the guilty mind.
The defendant is automatically liable regardless of whether the mens rea ever existed at all.
The defendant may be liable where the acts form one continuing transaction during which the mens rea was present.
The defendant cannot be liable unless the guilty act and guilty mind coincided at one precise instant.
Criminal Liability.w: Although actus reus and mens rea must coincide, the courts treat a series of connected acts as one continuing transaction. If the defendant had the mens rea at some point during that transaction, the coincidence requirement is satisfied even if the fatal act occurred later (Thabo Meli v R; R v Church).

n.0: The coincidence principle applies to offences against the person too.
n.1: Liability does not depend on death occurring at the precise moment of the guilty mind.
n.2: Liability still requires that mens rea existed during the transaction.
n.4: Exact instantaneous coincidence is not required; a continuing transaction suffices.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant kills the victim while having lost their self-control as a result of a qualifying trigger, in circumstances where a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint, might have reacted in a similar way. The defendant is charged with murder but seeks to reduce the offence to manslaughter. The court considers the partial defence of loss of control under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. The defendant had snapped after a sustained and frightening confrontation with the victim that evening. Which of the following best describes its effect?
o: If established, loss of control is a partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter.
If established, loss of control is a complete defence resulting in an acquittal.
Loss of control reduces murder to a lesser non-fatal offence against the person.
Loss of control has no effect on liability, because provocation was abolished with no replacement.
Loss of control applies only where the defendant also lacked the mens rea for murder.
Criminal Liability.w: Loss of control (ss.54-55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009) is a partial defence to murder only. If the defendant lost self-control due to a qualifying trigger and a normal person might have acted similarly, the conviction is reduced from murder to voluntary manslaughter.

n.1: It is a partial defence, not a complete one; it does not lead to acquittal.
n.2: It reduces murder to manslaughter, not to a non-fatal offence.
n.3: Provocation was replaced by the statutory loss of control defence.
n.4: It presupposes the mens rea for murder is present but partially excuses it.

Criminal Liability.q: A defendant is charged with an offence requiring intention or recklessness as to a particular circumstance. The defendant made a genuine mistake of fact, so that they did not have the state of mind the offence requires as to that circumstance. The offence requires a particular mens rea as to the circumstance. The defendant's mistake meant they lacked that mens rea. The offence the defendant faces is one built around a particular state of mind as to a circumstance, and the defendant genuinely got that circumstance wrong, so that on their own understanding of the facts they simply did not have the awareness the offence demands. Which of the following best describes the effect of the mistake of fact?
o: A mistake of fact provides a general defence to all offences automatically.
A mistake of fact is relevant only to sentencing, not to guilt.
A mistake of fact excuses liability only if it was reasonable, whatever the offence requires on these facts.
A mistake of fact is never relevant to criminal liability in any circumstances.
A genuine mistake of fact may mean the defendant lacked the required mens rea, so the offence is not made out.
Criminal Liability.w: Where an offence requires proof of a particular mens rea, a genuine mistake of fact that means the defendant did not have that state of mind can negate the mens rea, so the offence is not made out. For crimes requiring intention or subjective recklessness, the mistake need not be reasonable, though reasonableness may be required for some defences or strict liability offences.

n.0: It is not an automatic general defence to all offences; it operates by negating mens rea.
n.1: A mistake going to mens rea affects guilt, not merely sentence.
n.2: For subjective mens rea offences the mistake need not be reasonable to negate mens rea.
n.3: A mistake of fact can be relevant where it negates the required mens rea.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is convicted of a specified violent offence and is assessed as posing a significant risk of serious harm to the public from further such offences. The court is considering a sentence that provides for a longer period of protection than a standard determinate sentence. The defendant meets the dangerousness criteria for a specified offence. The court seeks to protect the public. The defendant has been convicted of a specified violent offence and the reports paint him as a continuing and significant danger of causing serious harm to others, so the judge is looking beyond an ordinary fixed term to a sentence that keeps the public protected for longer than a standard determinate sentence would. Which of the following best describes a sentence available for such a dangerous offender?
o: The court must impose a community order regardless of the risk posed.
Only a standard fine may be imposed on a dangerous offender.
The court must impose a suspended sentence in every case of dangerousness on these facts.
The court has no power to impose any longer or protective sentence.
An extended sentence, comprising a custodial term plus an extended licence period, may be imposed.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a defendant is convicted of a specified offence and found to be a dangerous offender (posing a significant risk of serious harm from further specified offences), the court may impose an extended sentence, comprising an appropriate custodial term plus an extended period of licence, to provide additional public protection (with a life sentence available in the most serious cases).

n.0: A community order is not mandated for a dangerous offender; protective custodial sentences are available.
n.1: A fine is plainly inadequate and not the protective sentence for a dangerous offender.
n.2: A suspended sentence is not required; extended (or life) sentences address dangerousness.
n.3: The court does have powers to impose longer, protective sentences for dangerous offenders.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A privately funded defendant is acquitted at trial after incurring legal costs in defending the proceedings. The defendant asks whether they can recover any of their costs. The defendant was not legally aided and has been acquitted. The defendant wishes to recover defence costs. Having paid privately to defend himself, the defendant has been cleared at trial and is now considerably out of pocket for his legal costs, so he is asking whether, having been acquitted, he can get any of that expenditure back and, if so, from where. Which of the following best describes the position on a defendant's costs order?
o: The acquitted defendant may recover costs only from the individual prosecutor personally on these facts as a general rule.
The acquitted defendant must apply to the Court of Appeal to recover any costs.
The court may make a defendant's costs order for reasonable costs from central funds, though the amount recoverable may be capped.
The acquitted defendant automatically recovers all costs in full without limit.
An acquitted defendant can never recover any of their defence costs.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: An acquitted defendant may be awarded a defendant's costs order, allowing recovery of some or all reasonable costs incurred, generally payable out of central funds. However, recovery for privately funded defendants is subject to caps (often at legal aid rates), so the full costs incurred may not be recovered.

n.0: A defendant's costs order is generally paid from central funds, not by the prosecutor personally.
n.1: The trial court can make the order; an application to the Court of Appeal is not required.
n.3: Recovery is not automatic and unlimited; caps commonly apply.
n.4: An acquitted defendant can, in appropriate cases, recover costs, so 'never' is wrong.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The police wish to interview a suspect about an offence and later rely on what is said as evidence. The suspect's solicitor is advising on how interviews must be conducted and recorded, and when questioning must stop. The suspect is detained at the police station. The solicitor considers the conduct of police interviews under PACE and the Codes of Practice. The police wanted the suspect's answers to stand up as evidence if the matter went to court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Interviews must generally be recorded and conducted under caution, and questioning must cease once there is sufficient evidence to charge.
Interviews need not be recorded and may be conducted informally without any caution.
Interviews may be conducted only in writing and never by audio recording.
The police may continue interviewing a suspect indefinitely even after deciding to charge them.
The police may interview a suspect who has asked for a solicitor before the solicitor arrives, without restriction on these facts.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE and the Codes, a suspect must be cautioned before questioning about an offence, interviews at the police station must generally be audio-recorded, and questioning must cease once the officer believes there is sufficient evidence for a realistic prospect of conviction and the suspect has been given the opportunity to give their account.

n.1: Interviews must be recorded and conducted under caution, not informally.
n.2: Interviews are audio-recorded, not only in writing.
n.3: Questioning must stop once there is sufficient evidence to charge.
n.4: Interviewing before a requested solicitor arrives is restricted, not unrestricted.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At a Crown Court trial the admissibility of the defendant's confession is disputed, and the judge must resolve whether it can be put before the jury before the jury hears it. The defendant's solicitor asks how the disputed admissibility is determined. The solicitor considers the procedure for determining the admissibility of a confession (the voir dire). The parties disagreed sharply over whether the jury should ever hear the disputed confession. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The confession is automatically put before the jury without any ruling on admissibility on these facts.
Admissibility is determined only after the jury has returned its verdict.
The jury decides whether the confession is admissible after hearing all the evidence.
The judge determines admissibility in a trial within a trial (voir dire) in the absence of the jury.
Admissibility is decided by the prosecution, which chooses what the jury hears.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where the admissibility of a confession is disputed in the Crown Court, the judge determines the issue in a 'trial within a trial' (voir dire), hearing evidence and argument in the absence of the jury, and rules on admissibility before the jury hears the confession.

n.0: Disputed confessions are not automatically put to the jury without a ruling.
n.1: Admissibility is decided before, not after, the verdict.
n.2: Admissibility is a question of law for the judge, not the jury.
n.4: The prosecution does not decide admissibility; the judge does.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At trial the defendant, having pleaded not guilty, decides not to give evidence in their own defence, despite there being evidence calling for an answer. The prosecution invites the court to draw a conclusion from the defendant's silence at trial. The defendant's solicitor advises on the consequences of not testifying. The solicitor considers adverse inferences from a defendant's silence at trial under the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994. The evidence plainly called for an explanation, yet the defendant chose to stay silent at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant commits a separate offence by declining to give evidence at trial.
The court may draw an adverse inference from the defendant's failure to give evidence where the case calls for an answer.
An adverse inference is drawn automatically whenever a defendant is charged with an offence on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant must always give evidence, or the case is automatically proved against them.
No inference of any kind may ever be drawn from a defendant not giving evidence at trial.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.35 Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, where a defendant who is not prevented by their physical or mental condition declines to give evidence at trial without good cause, and the case calls for an answer, the court may draw such inferences as appear proper from that failure (though a conviction cannot be based on the inference alone).

n.0: Not testifying is not itself a criminal offence.
n.2: Inferences are not drawn merely from being charged; they relate to silence at trial where a case is to answer.
n.3: The prosecution must still prove its case; guilt is not automatic.
n.4: An inference may be drawn from failure to testify in appropriate circumstances.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A court is minded to grant a defendant bail, but has some concerns about the risk of the defendant failing to attend or interfering with the case. Rather than refusing bail outright, the court considers whether it can grant bail subject to requirements designed to address those risks, such as residence, reporting or a curfew. The defendant's solicitor considers the imposition of conditions on bail. The court wanted to release the defendant but needed reassurance that they would behave properly. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court may grant bail subject to conditions, such as residence, reporting to a police station, or a curfew, to address identified risks.
The court may only ever grant unconditional bail and can attach no conditions of any kind on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may impose conditions only in cases involving offences of dishonesty.
Conditions may be imposed only after the defendant has been convicted at trial.
The court may attach conditions only if the defendant agrees to pay a fine in advance.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where necessary to address the risks that would otherwise justify refusing bail, the court may grant conditional bail, imposing requirements such as residence at a specified address, reporting to a police station, a curfew, surety or security, or a prohibition on contacting witnesses.

n.1: The court can attach conditions; bail is not limited to unconditional bail.
n.2: Conditions are not confined to dishonesty offences.
n.3: Bail conditions apply before trial, not only after conviction.
n.4: Conditions do not depend on the defendant paying a fine in advance.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: After conviction, the defendant's solicitor prepares to advance mitigation on the offender's behalf, and the court will weigh factors that make the offending more or less serious in deciding the sentence within the guideline range. The solicitor considers aggravating and mitigating factors in sentencing. The defence wanted to highlight the offender's remorse and previously blameless life. Which of the following best describes their role?
o: Mitigating factors increase the sentence, while aggravating factors reduce it.
Aggravating factors increase the seriousness and sentence, while mitigating factors reduce it, moving the sentence within the range.
Aggravating and mitigating factors are irrelevant, and the sentence is fixed by the offence alone on these facts as a general rule.
Aggravating and mitigating factors are considered only where the defendant pleads not guilty.
Only aggravating factors are ever considered by the court; mitigation is ignored.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: In sentencing, the court assesses the seriousness of the offence and adjusts the sentence within the guideline range according to aggravating factors (such as previous convictions, planning, or a vulnerable victim), which increase seriousness, and mitigating factors (such as remorse, good character, or personal circumstances), which reduce it.

n.0: The roles are reversed in this option.
n.2: These factors are highly relevant; the sentence is not fixed by the offence alone.
n.3: These factors apply to sentencing regardless of plea.
n.4: Both aggravating and mitigating factors are considered.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant aged 15 is charged with a very serious offence, such as a homicide or another grave crime for which a long custodial sentence is available for adults. Youths are usually dealt with in the youth court, but this offence falls within a special category. The defendant is under 18 but charged with a grave crime. The usual youth court venue is in question. The accused is only fifteen and would ordinarily have their case dealt with in the youth court, but the charge is of the gravest kind, a homicide, the sort of offence for which the adult courts hold far greater sentencing powers, which throws the usual choice of venue into doubt. Which of the following best describes where such a case may be tried?
o: The case may be sent to the Crown Court, as certain grave crimes (including homicide) fall outside the youth court's usual jurisdiction.
The case cannot be tried at all until the defendant turns 18.
The case must be tried in the adult magistrates' court.
The case must always be tried in the youth court whatever the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The case must be tried by a jury in the youth court.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Although defendants under 18 are generally dealt with in the youth court, certain grave crimes are exceptions. Homicide offences must be sent to the Crown Court, and other specified grave crimes (where a long sentence may be required) may be sent there, so a youth charged with such an offence can be tried in the Crown Court.

n.1: The case can be tried while the defendant is under 18; it need not wait until they are 18.
n.2: Youths are not tried in the adult magistrates' court; the alternatives are the youth court or Crown Court.
n.3: Not all youth cases stay in the youth court; grave crimes are exceptions.
n.4: The youth court does not sit with a jury; jury trial is in the Crown Court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A vulnerable and frightened witness is due to give evidence at a Crown Court trial, and there is concern that giving evidence in the ordinary way, in open court in front of the defendant, would prevent them giving their best evidence. The prosecution wishes to help the witness give evidence effectively. The solicitor considers the availability of special measures for witnesses. The witness was terrified of the defendant and dreaded having to face them across the courtroom. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Special measures are available only in cases involving offences of dishonesty.
The court may direct special measures, such as a screen or a live video link, to help vulnerable or intimidated witnesses give their best evidence.
Special measures may be used only after the witness has already broken down in court.
All witnesses must always give evidence in open court in the ordinary way, with no assistance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Special measures are available only to the defendant and never to prosecution witnesses.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The court may grant special measures directions to assist eligible vulnerable or intimidated witnesses in giving their best evidence — for example the use of screens, giving evidence by live link, video-recorded evidence in chief, or the removal of wigs and gowns — under the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999.

n.0: Special measures are not confined to dishonesty offences.
n.2: Special measures are arranged in advance, not only after a witness breaks down.
n.3: Not all witnesses must give evidence in the ordinary way; special measures may assist.
n.4: Special measures are for eligible witnesses generally, not only the defendant.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A judge is sentencing an offender for an offence for which the Sentencing Council has issued a definitive sentencing guideline. The judge is considering how much regard must be had to that guideline in deciding the sentence. The defendant's solicitor refers the court to the relevant guideline. The solicitor considers the status of sentencing guidelines. A definitive guideline set out the categories and ranges for exactly this kind of offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must follow the relevant sentencing guideline unless satisfied it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.
Sentencing guidelines apply only in the Crown Court and never in the magistrates' court on these facts as a general rule.
Sentencing guidelines fix a single mandatory sentence that the judge cannot vary at all.
Sentencing guidelines are relevant only where the offender pleads not guilty.
Sentencing guidelines are purely advisory and the court may ignore them entirely.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: By statute, a court must, in sentencing an offender, follow any relevant sentencing guideline unless it is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. Guidelines set offence ranges and category starting points, within which the judge applies aggravating and mitigating factors.

n.1: Guidelines apply in the magistrates' court as well as the Crown Court.
n.2: Guidelines provide ranges and starting points, not a single immovable sentence.
n.3: Guidelines apply regardless of plea (with credit given separately for a guilty plea).
n.4: Guidelines are not merely advisory; the court must generally follow them.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is convicted after a trial in the magistrates' court and wishes to challenge both the conviction and the sentence. The defendant's solicitor advises on the route of appeal available against a decision of the magistrates' court on the facts and merits. The solicitor considers an appeal from the magistrates' court to the Crown Court. The defendant felt the magistrates had got both the verdict and the sentence badly wrong. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An appeal from the magistrates' court is decided by a different bench of magistrates.
A defendant convicted in the magistrates' court may appeal to the Crown Court against conviction and/or sentence, by way of a rehearing.
An appeal from the magistrates' court is available only against sentence and never conviction on these facts as a general rule.
An appeal from the magistrates' court lies directly to the Supreme Court.
There is no right of appeal from the magistrates' court to any other court.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A defendant convicted in the magistrates' court may appeal to the Crown Court against conviction (if they pleaded not guilty) and/or sentence. The appeal takes the form of a complete rehearing before a judge and (usually) two magistrates.

n.0: The appeal is heard in the Crown Court, not by a fresh magistrates' bench.
n.2: Appeal to the Crown Court can be against conviction as well as sentence.
n.3: The appeal lies to the Crown Court, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.4: There is a right of appeal from the magistrates' court to the Crown Court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an offence that can only be tried in the Crown Court because of its seriousness, such as robbery or a serious offence against the person. On the defendant's first appearance in the magistrates' court, the magistrates must deal with the case appropriately given its classification. The defendant's solicitor explains what happens at that first hearing. The solicitor considers the procedure for an indictable-only offence. The charge was a serious one that could only ever be dealt with by the higher court. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The defendant may choose to have the indictable-only offence tried in the magistrates' court.
The case is discontinued because indictable-only offences cannot be tried anywhere.
The magistrates' court tries the indictable-only offence itself without involving the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule.
The prosecution must obtain the defendant's consent before the case can go to the Crown Court.
The magistrates' court sends the case forthwith to the Crown Court for trial, dealing only with preliminary matters such as bail.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: An indictable-only offence must be tried in the Crown Court. Under s.51 Crime and Disorder Act 1998, the magistrates' court sends the defendant forthwith to the Crown Court for trial at the first hearing, dealing only with preliminary matters such as bail and legal aid.

n.0: There is no option to have an indictable-only offence tried summarily.
n.1: Indictable-only offences are tried in the Crown Court, not discontinued.
n.2: The magistrates cannot try an indictable-only offence themselves.
n.3: The sending does not depend on the defendant's consent.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is refused bail by the magistrates' court and remanded in custody, but wishes to challenge that decision and seek release pending trial. The defendant's solicitor advises on the options for challenging a refusal of bail. The solicitor considers the ability to make further bail applications and appeals. The defendant maintained a strong case for release and wanted to challenge being kept in custody. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant may challenge a refusal of bail only after the trial has concluded.
The defendant may reapply for bail only once every year during the proceedings.
The defendant may make a further bail application and, in appropriate cases, appeal a refusal of bail to the Crown Court.
A refusal of bail by the magistrates is final and can never be challenged in any way on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant may appeal a refusal of bail only to the Supreme Court.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A defendant who is refused bail may make a further application to the magistrates (with a full argument at the first two hearings, and thereafter if there is a change of circumstances) and may, in appropriate cases, appeal a refusal of bail to the Crown Court (or a judge in chambers).

n.0: Bail can be challenged before trial, not only after.
n.1: Reapplication is not limited to once a year; it follows the rules on repeat applications.
n.3: A refusal of bail is not final; further applications and an appeal are possible.
n.4: The appeal is to the Crown Court, not directly the Supreme Court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant made a confession to the police, but the defence alleges that it was obtained by oppression, or in circumstances likely to render it unreliable. The prosecution wishes to rely on the confession at trial. The defendant's solicitor seeks to have the confession ruled inadmissible. The solicitor considers the exclusion of a confession under section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The defendant said the confession had been beaten out of them during a long, aggressive interview. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defence must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the confession was unreliable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A confession is always admissible once it has been made, however it was obtained.
The court must exclude the confession if it may have been obtained by oppression or be unreliable, unless the prosecution disproves this.
A confession can be excluded only if the police acted in bad faith deliberately.
The court may exclude a confession only if the defendant later pleads not guilty.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.76 PACE 1984, where it is represented that a confession was or may have been obtained by oppression, or in consequence of anything said or done likely to render it unreliable, the court must not allow it to be given in evidence unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that it was not so obtained.

n.0: The prosecution must prove the confession was not so obtained; the burden is not on the defence.
n.1: A confession is not always admissible; s.76 provides for exclusion.
n.3: Exclusion does not require deliberate bad faith; unreliability suffices.
n.4: Exclusion under s.76 does not depend on the plea.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The prosecution wishes to rely on a written statement of a witness who has since died and so cannot attend to give oral evidence. The statement is relevant to the case. The maker of the statement is unavailable because they have died. The prosecution seeks to adduce the statement as hearsay. A key witness whose written account supports the prosecution has since died and can no longer come to court to be examined, and the prosecution, anxious not to lose that evidence altogether, wants to put the statement before the jury despite the defence being unable to cross-examine its maker. Which of the following best describes the basis for admitting it?
o: It may be admissible as hearsay where the witness is unavailable for a specified reason, such as death, subject to safeguards.
It is admissible automatically because the witness has died, with no conditions on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It may be admitted only if the defence agrees to its admission.
Hearsay is never admissible in criminal proceedings under any circumstances.
It may be admitted only if corroborated by at least two other witnesses.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Hearsay is admissible in criminal proceedings only in defined circumstances. One route (s.116 Criminal Justice Act 2003) admits a statement where the maker is unavailable for a specified reason, such as death, and other conditions and safeguards are met. The court retains powers to exclude, and there are fairness protections given the inability to cross-examine.

n.1: Admission is not automatic on death; statutory conditions and safeguards apply.
n.2: Defence agreement is one route to admitting hearsay, but not the only one; unavailability is a distinct basis.
n.3: Hearsay can be admissible in defined circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: There is no rule requiring corroboration by two other witnesses.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect who is detained at a police station has a mental health condition that makes them vulnerable, and the custody officer must ensure appropriate safeguards are in place for the interview and detention. The suspect's solicitor is concerned that the suspect understands what is happening and is treated fairly. The solicitor considers the safeguards for a vulnerable adult suspect under PACE Code C. The suspect struggled to follow what was being said and became distressed during the process. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A vulnerable adult suspect is treated in exactly the same way as any other adult, with no extra safeguards on these facts as a general rule.
A vulnerable adult suspect requires safeguards only if charged with a serious offence.
A vulnerable adult suspect loses the right to legal advice because of their condition.
A vulnerable adult suspect may not be interviewed at all in any circumstances.
A vulnerable adult suspect must have an appropriate adult present and be afforded additional safeguards during detention and interview.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE Code C, a suspect who is mentally vulnerable or has a mental disorder must be treated as a vulnerable person, requiring an appropriate adult to be present for interview and other key steps, along with additional safeguards to ensure they understand their position and are treated fairly.

n.0: Vulnerable adults receive additional safeguards, not identical treatment.
n.1: The safeguards apply regardless of the seriousness of the offence.
n.2: Vulnerability does not remove the right to legal advice; it adds safeguards.
n.3: A vulnerable adult can be interviewed with the proper safeguards.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A youth aged 16 is convicted of an offence in the youth court. The court must decide on an appropriate sentence, applying the distinct sentencing framework that applies to children and young people, whose principal aim differs from that for adults. The young person's solicitor advises on youth sentencing. The solicitor considers the sentencing of young offenders. The young person had pleaded guilty and it was their first appearance before any court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Youth sentencing aims principally to prevent offending by children, with distinct orders like referral and rehabilitation orders.
Youth sentencing is aimed principally at maximising the punishment of the child.
Young offenders are sentenced in exactly the same way as adults, with identical orders on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Young offenders can never be given any sentence and must always be discharged.
The only sentence available for a young offender is immediate custody.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The youth justice system has, as a principal aim, the prevention of offending by children and young people, and the welfare of the child must be considered. A distinct range of sentences applies, including referral orders (often for first-time offenders pleading guilty), youth rehabilitation orders, and detention only as a last resort.

n.1: The principal aim is preventing offending, not maximising punishment.
n.2: Youths are not sentenced identically to adults; a distinct regime applies.
n.3: Young offenders can be sentenced; discharge is only one option.
n.4: Custody is a last resort, not the only option, for young offenders.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant has been convicted following a trial in the Crown Court and wishes to appeal against the conviction, arguing that it is unsafe. The defendant's solicitor advises on the court to which such an appeal lies and what is required to bring it. The solicitor considers an appeal against conviction from the Crown Court. The defendant believed the jury had been misdirected and that the conviction could not stand. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An appeal against a Crown Court conviction succeeds only if the defendant is factually innocent on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An appeal against conviction lies to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with permission, and succeeds if the conviction is unsafe.
An appeal against a Crown Court conviction lies to the magistrates' court for a rehearing.
There is no right of appeal against a conviction in the Crown Court.
An appeal against a Crown Court conviction may be brought at any time without permission.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A defendant convicted in the Crown Court may appeal against conviction to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally requiring leave (permission). The Court of Appeal will allow the appeal if it thinks the conviction is unsafe.

n.0: The test is whether the conviction is unsafe, not proof of factual innocence.
n.2: The appeal lies to the Court of Appeal, not down to the magistrates' court.
n.3: There is a right of appeal against Crown Court conviction to the Court of Appeal.
n.4: Permission (leave) is generally required, and there are time limits.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At trial the prosecution wishes to rely on a statement made out of court by a person who is not called as a witness, to prove the truth of its contents — hearsay evidence. The defence argues it is inadmissible. The defendant's solicitor considers the circumstances in which hearsay may be admitted in criminal proceedings under the Criminal Justice Act 2003. A key witness had since died and only their earlier written statement remained available. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Hearsay is admissible in criminal proceedings only in defined circumstances, such as where a statutory exception or the interests of justice apply.
Hearsay is freely admissible in criminal proceedings in the same way as any direct evidence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Hearsay is admissible in criminal cases only if it favours the prosecution.
Hearsay is entirely inadmissible in criminal proceedings in every case without exception.
Hearsay is admissible only where the defendant consents to its admission.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, hearsay is admissible in criminal proceedings only where it falls within a permitted category — for example where a witness is unavailable for a specified reason, under a statutory or preserved common-law exception, by agreement, or where the court is satisfied it is in the interests of justice to admit it.

n.1: Hearsay is not freely admissible like direct evidence in criminal cases.
n.2: The rules apply to prosecution and defence hearsay alike.
n.3: Hearsay can be admitted in defined circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Admissibility does not depend simply on the defendant's consent.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant appears in the magistrates' court charged with an either-way offence. Before any decision on allocation, the defendant is asked to indicate how they would plead if the matter proceeded to trial. The defendant indicates a guilty plea. The defendant has indicated a guilty plea at the plea before venue stage. The magistrates now consider what happens next. Facing an either-way charge in the magistrates' court, the defendant is asked at the outset, before any decision on where the case should be tried, to indicate the plea he would enter, and he indicates that he would plead guilty, which shapes what the magistrates do next. Which of the following best describes the effect of indicating a guilty plea at plea before venue?
o: The indication of a guilty plea is ignored and treated as a not guilty plea.
The court must acquit the defendant despite the indicated guilty plea.
The court proceeds to sentence (or commits for sentence to the Crown Court if its powers are insufficient), with no allocation or trial needed.
The court must still hold a full allocation hearing and then a trial on the merits on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court must send the case to the Crown Court for a jury to decide guilt.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: At the plea before venue stage for an either-way offence, if the defendant indicates a guilty plea, the court treats the matter as a summary conviction and proceeds to sentence, or commits the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence if its own sentencing powers are insufficient. Allocation and trial only arise where a not guilty plea is indicated.

n.0: An indicated guilty plea is acted upon, not ignored.
n.1: An admitted guilty plea leads to sentence, not acquittal.
n.3: No full allocation and trial are needed once a guilty plea is indicated.
n.4: A guilty plea does not lead to a jury deciding guilt; guilt is admitted.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is remanded in custody awaiting Crown Court trial. The applicable custody time limit is about to expire, but the trial cannot start in time. The prosecution wishes the defendant to remain in custody and applies to extend the custody time limit. The custody time limit is close to expiry before trial. The prosecution seeks an extension. The defendant has been held in custody awaiting his Crown Court trial, the maximum period he can lawfully be kept there before trial is about to run out, but the trial simply cannot be got on in time, and the prosecution, wanting him to stay in custody, applies to push the limit back. Which of the following best describes when the court may extend the custody time limit?
o: The custody time limit can never be extended in any circumstances.
The limit may be extended only with the defendant's consent.
The court must extend the limit automatically on the prosecution's request on these facts as a general rule.
The limit may be extended for any reason the prosecution chooses.
Where the prosecution shows good and sufficient cause and that it has acted with due diligence and expedition.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Custody time limits cap how long a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial. The court may extend a limit only if satisfied there is good and sufficient cause to do so and that the prosecution has acted with all due diligence and expedition. If the limit expires without extension, the defendant is entitled to bail.

n.0: Custody time limits can be extended where the statutory test is met.
n.1: The defendant's consent is not required to extend the limit.
n.2: Extension is not automatic on request; the court must be satisfied of the test.
n.3: Extension requires good and sufficient cause and due diligence, not any reason at all.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: Following a person's arrest, the police wish to search the arrested person and, in some circumstances, the premises where they were arrested or which they occupy, for evidence relating to the offence. The suspect's solicitor considers the extent of the police powers of search that arise on and after arrest. The solicitor considers the search powers under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The police believed evidence of the offence might be found on the suspect or at their home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The police may search any premises anywhere in the country without any limit or condition on these facts as a general rule.
The police may never search an arrested person or any premises in any circumstances.
The police may search only if the arrested person expressly agrees to the search.
The police may search premises only after obtaining a conviction against the suspect.
The police have statutory powers, subject to conditions, to search an arrested person and certain premises for evidence.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: PACE 1984 confers powers, subject to conditions, to search an arrested person (s.32) for evidence or items that might assist escape or cause harm, to enter and search premises where the person was when or immediately before arrest (s.32), and to search premises occupied or controlled by a person under arrest for an indictable offence (s.18), among other search powers.

n.0: Search powers are subject to conditions and limits, not unlimited.
n.1: The police do have search powers on and after arrest.
n.2: A lawful search does not depend on the arrested person's agreement.
n.3: Search powers arise on arrest/investigation, not only after conviction.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A 15-year-old is arrested and detained at a police station and is to be interviewed about an alleged offence. The custody officer is aware that special safeguards apply to the interviewing of juveniles and certain vulnerable suspects. The young person's solicitor asks who must be present to support the juvenile during the interview. The solicitor considers the requirement for an appropriate adult under PACE Code C. The teenager was frightened and had no adult with them when first brought into the station. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A juvenile may be interviewed alone, with no adult or solicitor present, to speed up the process on these facts.
An appropriate adult is required only for suspects aged under 10 years.
A juvenile requires only a solicitor and never any appropriate adult.
An appropriate adult replaces the need for the juvenile to have any legal advice.
A juvenile (or vulnerable suspect) must have an appropriate adult present for the interview, in addition to any solicitor.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE Code C, a juvenile (a person under 18) or a mentally vulnerable suspect must have an appropriate adult present. The appropriate adult's role is to support and advise the suspect and observe fair conduct; this is in addition to, and does not replace, the right to legal advice.

n.0: A juvenile cannot be interviewed alone without the required safeguards.
n.1: The safeguard applies to under-18s (and vulnerable adults), not only under-10s.
n.2: An appropriate adult is required in addition to a solicitor, not instead of one.
n.3: The appropriate adult does not replace the right to legal advice.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect is detained at a police station and wants a family member to be told where they are, being anxious that relatives will not know what has happened to them. The suspect asks the custody officer whether they have any right to have someone informed of their arrest and detention. The solicitor considers the right to have someone informed under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The suspect had young children at home and was desperate for their family to know where they were. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may have someone informed only if they pay a fee for the call on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The suspect has a right to have someone told of their arrest, though it may be delayed for serious offences.
The suspect has no right to have anyone informed of their arrest at all.
The suspect may only have someone informed after they have been charged.
The police must contact the suspect's employer, but never a family member.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.56 PACE 1984, a detained person has the right, if they request it, to have one friend, relative or other person told of their arrest and where they are being held. This right may be delayed (not denied) for up to 36 hours in limited circumstances where an indictable offence is involved and authorised by a senior officer.

n.0: No fee is required to exercise the right.
n.2: There is a right to have someone informed.
n.3: The right arises on detention, not only after charge.
n.4: The suspect chooses who is informed; it is not the employer only.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: During a police interview under caution, with legal advice available, a suspect fails to mention a fact which they later rely on in their defence at trial, being a fact they could reasonably have been expected to mention at the time. At trial the defence advances that fact. The fact was one the suspect could reasonably have mentioned when questioned but did not. The suspect later relies on it. When questioned under caution, with a solicitor available to advise, the suspect said nothing about a fact that they could easily have raised at the time, only to build their trial defence around that very fact later, prompting the court to consider what may properly be made of the earlier silence. Which of the following best describes the potential consequence?
o: The prosecution must prove the suspect deliberately lied in interview.
No inference can ever be drawn from what a suspect fails to say in interview on these facts as a general rule.
The failure has consequences only if the suspect had no solicitor present.
The court may draw such adverse inferences as appear proper from the failure to mention the fact when questioned.
The failure automatically renders the later defence inadmissible.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, where a suspect, when questioned under caution, fails to mention a fact later relied on in their defence, which they could reasonably have been expected to mention, the court may draw such adverse inferences as appear proper. Safeguards apply, including that a conviction cannot be based solely on such an inference.

n.0: The provision does not require proof that the suspect lied; it concerns unmentioned facts.
n.1: Adverse inferences can be drawn from a relevant failure to mention facts, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Adverse inferences may be drawn even where a solicitor was present, subject to safeguards (though legal advice to remain silent is relevant).
n.4: The failure does not render the later defence inadmissible; it may attract an inference.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an offence and is considering whether to plead guilty. The defendant's solicitor advises on how the timing of a guilty plea may affect the sentence ultimately imposed, in particular the reduction that may be given for admitting guilt. The solicitor considers credit for a guilty plea in sentencing. The defendant was weighing up whether to admit the offence now or to contest it at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A guilty plea increases the sentence, because it shows the offender committed the offence on these facts as a general rule.
A guilty plea has no effect at all on the sentence the court imposes.
A guilty plea entered at the door of the court attracts the maximum possible reduction.
A guilty plea attracts a reduction in sentence, greatest (up to about one third) where the plea is entered at the first opportunity.
A guilty plea always results in the offender receiving no punishment whatsoever.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: An offender who pleads guilty is entitled to a reduction in sentence to reflect the plea. The reduction is greatest (up to around one third) where the guilty plea is indicated at the first stage of proceedings, and the level of reduction decreases the later the plea is entered.

n.0: A guilty plea reduces, rather than increases, the sentence.
n.1: A guilty plea does affect sentence, attracting a reduction.
n.2: A late plea attracts a smaller reduction, not the maximum.
n.4: A guilty plea reduces but does not eliminate punishment.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is on trial in the Crown Court, and a question arises about the respective functions of the judge and the jury in reaching a verdict — in particular who decides questions of law and who decides questions of fact. The defendant's solicitor explains the division of roles at a Crown Court trial. The solicitor considers the roles of judge and jury in the Crown Court. The defendant wanted to understand who would actually decide whether they were guilty. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The jury decides all questions of law, and the judge decides all questions of fact.
The jury and the judge decide the verdict jointly by a majority of all of them together on these facts.
The judge decides questions of law and directs the jury, while the jury decides the facts and returns the verdict.
The prosecution decides questions of law, and the jury simply confirms the verdict.
The judge alone decides both the law and the facts, and there is no jury.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: In the Crown Court there is a division of function: the judge decides questions of law (such as admissibility of evidence), manages the trial and directs the jury on the law, while the jury is the tribunal of fact, deciding the facts and returning the verdict of guilty or not guilty.

n.0: The jury decides facts, not questions of law.
n.1: The verdict is the jury's, reached separately from the judge.
n.3: Questions of law are for the judge, not the prosecution.
n.4: Crown Court trials are decided with a jury as the tribunal of fact.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant of previous good character, with no relevant convictions, stands trial. The defence wishes the jury to be told that the defendant's good character is relevant to how they should assess the case. The defendant's solicitor considers the direction the judge should give about the defendant's good character. The solicitor considers the good character direction in a Crown Court trial. The defendant had never been in trouble before and had an unblemished record over many years. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The judge must ignore the defendant's good character entirely and give no direction about it on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The judge should direct the jury that the defendant's good character is relevant to their credibility and to the likelihood of their having offended.
Good character is relevant only to sentence and never to the jury's consideration of guilt.
The judge must direct the jury that good character proves the defendant is innocent.
Good character can be considered only if the prosecution agrees that it is relevant.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a defendant is of good character, the judge should generally give a good character direction, telling the jury that this is relevant to the defendant's credibility (the first limb) and to the likelihood of their having committed the offence (the second, propensity limb), so that the jury may take it into account in the defendant's favour.

n.0: Good character is relevant to the jury's assessment; it is not ignored.
n.2: Good character is relevant to guilt (credibility and propensity), not only sentence.
n.3: Good character does not prove innocence; it is a factor in the defendant's favour.
n.4: The direction does not depend on the prosecution agreeing to relevance.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At trial the prosecution seeks to rely on evidence that the defence says was obtained unfairly — for example evidence obtained following serious breaches of PACE or its Codes — such that admitting it would adversely affect the fairness of the proceedings. The defendant's solicitor applies to have the evidence excluded. The solicitor considers the court's discretion to exclude evidence under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The evidence had been obtained after serious breaches of the codes governing police conduct. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must admit all evidence the prosecution wishes to rely on, whatever its effect on fairness on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may exclude evidence only where it was obtained by torture and in no other case.
The court may exclude evidence only if the defendant did not have a solicitor present.
The court may exclude prosecution evidence whose admission would so unfairly affect the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted.
The court has no power to exclude any evidence in criminal proceedings.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.78 PACE 1984, the court has a discretion to refuse to allow evidence on which the prosecution proposes to rely if it appears that, having regard to all the circumstances (including how the evidence was obtained), its admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted.

n.0: The court can exclude unfairly obtained prosecution evidence under s.78.
n.1: Section 78 is not limited to evidence obtained by torture.
n.2: Exclusion is not confined to cases where no solicitor was present.
n.4: The court does have powers to exclude evidence (ss.76 and 78).

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant charged with an offence applies for bail, but the prosecution objects, arguing that if released the defendant would fail to attend the next hearing, commit further offences, or interfere with witnesses. The court must decide whether the presumption in favour of bail is displaced. The defendant's solicitor considers the grounds on which bail may be refused. The solicitor considers the exceptions to bail under the Bail Act 1976. The defendant faced serious charges and the prosecution feared they might abscond or intimidate witnesses. Which of the following best describes them?
o: Bail may be refused only where the defendant cannot afford a solicitor.
Bail may be refused only where the defendant has already been convicted of the offence.
Bail may never be refused once a defendant has requested it.
Bail may be refused for any reason at all, without the court needing to identify any ground on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Bail may be refused where there are substantial grounds to believe the defendant would fail to surrender, commit offences, or interfere with witnesses.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: For an imprisonable offence, the main exceptions to the right to bail arise where the court is satisfied there are substantial grounds for believing that, if released, the defendant would fail to surrender to custody, commit further offences, or interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice (among other grounds).

n.0: Inability to afford a solicitor is not a ground for refusing bail.
n.1: Bail can be refused before conviction where the statutory grounds are met.
n.2: Bail can be refused where grounds exist, notwithstanding a request.
n.3: The court must identify a statutory ground; it is not an unfettered discretion.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The police have finished interviewing a suspect and must decide what to do next: whether there is sufficient evidence to charge, or whether the suspect should be released while enquiries continue. The custody officer is considering the options at the end of detention. The suspect's solicitor advises on the possible outcomes. The solicitor considers the decisions available at the end of the period of detention under PACE. The evidence was thin and the custody officer had to decide what to do as the clock ran down. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect can only ever be released on payment of a financial penalty.
The suspect must always be released with no further action once the interview ends.
The suspect must always be charged at the end of the detention period, whatever the evidence on these facts as a general rule.
The only option available is to keep the suspect in custody indefinitely.
The suspect may be charged, released under investigation, released on pre-charge bail, or released with no further action.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: At the end of detention the custody officer decides the outcome: if there is sufficient evidence, the suspect may be charged (and then bailed or remanded); otherwise the suspect may be released under investigation, released on pre-charge (police) bail (with conditions where appropriate), or released with no further action.

n.0: Release is not conditional on paying a financial penalty.
n.1: Release with no further action is only one of several options.
n.2: Charge is not mandatory regardless of evidence.
n.3: Indefinite custody is not an option; detention is time-limited.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is to be tried summarily in the magistrates' court for an either-way offence that the magistrates have agreed to keep. On conviction, the magistrates consider the sentence, and the question arises of the maximum custodial sentence the magistrates' court can impose for a single either-way offence. The trial is summary in the magistrates' court. The court is considering its sentencing powers. Having tried and convicted the defendant of an either-way offence it agreed to keep, the magistrates now turn to sentence and confront the fact that the offending looks serious, prompting the bench to check the ceiling on the custodial term they are actually permitted to pass for a single such offence. Which of the following best describes the magistrates' sentencing powers?
o: The magistrates' court may impose up to 10 years' custody for an either-way offence.
The magistrates' court must always commit every convicted defendant to the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The magistrates' court has a limited maximum custodial sentence and must commit to the Crown Court for sentence if greater punishment is needed.
The magistrates' court may impose any length of custodial sentence, including life.
The magistrates' court has no power to impose any custodial sentence at all.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The magistrates' court's custodial sentencing powers are capped (limited to a statutory maximum per offence, historically six months for a single either-way offence, with a higher aggregate for two). Where the court considers its powers insufficient to reflect the seriousness of the offending, it may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence.

n.0: The cap is far below 10 years for an either-way offence.
n.1: Not every convicted defendant is committed; only where the magistrates' powers are insufficient.
n.3: The magistrates cannot impose any length of sentence, let alone life.
n.4: The magistrates do have power to impose custodial sentences, subject to the cap.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is released on bail with a duty to attend court on a specified date, but without reasonable cause fails to attend, and no legitimate excuse is offered. The court and prosecution consider the consequences of the defendant's non-attendance. The defendant's solicitor advises on the position where a defendant fails to surrender to bail. The solicitor considers the offence of failing to surrender under the Bail Act 1976. The defendant had simply not turned up on the appointed day, offering no explanation at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Failing to surrender is an offence only where the defendant is later acquitted of the main charge on these facts as a general rule.
Failing to surrender to bail has no legal consequences of any kind.
Failing without reasonable cause to surrender to custody is a criminal offence, and the court may issue a warrant for arrest.
Failing to surrender can only ever result in a small fixed penalty notice.
Failing to surrender simply means the hearing is adjourned with no other consequence.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A defendant released on bail who fails without reasonable cause to surrender to custody at the appointed time and place commits an offence under the Bail Act 1976. The court may issue a warrant for the defendant's arrest and may also revoke or vary bail.

n.0: The offence does not depend on the outcome of the main charge.
n.1: Failing to surrender has serious consequences; it is not without effect.
n.3: It is an offence carrying real penalties, not merely a fixed penalty notice.
n.4: It leads to more than a mere adjournment; it is an offence and a warrant may issue.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect detained for an indictable offence asks to consult a solicitor. The police wish to delay access to legal advice because they believe allowing it immediately would lead to interference with evidence connected with the offence. The offence is indictable and the police rely on specified statutory grounds. The suspect has requested legal advice. The suspect, held for a serious indictable offence, has asked to speak to a solicitor, but the investigating team fears that letting that happen straight away could tip off associates or lead to evidence being tampered with, and they want to know whether, and how far, that fundamental right can be held back. Which of the following best describes the police power to delay access to legal advice?
o: Access may be delayed only for an indictable offence, on the authority of a superintendent, for up to 36 hours, on specified grounds.
Access to legal advice can never be delayed under any circumstances.
Access to legal advice may be delayed at the discretion of any officer for any offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Access may be delayed only with the consent of the suspect's chosen solicitor.
Access may be delayed indefinitely until the investigation is complete.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The right to legal advice is fundamental, but access may exceptionally be delayed where the detainee is held for an indictable offence, a superintendent (or above) authorises the delay, and there are reasonable grounds to believe that immediate access would, for example, lead to interference with evidence or harm to others. The maximum delay is 36 hours.

n.1: Access can be delayed in exceptional, tightly defined circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Delay is not at the discretion of any officer for any offence; strict conditions apply.
n.3: The solicitor's consent is not the basis for delaying access.
n.4: Delay is capped (36 hours), not available indefinitely.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The prosecution holds material that would normally have to be disclosed to the defence, but disclosing it would create a real risk of serious prejudice to an important public interest, such as revealing the identity of an informant or a sensitive investigative technique. The prosecution wishes to withhold the material lawfully. The material is sensitive and its disclosure could harm an important public interest. The prosecution seeks to avoid disclosing it. The prosecution is holding material that in the ordinary way it would have to hand over, but revealing it could betray the identity of an informant or expose a sensitive method, risking real harm to an important public interest, and the prosecution is anxious to keep it back without falling foul of its disclosure duties. Which of the following best describes the proper course?
o: The prosecution must apply to the court for a public interest immunity ruling on whether the material can be withheld.
The defence must consent before any material can ever be withheld.
The prosecution must always disclose the material regardless of the public interest on these facts as a general rule.
The prosecution may destroy the material so that it need not be disclosed.
The prosecution may simply decide for itself not to disclose the material.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where disclosable material is sensitive and its disclosure would risk serious harm to an important public interest, the prosecution must not simply withhold it unilaterally; it must apply to the court for a ruling on public interest immunity. The court balances the public interest in non-disclosure against the defendant's right to a fair trial and decides what, if anything, may be withheld.

n.1: Defence consent is not the mechanism; the court rules on PII.
n.2: Not all such material must be disclosed; PII may justify withholding, subject to the court.
n.3: Destroying material would be improper and potentially an abuse of process.
n.4: The prosecution cannot decide for itself to withhold; it must seek a court ruling.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant who has spent a period in custody on remand awaiting trial is sentenced to imprisonment. The defendant asks whether the time already spent in custody before sentence counts towards the sentence to be served. The defendant was remanded in custody before conviction and sentence. A custodial sentence is now imposed. By the time sentence is passed the defendant has already spent a good stretch behind bars on remand while awaiting trial, and they naturally want to know whether that period already served counts towards the prison term the judge is now imposing or whether it simply falls away. Which of the following best describes how the remand time is treated?
o: Time on remand counts only if the judge expressly orders it in each case.
Time spent in custody on remand generally counts automatically towards the custodial sentence.
Time on remand can only be credited if the defendant applies to the Court of Appeal.
Time spent on remand is always ignored and never counts towards the sentence.
Time on remand doubles the credit given for a guilty plea.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Time spent in custody on remand before sentence generally counts automatically towards a custodial sentence: the days are administratively credited against the term to be served, so the defendant is not required to serve that time again. This is distinct from any separate reduction for a guilty plea.

n.0: Crediting is generally automatic and does not require an express order in each case.
n.2: No application to the Court of Appeal is needed for remand time to count.
n.3: Remand time is not ignored; it generally counts towards the sentence.
n.4: Remand time is credited against the sentence; it does not double the guilty-plea discount.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is to stand trial, and the prosecution holds material gathered during the investigation which it does not intend to use as evidence, some of which might undermine the prosecution case or assist the defence. The defendant's solicitor wants to ensure this material is disclosed. The solicitor considers the prosecution's duty of disclosure of unused material under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. Some of the material the police had gathered plainly pointed away from the defendant's guilt. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The prosecution has no duty to disclose anything to the defence at any stage.
The prosecution must disclose unused material only after the trial has concluded.
The prosecution must disclose unused material that might reasonably undermine its case or assist the defence.
The prosecution must disclose only material that strengthens the prosecution case.
The prosecution need only disclose the evidence it intends to rely on and nothing else on these facts.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the CPIA 1996, the prosecution is under a duty to disclose to the defence any material in its possession which has not been used as evidence and which might reasonably be considered capable of undermining the prosecution case or of assisting the defence case.

n.0: There is a statutory duty of disclosure to the defence.
n.1: Disclosure is made before trial to allow a fair trial, not after it.
n.3: The duty concerns material undermining the prosecution or assisting the defence, not material that strengthens the prosecution.
n.4: Disclosure extends to relevant unused material, not just the used evidence.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At a Crown Court trial the prosecution case depends significantly on the identification of the defendant by an eyewitness, and there is a recognised risk that even an honest witness may be mistaken about identity. The defence is concerned that the jury should be warned about the dangers of identification evidence. The defendant's solicitor considers the direction required where identification is disputed. The solicitor considers the Turnbull direction. The witness had seen the offender only briefly and in poor light on the night in question. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The judge must direct the jury to accept identification evidence without question on these facts as a general rule.
The judge should give a Turnbull warning about the special need for caution before convicting on identification evidence.
The jury alone decides whether any warning about identification is necessary.
No warning about identification evidence is ever required in a criminal trial.
Identification evidence is automatically inadmissible whenever it is disputed.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where the case against a defendant depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification evidence, the judge must give the jury a Turnbull warning: to exercise special caution before convicting on such evidence, explaining why mistakes can occur, and directing the jury to examine the circumstances of the identification.

n.0: The jury should be warned to be cautious, not to accept identification without question.
n.2: The requirement to warn is a matter of law for the judge, not the jury's choice.
n.3: A Turnbull warning is required in disputed-identification cases.
n.4: Disputed identification evidence is not automatically inadmissible; it is subject to the warning.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an offence and brought before the magistrates' court, where the question of bail arises pending the next hearing. The defendant has a settled home, a job, and no history of failing to attend court. The prosecution has not raised any strong objection. The defendant's solicitor advises on the starting point for bail. The solicitor considers the presumption in favour of bail under the Bail Act 1976. The defendant had strong community ties and had never previously failed to attend a court hearing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Bail is entirely at the personal discretion of the police and cannot be considered by the court.
Bail can never be granted to a defendant who has been charged with any offence.
There is a presumption against bail, so a defendant must always be remanded in custody before trial on these facts.
Bail is granted only where the defendant pays a cash sum to the court in advance.
There is a general presumption in favour of bail, so bail should be granted unless a statutory ground for refusing it applies.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the Bail Act 1976 there is a general presumption in favour of bail for a defendant in criminal proceedings. Bail should be granted unless the court is satisfied that one of the statutory exceptions (grounds for refusing bail) applies on the facts.

n.0: The court, not only the police, considers bail; there is a legal framework.
n.1: Bail is available for charged defendants, subject to the exceptions.
n.2: The presumption is in favour of, not against, bail.
n.3: A cash payment in advance is not the basis for granting bail.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: Before sentencing an offender, particularly where a community or custodial sentence is being considered, the court wishes to obtain information about the offender's background, circumstances and suitability for particular sentences. The defendant's solicitor considers what the court will typically obtain to assist it in sentencing. The solicitor considers the use of a pre-sentence report. The court wanted a fuller picture of the offender before deciding how to deal with them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court may obtain a pre-sentence report from the probation service to assist it in deciding the appropriate sentence.
A pre-sentence report is prepared by the victim to describe the impact of the offence.
The court must sentence immediately without ever obtaining any information about the offender on these facts.
A pre-sentence report is prepared by the prosecution to argue for the harshest sentence.
A pre-sentence report is required only where the offender pleads not guilty.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A pre-sentence report, prepared by the probation service, provides the court with information about the offender, an assessment of the offending and the risk they pose, and the suitability of various sentencing options. The court will normally obtain one before imposing a community order or custody, unless it considers it unnecessary.

n.1: A victim personal statement is separate from the probation pre-sentence report.
n.2: The court can obtain information via a pre-sentence report; it need not sentence blind.
n.3: A pre-sentence report is prepared by probation, not the prosecution.
n.4: A pre-sentence report relates to sentencing after conviction, regardless of plea.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: During the police investigation, the suspect's solicitor is offered access to the material the police hold before the interview, so as to advise the suspect properly. The police propose to disclose only limited information. The solicitor is aware of the position on pre-interview disclosure to the defence at the police station. The solicitor considers pre-interview disclosure by the police. The solicitor needed enough information about the allegation to advise the suspect sensibly. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The police may deliberately mislead the solicitor about the evidence before interview.
The police should give sufficient disclosure to allow the solicitor to advise the suspect, though they need not reveal all their evidence pre-interview.
The police are not required to give the defence any information at all before interview.
Pre-interview disclosure is a matter solely for the suspect and not the solicitor.
The police must disclose the entirety of their evidence and case file before any interview on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
