Criminal Law & Practice.w: Before interview, the police are not obliged to disclose all their evidence, but they should provide sufficient information about the alleged offence to enable the suspect's solicitor to give proper advice. Inadequate disclosure may be a ground for advising the suspect to give a 'no comment' interview.

n.0: The police must not mislead the solicitor about the evidence.
n.2: Some disclosure sufficient for advice is expected, so it is not 'nothing at all'.
n.3: Pre-interview disclosure is given to the solicitor to enable proper advice.
n.4: The police need not disclose their entire case pre-interview.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an either-way offence and appears in the magistrates' court. The court must go through a particular process to determine whether the case will be dealt with in the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, starting with the defendant indicating their plea. The defendant's solicitor explains the procedure. The solicitor considers plea before venue and allocation for an either-way offence. The defendant wanted to understand whether the case would stay in the magistrates' court or go higher. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The magistrates alone decide the court of trial and the defendant has no say at all.
The defendant must be tried in the magistrates' court whatever the circumstances.
The prosecution alone chooses the court of trial for an either-way offence.
An either-way offence is automatically sent to the Crown Court without any plea or allocation on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The defendant indicates a plea; if not guilty, the court decides allocation, and the defendant may elect Crown Court trial if the magistrates accept jurisdiction.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: For an either-way offence, there is first a plea before venue: the defendant indicates plea. If they indicate not guilty (or no plea), the court conducts allocation, deciding whether the case is suitable for summary trial; if the magistrates accept jurisdiction, the defendant may consent to summary trial or elect trial by jury in the Crown Court.

n.0: The defendant has a say (electing Crown Court trial), so the magistrates do not decide alone.
n.1: The defendant may elect Crown Court trial, so magistrates' trial is not compulsory.
n.2: The choice is not the prosecution's alone.
n.3: An either-way offence is not automatically sent up without plea and allocation.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: During prosecution disclosure the defence realises that further unused material has come to light after the initial disclosure was made, and is concerned that relevant material might not be provided as the case develops. The defendant's solicitor considers whether the prosecution's disclosure obligation is a one-off or a continuing one. The solicitor considers the continuing duty of disclosure under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. Fresh material kept surfacing as the investigation continued after the first disclosure was given. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The prosecution's duty ends the moment the defendant enters a plea.
The prosecution need only disclose further material if the defence pays for a further search.
The prosecution is under a continuing duty to review and disclose unused material that meets the test throughout the proceedings.
The prosecution's duty of disclosure is discharged once and for all by the initial disclosure on these facts as a general rule.
The prosecution must disclose further material only after the verdict has been given.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the CPIA 1996, the prosecution's duty of disclosure is a continuing one: it must keep the question of disclosure under review throughout the proceedings and disclose any further unused material that satisfies the disclosure test as it comes to light, including in response to the defence statement.

n.0: The duty continues after the plea, throughout the proceedings.
n.1: Further disclosure does not depend on the defence paying for a search.
n.3: The duty is continuing, not discharged by the initial disclosure alone.
n.4: Disclosure is made during the proceedings to ensure a fair trial, not after the verdict.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: An offence has been reported in which the key issue is the identity of the offender, and a witness saw the culprit. The police wish to test whether the witness can identify the suspect, and must follow the correct procedure so that any identification evidence is fair and admissible. The suspect's solicitor advises on identification procedures. The solicitor considers identification procedures under PACE Code D. A witness had glimpsed the culprit and the whole case turned on whether they picked out the suspect. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Identification evidence is never admissible in criminal proceedings under any circumstances.
No identification procedure is ever required, whatever the issues in the case.
The police may simply show the witness a single photograph of the suspect and treat that as reliable on these facts as a general rule.
The witness may identify the suspect only by being shown the suspect alone in the cell.
Where identity is disputed, the police should normally hold a formal identification procedure such as a video identification (VIPER).
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE Code D, where the identity of the suspect is in dispute and a witness may be able to identify them, the police should normally hold a formal identification procedure — usually a video identification (VIPER) parade, or an identification parade or group identification — conducted fairly to test the witness's ability to identify the suspect.

n.0: Identification evidence is admissible if obtained properly.
n.1: A procedure is generally required where identity is disputed.
n.2: Showing a single photograph is not the proper procedure.
n.3: Showing the suspect alone (a confrontation) is not the normal fair procedure.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant's solicitor is advising on where a case will be tried, which depends on how the offence is classified. Offences in England and Wales fall into different categories that determine the court of trial. The offence in question is one that can be tried in either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court depending on various factors. The solicitor considers the classification of criminal offences. The offence carried a range of possible sentences and could be dealt with at different levels. Which of the following best describes the classification of an offence that may be tried in either court?
o: It is an offence that can only ever be dealt with by a fixed penalty notice on these facts.
It is an indictable-only offence, triable only in the Crown Court.
It is an either-way offence, triable either in the magistrates' court or in the Crown Court.
It is an offence that is not triable in any court in England and Wales.
It is a summary-only offence, triable only in the magistrates' court.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Criminal offences are classified as summary-only (tried in the magistrates' court), indictable-only (tried in the Crown Court), or either-way. An either-way offence may be tried in either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, depending on the plea-before-venue and allocation decisions.

n.0: An either-way offence is not dealt with merely by a fixed penalty.
n.1: An indictable-only offence is tried only in the Crown Court.
n.3: The offence is triable; the question is which court.
n.4: A summary-only offence is tried only in the magistrates' court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is convicted in the magistrates' court of an either-way offence, and the magistrates consider that their own sentencing powers are insufficient to reflect the seriousness of the offending. They wish to ensure a more severe sentence can be imposed than they are able to give. The defendant's solicitor explains what the magistrates can do. The solicitor considers committal for sentence to the Crown Court. The offending was more serious than the magistrates could properly punish within their limited powers. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The magistrates may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence where their sentencing powers are inadequate.
The magistrates may commit for sentence only where the defendant consents to it.
The magistrates must impose whatever sentence they can, even if plainly too lenient.
The magistrates must acquit the defendant if they cannot impose an adequate sentence.
The magistrates may increase their own sentencing powers to any level they consider fit on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a defendant is convicted in the magistrates' court of an either-way offence and the magistrates consider that the appropriate sentence is greater than their limited sentencing powers allow, they may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence, where the greater powers of the Crown Court are available.

n.1: Committal for sentence does not require the defendant's consent.
n.2: The magistrates are not confined to imposing an inadequate sentence; they may commit for sentence.
n.3: They do not acquit a convicted defendant for want of sentencing power.
n.4: Magistrates cannot unilaterally increase their statutory sentencing powers.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The prosecution wishes to adduce evidence of the defendant's previous convictions for similar offences, to show that the defendant has a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged, making it more likely they committed this one. The evidence is of the defendant's bad character. The prosecution relies on a statutory gateway. The prosecution wants the jury to hear that the defendant has a string of previous convictions for offences just like the one now charged, arguing that this shows a tendency to behave in the way alleged and makes guilt more likely, and it must bring the material within the statutory scheme governing such evidence. Which of the following best describes the basis for admitting such evidence?
o: It may be admitted only after the defendant has been convicted.
Evidence of a defendant's bad character is never admissible in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It may be admitted automatically without reference to any gateway or safeguard.
It may be admitted through the gateway allowing relevant evidence of the defendant's propensity to commit offences of the kind charged.
It may be admitted only if the defendant consents to its use.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, evidence of a defendant's bad character is admissible only through one of the statutory gateways. One gateway admits evidence relevant to an important matter in issue between the defendant and prosecution, which can include propensity to commit offences of the kind charged; the court may still exclude it if admission would be unfair.

n.0: Such evidence may be admitted at trial, not only after conviction.
n.1: Bad character evidence can be admissible through a gateway, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Admission is through gateways with safeguards, not automatic.
n.4: The defendant's consent is not required for a prosecution gateway to apply.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At a criminal trial, a question arises about who must prove the case and to what standard, because the defendant argues that they need not prove their innocence. The prosecution asserts the defendant is guilty. The defendant's solicitor explains the fundamental position on proof in a criminal trial. The solicitor considers the burden and standard of proof in criminal proceedings. The defendant maintained they had done nothing wrong and were not required to prove anything. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The prosecution need only prove guilt on the balance of probabilities, as in civil cases.
The defendant bears the burden of proving their innocence on the balance of probabilities.
There is no burden or standard of proof in criminal proceedings; the court decides on impression on these facts.
The prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt, and must do so beyond reasonable doubt (so that the court is sure).
Both sides share the burden of proof equally throughout the criminal trial.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: In a criminal trial the legal burden of proving the defendant's guilt rests on the prosecution, which must prove each element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt (that is, so that the tribunal of fact is sure). The defendant does not have to prove innocence (subject to limited reverse-burden exceptions).

n.0: The criminal standard is beyond reasonable doubt, not the balance of probabilities.
n.1: The defendant generally does not bear the burden of proving innocence.
n.2: There is a defined burden and standard of proof in criminal cases.
n.4: The burden is on the prosecution, not shared equally.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is remanded in custody awaiting trial, and the defendant's solicitor is concerned about how long the defendant can be held in custody before the trial must take place. There are statutory limits designed to prevent excessive pre-trial detention. The solicitor considers custody time limits in criminal proceedings. The defendant had already spent a considerable time on remand awaiting a trial date. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Custody time limits apply only to defendants who have already been convicted.
A defendant may be held in custody before trial for a maximum of only 24 hours on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Custody time limits may never be extended in any circumstances whatsoever.
Custody time limits restrict how long a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial, and may be extended by the court on application.
There is no limit on how long a defendant may be held in custody before trial.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Custody time limits set the maximum period a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial (for example a set number of days in the magistrates' court or before Crown Court trial). If the limit is reached without trial, the defendant must be released on bail unless the prosecution successfully applies to extend the limit on the statutory grounds.

n.0: Custody time limits concern pre-trial (unconvicted) detention.
n.1: The limits are measured in weeks/months, not a mere 24 hours.
n.2: Custody time limits can be extended on the statutory grounds.
n.4: There are custody time limits, so detention is not unlimited.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an either-way offence and, at the plea before venue stage, indicates a guilty plea. The defendant's solicitor advises on what the magistrates' court can then do, given the defendant has indicated guilt to an either-way offence. The solicitor considers the position where a guilty plea is indicated to an either-way offence. The defendant accepted the charge and simply wanted the matter dealt with as quickly as possible. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court proceeds to sentence, and may commit to the Crown Court for sentence if its powers are inadequate.
The court can take no further step until the prosecution consents to sentencing on these facts as a general rule.
The court must send the case to the Crown Court for a trial of the issue.
The court must automatically acquit the defendant once a plea is indicated.
The court must hold a full jury trial despite the guilty plea being indicated.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a defendant indicates a guilty plea to an either-way offence at plea before venue, the magistrates deal with the matter as a guilty plea and proceed to sentence (there is no allocation for trial). If the magistrates' sentencing powers are insufficient, they may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence.

n.1: Sentencing does not require the prosecution's consent.
n.2: A guilty plea leads to sentencing, not a trial of the issue.
n.3: An indicated guilty plea does not lead to acquittal.
n.4: There is no jury trial where guilt is admitted.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant pleads guilty to an offence, but the defence and prosecution disagree about the factual basis of the plea — the defendant admits the offence but on a significantly less serious version of the facts than the prosecution alleges, and the difference would materially affect sentence. The court must resolve the dispute before sentencing. The solicitor considers how such a factual dispute after a guilty plea is resolved. The two sides put forward sharply different accounts of how the offence had been committed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The guilty plea is automatically withdrawn whenever the facts are disputed.
The court must simply accept the prosecution's version of the facts without any hearing.
The dispute is resolved by a full jury trial of the whole offence again.
The court may hold a Newton hearing to determine the disputed facts before sentencing.
The court must sentence on the defence version of the facts in every case.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a defendant pleads guilty but there is a significant dispute about the factual basis that would affect sentence, the court may hold a Newton hearing: the judge hears evidence and determines the disputed facts (to the criminal standard) before proceeding to sentence on the facts as found.

n.0: The guilty plea stands; the facts are resolved by a Newton hearing.
n.1: The court does not simply accept the prosecution's version without resolving the dispute.
n.2: A Newton hearing, not a full jury trial, resolves the factual dispute after a guilty plea.
n.4: The court does not automatically adopt the defence version.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect is detained at the police station, and their continued detention must be kept under review to ensure that the grounds for detention still exist and that the detention remains lawful. The suspect's solicitor asks about the requirement for periodic review of detention. The solicitor considers detention reviews under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The suspect had already been held for several hours and the grounds needed to be reconsidered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Once detention is authorised, it need never be reviewed again during the period in custody on these facts as a general rule.
Detention reviews may be carried out only by the arresting officer in the case.
Detention is reviewed only by the magistrates' court and never by any police officer.
Detention must be periodically reviewed by a review officer to check that the grounds for detention continue to apply.
Detention reviews are required only for suspects charged with murder.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE 1984, a detained person's detention must be reviewed periodically by a review officer (of at least inspector rank, not directly involved in the investigation) — the first review within 6 hours of detention being authorised and thereafter at intervals of no more than 9 hours — to confirm the grounds for detention still exist.

n.0: Detention must be reviewed periodically, not authorised once and forgotten.
n.1: The review officer must not be involved in the investigation, so not the arresting officer.
n.2: Reviews are conducted by a review officer, not only the magistrates.
n.4: Reviews apply generally, not only to murder suspects.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant charged with an indictable offence applies for bail. The prosecution objects, arguing there are substantial grounds to believe the defendant would fail to surrender, commit further offences, or interfere with witnesses if released. There is a general right to bail, but the offence is indictable and the prosecution relies on the statutory exceptions. The defendant, charged with a serious indictable matter, seeks release pending trial, but the prosecution resists, pointing to a real risk that the defendant would abscond, offend again, or lean on witnesses, and the court must apply the statutory exceptions to the ordinary right to bail. Which of the following best describes when bail may be refused on these grounds?
o: Bail may be refused only if the defendant has previous convictions.
Bail may be refused on substantial grounds to believe the defendant would fail to surrender, offend, or interfere with witnesses.
Bail may be refused only for offences carrying a life sentence.
Bail must always be granted regardless of the risks the defendant poses.
Bail may be refused only where the defendant consents to being remanded on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: There is a general presumption in favour of bail under the Bail Act 1976, but it may be rebutted. For an indictable (imprisonable) offence, the main exceptions allow bail to be refused where the court is satisfied there are substantial grounds for believing the defendant would fail to surrender, commit an offence while on bail, or interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct justice.

n.0: Bail can be refused without previous convictions, on the substantial-grounds test.
n.2: Refusal is not limited to offences carrying a life sentence.
n.3: The right to bail is not absolute; it can be refused on the statutory grounds.
n.4: The defendant's consent is not required to refuse bail.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect is being detained at a police station in connection with an indictable offence. The standard maximum period of detention without charge is approaching, but the police wish to detain the suspect for longer to continue their investigation. The offence is indictable and the initial detention limit is nearly reached. The police seek to extend detention lawfully. The investigation is not complete and the police are keen to hold the suspect longer, but the clock on the ordinary detention limit for the indictable matter is running down, so the custody team needs to know who can authorise further detention and how far it can lawfully be stretched. Which of the following best describes how detention without charge may be extended beyond the initial limit?
o: Detention without charge can never exceed the initial 24 hours in any circumstances.
A superintendent may authorise up to 36 hours, and a magistrates' court may extend detention up to a maximum of 96 hours.
Only the Crown Court may authorise any extension of detention without charge.
Detention may be extended to any length simply on the authority of the investigating officer on these facts as a general rule.
A custody officer alone may extend detention indefinitely as needed.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE, the basic limit on detention without charge is 24 hours. For an indictable offence, a superintendent (or above) may authorise continued detention up to 36 hours, and a magistrates' court may issue and extend a warrant of further detention, up to an overall maximum of 96 hours from the relevant time, after which the suspect must be charged or released.

n.0: Detention can exceed 24 hours for indictable offences via the extension procedures.
n.2: Extensions are authorised by a superintendent and then the magistrates' court, not the Crown Court.
n.3: The investigating officer cannot extend detention to any length at will.
n.4: A custody officer cannot extend detention indefinitely; the statutory scheme and time limits apply.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: An offender is convicted of an offence that is serious enough to pass the community sentence threshold but does not require custody. The court wishes to impose a sentence in the community with requirements tailored to the offending and the offender. The defendant's solicitor advises on this kind of sentence. The solicitor considers community orders for adult offenders. The offence crossed the threshold for a community penalty but plainly did not require prison. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A community order may be imposed only on offenders who plead not guilty.
A community order allows the court to impose one or more requirements, such as unpaid work, a curfew or rehabilitation activity.
A community order can consist only of a fine and nothing else.
A community order requires the offender's employer to supervise them at work on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A community order is simply another name for an immediate prison sentence.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A community order enables the court to impose one or more requirements on the offender — for example an unpaid work requirement, a curfew, a rehabilitation activity requirement, a programme, or an exclusion — tailored to the offence and the offender, as an alternative to custody where the community threshold is met.

n.0: A community order is available regardless of plea.
n.2: A community order comprises requirements, not only a fine.
n.3: Supervision is by the probation service, not the offender's employer.
n.4: A community order is served in the community, not in prison.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A 16-year-old is charged with a criminal offence which, for an adult, would be an either-way matter, but which is not a grave crime requiring Crown Court trial. The young person's solicitor advises on which court will normally deal with a defendant of this age. The solicitor considers the jurisdiction of the youth court. The young defendant and their family wanted to know which court would hear the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defendant under 18 may choose to be tried in any court they prefer.
A defendant under 18 is always sent to the Crown Court for trial whatever the offence on these facts.
A defendant under 18 is always tried in the adult magistrates' court alongside adults.
A defendant under 18 is generally dealt with in the youth court, save for certain grave or specified cases.
A defendant under 18 cannot be prosecuted for any criminal offence at all.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Defendants under 18 are generally dealt with in the youth court, a specialist part of the magistrates' court. There are exceptions where a young defendant may be sent to the Crown Court — for example homicide, certain grave crimes, or where jointly charged with an adult in some circumstances.

n.0: A young defendant does not freely choose the court; the rules on jurisdiction govern.
n.1: Under-18s are not always sent to the Crown Court.
n.2: Under-18s are dealt with in the youth court, not routinely the adult court.
n.4: Those over the age of criminal responsibility can be prosecuted.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: Identification of the defendant is disputed. The police failed to hold an identification procedure (such as a video identification) when one should have been held under the relevant Code of Practice, thereby breaching the Code. Identification is in issue and a required identification procedure was not held. The defence challenges the identification evidence. The case turns on whether the defendant is the person the witness saw, and it emerges that the police never held the identification procedure that the relevant Code of Practice required in the circumstances, so the defence is pressing the point that this breach should count against the identification evidence. Which of the following best describes the potential consequence of the breach of the Code?
o: The breach automatically results in the defendant's acquittal.
The breach means the identification evidence is automatically conclusive of guilt on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The breach means the prosecution must be stopped and cannot continue at all.
The breach has no effect on the admissibility or weight of the evidence.
The court may exclude or attach reduced weight to the identification evidence, and give appropriate directions, in light of the breach.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where the police breach Code D by failing to hold a required identification procedure, the court may exclude the identification evidence (for example under s.78 PACE as unfair) or admit it while directing the jury about the breach and the resulting disadvantage to the defence. The breach affects admissibility and weight; it is not automatically fatal to the prosecution or determinative of guilt.

n.0: A Code breach does not automatically acquit the defendant.
n.1: The breach undermines, rather than strengthens, the identification evidence.
n.2: The breach does not automatically halt the whole prosecution.
n.3: The breach can affect admissibility or weight; it is not without effect.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: The police wish to take samples from a suspect in custody to assist their investigation. Some samples they want are 'intimate' samples and others are 'non-intimate'. The rules on consent and authorisation differ between the two categories. The police are considering what is required to take each type of sample. The distinction between intimate and non-intimate samples is in issue. To build the case the police want to take a range of samples from the detained suspect, some of them intrusive and some routine, and the custody officer needs to be clear that the requirements for taking them are not the same across the board depending on how the sample is classified. Which of the following best describes the position under PACE?
o: Intimate samples may be taken without consent, but non-intimate samples always require consent on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Both intimate and non-intimate samples may always be taken without consent or authorisation.
Only a doctor may authorise the taking of any sample, intimate or non-intimate.
An intimate sample generally needs the suspect consent and an officer authorisation, whereas a non-intimate sample may be taken without consent if authorised.
Neither intimate nor non-intimate samples may ever be taken without a court order.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE, an intimate sample (such as blood or a swab from a body orifice other than the mouth) generally requires both the suspect's written consent and authorisation by an officer of appropriate rank; refusal may allow adverse inferences. A non-intimate sample (such as a mouth swab or hair) may be taken without consent where authorised, using reasonable force if necessary.

n.0: This reverses the position: intimate samples need consent; non-intimate can be taken without it if authorised.
n.1: Intimate samples require consent, so it is not true that all samples may be taken without consent.
n.2: Authorisation is by an officer of appropriate rank; a doctor takes intimate samples but does not authorise them.
n.4: Samples can be taken under the PACE scheme without a court order.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect is arrested and detained at a police station on suspicion of an offence. The custody officer authorises detention, and the police wish to hold the suspect while they investigate. The suspect's solicitor is concerned about how long the suspect can be held without charge. The offence is not one carrying extended terrorism powers. The solicitor considers the basic detention time limits under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The police wanted to hold the suspect for as long as possible while they gathered further evidence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A suspect may be detained for up to one week on the authority of the custody officer alone on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There are no time limits on police detention before charge under PACE.
Detention without charge is up to 24 hours, extended to 36 by a superintendent and 96 by the magistrates.
A suspect may never be detained for more than 6 hours without being charged.
A suspect may be detained without charge indefinitely until the investigation is complete.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE 1984, the basic maximum period of detention without charge is 24 hours from the relevant time. A superintendent may authorise up to 36 hours, and further detention up to a maximum of 96 hours requires a warrant of further detention from the magistrates' court.

n.0: Extension beyond 36 hours requires magistrates, not the custody officer alone.
n.1: PACE imposes clear detention time limits.
n.3: The basic limit is 24 hours, not 6.
n.4: Detention without charge is time-limited, not indefinite.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: In a Crown Court case, the defence serves a defence statement. At trial, the defence advances a positive case that was not mentioned in that statement, departing from it without explanation. The defence statement did not set out the case now run at trial. The departure is unexplained. The defence had served a statement setting out its case, but at trial counsel runs a positive account that the earlier statement never mentioned, departing from it without any explanation, and the judge must consider what, if anything, may flow from that discrepancy. Which of the following best describes the consequence of a fault in the defence statement?
o: The defence statement fault has no consequences of any kind.
The prosecution is barred from cross-examining the defendant on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant automatically loses the right to give evidence.
The defendant's trial must be stopped and the case dismissed.
The court or jury may draw such inferences as appear proper from the fault in the defence statement.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, faults in a defence statement, such as failing to disclose a defence later relied on, or departing from the statement at trial, may allow the court or jury to draw such inferences as appear proper. It does not automatically end the trial or bar the defence, but it can damage the defendant's credibility.

n.0: There are potential consequences (adverse inferences), so it is not consequence-free.
n.1: The prosecution is not barred from cross-examining; indeed the fault may be explored.
n.2: The defendant does not automatically lose the right to give evidence.
n.3: A defence statement fault does not require the case to be dismissed.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant's case has been sent to the Crown Court for trial, and following prosecution disclosure the defence must set out the nature of its case in a formal document. The defendant's solicitor advises on the obligation to serve this document and the consequences of not doing so. The solicitor considers the defence statement under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. The case had been sent up for trial and the prosecution had already served its disclosure. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defence statement is required only where the defendant intends to plead guilty.
The defence statement must set out all the evidence the defence will call, word for word.
In the Crown Court the defence must serve a defence statement, and adverse inferences may follow from failing to do so.
A defence statement is required only in the magistrates' court and never in the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The defence never has to reveal any part of its case before the trial begins.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Following prosecution disclosure, the defendant in Crown Court proceedings must serve a defence statement setting out the nature of the defence, the matters of fact on which issue is taken with the prosecution, and any points of law relied on. Failure to serve one, or inconsistency with the defence run, may permit adverse comment or inferences.

n.0: A defence statement is relevant to contested (not guilty-plea) cases.
n.1: It sets out the nature of the defence, not every word of the evidence.
n.3: It is compulsory in the Crown Court (and voluntary in the magistrates' court).
n.4: The defence must reveal the nature of its case via the defence statement in the Crown Court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A person attends a police station voluntarily to help with an investigation, having not been arrested. They are asked questions and become concerned about their status and whether they are free to leave. The person's solicitor advises them about the position of a voluntary attender at the police station. The solicitor considers the rights of a person attending the police station voluntarily. The person had come in of their own accord and was growing uneasy about whether they could go. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A voluntary attender may never leave once questioning has begun.
A voluntary attender need not be cautioned before being questioned about an offence.
A voluntary attender has no right to legal advice because they have not been arrested.
A voluntary attender is automatically detained and loses all rights on entering the police station on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A voluntary attender is free to leave at any time unless arrested, and is still entitled to free legal advice and to be cautioned before questioning about an offence.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A person who attends the police station voluntarily and has not been arrested is free to leave at will unless and until they are arrested. They remain entitled to free and independent legal advice, and must be cautioned before being questioned about an offence.

n.0: A voluntary attender may leave unless arrested.
n.1: A caution is still required before questioning about an offence.
n.2: A voluntary attender is entitled to free legal advice.
n.3: A voluntary attender is not automatically detained on entering.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant convicted and sentenced in the Crown Court considers that the sentence imposed was manifestly excessive or wrong in principle, and wishes to challenge it. The conviction itself is not challenged, only the sentence. The defendant was sentenced in the Crown Court following trial on indictment. The defendant seeks to appeal the sentence. The defendant does not quarrel with the jury's verdict but is aggrieved by the length of the sentence, considering it manifestly excessive and out of line with principle, and wants to know which court can be asked to look again at a sentence passed in the Crown Court after a trial on indictment. Which of the following best describes the route of appeal against sentence?
o: An appeal against sentence lies directly to the Supreme Court.
An appeal against sentence lies to the High Court by way of case stated only on these facts.
There is no right of appeal against a Crown Court sentence.
An appeal against sentence lies to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave.
An appeal against sentence lies to the magistrates' court for rehearing.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A defendant sentenced in the Crown Court following trial on indictment may appeal against sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave (permission). The Court of Appeal may reduce (but not increase, on the defendant's own appeal) the sentence if it is manifestly excessive or wrong in principle.

n.0: The first appeal is to the Court of Appeal, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.1: Case stated to the High Court applies to magistrates' and the Crown Court's appellate decisions, not a Crown Court sentence on indictment.
n.2: There is a right of appeal against sentence, generally with leave.
n.4: Appeal from the Crown Court does not go to the magistrates' court for a rehearing.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant appears before the magistrates' court for the first time charged with a summary offence. The court must deal with the initial steps of the case at this first hearing, such as taking the plea and giving directions or proceeding to trial or sentence. The defendant's solicitor explains what happens at the first hearing of a summary matter. The solicitor considers the first hearing in the magistrates' court for a summary offence. The defendant appeared for the first time and the court needed to move the matter forward. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The first hearing is used only to send the case to the Crown Court for trial.
The court must adjourn every summary case for at least six months before doing anything on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The defendant is asked to enter a plea; a guilty plea leads to sentence, while a not guilty plea leads to directions for a summary trial.
The first hearing always results in the case being discontinued by the court.
The defendant may not enter any plea at the first hearing under any circumstances.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: At the first hearing of a summary offence the defendant is asked to enter a plea. If they plead guilty, the court proceeds to sentence (immediately or after reports). If they plead not guilty, the court identifies the issues and gives case management directions, fixing a date for summary trial.

n.0: Summary offences are tried in the magistrates' court, not sent to the Crown Court.
n.1: There is no rule requiring a six-month adjournment of every case.
n.3: The first hearing does not automatically discontinue the case.
n.4: A plea is normally taken at the first hearing.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A suspect is about to be interviewed under caution at the police station. The interviewing officer administers the standard caution before questioning. The suspect's solicitor advises the suspect about the effect of the caution and the consequences of remaining silent. The offence is one where the suspect could later rely on facts in their defence. The solicitor considers the caution and the drawing of adverse inferences from silence. The suspect intended to give an account at trial and had to decide whether to answer questions now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may remain silent, but a court may draw an adverse inference if they later rely on a fact they could reasonably have mentioned when questioned.
The suspect must answer all questions put to them, or they commit a separate criminal offence.
The suspect may remain silent only if they have first been formally charged with the offence.
An adverse inference is drawn automatically from any silence, regardless of the defence later run on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The suspect's silence can never be mentioned or held against them in any way at trial.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The caution warns that the suspect need not say anything, but that it may harm their defence if they do not mention when questioned something they later rely on in court. Under s.34 Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, a court may draw such adverse inferences from a failure to mention a fact later relied on which the suspect could reasonably have been expected to mention.

n.1: Silence is not itself an offence; the consequence is a possible adverse inference.
n.2: The inference relates to pre-charge questioning under caution, not only post-charge silence.
n.3: Inferences are not automatic; they depend on the facts later relied on and reasonableness.
n.4: Silence can, in defined circumstances, lead to an adverse inference at trial.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant has been convicted and the court must decide on sentence. The judge is considering the purposes that sentencing is intended to serve when deciding how to deal with the offender. The defendant's solicitor makes submissions in mitigation. The solicitor considers the statutory purposes of sentencing for adult offenders. The offence was moderately serious and the court had a wide range of sentencing options open to it. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The sole purpose of sentencing is to raise revenue for the state through fines.
Sentencing has no defined purposes and is entirely at the whim of the individual judge.
The only purpose of sentencing is to punish the offender as severely as possible.
Sentencing purposes include punishment, reduction of crime (including deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public, and reparation.
The only purpose of sentencing is to compensate the offender for the inconvenience of prosecution on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The statutory purposes of sentencing for adults include the punishment of offenders, the reduction of crime (including by deterrence), the reform and rehabilitation of offenders, the protection of the public, and the making of reparation by offenders to persons affected by their offences.

n.0: Raising revenue is not the purpose of sentencing.
n.1: There are defined statutory purposes, not unfettered whim.
n.2: Maximum severity is not the sole purpose; several purposes apply.
n.4: Sentencing is not to compensate the offender.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is being sentenced for several separate offences at the same time. The judge is considering whether the sentences should run at the same time or one after another, and must ensure the overall sentence is just and proportionate to the totality of the offending. The defendant faces sentence for multiple offences together. The court must fix the overall length. The defendant comes up for sentence on a handful of distinct offences at once, and the judge must decide whether the individual terms should sit alongside one another or stack up one after the next, while making sure the total the defendant ends up serving genuinely fits the overall seriousness of what they did. Which of the following best describes the principle the court applies?
o: Every sentence for every offence must always run consecutively without exception on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court must simply add the maximum for each offence together.
The totality principle: whether sentences run concurrently or consecutively, the overall sentence must be just and proportionate.
The court may only ever sentence for the single most serious offence.
Every sentence must always run concurrently, so only the longest is served.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: When sentencing for more than one offence, the court decides whether sentences run concurrently (together) or consecutively (one after another), but must apply the totality principle: the overall sentence must be just and proportionate to the totality of the offending, and not simply the arithmetic sum of the individual sentences.

n.0: Sentences do not always run consecutively; the court has a choice, subject to totality.
n.1: The court does not simply add the maxima together; totality governs.
n.3: The court sentences for all the offences, not only the most serious one.
n.4: Sentences do not always run concurrently; consecutive sentences are permissible.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A police officer wishes to arrest a person whom the officer suspects of having committed an offence. The suspect's solicitor later challenges the lawfulness of the arrest, and the issue is whether the officer had the necessary grounds. There was no arrest warrant. The solicitor considers the requirements for a lawful arrest without warrant under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The officer acted on a hunch and the defence later questioned whether the arrest had been lawful. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A police officer may arrest only where they have already obtained a warrant from the court on these facts as a general rule.
A police officer may arrest only after the suspect has confessed to the offence.
A police officer may arrest a person only if that person consents to being arrested.
The officer must have reasonable grounds to suspect involvement in an offence and reasonable grounds to believe arrest is necessary.
A police officer may arrest anyone at any time without any grounds whatsoever.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under s.24 PACE 1984, a constable may arrest without warrant a person whom they have reasonable grounds to suspect is committing, has committed or is about to commit an offence, provided the constable also has reasonable grounds to believe that arrest is necessary for one of the statutory reasons (such as to allow prompt investigation).

n.0: Arrest without warrant is permitted where the statutory conditions are met.
n.1: A confession is not a precondition to a lawful arrest.
n.2: Arrest does not depend on the suspect's consent.
n.4: Arrest requires reasonable grounds; it is not permitted without grounds.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: An offender has been convicted of an offence and the court is considering whether to impose a custodial sentence. The defendant's solicitor argues that imprisonment is not justified in this case. The court must apply the correct test before it can impose a prison sentence. The solicitor considers the custody threshold for an adult offender. The offending was on the borderline between a community penalty and a short custodial term. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A custodial sentence may be imposed only where the offence is so serious that neither a fine nor a community sentence can be justified.
A custodial sentence must be imposed for every offence of which a defendant is convicted.
There is no threshold for custody, and the judge may imprison for any offence at will.
A custodial sentence may be imposed only where the offender has previous convictions.
A custodial sentence may be imposed whenever the victim asks the court to imprison the offender on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: The custody threshold provides that a court must not pass a custodial sentence unless it is of the opinion that the offence (or the combination of the offence and associated offences) was so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community sentence can be justified for it.

n.1: Custody is not mandatory for every conviction.
n.2: There is a custody threshold; the judge cannot imprison for any offence at will.
n.3: The threshold turns on seriousness, not solely on previous convictions.
n.4: The victim's wishes do not determine whether the threshold is met.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is charged with an offence that can only be dealt with in the magistrates' court, being a relatively minor matter such as a low-level public order or driving offence. The defendant's solicitor explains where such a case will be heard and by whom it will be tried. The solicitor considers the trial of a summary-only offence. The matter was a minor one that the police had charged as a straightforward summary offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A summary-only offence can be tried in any court the defendant selects.
A summary-only offence cannot be tried at all and must be discontinued.
A summary-only offence must always be sent to the Crown Court for trial on indictment.
A summary-only offence may be tried in the Crown Court before a jury at the defendant's choice on these facts.
A summary-only offence is tried in the magistrates' court, with no right to trial by jury in the Crown Court.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: A summary-only offence is triable only in the magistrates' court (before a bench of magistrates or a district judge). There is no right to elect Crown Court trial by jury for a summary-only offence.

n.0: The defendant cannot select any court for a summary-only offence.
n.1: Summary-only offences are tried in the magistrates' court, not discontinued.
n.2: Summary-only offences are not sent to the Crown Court for jury trial.
n.3: There is no right to jury trial for a summary-only offence.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A person has been arrested and is being held at a police station. Before being interviewed, they ask whether they are entitled to speak to a solicitor, and whether they will have to pay for legal advice at the police station. They have limited means. The solicitor considers the detained suspect's right to legal advice under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The suspect was worried about the cost, having very little money, and unsure of their rights. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may consult a solicitor only after the police interview has finished.
The suspect has a right to free and independent legal advice, which can be exercised at any time while in detention.
The suspect has no right to legal advice until they have been formally charged.
The suspect is entitled to legal advice only if the offence is triable on indictment on these facts as a general rule.
The suspect must pay privately for any legal advice received at the police station.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under PACE 1984 (s.58) and Code C, a person held in custody is entitled, if they request it, to consult a solicitor privately at any time, and free and independent legal advice is available at the police station regardless of means.

n.0: The suspect can consult a solicitor before and during interview, not only after.
n.2: The right to advice arises during detention, not only after charge.
n.3: The right is not limited to indictable offences.
n.4: Police station advice is free; the suspect does not have to pay privately.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: At trial the prosecution wishes to adduce evidence of the defendant's previous convictions and other misconduct, arguing it is relevant to the defendant's propensity to commit offences of the kind charged. The defence objects to this bad character evidence. The defendant's solicitor considers the admissibility of the defendant's bad character under the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The defendant had several previous convictions for very similar offences to the one now charged. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Evidence of the defendant's bad character is always admissible without restriction.
Evidence of the defendant's bad character is admissible only if it passes through one of the statutory gateways in the Criminal Justice Act 2003.
Bad character evidence is admissible only where the defendant chooses to reveal it.
Evidence of the defendant's bad character can never be admitted in any circumstances.
Bad character evidence is admissible only in the magistrates' court and never the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, evidence of a defendant's bad character is admissible only if it comes within one of the statutory gateways (for example, relevant to an important matter in issue such as propensity, or where the defendant attacks another's character), and the court may exclude it, notably where its admission would be unfair.

n.0: Bad character is not admissible without restriction; the gateways apply.
n.2: Admissibility does not depend on the defendant choosing to reveal it.
n.3: It can be admitted through a gateway, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: The bad character regime applies in both the magistrates' court and the Crown Court.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant is convicted in the magistrates' court of an either-way offence after the magistrates accepted jurisdiction and tried the case. During sentencing, the magistrates conclude that the offending is so serious that their sentencing powers are insufficient to deal with it properly. The magistrates' sentencing powers are inadequate for the seriousness of the offence. The defendant has been convicted summarily. The magistrates accepted jurisdiction and tried the either-way matter themselves, but on conviction the true gravity of the offending has become clear and plainly calls for more punishment than the bench can impose, so they must decide what step allows a sufficient sentence to be passed. Which of the following best describes what the magistrates may do?
o: They must order a retrial before a different bench of magistrates.
They may refer the sentence to the Court of Appeal for determination.
They must discharge the defendant because their powers are insufficient.
They may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence, where greater sentencing powers are available.
They must impose the maximum sentence within their own powers and take no other step on these facts.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where, following summary conviction of an either-way offence, the magistrates consider that greater punishment is warranted than they can impose, they may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence. The Crown Court then sentences using its full powers, as if the defendant had been convicted on indictment.

n.0: A retrial before another bench is not the mechanism.
n.1: Sentence is not referred to the Court of Appeal by the magistrates in this way.
n.2: Insufficiency of powers leads to committal for sentence, not discharge.
n.4: They are not confined to their own maximum; committal for sentence is available.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: An offender is convicted of a low-level offence, and the court considers whether a financial penalty is an appropriate way of dealing with the matter, taking into account the seriousness of the offence and the offender's means. The defendant's solicitor makes submissions about the offender's ability to pay. The solicitor considers the imposition of a fine as a sentence. The offender was of modest means and the court had to set a penalty they could realistically pay. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A fine must reflect the seriousness of the offence but the court must also take account of the offender's financial circumstances.
A fine may never be imposed as a sentence for a criminal offence.
A fine is fixed at the same amount for every offender regardless of means or offence.
A fine is payable only where the offender agrees to pay it voluntarily.
A fine is set solely by reference to the offender's income, ignoring the offence entirely on these facts as a general rule.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: When imposing a fine, the court must fix an amount that reflects the seriousness of the offence, but must also take into account the offender's financial circumstances (their ability to pay), so the same offence may attract different fines for offenders of different means.

n.1: A fine is a recognised sentence for many offences.
n.2: A fine is not a single fixed amount for all; seriousness and means both matter.
n.3: A fine is imposed by the court, not dependent on voluntary agreement.
n.4: Seriousness is relevant as well as means; the offence is not ignored.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant convicted on indictment receives a sentence that the Attorney General considers to be unduly lenient, given the seriousness of the offending. The offence is one to which the relevant scheme applies. The sentence passed in the Crown Court is said to be far too low. The Attorney General wishes to have it reviewed. After a Crown Court trial the sentence handed down strikes many, including the Attorney General, as far too soft for offending of this gravity, the offence is one within the relevant scheme, and the Attorney General is looking for a way to have that lenient sentence reviewed and, if appropriate, increased. Which of the following best describes the mechanism available?
o: The sentence may be increased only if the defendant also appeals against conviction on these facts as a general rule.
There is no mechanism to challenge a sentence for being too lenient.
The Attorney General may simply increase the sentence without any court involvement.
The prosecution witnesses may appeal the sentence themselves.
The Attorney General may refer the sentence to the Court of Appeal as unduly lenient for the offences within the scheme.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, the Attorney General may, for certain offences, refer a Crown Court sentence to the Court of Appeal where it appears unduly lenient. The Court of Appeal may then increase the sentence. This is separate from the defendant's own right to appeal against sentence.

n.0: An unduly lenient reference does not depend on the defendant appealing conviction.
n.1: There is a mechanism (the unduly lenient sentence scheme) to challenge over-lenient sentences.
n.2: The Attorney General cannot increase the sentence personally; it must be referred to the Court of Appeal.
n.3: Witnesses have no right to appeal the sentence.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A case involving an indictable offence has been sent to the Crown Court. Before trial, the court holds a hearing at which the defendant enters a plea and, if not guilty, directions are given to prepare the case for trial, including on issues, witnesses and timetabling. This is the first hearing in the Crown Court following the sending. The court manages the progress of the case. The indictable case has been sent up from the magistrates, and the Crown Court now lists the first hearing at which the defendant will be arraigned and, if the plea is not guilty, the judge will set the case on course for trial with directions on issues, witnesses and timetable. Which of the following best identifies this hearing?
o: A plea and trial preparation hearing (PTPH).
A voir dire to determine the admissibility of evidence.
An allocation hearing to decide the mode of trial.
A Newton hearing to resolve a factual dispute for sentence.
A committal for sentence hearing.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: In the Crown Court, the first hearing after a case is sent is generally the plea and trial preparation hearing (PTPH), at which the defendant is arraigned (enters a plea) and, if a not guilty plea is entered, the judge gives case management directions to prepare the matter for trial.

n.1: A voir dire is a trial within a trial on admissibility, not the initial preparation hearing.
n.2: Allocation (mode of trial) occurs in the magistrates' court, not as the Crown Court's PTPH.
n.3: A Newton hearing resolves a factual dispute relevant to sentence after a guilty plea, not this preparatory hearing.
n.4: Committal for sentence is a separate process from the magistrates, not the Crown Court's PTPH.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant of limited means is charged with a criminal offence and wishes to be represented, but cannot afford to pay privately for a solicitor to conduct the case in the magistrates' or Crown Court. The defendant's solicitor advises on the availability of public funding for criminal defence. The solicitor considers eligibility for a criminal legal aid representation order. The defendant was on a low income and could not begin to fund a defence privately. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Criminal legal aid is never available for the defence of a criminal charge.
Criminal legal aid is available only to defendants who intend to plead guilty.
Criminal legal aid depends on satisfying both a means test and the interests of justice (merits) test.
Criminal legal aid is available to every defendant automatically, regardless of means or the case.
Criminal legal aid depends only on the seriousness of the offence and not on the defendant's means.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Eligibility for a criminal legal aid representation order generally depends on satisfying both the means test (the defendant's financial circumstances) and the interests of justice test (factors such as risk of loss of liberty, complexity of the case, and ability to understand proceedings).

n.0: Criminal legal aid is available where the tests are satisfied.
n.1: Legal aid is not confined to those pleading guilty.
n.3: Legal aid is not automatic for everyone; the tests must be met.
n.4: Both means and interests of justice are relevant, not only the offence's seriousness.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant faces an either-way offence. At the allocation (mode of trial) stage, the magistrates consider whether the case is suitable for summary trial, taking into account the likely sentence and whether their sentencing powers would be adequate. The offence is either-way and allocation is being decided. The magistrates assess the adequacy of their powers. At the allocation stage for the either-way charge the magistrates weigh whether the case is really one for them, taking a view on the likely sentence and whether their limited powers could do it justice, and they must know what follows if they conclude those powers would fall short. Which of the following best describes what the magistrates do if they consider their powers insufficient?
o: They must try the case themselves regardless of the likely sentence.
They decline jurisdiction and the case proceeds to the Crown Court for trial.
They automatically grant the defendant bail and take no further step.
They must acquit the defendant if their powers are insufficient.
They refer the allocation decision to the Court of Appeal.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: At allocation for an either-way offence, if the magistrates consider that their sentencing powers would be inadequate or the case is otherwise more suitable for the Crown Court, they decline jurisdiction and the case is sent to the Crown Court for trial. If they accept jurisdiction, the defendant may still elect Crown Court trial.

n.0: They do not have to try a case they consider beyond their powers; they can decline jurisdiction.
n.2: Declining jurisdiction, not automatic bail, is the relevant step.
n.3: Insufficiency of sentencing powers does not lead to acquittal.
n.4: Allocation is not referred to the Court of Appeal.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A magistrates' court grants a defendant bail over the prosecution's objection in respect of an indictable-only offence. The prosecution considers whether it can challenge the decision to grant bail. Bail has just been granted at the magistrates' court against the prosecution's objection. The prosecution wishes to have the grant reconsidered. Over the prosecution's strenuous objection the magistrates have just released the defendant on bail in an indictable-only matter, and the prosecutor, dismayed at the decision and worried about the risk the defendant poses, wants to know whether anything can be done to have that grant of bail looked at again. Which of the following best describes the prosecution's position?
o: The prosecution may appeal only to the Supreme Court against the grant of bail.
The prosecution may overturn the grant of bail by its own decision without a court.
The prosecution may in certain cases appeal to the Crown Court against the grant of bail.
The prosecution has no means of challenging a grant of bail once made.
The prosecution may simply re-arrest the defendant without any further process.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a magistrates' court grants bail in respect of an imprisonable offence and the prosecution had opposed it, the prosecution may (having given the requisite notice) appeal against the grant of bail to the Crown Court, which will hear the matter afresh. This provides a check on decisions to release defendants the prosecution considers should be remanded.

n.0: The prosecution's bail appeal lies to the Crown Court, not the Supreme Court.
n.1: The prosecution cannot overturn bail by its own decision; it must appeal to a court.
n.3: The prosecution is not without means; it may appeal in appropriate cases.
n.4: The prosecution cannot simply re-arrest to circumvent the bail decision.

Criminal Law & Practice.q: A defendant (or the prosecution) considers that the magistrates' court made an error of law or acted in excess of jurisdiction in reaching its decision, and wishes to challenge the decision on that legal basis rather than by a rehearing of the facts. The solicitor considers the route for challenging a magistrates' court decision on a point of law. The defendant argued the magistrates had misdirected themselves on the meaning of the offence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A point of law can be challenged only by the prosecution and never by the defence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A point of law can only ever be challenged by a full rehearing in the Crown Court.
A point of law is challenged by appealing directly to the Court of Appeal.
The decision may be challenged by appeal to the High Court by way of case stated, or by judicial review, on a point of law or jurisdiction.
There is no way to challenge a magistrates' court decision on a point of law.
Criminal Law & Practice.w: Where a magistrates' court decision is challenged on the ground that it was wrong in law or in excess of jurisdiction, the challenge is made to the High Court (Divisional Court) by way of appeal by case stated, or by judicial review, rather than by the factual rehearing available in the Crown Court.

n.0: Case stated is available to either party, not only the prosecution.
n.1: A point of law goes to the High Court by case stated/judicial review, not a Crown Court rehearing.
n.2: The route is to the High Court, not directly to the Court of Appeal.
n.4: There is a route to challenge on a point of law.
